div.p: Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war of the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, how they fought against each other, beginning as soon as it broke out and expecting that it would be great and more worthy of account than any that had gone before, judging from the fact that both sides were at their peak for it in every kind of preparation, and seeing the rest of the Hellenic world taking sides with one or the other, some at once, others intending to.
For this was indeed the greatest upheaval that had happened to the Hellenes and to some part of the barbarians, and, so to speak, to the greater part of mankind.

For the events before it and those still more ancient were impossible to discover clearly because of the length of time, but from the evidence which I find I can trust when I look back as far as possible, I do not think they were great, either in their wars or in other respects.

For it is plain that what is now called Hellas was not in old times settled firmly, but that migrations were frequent in earlier times, and each people readily left its own land when forced by some people that was always more numerous.

For there was no commerce, and they did not mix with one another without fear either by land or by sea, and each tilled their own land only enough to live on it, having no surplus of wealth and planting no trees, since it was uncertain when someone would come and, as they were also without walls, take it from them; and thinking that they could get the necessary food for each day anywhere, they moved away without difficulty, and for this reason they were strong neither in the size of their cities nor in any other resource.

And the best of the land always had the most changes of inhabitants, the districts now called Thessaly and Boeotia and most of the Peloponnese except Arcadia, and of the rest whatever was most fertile.
For because of the goodness of the land, the greater power that arose for some caused factions by which they were ruined, and at the same time they were more exposed to plots from foreign peoples.
Attica, at any rate, which because of the thinness of its soil was free from faction for the longest time, was always inhabited by the same people.

And this is not the least proof of my statement that it was because of the migrations that the other parts did not grow in the same way: for from the rest of Hellas those who were driven out by war or faction, the most powerful, withdrew to the Athenians as to a secure place, and becoming citizens from very early times they made the city still greater in number of people, so that later they even sent out colonies to Ionia, as Attica was not large enough.
This too shows me not least the weakness of the ancients: for before the Trojan war Hellas appears to have done nothing in common before;

and, it seems to me, it did not yet have this name as a whole, but before Hellen, the son of Deucalion, this name did not exist at all, and the several peoples, the Pelasgian most widely among others, gave their own names to their districts; but when Hellen and his sons had become strong in Phthiotis and were called in to help the other cities, they came one by one to be called Hellenes more and more through this contact, but for a long time it could not prevail among them all.

Homer gives the best evidence: for though he lived much later even than the Trojan war, he nowhere names them all together, nor anyone except those with Achilles from Phthiotis, who were also the first Hellenes, but in his poems he calls them Danaans and Argives and Achaeans. Nor has he spoken of barbarians, because the Hellenes, as it seems to me, had not yet been set apart under one name as their opposite.

At any rate those who were called Hellenes one by one, city by city, as they understood one another, and later all together, did nothing together before the Trojan war, because of weakness and lack of contact with one another. But even for this expedition they came together only when they were already making more use of the sea.

For Minos is the earliest of those known to us by tradition who acquired a navy, and he controlled most of what is now the Hellenic Sea, and ruled the Cyclades islands and was the first founder of most of them, after driving out the Carians and installing his own sons as governors; and he cleared piracy from the sea, as is likely, as far as he could, so that his revenues would come to him more readily.

For in old times the Hellenes and those of the barbarians who lived on the coast of the mainland and all who held islands, when they began to cross over to one another in ships more often, turned to piracy, led by men who were not the weakest, for the sake of their own gain and of food for the weak, and falling upon cities that were unwalled and settled in villages they plundered them and got most of their living from this, since this work did not yet bring any shame but rather even some glory;

this is shown both by some of the mainland peoples even now, for whom it is an honour to do this well, and by the ancient poets, who everywhere alike ask those who sail in whether they are pirates, as if neither those who are asked disowned the work nor those who wanted to know reproached them for it.
for all Hellas used to carry weapons because their dwellings were unprotected and travel between them was unsafe, and they made living with arms their habit, like the barbarians.
And the fact that these parts of Hellas still live in this way is a sign of the ways of life that were once alike for all.

The Athenians were among the first to lay aside their iron and to change to an easier and more luxurious way of life. And it is not long since the older men among their wealthy, because of this delicate living, stopped wearing linen tunics and tying their hair up in a knot on their heads fastened with golden grasshoppers; from them this dress also prevailed for a long time among the older men of the Ionians, because of their kinship.
The Lacedaemonians in turn were the first to use a moderate dress after the present fashion, and in other respects those who owned more lived as much as possible on equal terms with the many.

They were also the first to strip naked and, undressing in public, to anoint themselves with oil when they exercised; but in old times even in the Olympic games the athletes competed wearing loincloths about their private parts, and it is not many years since this stopped. And even now among some of the barbarians, especially those of Asia, prizes for boxing and wrestling are set, and they do this wearing loincloths.
And one could show many other ways in which the ancient Hellenic world lived like the barbarian world of today.

Of the cities, those which were founded most recently, when navigation was already easier, having more surplus of wealth, were built with walls on the very shores and took over the isthmuses, both for commerce and for the strength of each against their neighbours; but the old ones, because piracy long prevailed, were founded farther from the sea, both those on the islands and those on the mainland (for they plundered one another and all the others who lived on the coast without being seafarers), and to this day they are still situated inland.

And the islanders were no less pirates, being Carians and Phoenicians: for these indeed settled most of the islands. And here is the evidence: when Delos was purified by the Athenians in this war and all the graves of those who had died on the island were removed, over half were found to be Carians, recognized by the style of the weapons buried with them and by the way they still bury today.
But when the navy of Minos had been established, sailing between peoples became easier (for the evil-doers from the islands were driven out by him, when he also colonized most of them),
And when they were already more in this condition, later in time they made the expedition against Troy.
And Agamemnon, it seems to me, gathered the fleet because he surpassed those of his time in power, and not so much because he led the suitors of Helen bound by the oaths to Tyndareus.

And those of the Peloponnesians who have received the clearest account by tradition from men of earlier times say that Pelops first, by the great wealth which he brought with him from Asia to a needy people, acquired power and, although he was a newcomer, nevertheless gave his name to the country, and that later still greater things fell to his descendants, when Eurystheus had been killed in Attica by the Heraclidae, and Atreus was his mother's brother, and Eurystheus, when he set out on his expedition, had entrusted Mycenae and the rule to Atreus because of their kinship (he happened to be in exile from his father because of the death of Chrysippus), and when Eurystheus did not return, Atreus, as the Mycenaeans also wished it out of fear of the Heraclidae, and since he seemed to be powerful and had courted the multitude, took over the kingship of the Mycenaeans and of all whom Eurystheus ruled, and the Pelopidae became greater than the Perseidae.
And it seems to me that Agamemnon, having inherited this and at the same time being stronger than the others in naval power, gathered the expedition and made it not so much by favour as by fear.

For he clearly arrived himself with the most ships and also supplied the Arcadians with them, as Homer has shown, if he is sufficient evidence for anyone. And at the handing down of the sceptre he has said that he
ruled over many islands and all Argos:
Hom. Il. 2.108so, being a mainlander, he would not have ruled over islands except the neighbouring ones (and these would not be many), unless he also had some navy. And we must also judge from this expedition what those before it were like.

And because Mycenae was small, or if any town of that time does not now seem considerable, one would not be using an exact proof if one disbelieved that the expedition was as great as the poets have said and as the tradition holds.

For if the city of the Lacedaemonians were deserted, and the temples and the foundations of its buildings were left, I think that after a long time had passed there would be great disbelief among later men that their power matched their fame (and yet they occupy two of the five parts of the Peloponnese, and lead the whole of it and many allies outside it; but nevertheless, since the city is not built together and does not have costly temples and buildings, but is settled in villages in the old manner of Hellas, it would appear inferior), whereas if the Athenians suffered this same thing, their power would be judged from the visible appearance of the city to be double what it is.

It is not reasonable, then, to disbelieve it, nor to look at the appearance of cities rather than their power, but to believe that that expedition was the greatest of those before it, but fell short of those of today, if here too we must trust the poetry of Homer, which it is likely that he, being a poet, embellished towards the greater, but even so it appears rather inferior.

For he has made it of twelve hundred ships, those of the Boeotians with a hundred and twenty men, and those of Philoctetes with fifty, showing, as it seems to me, the largest and the smallest: at any rate he made no mention of the size of others in the catalogue of ships. And that they were all both rowers and fighting men he has shown in the ships of Philoctetes: for he has made all the oarsmen archers. And it is not likely that many passengers sailed with them apart from the kings and those highest in office, especially as they were going to cross the open sea with the equipment of war, and moreover did not have their boats decked, but fitted out in the old manner, rather like pirate ships.
Looking, then, at the mean between the largest and the smallest ships, they do not appear to have come in great numbers, considering that they were sent from all Hellas in common.

The cause was not so much the lack of men as the lack of money. For through want of food they brought a smaller army, and only as large as they hoped could live on the country while fighting, and when on arrival they won a battle (and this is clear: for they would not have built the wall around their camp), they evidently did not use their whole force even then, but turned to farming the Chersonese and to piracy through want of food. And for this reason the Trojans, since the Greeks were scattered, held out by force for those ten years, being a match for those who were left behind at any time.

But if they had come with an abundance of food and, being together, without piracy and farming, had carried on the war continuously, they would easily have won in battle and taken the city, since even when not together, but with the part that was present at any time, they held out, and if they had sat down to a siege they would have taken Troy in less time and with less trouble.
since even after the Trojan war Hellas was still moving about and being resettled, so that it did not grow by being at rest.

For the return of the Hellenes from Ilium, happening after a long time, brought many changes, and factions arose in the cities in many places, and those who were driven out by them founded the cities.

For the present Boeotians, driven out of Arne by the Thessalians in the sixtieth year after the capture of Ilium, settled the land now called Boeotia, but formerly Cadmeis (but there was also a portion of them in this land earlier, some of whom also marched against Ilium), and the Dorians in the eightieth year occupied the Peloponnese with the Heraclidae.

And with difficulty, after a long time, Hellas came to be securely at rest and, no longer subject to migrations, sent out colonies, and the Athenians settled Ionia and most of the islands, and the Peloponnesians most of Italy and Sicily and some places of the rest of Hellas. And all these were founded after the Trojan war.

And as Hellas became more powerful and made the acquisition of money still more than before, tyrannies were established in most of the cities, as revenues became greater (before there had been hereditary kingships with fixed privileges), and Hellas fitted out navies, and they applied themselves more to the sea.
The Corinthians are said to have been the first to handle naval matters most nearly in the present manner, and triremes are said to have been built first in Hellas at Corinth.
And Ameinocles, a Corinthian shipwright, evidently also built four ships for the Samians: and it is about three hundred years to the end of this war since Ameinocles went to the Samians.
And the oldest sea battle that we know of is that of the Corinthians against the Corcyraeans: and to this too it is about two hundred and sixty years up to the same time.

For the Corinthians, living in their city on the Isthmus, always had a market, since the Hellenes of old, both those within the Peloponnese and those outside, mixed with one another more by land than by sea through their territory, and they were powerful in wealth, as has been shown by the old poets too: for they named the place wealthy. And when the Hellenes took more to sailing, they acquired ships and put down piracy, and, offering a market both ways, they made their city powerful by its revenue of money.

And the Ionians later had a great navy, in the time of Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, and of Cambyses his son, and, fighting against Cyrus, they controlled the sea along their own coast for some time. And Polycrates, tyrant of Samos in the time of Cambyses, being strong in his navy, made others of the islands subject to him, and took Rhenea and dedicated it to the Delian Apollo. And the Phocaeans, while founding Massalia, defeated the Carthaginians in a sea battle:

for these were the most powerful of the navies. And even these, though they arose many generations after the Trojan war, evidently used few triremes, but were still fitted out with fifty-oared ships and long boats, like those earlier ones.

And a little before the Persian wars and the death of Darius, who was king of the Persians after Cambyses, triremes came to be in large numbers for the tyrants around Sicily and for the Corcyraeans: for these were the last navies worth mentioning established in Hellas before the expedition of Xerxes.

For the Aeginetans and the Athenians, and any others, possessed small ones, and most of these fifty-oared ships: and it was late, from the time when Themistocles persuaded the Athenians, while at war with the Aeginetans and at the same time with the barbarian expected, to build the ships with which they also fought at sea: and these did not yet have decks throughout.

Such, then, were the navies of the Hellenes, both the ancient ones and those that arose later. Yet those who applied themselves to them gained no small strength, both by revenue of money and by rule over others: for they sailed against the islands and subdued them, especially those who did not have sufficient land.

But no war by land, from which any power was also gained, took place: all the wars there were, as many as did occur, were each against their own neighbours, and the Hellenes did not go out on foreign expeditions far from their own land to subdue others. For the subjects had not joined together around the greatest cities, nor again did they themselves make common expeditions on equal terms, but rather the neighbours fought against one another, each on their own.
Most of all, in the war that took place long ago between the Chalcidians and the Eretrians, the rest of the Hellenic world was also divided into alliance with one side or the other.

And obstacles to growth arose for different peoples in different places, and against the Ionians, when their affairs had advanced greatly, Cyrus and the Persian kingdom, having overthrown Croesus, marched against everything within the river Halys towards the sea and enslaved the cities on the mainland, and later Darius, strong with the navy of the Phoenicians, also the islands.

And the tyrants, as many as there were in the Hellenic cities, looking ahead only to their own interest, both for their own person and for increasing their own house, governed the cities with as much safety as they possibly could, and no deed worth mentioning was done by them, except perhaps against their own neighbours in each case: for those in Sicily advanced furthest in power. Thus on all sides Hellas was held back for a long time from achieving anything notable in common, and was less daring city by city.

But when the tyrants of the Athenians and those of the rest of Hellas, which had long been ruled by tyrants even before, most of them and the last, except those in Sicily, had been put down by the Lacedaemonians (for Lacedaemon, after its founding by the Dorians who now inhabit it, although it had suffered faction for the longest time we know of, nevertheless from very early times had good laws and was always free of tyrants: for it is about four hundred years and a little more to the end of this war since the Lacedaemonians have used the same constitution, and being powerful because of this they also settled affairs in the other cities), not many years after the removal of the tyrants from Hellas the battle at Marathon between the Medes and the Athenians also took place.

And in the tenth year after it the barbarian came again with the great expedition against Hellas to enslave it. And with a great danger hanging over them the Lacedaemonians led the Hellenes who fought together, since they were foremost in power, and the Athenians, as the Medes advanced, resolved to leave their city and, packing up their goods, embarked on their ships and became seamen. And having driven back the barbarian in common, not long afterwards both the Hellenes who had revolted from the King and those who had fought together divided themselves between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians. For these were clearly the greatest in power: for the one were strong by land, the other by ships.

And for a short time the alliance held together, then the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians quarrelled and made war on each other with their allies: and if any of the other Hellenes anywhere fell out, they now went over to these. So from the Persian wars to this war, sometimes making truces, sometimes fighting either each other or their own allies who revolted, they prepared well for war and became more experienced, getting their practice amid dangers.

And the Lacedaemonians led their allies without making them pay tribute, but took care that they were governed by oligarchies suited to their own interest alone, while the Athenians in time took over the ships of the cities, except those of the Chians and Lesbians, and assigned money for all to pay. And their own resources for this war became greater than when they had once been at their strongest with the alliance intact.

Such, then, I found ancient times to be, though it is hard to trust every piece of evidence in turn. For men accept from one another the reports of past events, even if they concern their own country, equally without testing them.

The mass of the Athenians, for example, think that Hipparchus was killed by Harmodius and Aristogeiton while he was tyrant, and do not know that Hippias ruled as the eldest of the sons of Pisistratus, and Hipparchus and Thessalus were his brothers, and that Harmodius and Aristogeiton, suspecting on that day and at the last moment that something had been disclosed to Hippias by those who were in the plot with them, kept away from him as being forewarned, but, wishing to do something before they were arrested and to take the risk, they came upon Hipparchus near the so-called Leocorium while he was arranging the Panathenaic procession and killed him.

And there are many other things, still existing even now and not forgotten through time, which the other Hellenes too wrongly believe, as that the kings of the Lacedaemonians each cast not one vote, but two, and that they have the Pitanate company, which never even existed. So little trouble do most people take in the search for truth, and they turn rather to what is ready to hand.

But from the evidence I have given one would still not be wrong in believing that things were very much as I have described, and not trusting more what the poets have sung about them, embellishing them towards the greater, nor what the prose writers have composed to be more attractive to the hearing than true, since they cannot be checked and most of them have through time won their way, beyond belief, into the realm of fable, but holding that they have been found out from the clearest evidence sufficiently, considering that they are ancient.

And this war, although men always judge the present war, while they are fighting it, to be the greatest, but when it has ended admire the old ones more, will nevertheless show to those who look at it from the facts themselves that it was greater than they.

And as for what each side said in speeches, either when about to go to war or when already in it, it was hard to remember the exact words spoken, both for me with what I heard myself and for those who reported to me from elsewhere: but as each speaker seemed to me most likely to have said what was required about the matters at hand in each case, keeping as close as possible to the general sense of what was actually said, so it has been written.

And as for the facts of what was done in the war, I did not think it right to write them down learning them from the first person I met, nor as it seemed to me, but going through with as much accuracy as possible each event both at which I was present myself and those I heard of from others.
And they were found out with labour, because those present at each event did not say the same things about the same events, but as each had goodwill towards one side or the other, or memory.

And for listening, perhaps, the absence of fable in them will seem less pleasing: but as many as wish to look at the clear truth both of what happened and of what will one day, by human nature, happen again in the same or a similar way, if they judge it useful, that will be enough. It has been composed as a possession for all time rather than as a prize piece to be heard for the moment.

Of earlier events the greatest achieved was the Persian war, and yet this had a quick decision in two sea battles and two land battles. But this war went on to a great length, and sufferings happened in it to Hellas such as no others in an equal time.

For never were so many cities taken and made desolate, some by barbarians, others by the Hellenes themselves fighting one another (and some even changed their inhabitants when captured), nor so many exiles of men and so much killing, some in the war itself, some because of faction.

And things formerly told by hearsay, but more rarely confirmed in fact, became not incredible, about earthquakes, which affected the largest part of the earth at once and were the most violent as well, and eclipses of the sun, which happened more often than is remembered from earlier time, and great droughts in some places and from them also famines, and that which did not least harm and in part destroyed, the plague: for all these things attacked together with this war.
And the Athenians and Peloponnesians began it by breaking the thirty years' truce which they had made after the capture of Euboea.
As to why they broke it, I have first written the causes and the disputes, so that no one may ever have to ask from what origin so great a war arose among the Hellenes.

For the truest cause, but the least spoken of, I believe to be that the Athenians, becoming great and causing fear to the Lacedaemonians, forced them into war: but the causes openly stated by each side were these, from which they broke the truce and entered into the war.
Epidamnus is a city on the right as you sail into the Ionian gulf: and the Taulantians live near it, barbarians, an Illyrian people.

The Corcyraeans colonized it, and its founder was Phalius son of Eratoclides, a Corinthian by birth, of the descendants of Heracles, who was called from the mother city according to the ancient custom. And some Corinthians and others of the Dorian race also took part in the settlement.
And as time went on the power of the Epidamnians became great and populous;
but after being in faction among themselves for many years, as it is said, they were ruined by a war with the neighbouring barbarians and were deprived of much of their power.
And finally, before this war, their people drove out the powerful men, and these came against them with the barbarians and plundered those in the city both by land and by sea.

And the Epidamnians in the city, since they were hard pressed, sent envoys to Corcyra as being their mother city, asking them not to stand by while they were being destroyed, but to reconcile the exiles to them and to put an end to the war with the barbarians.
And they made these requests sitting as suppliants in the temple of Hera. But the Corcyraeans did not accept their supplication, but sent them away with nothing done.

And the Epidamnians, realizing that there was no help for them from Corcyra, were at a loss how to deal with the present situation, and sending to Delphi they asked the god whether they should hand over their city to the Corinthians as their founders and try to get some help from them. And he answered them to hand it over and to make them their leaders.

And the Epidamnians went to Corinth and, according to the oracle, handed over the colony, pointing out that their founder was from Corinth and making known the oracle, and they asked them not to stand by while they were being destroyed, but to come to their aid.

And the Corinthians undertook the help both in accordance with justice, believing that the colony was no less theirs than the Corcyraeans', and at the same time also out of hatred of the Corcyraeans, because these neglected them although they were their colonists:

for they neither gave them the customary privileges at the common festivals nor began the sacrifices with a Corinthian man, as the other colonies did, but they despised them, and being in their wealth at that time equal to the richest of the Hellenes and in their preparation for war more powerful, and sometimes boasting that they were far superior in their navy and in accordance with the earlier settlement of the Phaeacians in Corcyra, who had fame in matters of ships (for which reason they also equipped their navy all the more and were not without power: for they had a hundred and twenty triremes when they began the war),

having complaints, then, about all these things, the Corinthians gladly sent the help to Epidamnus, ordering any settler who wished to go there, and garrison troops of Ambraciots and Leucadians and of themselves.
And they went by land to Apollonia, a colony of the Corinthians, for fear of the Corcyraeans, lest they should be stopped by them in crossing by sea.

And when the Corcyraeans learned that the settlers and garrison troops had come to Epidamnus and that the colony had been given to the Corinthians, they were angry: and sailing at once with twenty-five ships, and later with another fleet, they ordered them insultingly to receive the exiles (for the exiles of the Epidamnians had come to Corcyra, pointing to tombs and kinship, which they put forward in asking to be restored) and to send away the garrison troops whom the Corinthians had sent and the settlers.

But the Epidamnians did not listen to any of these demands, and the Corcyraeans marched against them with forty ships together with the exiles, intending to restore them, and taking the Illyrians with them as well.

And sitting down before the city they proclaimed that any of the Epidamnians who wished and the foreigners might leave unharmed: otherwise, they would treat them as enemies. And when they did not obey, the Corcyraeans (the place is an isthmus) besieged the city,

and the Corinthians, when messengers came to them from Epidamnus saying that they were being besieged, prepared an expedition, and at the same time proclaimed a colony to Epidamnus, that anyone who wished should go on equal and like terms: and if anyone did not want to sail with them at once, but wished to share in the colony, he could stay behind by paying down fifty Corinthian drachmas. And there were many both who sailed and who paid down the money.

And they also asked the Megarians to escort them with ships, in case they should be prevented by the Corcyraeans from sailing: and these prepared to sail with them with eight ships, and the Paleans of Cephallenia with four. And they asked the Epidaurians, who supplied five, and the Hermionians one, and the Troezenians two, and the Leucadians ten and the Ambraciots eight. And they asked the Thebans for money, and the Phliasians, and the Eleans for unmanned ships and money. And of the Corinthians themselves thirty ships were prepared and three thousand hoplites.

And when the Corcyraeans learned of the preparation, they came to Corinth with envoys of the Lacedaemonians and Sicyonians, whom they took with them, and ordered the Corinthians to withdraw the garrison troops and settlers in Epidamnus, on the ground that they had no part in Epidamnus.

But if they made any claim, they were willing to submit to arbitration in the Peloponnese before cities which both sides should agree on: and whichever side the colony should be judged to belong to, these should have it. And they were also willing to refer it to the oracle at Delphi.

But they did not allow them to make war: otherwise, they said, they themselves too would be forced, if those used violence, to make friends whom they did not want, others than those they now had, for the sake of help.

And the Corinthians answered them that, if they withdrew the ships and the barbarians from Epidamnus, they would consider it: but before that it was not right that the one side should be besieged and they themselves go to arbitration.

And the Corcyraeans replied that, if those too withdrew their men in Epidamnus, they would do this: and they were also ready for both sides to remain where they were, and to make a truce until the decision was given.

But the Corinthians did not listen to any of these proposals, but when their ships were manned and the allies were present, they sent a herald ahead first to declare war on the Corcyraeans, and putting out with seventy-five ships and two thousand hoplites they sailed against Epidamnus to make war against the Corcyraeans:

and the commanders of the ships were Aristeus son of Pellichus, Callicrates son of Callias and Timanor son of Timanthes, and of the infantry Archetimus son of Eurytimus and Isarchidas son of Isarchus.

And when they were at Actium in the land of Anactorium, where the temple of Apollo is, at the mouth of the Ambracian gulf, the Corcyraeans sent ahead a herald to them in a light boat to forbid them to sail against them, and at the same time manned their ships, strengthening the old ones so that they would be seaworthy and repairing the others.

And when the herald reported nothing peaceful from the Corinthians and their ships were manned, eighty in number (for forty were besieging Epidamnus), they put out against them and, drawing up in line, fought a sea battle:

and the Corcyraeans won by far and destroyed fifteen ships of the Corinthians. And on the same day it happened that those who were besieging Epidamnus also brought it to terms by an agreement that the newcomers should be sold, and that they should keep the Corinthians in chains until something else should be decided.
And after the sea battle the Corcyraeans set up a trophy on Leucimme, a headland of Corcyra, and killed the other prisoners whom they had taken, but kept the Corinthians in chains.

And later, when the Corinthians and their allies, defeated with their ships, had returned home, the Corcyraeans controlled the whole sea in those parts, and sailing to Leucas, the colony of the Corinthians, they ravaged the land and burned Cyllene, the port of the Eleans, because they had supplied ships and money to the Corinthians.

And for most of the time after the sea battle they controlled the sea and sailed against the allies of the Corinthians and did them harm, until the Corinthians, as the summer was coming round, sent ships and an army, since their allies were suffering, and encamped at Actium and around Chimerium in Thesprotis to guard both Leucas and the other cities that were friendly to them.

And the Corcyraeans also encamped opposite them at Leucimme with ships and infantry. And neither side sailed against the other, but after sitting opposite each other this summer, when winter had already come, both sides returned home.

And during the whole year after the sea battle and the next the Corinthians, bearing the war against the Corcyraeans with anger, built ships and prepared the strongest fleet of ships, gathering rowers both from the Peloponnese itself and from the rest of Hellas, persuading them with pay.

And the Corcyraeans, learning of their preparation, were afraid, and (for they were in treaty with none of the Hellenes, and had not enrolled themselves either in the treaty of the Athenians or in that of the Lacedaemonians) they decided to go to the Athenians to become their allies and to try to get some help from them.

And the Corinthians, learning this, also came themselves to Athens as envoys, so that the addition of the Athenian navy to that of the Corcyraeans should not become an obstacle to them in settling the war as they wished.
And when an assembly was held they came to a debate, and the Corcyraeans spoke as follows.

‘It is right, Athenians, that those who come to their neighbours, as we do now, to ask for help, without any great service or alliance owed to them beforehand, should first show, above all that what they ask is also advantageous, or if not, at least that it is not harmful, and then that they will also show lasting gratitude: and if they establish none of this clearly, they should not be angry if they fail.
And the Corcyraeans, together with the request for alliance, have sent us trusting that they can also give you firm assurances on these points.
But it has happened that the same policy is both inconsistent with our request towards you and disadvantageous to our own interests at present.

For having never before been anyone's allies of our own will, we have now come to ask this of others, and at the same time because of this we stand isolated in the present war with the Corinthians. And what formerly seemed our prudence, not to share danger in a foreign alliance at the will of a neighbour, has now turned out to appear folly and weakness.

The sea battle that took place, then, we fought off the Corinthians by ourselves alone: but since they have set out against us with a greater force from the Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas, and we see that we are unable to prevail with our own power alone, and at the same time the danger is great if we come under them, we must ask for help both from you and from everyone else, and we deserve pardon if we venture on a course opposed to our former inaction, not from wickedness, but rather from an error of judgment.

‘And if you listen to us, the chance of our request will be favourable to you in many ways, first because you will give your help to people who are wronged and who do not harm others, then because by receiving people in danger about the greatest things you will lay up gratitude with a testimony to be remembered forever: and we possess the largest navy except yours.

And consider: what good fortune could be rarer, or more painful to your enemies, than if the power which you would have valued at much money and gratitude to have added to you, this is present, offering itself unasked, without dangers and expense, and bringing besides a name for virtue among the many, gratitude from those you will help, and strength to yourselves: all of which in all time have come together for few indeed, and few who ask for alliance come offering to those they call on no less security and honour than they will receive.

And if any of you thinks that the war, for which we would be useful, will not come, he is wrong in his judgment and does not perceive that the Lacedaemonians are eager for war out of fear of you and that the Corinthians are powerful with them and are your enemies and are seizing on us first now for an attack on you, so that we may not stand together against them in our common hatred and they may not fail to achieve one of two things first, either to harm us or to strengthen themselves.
And it is our task, in turn, to anticipate them, we by offering, you by accepting the alliance, and to plot against them first rather than to counter their plots.

‘And if they say that it is not just for you to receive their own colonists, let them learn that every colony, when it is treated well, honours its mother city, but when it is wronged, becomes estranged: for colonists are not sent out to be slaves, but to be the equals of those who are left behind.
And that they did wrong is clear: for when invited to arbitration about Epidamnus they chose to pursue their complaints by war rather than by fair means.

And let what they do to us, their kinsmen, be some evidence to you, so that you are not led astray by their deceit and do not serve them when they ask you directly: for he who has the fewest regrets from doing favours to his opponents would remain the safest.
Nor will you break the treaty of the Lacedaemonians by receiving us, who are allies of neither side:
for it is said in it that whichever of the Hellenic cities is an ally of no one may go to whichever side it pleases.

And it is outrageous if these men may man their ships from those under the treaty and besides from the rest of Hellas and not least from your subjects, but will shut us out from the alliance open to us and from help from anywhere else, and then will count it as a wrong if you are persuaded to grant what we ask.

But we shall have far more ground for complaint if we do not persuade you: for you will reject us, who are in danger and are not your enemies, while you will not only not stop these men, who are enemies and are attacking us, but you will even stand by while they gain power from your empire: which is not just, but you should either stop the mercenaries from your empire on their side too, or else send us help to whatever extent you are persuaded, but above all receive us openly and help us.

And many, as we suggested at the beginning, are the advantages we point out, and the greatest is that the same people were our enemies, which is the clearest pledge, and these are not weak, but able to harm those who desert them: and when the alliance offered is a naval and not a continental one, its loss is not the same, but above all, if you can, you should allow no one else to possess ships, and if not, you should have as your friend whoever is strongest.

‘And whoever thinks that these things are said to be advantageous, but fears that if he is persuaded by them he will break the treaty, let him know that his fear, when it has strength, will frighten his opponents more, while his confidence, if he does not receive us, being weak against strong enemies, will be less to be feared, and at the same time that he is now deliberating not about Corcyra more than about Athens, and is not providing what is best for it, when, looking only to the moment, he hesitates in view of the coming and all but present war to gain a place which is made a friend or an enemy with the greatest consequences.

For it lies well for the coasting voyage to Italy and Sicily, so as neither to allow a navy to come from there to the Peloponnesians nor to let one from here pass to those parts, and for other purposes it is most advantageous.

And in the briefest summary, both as a whole and in each point, you may learn from this not to abandon us: there are three navies worth mentioning among the Hellenes, yours and ours and that of the Corinthians: and if you stand by while two of these come together and the Corinthians seize us first, you will fight at sea against the Corcyraeans and the Peloponnesians together, but if you receive us you will be able to contend against them with more ships, namely ours.’
Such things the Corcyraeans said: and the Corinthians after them spoke as follows.

‘Since these Corcyraeans have made their speech not only about your receiving them, but also to show that we do wrong and that they are unjustly attacked, we too must first deal with both these points and so go on to the rest of our argument, so that you may know in advance more surely the claim we make and may not reject the request of these men without due consideration.

‘They say that out of prudence they have never yet accepted an alliance with anyone: but they adopted this policy for villainy and not for virtue, wanting to have no ally as a witness to their wrongdoings, nor to be ashamed when they call one in.

And at the same time their city, lying in a self-sufficient position, makes them judges of the wrongs they do to anyone rather than having them judged by agreements, because, while they sail out least to their neighbours, they most often receive others who put in there by necessity.

And they have put forward this fair-seeming refusal of treaties not so that they may not share in others' wrongdoing, but so that they may do wrong by themselves, and that where they are stronger they may use force, where they escape notice they may take more, and if they gain anything anywhere they may feel no shame:
and yet if they were good men, as they claim, the less open to attack they were to their neighbours, the more clearly they could have shown their virtue by giving and receiving what is just.

But they are not like this either towards others or towards us, but, though they are our colonists, they have always stood aloof and now they are making war, saying that they were not sent out to be badly treated.
But we for our part say that we did not found the colony to be insulted by them, but to be their leaders and to be shown proper respect.
The other colonies at any rate honour us, and we are loved most of all by our colonists:

and it is clear that, if we are pleasing to the majority, we could not rightly be displeasing to these alone, and we would not be making an extraordinary expedition against them unless we were also being wronged in some exceptional way.
And it would have been honourable, even if we were in the wrong, for them to yield to our anger, and shameful for us to force their moderation:

but in their insolence and the licence of their wealth they have committed many other wrongs against us, and Epidamnus, which was ours, they did not claim while it was being harmed, but when we came to help it they seized it by force and hold it.

‘And they say indeed that they were willing earlier to submit to arbitration, but it is not the one who has the advantage and makes the challenge from a safe position who should be thought to say anything, but the one who puts his deeds and likewise his words on an equal footing before the contest.

But these men offered the fair-seeming arbitration not before they besieged the place, but when they thought that we would not stand by. And they have come here not only having done wrong themselves there, but now also asking you not to be their allies, but their partners in wrongdoing, and to receive them while they are at odds with us:

they ought to have come to you when they were safest, and not at a time when we have been wronged and they are in danger, nor when you, who did not then share in their power, will now give them a share of your help, and, having had no part in their wrongdoings, will have an equal share of the blame from us, but they should long ago have shared their power and so have the results in common too.
‘That we ourselves come with proper complaints, then, and that these men are violent and grasping has been shown: and you must learn that you would not justly receive them.

For if it is stated in the treaty that any of the unenrolled cities may go to whichever side it wishes, the agreement is not for those who go to the harm of others, but for one who, not depriving another of himself, needs safety, and for one who will not bring war instead of peace to those who receive him, if they are prudent: which you would now suffer if you were not persuaded by us.
For you would not become helpers to these men only, but also enemies to us instead of treaty partners: for if you go with them, we must defend ourselves against them not without you too.

And yet you ought by rights, above all, to stand aside from both, or if not, on the contrary to go against these men with us (for you are in treaty with the Corinthians, but with the Corcyraeans you have never yet been even in a truce), and not to establish the rule of receiving those who revolt from others.

For neither did we, when the Samians revolted, cast our vote against you, when the other Peloponnesians were divided in their vote on whether they should help them, but we openly said in opposition that each one should punish his own allies himself.
For if you receive and help those who do wrong, it will become clear that no fewer of your own will come over to us, and you will set the rule against yourselves rather than against us.

‘These, then, are the claims of right we have against you, sufficient according to the laws of the Hellenes, and we also have this advice and claim to gratitude, which, since we are neither enemies so as to harm you nor again friends so as to make use of you, we say ought to be repaid to us at the present time.

For once, when you were short of warships for the war against the Aeginetans before the Persian wars, you received twenty ships from the Corinthians: and this service, and the one regarding the Samians, when because of us the Peloponnesians did not help them, gave you the victory over the Aeginetans and the punishment of the Samians, and came at such moments when men, going against their own enemies, are most heedless of everything compared to winning:

for they consider the one who helps them a friend, even if he was an enemy before, and the one who opposes them an enemy, even if he happens to be a friend, since they even manage their own affairs worse for the sake of the immediate contest.

‘Bearing this in mind, let every younger man, having learned it from an older, think it right to repay us in like manner, and let him not think that these things are said justly, but that, if he goes to war, the advantage lies elsewhere.

For advantage follows most where one does least wrong, and the future war with which the Corcyraeans frighten you and urge you to do wrong still lies in obscurity, and it is not worth being carried away by it to gain an open enmity with the Corinthians, already present and not in the future, but it is wiser rather to remove the suspicion that existed before because of the Megarians (for the latest favour, coming at the right moment,
even if it is smaller, can cancel a greater complaint),

nor to be drawn on by this, that they offer a great naval alliance: for not wronging one's equals is a firmer power than gaining an advantage through dangers, carried away by what is immediately visible.

And we, having fallen into the situation about which we ourselves declared in Lacedaemon that each should punish his own allies himself, now claim to receive the same from you, and that you, having been helped by our vote, should not harm us by yours.
Repay like for like, knowing that this is that moment when the one who helps is most a friend and the one who opposes most an enemy.
And do not receive these Corcyraeans as allies against our will, nor help them in their wrongdoing.
And by doing this you will act properly and will decide what is best for yourselves.’

Such things the Corinthians too said. And the Athenians, having heard both sides, held an assembly twice, and in the first they accepted the arguments of the Corinthians no less, but on the next day they changed their minds, deciding not to make an alliance with the Corcyraeans such as to have the same enemies and friends (for if the Corcyraeans asked them to sail with them against Corinth, their treaty with the Peloponnesians would be broken), but they made a defensive alliance to help each other, if anyone went against Corcyra or Athens or the allies of these.

For it seemed that the war with the Peloponnesians would come for them even so, and they did not want to give up Corcyra to the Corinthians when it had so large a navy, but rather to make them clash with each other as much as possible, so that, if need arose, they might go to war with the Corinthians and the others who had navies when these were weaker.
At the same time the island seemed to them to lie well on the coasting route to Italy and Sicily.
With such a purpose the Athenians received the Corcyraeans, and not long after the Corinthians had left they sent ten ships to them as helpers:
and their commanders were Lacedaemonius son of Cimon, Diotimus son of Strombichus and Proteas son of Epicles.

And they instructed them not to fight a sea battle with the Corinthians unless these sailed against Corcyra and were about to land there or at any of their places: but in that case to stop them as far as they could. And they gave these instructions in order not to break the treaty.

So the ships arrived at Corcyra, and the Corinthians, when they were ready, sailed against Corcyra with a hundred and fifty ships. And there were ten of the Eleans, twelve of the Megarians and ten of the Leucadians, twenty-seven of the Ambraciots and one of the Anactorians, and ninety of the Corinthians themselves:
and the commanders of these were from each city separately, and of the Corinthians Xenoclides son of Euthycles with four others.
And when, sailing from Leucas, they reached the mainland opposite Corcyra, they anchored at Chimerium in the land of Thesprotis.

It is a harbour, and above it, away from the sea, lies a city in the Elaeatis district of Thesprotis, Ephyre. And near it the Acherusian lake flows out into the sea: and the river Acheron, flowing through Thesprotis, empties into it, from which it also has its name. And the river Thyamis also flows there, dividing Thesprotis and Cestrine, and between them the headland of Chimerium rises.
So the Corinthians anchored at this point of the mainland and made a camp.

And the Corcyraeans, when they learned that they were sailing towards them, manned a hundred and ten ships, which Miciades, Aesimides and Eurybatus commanded, and encamped on one of the islands which are called Sybota: and the ten Attic ships were present too.
And on the headland of Leucimme they had their infantry and a thousand hoplites of the Zacynthians who had come to help.
And the Corinthians too had many of the barbarians on the mainland who had come to help them: for the mainlanders in this region have always been their friends.
And when the Corinthians were ready, they took food for three days and put out by night from Chimerium as for a sea battle,
and at dawn, as they sailed, they saw the ships of the Corcyraeans out at sea and sailing against them.

And when they caught sight of each other, they drew up in line against each other, the Attic ships on the right wing of the Corcyraeans, while they themselves held the rest, forming three divisions of their ships, each of which was commanded by one of the three commanders.

So the Corcyraeans were drawn up, and of the Corinthians the Megarian ships and the Ambraciot ships held the right wing, and in the centre were the other allies, each in their own place: and the left wing the Corinthians themselves held with their best-sailing ships, opposite the Athenians and the right of the Corcyraeans.

And when the signals had been raised on each side, they engaged and fought the sea battle, both sides having many hoplites on their decks, and many archers and javelin-men, being equipped still rather unskilfully in the old manner.
And the sea battle was hard fought, not so much in skill, but rather resembling a land battle more.

For when they rammed each other, they did not easily get free because of the number and crowding of the ships, and also because they trusted rather more for victory in the hoplites on the deck, who took their stand and fought while the ships stayed still: and there was no breaking through the line, but they fought the sea battle more with spirit and strength than with skill.

Everywhere, then, there was much uproar and the sea battle was confused, and in it the Attic ships, coming to the support of the Corcyraeans wherever they were hard pressed, caused fear to their opponents, but did not begin fighting, since their commanders feared the instructions of the Athenians.

And the right wing of the Corinthians suffered most: for the Corcyraeans with twenty ships routed them and chased them in disorder to the mainland, and sailing up to their camp and landing, they burned the deserted tents and plundered their goods.

In this part, then, the Corinthians and their allies were defeated and the Corcyraeans prevailed: but where the Corinthians themselves were, on the left, they won by far, since the twenty ships of the Corcyraeans, from their smaller number, were not present, being away in the pursuit.

And the Athenians, seeing the Corcyraeans hard pressed, now began to help them more without disguise, at first holding back so as not to ram anyone: but when the rout was clearly happening and the Corinthians were pressing on, then indeed everyone set to work and no distinction was made any longer, but it came to this point of necessity, that the Corinthians and Athenians attacked each other.

And when the rout had happened, the Corinthians did not take in tow the hulls of the ships they had disabled, but turned to the men, sailing through to kill rather than to take prisoners, and they killed their own friends without knowing it, not having noticed that those on the right wing had been defeated.

For since there were many ships on both sides and they covered a great part of the sea, when they had engaged each other, they could not easily distinguish who were winning and who were losing: for this sea battle of Hellenes against Hellenes was indeed the greatest in number of ships of those before it.

And when the Corinthians had chased the Corcyraeans to the land, they turned to the wrecks and their own dead, and they got hold of most of them so as to bring them to Sybota, where the land army of the barbarians had come to help them: and Sybota is a deserted harbour of Thesprotis. And having done this, they gathered again and sailed against the Corcyraeans.
And these, with their seaworthy ships and all that were left, together with the Attic ships, sailed against them in turn, fearing that they might try to land on their territory.

And it was already late and the paean had been sung by them for the attack, when the Corinthians suddenly began to back water, having caught sight of twenty Athenian ships sailing up, which the Athenians had sent out later as helpers after the ten, fearing, as indeed happened, that the Corcyraeans would be defeated and their own ten ships would be too few to defend them.
So the Corinthians, seeing these first and suspecting that they were from Athens, and not as many as they saw but more, began to withdraw.

But the Corcyraeans did not see them, for they were sailing up rather out of their sight, and they wondered at the Corinthians backing water, until some saw them and said that ships were sailing up over there. Then they too withdrew: for it was already getting dark, and the Corinthians turned away and broke off.
Thus they parted from each other, and the sea battle ended at nightfall.

And to the Corcyraeans, encamped at Leucimme, these twenty ships from Athens, which Glaucon son of Leagrus and † Andocides son of Leogoras † commanded, making their way through the dead and the wrecks, sailed into the camp not long after they were seen.
And the Corcyraeans (for it was night) were afraid that they were enemies, but then they recognized them: and the ships anchored.

And on the next day the thirty Attic ships and as many of the Corcyraean ships as were seaworthy put out and sailed against the harbour at Sybota, where the Corinthians lay at anchor, wanting to know whether they would fight a sea battle.

And these, having put out their ships from the land and drawn them up in line out at sea, kept still, not intending to begin a sea battle of their own accord, seeing that fresh ships had arrived from Athens and that many difficulties had befallen them, both about the guarding of the prisoners whom they had in their ships, and because there was no means of repairing the ships in a deserted place:

and they were considering rather how they would make the voyage home, fearing that the Athenians, thinking that the treaty had been broken because they had come to blows, would not let them sail away.
So they decided to put some men in a boat without a herald's staff and send them to the Athenians to test them. And they sent them, and these spoke as follows.

‘You do wrong, men of Athens, by beginning war and breaking the treaty: for when we are punishing our own enemies you stand in our way, raising arms against us. And if it is your intention to prevent us from sailing against Corcyra or anywhere else we may wish, and you are breaking the treaty, take us here first and treat us as enemies.’
So they said such things: and of the Corcyraeans the whole army, as far as it heard, shouted out at once to seize them and kill them, but the Athenians answered as follows.

‘We are neither beginning war, men of the Peloponnese, nor breaking the treaty, but we have come to help these Corcyraeans, who are our allies. If, then, you wish to sail anywhere else, we do not prevent you: but if you sail against Corcyra or to any of their places, we shall not stand by, as far as we are able.’

When the Athenians had answered in this way, the Corinthians prepared for the voyage home and set up a trophy at Sybota on the mainland: and the Corcyraeans took up the wrecks and dead that had been carried towards them by the current and by the wind, which had risen in the night and scattered them everywhere, and they set up a rival trophy at Sybota on the island, as having won.

And each side claimed the victory with the following reasoning: the Corinthians, having prevailed in the sea battle until night, so as to bring in the most wrecks and dead, and having no fewer than a thousand men as prisoners and having sunk about seventy ships, set up a trophy: and the Corcyraeans, having destroyed about thirty ships, and having, when the Athenians came, taken up the wrecks and dead on their side, and because on the day before the Corinthians had backed water and withdrawn from them when they saw the Attic ships, and when the Athenians came, did not sail out against them from Sybota, for these reasons set up a trophy.

So each side claimed to have won: and the Corinthians, sailing away home, took Anactorium, which is at the mouth of the Ambracian gulf, by deceit (it was held in common by the Corcyraeans and them), and having settled Corinthian colonists in it they withdrew home, and of the Corcyraeans they sold eight hundred who were slaves, and two hundred and fifty they kept in chains and treated with much care, so that when they returned they might win Corcyra over for them: and most of these happened to be the first men of the city in power as well.

So Corcyra survived the war with the Corinthians in this way, and the ships of the Athenians withdrew from it: and this was the first cause of the war for the Corinthians against the Athenians, that they had fought at sea against them on the side of the Corcyraeans during the treaty.
And immediately after this the following differences also arose between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians, leading to war.

For while the Corinthians were contriving how to take revenge on them, the Athenians, suspecting their enmity, ordered the Potidaeans, who live on the isthmus of Pallene, colonists of the Corinthians, but their own allies paying tribute, to pull down their wall on the side of Pallene and to give hostages, and to send away the magistrates and in future not to receive those whom the Corinthians sent each year, fearing that they would revolt, persuaded by Perdiccas and the Corinthians, and would lead the other allies in Thrace to revolt with them.
The Athenians were making these preparations regarding the Potidaeans immediately after the sea battle at Corcyra:
for the Corinthians were now openly hostile, and Perdiccas son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, had become an enemy, although he had been an ally and friend before.
And he became an enemy because the Athenians had made an alliance with Philip, his own brother, and Derdas, who were jointly opposing him.

And in his fear he was intriguing, sending to Lacedaemon, so that war might come about for them against the Peloponnesians, and he was trying to win over the Corinthians for the sake of the revolt of Potidaea:

and he also made proposals to the Chalcidians in Thrace and to the Bottiaeans to join in the revolt, thinking that, if he had these places as allies, since they were neighbours, he could more easily wage the war with them.

And the Athenians, learning of this and wishing to forestall the revolts of the cities (for they happened to be sending thirty ships and a thousand hoplites against his land, with Archestratus son of Lycomedes and † ten † others in command), instructed the commanders of the ships to take hostages from the Potidaeans and to pull down their wall, and to keep watch over the neighbouring cities so that they would not revolt.

And the Potidaeans, having sent envoys to the Athenians too, to see if they could somehow persuade them to make no changes concerning them, and having also gone to Lacedaemon with the Corinthians, [were working] to get help ready, if it were needed, since from Athens, after negotiating for a long time, they had obtained nothing favourable, but the ships against Macedonia were sailing against them just the same, and the authorities of the Lacedaemonians promised them that, if the Athenians went against Potidaea, they would invade Attica, then indeed at this moment they revolted, together with the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, having sworn a common oath.

And Perdiccas persuaded the Chalcidians to abandon and pull down their cities on the sea and to move inland to Olynthus and to make this one strong city: and to those who abandoned their cities he gave part of his own land of Mygdonia around lake Bolbe to cultivate, as long as the war with the Athenians lasted. And they moved inland, pulling down their cities, and prepared for war:
and the thirty ships of the Athenians arrived in Thrace, and found Potidaea and the other places already in revolt.

And the commanders, thinking that it was impossible to fight both Perdiccas with their present force and the places that had revolted with him, turned to Macedonia, against which they had also been sent in the first place, and establishing themselves there they made war together with Philip and the brothers of Derdas, who had invaded with an army from the interior.

And meanwhile the Corinthians, since Potidaea had revolted and the Attic ships were around Macedonia, fearing for the place and thinking the danger their own, sent volunteers of their own and of the other Peloponnesians, persuaded with pay, sixteen hundred hoplites in all and four hundred light troops.
And their commander was Aristeus son of Adimantus, and not least out of friendship for him most of the soldiers from Corinth followed as volunteers: for he had always been friendly to the Potidaeans.
And they arrived in Thrace on the fortieth day after Potidaea revolted.

And the news of the cities also came at once to the Athenians, that they had revolted, and when they learned that the men with Aristeus were also coming, they sent two thousand of their own hoplites and forty ships against the places in revolt, and Callias son of Calliades with four others as commanders,
who, arriving in Macedonia, first found the earlier thousand, who had just taken Therme and were besieging Pydna.

And they too sat down before Pydna and besieged it, but then they made an agreement and a forced alliance with Perdiccas, since Potidaea and the arrival of Aristeus were pressing them, and withdrew from Macedonia,

and arriving at Beroea and from there at Strepsa, they first made an attempt on the place and, not taking it, marched by land towards Potidaea, with three thousand hoplites of their own, and many of the allies besides, and six hundred Macedonian horsemen, those with Philip and Pausanias: and at the same time seventy ships sailed along the coast.
And advancing little by little, they arrived on the third day at Gigonus and encamped.
And the Potidaeans and the Peloponnesians with Aristeus, awaiting the Athenians, were encamped on the side towards Olynthus on the isthmus, and had set up a market outside the city.

The allies, then, had chosen Aristeus as commander of all the infantry, and Perdiccas of the cavalry: for he had at once revolted again from the Athenians and was fighting with the Potidaeans, having appointed Iolaus as commander in his place.

And the plan of Aristeus was that he, keeping his own army on the isthmus, should watch for the Athenians, if they came on, and that the Chalcidians and the allies outside the isthmus and the two hundred horse from Perdiccas should stay at Olynthus, and when the Athenians advanced against them, should come to help in their rear and put the enemy between them.

But Callias, the commander of the Athenians, and his colleagues sent away the Macedonian horsemen and a few of the allies towards Olynthus, so that they might prevent those there from coming to help, and they themselves broke up their camp and advanced against Potidaea.
And when they reached the isthmus and saw their opponents preparing as for battle, they too drew up against them, and not long afterwards they engaged.

And the wing of Aristeus itself, and the picked men of the Corinthians and the others who were around him, routed the part opposite them and went out in pursuit for a long way: but the rest of the army of the Potidaeans and Peloponnesians was defeated by the Athenians and fled for refuge into the wall.

And Aristeus, returning from the pursuit, when he saw the rest of the army defeated, was at a loss which way he should go and risk it, either towards Olynthus or into Potidaea: and he decided to gather his men together into as small a space as possible and to force his way into Potidaea at a run, and he got through along the breakwater through the sea, under fire and with difficulty, losing a few men, but saving most of them.

And the helpers of the Potidaeans from Olynthus (it is about sixty stades away and is in sight), when the battle began and the signals were raised, advanced a little way as if to help, and the Macedonian horsemen drew up against them to stop them: but when the victory of the Athenians was quickly happening and the signals were pulled down, they withdrew again into the wall and the Macedonians went back to the Athenians: and the cavalry joined neither side.

And after the battle the Athenians set up a trophy and gave back the dead under truce to the Potidaeans: and there died of the Potidaeans and their allies a little less than three hundred, and of the Athenians themselves a hundred and fifty, and Callias the commander.

And the Athenians at once walled off the side towards the isthmus and kept guard there: but the side towards Pallene was unwalled: for they did not think they were strong enough both to keep guard on the isthmus and to cross over to Pallene and build a wall there, fearing that the Potidaeans and the allies would attack them when they were divided.

And the Athenians in the city, learning that Pallene was unwalled, some time later sent sixteen hundred hoplites of their own and Phormio son of Asopius as commander: and he, arriving at Pallene and setting out from Aphytis, led his army up to Potidaea, advancing little by little and at the same time ravaging the land, and when no one came out to battle, he walled off the side towards Pallene [with a wall].
And so Potidaea was now besieged in force on both sides, and from the sea by ships blockading it at the same time.

And Aristeus, since it had been walled off and he had no hope of safety unless something came from the Peloponnese or something else unexpected happened, advised that all except five hundred should wait for a wind and sail out, so that the food might hold out longer, and he himself was willing to be one of those who stayed: but when he did not persuade them, wishing to make the next preparations and to see that things outside would be as good as possible, he sailed out, escaping the notice of the guard of the Athenians.

And staying among the Chalcidians he helped in the war in other ways and, setting an ambush near the city of the Sermylians, killed many of them, and he negotiated with the Peloponnese to see how some help might come.
And after the walling off of Potidaea, Phormio with his sixteen hundred men ravaged Chalcidice and Bottice and took some towns as well.

So between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians these grievances had arisen beforehand against each other, for the Corinthians, that the Athenians were besieging Potidaea, which was their own colony, and men of the Corinthians and Peloponnesians who were in it, and for the Athenians against the Peloponnesians, that they had caused a city of their own, an ally and tribute-paying, to revolt, and had come and fought openly against them with the Potidaeans. However, the war had not yet broken out, but there was still a truce: for the Corinthians had done this on their own account.

But with Potidaea under siege they did not keep quiet, since their men were inside and at the same time they feared for the place: and they at once called the allies to Lacedaemon and, when they came there, loudly accused the Athenians of having broken the treaty and of wronging the Peloponnese.
And the Aeginetans, not sending envoys openly, since they feared the Athenians, but secretly, did not least help them urge on the war, saying that they were not autonomous according to the treaty.
And the Lacedaemonians, having summoned besides any of the allies and anyone else who said he had been wronged in any way by the Athenians, held their own customary assembly and told them to speak.

And others came forward and made their complaints, each one, and in particular the Megarians, pointing out many other differences too, but above all that they were excluded from the harbours in the Athenian empire and from the Attic market, contrary to the treaty.
And the Corinthians, coming forward last, after letting the others first stir up the Lacedaemonians, spoke as follows.

‘The trustworthiness, Lacedaemonians, of your own constitution and dealings with each other makes you more distrustful towards others if we say anything: and from it you have moderation, but you show rather more ignorance in dealing with affairs abroad.

For though we often told you beforehand what harm we were going to suffer from the Athenians, you did not take in each time what we were teaching you, but rather suspected the speakers of speaking for the sake of their own private differences: and for this reason it is not before we suffer, but when we are in the midst of the deed, that you have called these allies together, among whom it is fitting that we should speak not least, inasmuch as we also have the greatest complaints, being insulted by the Athenians and neglected by you.

‘And if they were wronging Hellas somewhere out of sight, there would be need of instruction besides, as to people who did not know: but as it is, why need we speak at length, when you see that some have been enslaved, and that they are plotting against others, not least against our allies, and have long been prepared in advance, in case they should ever go to war?

For otherwise they would not have taken Corcyra and be holding it against our will and be besieging Potidaea, of which the one is the most convenient place for use against Thrace, while the other would have provided the Peloponnesians with the largest navy.

And of this you are the cause, both by first allowing them to strengthen their city after the Persian wars and later to build the long walls, and by depriving of freedom right up to now not only those enslaved by them, but now also your own allies: for it is not the one who enslaves, but the one who could stop it but stands by, who more truly does it, if indeed he also claims the reputation of virtue as the liberator of Hellas.

And with difficulty have we met now at least, and not even now on clear terms. For we ought no longer to be considering whether we are being wronged, but how we shall defend ourselves: for those who act, having made their plans, are already advancing against those who have not decided, and without delay.

And we know by what road the Athenians go, and that they advance little by little against their neighbours. And while they think they are unnoticed because of your lack of perception, they are less bold, but when they learn that you know and stand by, they will press on hard.

For you alone of the Hellenes, Lacedaemonians, keep quiet, defending yourselves against someone not by your power, but by delay, and you alone put down the growth of your enemies not when it is beginning but when it is doubling.

And yet you were said to be safe, but your reputation, it seems, outran the reality. For we ourselves know that the Mede came from the ends of the earth to the Peloponnese before your forces went out to meet him worthily, and now you stand by while the Athenians are not far away, like him, but near, and instead of attacking them yourselves you prefer to defend yourselves when they attack, and to put yourselves at the mercy of chance by fighting against men much more powerful, knowing that even the barbarian failed mostly through his own fault, and that against the Athenians themselves we have often already prevailed more through their mistakes than through help from you, since your hopes have already ruined some who were even unprepared because they trusted them.
And let none of you think that these things are said out of enmity rather than as complaint: for complaint is against friends who make mistakes, but accusation against enemies who have done wrong.

‘And at the same time we think that we, if anyone, are entitled to bring reproach on our neighbours, especially when great interests are at stake, about which you do not seem to us to perceive anything, nor ever to have considered against what sort of men, the Athenians, and how far, how completely different from you, the contest will be.

For they are innovators and quick both to conceive and to carry out in deed whatever they decide: but you are for preserving what you have and devising nothing new, and in deed not even achieving what is necessary.

Again, they are daring beyond their power and take risks beyond their judgment, and in dangers they are hopeful: but your way is to do less than your power allows, and not to trust even what is certain in your judgment, and to think that you will never be freed from dangers.

And indeed they are unhesitating against you who delay, and they go abroad against you who stay most at home: for they think that by being away they may gain something, while you think that by going out you may harm even what you have.
And when they defeat their enemies they follow up furthest, and when they are defeated they fall back least.
Moreover they use their bodies for their city as if they were most foreign to them, but their minds as most their own for doing something on its behalf.

And whatever they have planned and do not carry through, they think they are deprived of their own, and whatever they go after and gain, they think they have achieved little compared with what they will get in the future. And if they should fail in some attempt, they hope for other things instead and make up the loss: for they alone possess as soon as they hope whatever they plan, because they quickly set their hand to whatever they decide.

And they toil at all these things with labours and dangers throughout their whole life, and they enjoy least what they have because they are always acquiring, and they think no festival is anything other than doing what is needed, and they consider untroubled quiet no less a misfortune than laborious activity:
so that if someone summed them up by saying that they were born neither to have quiet themselves nor to let other men have it, he would speak rightly.

‘And yet, when such a city stands opposed to you, Lacedaemonians, you delay, and you think that quiet lasts longest not for those men who act justly with their power, but with their spirit make it clear that, if they are wronged, they will not tolerate it, but you practise fairness on the principle of not harming others and of not being harmed yourselves in defending yourselves.
But you would hardly achieve this even if you lived next to a city like yourselves: and now, as we also showed just now, your ways are old-fashioned compared to theirs.
