And necessarily, as in an art, what is new always prevails: and for a city at peace unchanged customs are best, but for those who are forced to face many things there is need of much innovation too. Because of this the affairs of the Athenians, through their great experience, have been made new more than yours.

So up to this point let your slowness be limited: and now help the others and the Potidaeans, as you promised, by quickly invading Attica, so that you do not abandon men who are friends and kinsmen to their worst enemies, and do not turn the rest of us in despair to some other alliance.

And we would be doing nothing unjust either before the gods of oaths or before men who perceive it: for it is not those who, being left alone, go over to others who break treaties, but those who do not help those with whom they have sworn alliance.
But if you are willing to be zealous, we shall stay: for we would not be acting piously if we changed sides, nor would we find others more congenial.
In view of this, deliberate well, and try not to lead a Peloponnese lesser than your fathers handed down to you.’

Such were the words of the Corinthians. Now an embassy of the Athenians happened to be present at Lacedaemon beforehand on other business, and when they learned of the speeches, they decided that they ought to come before the Lacedaemonians, not to make any defence on the charges which the cities were bringing, but to show on the question as a whole that they should not decide quickly, but consider it at greater length. At the same time they wished to make plain how great the power of their own city was, and to remind the older men of what they knew and to give the younger an account of what they had no experience of, thinking that as a result of their words the Lacedaemonians would turn to keeping quiet rather than to making war.

So they approached the Lacedaemonians and said that they too wished to speak to their assembly, if nothing prevented it. The Lacedaemonians told them to come forward, and the Athenians came forward and spoke as follows.

‘Our embassy did not come here to dispute with your allies, but on the business for which our city sent us; but perceiving that there is no small outcry against us, we have come forward, not to answer the charges of the cities (for it is not before you as judges that either our words or theirs would be spoken), but so that you may not, persuaded by your allies, lightly take the worse decision about matters of great importance, and at the same time wishing, regarding the whole case that has been raised against us, to show that we do not hold what we have acquired unreasonably, and that our city is worthy of account.

‘Now what need is there to speak of very ancient matters, for which hearsay reports are witnesses rather than the sight of those who will hear them? But the Persian Wars and all that you yourselves know of we must speak of, even if it will be rather tiresome to us to be always bringing them forward: for when we were doing those deeds, the risk was run for a benefit, in the substance of which you had a share, and we should not be deprived of the whole of the credit, if it is of any benefit.
And it will be said not so much for the sake of deprecation as of testimony and of showing against what kind of city the struggle will be set for you if you do not take good counsel.

For we say that at Marathon we alone faced the danger in the front line against the barbarian, and that when he came the second time, not being able to defend ourselves by land, we embarked on our ships with all our people and joined in the sea-fight at Salamis, which prevented him from sailing against the Peloponnese city by city and ravaging it, since you would have been unable to help one another against many ships.
And he himself gave the greatest proof of this: for when he had been defeated with his ships, as if his power were no longer equal, he withdrew in haste with the greater part of his army.

Such then being the outcome, and it having been clearly shown that the cause of the Hellenes depended on their ships, we contributed the three most useful things to it, the largest number of ships, the shrewdest man as general, and the most unhesitating zeal: of the four hundred ships, a little less than two-thirds, and Themistocles as commander, who was most responsible for the sea-fight taking place in the strait, which most clearly saved the cause, and for this very reason you honoured him most of all the foreigners who have come to you;

and we showed a zeal by far the most daring, since, when no one was helping us by land, and the rest up to our borders were already enslaved, we resolved, after abandoning our city and sacrificing our property, not even so to forsake the common cause of the remaining allies, nor by scattering to become useless to them, but to embark on our ships and face the danger, and not to be angry because you had not come to our aid beforehand.

So we say that we ourselves benefited you no less than we received this benefit. For you came to our aid from cities that were still inhabited and with a view to occupying them in future, when you were afraid for yourselves more than for us (at any rate, while we were still safe, you did not come); but we, setting out from a city that no longer existed, and running the risk for one that existed only in slender hope, helped to save both you in your part and ourselves.

But if we had gone over to the Mede earlier, fearing for our land as others also did, or if we had not dared afterwards to embark on our ships, as being ruined men, there would no longer have been any need for you, not having enough ships, to fight at sea, but his affairs would have gone forward quietly just as he wished.
‘Do we deserve, Lacedaemonians, both for the sake of our zeal at that time and the shrewdness of our judgment, to be so excessively envied by the Hellenes, at least for the empire that we hold?

For we did not take this very empire by force, but because you were unwilling to stay on to deal with what remained of the barbarian, and the allies came to us and themselves asked us to become their leaders:
and from the very nature of the thing we were compelled at first to advance it to its present state, chiefly from fear, then also from honour, and later also from self-interest.

And it no longer seemed safe, when we were hated by most, and some had already revolted and been subdued, and you were no longer friendly to us as before, but suspicious and at variance, to let it go and run the risk: for the revolts would have been to you.
And no one can be blamed for making the best arrangement of his interests when the greatest dangers are at stake.

You at any rate, Lacedaemonians, lead the cities in the Peloponnese after settling them to your own advantage; and if at that time you had held out to the end and been hated in your leadership, as we were, we know well that you would have become no less burdensome to the allies and would have been forced either to rule with a strong hand or to be in danger yourselves.

So neither have we done anything remarkable or contrary to human ways, if we accepted an empire that was offered and did not give it up, overcome by the 〈three〉 greatest motives, honour and fear and self-interest, nor again were we the first to begin such a thing, but it has always been established that the weaker is held down by the stronger, and at the same time we thought ourselves worthy of it and were thought so by you too, until now, calculating your interests, you use the plea of justice, which no one yet, when a chance offered to gain something by strength, put forward and so turned away from having the advantage.
And they are worthy of praise who, having followed human nature so far as to rule over others, become more just than their existing power requires.
We think at any rate that others, if they took our position, would best show whether we are at all moderate; but for us even from our fairness ill repute rather than praise has unreasonably resulted.
‘For though we are at a disadvantage in the suits under contract with the allies and have made the judgments in our own courts under equal laws, we are thought to be litigious.

And none of them considers why this is not made a reproach to those who hold empire elsewhere too and are less moderate than we are towards their subjects: for those who are able to use force have no need besides to go to law.

But these, accustomed to deal with us on an equal footing, if they are worsted in anything, however little, contrary to their notion that it ought not to be so, either by a judgment or by the power that our empire gives, are not grateful at not being deprived of the greater part, but bear the loss more hardly than if we had from the first set the law aside and openly taken advantage of them. In that case not even they themselves would have argued that the weaker ought not to give way to the stronger.
And men, it seems, are more angry when wronged than when coerced: for the one is thought to be getting the worse of it from an equal, the other being compelled by a superior.
At any rate under the Mede they endured sufferings more terrible than these, but our rule is thought to be harsh, naturally enough: for the present is always heavy to subjects.

You at any rate, if you overthrew us and ruled yourselves, would soon change the goodwill that you have gained through fear of us, if you are going to think now as you showed signs of then, when you led against the Mede for a short time. For you have customs at home that do not mix with those of others, and besides each one of you, when he goes abroad, follows neither these nor those which the rest of Hellas observes.

‘Deliberate slowly, then, as about no small matters, and do not, persuaded by the opinions and complaints of others, take on trouble of your own. And recognise beforehand how great the incalculable element in war is, before you are in it:
for when it is drawn out it usually comes round to chances, from which we are equally far off, and which way it will turn out is risked in the dark.
And men, when they go to war, take to deeds first, which they ought to do later, and only when they are suffering do they resort to words.

But we, being not yet in any such error ourselves nor seeing you in one, tell you, while good counsel is still a free choice for both of us, not to break the treaty or transgress the oaths, but to settle our differences by arbitration according to the agreement. Otherwise, calling to witness the gods by whom the oaths were sworn, we shall try to defend ourselves against those who begin war, in whatever way you lead.’

Such were the words of the Athenians. And when the Lacedaemonians had heard both the charges of the allies against the Athenians and what the Athenians said, they made everyone withdraw and deliberated by themselves about the present situation.

And the opinions of the majority tended to the same conclusion, that the Athenians were already in the wrong and that they must go to war quickly; but Archidamus their king, a man who was thought to be both intelligent and prudent, came forward and spoke as follows.

‘I myself have already had experience of many wars, Lacedaemonians, and I see those of you who are of the same age, so that no one would desire the business out of inexperience, as most men might, nor because he thought it good and safe.
And you would find that this war about which you are now deliberating would not be the least, if one considered it soberly.

For against Peloponnesians and our neighbours our strength is of a similar kind, and it is possible to move quickly against each of them; but against men who have a land far away and moreover are most experienced at sea and are best equipped with everything else, with private and public wealth and ships and horses and arms and a population such as there is in no other single Hellenic place, and who besides have many allies paying tribute, how should we lightly take up war against these, and trusting in what should we hurry on unprepared?

In our ships? But we are inferior; and if we are to practise and prepare against them, time will be needed. In our money, then? But in this we are still far more deficient, and we neither have it in a common treasury nor readily contribute it from our private means.
Perhaps someone might be confident because we are superior to them in arms and in numbers, so as to invade and ravage their land.
But they have much other land which they rule, and they will import by sea what they need.
And if, again, we try to make their allies revolt, we shall have to help these too with ships, since they are for the most part islanders.
What sort of war, then, will ours be? For unless we either defeat them at sea or take away the revenues from which they maintain their navy, we shall suffer the greater harm.
And in that case it will no longer even be honourable to make peace, especially if we are thought to have begun the quarrel rather than they.

For let us certainly not be buoyed up by that hope, that the war will be quickly ended if we ravage their land. I fear rather that we may even leave it behind to our children: so unlikely is it that the Athenians, with their spirit, will either be slaves to their land or be dismayed by the war like inexperienced men.

‘Yet I do not bid you callously allow them to harm our allies and not detect them in their plotting, but not yet to take up arms, and to send and make complaint without showing too plainly either war or that we shall give way, and meanwhile to equip our own side also by winning over allies, both Hellenes and barbarians, if from anywhere we can gain any added power either of ships or of money (and it is no cause of reproach, for those who like us are plotted against by the Athenians, to save themselves by taking on not only Hellenes but also barbarians), and at the same time let us develop our own resources.
And if they listen at all to our envoys, that is best; but if not, after two or three years have passed, we shall go against them, if we decide to, better fortified by then.

And perhaps, seeing by then our preparation and our words hinting at the same, they would be more ready to yield, both because they still have their land unravaged and because they are deliberating about goods that are present and not yet destroyed.

For do not think that their land is anything other than a hostage in your hands, and no less so the better it is cultivated: you should spare it as long as possible, and not drive them to desperation and so have them harder to deal with.
For if, unprepared and hurried on by the complaints of the allies, we ravage it, see to it that we do not bring about something more shameful and more perplexing for the Peloponnese.

For complaints, both of cities and of private persons, can be settled; but a war taken up by all for the sake of private interests, of which it is not possible to know how it will go, is not easy to end with honour.
‘And let no one think it cowardice that many do not quickly attack a single city.

For they too have allies no fewer than ours who pay them money, and war is not a matter of arms so much as of expenditure, through which arms are of use, especially for a land power against a sea power.

Let us therefore first provide this, and not be carried away beforehand by the speeches of the allies, but as we shall bear the greater part of the blame for the outcome either way, let us also at leisure look ahead somewhat at it.

And the slowness and delay for which they most blame us, do not be ashamed of. For if you hurry, you would end the war more slowly because you begin it unprepared, and at the same time we have always inhabited a city that is free and most highly renowned.

And this quality can very well be sensible self-control: for because of it we alone neither become insolent in success nor give way to misfortunes as much as others; and we are not carried away by pleasure when people urge us with praise towards dangers contrary to our judgment, and if anyone tries to provoke us with accusation, we are not any the more persuaded by being annoyed.

We are both warlike and well-counselled because of our good order, warlike because a sense of shame has the greatest share in self-control, and courage in shame, and well-counselled because we are educated too unlearnedly to despise the laws and with too much severity in self-control to disobey them, and because we are not too clever in useless things, so as to find fine fault in words with the preparations of the enemy and then fail to go against them in deed in like manner, but we are taught to think that the plans of our neighbours are much like ours, and that the chances that befall are not to be determined by reasoning.

And we always prepare in deed against our opponents on the assumption that they plan well; and we must not rest our hopes on them as being likely to make mistakes, but on ourselves as taking safe precautions. And we must not think that man differs much from man, but that he is best who is trained in the hardest school.

‘These practices, then, which our fathers handed down to us and which we ourselves keep, having always benefited by them, let us not give up, nor in haste decide in a short part of a day about many lives and much property and many cities and honour, but at leisure. And we can do this more than others because of our strength.

And send to the Athenians about Potidaea, and send about the wrongs which the allies say they suffer, especially since they are ready to submit to arbitration: and against one who offers it, it is not lawful to go first as against a wrongdoer. But prepare for the war at the same time. For in this way you will decide best and most formidably for your opponents.’
Such were the words of Archidamus; and Sthenelaidas, who was one of the ephors at that time, came forward last and spoke [to the Lacedaemonians ] as follows.

‘The many words of the Athenians I do not understand: for though they praised themselves a great deal, they nowhere denied that they are wronging our allies and the Peloponnese; and yet if they were good then against the Medes but are bad towards us now, they deserve double punishment, because they have become bad instead of good.
But we are the same both then and now, and if we are wise we shall not look on while our allies are wronged, nor delay to avenge them: they are no longer delaying in their suffering.

For others have much money and ships and horses, but we have good allies, whom we must not betray to the Athenians, nor decide the matter by lawsuits and words when they are not being harmed in words, but we must avenge them quickly and with all our strength.
And let no one tell us that it is fitting for us to deliberate when we are wronged, but rather it is fitting for those who intend to do wrong to deliberate for a long time.
Vote, therefore, Lacedaemonians, for the war, as is worthy of Sparta, and do not let the Athenians become greater, nor let us betray our allies, but with the gods let us go against the wrongdoers.’
Having said this, he himself, being ephor, put the question to the assembly of the Lacedaemonians.

But he (for they decide by shouting and not by ballot) said that he could not tell which shout was the louder, and wishing that they should declare their opinion openly and so be the more eager for war, he said, ‘Whoever of you, Lacedaemonians, thinks that the treaty has been broken and that the Athenians are in the wrong, let him stand up and go to that place,’ pointing out a place to them, ‘and whoever does not think so, to the other side.’ And they stood up and divided,
and those who thought that the treaty had been broken were far more numerous.

And they summoned the allies and told them that in their own view the Athenians were in the wrong, but that they wished to call together all the allies as well and put it to the vote, so that they might make the war after deliberating in common, if it was so decided.
And the allies went away home having accomplished this, and the envoys of the Athenians later, after dealing with the business on which they had come:
and this decision of the assembly, that the treaty had been broken, was made in the fourteenth year of the thirty years' treaty, which had been made after the affair of Euboea.

And the Lacedaemonians voted that the treaty had been broken and that they must go to war, not so much because they were persuaded by the speeches of the allies as because they feared that the Athenians might become more powerful, seeing that most of Hellas was already subject to them.
For the Athenians came to the position in which they grew great in the following way.

When the Medes had withdrawn from Europe, defeated both by sea and by land by the Hellenes, and those of them who had fled with their ships to Mycale had been destroyed, Leotychides, the king of the Lacedaemonians, who was the leader of the Hellenes at Mycale, went away home with the allies from the Peloponnese, but the Athenians and the allies from Ionia and the Hellespont, who had already revolted from the King, stayed on and besieged Sestos, which the Medes held, and after wintering there they took it when the barbarians had abandoned it, and after this they sailed away from the Hellespont, each to their own cities.

And the Athenian people, when the barbarians had left their land, at once began to bring back their children and wives and the remaining furniture from where they had placed them for safety, and prepared to rebuild the city and the walls: for only short stretches of the circuit wall were standing, and most of the houses had fallen, though a few were left, in which the Persian nobles themselves had quartered.

But the Lacedaemonians, perceiving what was intended, came with an embassy, partly because they themselves would have preferred to see neither them nor anyone else having a wall, but more because the allies urged them on and feared both the size of their navy, which had not existed before, and the daring they had shown in the Persian war.

And they asked them not to build walls, but rather to join them in pulling down the circuit walls of all those outside the Peloponnese whose walls were standing, not revealing to the Athenians their real wish and suspicion, but saying that the barbarian, if he came again, would then have no strong place from which to set out, as now from Thebes; and they said that the Peloponnese was a sufficient refuge and base for all.

But the Athenians, on the advice of Themistocles, answered the Lacedaemonians, when they had said this, that they would send envoys to them about what they were saying, and at once sent them away; and Themistocles told them to send himself to Lacedaemon as quickly as possible, but, after choosing other envoys besides himself, not to send them out at once, but to hold them back until they had raised the wall high enough to fight from at the height most needed; and that all in the city, the whole people, should build the wall [themselves and their wives and children ], sparing no private or public building from which there would be any help for the work, but pulling everything down.
And having given these instructions and hinted that he himself would do the rest there, he departed.

And when he came to Lacedaemon he did not go to the authorities, but delayed and made excuses. And whenever any of those in office asked him why he did not come before the assembly, he said that he was waiting for his fellow envoys, who had been left behind because of some business, but that he expected them to come soon and was surprised that they were not yet there.

And those who heard him believed Themistocles because of their friendship for him, but when others arrived and clearly reported that the wall was being built and was already gaining height, they did not know how they should disbelieve it.
And he, learning of this, told them not to be misled by words rather than to send men of their own who were trustworthy and would report faithfully after looking.

So they sent them, and concerning them Themistocles sent secretly to the Athenians, telling them to detain them as unobtrusively as possible and not to let them go until they themselves had returned (for his fellow envoys, Abronichus son of Lysicles and Aristides son of Lysimachus, had already come to him, reporting that the wall was high enough), for he feared that the Lacedaemonians, when they heard the truth clearly, would no longer let them go.

So the Athenians detained the envoys, as they had been instructed, and Themistocles, coming before the Lacedaemonians, then at last said openly that their city was already walled so as to be able to protect its inhabitants, and that if the Lacedaemonians or the allies wished to send any embassy to them, they should come in future as to men who could distinguish both what was in their own interests and what was in the common interest.

For when it had seemed better to abandon their city and embark on their ships, they said, they had decided on it and dared it without them, and in whatever, again, they had deliberated with them, they had shown themselves second to none in judgment.
So it seemed to them that now too it was better for their own city to have a wall, and that it would be more useful both for their citizens in particular and for all the allies:

for it was not possible to deliberate on equal or similar terms for the common good except on the basis of a matching strength. Either, then, he said, they must all be allies without walls, or they must consider this too to be right.

And the Lacedaemonians, when they heard this, did not show open anger against the Athenians (for they had not sent the embassy to prevent them, but, as they claimed, to give advice to the common cause, and at the same time they happened to be very friendly to them at that time because of their zeal against the Mede), but, failing in their wish, they were secretly annoyed. And the envoys of each side went away home without complaint.
In this way the Athenians walled their city in a short time.

And the building still shows even now that it was done in haste: for the foundations are laid with stones of every kind, in some places not even fitted together, but as each was brought at the time, and many gravestones from tombs and worked stones were built in. For the circuit of the city was extended further on every side, and for this reason they hurried, moving everything alike.

And Themistocles also persuaded them to build the rest of the Piraeus (it had been begun before, in his term of office which he held as archon of the Athenians for a year), thinking that the place was fine, having three natural harbours, and that their having become a seafaring people would contribute greatly towards
acquiring power (for he was the first who dared to say that they must hold on to the sea), and he at once helped to lay the foundations of the empire.

And on his advice they built the wall of the thickness that is still visible now around the Piraeus: for two wagons, meeting one another, brought up the stones. And inside there was neither rubble nor clay, but large stones built together and cut square, bound to one another on the outside with iron and lead. And the height was completed to about half of what he intended.

For he wanted to repel the attacks of the enemy by its size and thickness, and he thought that the guarding would be enough for a few men, and the least serviceable, and that the rest would man the ships.

For he was most devoted to the ships, having seen, as it seems to me, that the approach of the King's army by sea was easier than that by land; and he thought the Piraeus more useful than the upper city, and often advised the Athenians, if they were ever overpowered by land, to go down to it and resist all comers with their ships.
So the Athenians were walled in this way and made their other preparations immediately after the withdrawal of the Medes.

And Pausanias son of Cleombrotus was sent out from Lacedaemon as general of the Hellenes with twenty ships from the Peloponnese; and the Athenians also sailed with them with thirty ships, and a number of the other allies.
And they made an expedition to Cyprus and subdued most of it, and afterwards to Byzantium, which the Medes held, and took it by siege during this command.

But since he was already acting violently, the other Hellenes were aggrieved, and not least the Ionians and all who had recently been freed from the King; and they went to the Athenians and asked them to become their leaders on the ground of kinship and not to give way to Pausanias if he used violence anywhere.
And the Athenians accepted their proposals and turned their attention to them, intending not to overlook it and to settle everything else as seemed best to them.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians recalled Pausanias to question him about what they were hearing: for much wrongdoing was alleged against him by the Hellenes who arrived, and his conduct seemed more an imitation of a tyranny than a generalship.
And it happened that he was recalled at the very time when the allies, out of hatred for him, went over to the Athenians, except the soldiers from the Peloponnese.

And when he came to Lacedaemon he was found guilty of wrongs done privately to particular persons, but on the most serious charges he was acquitted of wrongdoing; and not least he was accused of Medism, and it seemed to be very clear.
And they no longer sent him out as commander, but Dorcis and some others with him, with no large army; and the allies no longer granted the leadership to these.

And they, perceiving this, went away, and afterwards the Lacedaemonians sent out no others, fearing that those who went abroad would become corrupted, as they had seen in the case of Pausanias, and wishing also to be rid of the Persian war and thinking the Athenians capable of leading and friendly to them at that time.

And when the Athenians had taken over the leadership in this way, with the consent of the allies because of their hatred of Pausanias, they fixed which of the cities were to provide money against the barbarian and which ships: for the declared aim was to avenge what they had suffered by ravaging the King's land.

And the office of the Hellenotamiae was then first established by the Athenians, who received the tribute: for so the contribution of money was named. And the first tribute assessed was four hundred and sixty talents. And their treasury was Delos, and the meetings were held in the temple.

And leading allies who were at first autonomous and deliberated in common meetings, they undertook the following enterprises in war and in the management of affairs between this war and the Persian war, against the barbarian, and against their own allies when they revolted, and against those of the Peloponnesians who came into conflict with them on each occasion.

And I have written of them and made this digression from my account for this reason, that this period was omitted by all those before me, and they composed either the history of Hellas before the Persian Wars or the Persian Wars themselves; and Hellanicus, who is the one who did touch on these matters in his Attic history, mentioned them briefly and without accuracy as to the dates. At the same time it also gives an explanation of how the empire of the Athenians was established.
First they took by siege Eion on the Strymon, which the Medes held, and enslaved its people, under the command of Cimon son of Miltiades.
Then they enslaved Scyros, the island in the Aegean, which the Dolopians inhabited, and settled it themselves.
And they had a war with the Carystians, without the rest of the Euboeans, and in time they came to terms by agreement.

And after this they made war on the Naxians when they revolted and reduced them by siege, and this was the first allied city to be enslaved contrary to the established rule, and afterwards the others too, as it happened with each.

And there were various causes of the revolts, and the greatest were arrears in tribute and ships and desertion from service, if this happened in any case: for the Athenians exacted strictly and were burdensome, applying compulsion to men who were not accustomed to hardship or willing to endure it.

And in other ways too the Athenians were somehow no longer as popular as rulers as before, and they did not serve with them on an equal footing, and it was easy for them to bring back those who revolted.

For this the allies themselves were responsible: for because of this reluctance to serve on campaigns, most of them, so as not to be away from home, arranged to pay money instead of ships, the corresponding expense, and the navy of the Athenians grew from the expenditure which they contributed, while they themselves, whenever they revolted, found themselves unprepared and inexperienced for war.

And after this there took place also the land battle and sea battle at the river Eurymedon in Pamphylia between the Athenians and their allies and the Medes, and the Athenians won both on the same day under the command of Cimon son of Miltiades, and took and destroyed the Phoenician triremes, two hundred in all.

And some time later it happened that the Thasians revolted from them, having quarrelled about the trading-posts on the opposite coast of Thrace and the mine which they owned. And the Athenians sailed against Thasos with ships, won a sea-fight, and landed on the island,

and having sent ten thousand settlers of their own and of their allies to the Strymon about the same time to colonise what was then called Nine Ways, but is now Amphipolis, they themselves took Nine Ways, which the Edonians held, but when they advanced into the interior of Thrace they were destroyed at Drabescus in Edonia by all the Thracians together, to whom the place [Nine Ways] was hostile as it was being founded.
And the Thasians, defeated in battle and besieged, called on the Lacedaemonians and asked them to help them by invading Attica.

And they promised to do so, without the knowledge of the Athenians, and intended to, but were prevented by the earthquake that occurred, during which their Helots and, of the perioeci, the Thuriats and Aethaeans revolted and went to Ithome. And most of the Helots were the descendants of the old Messenians who had then been enslaved; hence they were all called Messenians.

So the Lacedaemonians were engaged in a war against those on Ithome, and the Thasians, in the third year of the siege, came to terms with the Athenians, pulling down their wall and handing over their ships, agreeing to pay at once the money they owed and to pay tribute in future, and giving up the mainland and the mine.
And the Lacedaemonians, as the war against those on Ithome dragged on for them, called in their other allies and the Athenians; and they came under the command of Cimon in no small numbers.

And they called them in chiefly because they were thought to be skilled at assaulting walls, but since the siege had become long, they seemed to fall short in this: for otherwise they would have taken the place by force.

And from this expedition a disagreement between the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians first became open. For the Lacedaemonians, when the place was not taken by force, fearing the daring and the revolutionary spirit of the Athenians, and regarding them at the same time as of another race, lest, if they stayed on, they might be persuaded by those on Ithome to start some revolution, sent them alone of the allies away, not revealing their suspicion, but saying that they had no further need of them.

But the Athenians realised that they were not being sent away for the better reason, but because some suspicion had arisen, and taking it ill and thinking they had not deserved to be treated so by the Lacedaemonians, as soon as they had withdrawn they gave up the alliance made with them against the Mede and became allies of the Argives, their enemies, and at the same time the same oaths and alliance were made by both with the Thessalians.

And those on Ithome, in the tenth year, since they could no longer hold out, came to terms with the Lacedaemonians on condition that they would leave the Peloponnese under truce and never set foot in it again; and if anyone was caught, he was to be the slave of whoever took him.
And the Lacedaemonians had also before this an oracle from Delphi, to let go the suppliant of Zeus of Ithome.

And they went out, themselves and their children and wives, and the Athenians, receiving them because of their hatred of the Lacedaemonians by now, settled them at Naupactus, which they happened to have recently taken from the Ozolian Locrians who held it.

And the Megarians too went over to an alliance with the Athenians, revolting from the Lacedaemonians, because the Corinthians were pressing them in a war about boundaries; and the Athenians held Megara and Pegae, and built for the Megarians the long walls from the city to Nisaea and garrisoned them themselves. And it was not least from this that the violent hatred of the Corinthians against the Athenians first began.

And Inaros son of Psammetichus, a Libyan, king of the Libyans who border on Egypt, setting out from Marea, the city above Pharos, caused most of Egypt to revolt from King Artaxerxes, and having made himself ruler, he called in the Athenians.

And they (for they happened to be campaigning against Cyprus with two hundred ships of their own and of their allies) came, leaving Cyprus, and sailing up from the sea into the Nile, being masters of the river and of two parts of Memphis, they made war on the third part, which is called the White Wall; and inside it were those of the Persians and Medes who had fled there and those of the Egyptians who had not joined the revolt.

And when the Athenians landed from their ships at Halieis, a battle took place against the Corinthians and Epidaurians, and the Corinthians won. And later the Athenians fought a sea-battle off Cecryphalea against a Peloponnesian fleet, and the Athenians won.

And after this, when war had broken out between the Athenians and the Aeginetans, a great sea-battle took place off Aegina between the Athenians and the Aeginetans, and the allies of each side were present, and the Athenians won and, having taken seventy of their ships, landed on the island and besieged the city, under the command of Leocrates son of Stroebus.

Then the Peloponnesians, wishing to help the Aeginetans, first sent across to Aegina three hundred hoplites, auxiliaries of the Corinthians and Epidaurians, while the Corinthians with their allies seized the heights of Geraneia and came down into the Megarid, thinking that the Athenians would be unable to help the Megarians, with a large army absent both in Aegina and in Egypt; and that if they did help them, they would withdraw from Aegina.
But the Athenians did not move the army at Aegina, and of those left in the city the oldest and the youngest came to Megara under the command of Myronides.
And after an indecisive battle against the Corinthians they separated from one another, and each side thought that it had not had the worse of the action.

And the Athenians (for they had in fact rather won) set up a trophy when the Corinthians had gone away; but the Corinthians, reproached by the older men in the city, made their preparations and, coming about twelve days later, set up a rival trophy themselves as though they had won. And the Athenians, sallying out from Megara, killed those who were setting up the trophy and engaged the rest and defeated them.

And the defeated men retreated, and a not small part of them, hard pressed and missing the road, rushed into the land of a private person, which happened to be enclosed by a great ditch, and there was no way out.

And the Athenians, seeing this, shut them in in front with their hoplites and, placing their light troops in a circle round them, stoned to death all who had gone in, and this was a great disaster for the Corinthians. And the main body of their army went back home.
And about this time the Athenians also began to build the long walls to the sea, the one to Phalerum and the one to the Piraeus.

And when the Phocians made an expedition against Doris, the mother country of the Lacedaemonians, against Boeum and Cytinium and Erineum, and took one of these towns, the Lacedaemonians, under the leadership of Nicomedes son of Cleombrotus on behalf of King Pleistoanax son of Pausanias, who was still young, went to the help of the Dorians with fifteen hundred hoplites of their own and ten thousand of their allies, and having compelled the Phocians by agreement to give back the town, they began to withdraw again.

And by sea, if they wished to cross by the Crisaean gulf, the Athenians were going to sail round with their ships and stop them; and to march through Geraneia did not seem safe to them, since the Athenians held Megara and Pegae. For Geraneia was hard to pass and was always guarded by the Athenians, and at that time they perceived that they were going to stop them this way too.

So they decided to wait in Boeotia and consider in what way they could most safely get through. And to some extent men of the Athenians were also inviting them in secretly, hoping to put an end to the democracy and to the building of the long walls.
And the Athenians went out against them with their whole force, and a thousand Argives, and the other allies in their several contingents; and they came to fourteen thousand in all.
And they marched against them, thinking that they were at a loss how to get through, and partly too from suspicion of an attempt to overthrow the democracy.
And some Thessalian horsemen also came to the Athenians in accordance with the alliance, who went over to the Lacedaemonians during the action.
And when a battle took place at Tanagra in Boeotia, the Lacedaemonians and their allies won, and there was great slaughter on both sides.

And the Lacedaemonians went into the Megarid and cut down the trees and went back home again through Geraneia and the Isthmus; and on the sixty-second day after the battle the Athenians marched against the Boeotians under the command of Myronides,

and having defeated the Boeotians in battle at Oenophyta they became masters of the land of Boeotia and Phocis, and pulled down the wall of the Tanagraeans and took a hundred of the richest men of the Opuntian Locrians as hostages, and finished their own long walls.
And after this the Aeginetans also came to terms with the Athenians, pulling down their walls, handing over their ships, and agreeing to pay tribute for the future.

And the Athenians sailed round the Peloponnese under the command of Tolmides son of Tolmaeus, and burned the dockyard of the Lacedaemonians and took Chalcis, a city of the Corinthians, and defeated the Sicyonians in battle during a landing on their territory.
And the Athenians and their allies in Egypt stayed on, and many forms of war befell them.

For at first the Athenians were masters of Egypt, and the King sent Megabazus, a Persian, to Lacedaemon with money, so that he might draw the Athenians away from Egypt by persuading the Peloponnesians to invade Attica.

who, arriving by land, defeated the Egyptians and their allies in battle and drove the Hellenes out of Memphis and finally shut them up in the island of Prosopitis and besieged them on it for a year and six months, until, by draining the canal and diverting the water elsewhere, he left the ships on dry ground and made most of the island mainland, and crossed over and took the island on foot.
Thus the cause of the Hellenes was ruined after six years of war; and a few out of many, making their way through Libya to Cyrene, were saved, but most perished.

And Egypt came again under the King, except Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes: him they could not take because of the size of the marsh, and besides, the marsh-dwellers are the most warlike of the Egyptians.
And Inaros, the king of the Libyans, who had managed the whole affair in Egypt, was taken by treachery and impaled.

And fifty triremes from Athens and the rest of the confederacy, sailing to Egypt as a relief force, put in at the Mendesian mouth, knowing nothing of what had happened; and land forces falling on them from the shore and a Phoenician fleet from the sea destroyed most of the ships, while the smaller part escaped back again.
Thus ended the great expedition of the Athenians and their allies to Egypt.

And Orestes son of Echecratides, the king of the Thessalians, being an exile from Thessaly, persuaded the Athenians to restore him; and taking with them the Boeotians and Phocians, who were their allies, the Athenians marched against Pharsalus in Thessaly. And they were masters of the land as far as they could go without moving far from their camp (for the Thessalian horsemen kept them in check), but they did not take the city, nor did anything else go forward for them of what they had come for, but they went back again with Orestes without having achieved anything.

And not long after this a thousand Athenians embarked on the ships at Pegae (for they themselves held Pegae) and sailed along the coast to Sicyon under the command of Pericles son of Xanthippus, and, having landed, defeated in battle those of the Sicyonians who engaged them.
And at once, taking the Achaeans with them and sailing across, they marched against Oeniadae in Acarnania and besieged it, but did not take it, and went back home.
And later, after an interval of three years, a five years' truce was made between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians.
And the Athenians abstained from war in Hellas, but made an expedition against Cyprus with two hundred ships of their own and of their allies under the command of Cimon.
And sixty of these ships sailed to Egypt, at the request of Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes, while the rest besieged Citium.

But when Cimon died and a famine occurred they withdrew from Citium, and sailing off Salamis in Cyprus they fought the Phoenicians and Cyprians and Cilicians by sea and by land at the same time, and having won both battles they went back home, and with them the ships [that had] come back from Egypt.

And after this the Lacedaemonians undertook the so-called Sacred War, and having gained control of the temple at Delphi, they handed it over to the Delphians; and again later, after they had withdrawn, the Athenians made an expedition, gained control of it, and handed it over to the Phocians.

And some time after this, when the Boeotian exiles held Orchomenus and Chaeronea and some other places in Boeotia, the Athenians marched against these places, which were hostile, with a thousand hoplites of their own and contingents of their allies, under the command of Tolmides son of Tolmaeus. And having taken Chaeronea and enslaved its people, they began to withdraw after setting up a garrison.

But as they were marching, at Coronea, the Boeotian exiles from Orchomenus attacked them, and with them Locrians and Euboean exiles and all who were of the same mind, and having won the battle they killed some of the Athenians and took others alive.
And the Athenians evacuated all Boeotia, making a treaty on condition that they would get their men back.
And the Boeotian exiles returned, and they and all the others became independent again.

And not long after this Euboea revolted from the Athenians, and when Pericles had already crossed over to it with an army of Athenians, news was brought to him that Megara had revolted and the Peloponnesians were about to invade Attica and the Athenian garrison had been destroyed by the Megarians, except those who had escaped to Nisaea; and the Megarians had revolted after calling in the Corinthians and Sicyonians and Epidaurians. And Pericles brought the army back again in haste from Euboea.

And after this the Peloponnesians invaded Attica as far as Eleusis and Thria and ravaged it, under the leadership of Pleistoanax son of Pausanias, king of the Lacedaemonians, and without advancing any further they went back home.

And the Athenians crossed over again to Euboea under the command of Pericles and subdued the whole of it, and settled the rest by agreement, but they expelled the Hestiaeans and occupied their land themselves.

And not long after withdrawing from Euboea they made a thirty years' treaty with the Lacedaemonians and their allies, giving back Nisaea and Pegae and Troezen and Achaea: for these were the places of the Peloponnesians that the Athenians held.

And in the sixth year a war broke out between the Samians and the Milesians about Priene, and the Milesians, getting the worse of the war, came to the Athenians and loudly accused the Samians. And they were supported also by private individuals from Samos itself who wished to change the constitution.

So the Athenians sailed to Samos with forty ships and established a democracy, and took hostages from the Samians, fifty boys and as many men, and placed them in Lemnos, and left a garrison behind and withdrew.

But there were some of the Samians who did not stay, but fled to the mainland, and having made an alliance with the most powerful of those in the city and with Pissuthnes son of Hystaspes, who then held Sardis, and having collected about seven hundred mercenaries, they crossed over to Samos by night,

and first they rose against the democrats and overpowered most of them, then they stole their own hostages away from Lemnos and revolted, and handed over to Pissuthnes the Athenian garrison and the officials who were with them, and at once prepared to march against Miletus. And the Byzantines also revolted with them.

And when the Athenians learned of it, they sailed against Samos with sixty ships, but did not use sixteen of the ships (for some had happened to go to Caria to look out for the Phoenician ships, and others to Chios and Lesbos to send round for help), and with forty-four ships, under the command of Pericles with nine others, they fought a sea-battle off the island of Tragia against seventy Samian ships, of which twenty were troop-carriers (and they all happened to be sailing from Miletus), and the Athenians won.

And later forty ships from Athens and twenty-five from Chios and Lesbos came to help them, and having landed and being superior with their infantry, they besieged the city with three walls and from the sea at the same time.

And Pericles, taking sixty ships from those on blockade, went in haste towards Caunus and Caria, since news had come that Phoenician ships were sailing against them; for Stesagoras and others had also gone from Samos with five ships to fetch the Phoenician ships.

Meanwhile the Samians made a sudden sally and fell on the camp, which was unfortified, and destroyed the ships on guard and defeated in a sea-battle those that put out against them, and were masters of the sea off their coast for about fourteen days, and brought in and carried out what they wished.

And the Samians fought a short sea-battle, but being unable to hold out they were reduced by siege in the ninth month and surrendered on terms, pulling down their wall, giving hostages, handing over their ships, and agreeing to pay back the money spent in instalments. And the Byzantines also agreed to be subjects as before.
And after this, not many years later, there now took place the events already described, the affair of Corcyra and the affair of Potidaea and all that became the occasion of this war.

And all these actions of the Hellenes against one another and against the barbarian took place in about fifty years between the retreat of Xerxes and the beginning of this war; during which the Athenians made their empire more firmly established and themselves advanced to great power, while the Lacedaemonians, though they perceived it, did not try to stop them except for a short time, and kept quiet most of the time, being even before this not quick to go to war unless they were compelled, and partly also being held back by wars at home, until at last the power of the Athenians was plainly rising and they were laying hands on their alliance. Then they no longer thought it bearable, but decided that they must attack it with all their zeal and destroy that strength, if they could, by taking up this war.

So the Lacedaemonians themselves had decided that the treaty had been broken and that the Athenians were in the wrong, but they sent to Delphi and asked the god whether it would be better for them if they went to war; and he answered them, as it is said, that if they made war with all their might, victory would be theirs, and he said that he himself would help them, whether called on or uncalled.

And they summoned the allies again and wished to put to the vote whether they should go to war. And when the envoys had come from the alliance and a meeting was held, the others said what they wished, most of them accusing the Athenians and demanding that the war should take place, and the Corinthians, who had already earlier begged each of the cities privately to vote for the war, fearing for Potidaea that it might be lost first, being present then too and coming forward last, spoke as follows.

‘We could no longer blame the Lacedaemonians, men of the alliance, for not having voted for the war themselves and for not having now brought us together for this. For leaders should, while managing their own affairs on an equal footing, look ahead to the common interests, just as in other respects they are honoured before all.

And those of us who have already had dealings with the Athenians do not need teaching to be on their guard against them; but those who live more inland and not on a trade route should know that, if they do not help those on the coast, they will find it harder to bring down their produce and in turn to get what the sea gives to the mainland, and they should not be bad judges of what is now being said, as though it did not concern them, but should expect that, if they abandoned the coast, the danger might one day advance even as far as themselves, and that they are deliberating now no less about themselves.

For this reason they should not hesitate to take up war instead of peace. For it is the part of prudent men to keep quiet, if they are not wronged, but of brave men, when they are wronged, to go from peace to war, and when a good opportunity offers to come to terms again after war, and neither to be elated by success in war nor to suffer wrong because one is delighted with the quiet of peace.

For he who hesitates because of pleasure would very soon be robbed, if he kept quiet, of the delight of the ease for the sake of which he hesitates, and he who goes too far because of success in war has not considered that he is elated by an untrustworthy confidence.

For many plans badly conceived have succeeded because they met with opponents who were even more ill-advised, and still more that seemed well planned have turned out, on the contrary, disgracefully: for no one carries out a thing in action with the same confidence as he conceives it, but we form our opinions in security, and in the action we fall short through fear.
‘And we are now stirring up the war because we are wronged and have sufficient grounds of complaint, and when we have punished the Athenians, we will lay it down in good time.
And it is likely that we shall prevail for many reasons, first because we are superior in numbers and in military experience, then because we all alike go to carry out orders,

and a navy, in which they are strong, we shall equip from the resources that each of us has and from the money at Delphi and Olympia: for by taking a loan we are able to lure away their foreign sailors with higher pay. For the power of the Athenians is bought rather than their own; but ours would be less liable to this, since its strength lies more in men than in money.

And in all likelihood they will be overcome by a single victory at sea; and if they hold out, we too shall practise naval matters over a longer time, and when we have brought our skill to equality, we shall surely prevail in courage at least. For the good that we have by nature they could not acquire by teaching; but the superiority that they have in skill can be removed by us with practice.

And we shall contribute money so as to have it for these purposes; or it would be a terrible thing if their allies do not refuse to pay for their own slavery, while we shall not spend money in order to punish our enemies and at the same time save ourselves, and in order not to be robbed of it by them and suffer harm by that very money.

And we have other ways of waging the war too, the revolt of their allies, which is the surest way of taking away the revenues on which their strength rests, and the building of a fort in their country, and all the other things that one could not foresee now. For war least of all proceeds on fixed terms, but itself devises most things out of itself to meet the occasion; in which he who deals with it calmly is the more secure, while he who grows angry with it suffers no smaller falls.

‘And let us consider also that if our disputes were each of us with rivals about the boundaries of land, it would be bearable; but as it is, the Athenians are a match for all of us together and still stronger than any one city, so that unless we resist them all together and nation by nation and each city with one mind, they will master us without effort, since we are divided. And let everyone know that defeat, however terrible it may be to hear, brings nothing else than outright slavery:

and for this even to be put in doubt in words is a disgrace to the Peloponnese, and that so many cities should suffer at the hands of one. In this case we would be thought either to suffer it justly or to put up with it out of cowardice and to show ourselves worse than our fathers, who freed Hellas, while we do not secure even our own freedom, but allow a city to be set up as a tyrant, though we claim to put down the sole rulers in a single city.

And we do not know how this conduct is free from the three greatest faults, stupidity or weakness or negligence. For surely you have not escaped these and gone on to that contempt which has harmed the most people, which, from tripping up many, has had its name changed to the opposite one, folly.

Now what need is there to blame what is past at greater length than is useful for the present? But for the sake of the future we must take on further hardship in helping the present (for it is your ancestral custom to win excellence from labours), and not change the custom, if you now have a little advantage in wealth and resources (for it is not right that what was gained in poverty should be lost in abundance), but go into the war with confidence for many reasons, since the god has given an oracle and has himself promised to help, and all the rest of Hellas will join in the struggle, partly from fear, partly from self-interest.

And you will not be the first to break the treaty, which even the god, in bidding you make war, considers to have been transgressed, but rather you will help it when it has been violated: for it is not those who defend themselves who break it, but those who attack first.

‘So, since it is in every way a good opportunity for you to go to war, and we advise this in common, if indeed it is most certain that the same interests serve both cities and individuals, do not delay to bring help to the Potidaeans, who are Dorians and are being besieged by Ionians, which used to be the opposite way, and to pursue the freedom of the others, since it is no longer possible to wait while some are already being harmed, and others, if we are known to have met but not to dare to defend ourselves, will not long after suffer the same:

but, believing that you have come to a point of necessity, men of the alliance, and at the same time that this is the best advice, vote for the war, not fearing its immediate danger, but desiring the more lasting peace that will come from it: for peace is made more secure by war, but to refuse to go to war out of a love of quiet is not equally free of danger.

And believing that the city that has been set up as a tyrant in Hellas has been set up against all alike, so that it already rules some and intends to rule others, let us attack it and bring it under, and both live ourselves without danger for the future and free the Hellenes who are now enslaved.’ Such were the words of the Corinthians.
And the Lacedaemonians, when they had heard the opinion of all, put the vote to all the allies who were present in turn, both the greater and the smaller city; and the majority voted for war.

But although it had been decided, it was impossible for them to set to work at once, since they were unprepared, and it was decided that each should provide what was suitable and that there should be no delay. Even so, while they were getting ready what was needed, not a year, but less, went by before they invaded Attica and openly took up the war.
And during this time they sent embassies to the Athenians making complaints, so that they might have the greatest possible pretext for going to war, if the Athenians paid no attention.
And first the Lacedaemonians sent envoys and bade the Athenians drive out the curse of the goddess; and the curse was as follows.
Cylon was an Athenian, a victor at Olympia, of old times, of noble birth and powerful, and he had married a daughter of Theagenes, a Megarian, who at that time was tyrant of Megara.
And when Cylon consulted the oracle at Delphi, the god answered him that he should seize the acropolis of the Athenians at the greatest festival of Zeus.

And he, having received a force from Theagenes and persuaded his friends, when the Olympic festival in the Peloponnese came round, seized the acropolis with a view to a tyranny, thinking that this was the greatest festival of Zeus and that it somehow concerned him, since he had won at Olympia.

But whether the greatest festival meant was in Attica or somewhere else, he did not go on to consider, and the oracle did not make it clear (for the Athenians too have the Diasia, as it is called, the greatest festival of Zeus Meilichios, outside the city, at which the whole people sacrifice many offerings, not victims, but 〈pure〉 offerings of the country), but thinking that he understood rightly, he set about the deed.
And the Athenians, perceiving it, came in a body from the fields to oppose them and sat down before them and besieged them.

But as time went on, the Athenians, worn out by the blockade, went away, most of them, entrusting the guarding to the nine archons with full powers to manage everything as they judged best; and at that time the nine archons conducted most of the affairs of state.
And those besieged with Cylon were in a bad state from lack of food and water.
So Cylon and his brother escaped; and the others, as they were hard pressed and some were even dying of hunger, sat down as suppliants at the altar on the acropolis.

And those of the Athenians who had been entrusted with the guarding raised them up, when they saw them dying in the temple, on condition that they would do them no harm, led them away and killed them; and some who had sat down at the altars of the Awful Goddesses as they passed, they put to death as well. And because of this both they and their descendants were called accursed and offenders against the goddess.

So the Athenians drove out these accursed men, and later Cleomenes the Lacedaemonian also drove them out with the help of an Athenian faction, driving out the living and taking up and casting out the bones of the dead; yet they returned later, and their descendants are still in the city.

It was this curse, then, that the Lacedaemonians bade them drive out, ostensibly to avenge the gods first, but knowing that Pericles son of Xanthippus was involved in it on his mother's side and thinking that if he were banished their affairs with the Athenians 〈would〉 go more easily.
Yet they did not so much hope that he would suffer this as that it would bring him into discredit with the city, as if the war would be partly due to his misfortune.
For being the most powerful man of his time and leading the state, he opposed the Lacedaemonians in everything, and would not let the Athenians give way, but urged them on to the war.

And the Athenians in return bade the Lacedaemonians drive out the curse of Taenarus: for the Lacedaemonians had once raised up some suppliants of the Helots from the temple of Poseidon [at Taenarus], led them away and killed them, because of which they themselves believe that the great earthquake at Sparta happened.
And they bade them drive out also the curse of the goddess of the Brazen House; and it came about as follows.

When Pausanias the Lacedaemonian was first recalled by the Spartans from his command in the Hellespont and was tried by them and acquitted of wrongdoing, he was no longer sent out officially, but privately he took a trireme of Hermione on his own, without the Lacedaemonians, and came to the Hellespont, nominally for the Hellenic war, but in fact to carry on his intrigues with the King, as he had first attempted, aiming at the rule of Hellas.
And he had first laid up a service with the King from the following circumstance and made the beginning of the whole affair:

for having taken Byzantium on his former visit after the return from Cyprus (the Medes held it, and some connections and kinsmen of the King were captured in it), he then sent these men whom he had taken back to the King without the knowledge of the other allies, giving out that they had escaped from him.

And he managed this with Gongylus of Eretria, to whom he had entrusted Byzantium and the prisoners. And he also sent Gongylus carrying a letter to him; and the following was written in it, as was afterwards discovered:

‘Pausanias, the commander of Sparta, wishing to do you a favour, sends back to you these men whom he took by the spear, and I propose, if it seems good to you too, to marry your daughter and to make Sparta and the rest of Hellas subject to you. And I think I am able to do this, acting in concert with you. If then any of this pleases you, send a trustworthy man to the coast, through whom we shall conduct our communications in future.’

So much the writing revealed, and Xerxes was pleased with the letter and sent Artabazus son of Pharnaces to the coast and ordered him to take over the satrapy of Dascylium, removing Megabates, who had governed it before, and he gave him a letter in reply to send across as quickly as possible to Pausanias at Byzantium and to show him the seal, and, if Pausanias gave him any instructions about his own affairs, to carry them out as well and as faithfully as possible.
And he, on arriving, did everything else as he had been told and sent the letter across:

and the following was written in reply: ‘Thus says King Xerxes to Pausanias. For the men whom you saved for me from Byzantium across the sea, a benefaction shall lie recorded for you in our house for ever, and I am pleased with the words that come from you. And let neither night nor day stop you so that you neglect to do any of the things you promise me, and do not be hindered by the expense of gold and silver or by the size of an army, if it must come anywhere, but with Artabazus, a good man, whom I have sent to you, carry on my affairs and yours with confidence, as will be most honourable and best for both of us.’

When Pausanias received this letter, though he had already been held in great esteem by the Hellenes because of his command at Plataea, he was then much more elated and could no longer live in the established manner, but he went out from Byzantium dressed in Median clothes, and as he travelled through Thrace, Medes and Egyptians formed his bodyguard, and he had a Persian table served for him and could not conceal his purpose, but by small acts revealed beforehand what he intended in his mind to do on a greater scale later.
And he made himself hard of access and showed so harsh a temper towards all alike that no one could approach him; and it was not least for this reason that the alliance went over to the Athenians.

And the Lacedaemonians, perceiving this, recalled him the first time for these very reasons, and when, having sailed out the second time in the ship of Hermione without their orders, he was seen to be acting in the same way, and after being forcibly driven out of Byzantium by the Athenians by siege he did not return to Sparta, but settled at Colonae in the Troad and was reported to them to be intriguing with the barbarians and to be making his stay there for no good purpose, then at last they no longer held back, but the ephors sent a herald and a scytale and told him not to stay behind the herald, or else the Spartans declared war on him.

And he, wishing to be as little suspected as possible and trusting that he could get rid of the charge with money, returned to Sparta the second time. And at first he was thrown into prison by the ephors (and the ephors have the power to do this to the king), then later he managed to get out and offered himself for trial to any who wished to bring proofs against him.

And the Spartans had no clear evidence, neither his enemies nor the whole city, on the strength of which they could confidently punish a man who was of the royal family and held high office at the time (for he was regent for Pleistarchus son of Leonidas, who was king and still young, being his cousin),

but by his contempt for the laws and his imitation of the barbarians he gave rise to many suspicions that he did not wish to be on an equal footing with the present order, and they examined his other actions, whether he had anywhere departed in his way of life from the established customs, and recalled that once, on the tripod at Delphi, which the Hellenes had dedicated as first-fruits of the spoils from the Medes, he had thought fit to have the following couplet inscribed privately on his own account:
Leader of the Hellenes, when he destroyed the army of the Medes,
Pausanias dedicated this memorial to Phoebus.

The Lacedaemonians, then, had at once chiselled this couplet off the tripod at that time and inscribed by name all the cities that had joined in overthrowing the barbarian and set up the offering; yet even then this was thought to be a crime of Pausanias, and when he was now in this position, it seemed much more to have been done in keeping with his present intentions.
And they learned also that he was intriguing with the Helots, and so it was: for he promised them freedom and citizenship if they would rise with him and help him carry out the whole plan.

But not even so, and not even trusting certain informers among the Helots, did they think fit to take any extreme measure against him, following the practice which they usually observe towards themselves, not to be quick to make any irrevocable decision about a Spartan man without indisputable proofs, until at last, as it is said, the man who was to carry the last letters for the King to Artabazus, a man from Argilus, who had once been his favourite and was most trusted by him, became an informer, being afraid on reflection that none of the messengers before him had ever come back, and having counterfeited the seal, so that, if he was mistaken in his suspicion or if Pausanias asked to make some change in them, he should not find out, he opened the letters, in which, suspecting that some such instruction had been added, he found himself too written down to be killed.

Then indeed the ephors, when he showed them the letters, believed more, but wishing still to hear Pausanias himself saying something with their own ears, by arrangement the man went to Taenarus as a suppliant and built a hut divided in two by a partition, in which he hid some of the ephors inside, and when Pausanias came to him and asked the reason for his supplication, they perceived everything clearly, as the man reproached him with what had been written about him and set out the rest point by point, saying that he had never yet exposed him to any danger in his services to the King, yet he had been honoured with death just like the mass of his servants, while Pausanias admitted these very things and told him not to be angry about the present situation, but gave him a pledge of safety for leaving the temple and asked him to go as quickly as possible and not to hinder what was being done.

Having heard everything exactly, the ephors went away for the time being, and, now knowing for certain, they prepared to make the arrest in the city. And it is said that when he was about to be arrested in the street, he saw the face of one of the ephors as he approached and knew why he was coming, and when another made a hidden nod and showed him out of goodwill, he ran to the temple of the goddess of the Brazen House and took refuge there first; and the precinct was near. And entering a small building which belonged to the temple, so as not to suffer in the open air, he kept quiet.

And they were too late in their pursuit at the moment, but after this they took off the roof of the building and, watching till he was inside and cutting him off, walled up the doors, and sitting down before it they starved him out.
And when he was about to expire, just as he was in the building, perceiving it they brought him out of the temple while he was still breathing, and when he had been brought out he died at once.

And they intended to throw him into the Caeadas [where they throw criminals]; but then they decided to bury him somewhere near. But the god at Delphi afterwards ordered the Lacedaemonians to move the tomb to where he died (and he now lies in the forecourt of the precinct, as the inscribed stelae show), and, as what had been done was a curse on them, to give back two bodies instead of one to the goddess of the Brazen House. And they made two bronze statues and dedicated them as if in place of Pausanias.
And the Athenians, since the god too had judged it a curse, ordered the Lacedaemonians in turn to drive it out.

Concerning the Medism of Pausanias, the Lacedaemonians sent envoys to the Athenians and accused Themistocles also as an accomplice, as they found from the evidence about Pausanias, and they demanded that he be punished with the same penalty.

And they, being persuaded (for he happened to have been ostracized, and was living in Argos, but also visiting the rest of the Peloponnese), sent, together with the Lacedaemonians, who were ready to join in the pursuit, men who had been told to bring him wherever they came upon him.

But Themistocles, learning of it beforehand, fled from the Peloponnese to Corcyra, being their benefactor. But when the Corcyraeans said that they were afraid to keep him and so incur the hatred of the Lacedaemonians and Athenians, he was conveyed by them to the mainland opposite.

And being pursued by those who had been assigned the task, according to their information about where he was going, he was forced in a certain difficulty to put up with Admetus, king of the Molossians, who was not friendly to him.
And Admetus happened not to be at home, but Themistocles, becoming a suppliant of his wife, was instructed by her to take their child and sit down at the hearth.

And when Admetus came not long afterwards, he declared who he was, and asked him not, if he himself had perhaps opposed him in some request to the Athenians, to take vengeance on him as an exile; for in that case he would suffer harm from Admetus when he was far weaker in his present state, whereas it was noble to take vengeance on equals on equal terms. And besides, he himself had opposed Admetus in some request, and not in a matter of saving his life, whereas Admetus, if he gave him up (telling by whom and for what he was pursued), would deprive him of the salvation of his life.

And Admetus, hearing him, raised him up together with his own son, just as he had been sitting holding him, and this was the most solemn form of supplication, and not long afterwards, when the Lacedaemonians and Athenians came and said much, he did not give him up, but sent him away, as he wished to travel to the King, to the other sea on foot, to Pydna, the city of Alexander.

There, finding a merchant ship putting out for Ionia and going on board, he was carried down by a storm to the camp of the Athenians, which was besieging Naxos. And (for he was unknown to those on the ship), being afraid, he told the captain who he was and why he was fleeing, and said that if he did not save him, he would say that he was taking him because he had been bribed with money; and that safety lay in nobody leaving the ship until sailing became possible; and that if he complied, he would repay the favour worthily. And the captain did this, and after riding at anchor for a day and a night off the camp, he afterwards arrived at Ephesus.

And Themistocles rewarded him with a gift of money (for there came to him afterwards both from Athens, from his friends, and from Argos, what had been secretly deposited), and travelling inland with one of the Persians of the coast, he sent a letter to King Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes, who had recently come to the throne.

And the letter declared: ‘I, Themistocles, have come to you, who of all the Greeks did the most harm to your house, for as long as I was forced to defend myself against your father when he attacked me, but far more good, when the retreat was safe for me but dangerous for him in turn. And a kindness is owed to me (here he wrote of the advance warning from Salamis of the withdrawal, and of the non-destruction of the bridges at that time, which he falsely claimed as due to himself), and now I am here, able to do you great good, pursued by the Greeks on account of my friendship with you. And I wish to wait a year and then explain to you myself the matters for which I have come.’

and arriving after the year, he became great at his court, such as no Greek ever yet was, both because of his previous reputation and the hope of the Greek world, which he held out to him that he would enslave, but most of all from his appearing intelligent when he gave proof of it.

For Themistocles was a man who had shown the strength of his nature most surely and in this respect was exceptionally worthy of admiration, more than any other; for by his native intelligence, and without either having learned anything about it beforehand or learning afterwards, he was the best judge of present affairs with the least deliberation, and the best guesser of what was to come, furthest into the future; and what he had in hand he was also able to explain, and what he had no experience of, he was not incapable of judging adequately; and he especially foresaw the better or the worse while it was still unseen. And, to sum it up, by the power of his nature and with the shortness of his preparation, this man was indeed the ablest at improvising what was needed.
And he ended his life by illness; but some say that he died by his own will, by poison, thinking it impossible to accomplish what he had promised the King.

Now his monument is in Magnesia in Asia, in the market-place; for he ruled this country, the King having given him Magnesia for bread, which brought in fifty talents a year, Lampsacus for wine (for it was thought to be the richest in wine of the places of that time), and Myus for relish.
