And his relatives say that his bones were brought home at his own order and buried in Attica secretly from the Athenians; for it was not lawful to bury him, as he was exiled for treason. So the affairs of Pausanias the Lacedaemonian and Themistocles the Athenian, who had become the most famous of the Greeks of their time, ended thus.

The Lacedaemonians, then, on the first embassy made such demands and received such counter-demands concerning the expulsion of the accursed; but later, visiting the Athenians, they ordered them to withdraw from Potidaea and to leave Aegina independent, and above all and most clearly they declared that if they revoked the decree about the Megarians there would be no war, the decree in which it had been stated that they should not use the harbours in the Athenian empire nor the Attic market.
But the Athenians neither obeyed in the other matters nor revoked the decree, charging the Megarians with cultivating the sacred land and the undefined land and with receiving runaway slaves.

Finally, when the last envoys had come from Lacedaemon, Ramphias and Melesippus and Agesander, and said nothing of what they had usually said before, but only this, that ‘The Lacedaemonians want there to be peace, and there would be if you left the Greeks independent,’ the Athenians held an assembly and put the question up for discussion among themselves, and they resolved to deliberate about everything once and then give their answer.

And many others came forward and spoke, taking both sides in their opinions, both that they must go to war and that the decree should not be an obstacle to peace, but should be revoked, and Pericles, son of Xanthippus, came forward, a man at that time the first of the Athenians, most able both in speaking and in acting, and advised as follows.

‘I always hold to the same opinion, Athenians, not to give way to the Peloponnesians, although I know that people are not persuaded to go to war and act in the deed with the same temper, but change their opinions according to what befalls them. And I see that now too similar and nearly identical advice must be given by me, and I require those of you who are persuaded to support the common decisions, even if we should perhaps suffer some setback, or else, when we succeed, not to claim any share of the wisdom. For it is possible for the course of events to go no less unaccountably than the plans of man; and that is why we are accustomed to blame fortune for whatever turns out contrary to reason.

‘And the Lacedaemonians were clearly plotting against us before, and now not least. For although it was agreed that we should give and accept arbitration of our differences with each other, and that each side should keep what we have, they themselves have never yet asked for arbitration nor do they accept it when we offer it, but they want to settle their complaints by war rather than by words, and they are here already giving orders and no longer making complaints.

For they order us to withdraw from Potidaea and to leave Aegina independent and to revoke the decree about the Megarians; and these last who have come even proclaim that we should leave the Greeks independent.

And let none of you think that we would be going to war over a small thing if we did not revoke the decree about the Megarians, which they put forward above all, saying that if it were revoked there would be no war, and do not leave in your own minds a charge that you went to war for a trifle.

Decide, then, right now either to submit before suffering any harm, or, if we go to war, as to me at least seems better, not to give way on either a great or a small pretext alike, nor to hold what we have acquired in fear; for the same enslavement is meant by both the greatest and the least claim, when it is imposed by equals on their neighbours before any arbitration.
‘As for the war and the resources of each side, learn, as you hear them point by point, that we shall not have the weaker.

For the Peloponnesians work their own land, and they have no money either privately or in common, and then they are inexperienced in long wars and wars overseas, because owing to poverty they themselves wage only brief wars against each other.

and it is accumulated wealth rather than forced contributions that sustains wars. And people who work their own land are readier to wage war with their bodies than with money, being confident that their bodies will survive the dangers, but not sure that their money will not be spent first, especially if, contrary to their expectation, as is likely, the war is drawn out for them.

For in a single battle the Peloponnesians and their allies are able to hold out against all the Greeks, but they are unable to wage war against an opposing force unlike their own, as long as, not having one council, they do not carry anything out quickly on the spot, and, all having an equal vote and not being of the same race, each pursues his own interest; and from this nothing usually gets accomplished.

For some want above all to take vengeance on someone, others above all not to ruin their own property. And meeting only after long intervals, they consider the common interests in a small fraction of the time, but for the greater part they attend to their own affairs, and each thinks that he will do no harm by his own neglect, but that it is the concern of someone else to look ahead on his behalf, so that, because this same notion is held by all individually, it escapes notice that the common cause is being ruined as a whole.
‘And most important, they will be hindered by their lack of money, as they delay while providing it slowly; but the opportunities of war do not wait.
Nor indeed is their fortification of a post in our land or their navy worth fearing.
For it is difficult even in peace to establish a rival city, still more in hostile territory and when we have fortified ourselves against them no less than they against us;
for we have more experience of land warfare from our navy than they have from their land warfare of naval matters.
And becoming skilled in the sea will not easily come to them.

For not even you, though you have practised it ever since the Persian Wars, have yet mastered it; how then could men who are farmers and not seamen, and who besides will not even be allowed to practise, because they will always be blockaded by us with many ships, achieve anything worthwhile?

For against a few blockading ships they might even take the risk, emboldening their ignorance by their numbers, but when shut in by many they will keep quiet, and through lack of practice they will be less skilful and for that very reason also more hesitant.
And seamanship is a matter of skill, like anything else, and it cannot be practised as a sideline, whenever the chance arises, but rather nothing else can be a sideline to it.

‘And if they should lay hands on the funds at Olympia or Delphi and try to lure away the foreigners among our sailors with higher pay, that would be dangerous if we were not a match for them by embarking ourselves and our resident aliens; but as it is, we have this, and, what is best, we have citizens as helmsmen and the rest of the crews more numerous and better than all the rest of Greece.
And in the face of the danger none of the foreigners would agree to be exiled from his own land and, with less hope as well, to fight on their side for the sake of a few days' high pay.
‘And the situation of the Peloponnesians seems to me to be such or nearly so, while ours seems to be free of the faults I found in theirs and to have other great advantages beyond comparison.

And if they march against our land on foot, we shall sail against theirs, and it will no longer be an equal thing for some part of the Peloponnese to be laid waste and for all of Attica; for they will not be able to take other land in its place without a battle, whereas we have much land both on the islands and on the mainland;

for the mastery of the sea is a great thing. But consider: if we were islanders, who would be harder to capture? And now we must, thinking ourselves as near to this as possible, give up the land and our houses, but keep guard over the sea and the city, and not, angered over these things, fight it out with the Peloponnesians, who are far more numerous (for if we win, we shall fight again against no fewer, and if we fail, the resources of our allies, from which we draw our strength, are lost as well; for they will not keep quiet when we are not able to march against them), and not lament for houses and land, but for lives; for it is not these things that acquire men, but men who acquire these things. And if I thought I could persuade you, I would tell you to go out yourselves and lay them waste and show the Peloponnesians that it is not for the sake of these that you will submit.

‘And I have many other reasons to hope that we shall prevail, if you are willing not to extend your empire while you are at war and not to take on self-chosen dangers; for I am more afraid of our own mistakes than of the plans of our enemies.

But those matters will be made clear in another speech, at the same time as the events; now let us send these envoys away with this answer: that we will allow the Megarians to use our market and harbours if the Lacedaemonians also stop their expulsions of foreigners, both of us and of our allies (for the treaty forbids neither that nor this), and that we will leave the cities independent if they were also independent when we made the treaty, and when they too allow their own cities to be independent not in a way that suits themselves [the Lacedaemonians], but as each of them wishes; and that we are willing to submit to arbitration according to the agreement, and that we will not begin a war, but we will defend ourselves against those who begin it. For this is a just answer and at the same time one befitting this city to give.

But you must know that war is inevitable, and that if we accept it willingly, we shall find our enemies less pressing, and that from the greatest dangers both city and individual win the greatest honours.

Our fathers, at any rate, withstood the Persians, starting not from resources like these, but even abandoning what they had, and by judgement more than by fortune and by daring greater than their power they drove back the barbarian and brought our affairs to their present state. We must not fall short of them, but must defend ourselves against our enemies in every way and try to hand these things on to those who come after us no less great.’

Such were the words of Pericles, and the Athenians, thinking that he was advising them best, voted what he urged, and answered the Lacedaemonians according to his opinion, both in detail as he had stated it and on the whole, that they would do nothing on command, but were ready to settle their complaints by arbitration according to the agreement on fair and equal terms. And the envoys went back home and no longer came on embassies afterwards;

these were the grievances and differences that arose on both sides before the war, beginning directly from the events at Epidamnus and Corcyra; but they nevertheless had dealings with each other during them and visited each other, without heralds, though not without suspicion; for what was happening was a breaking of the treaty and a pretext for war.

From this point the war now begins between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians and the allies of each, during which they no longer had dealings with each other without heralds, and, once it had started, fought continuously; and it has been written in order, as each thing happened, by summers and winters.

For the thirty years' treaty that was made after the capture of Euboea lasted fourteen years; but in the fifteenth year, when Chrysis was in the forty-eighth year of her priesthood at Argos, and Aenesias was ephor in Sparta, and Pythodorus still had two months as archon at Athens, in the sixth month after the battle at Potidaea and at the beginning of spring, a little more than three hundred men of the Thebans (they were led by the Boeotarchs Pythangelus son of Phyleides and Diemporus son of Onetorides) entered Plataea in Boeotia, an ally of the Athenians, with arms about the first sleep.

Men of the Plataeans, Naucleides and his associates, brought them in and opened the gates, wishing, for the sake of their own power, to destroy those of the citizens who were opposed to them and to bring the city over to the Thebans.

They arranged this through Eurymachus son of Leontiades, a very powerful man among the Thebans. For the Thebans, foreseeing that the war would come, wished to seize Plataea, which had always been at odds with them, beforehand, while it was still peace and the war had not yet openly broken out. And for this reason they also got in more easily without being noticed, since no guard had been posted.

And grounding their arms in the market-place, they did not comply with those who had brought them in so as to set to work at once and go against the houses of their enemies, but resolved to make conciliatory proclamations and to bring the city rather to an agreement and friendship (and the herald proclaimed that if anyone wished to be an ally according to the ancestral customs of all the Boeotians, he should ground his arms beside them), thinking that in this way the city would easily come over to them.

And the Plataeans, when they perceived that the Thebans were inside and that the city had been suddenly seized, were terrified, and thinking that far more had come in (for they could not see in the night), they came to terms, and having accepted the proposals they kept quiet, especially since the Thebans were taking no violent measures against anyone.

But while they were somehow doing this, they noticed that the Thebans were not many, and thought that by attacking they would easily overpower them; for the majority of the Plataeans did not wish to revolt from the Athenians.

So it seemed that the attempt must be made, and they gathered together by digging through the party walls between their houses, so that they would not be seen going through the streets, and they set wagons without the draught animals in the streets, so that they would serve as a wall, and they made the other preparations as each seemed likely to be useful for the present circumstances.

And when things were ready as far as was possible, waiting for the time when it was still night and just before dawn, they went out of their houses against them, so that they would not be attacking men made bolder by daylight and they would meet them on equal terms, but men who, being more frightened at night, would be inferior to their own knowledge of the city. And they attacked at once and came to close quarters quickly.
And the Thebans, when they realized that they had been deceived, closed ranks among themselves and pushed back the attacks wherever they fell on them.

And twice or three times they drove them back, but then, as the Plataeans attacked with a great uproar, and the women and the slaves at the same time shouted and screamed from the houses and pelted them with stones and tiles, and as much rain also fell during the night, they became afraid and, turning, fled through the city, most of them being unacquainted in the darkness and mud with the ways by which they could escape (for these events happened at the end of the month), while their pursuers were well acquainted with how to prevent their escape, so that most of them were killed.

And one of the Plataeans shut the gates by which they had entered, which were the only ones open, using the butt-spike of a spear instead of a bolt-pin in the bar, so that there was no longer a way out even there either.

And being pursued through the city, some of them climbed onto the wall and threw themselves outside, and most of these perished, while others, at a deserted gate, where a woman gave them an axe, got out unnoticed after cutting through the bar, not many (for the discovery was quickly made), and others perished scattered in different parts of the city.

But the greatest number, and those who had kept together most, rushed into a large building which was part of the wall and whose doors happened to be open, thinking that the doors of the building were gates and a direct way out.
And the Plataeans, seeing them trapped, deliberated whether they should burn them as they were, setting fire to the building, or deal with them in some other way.
Finally these and all the other Thebans who survived, wandering about the city, agreed to surrender themselves and their arms to the Plataeans, to deal with as they wished.
So those in Plataea had fared thus;

and the rest of the Thebans, who were to have arrived with their whole force while it was still night, in case things did not go well for those who had entered, were coming to help when the news of what had happened was told to them on the way.
And Plataea is seventy stades distant from Thebes, and the rain that fell during the night made them come more slowly; for the river Asopus had risen high and was not easy to cross.
And marching in the rain and crossing the river with difficulty, they arrived too late, when the men had already been partly killed and partly taken alive.

And when the Thebans learned what had happened, they plotted against those of the Plataeans outside the city; for there were both people in the fields and property, as was natural when an unexpected misfortune had happened in peacetime; for they wanted to have whomever they might catch to set against those inside, in case any of them had in fact been taken alive. And they were planning this,

but the Plataeans, while they were still deliberating, suspected that something of this kind would happen and, fearing for those outside, sent out a herald to the Thebans, saying that they had not acted piously in what they had done, in trying to seize their city during a treaty, and they told them not to harm what was outside; otherwise, they said, they too would kill the men of theirs whom they held alive; but if the Thebans withdrew from their land, they would give the men back to them.

This is what the Thebans say, and they say that the Plataeans swore to it; but the Plataeans do not agree that they promised to give back the men at once, but only after negotiations, if they came to some agreement, and they deny that they swore to it.

At any rate the Thebans withdrew from the land having done no harm; and the Plataeans, as soon as they had quickly brought in their property from the country, killed the men at once. And those captured were one hundred and eighty, and Eurymachus was one of them, with whom the traitors had negotiated.

And having done this, they sent a messenger to Athens and gave back the dead under a truce to the Thebans, and they settled affairs in the city with a view to the present situation as seemed best to them.

And what had happened concerning the Plataeans was reported to the Athenians at once, and they immediately arrested all the Boeotians who were in Attica and sent a herald to Plataea, telling him to say that they should take no drastic step concerning the Thebans whom they held, until they too had deliberated about them;

for it had not been reported to them that they were dead. For the first messenger had gone out at the very moment of the entry of the Thebans, and the second when they had just been defeated and captured; and of what happened later they knew nothing. So the Athenians gave their orders without knowing; and the herald, on arriving, found the men killed.
And after this the Athenians marched to Plataea, brought in grain and left a garrison there, and took out the least useful of the people together with the women and children.

Now that the affair at Plataea had happened and the treaty had been clearly broken, the Athenians prepared for war, and the Lacedaemonians and their allies prepared too, both intending to send embassies to the King and elsewhere to the barbarians, from wherever either side hoped to gain some help, and making allies of the cities that were outside their own power.

And the Lacedaemonians, in addition to the ships already there, ordered those in Italy and Sicily who had chosen their side to build ships in proportion to the size of their cities, so that the whole number would be five hundred ships, and to prepare a fixed sum of money, and otherwise to keep quiet and to receive the Athenians with a single ship until these preparations were made.

And the Athenians reviewed their existing alliance and sent embassies more to the places around the Peloponnese, Corcyra and Cephallenia and the Acarnanians and Zacynthus, seeing that, if these were firmly friendly to them, they would wage war on the Peloponnese from all around.

And neither side had small plans, but both were eager for the war, not unnaturally; for at the beginning everyone grasps more eagerly, and at that time there was also a great number of young men in the Peloponnese and a great number in Athens, who through inexperience took up the war not unwillingly, and all the rest of Greece was in suspense as the leading cities came into conflict.
And many oracles were being spoken, and soothsayers chanted many, both among those who were about to go to war and in the other cities.

Moreover Delos was shaken by an earthquake a little before this, though it had never before been shaken within the memory of the Greeks; and it was said and believed to be a sign of what was about to happen. And if anything else of this sort happened to occur, it was all searched out.

And the goodwill of men inclined by far rather toward the Lacedaemonians, especially as they had proclaimed that they were liberating Greece. And every individual and city was eager, if in any way they could, to help them both in word and in deed; and each thought that the cause was hindered in whatever he himself would not be present for.
So angry were most people with the Athenians, some wishing to be freed from their rule, others fearing that they would be ruled.
With such preparation and such a spirit, then, they set out, and each side entered the war with the following cities as allies.

These were the allies of the Lacedaemonians: all the Peloponnesians within the Isthmus except the Argives and the Achaeans (these were friendly to both sides; of the Achaeans the Pellenians alone joined in the war at first, but later all of them did too), and outside the Peloponnese the Megarians, Boeotians, Locrians, Phocians, Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians.

and that of the Athenians was the Chians, Lesbians, Plataeans, the Messenians in Naupactus, most of the Acarnanians, the Corcyraeans, the Zacynthians, and other cities which were tributary among the following peoples: Caria on the sea, the Dorians neighbouring the Carians, Ionia, the Hellespont, the places towards Thrace, the islands that lie between the Peloponnese and Crete toward the rising sun, and all the Cyclades except Melos and Thera.
Of these, a navy was provided by the Chians, Lesbians, and Corcyraeans, and the others provided infantry and money.
Such was the alliance of each side and their preparation for the war.

Immediately after the events at Plataea the Lacedaemonians sent word around the Peloponnese and to their allies outside it for the cities to prepare an army and such provisions as it was fitting to have for an expedition abroad, intending to invade Attica.
And when each were ready, at the appointed time two-thirds of the forces from each city assembled at the Isthmus.

And when the whole army had been gathered, Archidamus, the king of the Lacedaemonians, who was leading this expedition, called together the generals of all the cities and those highest in office and of most account, and spoke to them as follows.

‘Peloponnesians and allies, our fathers too made many campaigns both in the Peloponnese itself and outside it, and the older among us ourselves are not inexperienced in wars; yet never before have we set out with a greater force than this, but we are now going against a very powerful city, and we ourselves are marching in the greatest numbers and the best condition.

It is right, then, that we should appear neither worse than our fathers nor falling short of our own reputation. For all Greece is stirred up by this enterprise and is paying attention, wishing us well because of its hatred of the Athenians, so that we may accomplish what we intend.

Therefore, even if we seem to some to be attacking in great numbers and it seems very safe that the enemy will not come to battle with us, we must not on this account advance any less carefully prepared, but the leader and the soldier of each city must always, as far as concerns himself, expect that he will come into some danger.

For the course of wars is uncertain, and attacks mostly come about suddenly and in anger; and often a smaller force, being afraid, has defended itself better against a larger one, because the latter through contempt was unprepared.

And in enemy country one must always march bold in spirit, but in practice be prepared as if afraid; for in this way men would be most courageous for attacking the enemy and safest against being attacked.

And we are not going against a city so incapable of defending itself, but one best prepared in every way, so that we must fully expect that they will come out to battle, if they have not set out already, before we are there, then at least when they see us in their land ravaging and destroying their property.
For anger falls upon all men when they see themselves suffering something unaccustomed before their eyes and at that very moment; and those who use reasoning least set to action most with passion.
And the Athenians are likely to do this even more than others, since they claim to rule others and to invade and ravage their neighbours' land rather than to see their own ravaged.

Since, then, you are marching against so great a city and will win the greatest glory for your ancestors and yourselves, for better or worse, according to the outcome, follow wherever you are led, holding order and watchfulness above all and receiving commands promptly; for this is the finest and safest thing, that many should be seen to act with one discipline.’

Having said this and dismissed the assembly, Archidamus first sent Melesippus son of Diacritus, a Spartiate, to Athens, in case the Athenians should be more inclined to give way now that they saw them already on the march.

But they did not admit him into the city or before the assembly; for there was a proposal of Pericles which had carried earlier not to admit a herald or an embassy from the Lacedaemonians once they had taken the field; so they sent him away before hearing him and ordered him to be beyond the borders that same day, and in future, if they wanted anything, to withdraw to their own territory and send envoys from there. And they sent escorts with Melesippus, so that he should communicate with no one.
And when he was at the border and was about to part from them, he said this much before he went on his way: ‘This day will be the beginning of great evils for the Greeks.’
And when he reached the camp and Archidamus learned that the Athenians would not yet give way at all, then at last he set out with his army and advanced into their land.
And the Boeotians provided their contingent and their cavalry to march with the Peloponnesians, and with the rest they went to Plataea and ravaged the land.

While the Peloponnesians were still gathering at the Isthmus and were on the march, before they invaded Attica, Pericles son of Xanthippus, who was general of the Athenians with nine others, when he learned that the invasion would take place, suspected, because Archidamus happened to be his guest-friend, that perhaps either he himself, wishing to do him a personal favour, might pass over his lands and not ravage them, or this might also happen at the order of the Lacedaemonians to discredit him, just as they had demanded that the curse be driven out on his account, and so he declared to the Athenians in the assembly that Archidamus was indeed his guest-friend, but that this would not be to the harm of the city, and that if the enemy did not ravage his own lands and houses like those of the others, he gave them up to be public property, so that no suspicion should arise against him on this account.

And he advised them about the present situation the same things as before, to prepare for the war and bring in their property from the fields, and not to go out to battle, but to come into the city and guard it, and to fit out the navy, in which they were strong, and to keep the allies well in hand, saying that their strength came from the money these paid, and that most things in war were won by judgement and abundance of money.

And he told them to take courage, since six hundred talents of tribute came in on average each year from the allies to the city, not counting the other revenue, and there were still at that time on the Acropolis six thousand talents of coined silver (for the greatest amount had been nine thousand seven hundred, from which money had been spent on the Propylaea of the Acropolis and the other buildings and on Potidaea),

and besides, the uncoined gold and silver in private and public offerings and all the sacred vessels for the processions and the games and the Persian spoils and anything else of the kind were worth not less than five hundred talents.

And in addition he added the not inconsiderable money from the other temples, which they could use, and, if they were completely cut off from everything, even the gold plates on the goddess herself; and he showed that the statue had forty talents' weight of refined gold, and that it was all removable. And he said that if they used it for their safety they must restore no less again.
So he encouraged them with regard to money, and said that there were thirteen thousand hoplites, not counting the sixteen thousand in the garrisons and on the battlements.

For that was the number who kept guard at first whenever the enemy invaded, drawn from the oldest and the youngest, and from as many of the resident aliens as were hoplites. For the Phalerian wall was thirty-five stades long to the circuit of the city, and of the circuit itself the guarded part was forty-three (there is a part of it which was also left unguarded, the part between the long wall and the Phalerian), and the long walls to the Piraeus were forty stades, of which the outer one was guarded; and the whole circuit of the Piraeus together with Munychia was sixty stades, and the part under guard was half of this.
And he showed that there were twelve hundred cavalry including mounted archers, sixteen hundred archers, and three hundred seaworthy triremes.

For these were the resources the Athenians had, and no less in each case, when the invasion of the Peloponnesians was first about to take place and they were entering the war. And Pericles said other things too, as he was accustomed to, to prove that they would prevail in the war.

And the Athenians, hearing him, were persuaded and brought in from the fields their children and women and the other furnishings which they used at home, even pulling down the woodwork of the houses themselves; and they sent their sheep and draught animals across to Euboea and to the islands lying off the coast.
And the removal was hard for them, because most of them had always been accustomed to live in the fields.

This had been the case for the Athenians more than for others from very ancient times. For in the time of Cecrops and the first kings down to Theseus, Attica had always been inhabited in separate towns, which had their own town halls and magistrates, and when they had nothing to fear, they did not come together to consult with the king, but each managed its own affairs and deliberated by itself; and some of them even made war at times, as the Eleusinians with Eumolpus did against Erechtheus.

But when Theseus became king, being powerful as well as intelligent, he organized the country in other respects, and abolishing the council-houses and magistracies of the other towns in favour of the present city, appointing one council-house and town hall, he united them all, and while each continued to occupy its own land as before, he compelled them to use this one city, which, since all now contributed to it, became great and was handed down by Theseus to those who came after; and from that time the Athenians still even now celebrate the Synoikia, a public festival for the goddess.
Before this, what is now the Acropolis was the city, together with the area below it, facing mostly south.

And this is the evidence: for the temples on the Acropolis itself † are also those of other gods, and those outside are built more toward this part of the city, the temple of Olympian Zeus, the Pythium, the temple of Earth, and that of Dionysus in the Marshes, in whose honour the more ancient Dionysia are celebrated [on the twelfth day] in the month Anthesterion, as the Ionians who derive from Athens still even now observe. And other ancient temples are also built in this area.

And the fountain, which is now called Enneacrunus (Nine Spouts) since the tyrants arranged it so, but which long ago, when the springs were open, was named Callirrhoe, was used by the people of that time, since it was near, for the most important purposes, and still even now, from ancient custom, it is usual to use its water before weddings and for other sacred rites;
and because of the ancient settlement there, the Acropolis too is still called the city by the Athenians to this day.

So the Athenians for a long time lived independently in the country, and even after they were united, because of custom, most of them, both of the early times and of those later down to this war, having been born and having lived in the fields, did not readily move with their whole households, especially since they had only recently restored their establishments after the Persian Wars;

and they were dejected and took it hard to leave their houses and the temples which had always been ancestral to them from their ancient form of government, and to be about to change their way of life, and each of them felt he was leaving nothing less than his own city.

And when they arrived in the city, a few had dwellings and refuge with some friends or relatives, but most of them settled in the empty parts of the city and in the temples and all the hero-shrines except the Acropolis and the Eleusinium and any other place that could be securely locked; and the so-called Pelargicum below the Acropolis, which was even under a curse forbidding its habitation, and which the ending of a Pythian oracle also forbade, saying, ‘The Pelargicum is better unused,’ was nevertheless occupied because of the immediate necessity.

And it seems to me that the oracle came true in a way opposite to what they expected; for it was not because of the unlawful occupation that the misfortunes came upon the city, but because of the war that the necessity of occupying it arose, and the oracle, without naming the war, foresaw that it would never be occupied for any good.
And at the same time they also set about preparing for the war, gathering allies and fitting out an expedition of a hundred ships against the Peloponnese.
And they were at this stage of preparation.

for Oenoe, lying on the border between Attica and Boeotia, had been walled, and the Athenians used it as a fort whenever war broke out. So they were preparing their assaults and spent time around it in other ways too.

And Archidamus incurred no small blame from this, since he was thought to have been soft also in the gathering of the war and favourable to the Athenians, as he had not urged them eagerly to go to war; and when the army was gathering, the delay that took place at the Isthmus and the slowness during the rest of the march brought him into discredit, but most of all the halt at Oenoe.

For the Athenians were bringing in their property during this time, and the Peloponnesians thought that by advancing quickly they could have caught everything still outside, had it not been for his delay.

In such anger did the army hold Archidamus during the halt. But he, expecting, as is said, that the Athenians would give way somewhat while their land was still unharmed, and would shrink from allowing it to be laid waste, held back.

When, however, after attacking Oenoe and trying every means they were unable to take it, and the Athenians sent no herald, then at last they set out from it, about the eightieth day after what happened at Plataea [of the Thebans who entered], in mid-summer, when the grain was ripe, and invaded Attica; and they were led by Archidamus son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians.

And encamping, they first ravaged Eleusis and the Thriasian plain and put to flight a detachment of the Athenian cavalry near the place called Rheiti; then they advanced, keeping Mount Aegaleos on their right, through Cropia, until they reached Acharnae, the largest place in Attica of the so-called demes, and encamping there they made a camp and, staying a long time, ravaged the land.
Archidamus is said to have remained around Acharnae in battle order with the following intention, and not to have gone down into the plain on that invasion;
for he hoped that the Athenians, flourishing with a great number of young men and prepared for war as never before, would perhaps come out against him and would not allow their land to be ravaged.
So, since they had not met him at Eleusis and the Thriasian plain, he tried, by encamping around Acharnae, whether they would come out;

for at the same time the place seemed to him suitable for encamping, and at the same time the Acharnians, being a large part of the city (for there were three thousand hoplites), seemed unlikely to allow their own property to be destroyed, but likely to urge everyone to battle as well. And even if the Athenians did not come out against that invasion, he could then in future ravage the plain with less fear and advance up to the city itself; for the Acharnians, having been deprived of their own property, would not be equally eager to run risks for that of the others, and there would be dissension in their counsels.
Such was the intention of Archidamus at Acharnae.

As for the Athenians, as long as the army was around Eleusis and the Thriasian plain, they still had some hope that they would not advance nearer, remembering also that Pleistoanax son of Pausanias, king of the Lacedaemonians, when he had invaded Attica as far as Eleusis and Thria with an army of Peloponnesians fourteen years before this war, had gone back again without advancing any further (and it was for this that he was banished from Sparta, since he was thought to have been bribed [to retreat]);

but when they saw the army around Acharnae, sixty stades from the city, they no longer thought it bearable, but, as was natural, when their land was being ravaged before their eyes, a thing which the younger men had never yet seen, nor the older ones except in the Persian Wars, it seemed terrible to them, and everyone, and the young men most of all, thought they should go out and not stand by and watch.

And gathering in groups they were in great dispute, some urging them to go out, others not allowing it. And soothsayers chanted oracles of every kind, which each was eager to listen to according to his inclination. And the Acharnians, thinking that they themselves were no small part of the Athenians, since it was their land that was being ravaged, pressed most of all for the sally. And the city was provoked in every way, and they were angry with Pericles, and remembered nothing of what he had advised before, but abused him because, though he was general, he did not lead them out, and they held him responsible for all that they were suffering.

But Pericles, seeing them angry at the present situation and not thinking in the best way, and being confident that he was right in his decision not to go out, did not call an assembly or any meeting of them, so that they should not make some mistake by coming together in anger rather than with judgement, and he guarded the city and kept it as quiet as he could.

He did, however, keep sending out cavalry to prevent advance parties from the army from falling on the fields near the city and doing damage; and there was a brief cavalry fight at Phrygii between one squadron of the Athenian cavalry, with the Thessalians with them, and the Boeotian cavalry, in which the Athenians and Thessalians had no worse of it, until the hoplites came to the support of the Boeotians and they were put to flight, and not many of the Thessalians and Athenians were killed; they recovered their bodies, however, the same day without a truce.

And the Peloponnesians set up a trophy on the next day. This help of the Thessalians came to the Athenians in accordance with their old alliance, and there came to them Larisaeans, Pharsalians, [Parasians], Crannonians, Pyrasians, Gyrtonians, and Pheraeans. And they were led from Larisa by Polymedes and Aristonous, one from each faction, and from Pharsalus by Meno; and the others also had commanders city by city.
And the Peloponnesians, since the Athenians did not come out against them to battle, set out from Acharnae and ravaged some other demes between Mount Parnes and Mount Brilessus.

While they were in the land, the Athenians sent around the Peloponnese the hundred ships which they had been preparing, and a thousand hoplites on them and four hundred archers; and the generals were Carcinus son of Xenotimus, Proteas son of Epicles, and Socrates son of Antigenes.

And they set out with this force and sailed around, while the Peloponnesians, after staying in Attica for as long as they had provisions, withdrew through Boeotia, not by the way they had invaded; and passing Oropus they ravaged the land called Graice, which the Oropians, subjects of the Athenians, inhabit. And on arriving in the Peloponnese they dispersed each to their own cities.

After they had withdrawn, the Athenians set up guards by land and by sea, as they intended to keep guard throughout the whole war; and they decided to set apart a thousand talents from the money on the Acropolis as a special reserve and not to spend it, but to wage the war with the rest; and if anyone should propose or put to the vote that this money be used for anything else, except if the enemy should sail against the city with a fleet and it should be necessary to defend it, they made death the penalty.

And together with this money they set apart a hundred triremes each year, the best ones, and trierarchs for them, none of which was to be used for anything else than, together with the money, for that same danger, if the need arose.

Meanwhile the Athenians in the hundred ships around the Peloponnese, and the Corcyraeans with them, who had come to their aid with fifty ships, and some others of the allies there, did damage in various places as they sailed around, and landing at Methone in Laconia they attacked the wall, which was weak and had no men in it.

But Brasidas son of Tellis, a Spartiate, happened to be in command of a garrison in this district, and learning of it he came to the help of those in the place with a hundred hoplites. And running through the army of the Athenians, which was scattered over the country and had turned toward the wall, he threw himself into Methone, and losing a few of his men in the dash, he saved the city, and for this daring deed he was the first in the war to be praised in Sparta.

And the Athenians set out and sailed along the coast, and putting in at Pheia in Elis they ravaged the land for two days and defeated in battle three hundred picked men from Hollow Elis and from the local perioeci of the Eleans who had come to help.

But when a strong wind came down and they were caught by the storm in a place without a harbour, most of them went on board the ships and sailed around the promontory called Ichthys to the harbour at Pheia, but meanwhile the Messenians and some others who could not get on board went by land and took Pheia.

And later the ships sailed around and picked them up, and they put out to sea, abandoning Pheia, and the main army of the Eleans had already come up to help. And the Athenians sailed on along the coast to other places and ravaged them.
About this same time the Athenians sent out thirty ships around Locris and at the same time as a guard for Euboea; and their general was Cleopompus son of Clinias.
And making landings he ravaged some places on the coast and took Thronium, and received hostages from them, and at Alope he defeated in battle the Locrians who had come to help.

In this same summer the Athenians also expelled the Aeginetans from Aegina, themselves and their children and wives, charging that they were not least responsible for the war; and it seemed safer to hold Aegina, which lies off the Peloponnese, by sending settlers of their own. And not long afterwards they sent out the settlers to it.

And to the Aeginetans who had been expelled the Lacedaemonians gave Thyrea to live in and its land to occupy, both because of their quarrel with the Athenians and because the Aeginetans had been their benefactors at the time of the earthquake and the revolt of the Helots. And the land of Thyrea is on the border of Argolis and Laconia, extending down to the sea. And some of them settled there, while others were scattered throughout the rest of Greece.

In the same summer, at the new moon by the lunar calendar, which seems to be the only time when it can happen, the sun was eclipsed after midday and became full again, after it had become crescent-shaped and some stars had appeared.

And in the same summer the Athenians made Nymphodorus son of Pytheas, a man of Abdera, whose sister Sitalces had married and who had great influence with him, though they had previously considered him an enemy, their proxenus, and summoned him, wishing Sitalces son of Teres, king of the Thracians, to become their ally.
This Teres, the father of Sitalces, was the first to establish the great kingdom of the Odrysians over most of the rest of Thrace; for a large part of the Thracians is also independent.

This Teres is in no way related to the Tereus who took Procne, daughter of Pandion, from Athens as his wife, nor were they from the same Thrace, but the one [Tereus] lived in Daulia, in the land now called Phocis, which was then inhabited by Thracians, and it was in this land that the women did the deed concerning Itys (and by many of the poets too, when they mention the nightingale, the bird is called Daulian), and it is also likely that Pandion contracted the marriage alliance of his daughter at such a short distance for mutual help rather than at a distance of many days' journey to the Odrysians. And Teres, who did not even have the same name, was the first king to come to power over the Odrysians.
It was his son Sitalces whom the Athenians were making their ally, wishing him to help them subdue the places towards Thrace and Perdiccas.

And Nymphodorus, coming to Athens, concluded the alliance with Sitalces and had Sadocus, his son, made an Athenian, and undertook to end the war in Thrace; for he said he would persuade Sitalces to send the Athenians a Thracian army of cavalry and peltasts.
And he also reconciled Perdiccas with the Athenians and persuaded them to give Therma back to him; and Perdiccas at once joined the Athenians and Phormio in a campaign against the Chalcidians.
Thus Sitalces son of Teres, king of the Thracians, became an ally of the Athenians, and so did Perdiccas son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians.

And the Athenians in the hundred ships, who were still around the Peloponnese, took Sollium, a town of the Corinthians, and handed over the land and the city to the Palaereans alone of the Acarnanians to occupy; and Astacus, of which Evarchus was tyrant, they took by storm, and having driven him out they brought the place into their alliance.

And sailing to the island of Cephallenia they won it over without a battle; and Cephallenia lies opposite Acarnania and Leucas, and it consists of four cities, the Paleans, Cranians, Samaeans, and Pronnaeans. And not long afterwards the ships returned to Athens.

About the autumn of this summer the Athenians in full force, themselves and the resident aliens, invaded the territory of Megara under the command of Pericles son of Xanthippus. And the Athenians in the hundred ships around the Peloponnese (for they happened to be already at Aegina on their way back home), when they learned that the men from the city were at Megara in full force, sailed to them and joined them.

And this was indeed the largest army of Athenians ever assembled together, since the city was still at its height and had not yet been struck by the plague; for the Athenians themselves were not fewer than ten thousand hoplites (besides these there were the three thousand at Potidaea), and resident aliens joined the invasion, no fewer than three thousand hoplites, and besides these there was the rest of the crowd of light-armed troops, not a small one. And after ravaging most of the land they withdrew.
And there were also other invasions of the Athenians later in the war, every year, into the territory of Megara, both by cavalry and in full force, until Nisaea was taken by the Athenians.
These things happened in this summer after the withdrawal of the Peloponnesians from Attica.

In the following winter Evarchus the Acarnanian, wishing to return to Astacus, persuaded the Corinthians to sail with forty ships and fifteen hundred hoplites and restore him, and he himself also hired some mercenaries; and the commanders of the army were Euphamidas son of Aristonymus, Timoxenus son of Timocrates, and Eumachus son of Chrysis.
And they sailed and restored him; and wishing to win over some places in the rest of Acarnania along the sea, and having made the attempt, when they were unable to, they sailed away home.

And putting in at Cephallenia on their voyage along the coast and making a landing in the territory of the Cranians, they were deceived by them under some agreement and lost some of their men, when the Cranians attacked them unexpectedly, and putting out to sea with some difficulty they made their way home.
In the same winter the Athenians, following their ancestral custom, held at public expense the funeral of those who had been the first to die in this war, in the following way.
They lay out the bones of the dead two days beforehand, having set up a tent, and each person brings to his own whatever offering he wishes;
And anyone who wishes, both citizens and foreigners, joins in the procession, and the women who are relatives are present at the grave, lamenting.

They then lay them in the public burial-place, which is in the most beautiful suburb of the city, and in it they always bury those who died in the wars, except, at least, those at Marathon; for, judging their valour to be outstanding, they made their grave there on the spot.

And when they have covered them with earth, a man chosen by the city, who is thought to be not unintelligent in judgement and is pre-eminent in reputation, speaks over them the fitting praise; and after this they depart.
This is how they bury them; and throughout the whole war, whenever the occasion arose for them, they followed the custom.

Over these first ones, then, Pericles son of Xanthippus was chosen to speak. And when the time came, he went forward from the tomb onto a high platform that had been built, so that he might be heard by as much of the crowd as possible, and spoke as follows.

‘Most of those who have already spoken here praise the man who added this speech to the custom, saying that it is fine for it to be delivered over those who are buried after dying in the wars. But to me it would have seemed sufficient that, when men have proved brave in deed, their honours should also be shown in deed, such as you see now prepared at public expense around this grave, and that the virtues of many should not be put at risk in one man, to be believed according as he speaks well or badly.

For it is difficult to speak in due measure on a subject where even the appearance of truth is hardly established. For the hearer who knows the facts and is well-disposed might perhaps think that something has been set forth less fully than he wishes and knows, while the one without experience might think that some things are even exaggerated, through envy, if he hears of anything beyond his own nature. For praises spoken about others are tolerable only up to this point, as far as each man thinks that he himself is also able to do any of the things he has heard; but what goes beyond them they envy and so also disbelieve.
But since those of old judged that this was well, I too must follow the custom and try to meet the wishes and expectations of each of you as far as possible.

‘I shall begin first with our ancestors; for it is just and at the same time fitting, on such an occasion as this, that this honour of remembrance should be given to them. For the same people always inhabited this land in succession from generation to generation until now and handed it down free through their valour.

And they are worthy of praise, and still more so are our fathers; for in addition to what they received, they acquired, not without toil, the empire which we hold and left it to us of the present day.

And the greater part of it we ourselves, who are still now alive and mostly in the settled time of life, have increased, and we have made the city in every way most self-sufficient both for war and for peace.

Of these things, the deeds in war by which each possession was acquired, or any occasion when we ourselves or our fathers eagerly beat back a barbarian or Greek enemy attacking us, I shall pass over, since I do not wish to speak at length among those who know; but by what way of life we came to these things, and with what form of government and from what manners they became great, this I shall first make clear and then go on to the praise of these men, thinking that on the present occasion it would not be unfitting for this to be said and that it is profitable for the whole crowd, both of citizens and foreigners, to listen to it.

‘For we have a form of government that does not emulate the laws of our neighbours, but rather we ourselves are an example to some than imitators of others. And in name, because it is administered not for the few but for the many, it is called a democracy; and according to the laws, all have an equal share in private disputes, while according to reputation, as each man is well regarded in anything, he is preferred for public affairs not by rotation rather than by merit, nor again because of poverty, if he is able to do some good to the city, is he hindered by the obscurity of his rank.

And we conduct our public life freely, and also with regard to our suspicion of one another in our daily pursuits, not being angry with our neighbour if he does something for his pleasure, nor putting on looks of annoyance which, though harmless, are painful to see.

And while we associate without offence in private matters, in public matters we do not break the law, chiefly through fear, obeying those who are in office at any time and the laws, and especially those that are laid down for the help of those who are wronged and those which, though unwritten, bring acknowledged shame.

‘Moreover, we have provided very many relaxations from toil for the mind, observing games and sacrifices throughout the year, and fine private establishments, the daily delight in which drives away sorrow.
And because of the greatness of the city all things from every land come in, and it happens that we enjoy the goods produced here with no more familiar enjoyment than those of other men.

‘And we also differ from our opponents in our training for war in the following ways. For we keep our city open to all, and there is never a time when by expulsions of foreigners we keep anyone from learning or seeing anything which, if it were not concealed, one of our enemies might see and profit by, since we rely not so much on preparations and deceptions as on our own courage for action; and in education, they from their very youth pursue manliness by laborious training, while we, living a relaxed life, are no less ready to face equal dangers.

And here is the evidence: for the Lacedaemonians do not invade our land by themselves, but with all their allies, while we, invading our neighbours' land by ourselves, without difficulty, fighting on foreign soil against men defending their own homes, usually win.

And no enemy has ever yet met our whole force together, because of our attention to the navy at the same time and our sending of our own men by land on many missions; but if they engage somewhere with some part of it, when they have beaten some of us they boast that they have repulsed us all, and when they have been defeated, that they were beaten by all of us.

And yet if we are willing to face dangers with easy-going ease rather than laborious training, and with a courage that comes not so much from laws as from our way of life, we gain the advantage of not suffering beforehand from troubles to come, and of showing ourselves, when we come to them, no less daring than those who are always toiling, and in these respects the city is worthy of admiration, and in others as well.

‘For we love beauty with economy and we love wisdom without softness; and we use wealth as an opportunity for action rather than for boastful talk, and to be poor is not shameful for anyone to admit, but it is more shameful not to escape poverty by action.

And the same men care at once for their private affairs and for public ones, and others, who are occupied with their work, have no lack of knowledge of public affairs; for we alone regard the man who takes no part in these not as one who minds his own business, but as useless, and we ourselves either decide or at least think through public matters properly, not considering words a harm to deeds, but rather the harm to be not to have been instructed by discussion beforehand, before going into action as we must.

For we have this too as a distinction, that we are the same men who are most daring and who also think out what we are about to undertake; whereas in others ignorance brings boldness, and reflection brings hesitation. And those would rightly be judged strongest in spirit who know most clearly both what is terrible and what is pleasant and for this reason do not turn away from dangers.

And in matters of virtue we are opposite to most; for we acquire our friends not by receiving benefits but by conferring them. And the one who has done the favour is the more steadfast friend, so as to keep it owing through goodwill from the one to whom he gave it; while the one who owes in return is less keen, knowing that he will repay the kindness not as a favour, but as a debt.
And we alone help others fearlessly, not so much from calculation of advantage as from the confidence of freedom.

‘In short, I say that the whole city is the school of Greece, and that each single man among us would, it seems to me, show himself self-sufficient in the most varied forms of activity, and with the greatest grace and versatility.
And that this is not boastful talk for the present occasion rather than the truth of facts, the very power of the city, which we have acquired by these ways of life, shows.

For it alone of the cities of today proves greater than its reputation when put to the test, and it alone gives neither the enemy who attacks it cause for indignation at the kind of men by whom he suffers, nor its subjects cause for complaint that they are ruled by men unworthy.

And since we have shown our power with great proofs and certainly not without witnesses, we shall be admired by people now and in the future, and we have no further need of Homer to praise us, nor of anyone who will delight for the moment with his verses, but whose idea of the facts the truth will harm, but we have compelled every sea and land to become accessible to our daring, and everywhere we have established, together with our settlements, everlasting memorials of both harm and good.

It was for such a city, then, that these men, nobly resolving that it should not be taken from them, died fighting, and it is fitting that every one of those who are left should be willing to toil for it.

‘That is why I have spoken at such length about the city, making it a lesson that the contest is not for equal stakes for us and for those who have none of these advantages in like measure, and at the same time making the praise of those of whom I now speak clear by proofs.

And the greatest part of it has been spoken; for the things for which I praised the city, the virtues of these men and of men like them have adorned, and not for many of the Greeks would the account appear equal to their deeds, as it does for these men. And it seems to me that a man's virtue is shown by the death that these men have now met, whether as its first revelation or its final confirmation.

For even for those who were worse in other respects it is right that their bravery in war for their country should be put first; for by blotting out evil with good, they did more benefit in common than harm by their private conduct.

And none of these men became a coward because he valued more the further enjoyment of his wealth, nor, through the hope that belongs to poverty, that he might yet escape it and become rich, did he postpone the danger; but, considering vengeance on their enemies more desirable than these things, and thinking this also the most glorious of dangers, they resolved with it to take vengeance on the enemy and to give up the other things, entrusting to hope the uncertainty of success, but in action resolving to rely on themselves as to what was already before their eyes, and in the very act of defending themselves thinking it better even to suffer death than to save themselves by giving way, they fled from the shame of reproach, and endured the deed with their bodies, and in the briefest moment of fortune, at the peak of glory rather than of fear, they departed.

‘And these men proved such as befitted the city; and those who remain must pray for a safer spirit, but must not think it right to have a less daring one towards the enemy, considering its benefit not by words alone, which one could expound at length to you who know it just as well, telling of all the good things there are in defending ourselves against the enemy, but rather by beholding in deed each day the power of the city and becoming its lovers, and, when it appears great to you, by reflecting that it was men who acquired it by daring and by knowing what was needed and by having a sense of honour in action, and who, whenever they failed in an attempt, did not think it right to deprive the city of their valour as well, but offered it as the finest contribution.

For they gave their bodies in common and received each for himself the praise that never grows old and the most distinguished of tombs, not so much the one in which they lie, but the one in which their glory is left behind to be remembered forever, at every occasion for word or deed, in the minds of whoever comes upon it.

For the whole earth is the tomb of famous men, and not only does the inscription on columns in their own land mark it, but even in lands not their own an unwritten memorial lives on in each person, of their spirit rather than of their deed.
Emulate these men now, and, judging happiness to be freedom and freedom to be courage, do not look anxiously at the dangers of war.

For it is not the unfortunate, who have no hope of anything good, who would with more reason be unsparing of their lives, but those for whom a change to the opposite is still a risk while they live, and for whom the difference is greatest if they should stumble.
For to a man of spirit, at least, the humiliation that comes with cowardice is more painful than death, which comes unfelt, together with strength and common hope.

‘That is why I do not lament the parents of these men, those of you who are present, rather than comfort them. For they know that they were brought up amid changing fortunes; but happy are those who obtain the most glorious end, as these men now have, and the most glorious grief, as you have, and those for whom life was measured out so that their happiness and their end came together.

I know, indeed, that it is hard to persuade you of this, when you will often have reminders of them in the good fortune of others, in which you yourselves once also rejoiced; and grief is not for the good things one is deprived of without having experienced them, but for what one is robbed of after growing used to it.

And you who are past your prime, count as gain the greater part of your life in which you were fortunate, and consider that this remainder will be short, and be lightened by the good fame of these men. For the love of honour alone does not grow old, and in the useless time of life it is not making gain, as some say, that gives more delight, but being honoured.

But for those of you who are present as sons or brothers of these men, I see the contest as great (for everyone is accustomed to praise the one who is no more), and even by an excess of virtue you would hardly be judged not their equals, but a little inferior. For the living are envied in rivalry, but what is no longer in the way is honoured with a goodwill that has no rival.

And if I must also make some mention of womanly virtue, for those who will now be in widowhood, I will indicate it all in a brief exhortation. For great is your glory if you do not fall below the nature that is yours, and great is hers about whom there is the least talk among men, whether in praise or in blame.

‘I too have said in word, according to the law, whatever I had that was fitting, and in deed those who are being buried have in part already been honoured, while for the rest the city will bring up their children at the public expense from this time until manhood, offering a useful crown both to these men and to those left behind for such contests: for where the greatest prizes for virtue are set, there also the best men are citizens.
And now, having made lament each for the one who belongs to him, depart.’
Such was the funeral that took place in this winter; and when it had passed, the first year of this war came to an end.

As soon as summer began, the Peloponnesians and their allies, with two-thirds of their forces, as also the first time, invaded Attica (Archidamus son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, was in command), and settling down they ravaged the land.

And when they had not yet been many days in Attica, the plague first began to appear among the Athenians, though it was said to have struck before in many places, both around Lemnos and in other places, yet such a pestilence and so great a destruction of men was nowhere remembered to have happened.

For neither were the physicians able to cope at first, treating it in ignorance, but they themselves died most of all, as they most of all came near the sick, nor was any other human art of any use; and whatever supplications they made at sanctuaries, or the oracles and such things they made use of, all were useless, and in the end they gave them up, overcome by the evil.
It began first, as is said, in Ethiopia beyond Egypt, and then came down into Egypt and Libya and into the greater part of the King's land.

Into the city of the Athenians it fell suddenly, and it first attacked the people in the Piraeus, so that it was even said by them that the Peloponnesians had thrown poisons into the cisterns; for there were not yet fountains there. Later it reached the upper city too, and then they died much more.

Let each one, then, physician or layman, say about it what he thinks, from what it was likely to have arisen, and the causes which he considers sufficient to have had the power to bring about so great a change; I, however, will tell what it was like, and I will set out those things from which someone, looking at them, if it should ever fall upon us again, would best be able, knowing something in advance, not to fail to recognize it, since I both had the disease myself and myself saw others suffering.
For that year, as was agreed, happened to be of all years the most free of disease as regards other illnesses; but if anyone was already ill with something, everything ended in this.

The others, from no apparent cause, but suddenly while in good health, were seized first by strong heats in the head and redness and inflammation of the eyes, and the inner parts, both the throat and the tongue, immediately became bloody and gave out an unnatural and foul-smelling breath;

then after these came sneezing and hoarseness, and in no long time the pain went down to the chest with a violent cough; and when it settled in the stomach, it upset it, and every discharge of bile that has been named by physicians followed, and these with great distress.
And in most cases an empty retching fell upon them, producing a violent convulsion, which in some abated after this, in others only much later.

And the body, to one touching it from the outside, was neither very hot nor pale, but reddish, livid, broken out in small blisters and ulcers; but the inner parts burned so that they could not bear the covering of even very light garments and linen sheets, nor anything other than being naked, and would most gladly have thrown themselves into cold water. And many of the neglected people actually did this, into cisterns, gripped by unceasing thirst; and drinking more or less made no difference.

And the inability to rest and the sleeplessness pressed on them throughout. And the body, for as long as the disease was at its height, did not waste away, but held out against the suffering beyond expectation, so that either most of them perished on the ninth or seventh day from the inner heat, still having some strength, or, if they escaped, as the disease descended further into the bowels and a violent ulceration arose there and at the same time an uncontrolled diarrhoea set in, most of them later perished through the weakness it caused.
For the evil, first settled in the head, passed through the whole body, beginning from above, and if anyone survived the worst, its seizing of the extremities at least left its mark on him.

For it struck down to the private parts and to the fingers and toes, and many escaped with the loss of these, and there are some who lost their eyes too. And others were seized immediately upon recovering by forgetfulness of all things alike, and did not know either themselves or their friends.

For the form of the disease, proving beyond description, both fell upon each person in other respects more harshly than human nature can bear, and in this especially it showed that it was something other than one of the familiar diseases: the birds and four-footed animals that touch human bodies, although many lay unburied, either did not come near or, having tasted, perished.

And the evidence: there was a clear disappearance of such birds, and they were not seen either elsewhere or around anything of this kind; but the dogs gave more opportunity to perceive the outcome because they live with men.

Such, then, was the disease in its general form, passing over many other strange features, as it happened to affect each person differently, one from another. And no other of the usual illnesses troubled them during that time; and if any did occur, it ended in this.

Some died from neglect, others even while being carefully nursed. And there was not, so to speak, one single remedy established which those applying it were bound to help with; for what helped one person harmed another.
And no constitution showed itself sufficient against it, whether in strength or in weakness, but it carried off all alike, even those cared for with every regimen.

And the most terrible thing in the whole evil was the despondency whenever anyone perceived that he was sick (for turning at once in their minds to despair, they gave themselves up much more and did not resist), and that, catching the disease one from another through nursing, they died like sheep; and this caused the greatest mortality.

For if they were unwilling out of fear to visit one another, they perished alone, and many houses were emptied for lack of someone to nurse; if they did visit, they perished, and especially those who laid any claim to virtue: for out of shame they did not spare themselves in going in to their friends, since in the end even the members of the household grew weary of the lamentations for the dying, overcome by the greatness of the evil.

Yet those who had come through it had more pity for the dying and the suffering, because they knew it beforehand and were themselves by now in confidence; for it did not seize the same man twice, at least not so as to kill. And they were congratulated by the others, and they themselves, in their joy of the moment, also had some light hope for the time to come that they would never again be destroyed by any other disease.
And besides the existing suffering, the gathering from the fields into the city oppressed them still more, and not least those who had come in.

For since there were no houses, and they were living in stifling huts in the hot season of the year, the dying went on in no order, but dead men lay upon one another as they died, and half-dead people rolled about in the streets and around all the fountains in their longing for water.

And the sanctuaries in which they had set up their tents were full of corpses, as people died there; for as the evil overpowered them, men, not knowing what would become of them, turned to neglect of things sacred and profane alike.

And all the customs which they had previously observed concerning burials were thrown into confusion, and they buried their dead as each one could. And many turned to shameless modes of burial for lack of the necessary materials, because so many of their people had already died before; for some, getting ahead of those who had built them, placed their own dead on other people's pyres and set fire to them, while others threw the one they were carrying on top of another body as it burned, and went away.

In other respects too the disease first began greater lawlessness in the city. For a man more readily dared to do what he had previously concealed, that he did not do as he pleased, as they saw the change so swift, both of the prosperous who died suddenly and of those who had possessed nothing before but at once held the property of the others.
So they thought fit to take their enjoyments quickly and with a view to pleasure, regarding both their bodies and their wealth alike as things of a day.

And no one was eager to persevere in hardship for what was thought honourable, considering it uncertain whether he would perish before attaining it; but whatever was pleasant at once, and whatever was in any way profitable towards it, this became both honourable and useful.

And no fear of gods or law of men restrained them, since on the one hand they judged it all the same whether they were pious or not, from seeing all perishing alike, and on the other no one expected to live until a trial took place and to pay the penalty for his offences, but thought that a far greater penalty, already decreed against them, hung over them, and that before it fell it was reasonable to enjoy something of life.
Having fallen into such a calamity, the Athenians were hard pressed, with men dying inside the walls and the land being ravaged outside.

And in their misfortune they remembered, as was natural, also this verse, the older men saying that it had been sung long ago
‘A Dorian war will come, and plague along with it.’

A dispute then arose among the people that the word named in the verse by the ancients was not loimos, plague, but limos, famine, but at the time the view naturally prevailed that loimos had been said; for men made their memory fit what they were suffering. But if, I suppose, another Dorian war should ever come upon them after this one and a famine should happen to arise, they will in all likelihood sing it so.

Those who knew of it also remembered the oracle given to the Lacedaemonians, when, on their asking the god whether they should go to war, he answered that if they made war with all their might victory would be theirs, and said that he himself would help them.

Concerning the oracle, then, they supposed that what was happening matched it; for the disease began immediately after the Peloponnesians had invaded, and it did not enter the Peloponnese to any extent worth mentioning, but it spread over Athens most of all, and then also over the most populous of the other places. This is what happened concerning the disease.

The Peloponnesians, when they had laid waste the plain, advanced into the land called Paralus as far as Laurium, where the Athenians' silver mines are. And first they laid waste the part of it that looks towards the Peloponnese, and then the part turned towards Euboea and Andros.
But Pericles, who was general, held the same view then too as in the earlier invasion, that the Athenians should not go out against them.
While they were still in the plain, before they came to the coastal land, he prepared an expedition of a hundred ships against the Peloponnese, and when it was ready, he put to sea.

He took on the ships four thousand Athenian hoplites and three hundred horsemen in horse-transport ships, then made for the first time out of the old ships; and the Chians and Lesbians also joined the expedition with fifty ships.
When this force of the Athenians put to sea, they left the Peloponnesians in the coastal part of Attica.
Arriving at Epidaurus in the Peloponnese, they laid waste most of the land, and attacking the city they came to hope of taking it, but it did not succeed.
Putting to sea from Epidaurus they laid waste the land of Troezen and of Halieis and of Hermione; these are all on the coast of the Peloponnese.

Setting sail from there, they came to Prasiae, a coastal town of Laconia, and they laid waste part of the land and took the town itself and sacked it. Having done this they returned home. And they no longer found the Peloponnesians in Attica, but withdrawn.

During the whole time that the Peloponnesians were in the land of the Athenians and the Athenians were on the expedition with the ships, the disease was destroying the Athenians both in the army and in the city, so that it was even said that the Peloponnesians, fearing the disease, since they learned from deserters that it was in the city and at the same time saw them burying, left the land more quickly.
But in this invasion they remained for the longest time and laid waste the whole land; for they were about forty days in the land of Attica.

In the same summer Hagnon son of Nicias and Cleopompus son of Clinias, who were fellow generals of Pericles, taking the force which he had used, at once made an expedition against the Chalcidians in Thrace and against Potidaea, which was still under siege, and on arriving they brought siege engines against Potidaea and tried in every way to take it.
