But neither the capture of the city nor anything else went forward for them in a manner worthy of their preparation; for the disease came upon them there and pressed the Athenians very hard, destroying the army, so that even the earlier Athenian soldiers, who had been healthy in the time before, fell sick from the force with Hagnon. And Phormio and the sixteen hundred were no longer in the region of the Chalcidians.

So Hagnon returned with the ships to Athens, having lost to the disease one thousand and fifty of four thousand hoplites in about forty days; but the earlier soldiers remained on the spot and continued to besiege Potidaea.
After the second invasion of the Peloponnesians the Athenians, since their land had been laid waste for the second time and the disease and the war pressed on them at once, changed their minds,

and they held Pericles to blame, as having persuaded them to go to war and as the one through whom they had fallen into their misfortunes, and they were eager to come to terms with the Lacedaemonians; and having sent some envoys to them, they achieved nothing. And being at a loss in their minds on every side, they set upon Pericles.

He, seeing them angry at the present situation and doing everything just as he himself had expected, called an assembly (for he was still general), and wished to encourage them and, drawing off the angry part of their minds, to bring it to a gentler and less fearful state; and coming forward he spoke as follows.

‘The outbursts of your anger against me have come about as I expected (for I perceive their causes), and I called an assembly for this reason, to remind you and to reproach you if in anything you are wrongly either angry with me or giving way to your misfortunes.
For I think that a city that is successful as a whole benefits its private citizens more than one that prospers in each of its citizens but fails as a body.

For a man who is doing well in his own affairs, if his country is being destroyed, is nonetheless ruined with it, but one who is unfortunate in a fortunate country is much more likely to come through safely.

Since, then, a city is able to bear the misfortunes of individuals, but each single person is unable to bear hers, how should all not defend her, and not do what you are now doing: struck down by your misfortunes at home you are abandoning the common safety, and you hold to blame both me, who advised you to go to war, and yourselves, who voted with me?
And yet you are angry with me, a man who I think is inferior to no one in knowing what is needed and in explaining it, and who is a lover of his city and above money.

For one who knows but does not explain clearly is in the same position as if he had not thought of it; one who has both gifts but is ill-disposed to the city would not speak with the same devotion; and if this too is present, but he is overcome by money, everything would be sold for this one thing.

So if you were persuaded by me to go to war because you thought that these qualities were in me even moderately more than in others, I would not now reasonably bear the charge of doing wrong at least.

‘For to those who have had a choice and are fortunate in other respects, it is great folly to go to war; but if it was necessary either to give way and at once submit to their neighbours or to run risks and prevail, the one who flees the danger is more to blame than the one who faces it.

And I am the same and do not shift my ground; it is you who change, since it has happened that you were persuaded while unharmed but repent when suffering, and that my argument, in the weakness of your judgment, does not seem right, because the pain is already felt by each of you, while the proof of the benefit is still absent for all, and now that a great reversal, and that a sudden one, has fallen upon you, your mind is too humbled to persevere in what you resolved.
For what is sudden and unexpected and happens most against calculation enslaves the spirit; and this has happened to you, besides other things, not least in the matter of the disease.

Nevertheless, as you inhabit a great city and have been brought up in a character equal to it, you must be willing to endure even the greatest misfortunes and not obscure your reputation (for men think it equally right to blame whoever through weakness falls short of the fame he has and to hate the one who through boldness grasps at a fame that does not belong to him), but you must put away your private grief and take hold of the common safety.

‘As for the hardship of the war, and the fear that it may become great and we may prevail no better for it, let those arguments suffice for you too in which I have often shown on other occasions that it is wrongly suspected, but I will also make clear this point, which I think neither you yourselves have ever considered, though it is yours, concerning the greatness of your empire, nor I in my earlier speeches; nor would I have used it now, since it carries a rather boastful claim, if I did not see you dismayed beyond reason.

For you think that you rule only over your allies, but I declare that of the two parts open to man's use, land and sea, you are complete masters of the whole of one, both as far as you now hold it and further if you wish; and there is no one, neither the King nor any other nation of those now living, who will stop you from sailing with the naval force you now have.

So this power plainly does not compare with the use of houses and land, which you think it a great thing to have lost; nor is it reasonable to take their loss hard, rather than to make light of them, regarding them as a little garden and an ornament of wealth compared with this, and to recognize that freedom, if we hold on to it and keep it safe, will easily recover these things, while for those who submit to others even what they possessed before tends to be diminished, and to show yourselves not worse in both respects than your fathers, who with toil, and not receiving it from others, won this empire and moreover kept it safe and handed it down to you (and it is more shameful to be robbed of what you have than to fail in acquiring it), and to go to meet your enemies not with confidence alone, but also with contempt.
For boasting arises even from a lucky ignorance, and even in a coward, but contempt belongs to the one who also trusts in his judgment that he is superior to his opponents, which is our case.

And where fortune is equal, intelligence makes daring more secure out of a sense of superiority, and it trusts less in hope, whose strength lies in perplexity, and more in judgment based on what exists, whose foresight is more certain.

And it is reasonable for you to support the honour that the city enjoys from its rule, in which you all take pride, and not to flee the hardships, or else not to pursue the honours either; and not to think that you are fighting over one thing only, slavery instead of freedom, but also over loss of empire and the danger from the hatred you have incurred in your rule.

And it is no longer possible for you to give it up, even if anyone at the present time, out of fear, wishes to play the honest man by keeping quiet in this way; for you already hold it like a tyranny, which it seems unjust to have taken, but dangerous to let go.

And such men would very quickly ruin a city, if they persuaded others, even if they lived somewhere on their own, independent; for the quiet do not survive unless they are ranged alongside the active, and it is not of advantage in a ruling city, but in a subject one, to be a slave in safety.

‘But do not be led astray by such citizens nor be angry with me, with whom you yourselves voted for war, even if the enemy invaded and did just what was to be expected when you were unwilling to obey them, and this disease has come upon us beyond what we expected, the only thing of all that has happened that has proved beyond foresight. And because of it, I know, I am hated still more to some extent, not justly, unless you will also credit me whenever you do well in some way beyond expectation.
But one must bear what the gods send with resignation and what comes from the enemy with courage; for this was the custom in this city before, and now let it not be hindered in you.

And know that it has the greatest name among all men because it does not yield to misfortunes and has spent the most lives and labours on war, and that it possesses the greatest power to this day, of which a memory will be left for ever to those who come after, even if we should now give way a little at some time (for all things are by nature also bound to diminish), that we, Hellenes, ruled over the most Hellenes, and held out in the greatest wars against them both all together and one by one, and inhabited a city the richest in all things and the greatest.
And yet the man who prefers quiet may find fault with this, but the one who himself wishes to achieve something will emulate it; and anyone who does not possess it will envy it.

To be hated and offensive for the present has been the lot of all who have aspired to rule over others; but whoever accepts this odium for the greatest ends is well advised. For hatred does not hold out for long, but the splendour of the present and the glory for the future are left behind, remembered for ever.

So you, foreseeing what will be honourable for the future and what will not be shameful for the present, win both by your zeal now, and neither send heralds to the Lacedaemonians nor show that you are weighed down by your present hardships, since those who in the face of misfortunes are least troubled in spirit and resist most in action are the strongest, both among cities and among individuals.’
Saying such things, Pericles tried to release the Athenians from their anger against him and to lead their minds away from the present terrors.

And in public they were persuaded by his words and no longer sent to the Lacedaemonians and were more eager for the war, but in private they were grieved by their sufferings, the common people because, having started with less, they had been deprived even of that, and the powerful because they had lost fine estates in the country, with buildings and costly furnishings, and, greatest of all, because they had war instead of peace.
However, they did not all cease being angry with him before they had punished him with a fine.

But not long afterwards, as a crowd tends to do, they chose him general again and entrusted all their affairs to him, being by now duller to what each grieved over in his own affairs, while for what the whole city needed they thought him worth the most.

For as long as he was at the head of the city in peacetime, he led it with moderation and kept it safe, and it became greatest under him, and when the war broke out, he too evidently foresaw its power in this also.
He survived two years and six months; and when he died, his foresight regarding the war was recognized still more.

For he said that they would prevail if they kept quiet and looked after the navy and did not try to extend their empire during the war or put the city at risk; but they did all these things in the opposite way, and in other matters which seemed to have nothing to do with the war, out of private ambitions and private gain, they pursued policies that were bad both for themselves and for their allies, which when successful brought honour and benefit rather to individuals, but when they failed became a harm to the city for the war.

The reason was that he, being powerful through his standing and his judgment and having proved clearly most incorruptible by money, held the multitude in check freely, and was not led by it rather than leading it himself, because he did not, acquiring his power by improper means, say anything to please them, but, having it on the strength of his standing, could even contradict them to the point of anger.

At any rate, whenever he perceived them out of season confident in their arrogance, by speaking he struck them into fear, and when they were afraid without reason he restored them again to confidence. And it became in name a democracy, but in fact rule by the first man.
But those who came later, being more equal among themselves and each reaching to become first, turned to handing over even affairs to the people according to their pleasure.

From this, as was to be expected in a great city holding an empire, many other mistakes were made, and especially the voyage to Sicily, which was not so much an error of judgment about those whom they attacked, as that those who sent it out did not afterwards decide what would help those who had gone, but through private accusations about the leadership of the people they made matters in the camp less vigorous and were for the first time thrown into confusion among themselves in the affairs of the city.

Yet after failing in Sicily, both with the rest of their force and with the greater part of the navy, and being by now in civil strife in the city, they nevertheless held out for † three † years against both their earlier enemies and those from Sicily with them, and against most of their allies, who were now in revolt, and later against Cyrus, the King's son, who joined them and provided money to the Peloponnesians for the navy, and they did not give in before they had fallen upon one another in their private quarrels and been brought down.
So great was the abundance of reasons Pericles had then, from which he himself foresaw that the city would quite easily prevail in the war over the Peloponnesians alone.

In the same summer the Lacedaemonians and their allies made an expedition with a hundred ships against the island of Zacynthus, which lies opposite Elis; they are colonists of the Achaeans from the Peloponnese and were allies of the Athenians.

On board sailed a thousand Lacedaemonian hoplites, and Cnemus, a Spartan, was admiral. Landing in the country they ravaged most of it. And since the inhabitants would not come to terms, they sailed back home.

And at the end of the same summer Aristeus the Corinthian, and the Lacedaemonian envoys Aneristus, Nicolaus and Pratodamus, and Timagoras of Tegea, and Pollis of Argos in a private capacity, travelling to Asia to the King, to see if they could somehow persuade him to provide money and to join in the war, came first to Sitalces son of Teres in Thrace, wishing to persuade him, if they could, to abandon the alliance with the Athenians and march against Potidaea, where an army of the Athenians was besieging, and, as they had set out to do, to travel through his land across the Hellespont to Pharnaces son of Pharnabazus, who was to send them up to the King.

But envoys of the Athenians who happened to be with Sitalces, Learchus son of Callimachus and Ameiniades son of Philemon, persuaded Sadocus, Sitalces' son, who had been made an Athenian, to hand the men over to them, so that they might not cross to the King and harm his city as far as they could.

He, persuaded, seized them as they travelled through Thrace to the boat in which they were to cross the Hellespont, before they went on board, sending others along with Learchus and Ameiniades, and ordered them to hand them over to these; and they took them and brought them to Athens.

When they arrived, the Athenians, fearing that Aristeus might escape and do them still more harm, because even before this he had clearly been behind all the affairs of Potidaea and of the Thracian region, killed them all on the same day without trial, though they wished to say something, and threw them into a pit, thinking it right to defend themselves by the same means which the Lacedaemonians too had begun with, when they killed the traders of the Athenians and their allies whom they had caught sailing in merchant ships around the Peloponnese and threw them into pits. For at the beginning of the war the Lacedaemonians destroyed as enemies all whom they caught at sea, both those fighting on the side of the Athenians and those on neither side.

At about the same time, as the summer was ending, the Ambraciots too, both themselves and many of the barbarians whom they had raised, made an expedition against Amphilochian Argos and the rest of Amphilochia.
Their enmity towards the Argives first began from the following.

Amphilochian Argos and the rest of Amphilochia were founded on the Ambracian Gulf, after the Trojan War, by Amphilochus son of Amphiaraus, who on returning home was not pleased with the state of affairs in Argos, and he named it Argos after his own fatherland
(and this city was the largest in Amphilochia and had the most powerful inhabitants),

but many generations later, pressed by misfortunes, they brought in the Ambraciots, who bordered on the Amphilochian land, as fellow settlers, and they were made Hellenes in their present language then for the first time from the Ambraciots who settled with them; but the rest of the Amphilochians are barbarians.
So in time the Ambraciots expelled the Argives and held the city themselves.

When this happened the Amphilochians gave themselves over to the Acarnanians, and both together called in the Athenians as well, who sent them Phormio as general and thirty ships, and when Phormio arrived they took Argos by storm and enslaved the Ambraciots, and the Amphilochians and Acarnanians settled it in common.
After this the alliance between the Athenians and the Acarnanians was first made.

The Ambraciots first conceived their enmity towards the Argives from the enslavement of their own people, and later in the war they made this expedition with themselves and the Chaonians and some others of the neighbouring barbarians; and coming to Argos they were masters of the countryside, but since they could not take the city by assault, they went back home and dispersed by tribes. So much happened in the summer.

In the following winter the Athenians sent twenty ships around the Peloponnese with Phormio as general, who, setting out from Naupactus, kept guard so that no one should sail out of Corinth and the Crisaean Gulf or sail in, and six others to Caria and Lycia with Melesander as general, so that they might collect money there and not allow the Peloponnesian privateers, setting out from there, to harm the passage of the merchant ships from Phaselis and Phoenicia and the mainland in that region.
But Melesander, going up into Lycia with a force of the Athenians from the ships and of the allies, was killed, and lost part of his army, defeated in battle.

In the same winter the Potidaeans, since they were no longer able to hold out under siege, but the invasions of Attica by the Peloponnesians did not make the Athenians withdraw any more, and their grain had run out, and much else had already happened there concerning the food they were forced to eat, and some had even eaten one another, so then they made proposals for an agreement to the generals of the Athenians posted against them, Xenophon son of Euripides and Hestiodorus son of Aristocleides and Phanomachus son of Callimachus.
And these accepted them, seeing the hardship of the army in a wintry place, and since the city had already spent two thousand talents on the siege.
So they agreed on these terms, that they should go out, with their children and wives and the mercenaries, with one garment each, the women with two, and having a fixed sum of money for the journey.

And they went out under truce into Chalcidice and wherever each one could; but the Athenians blamed the generals for having made the agreement without them (for they thought they could have mastered the city on the terms they wanted), and later they sent settlers of their own to Potidaea and settled it. These things happened in the winter, and the second year of this war, which Thucydides wrote, came to an end.

In the following summer the Peloponnesians and their allies did not invade Attica, but marched against Plataea; Archidamus son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, was in command. And having encamped his army he was about to ravage the land; but the Plataeans at once sent envoys to him and spoke as follows:

‘Archidamus and Lacedaemonians, you are not acting justly, nor worthily either of yourselves or of the fathers from whom you come, in marching against the land of the Plataeans. For Pausanias son of Cleombrotus, the Lacedaemonian, after freeing Hellas from the Medes with those of the Hellenes who were willing to share the danger of the battle that took place in our land, sacrificed in the marketplace of the Plataeans to Zeus the Liberator and, calling together all the allies, gave back to the Plataeans their land and their city to hold and inhabit independent, and that no one should ever march against them unjustly or to enslave them; otherwise the allies then present should defend them with all their power.
These things your fathers gave us because of the courage and zeal shown in those dangers, but you are doing the opposite; for with the Thebans, our greatest enemies, you have come to enslave us.

Making witnesses of the gods who were invoked in the oaths then, and of your ancestral gods and of ours of the land, we tell you not to wrong the land of Plataea nor to transgress the oaths, but to let us live independent, just as Pausanias granted as our right.’

When the Plataeans had said this, Archidamus replied and said: ‘What you say is just, men of Plataea, if you act in accordance with your words. For just as Pausanias handed it over to you, be independent yourselves and help to free the others too, all who shared in the dangers of that time and swore the oaths with you and are now under the Athenians, and it is for their sake and for the liberation of the others that so great a preparation and a war have come about. Take part in this yourselves, preferably, and abide by the oaths; but if not, then, as we already proposed before, keep quiet, enjoying your own possessions, and be on neither side, but receive both sides as friends, and neither for war. And this will be enough for us.’

So much Archidamus said; and the envoys of the Plataeans, having heard this, went into the city, and after communicating what had been said to the people they answered him that it was impossible for them to do what he proposed without the Athenians (for their children and wives were with them), and that they also feared for the whole city, that when the Lacedaemonians had withdrawn the Athenians would come and not allow it, or that the Thebans, as being included in the oaths by the clause about receiving both sides, would again try to seize their city.

He, encouraging them on these points, said: ‘Then hand over your city and houses to us, the Lacedaemonians, and point out the boundaries of your land and your trees by number and anything else that can be counted; and move away yourselves wherever you wish, for as long as the war lasts; and when it has passed, we will give back to you whatever we have received. Until then we will hold it in trust, working the land and paying you a rent which will be enough for you.’

They, having heard this, went into the city again, and after deliberating with the people they said that they wished first to communicate his proposal to the Athenians, and if they persuaded them, to do it; and until then they asked him to make a truce with them and not to ravage the land. And he made a truce for the days within which they were likely to have returned, and did not lay waste the land.
The Plataean envoys went to the Athenians, and after deliberating with them came back again bringing the following message to those in the city:

‘The Athenians say, men of Plataea, that neither in the time before, since we became allies, have they ever abandoned you when you were wronged, nor will they now look on, but will help you with all their power. And they charge you, by the oaths which your fathers swore, to make no change in the alliance.’

When the envoys had reported this, the Plataeans resolved not to betray the Athenians, but to endure even seeing their land laid waste, if they must, and suffering whatever else might happen; and that no one should go out any more, but they should answer from the wall that it was impossible for them to do what the Lacedaemonians proposed.

When they had answered, then first King Archidamus set about calling the gods and heroes of the country to witness, speaking as follows: ‘Gods who hold the land of Plataea, and heroes, be witnesses that we did not come against this land unjustly at the beginning, but only after these men had first abandoned the common oath, the land in which our fathers, praying to you, defeated the Medes, and which you made favourable for the Hellenes to fight in, nor will we now do wrong if we take any action; for though we have made many reasonable proposals we do not obtain them. Consent then that those who began the wrong first be punished for it, and that those who seek vengeance lawfully obtain it.’

Having made this appeal to the gods he set the army to war, and first they fenced them round with a stockade of the trees which they had cut down, so that no one could go out, and then they began to heap up a mound against the city, hoping that it would be taken very quickly with so great an army at work.

So cutting timber from Cithaeron they built it up on either side, laying it crosswise like matting instead of walls, so that the mound would not spread out too far; and they carried into it wood and stones and earth and anything else that would help to complete it when thrown on.

And they went on heaping up the mound for † seventy † days and nights without a break, divided into relays, so that some were carrying while others took sleep and food; and the Lacedaemonian commanders of the allied contingents, together with those in charge of each city, forced them to the work.

The Plataeans, seeing the mound rising, put together a wooden wall and set it on their own wall where the mound was being heaped against it, and built bricks into it, taking them down from the nearby houses.

The timbers served them as a binding, so that the building should not be weak as it grew high, and it had coverings of skins and hides, so that the workers and the timbers should not be hit by fire-bearing arrows and should be in safety.

The height of the wall was raised greatly, and the mound rose against it no more slowly. And the Plataeans devised something like this: they broke through the wall where the mound touched it and carried the earth inside.
But the Peloponnesians, noticing it, rolled clay in reed mats and threw it into the breach, so that it would not spread out and be carried off like the earth.

They, shut off in this way, stopped this, but they dug a tunnel from the city and, judging where it was under the mound, again drew away the earth to their side from below; and for a long time they went unnoticed by those outside, so that, for all they threw on, they achieved less, as the mound was drawn away from below and kept settling into the space being emptied.

But fearing that even so they might not be able, few against many, to hold out, they devised this as well: they stopped working on the great building opposite the mound, and starting on either side of it from the low wall they built inwards into the city a crescent-shaped wall, so that, if the great wall were taken, this would hold out, and the enemy would have to heap a mound against it again and, as they advanced inside, would have double the labour and be more exposed on both sides.

And at the same time as the heaping up, the Peloponnesians also brought engines against the city, one of which, brought up over the mound against the great building, shook down a large part of it and frightened the Plataeans, and others at other parts of the wall, which the Plataeans broke off by throwing nooses round them, and they also hung great beams on long iron chains from both ends, from two poles leaning on the wall and stretching out over it, and having hauled them up crosswise, whenever the engine was about to strike somewhere, they let the beam go with the chains slack and not holding them in their hands, and the beam, falling with force, broke off the projecting head of the ram.

After this the Peloponnesians, since the engines did no good and the counter-wall was being built against the mound, thinking that it was impossible to take the city with the present means of attack, made preparations for the walling round.

But first they decided to try with fire, to see whether, if a wind arose, they could set fire to the city, which was not large; for they thought of every kind of means, if somehow it might be brought over to them without expense and siege.

Carrying bundles of brushwood they threw them from the mound, first into the space between the wall and the mound, and when it was quickly filled because of the many hands, they heaped them up further also over as much of the rest of the city as they could reach from the height, and throwing fire on with sulphur and pitch they set the wood alight.

And there was a blaze so great as no one had ever yet seen, at least up to that time, made by human hands; for before now in the mountains wood rubbed against itself by the winds has spontaneously sent up fire and flame from it.

This was great and came within very little of destroying the Plataeans, who had escaped everything else; for within a large part of the city it was not possible to come near, and if a wind had arisen carrying it on, which is just what the enemy hoped, they would not have escaped.
But as it was, this too is said to have happened, that heavy rain from the sky and thunder came and put out the flame, and so the danger was stopped.

The Peloponnesians, when they had failed in this too, leaving part of the army and dismissing the greater part, began to wall the city round in a circle, dividing the ground among the cities; and there was a ditch both inside and outside, from which they had made the bricks.
And when all was finished, about the rising of Arcturus, they left guards for half of the wall (the Boeotians guarded the other half), and withdrew with the army and dispersed to their cities.

The Plataeans had earlier removed their children and wives and the oldest men and the useless part of the population to Athens, and those left behind to be besieged were four hundred of themselves, eighty Athenians, and a hundred and ten women to make bread.
So many were they altogether when they settled down to the siege, and there was no one else within the wall, either slave or free. Such was the way the siege of Plataea was set up.

In the same summer, and at the same time as the expedition against Plataea, the Athenians with two thousand of their own hoplites and two hundred horsemen marched against the Chalcidians in Thrace and the Bottiaeans, when the grain was ripening; and Xenophon son of Euripides was in command, with two others.

Coming before Spartolus in Bottice they destroyed the grain. And it was also thought that the city would come over to them through some people inside who were negotiating. But those who did not want the same thing sent to Olynthus, and hoplites and an army came to guard the city; and when it sallied out of Spartolus, the Athenians engaged in battle under the city itself.

And the hoplites of the Chalcidians and some mercenaries with them were defeated by the Athenians and withdrew into Spartolus, but the horsemen and light troops of the Chalcidians defeated the horsemen and light troops of the Athenians;
and they had some peltasts, not many, from the land called Crousis. Just after the battle had taken place, other peltasts came to help from Olynthus.

And the light troops from Spartolus, when they saw them, emboldened by the newcomers and because they had not been defeated before, attacked the Athenians again with the Chalcidian horsemen and those who had come to help; and the Athenians withdrew to the two companies which they had left with the baggage.

And whenever the Athenians advanced, they gave way, but when they withdrew they pressed on them and hurled javelins. And the horsemen of the Chalcidians, riding up, charged wherever it seemed good, and, terrifying them not least, they routed the Athenians and pursued them a long way.

And the Athenians fled for refuge to Potidaea, and later, having recovered their dead under truce, returned to Athens with what was left of the army; four hundred and thirty of them had died, and all the generals. The Chalcidians and Bottiaeans set up a trophy and, having taken up their own dead, dispersed to their cities.

In the same summer, not long after this, the Ambraciots and Chaonians, wishing to subdue the whole of Acarnania and detach it from the Athenians, persuaded the Lacedaemonians to prepare a fleet from the allied states and to send a thousand hoplites against Acarnania, saying that, if they came with them with ships and infantry at once, since the Acarnanians from the coast would be unable to help, they would easily take Acarnania and become masters of Zacynthus and Cephallenia too, and the voyage round the Peloponnese would no longer be the same for the Athenians; and that there was hope of taking Naupactus too.
The Lacedaemonians, persuaded, at once sent Cnemus, who was still admiral, and the hoplites on a few ships, and sent word round to the fleet to make ready and sail as quickly as possible to Leucas.

And the Corinthians were especially eager in support of the Ambraciots, who were their colonists. And the fleet from Corinth and Sicyon and the places in that region was being prepared, but the one from Leucas and Anactorium and Ambracia, having arrived first, was waiting at Leucas.

Cnemus and the thousand hoplites with him, when they had crossed without being noticed by Phormio, who commanded the twenty Attic ships that were keeping guard around Naupactus, at once began preparing the expedition by land.

And with him were, of Hellenes, Ambraciots and Leucadians and Anactorians and the thousand Peloponnesians whom he himself had brought, and of barbarians, a thousand Chaonians, who have no king, whom Photius and Nicanor of the ruling family led in their yearly leadership. And with the Chaonians the Thesprotians, who have no king, also joined the expedition.

Sabylinthus, who was guardian of King Tharyps, who was still a boy, led the Molossians and Atintanians, and Oroedus, who was their king, the Paravaeans. And a thousand Orestians, whose king was Antiochus, joined the expedition with the Paravaeans, Antiochus having entrusted them to Oroedus.
And Perdiccas also sent, secretly from the Athenians, a thousand Macedonians, who came too late.

With this army Cnemus set out, without waiting for the fleet from Corinth, and passing through the territory of Argos they sacked Limnaea, an unwalled village. And they came to Stratus, the largest city of Acarnania, thinking that if they took this first, the rest would easily come over to them.

The Acarnanians, perceiving that a large army had invaded by land and that the enemy would at the same time be present from the sea with ships, did not join to help one another, but each guarded their own, and they sent to Phormio urging him to help; but he said that it was impossible, with a fleet about to sail out from Corinth, to leave Naupactus unguarded.

The Peloponnesians and their allies, forming three divisions of themselves, advanced towards the city of the Stratians, so that, encamping near, if they could not persuade them by words, they might attack the wall in deed.

And the Chaonians and the other barbarians advanced holding the centre, and on their right the Leucadians and Anactorians and those with them, and on the left Cnemus and the Peloponnesians and the Ambraciots; and they were far apart from one another, and at times were not even in sight of each other.

And the Hellenes advanced in order and on their guard, until they encamped in a suitable place; but the Chaonians, trusting in themselves and esteemed by the mainlanders in that region to be the most warlike, did not stop to occupy a camp, and rushing forward with the other barbarians, they thought they would take the city at the first shout and the achievement would be theirs.

The Stratians, recognizing that they were still advancing, and thinking that if they overcame them while isolated the Hellenes would no longer come against them in the same way, laid ambushes around the city, and when they were near, they attacked them, charging both from the city and from the ambushes.
And as they fell into panic, many of the Chaonians were killed, and the other barbarians, when they saw them give way, no longer stood their ground, but took to flight.
Neither of the Hellenic camps noticed the battle, because these had gone far ahead and they thought they were hurrying on to occupy a camp.

But when the barbarians in flight fell upon them, they took them in, and bringing their camps together they kept quiet there for the day, while the Stratians did not come to close quarters with them, because the rest of the Acarnanians had not yet come to help, but slung stones at them from a distance and brought them into difficulties; for it was not possible to move without armour. And the Acarnanians are thought to be the best at doing this.

When night came, Cnemus, withdrawing quickly with his army to the river Anapus, which is eighty stades distant from Stratus, recovered his dead the next day under truce, and since the Oeniadae had joined him out of friendship, he withdrew to them before the relief force came. And from there they all went home. And the Stratians set up a trophy for the battle against the barbarians.

The fleet from Corinth and the other allies from the Crisaean Gulf, which was to have joined Cnemus, so that the Acarnanians from the coast should not help those inland, did not arrive, but they were forced, about the same days as the battle at Stratus, to fight at sea against Phormio and the twenty ships of the Athenians that were on guard at Naupactus.
For Phormio was watching them as they sailed along out of the gulf, wanting to attack them in the open water.

The Corinthians and their allies were sailing not as for a sea battle, but equipped more for military transport to Acarnania, and not thinking that the Athenians with their twenty ships would dare to give battle against their own forty-seven; when, however, they saw them sailing along opposite while they themselves travelled along the shore, and, as they were crossing from Patrae in Achaea to the mainland opposite, towards Acarnania, they saw the Athenians sailing towards them from Chalcis and the river Evenus, and had not gone unnoticed when they slipped their moorings by night, then indeed they were forced to fight at sea in the middle of the strait.
There were generals for each of the cities that were contributing forces, and those of the Corinthians were Machaon and Isocrates and Agatharchidas.

And the Peloponnesians drew up their ships in a circle as large as they could without allowing a breakthrough, with the prows outward and the sterns inward, and they placed inside the light boats that sailed with them and five of their best-sailing ships, so that they could sail out over a short distance and give support wherever the enemy might attack.

The Athenians, drawn up in single file, sailed round them in a circle and drove them together into a small space, always brushing close past them and giving the impression that they were about to charge at once; but they had been told beforehand by Phormio not to attack until he himself gave the signal.

For he hoped that their order would not hold, like an infantry line on land, but that the ships would fall foul of one another and the boats would cause confusion, and that if the wind blew out of the gulf, which he was waiting for as he sailed round and which usually arose towards dawn, they would not stay still for any time; and he thought that the attack was in his own power, whenever he wished, since his ships sailed better, and that it would be finest then.

When the wind came down and the ships, already in a narrow space, were thrown into confusion by both at once pressing on them, the wind and the boats, and ship fell against ship and they pushed them apart with poles, and, using shouts and guarding against and abusing one another, they heard nothing either of the orders or of the boatswains, and, being inexperienced men unable to lift their oars in the rough water, they made the ships less obedient to the helmsmen, then indeed at this moment he gave the signal, and the Athenians, falling upon them, first sank one of the admirals' ships, and then destroyed the others too wherever they went, and brought them to such a state that none of them turned to resistance because of the confusion, but they fled to Patrae and Dyme in Achaea.

The Athenians, having pursued them and taken twelve ships and picked up most of the men from them, sailed off to Molycreum, and having set up a trophy on Rhium and dedicated a ship to Poseidon they returned to Naupactus.

And the Peloponnesians too sailed along at once with the remaining ships from Dyme and Patrae to Cyllene, the port of the Eleans; and Cnemus and the ships from Leucas, which were to have joined these, arrived at Cyllene from Leucas after the battle at Stratus.

The Lacedaemonians also sent Timocrates and Brasidas and Lycophron to the ships as advisers to Cnemus, ordering him to prepare better for another sea battle and not to be shut out of the sea by a few ships.

For it seemed to them, especially as they had attempted a sea battle for the first time, that the outcome was greatly against reason, and they did not think that their navy was so far inferior, but that there had been some cowardice, not setting the long-standing experience of the Athenians against their own brief practice. So they sent them off in anger.
And these, having arrived, with Cnemus sent round to the cities for more ships and equipped those already there as for a sea battle.

Phormio too sent men to Athens to report their preparations and to tell of the sea battle which they had won, and urging them to send him as many ships as possible quickly, since every single day there was always the expectation that he would have to fight at sea.

And they sent him twenty ships, but instructed the man bringing them to go first to Crete. For Nicias, a Cretan of Gortyn, who was their proxenus, persuaded them to sail against Cydonia, saying that he would bring it over to them, as it was hostile; but he was bringing them in to gratify the Polichnitans, neighbours of the Cydonians.
And he took the ships and went to Crete, and with the Polichnitans he ravaged the land of the Cydonians, and because of winds and weather unfit for sailing he spent no little time there;

and the Peloponnesians at Cyllene, during the time that the Athenians were held up around Crete, prepared as for a sea battle, sailed along to Panormus in Achaea, where the land army of the Peloponnesians had come to support them.
Phormio too sailed along to the Molycrian Rhium and anchored outside it with the twenty ships with which he had also fought the sea battle.

This Rhium was friendly to the Athenians, and the other Rhium, the one in the Peloponnese, is opposite; they are about seven stades of sea apart from each other, and this is the mouth of the Crisaean Gulf.
So at the Achaean Rhium, which is not far from Panormus, where their infantry was, the Peloponnesians too anchored with seventy-seven ships, when they saw the Athenians as well.

And for six or seven days they lay at anchor opposite one another, practising and preparing for the sea battle, the one side intending not to sail out beyond the Rhia into the open water, fearing their earlier disaster, the other not to sail into the narrows, thinking that a sea battle in a small space was in the enemy's favour.

Then Cnemus and Brasidas and the other generals of the Peloponnesians, wishing to fight the sea battle quickly before some help came from the Athenians too, first called the soldiers together, and seeing that most of them were afraid because of the earlier defeat and were not eager, they encouraged them and spoke as follows.
‘The sea battle that took place, men of the Peloponnese, if any of you perhaps fears the coming one because of it, gives no just ground for alarm.

For it was deficient in preparation, as you know, and we were sailing not so much for a sea battle as on a military expedition; and it also happened that not a few of the things that come from chance were against us, and perhaps inexperience too tripped us up somewhat, fighting at sea for the first time.

So defeat did not come about through our cowardice, nor is it right that the part of our spirit that was not conquered by force, but holds within itself some answer, should be blunted by the outcome of the misfortune, but you must consider that men may fail in their fortunes, but that the same men are always rightly brave in their spirit, and that, when courage is present, they cannot reasonably put forward inexperience and so be cowards in any case.

And your inexperience falls short by less than you excel in daring; and the skill of these men, which you fear most, if it has courage, will also have the presence of mind in danger to carry out what it has learned, but without spirit no art has strength against dangers. For fear drives out presence of mind, and art without valour is of no use.
So against their greater experience set your greater daring, and against the fear due to the defeat set the fact that you happened then to be unprepared.

You have the advantage of a greater number of ships and of fighting near a land that is your own, with hoplites present; and for the most part victory belongs to those who are more numerous and better prepared.
So we find not a single reason why we should reasonably fail; and all the mistakes we made before, these very things, now added to our experience, will give us instruction.
So take courage, helmsmen and sailors, and each of you follow according to his own part, not leaving the place where anyone is posted.

We will prepare the attack no worse than the former commanders, and we will give no one an excuse for being a coward; but if anyone should wish to be, he will be punished with the fitting penalty, while the brave will be honoured with the proper prizes of valour.’

Such was the encouragement the commanders gave to the Peloponnesians. And Phormio, himself fearing the dread of his soldiers and perceiving that they were gathering together among themselves and were afraid of the number of the ships, wished to call them together and encourage them and give an exhortation in the present situation.

For before he had always told them and prepared their minds beforehand that there was no number of ships so great, if it sailed against them, that it should not be withstood, and the soldiers had long ago taken this conviction among themselves, that as Athenians they should give way to no crowd of Peloponnesian ships;
but at that time, seeing them disheartened in view of the present sight, he wished to remind them to be confident, and calling the Athenians together he spoke as follows.
‘Seeing you, soldiers, frightened at the number of the enemy, I have called you together, not thinking it right that you should be in dread of things that are not terrible.

For first, because they have been defeated before and do not themselves think that they are a match for us, they have prepared this number of ships, and not on equal terms; then, as for what they chiefly trust in when they come against us, as if it belonged to them to be brave, they are confident for no other reason than that through their experience on land they are mostly successful, and they think it will do the same for them at sea as well.

But by right this advantage will now be ours rather, if it is theirs on land, since in spirit at least they are in no way superior, but we are each bolder in proportion as we are more experienced in something.

And the Lacedaemonians, leading them for the sake of their own reputation, bring most of them into danger against their will, since they would never, after being so badly defeated, have tried to fight at sea again.

So do not fear their daring. But you cause them far greater and better-founded fear, both because you have defeated them before and because they think that you would not be standing against them if you did not intend to do something worthy of the great odds.

For those who are a match for their enemies, like these men, mostly attack trusting more in their strength than in their resolve; but those who, from a much weaker position, and at the same time without being forced, dare to face them, have a great firmness of mind. Reckoning this, these men have come to fear us more for what is beyond expectation than they would a preparation in proportion.
Many armies too have before now fallen to smaller numbers through inexperience, and some also through lack of daring; and we now share in neither of these.

And I will not willingly fight the battle in the gulf, nor sail into it. For I see that against many unskilled ships, for a few experienced and better-sailing ships, a narrow space is not advantageous. For one could neither sail in to ram as one should, not having a view of the enemy from far off, nor withdraw when needed if hard pressed; and there is no breaking through the line or wheeling round, which are the work of better-sailing ships, but the sea battle would necessarily turn into a land battle, and in that the greater number of ships prevails.

For these things, then, I will make provision as far as I can; and you, keeping good order and staying by the ships, receive the orders sharply, especially as we are lying at anchor so close to each other, and in action consider discipline and silence of the greatest importance, which is useful in most matters of war and not least in a sea battle, and repel these men in a manner worthy of what you have achieved before.
The contest is a great one for you, either to destroy the Peloponnesians' hope in their navy or to bring the Athenians' fear about the sea nearer home.
Again I remind you that you have defeated most of them; and the minds of defeated men are not apt to be the same when facing the same dangers.’

Such was the encouragement Phormio too gave. The Peloponnesians, since the Athenians did not sail against them into the gulf and the narrows, wishing to draw them inside against their will, put out at dawn and sailed, having drawn up their ships four deep, along their own land, inwards up the gulf, with the right wing leading, just as they had lain at anchor;

and on this wing they placed twenty of their best-sailing ships, so that, if Phormio, thinking that they were sailing against Naupactus, should himself sail along to help there, the Athenians might not escape their attack by sailing outside their wing, but these ships might shut them in.

And he, just as they expected, fearing for the place, which was unguarded, when he saw them putting out, embarked against his will and in haste and sailed along the land; and the Messenian infantry at the same time came along to help.

The Peloponnesians, seeing them sailing along in single file and already inside the gulf and close to the land, which was what they most wanted, at one signal suddenly turned their ships and sailed in line abreast, as fast as each could, against the Athenians, and hoped to cut off all their ships.

But of these, eleven, the ones leading, escaped the wing of the Peloponnesians and their turn into the open water; but the others they overtook, drove ashore as they tried to escape, and disabled them, and they killed those of the Athenians who did not swim out.

And some of the ships they tied on and towed away empty (one they had already taken with its crew), but some, already being towed, the Messenians took back, coming to help and going into the sea with their arms, and boarding them and fighting from the decks.

Here, then, the Peloponnesians were victorious and disabled the Attic ships; but their twenty ships from the right wing were pursuing the eleven ships of the Athenians which had escaped their turn into the open water. And all but one ship got ahead of them and took refuge first in Naupactus, and putting in with their prows facing outward near the temple of Apollo they prepared to defend themselves if the enemy sailed against them towards the land.
And these, arriving later, were singing the paean as they sailed, as having won, and a single Leucadian ship, far ahead of the others, was chasing the one remaining Athenian ship.

But there happened to be a merchant ship lying at anchor out in deep water, round which the Attic ship, getting there first and sailing round it, rammed the pursuing Leucadian ship amidships and sank it.

So when this unexpected thing happened against all reason, fear fell upon the Peloponnesians, and at the same time, as they were pursuing in disorder because they had the upper hand, some of the ships let down their oars and stopped their course, doing an unwise thing in view of the enemy's counter-attack from close at hand, wishing to wait for the main body, and others even ran aground in the shallows through ignorance of the place.

The Athenians, seeing this happening, took courage, and at one word of command they raised a shout and rushed against them. And they, because of the mistakes already made and their present disorder, held out for a short time, but then turned in flight to Panormus, from where they had put out.

The Athenians, pursuing, took the six ships that were nearest, and recovered their own, which the enemy had disabled by the shore at first and taken in tow; and of the men they killed some and also took some alive.

On the Leucadian ship, which sank by the merchant ship, Timocrates the Lacedaemonian was sailing, and when the ship was being destroyed he killed himself, and was washed up in the harbour of Naupactus.

The Athenians, having withdrawn, set up a trophy at the place from which they had put out and won, and took up the dead and all the wrecks that were near their own shore, and gave back to the enemy theirs under truce.

The Peloponnesians too set up a trophy, as having won, for the rout of the ships which they had disabled by the shore; and the ship that they had taken they dedicated at the Achaean Rhium beside the trophy.
After this, fearing the reinforcements from the Athenians, they sailed under cover of night into the Crisaean Gulf and to Corinth, all except the Leucadians.

And the Athenians from Crete with the twenty ships, which were to have joined Phormio before the sea battle, arrived at Naupactus not long after the withdrawal of the ships. And the summer came to an end.

But before disbanding the fleet that had withdrawn to Corinth and the Crisaean Gulf, Cnemus and Brasidas and the other commanders of the Peloponnesians, at the beginning of the winter, at the suggestion of the Megarians, wished to make an attempt on the Piraeus, the harbour of the Athenians; and it was unguarded and not closed, naturally, because they were greatly superior with their navy.

It was decided that each of the sailors, taking his oar and his cushion and his oar-strap, should go on foot from Corinth to the sea on the side of Athens, and, arriving quickly at Megara, should launch from Nisaea, their dockyard, forty ships that happened to be there, and sail straight for the Piraeus;

for there was no fleet keeping guard in it, nor any expectation that the enemy would ever sail against it so suddenly, since they would not dare to do so openly at leisure, nor, if they planned it, would it fail to be perceived beforehand.

When they had decided, they set out at once; and arriving by night and launching the ships from Nisaea they sailed no longer to the Piraeus, as they had intended, being afraid of the danger (and a wind too is said to have prevented them), but to the promontory of Salamis that looks towards Megara; and there was a fort on it and a guard of three ships, so that nothing should sail in to or out of Megara. They attacked the fort and towed off the triremes empty, and falling on the rest of Salamis when the people did not expect it they plundered it.

And fire signals of enemy attack were raised towards Athens, and there was a panic no less than any in the war. For those in the city thought that the enemy had already sailed into the Piraeus, and those in the Piraeus that Salamis had been taken and that they were all but sailing in against them; which, if they had been willing not to hesitate, would easily have happened, and no wind would have prevented it.

At daybreak the Athenians, coming to help in full force to the Piraeus, launched ships, and embarking in haste and with much uproar they sailed with the ships to Salamis, while with the infantry they set up guards for the Piraeus.

The Peloponnesians, when they became aware of the relief force, having overrun most of Salamis and taken men and booty and the three ships from the fort of Budorum, sailed off in haste for Nisaea; for to some extent their ships also frightened them, having been launched after a long time and not being at all watertight. Arriving at Megara, they withdrew again to Corinth on foot;

and the Athenians, no longer finding them at Salamis, sailed back themselves too, and after this they now kept a stricter guard over the Piraeus for the future, by closing the harbours and by other precautions.

About the same time, as this winter was beginning, Sitalces son of Teres, the Odrysian, king of the Thracians, made an expedition against Perdiccas son of Alexander, king of Macedonia, and against the Chalcidians in the region of Thrace, wishing to exact the fulfilment of one of two promises and himself to fulfil the other.

For Perdiccas, having made him a promise if he would reconcile him to the Athenians when he was hard pressed by the war at the beginning, and would not bring back his brother Philip, who was his enemy, to make him king, did not perform what he had undertaken; and Sitalces himself had agreed with the Athenians, when he made the alliance, to put an end to the Chalcidian war in the region of Thrace.

For both reasons, then, he made the invasion, and he brought with him both Amyntas, the son of Philip, with a view to making him king of the Macedonians, and envoys of the Athenians, who happened to be present on this business, and Hagnon as commander; for the Athenians too were to join him against the Chalcidians with ships and as large an army as possible.

So, setting out from the Odrysians, he raised first the Thracians within Mount Haemus and Rhodope, as many as he ruled as far as the sea [toward the Euxine Sea and the Hellespont], then the Getae beyond Haemus, and all the other parts that were settled south of the river Ister, rather toward the sea of the Euxine; the Getae and the people of that region are both neighbours of the Scythians and equipped like them, all mounted archers.

He also summoned many of the mountain Thracians who are independent and carry short swords, who are called Dii, most of them inhabiting Rhodope; and some he won over with pay, while others followed as volunteers.

He also raised the Agrianians and Laeaeans and all the other Paeonian tribes that he ruled, and these were the outermost of his empire; for as far as the Laeaean Paeonians and the river Strymon, which flows from Mount Scombrus through the Agrianians and Laeaeans, [where] the empire was bounded on the side of the Paeonians, who were independent from there on.

On the side of the Triballi, who were also independent, the Treres and the Tilataeans formed the boundary; these live to the north of Mount Scombrus and extend toward the setting sun as far as the river Oscius. This river flows from the same mountain as the Nestus and the Hebrus; the mountain is uninhabited and large, adjoining Rhodope.

The empire of the Odrysians in its extent reached along the sea from the city of Abdera to the Euxine Sea as far as the river Ister; this land is a voyage round, by the shortest route, if the wind always stands astern, of four days and as many nights for a merchant ship; and by road, by the shortest route, an active man completes the journey from Abdera to the Ister in eleven days.

Such was its extent toward the sea, and inland, from Byzantium to the Laeaeans and to the Strymon (for here it reached farthest up from the sea), it is a journey of thirteen days for an active man to accomplish.

The tribute from all the barbarian land and from the Hellenic cities, as much as they brought in under Seuthes, who reigned after Sitalces and raised it to the very highest, was worth about four hundred talents of silver, which came in gold and silver; and gifts no less than these, of gold and silver, were brought in addition, apart from all that was woven, both embroidered and plain, and the other furnishings, and not only to him, but also to those who shared power with him and the nobles of the Odrysians.

For they had established, the opposite of the Persian kingdom, the custom, which existed also among the other Thracians, of taking rather than giving (and it was more shameful not to give when asked than to ask and not obtain), but nevertheless, because of their power, they made more use of it; for it was not possible to accomplish anything without giving gifts. So the kingdom came to a great height of strength.

For of all the kingdoms in Europe between the Ionian Gulf and the Euxine Sea it became the greatest in revenue of money and in general prosperity, but in strength for battle and the size of its army it was a distant second to that of the Scythians.

With this it is impossible, not only for those in Europe to compete, but even in Asia there is no single nation, one against one, that is able to stand against the Scythians if they are all of one mind. Nor indeed in general good counsel and intelligence about the affairs of life are they like other peoples.

Sitalces, then, ruling over so great a country, was preparing his army. And when everything was ready for him, he set out and marched against Macedonia, first through his own empire, then through Cercine, an uninhabited mountain which is the border between the Sinti and the Paeonians; and he marched across it by the road which he himself had made before by cutting down the forest, when he made an expedition against the Paeonians.
Crossing the mountain from the Odrysians, they had the Paeonians on their right and on their left the Sinti and Maedi. Having passed through it they arrived at Doberus in Paeonia.

On his march nothing of his army was lost, except perhaps by sickness, but it was increased; for many of the independent Thracians followed unsummoned in hope of plunder, so that the whole number is said to have been not less than a hundred and fifty thousand;

and of this the greater part was infantry, and about a third cavalry. Of the cavalry the Odrysians themselves furnished the most, and after them the Getae. Of the infantry the most warlike were the sword-bearers, the independent men who came down from Rhodope, while the rest of the crowd that followed was mixed and most formidable by its numbers.
So they gathered at Doberus and made preparations to invade over the mountain crest into lower Macedonia, which Perdiccas ruled.
For the Macedonians include also the Lyncestians and Elimiotes and other tribes of the upper country, which are allies and subjects of these, but have kingdoms of their own.

The Macedonia now by the sea was first acquired and ruled by Alexander, the father of Perdiccas, and his ancestors, who were originally Temenidae from Argos, after they had expelled by battle the Pierians from Pieria, who later settled Phagres and other places under Mount Pangaeus beyond the Strymon (and even now the land under Pangaeus toward the sea is called the Pierian Gulf), and from the land called Bottia the Bottiaeans, who now live as neighbours of the Chalcidians;

and of Paeonia they acquired a narrow strip along the river Axius reaching down from the interior as far as Pella and the sea, and beyond the Axius as far as the Strymon they occupy the land called Mygdonia, having driven out the Edonians.
They also expelled from what is now called Eordia the Eordians, of whom most perished, but a small part of them is settled around Physca, and from Almopia the Almopians.

These Macedonians also became masters of the other tribes, which they still hold even now, Anthemus, Grestonia, Bisaltia, and much of Macedonia proper. The whole is called Macedonia, and Perdiccas son of Alexander was their king when Sitalces invaded.
And these Macedonians, as a great army was coming against them, being unable to defend themselves, withdrew into the strongholds and the walled places, as many as there were in the country.

There were not many, but later Archelaus son of Perdiccas, when he became king, built those that now exist in the country, and cut straight roads, and in other respects organized matters for war with horses and arms and other equipment better than all the other eight kings who came before him put together.

The army of the Thracians invaded from Doberus first into the province that had formerly been Philip's, and took Idomene by storm, and Gortynia and Atalanta and some other places by agreement, as they came over out of friendship for Amyntas son of Philip, who was present; and they besieged Europus, but were unable to take it.

Then they advanced also into the rest of Macedonia, which lies to the left of Pella and Cyrrhus. They did not go beyond these into Bottiaea and Pieria, but ravaged Mygdonia and Grestonia and Anthemus.

The Macedonians did not even think of defending themselves with infantry, but, sending for additional horsemen from their allies in the interior, few against many, they charged into the army of the Thracians wherever it seemed good. And wherever they fell upon them, no one withstood men who were good horsemen and wore breastplates, but, being hemmed in by numbers, they put themselves in danger against a crowd many times their size, so that in the end they kept quiet, not thinking themselves strong enough to run risks against the greater force.

Sitalces held talks with Perdiccas about the matters for which he had made the expedition, and since the Athenians had not come with their ships, not believing that he would come, but had sent gifts and envoys to him, he sent part of his army against the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, and, having shut them up within their walls, ravaged their land.

While he was encamped in these regions, the peoples living to the south, the Thessalians and Magnesians and the other subjects of the Thessalians and the Hellenes as far as Thermopylae, feared that the army might advance against them too, and were in a state of preparation.
The Thracians beyond the Strymon to the north also feared, those who held the plains, the Panaeans and Odomantians and Droans and Dersaeans; they are all independent.
He also gave occasion for talk even among the Hellenes who were enemies of the Athenians, that the Thracians, led on by them in accordance with the alliance, might advance against them too.

But he, occupying Chalcidice and Bottice and Macedonia at once, was ravaging them, and since none of the things for which he had invaded was being accomplished, and his army had no food and was suffering from the winter, he was persuaded by Seuthes son of Sparadocus, his nephew and the most powerful after himself, to go away quickly. Perdiccas had secretly won Seuthes over by promising to give him his own sister and money with her.

And Sitalces, persuaded, after staying thirty days in all, eight of them among the Chalcidians, withdrew home with his army in haste; and Perdiccas afterwards gave his sister Stratonice to Seuthes, as he had promised. Such, then, were the events of the expedition of Sitalces.

The Athenians in Naupactus, in the same winter, after the fleet of the Peloponnesians had dispersed, made an expedition under the command of Phormio, sailing along the coast to Astacus and disembarking, into the interior of Acarnania with four hundred Athenian hoplites from the ships and four hundred Messenians, and they expelled from Stratus and Coronta and other places men who did not seem to be loyal, and, having restored Cynes son of Theolytus to Coronta, they went back again to their ships.

For against Oeniadae, whose people alone of the Acarnanians were always hostile, it did not seem possible to make an expedition while it was winter; for the river Achelous, flowing from Mount Pindus through Dolopia and the land of the Agraeans and Amphilochians and through the Acarnanian plain, past the city of Stratus in its upper course, and emptying into the sea by Oeniadae and surrounding their city with marshes, makes campaigning there in winter impossible because of the water.

Most of the Echinades islands also lie opposite Oeniadae, not at all far from the mouths of the Achelous, so that the river, being large, keeps depositing silt, and some of the islands have become mainland, and it is expected that all of them will suffer this in no very long time;

for the stream is large and full and muddy, and the islands are close together and become links binding the deposit to one another [so that it is not scattered], since they lie alternately and not in a row, and do not have straight passages for the water into the open sea.

They are uninhabited and not large. It is said also that when Alcmaeon son of Amphiaraus was wandering after the murder of his mother, Apollo directed him by oracle to inhabit this land, intimating that there was no release from his terrors until he should find and settle in a country which, when he killed his mother, had not yet been seen by the sun and was not yet land, since all the rest of the earth had been polluted by him.

And he, being at a loss, as they say, with difficulty noticed this deposit of the Achelous, and it seemed to him that enough land to sustain his body might have been heaped up since the time he had been wandering, no short time, after killing his mother. And settling in the places around Oeniadae, he became ruler and left to the country its name from his son Acarnan. Such are the stories about Alcmaeon that we have received.

The Athenians and Phormio, setting out from Acarnania and arriving at Naupactus, sailed back to Athens at the beginning of spring, bringing the free men among the prisoners from the sea battles, who were released man for man, and the ships that they had taken.
And this winter ended, and the third year of this war ended, which Thucydides wrote down.
In the following summer the Peloponnesians and their allies, when the grain was ripening, made an expedition into Attica; and Archidamus son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, led them.

And settling down they ravaged the land; and attacks were made, as usual, by the Athenian cavalry wherever there was opportunity, and they kept the great mass of the light-armed troops from going out beyond their camp and doing harm to the places near the city.
After staying as long as they had provisions, they withdrew and dispersed to their cities.

Immediately after the invasion of the Peloponnesians, Lesbos, except Methymna, revolted from the Athenians, having wished to do so even before the war, but the Lacedaemonians had not received them, and being forced to make even this revolt sooner than they had intended.

For they were waiting for the blocking of their harbours and the building of walls and the making of ships to be completed, and for all that had to come from the Pontus to arrive, archers and grain, and the things they were sending for.

For the Tenedians, being at odds with them, and the Methymnaeans, and, of the Mytilenaeans themselves, some men privately out of factional strife, proxeni of the Athenians, became informers to the Athenians that they were forcibly uniting Lesbos into Mytilene and were hurrying on all their preparations for revolt together with the Lacedaemonians and the Boeotians, who were their kinsmen; and that unless someone forestalled them at once, they would be deprived of Lesbos.

The Athenians (for they were worn out by the plague and by the war, which had just begun and was at its height) thought it a great matter to make an enemy besides of Lesbos, which had a fleet and unimpaired power, and at first they did not accept the accusations, giving greater weight to their wish that they not be true; when, however, even after sending envoys they could not persuade the Mytilenaeans to give up the union and the preparations, they became afraid and wanted to forestall them.
And they suddenly sent forty ships which happened to have been made ready to sail around the Peloponnese; Cleippides son of Deinias, with two others, was in command.

For it had been reported to them that there was a festival of Apollo Maloeis outside the city, at which the Mytilenaeans celebrate with the whole people, and that there was hope, if they made haste, of falling upon them suddenly, and if the attempt succeeded, well: if not, they were to tell the Mytilenaeans to hand over their ships and pull down their walls, and, if they did not obey, to make war.

And the ships departed; and the ten triremes of the Mytilenaeans, which happened to be with them as auxiliaries in accordance with the alliance, the Athenians detained, and they put the men from them under guard.

But a man who crossed from Athens to Euboea and went on foot to Geraestus, finding a merchant ship putting to sea, took passage and, arriving at Mytilene on the third day from Athens, reported the expedition to the Mytilenaeans.
And they did not go out to the temple of Maloeis, and barricaded and guarded the rest of the walls and harbours around the half-finished parts.
And the Athenians, sailing in not much later, when they saw this, the generals delivered their orders, and as the Mytilenaeans did not listen, they began war.

The Mytilenaeans, unprepared and forced suddenly to make war, made a sortie with their ships as if for a sea battle a little in front of the harbour, and then, being chased back by the Attic ships, they now made proposals to the generals, wishing, if they could, to get rid of the ships for the moment by some reasonable agreement.
And the generals of the Athenians accepted, being themselves afraid that they were not strong enough to make war against all Lesbos.

And having made an armistice, the Mytilenaeans sent to Athens one of the informers, who already repented, and others, to see if they could somehow persuade them to have the ships go away, on the ground that they would make no revolution.

Meanwhile they also sent envoys to Lacedaemon in a trireme, escaping the notice of the Athenian fleet, which was anchored at Malea to the north of the city; for they did not trust that matters with the Athenians would succeed.
And these, having made their way to Lacedaemon with hardship across the open sea, were negotiating for them that some help should come;

and when the envoys from Athens came back having accomplished nothing, the Mytilenaeans and the rest of Lesbos except Methymna went to war; these had come to the aid of the Athenians, as had the Imbrians and Lemnians and a few of the other allies.

And the Mytilenaeans made a sortie in full force against the camp of the Athenians, and a battle took place, in which the Mytilenaeans, though they did not get the worse of it, neither bivouacked on the field nor trusted themselves, but withdrew; then they kept quiet, wishing to run the risk with additional forces from the Peloponnese and elsewhere, if any should join them; for Meleas, a Laconian, and Hermaeondas, a Theban, had come to them, who had been sent out before the revolt, but, being unable to arrive ahead of the Athenian expedition, sailed in secretly after the battle in a trireme, and urged them to send another trireme and envoys with them; and they sent them.

The Athenians, much encouraged by the inactivity of the Mytilenaeans, summoned allies, who came much more quickly as they saw no strength on the part of the Lesbians, and, bringing their ships round to anchor to the south of the city, they fortified two camps, one on each side of the city, and established blockades at both harbours.

And they kept the Mytilenaeans from using the sea, but of the land, the Mytilenaeans and the other Lesbians, who had now come to their aid, controlled the rest, while the Athenians held the area around the camps, which was not large, and Malea served them rather as a station for their boats and a market. And the war around Mytilene was carried on in this way.

About the same time of this summer the Athenians also sent thirty ships round the Peloponnese and Asopius son of Phormio as general, since the Acarnanians had asked them to send them someone of Phormio's family, either a son or a kinsman, as commander.
And the ships, sailing along the coast, ravaged the coastal places of Laconia.

Then Asopius sent most of the ships back home, while he himself, with twelve, arrived at Naupactus, and later, having raised the Acarnanians in full force, he made an expedition against Oeniadae, and he sailed with the ships along the Achelous while the army on land ravaged the country.

And when they did not come over, he dismissed the infantry, and he himself, sailing to Leucas and making a landing at Nericus, was killed on his way back, he and part of his army, by the people of the place who came to the rescue and by a few guards.
And afterwards the Athenians, sailing away, recovered their dead from the Leucadians under a truce.

The envoys of the Mytilenaeans who had been sent out on the first ship, since the Lacedaemonians told them to be present at Olympia, so that the other allies too might hear them and deliberate, arrived at Olympia; it was the Olympiad in which Dorieus the Rhodian won for the second time.
And when after the festival they came to the conference, they spoke as follows.

‘The established custom among the Hellenes, Lacedaemonians and allies, we know; for those who revolt in wars and abandon their former alliance are held in favour by those who receive them, in so far as they benefit from them, but, considering them traitors to their former friends, they think the worse of them.

And this judgement is not unjust, if those who revolt and those from whom they separate should happen to be equal to one another in opinion and goodwill, and evenly matched in preparation and power, and if no reasonable pretext for the revolt existed; which was not the case between us and the Athenians.
Let no one think us worse, then, if, having been honoured by them in peace, we revolt from them in time of danger.

‘For we will speak first about justice and virtue, especially since we are seeking an alliance, knowing that neither does friendship between private men become firm nor a partnership between cities come to anything, unless they deal with one another with evident virtue and are alike in character in other respects; for from difference in thinking arise also the differences in actions.
Between us and the Athenians an alliance first came about when you withdrew from the Persian war, while they remained for the rest of the work.
We became allies, however, not to the Athenians for the enslavement of the Hellenes, but to the Hellenes for their liberation from the Persian.
