And as long as they led on equal terms, we followed eagerly; but when we saw them relaxing their hostility against the Persian and bringing on the enslavement of the allies, we were no longer without fear.

And the allies, being unable to unite and defend themselves because of the number of votes, were enslaved, except us and the Chians; but we, being independent, supposedly, and free in name, joined in their campaigns.

And we no longer had the Athenians as trustworthy leaders, taking the examples that had gone before as our guide; for it was not likely that they would subdue those whom they had made parties to the treaty together with us, and not do this to those who were left, if they were ever able to.

And if we had all still been independent, they would have been more reliable to us in making no revolution; but holding the majority in subjection, while dealing with us on equal terms, they were naturally going to bear it with more irritation that, while the majority had already yielded, ours alone still stood as an equal, especially as they themselves were becoming more powerful than before and we more isolated.
Only mutual fear is a sure basis for an alliance; for the one who wishes to transgress in some way is deterred by not being superior in making an attack.
And we were left independent for no other reason than in so far as it seemed to them that, for their empire, affairs could be won by fair-seeming words and an approach of policy rather than of force.

For at the same time they used us as evidence that those at least who had an equal vote would not be campaigning with them against their will, unless those whom they attacked were doing some wrong; and in the same way they also led the strongest against the weaker ones first, and, leaving the strongest to the last, they would find them weaker when everything else had been stripped away.
But if they had begun with us, while all still had their own strength and something to rally to, they would not have subdued them so easily.
And our navy caused them some fear that it might some day unite and, joining you or someone else, bring danger upon them.
And in part we also survived by courting their people and those who from time to time were their leaders.
We did not, however, think that we would have been able to do so for long, if this war had not broken out, taking the examples of their conduct towards the others.

What kind of friendship, then, was this, or what trustworthy freedom, in which we received each other against our real feelings, and they courted us in war out of fear, while we did the same to them in peace; and whereas for others it is goodwill above all that makes good faith firm, for us fear provided this security, and we were allies held more by dread than by friendship; and whichever side security should first give boldness, they were going to be the first to break the agreement in some way?

So if anyone thinks that we do wrong in revolting first because of their delay in the dangers against us, without ourselves waiting in turn to know clearly whether any of them will happen, he does not consider rightly.

For if we were able, on equal terms, both to plot in return and to delay in return, why did we need to be in their power on equal terms? But since attacking is always in their power, defending ourselves in advance must also be in ours.

‘With such pretexts and reasons, Lacedaemonians and allies, we revolted, clear enough for those who hear them to recognize that we acted reasonably, and sufficient to frighten us and turn us toward some means of safety, wishing to do so long ago, when, while still at peace, we sent to you about revolting, but being prevented because you did not receive us; now, however, when the Boeotians invited us, we at once responded, and we thought we would make a double revolt, from the Hellenes, so as not to join the Athenians in harming them but to join in freeing them, and from the Athenians, so as not to be destroyed by them ourselves later on but to act first.

Our revolt, however, has come about too soon and without preparation; for which reason you ought all the more to receive us as allies and send help quickly, so that you may be seen both defending those whom you should and at the same time harming your enemies.

And the opportunity is such as never before. For the Athenians have been ruined by disease and by the expenditure of money, and of their ships, some are around your coasts, while others have been posted against us.

so that it is not likely that they have ships to spare, if you invade them a second time this summer with ships and infantry together, but either they will not resist you when you sail against them, or they will withdraw from both our coasts.

And let no one think that he will incur a danger of his own for the sake of another's land. For to whoever thinks Lesbos is far away, it will provide its help from close at hand. For the war will not be in Attica, as some think, but in the places from which Attica draws its benefit.

Their revenue of money comes from the allies, and it will be still greater if they subdue us; for no one else will revolt, and our resources will be added to theirs, and we would suffer more terrible things than those who were slaves before.

But if you help us eagerly, you will gain a city that has a large navy, which is what you most need, and you will more easily overthrow the Athenians by drawing away their allies (for everyone will come over more boldly), and you will escape the charge that you had of not helping those who revolt. And if you are seen to be liberators, you will have the mastery in the war more securely.

‘Respecting, then, the hopes that the Hellenes place in you and Olympian Zeus, in whose temple we are as good as suppliants, come to the aid of the Mytilenaeans by becoming their allies, and do not abandon us, who are risking our own lives in a danger that is ours alone, but will give to all the common benefit of success, and a still more common harm, if we fail because you were not persuaded.
Be such men as the Hellenes think you and as our fear wishes.’

Such were the words of the Mytilenaeans. The Lacedaemonians and the allies, when they had heard them, accepted their arguments and made the Lesbians allies, and as for the invasion of Attica, they told the allies present to go quickly to the Isthmus with two thirds of their forces in order to carry it out, and they themselves arrived first, and prepared hauling-machines for the ships at the Isthmus in order to carry them across from Corinth to the sea on the side of Athens and to attack with ships and infantry at the same time.
And they were doing these things eagerly, but the other allies were assembling slowly and were busy gathering in their harvest and weary of campaigning.

The Athenians, perceiving that they were preparing because they judged them weak, and wishing to show that they had not judged rightly, but that they were able, without moving the fleet at Lesbos, also easily to repel the fleet coming from the Peloponnese, manned a hundred ships, embarking themselves, except the knights and the five-hundred-bushel men, and the resident aliens, and, putting out along the Isthmus, they made a display of their strength and landings on the Peloponnese wherever they pleased.

The Lacedaemonians, seeing how much things were contrary to their expectation, considered what had been said by the Lesbians untrue and, thinking the undertaking impossible, since their allies too were not present at the same time, and it was also reported that the thirty ships of the Athenians around the Peloponnese were ravaging their surrounding country, they went back home.
Later, however, they prepared a fleet to send to Lesbos, and ordered from the cities a total of forty ships, and appointed as admiral Alcidas, who was to sail with it.
The Athenians also went back with their hundred ships, when they saw that the others had too.

[And at the time when these ships were at sea, they had among the very largest numbers of ships in active service at once, in fine condition, but similar numbers and even more at the beginning of the war.

For a hundred were guarding Attica and Euboea and Salamis, and another hundred were around the Peloponnese, apart from those at Potidaea and in the other places, so that in all there were two hundred and fifty at the same time in one summer.
And it was this above all, together with Potidaea, that drained their money.

For hoplites at two drachmas were guarding Potidaea (each received a drachma a day for himself and for his servant), three thousand at first, of whom no fewer stayed throughout the siege, and sixteen hundred with Phormio, who left before the end; and all the ships drew the same pay. In this way, then, their money was drained at first, and this was the greatest number of ships they manned.]

The Mytilenaeans, at the same time that the Lacedaemonians were at the Isthmus, made an expedition by land against Methymna, as it was being betrayed to them, both they and their mercenaries; and having attacked the city, when it did not go as they expected, they went off to Antissa and Pyrrha and Eresus, and having made affairs in these cities more secure and strengthened their walls, they went back home in haste.

The Methymnaeans too, after they had withdrawn, made an expedition against Antissa; and when a sortie was made, being beaten by the Antissaeans and the mercenaries, many of them were killed and the rest withdrew in haste.

The Athenians, learning of this, that the Mytilenaeans were masters of the land and that their own soldiers were not enough to hem them in, sent, as autumn was now beginning, Paches son of Epicurus as general and a thousand of their own hoplites.
And they, rowing the ships themselves, arrived and walled Mytilene round in a circle with a single wall; and forts were built into it at some of the strong points.
And Mytilene was now firmly shut in on both sides, both by land and by sea, and winter was beginning.

The Athenians, being in further need of money for the siege, and having themselves then for the first time paid a property tax of two hundred talents, also sent out to the allies twelve money-collecting ships with Lysicles and four others as general.

He collected money and sailed about at various places, and having gone up from Myus in Caria through the plain of the Maeander as far as the hill of Sandius, when the Carians and Anaeitans attacked, he himself was killed and many of the rest of the army.

In the same winter the Plataeans (for they were still being besieged by the Peloponnesians and Boeotians), since they were hard pressed by their failing grain and there was no hope of help from Athens nor did any other means of safety appear, plotted, they and the Athenians besieged with them, at first that all should go out and climb over the walls of the enemy, if they could force their way, the attempt having been proposed to them by Theaenetus son of Tolmides, a seer, and Eupompidas son of Daimachus, who was also one of the generals;
then half of them somehow shrank from the danger, thinking it great, but about two hundred and twenty men persisted in the sortie voluntarily, in the following way.

They made ladders equal to the wall of the enemy; and they measured it by the layers of bricks, where their wall facing them happened not to be plastered over. Many counted the layers at once, and some were likely to miss but the majority to hit the true calculation, especially as they counted many times and at the same time were not far away, but the wall was easily seen as far as they wished.
The measure of the ladders they thus obtained, guessing the measure from the thickness of the brick.

The wall of the Peloponnesians was of the following construction. It had two rings, one against the Plataeans and one in case anyone should attack from outside from Athens, and the rings were about sixteen feet apart from each other.
This space between [the sixteen feet ] had been built up into quarters divided among the guards, and they were continuous, so that it appeared to be one thick wall with battlements on both sides.

And at every ten battlements there were large towers of the same width as the wall, reaching both to its inner face and likewise to the outer one, so that there was no passage beside a tower, but they went through the middle of them.

On nights, then, whenever there was rainy weather, they left the battlements and kept guard from the towers, which were a short distance apart and roofed above. Such, then, was the wall by which the Plataeans were blockaded.

And they, when they were ready, waited for a night stormy with rain and wind and at the same time moonless, and went out; and they were led by those who had been the authors of the attempt. And first they crossed the ditch which surrounded them, and then came up to the wall of the enemy unnoticed by the guards, who did not see ahead in the darkness and did not hear the noise of their approach, as the wind drowned it with its clatter;

and at the same time they went far apart from one another, so that their arms, striking against one another, might not betray them. And they were lightly equipped and had only the left foot shod, for safety against the mud.

So they approached the battlements at a space between towers, knowing that they were unguarded, first those carrying the ladders, and they set them up; then twelve light-armed men with a dagger and a breastplate went up, led by Ammeas son of Coroebus, who was the first to climb; and after him his followers went up, six to each of the two towers. Then other light-armed men came after these with short spears, whose shields others carried behind them, so that they might advance more easily, and they were to hand them over when they were close to the enemy.
When more of them were up, the guards in the towers noticed; for one of the Plataeans, taking hold of the battlements, knocked down a tile, which made a thud as it fell.

And at once there was a shout, and the army rushed to the wall; for it did not know what the danger was, since the night was dark and stormy, and at the same time the Plataeans left behind in the city went out and attacked the wall of the Peloponnesians on the opposite side from where their men were climbing over, so that they might pay as little attention as possible to them.
They were in an uproar, then, staying in their places, but no one dared to go to help from his own post, and they were at a loss to guess what was happening.
And their three hundred, who had been assigned to help wherever there was need, went outside the wall toward the shouting. And beacons signalling an enemy attack were raised toward Thebes;

but the Plataeans from the city also raised many beacons from the wall, prepared beforehand for this very purpose, so that the signals of the beacons might be unclear to the enemy and they might not come to help, thinking that what was happening was something other than it was, before their men who were going out should escape and reach safety.

Meanwhile, of the Plataeans who were climbing over, when the first of them had gone up and, killing the guards of each tower, had taken control, they themselves took position in the passages of the towers and guarded them so that no one might come to help through them, and, setting ladders from the wall against the towers and sending up more men, some kept off those coming to help from the towers, shooting at them both from below and from above, while meanwhile the greater number, having set up many ladders and at the same time pushed down the battlements, were climbing over through the space between the towers.
And each man as he got across stood on the edge of the ditch, and from there they shot arrows and threw javelins, if anyone, coming to help along the wall, tried to hinder the crossing.
When all had crossed, the men from the towers, the last of them coming down with difficulty, went to the ditch, and meanwhile the three hundred bore down on them carrying torches.

The Plataeans, then, standing on the edge of the ditch, saw them better out of the darkness, and shot arrows and threw javelins at their unprotected parts, while they themselves, being in obscurity, were less visible because of the torches, so that even the last of the Plataeans got across the ditch in time, though with difficulty and by force;

for ice had formed in it, not firm enough to walk on, but rather watery, as it is with an east wind [or a north wind], and the night, snowing a little with such a wind, had made the water in it deep, so that they crossed with their heads barely above it. And their escape came about rather because of the violence of the storm.

Setting out from the ditch, the Plataeans went in a body along the road leading to Thebes, having the shrine of the hero Androcrates on their right, thinking that they would least suspect that they had turned onto this road, the one toward the enemy; and at the same time they saw the Peloponnesians pursuing with torches along the road toward Cithaeron and Dryoscephalae, which leads to Athens.

And for six or seven stadia the Plataeans went along the road to Thebes, then, turning, went along the road leading toward the mountain to Erythrae and Hysiae, and, reaching the mountains, escaped to Athens, two hundred and twelve men out of a larger number; for there were some of them who turned back to the city before climbing over, and one archer was captured at the outer ditch.

The Peloponnesians, then, returned to their posts, giving up the pursuit; but the Plataeans in the city, knowing nothing of what had happened, and since those who had turned back reported to them that no one survived, sent out a herald when day came and asked for a truce to take up their dead, but, learning the truth, they desisted. So these men of the Plataeans escaped in this way by climbing over.

At the end of the same winter, Salaethus the Lacedaemonian was sent out from Lacedaemon to Mytilene in a trireme. And having sailed to Pyrrha and from there going on foot along a ravine, where the siege wall could be crossed, he got into Mytilene unnoticed, and told the magistrates that there would be an invasion of Attica and at the same time the forty ships would arrive which were to help them, and that he himself had been sent ahead for this reason and also to take charge of everything else.
And the Mytilenaeans took courage and were less inclined to come to terms with the Athenians. And this winter ended, and the fourth year of this war ended, which Thucydides wrote down.

In the following summer the Peloponnesians, after sending off the forty-two ships to Mytilene, appointing as commander Alcidas, who was their admiral, invaded Attica, they and their allies, so that the Athenians, harassed on both sides, might be less able to send help against the ships sailing to Mytilene.
This invasion was led by Cleomenes on behalf of Pausanias son of Pleistoanax, who was king and still young, being his father's brother.

They ravaged in Attica both the parts that had been cut down before, [and] whatever had grown up again, and all that had been left untouched in the earlier invasions; and this invasion was the hardest for the Athenians after the second.

For, constantly waiting to hear from Lesbos of some deed of the ships, as though they had already crossed, they went on and on, cutting down most of the land. But when nothing of what they expected came about and their grain had run out, they withdrew and dispersed to their cities.
The Mytilenaeans meanwhile, as the ships did not come to them from the Peloponnese but delayed, and their grain had run out, were forced to come to terms with the Athenians for the following reasons.
Salaethus, himself no longer expecting the ships either, armed with heavy armour the commons, who had before been light-armed, intending to make a sortie against the Athenians;

but they, when they had received arms, no longer obeyed their leaders, and, gathering in groups, they either ordered the men of power to bring the grain into the open and distribute it to all, or they said they would themselves come to terms with the Athenians and hand over the city.

And those in charge of affairs, realizing that they were not able to prevent it, and that they would be in danger if they were left out of the agreement, made an agreement jointly with Paches and the army, that the Athenians should be free to decide whatever they wished about the Mytilenaeans, and that they should receive the army into the city, and that the Mytilenaeans should send an embassy to Athens about themselves; and until they came back, Paches should neither imprison any of the Mytilenaeans nor enslave nor kill any.

This was the agreement, but those of the Mytilenaeans who had most dealt with the Lacedaemonians, being terrified, when the army came in, could not hold out, but sat down at the altars nevertheless; and Paches, raising them up on the promise that he would not harm them, placed them in Tenedos until the Athenians should decide something.
And having sent triremes to Antissa as well, he took it over, and arranged the other matters concerning the army as he thought best.

The Peloponnesians in the forty ships, who ought to have arrived quickly, wasted time sailing around the Peloponnese itself, and, proceeding at leisure on the rest of the voyage, escaped the notice of the Athenians in the city until they touched at Delos, and putting in from there at Icarus and Myconus, they first learned that Mytilene had been taken.

Wishing to know the exact truth, they sailed into Embatum in the territory of Erythrae; and it was about seven days since Mytilene had been taken when they sailed into Embatum. Having learned the truth, they deliberated on the situation, and Teutiaplus, a man of Elis, spoke to them as follows.
‘Alcidas and all of us Peloponnesians present here as commanders of the army, it seems to me that we should sail against Mytilene before our coming becomes known, just as we are.

For in all likelihood we shall find much lack of watchfulness, as with men who have newly taken a city, and especially by sea, where they do not expect that any enemy would come upon them and where our strength happens chiefly to lie; and it is likely that their infantry too is scattered among the houses rather carelessly, as befits victors.
If, then, we should fall upon them suddenly and by night, I hope that, with the help of those inside, if indeed anyone well disposed to us is left, the situation could be mastered.

And let us not shrink from the danger, considering that the element of surprise in war is nothing other than this sort of thing, and if a general were to guard against it in his own case and, seeing it in the enemy, were to attack, he would be most successful.’

He said this much but did not persuade Alcidas. Some others, of the exiles from Ionia and the Lesbians sailing with him, urged him, since he feared this danger, to seize one of the cities in Ionia or Cyme in Aeolis, so that, setting out from a city, they might bring Ionia to revolt (and there was hope of this; for their coming was unwelcome to no one) and might take away this revenue, the greatest of the Athenians, and at the same time, if the Athenians blockaded them, expense might fall on them; and they said they thought they would also persuade Pissuthnes to join in the war.
But he did not accept this either, but his mind was chiefly set, since he had come too late for Mytilene, on reaching the Peloponnese again as quickly as possible.
Setting out from Embatum he sailed along the coast, and putting in at Myonnesus in the territory of Teos, he slaughtered most of the prisoners whom he had taken on the voyage.

And when he anchored at Ephesus, envoys of the Samians from Anaea came and said that he was not freeing Hellas well if he destroyed men who were neither raising their hands against him nor enemies, but allies of the Athenians under compulsion; and that if he did not stop, he would bring few of his enemies into friendship but would make many more of his friends enemies.

And he was persuaded, and released all the men of Chios that he still held and some of the others; for the people, seeing the ships, did not flee, but rather approached them as if they were Attic ships, and they had not even the slightest expectation that, while the Athenians controlled the sea, Peloponnesian ships would ever cross over to Ionia.

From Ephesus Alcidas sailed in haste and took to flight; for he had been seen by the Salaminia and the Paralus while still anchored near Clarus (they happened to be sailing from Athens), and, fearing pursuit, he sailed through the open sea, intending not to touch land willingly anywhere other than the Peloponnese.

News came to Paches and the Athenians from Erythraea, and indeed it arrived from everywhere; for since Ionia was unwalled, great fear arose that the Peloponnesians, sailing along the coast, even if they did not intend to stay, might at the same time fall upon the cities and plunder them. And the Paralus and the Salaminia, having seen him at Clarus, reported it themselves as eyewitnesses.

And he made the pursuit in haste; and he pursued as far as the island of Patmos, but when they no longer appeared within reach, he turned back. And he considered it a gain, since he had not met them in the open sea, that they had not been caught anywhere and forced to make a camp and give him the trouble of guarding and blockading them.

Sailing back along the coast he also put in at Notium, which belongs to the Colophonians, where Colophonians had settled after the upper city had been taken by Itamenes and the barbarians, who had been brought in because of a private faction; and it was taken about the time when the second invasion of Attica by the Peloponnesians was taking place.

Now in Notium those who had fled there and settled there fell into faction again, and one party, bringing in mercenaries, Arcadians and barbarians, from Pissuthnes, kept them within a walled-off quarter, and those of the Colophonians from the upper city who had sided with the Persians came in with them and shared in the government, while the other party, who had slipped away from them and were exiles, brought in Paches.

And he invited Hippias, the commander of the Arcadians in the walled-off quarter, to a conference, on condition that, if he said nothing acceptable, he would restore him to the fortress safe and sound, and Hippias came out to him, and Paches kept him under guard but unbound, and himself, attacking the fortification suddenly and when they did not expect it, took it, and killed the Arcadians and all the barbarians who were in it; and afterwards, bringing Hippias in as he had agreed, when he was inside, he seized him and shot him down.

He handed Notium over to the Colophonians, except those who had sided with the Persians. And later the Athenians, sending out founders, resettled Notium under their own laws, gathering all the Colophonians from the cities, wherever there was one.

Paches, having arrived at Mytilene, brought Pyrrha and Eresus to submission, and, catching Salaethus the Lacedaemonian hidden in the city, sent him off to Athens, together with the men of the Mytilenaeans from Tenedos whom he had placed there, and anyone else who seemed to him to be responsible for the revolt;
and he also sent off the greater part of his army, and, remaining with the rest, he settled affairs in Mytilene and the rest of Lesbos as he thought best.

When the men and Salaethus arrived, the Athenians at once killed Salaethus, although he made some offers, among other things to lead the Peloponnesians away from Plataea (for it was still being besieged);

and concerning the men they held a debate, and in their anger they decided to kill not only those present but also all the Mytilenaeans who were of adult age, and to enslave the children and women, charging them with the revolt in general, because they had made it without being ruled like the others, and not least did the Peloponnesian ships contribute to their fury, having dared to venture over to Ionia to help them; for they thought that they had made the revolt after no brief deliberation.
So they sent a trireme to Paches as messenger of what had been decided, ordering him to put the Mytilenaeans to death quickly.

And on the next day there was at once a certain change of heart among them and the reflection that the decision taken was cruel and monstrous, to destroy a whole city rather than only those who were guilty.

When the envoys of the Mytilenaeans who were present and those of the Athenians who were acting with them perceived this, they prevailed on those in authority to put the question again; and they persuaded them more easily because it was clear to them as well that the majority of the citizens wished that someone would give them another chance to deliberate.

When an assembly had been called at once, various opinions were expressed by different speakers, and Cleon son of Cleaenetus, who had carried the earlier motion to kill them, being in other respects too the most violent of the citizens and at that time by far the most persuasive with the people, came forward again and spoke as follows.
‘Many times before now I for my part have recognized that a democracy is incapable of ruling others, but most of all in your present change of heart about the Mytilenaeans.

For because of your daily freedom from fear and plotting towards one another, you have the same attitude toward your allies too, and whenever you make a mistake because you were persuaded by their words or give in out of pity, you do not consider that you are being soft at your own peril and without winning the gratitude of the allies, not observing that the empire you hold is a tyranny, over men who plot against you and are ruled against their will, who obey you not because of any favours you may do them to your own harm, but because of whatever superiority you may gain through strength rather than through their goodwill.

And most terrible of all is if nothing of what we decide shall stand firm for us, and if we shall not recognize that a city that uses worse laws that are not changed is stronger than one with good laws that have no authority, and that ignorance with self-restraint is more useful than cleverness with licentiousness, and that the simpler men, compared with the more intelligent, on the whole govern cities better.

For the latter wish to appear wiser than the laws and to get the better of whatever is said for the public good, as if they could not show their judgement in other, greater matters, and through such conduct they mostly bring their cities to ruin; but the former, distrusting their own intelligence, are content to be less learned than the laws and less able to find fault with the speech of one who has spoken well, and, being judges on equal terms rather than competitors, they are mostly right.
So we too ought to act in this way, and not, carried away by cleverness and the contest of wits, advise your multitude against our own judgement.

‘I, then, am of the same opinion, and I wonder at those who have proposed to debate the Mytilenaeans again and have caused a waste of time, which is rather to the advantage of those who have done wrong (for the victim proceeds against the offender with his anger blunted, whereas retaliation that follows as closely as possible on the injury, being its match, exacts the fullest vengeance), and I wonder too who will be the one to speak against me and to claim to show that the wrongdoings of the Mytilenaeans are beneficial to us and that our misfortunes turn into harm for our allies.

And clearly either, trusting in his speaking, he would strive to show that what has been fully decided has not been decided, or, incited by gain, he will try to lead you astray by elaborating the speciousness of his speech.
And from contests of this kind the city gives the prizes to others, while it itself bears the dangers.

You are to blame, managing these contests badly, you who are accustomed to be spectators of words and listeners to deeds, judging future deeds from those who speak well, as to whether they are possible, and things already done, not taking what was done as more credible because seen than what was heard, from those who have made clever criticisms in speech;
and you are the best at being deceived by novelty in argument and at being unwilling to follow what has been approved, being slaves of every new paradox and despisers of what is customary,

and each of you wishing above all to be able to speak himself, or, if not, competing with those who speak in this way so as not to seem to follow behind them in understanding, but to praise a sharp point before it is out, and being eager to anticipate what is said and slow to foresee what will result from it,

seeking, so to speak, something other than the world in which we live, while not thinking adequately even about what is at hand; and, in a word, overcome by the pleasure of hearing and like men sitting as spectators of sophists rather than men deliberating about a city.
‘Trying to turn you away from these things, I declare that the Mytilenaeans have wronged you more than any single city.

For I, for my part, can pardon those who revolted because they were not able to bear your rule or because they were compelled by the enemy; but those who held an island with walls and feared our enemies only by sea, where they themselves too were not unprotected against them with their own force of triremes, and who lived independent and were honoured by us in the highest degree, and did such things, what else did these men do than plot and rise up against us rather than revolt (revolt, at any rate, belongs to those who suffer some violence), and seek to destroy us by taking their stand with our bitterest enemies? And yet that is more terrible than if they had gone to war against us by acquiring power on their own.

Neither did the misfortunes of their neighbours, those who had already revolted from us and been subdued, become a lesson to them, nor did their present prosperity give them hesitation about entering into danger; but becoming bold toward the future and having hopes greater than their power, though less than their desire, they took up war, thinking fit to put strength before justice; for at the moment when they thought they would prevail, they attacked us without being wronged.

It is usual for those cities to which unexpected prosperity comes most fully and most suddenly to turn to insolence; but for men, success that comes in accordance with reason is for the most part more secure than success beyond expectation, and they more easily, so to speak, ward off adversity than preserve prosperity.

The Mytilenaeans ought long ago to have been honoured by us no differently from the others, and they would not have come to this degree of insolence; for man is by nature disposed in any case to despise what courts him and to admire what does not yield.

Let them be punished, even now, as their wrongdoing deserves, and do not lay the blame on the few while you acquit the people. For all of them alike attacked you, even those who could have turned to us and now be back in their city; but, thinking the danger with the few to be safer, they joined in the revolt.

And consider your allies: if you impose the same penalties on those compelled by the enemy and on those who revolt willingly, who do you think will not revolt on a slight pretext, when either freedom comes with success or nothing irreparable is suffered with failure?

And we shall have risked our money and our lives against each city, and if we succeed, receiving a ruined city, you will be deprived thereafter of its future revenue, through which we are strong, and if we fail, we shall have enemies in addition to those we already have, and during the time when we should be resisting our present enemies, we shall be fighting our own allies.

‘We must not, then, hold out a hope, either trusted because of eloquence or bought with money, that they will receive pardon for having erred as humans do. For they did not do harm unwillingly, but plotted knowingly; and what is involuntary is pardonable.

I, then, both at that time first and now, insist that you do not reverse what has already been decided, and that you do not err through the three things most harmful to empire, pity and pleasure in speeches and clemency.

For pity is rightly given in return to those who are like-minded, and not to those who will not pity in return and are by necessity always enemies; and the orators who delight with words will have a contest in other, lesser matters as well, and not in one where the city, after a brief pleasure, will pay a great penalty, while they themselves receive good treatment in return for speaking well; and clemency is better given to those who are going to be friends in the future too than to those who remain the same and enemies no less.

And I say one thing in sum; if you obey me, you will do what is just to the Mytilenaeans and what is expedient at the same time, but if you decide otherwise, you will not win their gratitude, but will rather condemn yourselves. For if these men were right to revolt, you would be ruling when you ought not. But if, though it is not fitting, you nevertheless think fit to do this, then contrary to equity these men too must be punished in your interest, or else you must give up your empire and play the good man out of danger.

Resolve to punish them with the same penalty and not to appear, you who escaped, more insensible than those who plotted, considering what they would likely have done if they had defeated you, especially since they were the first to do wrong.

It is chiefly those who harm someone without a pretext who pursue him to the end and destroy him, suspecting the danger of an enemy who is left alive; for one who has suffered something without necessity is more dangerous if he escapes than an enemy on equal terms.

‘Do not, then, become traitors to yourselves, but, coming as near as possible in thought to what you suffered and how you would have valued above everything subduing them, now pay them back, not growing soft at their present plight nor forgetting the danger that once hung over you.

Punish these men as they deserve and set a clear example to the other allies, that whoever revolts will be punished with death. For if they know this, you will less often neglect the enemy and fight against your own allies.’

Such were the words of Cleon; and after him Diodotus son of Eucrates, who in the earlier assembly too had spoken most strongly against killing the Mytilenaeans, came forward then also and spoke as follows.

‘I neither blame those who have proposed a new decision about the Mytilenaeans, nor do I praise those who object to deliberating many times about the greatest matters, but I think that the two things most opposed to good counsel are haste and anger, of which the one usually goes with folly, the other with lack of education and narrowness of mind.

And whoever contends that words are not to be the teachers of actions is either unintelligent or has some private interest; unintelligent, if he thinks it possible to explain the future and what is not evident by any other means, and with an interest, if, wishing to win acceptance for something shameful, he thinks he could not speak well about what is not honourable, but that by slandering well he could intimidate both those who will speak against him and those who will listen.

And most troublesome of all are those who in addition accuse a speaker of making a display for money. For if they charged him with ignorance, the one who failed to persuade would go away seeming more unintelligent than dishonest; but when dishonesty is imputed, he becomes suspect if he persuades, and if he fails, he is considered dishonest as well as unintelligent.

And the city is not benefited by this; for through fear it is deprived of its counsellors. And it would prosper most if it had such citizens unable to speak; for then the people would least be persuaded to err.

The good citizen ought not to intimidate those who will speak against him, but to show himself the better speaker on equal terms, and the prudent city ought not to add honour to the one who gives good counsel most often, but also not to diminish what he already has, and as for the one whose opinion does not prevail, not only not to punish him but not even to dishonour him.

For in this way the successful speaker would be least likely, in order to be thought worthy of still greater honours, to say anything against his judgement and to win favour, and the unsuccessful one would not strive in the same way, by himself also saying something to win favour, to win over the multitude.

‘We do the opposite of this, and moreover, if anyone is even suspected of speaking for the sake of gain, though he nevertheless gives the best advice, we begrudge him the uncertain suspicion of gain and deprive the city of its evident benefit.

And it has come about that good advice given plainly is in no way less suspected than bad, so that the man who wishes to carry the most dangerous measures must win over the multitude by deceit, just as the man who gives better advice must lie in order to be believed.

And this is the only city which, because of its over-cleverness, it is impossible to benefit openly without deceiving it; for the one who openly gives something good is suspected in return of getting some secret advantage somehow.

But in view of the greatest interests, and in such a matter, we must claim to speak looking somewhat further ahead than you who consider things briefly, especially since we are accountable for our advice, while your listening is unaccountable.

For if both the one who persuaded and the one who followed suffered alike, you would judge more prudently; but as it is, whenever you fail, in whatever anger you happen to be in, you punish the single judgement of the one who persuaded you and not your own, though they were many and shared in the error.
‘I have come forward neither to speak in defence of the Mytilenaeans nor to accuse them. For the contest for us, if we are sensible, is not about their wrongdoing, but about our own good counsel.

For if I show them to be utterly guilty, I will not for that reason also bid you kill them, unless it is expedient, and if they should have some claim to pardon, I will not bid you spare them, if it should not appear good for the city.

I think we are deliberating about the future rather than the present. And as for this point which Cleon especially insists on, that it will be expedient for the future, so that there will be fewer revolts, to set the penalty of death, I too, insisting in turn on what is good for the future, hold the opposite view.

And I ask you not to reject the usefulness of my argument because of the speciousness of his. For his argument, being more just in view of your present anger against the Mytilenaeans, might perhaps attract you; but we are not in a lawsuit with them, so as to need what is just, but we are deliberating about them, how they may be useful to us.

‘Now in the cities the penalty of death is laid down for many offences, and these not equal to this one, but lesser; nevertheless, carried away by hope, men take the risk, and no one has yet entered into danger having condemned himself to failure in his plot.
And what city in revolt has ever attempted it thinking that the resources it had, either its own or through the alliance of others, were inferior?

All are by nature inclined to err, both in private and in public, and there is no law that will prevent this, since men have gone through every penalty, adding to them, in the hope that they might be wronged less by evildoers. And it is likely that in old times the penalties for the greatest crimes were milder, but as they were transgressed, in time most of them came to death; and even this is transgressed.

Either, then, some fear more terrible than this must be found, or this at least restrains nothing, but poverty, giving boldness through necessity, and abundance, giving greed through insolence and pride, and the other conditions of life, through the passion of men, as each is mastered by some irresistible power, lead them into dangers.

And hope and desire are present in everything, the one leading, the other following, and the one devising the plot, the other suggesting the ease of fortune, and they do the most harm, and, being unseen, are stronger than visible dangers.

And fortune contributes no less to these in urging men on; for sometimes, presenting itself unexpectedly, it leads one to run risks even with inferior means, and cities no less, inasmuch as the stakes are the greatest, freedom or rule over others, and each man, acting together with all, has irrationally rated himself too highly.

In short, it is impossible, and a sign of great simplicity, for anyone to think that, when human nature is eagerly set on doing something, it has any means of being turned back, either by the force of laws or by any other terror.

‘We must not, then, trusting in the penalty of death as a guarantee, make a worse decision, nor leave the rebels without hope that it will be possible to repent and to put an end to their error in the shortest time.

For consider that now, if a city that has revolted realizes that it will not prevail, it would come to terms while still able to pay the cost and to pay tribute for the future; but in the other case, what city do you think will not prepare itself better than now, and hold out under siege to the very last, if coming to terms slowly and quickly means the same?

And how is it not harmful to us to spend money sitting before a city because it will not come to terms, and, if we take it, to receive a ruined city and be deprived of its revenue for the future? And it is by this that we are strong against our enemies.

So we must not, acting as strict judges of the offenders, harm ourselves rather than see how, punishing moderately, we shall in future have cities strong in money at our disposal, and we must think fit to provide our protection not from the terror of the laws, but from the care of our actions.
Doing the opposite of this now, if we subdue some free people, ruled by force, who have revolted for their independence, as is natural, we think we must punish them harshly.

But we must not punish free men severely when they revolt, but guard them severely before they revolt and forestall them so that they do not even come to think of it, and, when we have prevailed, lay the blame on as few as possible.
‘And consider how greatly you would err in this too by obeying Cleon.

For now the people in all the cities are well disposed to you, and either they do not join the few in revolting or, if they are forced, they are at once hostile to those who caused the revolt, and you go to war having the multitude of the opposing city as your ally.

But if you destroy the people of the Mytilenaeans, who neither took part in the revolt and, when they got hold of arms, willingly handed over the city, first you will do wrong by killing your benefactors, and then you will bring about for the powerful men what they most wish; for when they cause cities to revolt they will at once have the people as their ally, since you will have shown beforehand that the same penalty is laid down alike for those who do wrong and for those who do not.
But even if they did wrong, you must pretend not to know, so that the only element still allied to us may not become hostile.

And I think this far more expedient for keeping our empire, that we should willingly be wronged rather than justly destroy those whom we ought not to; and Cleon's claim that the same punishment is both just and expedient is not found possible to be realized in it at the same time.

‘Recognizing that these proposals are better, and giving no more weight to pity or to clemency, by which I too do not allow you to be won over, but on the basis of the advice itself, obey me: judge at your leisure those of the Mytilenaeans whom Paches sent off as guilty, and let the rest live in their homes.
For this is good for the future and already formidable to the enemy; for whoever deliberates well is stronger against his opponents than one who attacks recklessly with the force of deeds.’

Such were the words of Diodotus. When these opinions, most nearly balanced against each other, had been expressed, the Athenians nevertheless came into a conflict of opinion and were almost equal in the show of hands, but the view of Diodotus prevailed.
And they at once sent off another trireme in haste, so that they might not find the city destroyed because the first had arrived before it; it had a lead of about a day and a night.

The envoys of the Mytilenaeans provided wine and barley for the ship and promised great rewards if they arrived first, and there was such haste on the voyage that they ate barley kneaded with wine and oil while rowing, and some slept by turns while others rowed.

By good fortune, no wind was contrary, and since the first ship was sailing without haste on a monstrous business, while this one was pressing on in such a way, the first arrived ahead only so much that Paches had read the decree and was about to carry out what had been decided, and the second put in right after it and prevented the destruction. By so little did Mytilene come to danger.

The rest of the men, whom Paches had sent off as being the most responsible for the revolt, the Athenians put to death on the motion of Cleon (they were a little more than a thousand), and they pulled down the walls of the Mytilenaeans and took over their ships.

Afterwards they did not impose a tribute on the Lesbians, but they divided the land, except that of the Methymnaeans, into three thousand lots, set apart three hundred of them as sacred to the gods, and to the rest they sent out settlers of their own, chosen by lot; with these the Lesbians agreed to pay in money two minas a year for each lot, and worked the land themselves.
The Athenians also took over the towns on the mainland that the Mytilenaeans controlled, and these were afterwards subject to the Athenians. So went the events at Lesbos.

In the same summer, after the capture of Lesbos, the Athenians, with Nicias son of Niceratus in command, made an expedition against the island of Minoa, which lies off Megara; the Megarians had built a tower on it and used it as a garrison post.

Nicias wanted the Athenians to keep their watch from there, at a shorter distance, and not from Budorum and Salamis, to prevent the Peloponnesians from making sailings out from there unobserved, both of triremes, as had also happened before, and by sending out privateers, and at the same time to let nothing sail in to the Megarians.

So, after first taking with engines from the sea two projecting towers on the side of Nisaea and clearing the entrance into the channel between the island and the mainland, he walled off also the side facing the mainland, where by a bridge across a shallow marsh help could come to the island, which is not far from the mainland.
When they had finished this in a few days, he afterwards left a fort on the island as well and a garrison, and withdrew with his army.
About the same time in this summer the Plataeans too, who no longer had food and could not endure the siege, came to terms with the Peloponnesians in the following way.

The Peloponnesians were assaulting their wall, and they were unable to defend themselves. The Lacedaemonian commander, recognising their weakness, did not want to take the place by force (for he had been told from Lacedaemon that, if a treaty were ever made with the Athenians and they agreed that each side should give back the places it held by war, Plataea should not have to be given back, on the ground that its people had come over of their own will), but he sent a herald to them saying that, if they were willing to hand over the city of their own accord to the Lacedaemonians and accept them as judges, they would punish the guilty, but no one contrary to justice.

So much the herald said; and they (for they were now at the last stage of weakness) handed over the city. And the Peloponnesians fed the Plataeans for some days, until the judges from Lacedaemon, five men, arrived.
When they had come, no accusation was put forward, but they called the Plataeans and asked them only this, whether they had done any good to the Lacedaemonians and their allies in the present war.

They asked to speak at greater length and put forward from among themselves Astymachus son of Asopolaus and Lacon son of Aeimnestus, who was proxenus of the Lacedaemonians; and they came forward and spoke as follows.

‘We made the surrender of our city, Lacedaemonians, trusting in you, not thinking that we would undergo a trial like this, but that it would be a more regular one, and we accepted to be tried before no other judges than you, as we now are, believing that we would be most likely to obtain fair treatment.

But now we fear that we have been disappointed in both at once; for we reasonably suspect that the trial is about the gravest matters and that you will not prove impartial, judging from the fact that no accusation was first made against us to which we must reply (instead we ourselves asked leave to speak) and that the question is short, so that to answer it truly goes against us, while a false answer can be refuted.

But being at a loss on every side, we are compelled, and it also seems safer, to say something and take the risk; for to men in our situation the word not spoken might give cause for reproach, that, if it had been spoken, it would have saved them.

Besides everything else, persuading you is also difficult for us. If we were strangers to each other, we might benefit by bringing in evidence on matters you did not know; but as it is, everything will be said to people who already know it, and we fear, not that you have already judged our virtues to be inferior to yours and make that itself a charge against us, but that to do a favour to others we are being brought before a judgment already decided.
Nevertheless, presenting the just claims we have, both regarding our quarrel with the Thebans and towards you and the other Greeks, we will remind you of our good deeds and try to persuade you.

‘To the short question, whether we have done any good to the Lacedaemonians and their allies in this war, we say that, if you ask us as enemies, you are not wronged if you have not been benefited, but if you regard us as friends, then you yourselves are rather at fault, who made war on us.

In the peace and against the Mede we have proved good men, since we have not now been the first to break the one, and in the other we alone of the Boeotians joined then in the attack for the freedom of Greece.

For though we are inland people, we fought in the sea battle at Artemisium, and in the battle that took place in our own land we stood by you and Pausanias; and if anything else dangerous happened to the Greeks at that time, we took part in all of it beyond our strength.

And to you, Lacedaemonians, in particular, at the very time when the greatest fear surrounded Sparta after the earthquake, when the Helots had revolted to Ithome, we sent out the third part of our own citizens to help; these things it is not right to forget.

‘Such we thought it right to be in the old and greatest events, and we became enemies only later. You were to blame for it; for when we asked for an alliance after the Thebans had oppressed us, you rejected us and told us to turn to the Athenians, since they were near, while you lived far away.
In the war, however, you have neither suffered nor been about to suffer anything out of the ordinary at our hands.

And if we refused to revolt from the Athenians when you told us to, we did no wrong; for they helped us against the Thebans when you held back, and to betray them was then no longer honourable, especially since we had received benefits from them and had ourselves asked to be taken in as allies and had been given a share of their citizenship, and it was reasonable to follow their orders willingly.
Whatever each of you have led your allies into, it is not the followers who are to blame if anything was done badly, but those who lead them into what is not right.
‘The Thebans have wronged us in many other ways, and the last wrong you yourselves know, because of which we are suffering these things.

For when they were seizing our city in time of truce and, besides, on a holy day, we rightly punished them according to the law established for all, that it is right to defend oneself against an attacking enemy, and now we should not reasonably be harmed because of them.
For if you take what is just by your immediate advantage and their hostility, you will show yourselves not true judges of what is right, but rather servants of expediency.

And yet, if they seem useful to you now, both we and the other Greeks were much more so then, when you were in greater danger. For now you attack others and are formidable, but at that critical time, when the barbarian was bringing slavery upon all, these men were with him.

And it is just to set against our present error, if indeed any error has been made, our zeal then; you will find the greater set against the lesser, and that it was at a time when it was rare for any of the Greeks to oppose courage to the power of Xerxes, and those were praised more who did not, for their own safety, pursue what was profitable to themselves with regard to the invasion, but were willing to dare the best course amid dangers.
We were among these and were honoured among the first, and now for the same reasons we fear that we shall be destroyed, because we chose the Athenians justly rather than you for profit.

And yet you ought to show that you judge the same things in the same way, and to consider your advantage to be nothing else than this: when the good among your allies always hold a lasting gratitude for their virtue, and what is useful to you at the moment is somehow secured as well.

‘Consider too that now you are regarded by most of the Greeks as an example of uprightness; but if you judge about us what is not fitting (for you will not judge this case in obscurity, but you are praised and we are not to be blamed), see to it that men do not refuse to accept that men better than they decided something unseemly about good men, or that spoils from us, the benefactors of Greece, are dedicated in the common temples.

It will seem a terrible thing that the Lacedaemonians should sack Plataea, and that, while your fathers inscribed our city on the tripod at Delphi because of its valour, you should wipe it out, house and home, from the whole Greek world for the sake of the Thebans.

For to such a depth of misfortune have we come, we who were being ruined when the Medes prevailed, and now before you, formerly our dearest friends, are being defeated by the Thebans, and have faced the two greatest trials, then, if we had not surrendered the city, of perishing by hunger, and now of being tried for our lives.

And we Plataeans, who were zealous for the Greeks beyond our strength, have been pushed aside by all, deserted and unaided; none of our allies of that time helps us, and you, Lacedaemonians, our only hope, we fear may not be steadfast.

‘And yet we ask you, both for the sake of the gods who once sanctioned our alliance and for our valour towards the Greeks, to relent and change your minds, if you have been persuaded in anything by the Thebans, and in return to ask of them the favour not to kill those whom it does not become you to kill, and to receive an honourable instead of a shameful gratitude, and not, by giving pleasure to others, to get disgrace in return yourselves;

for it is a short matter to destroy our bodies, but a laborious one to wipe out the infamy of it. For you will not be rightly punishing us as enemies, but as well-wishers who made war under compulsion.

So you would judge righteously if you granted safety to our lives and bore in mind that you received us willingly surrendering and holding out our hands (and the law of the Greeks is not to kill such men), and moreover that we have been your benefactors all along.

Look at the tombs of your fathers, who were killed by the Medes and buried in our land, and whom we honoured every year at public cost with garments and the other customary rites, bringing the first fruits of everything our land produced in its season, as well-wishers from a friendly land and allies to those who were once our comrades in arms. All this you would undo by judging wrongly.

Consider too: Pausanias buried them thinking he was laying them in a friendly land and among men of that kind; but you, if you kill us and make the Plataean land Theban land, what else will you be doing but leaving your fathers and kinsmen in a hostile land and among their murderers, deprived of the honours they now have? Besides, you will enslave the land in which the Greeks were freed, you will make desolate the temples of the gods to whom they prayed before defeating the Medes, and you will take away the ancestral sacrifices from those who founded and established them.

‘This is not in keeping with your reputation, Lacedaemonians, to offend against the common customs of the Greeks and against your ancestors, or to destroy us, your benefactors, because of another's enmity when you yourselves have not been wronged; you should rather spare us and relent in your judgment, taking a sober pity on us, considering not only how terrible is what we shall suffer, but also who we are that would suffer it, and how incalculable misfortune is, which may fall on anyone, even the undeserving.

And we, as befits us and as our need urges, beg you, calling on the gods who share the same altars and are common to the Greeks, to grant this; appealing to the oaths that your fathers swore never to forget us, we become suppliants at the tombs of your fathers and call on the dead not to let us fall into the hands of the Thebans, nor to be handed over, their dearest friends, to their bitterest enemies. We remind you too of that day on which we did the most glorious deeds with them, and now on this one are in danger of suffering the most terrible fate.

And doing what is necessary and hardest for men in our situation, ending our speech, since the danger to our life comes near with it, we now stop and say that we did not surrender the city to the Thebans (for rather than that we would have chosen to die by hunger, the most shameful death), but came over to you trusting you (and it is just, if we do not persuade you, to put us back in the same position and let us choose for ourselves the danger that befalls us),

and at the same time we adjure you that we, Plataeans, who were the most zealous for the Greeks, should not be handed over to the Thebans, our bitterest enemies, out of your hands and your good faith, suppliants as we are, Lacedaemonians, but that you become our saviours and do not, while freeing the other Greeks, destroy us.’

So spoke the Plataeans. The Thebans, afraid that the Lacedaemonians might give way somewhat in response to their speech, came forward and said that they too wished to speak, since the Plataeans had, against their own judgment, been given a longer speech than the answer to the question required. When the judges told them to, they spoke as follows.

‘We would not have asked to make a speech if they too had answered the question briefly and had not turned on us and made an accusation, and made a long defence of themselves on matters outside the issue and on which they had not even been charged, and praised themselves where no one had blamed them. But now we must answer the one and refute the other, so that neither our baseness nor their reputation may help them, but you may hear the truth about both before you judge.

‘We first came into conflict with them because, after we had founded Plataea later than the rest of Boeotia, and other places with it, which we held after driving out a mixed population, these men refused to be led by us, as had been arranged at first, but, separating themselves from the other Boeotians and transgressing the ancestral customs, when they were being compelled, went over to the Athenians and with them did us much harm, for which they also suffered in return.
‘When the barbarian came against Greece, they say that they alone of the Boeotians did not medize, and on this above all they pride themselves and abuse us.
We say that they did not medize because the Athenians did not either, and that in the same way, when the Athenians later attacked the Greeks, they alone of the Boeotians in turn atticized.

And yet consider in what circumstances each of us did this. For our city at that time happened to be governed neither as an oligarchy with equal rights nor as a democracy; but what is most opposed to the laws and to sound government, and nearest to a tyranny, a narrow clique of a few men, held power.

These men, hoping to gain still more power for themselves if the cause of the Mede prevailed, held down the people by force and brought him in; and the city as a whole did this when it was not mistress of itself, nor is it fair to reproach it for the errors it made while not under laws.

At any rate, after the Mede had left and the city had received its laws, you should consider whether, when the Athenians later attacked and tried to bring the rest of Greece and our land under their power, and through faction already held most of it, we fought at Coronea, defeated them and freed Boeotia, and whether now we are zealously helping to free the others, providing horses and equipment such as none of the other allies provide.
‘So much we say in defence regarding medism; but that you have wronged the Greeks more and are more deserving of every punishment, we will try to show.

You became allies and citizens of the Athenians, as you say, to get protection against us. Then you ought to have brought them in only against us, and not to have joined them in attacking others, since it was open to you, if you were ever led on by the Athenians against your will, to rely on the alliance of these Lacedaemonians, already made against the Mede, which you yourselves keep putting forward; it was enough both to keep us from you and, what matters most, to let you deliberate without fear. But willingly and no longer under compulsion you chose the side of the Athenians.

And you say that it would have been shameful to betray your benefactors; but it was much more shameful and unjust to betray all the Greeks, with whom you had sworn alliance, than the Athenians alone, the one party enslaving Greece, the other freeing it.

And the favour you returned them was not equal, nor free from shame; for you brought them in when you were being wronged, as you say, but you became their accomplices when they were wronging others. And yet it is more shameful not to return like favours than not to return those that were owed justly but are repaid in injustice.

And you made it plain that even then it was not for the sake of the Greeks that you alone did not medize, but because the Athenians did not either, and you wished to do the same as the one party and the opposite of the other.

And now you expect to be rewarded for what you did well because of others. But that is not reasonable; as you chose the Athenians, fight on their side, and do not bring up the alliance made then as if it must save you now.

For you abandoned it and, transgressing it, helped rather to enslave the Aeginetans and some others of those who had sworn it than tried to prevent it, and that not against your will, since you had the laws which you have up to now and no one was compelling you as we were compelled. And the last proposal we made before you were walled in, that you should keep quiet and help neither side, you did not accept.

Who then would more justly be hated by all the Greeks than you, who put forward your valour to their harm? And the good qualities you once showed, as you say, you have now shown were not your own, while what your nature always wanted has been exposed in its truth; for you went along with the Athenians when they took the unjust road.
‘This, then, is what we show concerning our involuntary medism and your voluntary atticism;
and as to the last wrong you say you suffered, that we came unlawfully in time of truce and on a holy day against your city, we do not think that in this either we are more at fault than you.

For if we ourselves had come against your city and fought and ravaged your land as enemies, we would be in the wrong; but if men of yours, the first in both wealth and birth, wishing to put an end to your foreign alliance and to restore you to the ancestral customs common to all the Boeotians, called us in of their own will, what wrong do we do? For those who lead break the law more than those who follow.

But, as we judge, neither they nor we did wrong; being citizens like you and having more at stake, they opened their own wall and brought us into their own city as friends, not as enemies, wishing that the worse among you should not become worse still and that the better should have what they deserve, acting as correctors of your thinking and not estranging the city from your persons but bringing it back into its kinship, making it the enemy of no one, but at peace with all alike.

The proof that we did not act as enemies is this: we wronged no one, and we proclaimed that anyone who wished to live as a citizen according to the ancestral customs of all the Boeotians should come over to us.

And you came over gladly and made an agreement and at first kept quiet, but later, when you saw that we were few, even if we might seem to have acted somewhat unfairly in entering without the consent of your people, you did not repay us in kind, by not using violence in deed and by persuading us with words to leave, but you attacked us against the agreement; those you killed in the fight we do not grieve for so much (for they suffered by a kind of law), but those who held out their hands, whom you took alive and then promised us not to kill, but lawlessly destroyed, how have you not done terrible things?

And after committing these three wrongs in a short time, the broken agreement, the later death of the men, and the false promise to us not to kill them if we did not harm your property in the fields, you nevertheless say that we broke the law and claim that you yourselves should not pay the penalty. No, not if these judges decide rightly; but for all of these you will be punished.

‘We have gone through these things at length, Lacedaemonians, both for your sake and for ours, so that you may know that you will be justly condemning them, and we that we have taken our vengeance still more righteously.

And do not be softened by hearing of their old virtues, if indeed there ever were any; such virtues ought to be a help to those who are wronged, but a double penalty to those who do something shameful, because they do wrong out of keeping with their character. And let them not be helped by lamentation and pity, calling upon the tombs of your fathers and their own desolation.

For we in turn show that our young men, destroyed by them, suffered a much more terrible fate; of their fathers some died at Coronea bringing Boeotia over to your side, while others, left behind as old men in desolate homes, make a much more just supplication to you to punish these men.
Men who suffer something undeserved are more worthy to receive pity, but those who suffer justly, as these do, are on the contrary a cause for rejoicing.

And their present desolation they have through their own fault; for they willingly rejected the better allies. They broke the law without having first suffered anything from us, judging out of hatred rather than justice, and they are not now paying back an equal penalty; for they will suffer a lawful sentence, and not holding out their hands after a battle, as they say, but having handed themselves over to trial by agreement.

So defend, Lacedaemonians, the law of the Greeks which these men have transgressed, and to us, who have suffered lawless treatment, give a just return for the zeal we have shown, and let us not be pushed aside before you by their words, but make an example for the Greeks that you will set up trials not of words but of deeds, for which, if they are good, a short report suffices, but if they are wrong, speeches adorned with fine phrases become veils.
But if leaders, as you now do, sum up the facts and give judgment towards all together, people will be less likely to seek fine words for unjust deeds.’

Such was the speech of the Thebans. The Lacedaemonian judges thought that the question, whether they had received any good from them in the war, would be a right one for them, because at other times, so they said, they had asked them to keep quiet according to the old treaty of Pausanias after the Mede, and when later, before the siege wall, they had proposed to them that they should be neutral according to that treaty, the Plataeans had not accepted, and so, considering that by their own just intention they were already released from the treaty and had been wronged by them, they brought them forward again one at a time and asked the same question, whether they had done any good to the Lacedaemonians and their allies in the war, and when they said no, they led them away and killed them, and made an exception of no one.
They put to death no fewer than two hundred of the Plataeans themselves, and twenty-five of the Athenians who had been besieged with them; and they enslaved the women.

The city they gave for about a year to some Megarians who had been driven out by faction, and to those of the Plataeans who supported their side and had survived, to live in; later they razed it entirely to the ground from its foundations and built near the temple of Hera an inn two hundred feet square, with rooms all around below and above, and they used the roofs and doors of the Plataeans, and from the other furniture that was within the wall, bronze and iron, they made couches and dedicated them to Hera, and they built for her a stone temple a hundred feet long. The land they made public property and leased for ten years, and the Thebans farmed it.
And almost wholly it was for the sake of the Thebans that the Lacedaemonians were so hostile towards the Plataeans, thinking that the Thebans would be useful in the war that was then just beginning.
So ended the affair of Plataea, in the ninety-third year after the Plataeans became allies of the Athenians.

The forty ships of the Peloponnesians which had come to help the Lesbians, after fleeing then across the open sea, pursued by the Athenians and caught in a storm off Crete, had come scattered from there back to the Peloponnese, and they found at Cyllene thirteen triremes of the Leucadians and Ambraciots, and Brasidas son of Tellis, who had come as adviser to Alcidas.

For the Lacedaemonians, since they had failed at Lesbos, wanted to enlarge their fleet and sail to Corcyra, which was in civil strife, while the Athenians had only twelve ships at Naupactus, so as to get there first before any larger fleet came to help from Athens, and Brasidas and Alcidas were making their preparations for this.

For the Corcyraeans were in civil strife ever since the prisoners taken in the sea battles off Epidamnus had come home to them, released by the Corinthians, nominally on bail of eight hundred talents given by their proxeni, but in fact persuaded to win Corcyra over for the Corinthians. And these men were intriguing, going to each of the citizens, to make the city revolt from the Athenians.

And when an Attic and a Corinthian ship arrived bringing envoys, and talks were held, the Corcyraeans voted to be allies of the Athenians according to the agreement, but friends of the Peloponnesians as before.
And (since Peithias was a volunteer proxenus of the Athenians and the leader of the people) these men brought him to trial, saying that he was enslaving Corcyra to the Athenians.
He was acquitted and in turn prosecuted the five richest men among them, saying that they were cutting vine-props from the precinct of Zeus and of Alcinous; the fine fixed for each prop was a stater.

When they had been convicted and had sat down at the temples as suppliants because of the size of the fine, so that they might pay it in instalments, Peithias (for he was also a member of the council) persuaded the council to apply the law.

They, since they were shut out by the law and at the same time learned that Peithias, while he was still a member of the council, intended to persuade the people to have the same friends and enemies as the Athenians, banded together and, taking daggers, suddenly entered the council and killed Peithias and others, both councillors and private citizens, about sixty; but some few who held the same views as Peithias took refuge in the Attic trireme, which was still there.

Having done this, they called the Corcyraeans together and said that this was for the best and that they would now be least likely to be enslaved by the Athenians, and that in future they should receive neither side, except with one ship, and keep quiet, and should consider any larger number hostile. When they had said this, they also compelled the people to ratify the proposal.
They also sent envoys at once to Athens, to explain that what had been done was advantageous and to persuade those who had fled there to do nothing harmful, so that there might be no reaction.
When they arrived, the Athenians arrested the envoys as revolutionaries, together with all those they had persuaded, and put them away in Aegina.
Meanwhile, those of the Corcyraeans who held power, when a Corinthian trireme and Lacedaemonian envoys arrived, attacked the people, and won the fight.

When night came on, the people took refuge on the acropolis and the high parts of the city, and gathered and established themselves there, and they held the Hyllaic harbour; the others seized the market-place, where most of them lived, and the harbour next to it and facing the mainland.

On the next day they skirmished a little, and both sides sent round into the fields, calling on the slaves and promising them freedom; and the mass of the household slaves joined the people as allies, while the other side got eight hundred mercenaries from the mainland.

After a day's interval there was another battle, and the people won, having the advantage both in the strength of their positions and in numbers; and the women boldly joined in with them, throwing tiles from the houses and enduring the uproar beyond their nature.

When the rout took place, late in the afternoon, the few, fearing that the people might come on and take the dockyard at the first shout and destroy them, set fire to the houses around the market-place and the tenements, so that there might be no approach, sparing neither their own nor others', so that much merchandise was burned up and the whole city was in danger of being destroyed, if a wind had risen to carry the flame towards it.

They stopped fighting, and both sides kept quiet and spent the night on guard; and the Corinthian ship slipped out to sea, since the people had won, and most of the mercenaries were secretly carried over to the mainland.
