On the following day Nicostratus son of Diitrephes, general of the Athenians, arrived to help from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenian hoplites; he negotiated a settlement and persuaded them to agree with one another to try ten men, the most guilty, who did not wait any longer, and that the rest should live together, making a treaty with one another and with the Athenians, so as to have the same enemies and friends.

Having done this, he was about to sail away; but the leaders of the people persuaded him to leave them five of his own ships, so that their opponents would be somewhat less inclined to make trouble, while they themselves would man the same number from their own people and send them with him.
He agreed, and they began to enrol their enemies for the ships. But these, fearing that they might be sent off to Athens, sat down in the temple of the Dioscuri.

Nicostratus tried to make them get up and reassured them. When he could not persuade them, the people armed themselves on this pretext, taking their distrust in refusing to sail with him to mean that they intended nothing sound, and took their arms from their houses, and they would have killed some of those they came upon, if Nicostratus had not prevented it.

The others, seeing what was happening, sat down in the temple of Hera as suppliants, and they were no fewer than four hundred. The people, fearing that they might start a revolution, persuaded them to get up and carried them over to the island in front of the temple of Hera, and provisions were sent to them there.

While the strife was at this stage, on the fourth or fifth day after the men had been carried over to the island, the Peloponnesian ships from Cyllene, where they had been lying at anchor since their voyage from Ionia, arrived, fifty-three in number; they were commanded by Alcidas, as before, and Brasidas sailed with him as adviser. They anchored at Sybota, a harbour of the mainland, and at dawn sailed against Corcyra.

The Corcyraeans, in great confusion and frightened both by the situation in the city and by the attack, at the same time prepared sixty ships and sent them out against the enemy as each was manned, although the Athenians urged them to let them sail out first and to come out afterwards themselves with all their ships together.
When their ships came near the enemy scattered, two immediately deserted, and in others the crews were fighting one another, and there was no order in anything they did.
The Peloponnesians, seeing the confusion, drew up twenty ships against the Corcyraeans, and the rest against the twelve ships of the Athenians, among which were the two ships Salaminia and Paralus.

The Corcyraeans, attacking badly and a few ships at a time, were in distress in their own part; the Athenians, fearing the enemy's numbers and being surrounded, did not attack the main body or the centre of the ships drawn up against them, but attacked on the wing and sank one ship. And after that, when the enemy had formed in a circle, they sailed round them and tried to throw them into confusion.

Those who were facing the Corcyraeans noticed this and, fearing that what had happened at Naupactus might happen again, came to help, and the ships, now united, made their attack on the Athenians together.

The Athenians now began to retire, backing water, and at the same time they wanted the Corcyraean ships to escape first as far as possible, while they themselves retired slowly and the enemy was drawn up against them.
Such was the sea battle, and it ended at sunset,

and the Corcyraeans, fearing that the enemy, as victors, might sail against the city and either take the men from the island on board or do something else violent, carried the men from the island back to the temple of Hera and guarded the city.
The enemy, though they had won the sea battle, did not dare to sail against the city, but with thirteen Corcyraean ships they had taken they sailed back to the mainland, from where they had set out.

On the next day they were no more inclined to sail against the city, although the citizens were in great confusion and fear, and although Brasidas, it is said, urged Alcidas to do so, but he did not have an equal vote; instead they landed on the promontory of Leucimme and ravaged the fields.

Meanwhile the people of the Corcyraeans, greatly afraid that the ships might sail against them, came to talks with the suppliants and the others about how the city might be saved, and persuaded some of them to go on board the ships; for in spite of everything they manned thirty, expecting the attack.

The Peloponnesians, after ravaging the land until midday, sailed away, and towards night it was signalled to them by fire that sixty Athenian ships were approaching from Leucas; these the Athenians had sent, under the general Eurymedon son of Thucles, when they learned of the strife and that the ships with Alcidas were about to sail against Corcyra.
So the Peloponnesians went home at once that night with all speed along the coast; and hauling their ships across the isthmus of Leucas, so that they would not be seen sailing round, they got away.

The Corcyraeans, when they saw that the Attic ships were approaching and those of the enemy had gone, took the Messenians, who had previously been outside, and brought them into the city, and, ordering the ships they had manned to sail round into the Hyllaic harbour, while they were sailing round, they killed any of their enemies they could catch; and they put ashore from the ships all those they had persuaded to go on board and made away with them, and going to the temple of Hera they persuaded about fifty of the suppliants to undergo trial and condemned them all to death.

Most of the suppliants, all who had not been persuaded, when they saw what was happening, killed one another there in the sanctuary, and some hanged themselves from the trees, and others made away with themselves each as best they could.

And for the seven days that Eurymedon, after his arrival, stayed with his sixty ships, the Corcyraeans kept slaughtering those of their fellow citizens whom they considered their enemies, bringing the charge against them of trying to overthrow the democracy, but some were killed also because of private enmity, and others for money owed to them, by those who had borrowed it;

death appeared in every form, and, as tends to happen in such times, there was nothing that did not happen, and worse still. For father killed son, and men were dragged from the temples and killed beside them, and some were even walled up in the temple of Dionysus and died there.

So savage was the course of the civil strife, and it seemed more so because it was among the first, since later practically the whole Greek world was convulsed, there being quarrels everywhere, the leaders of the people trying to bring in the Athenians and the few the Lacedaemonians. In peace they would have had no pretext nor been ready to call them in, but in war, and with alliances available to each side both for harming their opponents and for gaining advantage for themselves by the same means, calls for intervention were easily procured by those who wanted a revolution.

And many grievous things fell upon the cities through civil strife, things that happen and always will happen as long as human nature is the same, but more severe or milder and differing in their forms, according as each change of circumstances presents itself. For in peace and prosperity both cities and individuals have better dispositions because they do not fall into unwilling necessities; but war, taking away the easy supply of daily life, is a violent teacher and makes the tempers of most people like their circumstances.

So the affairs of the cities were in strife, and those that came later, hearing perhaps of what had happened before, went much further in the excess of inventing new ideas, both in the cunning of their attacks and the outrageousness of their revenges.

And they changed the usual meaning of words in relation to deeds as they thought right. Reckless daring was considered loyal courage to one's party, prudent delay specious cowardice, moderation a cover for unmanliness, and understanding in everything idleness in everything; frantic haste was counted part of a man, and plotting for safety a plausible pretext for backing out.

The violent man was always trusted, and the man who spoke against him suspected. A man who plotted and succeeded was clever, and one who detected a plot was still cleverer; but one who planned beforehand so as to need none of these things was a breaker-up of his party and afraid of his opponents. In short, the man who got in first against one about to do something bad was praised, and also the one who urged on someone who had not thought of it.

Indeed, kinship became more foreign than party, because party men were more ready to dare without excuse; for such associations are formed not for benefit under the established laws, but for gain against the existing ones. And they confirmed their pledges to each other not so much by divine law as by breaking the law together.

Fair words from opponents they accepted with watchfulness over their deeds, if those opponents had the upper hand, and not with generosity. To take revenge on someone was valued more than not to have been harmed first oneself. And oaths of reconciliation, if any were ever made, held for the moment, given by each side in its helplessness, when they had no strength from elsewhere; but at the chance moment, the one who was first to take courage, if he saw his enemy unguarded, took revenge more gladly because of the pledge than if it had been in the open, and he counted both the safety and that by winning through deceit he gained in addition a prize for cleverness. Most people, being villains, are more easily called clever than, being simple, called good, and they are ashamed of the latter and pride themselves on the former.

The cause of all these things was the desire for power arising from greed and ambition; and from them came the zeal of men engaged in rivalry. For the leaders in the cities, each side with a fair-sounding name, preferring political equality for the people or moderate aristocracy, while serving the common good in word, made it their prize, and striving in every way to get the better of each other they dared the most terrible deeds and pursued revenges still greater, not setting them within the bounds of justice and the advantage of the city, but limiting them by whatever gave pleasure to each side at the moment, and, gaining power either by an unjust vote of condemnation or by force, they were ready to satisfy their rivalry of the moment. So neither side respected piety, but those who managed to accomplish something odious under a fair pretext of words were better spoken of. The citizens in the middle were destroyed by both sides, either because they did not join the struggle or out of envy that they should survive.

And those of meaner intelligence mostly prevailed; for, fearing both their own deficiency and the intelligence of their opponents, lest they be worsted in words and be plotted against first by the versatility of their opponents' minds, they boldly went to deeds.
The others, contemptuously thinking that they would see it coming and that they had no need to take by deed what they could by intelligence, were caught unguarded and perished in greater numbers.

[In Corcyra, then, most of these things were first dared, and all that men ruled with insolence rather than moderation would do in retaliation against those who gave them the chance of revenge, and what some, wishing to be freed from their customary poverty, and above all through passion desiring to have their neighbours' goods, would resolve contrary to justice, and those who, not for gain, but attacking above all on equal terms, carried away by uncontrolled passion, would attack savagely and mercilessly.

And when the life of the city was thrown into confusion at this time, human nature, prevailing over the laws and accustomed to do wrong even against the laws, gladly showed itself ungoverned in passion, stronger than justice, and hostile to all superiority; for they would not have put revenge before religion and gain before doing no wrong, if envy had not had its harmful power.

And men think fit, in taking revenge on others, to abolish beforehand the common laws on such matters, on which rests the hope of all that they themselves may be saved if they fall, and not to leave them in force, in case someone in danger should ever need one of them.]

later the exiles of the Corcyraeans (for about five hundred of them had escaped) seized forts that were on the mainland, controlled the land of their own on the other side, and, setting out from there, plundered those on the island and did much harm, and a severe famine arose in the city.

They also sent envoys to Lacedaemon and Corinth about their return; and when nothing was achieved for them, later on they got boats and mercenaries ready and crossed over to the island, about six hundred in all,

and burning their boats, so that there might be no hope of anything other than controlling the land, they went up to Mount Istone, built a fort there, and began to destroy those in the city and controlled the land.
At the end of the same summer the Athenians sent twenty ships to Sicily, and Laches son of Melanopus as their general and Charoeades son of Euphiletus.

For the Syracusans and Leontines had gone to war with each other. Allies of the Syracusans were all the other Dorian cities except Camarina, which at the beginning of the war had also been enrolled in the alliance of the Lacedaemonians, though they had not actually fought in the war, and allies of the Leontines were the Chalcidian cities and Camarina; in Italy the Locrians were on the side of the Syracusans, and the Rhegians, because of kinship, on that of the Leontines.

So the allies of the Leontines sent to Athens and, on the ground of an old alliance and because they were Ionians, persuaded the Athenians to send them ships; for they were being shut out from both the land and the sea by the Syracusans.

And the Athenians sent them, on the pretext of kinship, but wishing that no grain should be brought to the Peloponnese from there, and making a preliminary test whether the affairs of Sicily could be brought under their control.
So, establishing themselves at Rhegium in Italy, they carried on the war with their allies. And the summer ended.
In the following winter the plague fell upon the Athenians a second time; it had never entirely left them at any time, but there had nevertheless been some respite.
The second time it lasted no less than a year, and the first time as much as two years, so that nothing distressed the Athenians and damaged their power more than this;
for no fewer than four thousand four hundred hoplites from the ranks died, and three hundred horsemen, and of the rest of the multitude a number that could not be found out.
At that time there also occurred the many earthquakes, at Athens, in Euboea, and in Boeotia, and especially at Orchomenus in Boeotia.

The Athenians in Sicily and the Rhegians, in the same winter, made an expedition with thirty ships against the islands called the islands of Aeolus; for in summer it was impossible to attack them because of the lack of water.

The Liparaeans, colonists of the Cnidians, occupy them. They live on one of the islands, which is not large and is called Lipara; and setting out from it they farm the others, Didyme, Strongyle and Hiera.

The people there believe that Hephaestus works as a smith on Hiera, because at night it is seen sending up much fire, and by day smoke. These islands lie off the land of the Sicels and the Messenians, and they were allies of the Syracusans.
The Athenians ravaged their land and, since they did not come over to them, sailed back to Rhegium. And the winter ended, and the fifth year of this war, which Thucydides wrote down, ended.

In the following summer the Peloponnesians and their allies came as far as the Isthmus intending to invade Attica, led by Agis son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, but when many earthquakes occurred they turned back again and there was no invasion.

About this time, while the earthquakes prevailed, at Orobiae in Euboea the sea, receding from what was then the land and rising in a wave, came over part of the city, and part of it flooded, and part of it subsided, and what was land before is now sea; and it destroyed the people who could not run up to the high ground in time.
And around Atalante, the island off Opuntian Locris, a similar flood occurred, and it carried away part of the Athenian fort and of two ships that had been drawn up wrecked one.
At Peparethus there was also a certain recession of the wave, but it did not flood; and an earthquake threw down part of the wall and the prytaneum and a few other houses.

In the same summer others were at war in Sicily, as it happened to each, and the Siceliots themselves, campaigning against one another, and the Athenians with their own allies; but what was most worth telling, done either by the allies with the Athenians or against the Athenians by their opponents, of these things I shall make mention.

Charoeades, the general of the Athenians, having already been killed by the Syracusans in battle, Laches, who now had the whole command of the ships, made an expedition with the allies against Mylae, a town of the Messenians. It happened that two tribes of the Messenians were on garrison duty at Mylae and had also laid an ambush for those coming from the ships.

The Athenians and their allies routed the men from the ambush and killed many, and attacking the fortification they compelled them by agreement to hand over the acropolis and to march with them against Messene.
And after this, when the Athenians and their allies came against them, the Messenians also came over themselves, giving hostages and providing the other pledges.

In the same summer the Athenians sent thirty ships round the Peloponnese, commanded by Demosthenes son of Alcisthenes and Procles son of Theodorus, and sixty ships and two thousand hoplites to Melos; their commander was Nicias son of Niceratus.
For they wanted to bring over the Melians, who, though islanders, were unwilling to obey or to join their alliance.

When they did not come over, though their land was being ravaged, the Athenians left Melos and sailed to Oropus in the Graean land, and putting in at nightfall the hoplites at once marched from the ships by land to Tanagra in Boeotia.
The Athenians from the city in full force, commanded by Hipponicus son of Callias and Eurymedon son of Thucles, met them at the same place by land at a signal.

And encamping, they spent that day ravaging the land of Tanagra and spent the night there. On the next day they defeated in battle the Tanagraeans who came out against them and some Thebans who had come to help, took the arms, set up a trophy, and withdrew, the one party to the city, the other to the ships.
And Nicias, sailing along the coast with the sixty ships, ravaged the seaboard of Locris and returned home.
About this time the Lacedaemonians founded Heraclea in Trachinia as a colony, with the following intention.

The Malians as a whole consist of three parts, Paralians, Hiereans and Trachinians; of these the Trachinians, having been ruined in war by the Oetaeans, who were their neighbours, at first intended to attach themselves to the Athenians, but, fearing that these might not be loyal to them, sent to Lacedaemon, choosing Tisamenus as envoy.
The Dorians, the mother city of the Lacedaemonians, also joined in the embassy with them, asking for the same things; for they too were being ruined by the Oetaeans.

So first they consulted the god at Delphi, and at his bidding they sent out the settlers, from themselves and from the perioeci, and they invited any of the other Greeks who wished to follow, except Ionians and Achaeans and some other peoples. Three Lacedaemonians led as founders, Leon, Alcidas and Damagon.

Once established, they walled the city anew, which is now called Heraclea, about forty stades from Thermopylae and twenty from the sea. They also prepared dockyards, and they closed off the side towards Thermopylae at the pass itself, so that it might be easy for them to guard.

The Athenians, when this city was being settled, were at first afraid and thought that it was being founded chiefly against Euboea, because the crossing to Cenaeum in Euboea is short. Afterwards, however, it turned out contrary to their expectation; for nothing terrible came from it.

The cause was that the Thessalians, who were powerful in these regions, and on whose land it was being founded, fearing that they might have neighbours of great strength, harassed and continually made war on the newly settled people, until they wore them out, although at first they had been very many (for everyone went boldly since the Lacedaemonians were founding it, thinking the city secure); but not least the governors from the Lacedaemonians themselves who came out ruined the affairs and reduced it to a small population, frightening most people away by governing harshly and in some things not fairly, so that their neighbours now more easily prevailed over them.

In the same summer, and about the same time that the Athenians were detained at Melos, the Athenians from the thirty ships around the Peloponnese first set an ambush at Ellomenus in Leucadia and killed some of the garrison, and then later came against Leucas with a larger force, with all the Acarnanians, who followed in full force except the Oeniadae, and with the Zacynthians and Cephallenians and fifteen ships of the Corcyraeans.

The Leucadians, though their land was being ravaged both outside and inside the isthmus, where Leucas and the temple of Apollo are, kept quiet, overpowered by numbers; the Acarnanians asked Demosthenes, the general of the Athenians, to wall them off, thinking that they could easily take them by siege and be rid of a city that was always hostile to them.

Demosthenes at this time was persuaded by the Messenians that it would be a fine thing for him, since so large an army had been gathered, to attack the Aetolians, who were enemies of Naupactus, and that, if he defeated them, he would easily win over to the Athenians the rest of the mainland there as well.

For they explained that the nation of the Aetolians, though large and warlike, lived in unwalled villages, and those far apart, and used light equipment, and so it would not be difficult to subdue it before they could come together to help one another.

They urged him to attack first the Apodotians, then the Ophioneans, and after them the Eurytanians, who are the largest part of the Aetolians, and are most unintelligible in speech and eaters of raw flesh, as is said; for once these were taken, the rest would easily come over too.

He was persuaded, out of a wish to please the Messenians and above all because he thought that without the forces of the Athenians, with his allies from the mainland together with the Aetolians, he could go by land against the Boeotians through the Ozolian Locrians to Cytinium in Doris, keeping Parnassus on his right, until he came down among the Phocians, who, he thought, would eagerly join the expedition because of their constant friendship with the Athenians or could be brought over by force (and Boeotia already borders on the Phocians); so he set out with his whole army from Leucas, against the will of the Acarnanians, and sailed along the coast to Sollium.

He communicated his plan to the Acarnanians, and when they did not accept it because he had not walled in Leucas, he himself with the rest of the army, Cephallenians, Messenians, Zacynthians and three hundred Athenian marines from his own ships (for the fifteen Corcyraean ships had gone away), made an expedition against the Aetolians.

He set out from Oeneon in Locris. These Ozolian Locrians were allies, and they were to meet the Athenians in the interior with their whole force; for being neighbours of the Aetolians and armed in the same way, they seemed likely to be of great help on the expedition through their experience of the Aetolians' way of fighting and of the country.

He camped with his army in the sanctuary of Nemean Zeus, where Hesiod the poet is said to have been killed by the people of that region, an oracle having told him that he would suffer this at Nemea, and at dawn he set out and marched into Aetolia.

And he took Potidania on the first day, Crocyleum on the second and Teichium on the third, and he stayed there and sent the booty away to Eupalium in Locris; for his intention was, after subduing the other places, then to return to Naupactus and make an expedition later against the Ophioneans, if they were unwilling to come to terms.

This preparation did not escape the Aetolians, either when it was first being planned, and once the army had invaded, they all came to help in great force, so that even the farthest of the Ophioneans, who reach down to the Malian Gulf, the Bomians and Callians, came to help.

The Messenians gave Demosthenes advice of this kind: just as at first, telling him that the capture of the Aetolians was easy, they urged him to go as quickly as possible against the villages and not to wait until they all gathered and drew up against him, but always to try to take the village in front of him.

He, persuaded by them and confident in his good fortune, since nothing opposed him, did not wait for the Locrians who were to come to his help (for he was most in need of light-armed javelin-men) but advanced against Aegitium, and attacking it took it by storm. For the people slipped away and sat on the hills above the town; for it lay on high ground, about eighty stades from the sea.

The Aetolians (for they had by now come to the help of Aegitium) attacked the Athenians and their allies, running down from the hills from all sides and throwing javelins at them, and when the Athenian army advanced, they retreated, and when it retreated, they pressed on; and for a long time the battle went on like this, pursuits and retreats, in both of which the Athenians had the worse.

So as long as their archers had their arrows and were able to use them, they held out (for the Aetolians, being light-armed men, were driven back when shot at); but when the captain of the archers was killed and his men were scattered, and the soldiers themselves were worn out, having been engaged for a long time in the same toil, and the Aetolians pressed on and kept throwing javelins, then at last they turned and fled, and falling into ravines with no way out and into places they did not know, they perished; for their guide on the roads, Chromon the Messenian, had happened to be killed.
every form of flight and destruction befell the army of the Athenians, and the survivors barely escaped to the sea and to Oeneon in Locris, from where they had set out.

Many of the allies were killed, and of the Athenians themselves about a hundred and twenty hoplites. So many in number and all of the same age, these men, truly the best who perished in this war from the city of the Athenians, were destroyed; and the other general, Procles, was killed too.

They took up their dead from the Aetolians under truce, withdrew to Naupactus, and later were carried to Athens by the ships. Demosthenes remained behind around Naupactus and those places, fearing the Athenians because of what had happened.
About the same time the Athenians in Sicily also sailed to Locris, and in a landing defeated those of the Locrians who came to help, and took a guard-post that was on the river Halex.

In the same summer the Aetolians, having earlier sent envoys to Corinth and to Lacedaemon, Tolophus the Ophionean, Boriades the Eurytanian and Tisander the Apodotian, persuaded them to send an army against Naupactus because it had brought in the Athenians.

And towards autumn the Lacedaemonians sent out three thousand hoplites of their allies. Of these, five hundred were from Heraclea, the city in Trachis, which was then newly founded; a Spartan, Eurylochus, commanded the army, and with him went the Spartans Macarius and Menedaeus.

When the army had been gathered at Delphi, Eurylochus sent a herald to the Ozolian Locrians; for the road to Naupactus went through their country, and at the same time he wanted to make them revolt from the Athenians.

Of the Locrians, the Amphissians helped him most, being afraid because of their enmity with the Phocians; and they themselves gave hostages first and persuaded the others, who feared the invading army, to give them too, first their neighbours the Myoneans (for on this side Locris is most difficult to invade), then the Ipneans, Messapians, Tritaeans, Chalaeans, Tolophonians, Hessians and Oeantheans. All these also joined the expedition. The Olpaeans gave hostages, but did not follow; and the Hyaeans did not give hostages until their village called Polis was taken.

When everything was ready and he had deposited the hostages at Cytinium in Doris, he advanced with his army against Naupactus through the Locrians, and on the march he took their towns Oeneon and Eupalium; for they did not come over.

When they were in the territory of Naupactus, and the Aetolians had now joined them, they ravaged the land and took the suburb, which was unwalled; and coming against Molycreium, a colony of the Corinthians but subject to the Athenians, they took it.

Demosthenes the Athenian (for he happened still to be around Naupactus after the events in Aetolia), learning of the army in advance and fearing for the town, went and persuaded the Acarnanians, with difficulty because of his withdrawal from Leucas, to help Naupactus.
And they sent with him on the ships a thousand hoplites, who went in and saved the place; for there was a danger that, since the wall was large and the defenders few, they would not hold out.

Eurylochus and those with him, when they saw that the army had entered and that it was impossible to take the city by force, withdrew, not to the Peloponnese, but to what is now called Aeolis, Calydon and Pleuron and the places there, and to Proschium in Aetolia.

For the Ambraciots came to them and persuaded them to attack with them Amphilochian Argos and the rest of Amphilochia, and Acarnania at the same time, saying that, if they got control of these, the whole mainland would become allied to the Lacedaemonians.

Eurylochus was persuaded, dismissed the Aetolians, and stayed quiet with his army in these regions, until he should have to help the Ambraciots when they had taken the field around Argos. And the summer ended.

The Athenians in Sicily, in the following winter, advancing with their Greek allies and with those of the Sicels who had been ruled by force by the Syracusans and had been their allies but had revolted and were fighting on their side, attacked Inessa, the Sicel town, whose acropolis the Syracusans held, and when they could not take it, they went away.
During the retreat the Syracusans from the fort attacked the allies, who were retreating behind the Athenians, and falling upon them routed part of the army and killed not a few.

And after this Laches and the Athenians made several landings from the ships in Locris, and at the river Caicinus they defeated in battle about three hundred of the Locrians who came to help, with Proxenus son of Capaton, and took their arms and went away.

In the same winter the Athenians also purified Delos, in accordance with some oracle. Pisistratus the tyrant had also purified it before, not the whole island, but as much of it as could be seen from the temple; but at this time the whole was purified in the following way.

They removed all the graves of the dead that were in Delos, and proclaimed that in future no one should die on the island or give birth there, but should be carried over to Rheneia. Rheneia is so short a distance from Delos that Polycrates, the tyrant of the Samians, who was powerful for some time with his navy and ruled the other islands and took Rheneia, dedicated it to Delian Apollo, binding it to Delos with a chain. And it was then, after the purification, that the Athenians first held the five-yearly festival, the Delia.

There had also been in old times a great gathering at Delos of the Ionians and the surrounding islanders; for they came to the festival with their wives and children, as the Ionians now do to the Ephesia, and a contest was held there, both athletic and musical, and the cities brought choruses.

Homer shows most clearly that it was so in these verses, which are from the hymn to Apollo:
But when, Phoebus, your heart delighted most in Delos,
where the Ionians in trailing robes gather for you
with their children and wives in your street;
there with boxing and dancing and song
they delight you, remembering you, whenever they hold the contest.

And that there was also a musical contest and that men went there to compete he shows again in these verses, which are from the same hymn; for after singing of the Delian chorus of women he ended his praise with these lines, in which he also mentioned himself:
But come, may Apollo be gracious, together with Artemis,
and farewell, all of you. And remember me hereafter too,
whenever some one of the men on earth,
another much-suffering stranger, comes here and asks:
‘Maidens, who is the sweetest of singers to you
who comes here, and in whom do you delight most?’
And all of you, answer well and with one voice:
‘A blind man, and he lives in rocky Chios.’

So much Homer testified, that there was in old times too a great gathering and festival at Delos; later the islanders and the Athenians still sent choruses with offerings, but the contests and most of the rest were abolished by misfortunes, it seems, until the Athenians at this time held the contest, and horse races too, which had not been held before.

In the same winter the Ambraciots, as they had promised Eurylochus when they kept his army back, made an expedition against Amphilochian Argos with three thousand hoplites, and invading the Argive land they seized Olpae, a strong fort on a hill by the sea, which the Acarnanians had once fortified and used as a common court of justice; it is about twenty-five stades from the city of the Argives, which is on the sea.

Some of the Acarnanians went to help at Argos, while the others encamped in the place in Amphilochia called Crenae, watching for the Peloponnesians with Eurylochus, so that they should not pass through to the Ambraciots unnoticed.

They also sent for Demosthenes, who had commanded the Athenians in Aetolia, to be their leader, and for the twenty Athenian ships that happened to be around the Peloponnese, commanded by Aristoteles son of Timocrates and Hierophon son of Antimnestus.

The Ambraciots at Olpae also sent a messenger to their city, asking the people to come to their help in full force, fearing that those with Eurylochus might not be able to get through the Acarnanians, and that they would either have to fight alone, or, if they wanted to retreat, it would not be safe.

The Peloponnesians with Eurylochus, when they learned that the Ambraciots had arrived at Olpae, set out from Proschium and went to help with all speed, and crossing the Achelous they advanced through Acarnania, which was empty because of the help sent to Argos, having on their right the city of the Stratians and its garrison, and on their left the rest of Acarnania.

And passing through the land of the Stratians they advanced through Phytia and then along the edge of Medeon, then through Limnaea; and they entered the land of the Agraeans, no longer Acarnanian but friendly to them.

Reaching Mount Thyamus, which belongs to the Agraeans, they went across it and came down into the Argive land when it was already night, and passing between the city of the Argives and the Acarnanian guard at Crenae they escaped notice and joined the Ambraciots at Olpae.

Having united, at daybreak they took up a position at the place called Metropolis and made a camp. Not long afterwards the Athenians arrived with the twenty ships in the Ambracian Gulf to help the Argives, and Demosthenes with two hundred Messenian hoplites and sixty Athenian archers.

The ships lay at anchor off the hill of Olpae on the sea side; the Acarnanians and a few of the Amphilochians (for most were held back by force by the Ambraciots) had already gathered at Argos and were preparing to fight their opponents, and they chose Demosthenes as leader of the whole allied force together with their own generals.

He led them up near Olpae and encamped, and a great ravine separated them. For five days they kept quiet, and on the sixth both sides drew up for battle. And (since the army of the Peloponnesians was larger and outflanked his) Demosthenes, fearing that he might be surrounded, placed in ambush in a sunken road overgrown with bushes hoplites and light troops, together about four hundred, so that at the moment of the clash itself they might rise up at the point where the enemy overlapped and get behind them.

When both sides were ready, they came to close quarters, Demosthenes holding the right wing with the Messenians and a few Athenians, while the rest was held by the Acarnanians, drawn up by tribes, and the Amphilochian javelin-men who were present, and the Peloponnesians and Ambraciots were drawn up mixed together, except the Mantineans; these were massed rather on the left, not holding the tip of the wing, but Eurylochus and those with him held the extreme left, opposite the Messenians and Demosthenes.

When they were already at close quarters and the Peloponnesians outflanked with their wing and were encircling the right of their opponents, the Acarnanians from the ambush came upon them from behind, attacked and routed them, so that they did not stand to resist and in their panic put the greater part of the army to flight too; for when they saw the division of Eurylochus, which was the strongest, being destroyed, they were much more afraid. And the Messenians, who were there with Demosthenes, carried through most of the work.
The Ambraciots and those on the right wing defeated those opposite them and pursued them to Argos; for they happen to be the most warlike of the peoples in that region.

But as they came back and saw that the main body had been defeated and the rest of the Acarnanians were pressing on them, they escaped with difficulty to Olpae, and many of them were killed, rushing in disorder and with no order at all, except the Mantineans; these kept their ranks best of the whole army in the retreat. And the battle ended late in the evening.

On the next day Menedaeus, since Eurylochus and Macarius were dead, had taken over the command himself, and being at a loss, after so great a defeat, how he could either stay and endure a siege, shut in by land and by sea by the Attic ships, or retreat and get away safely, he made a proposal about a truce and a retreat to Demosthenes and the Acarnanian generals, and at the same time about taking up the dead.

They gave back the dead, set up a trophy themselves, and took up their own dead, about three hundred in number; a retreat, however, they did not openly grant to all by treaty, but Demosthenes with his fellow generals, the Acarnanians, secretly made a treaty with the Mantineans and Menedaius and the other commanders of the Peloponnesians and those of them who were most considerable, allowing them to withdraw speedily, wishing to strip bare the Ambraciots and the hired crowd [of foreigners], and above all wanting to discredit the Lacedaemonians and Peloponnesians with the Hellenes there, as having betrayed them and preferred their own interest.
And they took up their dead and buried them hastily, as best they could, and those to whom it had been granted secretly planned their withdrawal;

but word was brought to Demosthenes and the Acarnanians that the Ambraciots from the city, in full force, in response to the first message from Olpae, were coming to help through the territory of the Amphilochians, wishing to join those in Olpae, and knowing nothing of what had happened.
And he immediately sent a part of his army to lay ambushes on the roads and to seize the strong positions in advance, and at the same time prepared to march against them with the rest of the army.

In the meantime the Mantineans and those included in the treaty went out on the pretext of gathering herbs and firewood and stole away in small groups, at the same time collecting the things they had supposedly gone out for; and when they had already advanced far from Olpae, they withdrew more quickly.

But the Ambraciots and the others, as many as † happened to have come out thus † together in a body, when they realized that they were going away, rushed off themselves too and ran at full speed, wishing to overtake them.

The Acarnanians at first thought that all alike were leaving without a truce and pursued the Peloponnesians too, and when some of their own generals tried to stop them, saying that a truce had been made with them, someone hurled a javelin at them, thinking that they were being betrayed; afterwards, however, they let the Mantineans and the Peloponnesians go, but killed the Ambraciots.

And there was much dispute and uncertainty as to whether a man was an Ambraciot or a Peloponnesian. And they killed about two hundred of them; the rest escaped into Agraïs, which was on the border, and Salynthius, the king of the Agraeans, being their friend, received them.

Meanwhile the Ambraciots from the city arrived at Idomene. Idomene consists of two high hills; of these the larger had been seized in advance, as night came on, by the men sent ahead by Demosthenes from the camp, who escaped notice and got there first (the smaller one the Ambraciots had happened to climb before), and they bivouacked there.
Demosthenes, after dining, set out with the rest of the army immediately at nightfall, he himself with half of it making for the pass, and the other half through the Amphilochian mountains.
And at dawn he fell upon the Ambraciots, who were still in their beds and had no previous knowledge of what had happened, but much rather thought that these were their own men;
So when he fell upon their army, they routed it, and killed most of them on the spot, while the rest rushed in flight over the mountains.

But the roads had been seized in advance, and at the same time the Amphilochians were familiar with their own country and were light-armed against hoplites, while the others were unfamiliar with it and did not know which way to turn, so they fell into ravines and into the ambushes laid beforehand and perished.

And after resorting to every form of flight, some turned even to the sea, which was not far off, and when they saw the Attic ships sailing along the coast, just at the moment of the action, they swam out to them, thinking in their immediate fear that it was better for them to be killed, if they must be, by those in the ships than by the barbarian and most hated Amphilochians.

And on the next day a herald came to them from the Ambraciots who had fled from Olpae to the Agraeans, to ask for the recovery of the dead whom they had killed after the first battle, when they were going out together with the Mantineans and those under the truce, without a truce themselves.
The herald, seeing the arms of the Ambraciots from the city, was amazed at their number; for he did not know of the disaster, but thought that they were those of the men with his own party.

And someone asked him what he was amazed at and how many of them had been killed, the questioner thinking in turn that the herald was from those at Idomene. He said about two hundred. The questioner replied and said, ‘Well, these arms do not appear to be those of two hundred,

but of more than a thousand.’ And again the other said, ‘Then they are not those of the men who fought with us.’ And he answered, ‘They are, if indeed it was you who were fighting at Idomene yesterday.’ ‘But we fought with no one yesterday, but the day before yesterday, in the retreat.’ ‘And yet we fought yesterday with these men, who came to help from the city of the Ambraciots.’

When the herald heard this and realized that the relief force from the city had perished, he cried out aloud and, stunned by the magnitude of the present calamity, went away at once without accomplishing his errand and no longer asked for the dead.

For this was indeed the greatest disaster to befall a single Hellenic city in an equal number of days in the course of this war. And I have not recorded the number of the dead, because the multitude said to have perished is incredible in proportion to the size of the city. I know, however, that if the Acarnanians and Amphilochians had been willing, in obedience to the Athenians and Demosthenes, to take Ambracia, they would have taken it at the first shout; but as it was, they feared that the Athenians, if they held it, would be more troublesome neighbours to them.

After this they allotted a third part of the spoils to the Athenians and divided the rest among their cities. And the Athenians' share was captured at sea, but the three hundred panoplies now dedicated in the Attic temples were set apart for Demosthenes, and he brought them with him when he sailed home; and at the same time his return, after the disaster in Aetolia, was made less fearful by this exploit.

The Athenians in the twenty ships also went away to Naupactus. And the Acarnanians and Amphilochians, after the Athenians and Demosthenes had gone, granted by treaty to the Ambraciots and Peloponnesians who had taken refuge with Salynthius and the Agraeans a withdrawal from Oeniadae, whither they had also moved from Salynthius.

And for the future the Acarnanians and Amphilochians made a treaty and alliance for a hundred years with the Ambraciots on these terms: that neither the Ambraciots should march with the Acarnanians against the Peloponnesians, nor the Acarnanians with the Ambraciots against the Athenians, but that they should help defend each other's territory, and that the Ambraciots should give back whatever places or hostages of the Amphilochians they held, and should not help Anactorium, which was hostile to the Acarnanians.

In the same winter the Athenians in Sicily made a landing from their ships on the territory of Himera together with the Sicels from the interior, who had invaded the borders of Himera, and they sailed against the islands of Aeolus.
Returning to Rhegium, they found Pythodorus son of Isolochus, a general of the Athenians, who had come to take over the ships which Laches had commanded.

For the allies in Sicily had sailed to Athens and persuaded the Athenians to help them with more ships; for the Syracusans controlled their land, and being shut out from the sea by a few ships, they were preparing by collecting a fleet, determined not to put up with it.
And the Athenians manned forty ships to send to them, partly thinking that the war there would be ended sooner, and partly wishing to give their fleet practice.
So they sent out one of the generals, Pythodorus, with a few ships, and intended to send Sophocles son of Sostratides and Eurymedon son of Thucles with the larger number of ships.

Pythodorus, having already taken over Laches' command of the ships, sailed at the end of the winter against the fort of the Locrians which Laches had previously taken, and being defeated in battle by the Locrians, he withdrew.

About this very spring the stream of fire flowed from Aetna, as also before, and destroyed some of the land of the Catanaeans, who live under Aetna the mountain, which is the highest mountain in Sicily.
This eruption is said to have happened in the fiftieth year after the previous eruption, and in all the eruption has occurred three times since Sicily has been inhabited by Hellenes.
These things happened in this winter, and the sixth year ended for this war, of which Thucydides wrote the history.

In the following summer, about the time the grain was coming into ear, ten ships of the Syracusans and an equal number of Locrian ships sailed to Messene in Sicily and occupied it, the inhabitants themselves having invited them, and Messene revolted from the Athenians.

The Syracusans did this chiefly because they saw that the place offered an approach to Sicily and feared that the Athenians might some day use it as a base and come against them with a greater force, and the Locrians out of hatred of the Rhegians, wishing to crush them from both sides.

And at the same time the Locrians had invaded the territory of the Rhegians in full force, so that they might not help the Messenians, and at the same time also because Rhegian exiles who were with them urged them on; for Rhegium had for a long time been in a state of faction, and it was impossible at the moment to resist the Locrians, for which reason they attacked all the more.
After ravaging the land the Locrians withdrew with their infantry, while the ships guarded Messene; and other ships that were being manned were to anchor there and carry on the war from there.

About the same time in the spring, before the grain was ripe, the Peloponnesians and their allies invaded Attica (Agis son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, was in command), and settling down there they ravaged the land.

The Athenians sent the forty ships to Sicily, as they had been preparing to do, and the remaining generals, Eurymedon and Sophocles; for Pythodorus, the third of them, had already arrived in Sicily before them.

And they told these, as they sailed past, also to look after those of the Corcyraeans in the city, who were being plundered by the exiles on the mountain; and sixty ships of the Peloponnesians had sailed there to help those on the mountain, thinking also, since there was a great famine in the city, that they would easily get control of affairs.
And to Demosthenes, who had been a private citizen since his return from Acarnania, at his own request they gave leave to use these ships, if he wished, around the Peloponnese.

And when they were sailing off Laconia and learned that the ships of the Peloponnesians were already at Corcyra, Eurymedon and Sophocles were for hurrying to Corcyra, but Demosthenes urged them first to put in at Pylos and do what was necessary and then make the voyage; and while they were objecting, by chance a storm came on and carried the ships to Pylos.

And Demosthenes at once urged them to fortify the place (for it was for this that he had sailed with them), and he pointed out that there was a great abundance of wood and stone, and that it was strong by nature and deserted, both itself and much of the country around; for Pylos is about four hundred stadia distant from Sparta and lies in what was once the land of Messenia, and the Lacedaemonians call it Coryphasium.

But they said there were many deserted headlands in the Peloponnese, if he wished to put the city to expense by occupying them. But to him this place seemed to have some advantage over any other, since there was a harbour close by and the Messenians, who were akin to it of old and spoke the same dialect as the Lacedaemonians, would do the greatest harm by using it as a base, and would at the same time be reliable guards of the place.

And when he could not persuade either the generals or the soldiers, having later also communicated his plan to the taxiarchs, he remained inactive because of the bad sailing weather, until the soldiers themselves, having nothing to do, were seized with an impulse to stand around and fortify the place.

And setting their hands to it they worked, having no iron tools for stone-cutting, but picking out stones and bringing them, and they put them together as each happened to fit; and the mud, wherever it had to be used, for lack of vessels they carried on their backs, stooping so that it would best stay on, and clasping their two hands behind them, so that it would not fall off.
And in every way they hastened to finish the most assailable points before the Lacedaemonians came up to help; for the greater part of the place was strong in itself and needed no wall.

They happened to be celebrating a festival and, when they heard of it, made light of it, thinking that, when they marched out, the enemy would either not stand against them or they would easily take the place by force; and the fact that their army was still at Athens also held them back somewhat.

The Athenians, having fortified the side of the place toward the mainland and the points that most needed it in six days, left Demosthenes there with five ships as a guard, and with the greater number of ships hastened on their voyage to Corcyra and Sicily.

The Peloponnesians who were in Attica, when they learned that Pylos had been occupied, returned home in haste, the Lacedaemonians and King Agis thinking that the affair at Pylos concerned them closely; and at the same time, having invaded early, while the grain was still green, most of them were short of food, and a storm that came on, more severe than usual for the season, distressed the army.
So for many reasons it came about that they withdrew sooner and that this invasion was the shortest; for they stayed fifteen days in Attica.

About the same time Simonides, a general of the Athenians, having gathered a few Athenians from the garrisons and a large number of the allies there, took Eion in Thrace, a colony of the Mendaeans which was hostile, as it was being betrayed to him. And when the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans came to help at once, he was driven out and lost many of his soldiers.

When the Peloponnesians had returned from Attica, the Spartans themselves and the nearest of the perioeci at once went to the help of Pylos, but the other Lacedaemonians were slower in coming, as they had just returned from another campaign.

They also sent word round the Peloponnese to come to the help of Pylos as quickly as possible, and they sent for their sixty ships at Corcyra, which were carried over the isthmus of Leucas and, escaping the notice of the Attic ships at Zacynthus, arrived at Pylos; and the land army was already there too.

But while the Peloponnesians were still sailing up, Demosthenes managed to send out two ships secretly in advance to tell Eurymedon and the Athenians in the ships at Zacynthus to come, as the place was in danger.

And the ships sailed in haste in accordance with Demosthenes' instructions; and the Lacedaemonians prepared to attack the fortification both by land and by sea, hoping to take easily a structure built in haste and held by few men.

And since they also expected the help of the Attic ships from Zacynthus, they had in mind, if they did not take it before, to block up the entrances of the harbour as well, so that the Athenians could not anchor in it.

For the island called Sphacteria, stretching along the harbour and lying close to it, makes it safe and its entrances narrow, on one side giving passage for two ships opposite the fortification of the Athenians and Pylos, and on the side toward the rest of the mainland for eight or nine; and it was all wooded and pathless because it was uninhabited, and about fifteen stadia in size.

The entrances, then, they intended to close tight with ships placed prow outwards; and fearing that the enemy might make war on them from this island, they carried hoplites across to it and posted others along the mainland.

For in this way both the island and the mainland would be hostile to the Athenians, as it had no landing place (for the parts of Pylos itself outside the entrance, toward the open sea, being without harbours, would give them no base from which to help their own men), while they themselves, without a sea battle or risk, would in all likelihood take the place by siege, since there was no grain in it and it had been occupied with little preparation.

When they had decided this, they began carrying the hoplites over to the island, choosing them by lot from all the companies. Others too had crossed over before, in turn, but the last, who were also caught there, were four hundred and twenty, with the Helots attending them; and their commander was Epitadas son of Molobrus.

Demosthenes, seeing that the Lacedaemonians were about to attack with ships and infantry at the same time, made preparations himself too, and the triremes that remained to him of those left behind he drew up under the fortification and fenced them round with a stockade, and the sailors from them he armed with poor shields, most of them made of wicker; for it was not possible to procure arms in a deserted place, but even these they took from a thirty-oared privateer and a light boat of some Messenians, who happened to come by. And of these Messenians there were about forty hoplites, whom he used along with the others.
for they themselves, never expecting to be beaten at sea, had not built the wall strong there, and if the enemy forced a landing the place became capable of being taken.
So at this point, going down to the very edge of the sea, he posted his hoplites to keep the enemy off, if he could, and exhorted them as follows.

‘Men who have joined in this danger with me, let none of you in such a necessity wish to appear clever by calculating all the danger surrounding us, but rather let him go to meet the enemy without reflection, full of good hope, and believing that he will survive even these perils. For whatever has come to necessity, as this has, admits of calculation least of all and requires the quickest risk.
And I see that most things are on our side, if we are willing to stand our ground and not, terrified by their numbers, betray the advantages we have.

For I consider the difficulty of landing at this place to be ours, which, if we stand our ground, becomes an ally, but if we give way, difficult though it is, will be easy to pass when no one prevents it, and we shall find the enemy more formidable, since his retreat will not be easy, if he is hard pressed by us too (for while they are on their ships they are very easy to repel, but once landed they are already on equal terms),

and we need not fear their numbers too much; for they will fight a few at a time, large though they are, because of the difficulty of bringing to shore, and it is not an army on land, greater on equal terms, but one on ships, for which many favourable conditions must come together at sea.

So I consider their difficulties a match for our numbers, and at the same time I ask you, who are Athenians and know by experience about landing from ships against others, that if anyone stands his ground and does not give way through fear of the splashing of oars and the terror of ships sailing in, the enemy can never force a landing, to stand your ground now yourselves and, defending yourselves at the very edge of the surf, to save both ourselves and the place.’
When Demosthenes had exhorted them this much, the Athenians took more courage and, going down further, posted themselves at the very edge of the sea.

The Lacedaemonians set out and attacked the fortification with their land army and at the same time with their ships, which numbered forty-three, and their admiral who sailed in command was Thrasymelidas son of Cratesicles, a Spartan. And he attacked just where Demosthenes expected.

And the Athenians defended themselves on both sides, from land and from sea; and the enemy, dividing into a few ships at a time, because it was not possible for more to put in, and resting in turns, made their attacks, using all eagerness and exhortation, in the hope of pushing them back and taking the fortification.

Of all men Brasidas was the most conspicuous. For being a trierarch and seeing that, because the place was difficult, the trierarchs and pilots, even where it seemed possible to put in, hesitated and took care of their ships for fear of smashing them, he shouted, saying that it was not fitting, out of sparing timber, to allow the enemy to have built a fort in their country, but he urged them to break their own ships and force a landing, and the allies not to hesitate, in return for great benefits, to give up their ships to the Lacedaemonians at the present moment, but to run them aground and, landing in any way, to master both the men and the place.

And he urged on the others in this way, and, compelling his own pilot to run the ship aground, made for the gangway; and trying to land he was beaten back by the Athenians, and having received many wounds he fainted, and when he fell into the outrigger his shield slipped off into the sea, and when it was carried ashore the Athenians picked it up and later used it for the trophy which they set up for this attack.
The others were eager, but they were unable to land, because of the difficulty of the ground and because the Athenians stood their ground and did not give way at all.

And fortune had turned around to such a point that the Athenians were fighting from land, and Laconian land at that, to ward off the Lacedaemonians sailing against them, while the Lacedaemonians were trying from ships to land on their own country, now hostile, against the Athenians; for at that time it contributed greatly to the reputation of the one people to be above all a land people and the strongest with infantry, and of the other to be a sea people and to excel most with their ships.

After making attacks that day and part of the next, they stopped; and on the third day they sent some of the ships to Asine for wood for engines, hoping that the wall by the harbour, though it was high, could be taken by engines, since landing was most possible there.
In the meantime the ships of the Athenians from Zacynthus arrived, forty in number; for some of the guard ships from Naupactus and four Chian ships had come to reinforce them.

And when they saw that both the mainland and the island were full of hoplites, and that the ships were in the harbour and not sailing out, being at a loss where to anchor, they sailed for the time to the island of Prote, which is not far away and uninhabited, and bivouacked there, and on the next day, having prepared for a sea battle, they put out to sea, in case the enemy were willing to sail out against them into the open water, and if not, intending to sail in themselves.

And the enemy neither put out against them nor happened to have done what they had intended, to block the entrances, but remaining quiet on the land they were manning their ships and preparing, if anyone sailed in, to fight a sea battle in the harbour, which was not small.

The Athenians, realizing this, rushed at them by each of the two entrances, and falling upon the greater number of the ships, which were already afloat and facing them, put them to flight, and pursuing them, as far as was possible in the short distance, damaged many, and took five, one of them with its crew; and they rammed the rest, which had fled to the land. Others were cut to pieces while still being manned, before they could put out; and some they even tied on and towed off empty, their crews having fled.

Seeing this, and deeply grieved at the disaster, because their men were being cut off on the island, the Lacedaemonians came to the rescue, and going into the sea in their armour they took hold of the ships and pulled them back; and in this each man thought that things were held up wherever he himself was not present in action.

And the tumult was great, with the manner of fighting of each side reversed around the ships; for the Lacedaemonians, from eagerness and consternation, were, so to speak, doing nothing other than fighting a sea battle from land, and the Athenians, winning and wishing to follow up their present good fortune as far as possible, were fighting a land battle from ships.
And after giving each other much trouble and inflicting wounds, they separated, and the Lacedaemonians saved their empty ships, except those taken at first.

When both sides had settled back in their camps, the Athenians set up a trophy and gave back the dead and took possession of the wrecks, and at once began sailing round the island and kept it under guard, as the men were cut off; and the Peloponnesians on the mainland, and those who had already come to help from all sides, remained in position at Pylos.

When what had happened at Pylos was reported at Sparta, they decided, regarding it as a great disaster, that the magistrates should go down to the camp and decide on the spot, seeing for themselves, whatever seemed best.

And when they saw that it was impossible to help the men and they were unwilling to run the risk of their either suffering something from hunger or being overpowered by force of numbers, they decided to make a truce with the generals of the Athenians, if they were willing, for the affairs at Pylos, and to send envoys to Athens about an agreement and to try to recover the men as quickly as possible.

When the generals accepted the proposal, a truce was made on these terms: that the Lacedaemonians should bring to Pylos and hand over to the Athenians the ships in which they had fought and all those in Laconia that were ships of war, and should not bear arms against the fortification either by land or by sea; that the Athenians should allow the Lacedaemonians on the mainland to send to the men on the island a fixed amount of grain, already kneaded, two Attic choenixes of barley-meal for each man, and two cotylae of wine and meat, and for a servant half of these; and that they should send these in under the eyes of the Athenians, and no boat should sail in secretly; and that the Athenians should guard the island no less than before, without landing on it, however, and should not bear arms against the army of the Peloponnesians either by land or by sea.

If either side violated any of these terms in any way whatever, the truce should then be at an end. It was to hold until the envoys of the Lacedaemonians should return from Athens; and the Athenians were to send them in a trireme and bring them back again. When they had come, this truce was to be at an end and the Athenians were to give back the ships in the same condition in which they received them.
The truce was made on these terms, and the ships, about sixty in number, were handed over, and the envoys were sent off. And when they arrived at Athens they spoke as follows.

‘The Lacedaemonians have sent us, Athenians, to arrange about the men on the island whatever we may persuade you to be at once advantageous to you and also likely to bring us most honour in our misfortune, as far as present circumstances allow.

And we shall not be speaking at greater length against our custom, but it is our local way, where few words suffice, not to use many, but to use more when there is occasion, by setting forth something important in words, to accomplish what is needed.
Receive them not in a hostile spirit, nor as if you were being instructed like men without understanding, but regard them as a reminder about good counsel addressed to those who know.

‘For it is in your power to make good use of your present good fortune, keeping what you hold and gaining honour and reputation besides, and not to suffer what happens to those men who obtain some good thing unexpectedly; for they always reach out for more in hope because their present good fortune too has come unexpectedly.

But those who have experienced the most changes of fortune in both directions have every reason to be most distrustful of their successes; and this would naturally apply most of all both to your city, through its experience, and to us.

Recognize this by looking also at our present misfortunes, we who, having the greatest prestige among the Hellenes, have come to you, though formerly we ourselves thought we had more power to grant what we have now come to ask of you.

And yet we did not suffer this either through lack of power or by growing insolent when greater power was added, but we were mistaken in judgment with the resources we always had, a thing in which all are equally liable.
So it is not reasonable for you, because of the present strength of your city and of what has been added to it, to think that fortune too will always be with you.

It is the mark of prudent men to treat their good things as uncertain, for safety (and the same men would also deal more wisely with misfortunes), and to consider that war does not keep company with a man in whatever portion of it he wishes to handle, but as his fortunes lead; and such men, failing least because they are not elated by trusting in its success, would be most likely to make peace while they are fortunate.

And this, Athenians, it is good for you to do now with regard to us, so that you may not some day later, if by not listening to us you should fail, as may well happen in many ways, be thought to have won by fortune even your present successes, when it is possible to leave behind for the future a reputation for strength and wisdom free from risk.

‘The Lacedaemonians invite you to a truce and an end of the war, offering peace and alliance and much friendship besides and intimacy between us, and asking in return for the men from the island, and thinking it better for both that the risk should not be run, whether they should escape by force if some chance of safety should present itself, or whether they should be besieged and rather be subdued.

And we think that great enmities would be most surely ended, not if one side, taking revenge and having got the upper hand in most of the war, binds the other by compulsory oaths and makes an agreement on unequal terms, but if, when it is possible to do the same, he turns to fairness and, conquering him in generosity too, contrary to what he expected, makes a moderate settlement.
For the adversary, now under obligation not to take revenge as one who has been forced, but to repay generosity in return, is more ready from a sense of shame to abide by what he has agreed.

And men do this toward their greater enemies more than toward those with whom they have had moderate differences; and it is their nature to give way gladly in turn to those who yield willingly, but against arrogance to take risks even against their better judgment.

‘For both of us reconciliation is good now, if ever, before something irreparable happens in the meantime and overtakes us, in which case you would necessarily have eternal enmity toward you, private as well as public, and you would be deprived of what we now offer.

While things are still undecided, and you are gaining reputation and our friendship, and our misfortune is being settled on moderate terms before anything disgraceful happens, let us be reconciled, and let us ourselves choose peace instead of war and give the other Hellenes a rest from evils; and they will regard you as chiefly responsible for this too. For they are fighting without knowing clearly which side began it; but if an end is made, which is now mostly in your power, they will give the gratitude to you.
And if you so decide, it is in your power to become firm friends of the Lacedaemonians, since they themselves invite it and you will have shown favour rather than force.

And consider in this how many good things are likely to be involved; for if we and you speak with one voice, know that the rest of the Hellenic world, being inferior, will honour us in the highest degree.’

The Lacedaemonians said this much, thinking that the Athenians had in the earlier time desired a truce but had been prevented by their own opposition, and that if peace were offered they would gladly accept it and give back the men.
But the Athenians, holding the men on the island, thought that the truce was already ready for them, whenever they wished to make it with them, and they reached for more.

They were urged on most of all by Cleon son of Cleaenetus, who was a popular leader at that time and most persuasive with the multitude; and he persuaded them to answer that the men on the island must first hand over their arms and themselves and be brought to Athens, and that when they had come, the Lacedaemonians must give back Nisaea and Pegae and Troezen and Achaea, which they had not taken in war, but by the earlier agreement, when the Athenians had conceded them because of misfortunes and at that time wanted a truce somewhat more, and then they might recover the men and make a truce for as long a time as both sides decided.
To the answer they made no reply, but they asked them to choose commissioners who, by speaking and listening about each point, would agree at leisure on whatever they could persuade each other of.

At this Cleon attacked them vehemently, saying that he had known even before that they had nothing honest in mind, and that it was clear now as well, since they were unwilling to say anything before the multitude, but wished to confer with a few men; but if they had anything sound in mind, he told them to say it to all.

The Lacedaemonians, seeing that it was not possible for them to speak before the multitude, even if they had decided to make some concession because of their misfortune, lest they be discredited with their allies by speaking and not obtaining it, and that the Athenians would not do what they proposed on moderate terms, withdrew from Athens without accomplishing anything.

When they arrived, the truce concerning Pylos was at once at an end, and the Lacedaemonians demanded back their ships, as had been agreed; but the Athenians, alleging an attack on the fortification in breach of the truce and other things which do not seem worth mentioning, did not give them back, insisting that it had been stated that, if there were any violation whatever, the truce was at an end. The Lacedaemonians objected and, protesting that the matter of the ships was an injustice, went away and resumed the war.

And the war around Pylos was carried on by both sides with all their might, the Athenians by day always sailing round the island with two ships in opposite directions (and at night all of them lay at anchor round it, except on the side toward the open sea, when there was wind; and twenty ships came to them from Athens for the blockade, so that there were seventy in all), and the Peloponnesians encamping on the mainland and making attacks on the wall, watching for an opportunity, if any should present itself, to save the men.
Meanwhile the Syracusans in Sicily and their allies, having brought up to the ships on guard at Messene the rest of the fleet which they had been preparing, were carrying on the war
from Messene (the Locrians urged them on most of all, out of hatred of the Rhegians, and they themselves had also invaded their land in full force),
and they wished to try a sea battle, seeing that the Athenians had only a few ships present, and learning that the greater number, those which were about to come, were blockading the island.

For if they were victorious with the fleet, they hoped, by blockading Rhegium by land and with ships, to subdue it easily, and that their situation would then become strong; for since Rhegium, the promontory of Italy, and Messene in Sicily lie close together, it would not be possible for the Athenians to lie in wait there and command the strait.

The strait is the sea between Rhegium and Messene, where Sicily is nearest to the mainland; and this is the so-called Charybdis, through which Odysseus is said to have sailed. Because of its narrowness, and because the sea falls into it from great open seas, the Tyrrhenian and the Sicilian, and is full of currents, it was naturally considered dangerous.

In this strait, then, the Syracusans and their allies, with a few more than thirty ships, were compelled late in the day to fight a sea battle over a vessel that was sailing through, putting out against sixteen ships of the Athenians and eight Rhegian ones.

And being defeated by the Athenians, they sailed away in haste, each as best they could, to their own camps, the one at Messene and the one at Rhegium, having lost one ship; and night came on during the action.

After this the Locrians left the territory of the Rhegians, and the ships of the Syracusans and their allies, gathering at Peloris in the territory of Messene, lay at anchor, and their infantry was with them.
The Athenians and Rhegians sailed up and, seeing the ships empty, attacked them, and through an iron grappling hook thrown upon it they themselves lost one ship, the men swimming away.

And after this, when the Syracusans had embarked on their ships and were being towed along the shore by a rope toward Messene, the Athenians attacked again, and when the enemy swung out to sea and rammed first, they lost another ship.
And having had no worse of it in the passage along the shore and in the sea battle that took place in this way, the Syracusans made their way into the harbour at Messene.

And the Athenians, since it was reported that Camarina was being betrayed to the Syracusans by Archias and his associates, sailed there; and meanwhile the Messenians, in full force, made an expedition by land and at the same time with their ships against Naxos, the Chalcidian city on their border.

And on the first day, having shut the Naxians within their walls, they ravaged the land, and on the next day they sailed round with their ships and ravaged the land along the river Acesines, while with their infantry they attacked the city.

Meanwhile many of the Sicels came down over the heights to help against the Messenians. And when the Naxians saw them, taking courage and encouraging one another that the Leontines and the other Hellenes, their allies, were coming to their aid, they rushed out suddenly from the city and fell upon the Messenians, and routing them they killed more than a thousand, and the rest got back home with difficulty; for the barbarians fell upon them on the roads and destroyed most of them.

And the ships, after putting in at Messene, later separated, each for home. The Leontines and their allies, together with the Athenians, at once marched against Messene, as it had been weakened, and attacking, the Athenians made attempts with their ships at the harbour, and the infantry against the city.

But the Messenians and some of the Locrians with Demoteles, who had been left behind as a garrison after the disaster, made a sally, and falling upon them suddenly routed the greater part of the army of the Leontines and killed many. Seeing this, the Athenians landed from their ships and came to help, and pursued the Messenians back into the city, falling upon them while they were in disorder; and after setting up a trophy they withdrew to Rhegium.
After this the Hellenes in Sicily made expeditions by land against one another without the Athenians.
At Pylos the Athenians were still besieging the Lacedaemonians on the island, and the camp of the Peloponnesians on the mainland remained in its position.

But the blockade was laborious for the Athenians through lack of food and water; for there was no spring except one on the acropolis of Pylos itself, and that not a large one, but most of them scraped away the shingle by the sea and drank such water as was to be expected.
And they were cramped for room, encamping in a small space, and as the ships had no anchorage, some took their meals on land in turn, while others lay at anchor out at sea.
