And the time, going on beyond all expectation, caused the greatest discouragement, since they had thought to reduce by siege within a few days men who were on a desert island and used brackish water.

The cause was that the Lacedaemonians had announced that anyone who wished might bring into the island ground grain and wine and cheese and any other food that might be useful for a siege, fixing a high price in silver, and promising freedom to any of the Helots who brought it in.

And others brought it in, running the risk, and especially the Helots, putting out from the Peloponnese from wherever they happened to be and coming to land while it was still night on the side of the island facing the open sea.

Above all they watched for a wind to carry them in; for they more easily escaped the notice of the guard of triremes whenever the wind blew from the sea; for it became impossible to lie at anchor around the island, while for them the landing was made without regard for cost; for they ran their boats aground, a value having been set on them in money, and the hoplites kept watch at the landing places of the island. But all who took the risk in calm weather were caught.

And divers swam in under water at the harbour too, drawing after them by a cord, in skins, poppy-seed mixed with honey and pounded linseed; at first they were not noticed, but later guards were set against them.
And both sides contrived in every way, the one to send in the food, the other not to let them escape notice.

At Athens, when they learned that the army was suffering hardship and that food was being brought in to the men on the island, they were at a loss and feared that winter might overtake their blockade, seeing that the conveyance of supplies around the Peloponnese would be impossible, the place being at the same time deserted, and since even in summer they were unable to send round enough, and that the blockade could not be maintained as the places were without harbours, but either, if they relaxed the watch, the men would survive, or, watching for stormy weather, they would sail away in the boats which brought them food.

And most of all they feared the Lacedaemonians, because they thought that it was because they had some strong ground that they no longer sent heralds to them; and they regretted not having accepted the truce.

But Cleon, aware of their suspicion against him over his preventing the agreement, said that those who brought the reports were not telling the truth. And when those who had come advised, if they did not believe them, to send some inspectors, he himself was chosen inspector by the Athenians together with Theagenes.

And realizing that he would be forced either to say the same as those whom he was slandering or, by saying the opposite, to be shown a liar, he advised the Athenians, seeing that they were also somewhat more inclined in their minds to make an expedition, that they should not send inspectors nor delay and let the opportunity slip, but if they thought the reports were true, should sail against the men.

And he pointed at Nicias son of Niceratus, who was a general, being his enemy and taunting him, saying that it was easy with a force, if the generals were men, to sail and take those on the island, and that he himself, if he were in command, would do it.

Nicias, since the Athenians were murmuring somewhat against Cleon, asking why he did not sail even now, if it seemed so easy to him, and at the same time seeing him taunting him, told him to take whatever force he wished and, as far as the generals were concerned, make the attempt.

Cleon at first, thinking that he was giving it up only in word, was ready, but when he realized that he really wanted to hand it over, he drew back and said that not he but Nicias was general, being already afraid and not thinking that he would dare to give way to him.

But again Nicias urged him and resigned the command at Pylos and made the Athenians witnesses of it. And they, as a crowd likes to do, the more Cleon tried to escape the voyage and to back out of what he had said, the more they urged Nicias to hand over the command and shouted to the other to sail.

So, having no way of getting out of what he had said any longer, he undertook the voyage, and coming forward he said that he was not afraid of the Lacedaemonians and that he would sail taking no one from the city, but the Lemnians and Imbrians who were present and the peltasts who had come to help from Aenus, and four hundred archers from elsewhere; and with these, he said, in addition to the soldiers at Pylos, within twenty days he would either bring the Lacedaemonians back alive or kill them on the spot.

His empty talk caused some laughter among the Athenians, but nevertheless the prudent among them were glad, reckoning that they would obtain one of two good things, either to be rid of Cleon, which they rather expected, or, if they were mistaken in this, that he would subdue the Lacedaemonians for them.
Having settled everything in the assembly, and the Athenians having voted him the expedition, he chose as colleague Demosthenes, one of the generals at Pylos, and made haste to put to sea.

He took Demosthenes as his colleague because he had learned that he was planning the landing on the island. For the soldiers, suffering because of the hardships of the place and rather besieged than besieging, were eager to run the risk. And the burning of the island had also given him further confidence.

For before, since it was mostly wooded and pathless because it had always been uninhabited, he had been afraid and thought that this was rather in favour of the enemy; for they could attack a large army after it had landed from a hidden position and do it harm. For to them the mistakes and preparations of the enemy would not be equally clear because of the wood, whereas all the mistakes of their own army would be plainly visible, so that the enemy could fall upon them unexpectedly wherever they wished; for the attack would be in their power.

And if, on the other hand, he should force his way to close quarters in thick country, he thought that the fewer, who knew the country, were stronger than the greater number who did not; and that their own army, large as it was, would be destroyed before they knew it, since there would be no view of where they ought to help one another.
It was not least from the disaster in Aetolia, which had been partly due to the wood, that these thoughts occurred to him.

But since the soldiers had been forced by the lack of room to put in at the edges of the island and take their morning meal with an outpost on guard, and someone had set fire to a little of the wood without meaning to, and after this a wind had sprung up, most of it was burned before they knew it.

So, seeing better that the Lacedaemonians were more numerous, having before suspected that they were sending in food for fewer, and that the island was easier to land on, he then prepared the attempt, as a thing worthy of the Athenians' making a greater effort, sending for troops from the allies nearby and making everything else ready.

Cleon, having sent a messenger ahead to him to say that he would come, and having the army which he had asked for, arrived at Pylos. And being together, they first sent a herald to the camp on the mainland, inviting them, if they wished, without risk to order the men on the island to hand over their arms and themselves to them, on condition that they should be kept in moderate custody until some agreement was reached about the main question.

When they did not accept, they waited one day, and on the next they put out by night, having embarked all the hoplites on a few ships, and a little before dawn they landed on both sides of the island, from the open sea and toward the harbour, being about eight hundred hoplites, and went at a run against the first guard post of the island.

For they had been disposed as follows: in this first post there were about thirty hoplites, the middle, the most level part and around the water, was held by most of them and Epitadas the commander, and a small part guarded the very end of the island facing Pylos, which was precipitous from the sea and least assailable from the land; for there was also an old fort there, made of stones picked up at random, which they thought would be useful to them, if a rather forced retreat should overtake them. So they were disposed.

The Athenians immediately destroyed the first guards, upon whom they ran, still in their beds and taking up their arms, having landed unnoticed, as they thought that the ships were sailing as usual to their station for the night.

And at daybreak the rest of the army also landed, from somewhat more than seventy ships all except the lowest rowers, each equipped as he was, and eight hundred archers and no fewer peltasts than these, and those of the Messenians who had come to help and all the others who were holding the area around Pylos, except the guards on the wall.

On Demosthenes' orders they separated into groups of two hundred and more, and in places fewer, occupying the highest points, so that the enemy, surrounded on all sides, might be in the greatest perplexity and might not know what to face, but might be exposed to attack on two sides from the multitude, if they attacked those in front, being shot at by those behind, and if those on the flanks, by those posted on either side.

And wherever they went, the enemy would always be at their backs, light-armed and the hardest to deal with, having their strength at long range in arrows and javelins and stones and slings, whom it was not even possible to come at; for they were victorious even when fleeing, and pressed upon them when they withdrew. With such a plan Demosthenes both originally conceived the landing and arranged it in the action;

and those with Epitadas, who were the greatest part of those on the island, when they saw that the first guard post had been destroyed and an army was advancing on them, formed up together and advanced on the hoplites of the Athenians, wishing to come to close quarters; for these were posted opposite them, and the light-armed on the flank and at the rear.

They were not able, however, to engage the hoplites or to make use of their own experience; for the light-armed, shooting from both sides, kept them back, and at the same time the hoplites did not advance against them, but stayed quiet; the light-armed they routed wherever they ran at them and pressed them hardest, and these turned round and defended themselves, being men lightly equipped and easily getting a start in flight, because of the difficulty of the ground and its roughness from the former lack of inhabitants, where the Lacedaemonians in their armour could not pursue.

For some short time, then, they skirmished with each other in this way; but when the Lacedaemonians were no longer able to dash out quickly where they were attacked, the light-armed, realizing that they were already slower in defending themselves, and having themselves gained the greatest confidence from the sight, since they appeared many times more numerous, and having become accustomed to their no longer seeming so formidable to them, because they had not at once suffered as much as they had expected, as when they first landed with their spirits enslaved at the thought of going against Lacedaemonians, despising them and raising a shout, they rushed at them in a body and pelted them with stones and arrows and javelins, whatever each had at hand.

The shout raised with the charge struck consternation into men unaccustomed to such fighting, and the dust from the newly burned wood went up thick into the air, and it was impossible to see what was in front of one because of the arrows and stones from many men flying at the same time with the dust.

And the action then became hard for the Lacedaemonians; for their felt caps did not keep out the arrows, and the javelins broke off in them when they were struck, and they could do nothing for themselves, being shut off from seeing ahead, and, because of the louder shouting of the enemy, not hearing the orders given among them, with danger standing around them on all sides and having no hope of how they should defend themselves and be saved.

At last, since many were now being wounded because they kept turning back and forth on the same spot, they closed ranks and went to the farthest fort on the island, which was not far off, and to their own guards.

And when they gave way, then the light-armed, emboldened, pressed upon them with still louder shouting, and those of the Lacedaemonians who were caught as they retreated were killed, while most of them escaped to the fort and posted themselves with the guards there all along it, to defend it wherever it was assailable.
And the Athenians, following, were unable to go round them and encircle them because of the strength of the place, but approaching from the front they tried to drive them out.

And for a long time and most of the day both sides, suffering from the battle and thirst and the sun, held out, the one trying to drive the enemy from the height, the other not to give way; and the Lacedaemonians defended themselves more easily than before, since there was no encircling of them on the flanks.

When it was endless, the general of the Messenians came to Cleon and Demosthenes and said that they were toiling in vain; but if they were willing to give him some part of the archers and the light-armed to go round to the enemy's rear by whatever path he himself could find, he thought he would force the approach.

Having received what he asked for, he set out from a hidden spot so that the enemy should not see him, and advancing wherever the cliffs of the island allowed a foothold, and where the Lacedaemonians, trusting in the strength of the place, kept no guard, he got round with great difficulty and barely, unnoticed, and suddenly appearing on the height at their rear, he struck the one side with consternation by the unexpectedness of it, and greatly strengthened the other, who saw what they were expecting.

And the Lacedaemonians, now being shot at from both sides and finding themselves in the same misfortune, to compare small with great, as that at Thermopylae, for those men were destroyed when the Persians came round by the path, and these men too, now exposed on both sides, no longer held out, but, fighting few against many and with weakness of body through lack of food, they began to give way, and the Athenians were already masters of the approaches.

Cleon and Demosthenes, realizing [that], if they gave way even a little more, they would be destroyed by their own army, stopped the battle and held back their own men, wishing to bring them to the Athenians alive, in the hope that perhaps, on hearing the proclamation, they might be broken in spirit so as to hand over their arms and yield to the present danger.
And they proclaimed that, if they wished, they should hand over their arms and themselves to the Athenians, for these to decide as they thought fit.

When they heard this, most of them lowered their shields and waved their hands, showing that they accepted the proclamation. After this, when the armistice had been made, Cleon and Demosthenes met for a conference, and on their side Styphon son of Pharax, since of their earlier commanders the first, Epitadas, had died, and the one chosen after him, Hippagretas, was lying among the dead, still alive but taken for dead, and he himself had been chosen third to command according to law, if anything should happen to those men.
Styphon and those with him said that they wished to send a herald across to the Lacedaemonians on the mainland to ask what they ought to do.

And as the Athenians let none of them go, but themselves called heralds from the mainland, and questions were exchanged two or three times, the last man who sailed across to them from the Lacedaemonians on the mainland reported that [the] ‘Lacedaemonians bid you yourselves decide about yourselves, doing nothing dishonourable’; and they, after consulting among themselves, handed over their arms and themselves.

And that day and the following night the Athenians kept them under guard; and on the next day the Athenians set up a trophy on the island and made all other preparations for the voyage, and distributed the men among the trierarchs for safekeeping, while the Lacedaemonians sent a herald and carried their dead across.

The number of those who died on the island and were taken alive was as follows; four hundred and twenty hoplites in all had crossed over; of these, three hundred less eight were brought away alive, and the rest had died. And of those taken alive about a hundred and twenty were Spartans. Of the Athenians not many were killed; for the battle was not a pitched one.
The whole time during which the men [who were] on the island were besieged, from the sea battle to the battle on the island, was seventy-two days.

For about twenty of these days, during which the envoys were away about the truce, they were given rations, and for the rest they were fed by those who sailed in secretly. And there was some grain on the island and other food was found there; for the commander Epitadas had been giving each man less than his means allowed.

So the Athenians and the Peloponnesians withdrew with their armies from Pylos, each homeward, and Cleon's promise, mad as it was, came true; for within twenty days he brought the men, as he had undertaken.

And of all the events of the war this was the most contrary to expectation for the Hellenes; for they thought that the Lacedaemonians would not give up their arms either through hunger or through any necessity, but that, keeping them and fighting as best they could, they would die.

And they did not believe that those who surrendered were like those who had died, and when one of the allies of the Athenians some time later asked one of the prisoners from the island, to vex him, whether their dead were brave men, he answered him that the spindle, meaning the arrow, would be worth a great deal if it could pick out the brave, making it clear that whoever happened to be in the way of the stones and arrows was killed.

When the men had been brought, the Athenians decided to keep them in chains until some agreement was reached, but if the Peloponnesians before that invaded their land, to bring them out and kill them.

They established a garrison at Pylos, and the Messenians from Naupactus, as to their fatherland (for Pylos is in what was once the land of Messenia), sent there the most suitable of their own men and plundered Laconia and did very great harm, as they spoke the same dialect.

The Lacedaemonians, having had no experience in former times of raiding and of such warfare, since the Helots were deserting and they feared that some revolution might go still further among them in the country, did not bear it easily, but, although not wishing to let the Athenians see it, they kept sending envoys to them and tried to recover both Pylos and the men.
But the Athenians kept reaching for more and sent them away unsuccessful, though they came often. These were the events at Pylos.

In the same summer, immediately after this, the Athenians made an expedition against Corinthian territory with eighty ships and two thousand of their own hoplites, and two hundred cavalry on horse-transport ships; and of the allies the Milesians and Andrians and Carystians also went with them, and Nicias son of Niceratus was general with two others.

Sailing, they put in at dawn between Chersonesus and Rheitus on the beach of the place above which is the Solygeian hill, on which the Dorians of old established themselves and made war on the Corinthians in the city, who were Aeolians; and there is now a village on it called Solygeia. From this beach where the ships put in, this village is twelve stadia distant, the city of the Corinthians sixty, and the Isthmus twenty.

The Corinthians, having learned in advance from Argos that the army of the Athenians would come, had long before come to the Isthmus to help, all of them except those beyond the Isthmus; and in Ambracia and in Leucas five hundred of them were away as a garrison; and the rest in full force were watching where the Athenians would put in.

But when the Athenians escaped their notice by sailing in at night and the signals were raised to them, they left half of their men at Cenchreae, in case the Athenians should go against Crommyon, and hastened to the rescue.

And Battus, one of the two generals (for there were two present at the battle), taking a company, went to the village of Solygeia to guard it, as it was unwalled, while Lycophron engaged with the rest.
And first the Corinthians attacked the right wing of the Athenians, which had just landed in front of Chersonesus, and then the rest of the army too. And the battle was fierce and all hand to hand.

And the right wing of the Athenians and Carystians (for these were posted at the end) received the Corinthians and pushed them back with difficulty; but they, retreating to a stone wall (for the ground was all uphill), pelting them with stones from above, and raising the paean, came on again, and when the Athenians received them the battle was hand to hand again.

And a company of the Corinthians, coming to the help of their own left wing, routed the right wing of the Athenians and pursued it to the sea; but again from the ships the Athenians and the Carystians turned back.

The rest of the army on both sides fought continuously, and especially the right wing of the Corinthians, where Lycophron was, defending itself against the left of the Athenians; for they expected them to make an attempt on the village of Solygeia.

For a long time, then, they held out without giving way to each other; then (for the cavalry were of use to the Athenians fighting with them, as the others had no horses) the Corinthians turned and withdrew to the hill and grounded their arms and no longer came down, but stayed quiet.

In this rout most of them were killed on the right wing, and Lycophron the general. The rest of the army, in this way, without much pursuit or hasty flight taking place, when it was forced back, withdrew to the high ground and established itself there.
The Athenians, as they no longer came against them to fight, stripped the dead and took up their own, and at once set up a trophy.

To the half of the Corinthians who were stationed at Cenchreae as guards in case the enemy should sail against Crommyon, the battle was not visible because of Mount Oneium; but when they saw the dust and [when] they realized, they came to help at once. And the older men of the Corinthians from the city also came to help when they perceived what had happened.

The Athenians, seeing them all advancing together, and thinking that help from the nearby neighbouring Peloponnesians was coming on, withdrew in haste to their ships, taking the spoils and their own dead except two, whom they left behind, being unable to find them.

And going on board their ships they crossed over to the islands lying off the coast, and from them, sending a herald, they recovered under truce the dead whom they had left behind. There were killed in the battle two hundred and twelve of the Corinthians, and of the Athenians a few less than fifty.

Setting out from the islands, the Athenians sailed on the same day to Crommyon in Corinthian territory; it is a hundred and twenty stadia distant from the city. And having anchored there they ravaged the land and bivouacked for the night.

On the next day, sailing along the coast, they came first to the territory of Epidaurus and, after making a landing, they arrived at Methana, between Epidaurus and Troezen, and cutting off the isthmus of the peninsula they fortified it, [on which Methone is,] and setting up a fort there they plundered for the time after that the territory of Troezen and Halieis and Epidaurus. And with the ships, when they had fortified the place, they sailed away home.

At the same time as these things were happening, Eurymedon and Sophocles too, after they had set out from Pylos for Sicily with the ships of the Athenians, arrived at Corcyra and made an expedition with the men from the city against the Corcyraeans established on Mount Istone, who had crossed over there after the revolution and were then masters of the land and were doing much harm.

Attacking, they took the stronghold, and the men, having fled together to some high ground, came to terms that they should hand over their mercenaries, and that, after they had given up their arms, the people of the Athenians should decide about them.

And the generals carried them across under truce to the island of Ptychia for safekeeping, until they should be sent to Athens, on condition that, if anyone was caught running away, the truce should be at an end for all.
But the leaders of the people of the Corcyraeans, fearing that the Athenians would not kill them when they came there, contrived something like this;

they persuaded a few of those on the island, by secretly sending friends and instructing them to say, as if out of goodwill, that it would be best for them to run away as quickly as possible, and that they themselves would get a boat ready; for the generals of the Athenians were indeed about to hand them over to the people of the Corcyraeans.
And when they had persuaded them, and they were caught sailing away in the boat which the others had contrived, the truce was broken and they were all handed over to the Corcyraeans.

And what contributed not least to this, so that the pretext became exact and those who devised it set about it with less fear, was that the generals of the Athenians made it plain that they would not wish the men to be conveyed by others, since they themselves were sailing to Sicily, and the honour to go to those who brought them.

The Corcyraeans took them over and shut them up in a large building, and later, leading them out twenty men at a time, they led them through two lines of hoplites posted on either side, bound to one another and being struck and stabbed by those posted along the lines, if anyone saw among them a personal enemy; and men with whips walking beside them hurried on the way those who went more slowly.

And up to sixty men they led out and killed in this way without those in the building noticing (for they thought that they were leading them away to move them somewhere else); but when they perceived it and someone told them, they called on the Athenians and urged them, if they wished, to kill them themselves, and they were no longer willing to come out of the building, and said that as far as they could they would allow no one to come in.
Nor did the Corcyraeans themselves intend to force their way in by the doors, but climbing up onto the top of the building and breaking through the roof they threw tiles and shot arrows down at them.

They defended themselves as best they could, and at the same time most of them killed themselves, thrusting into their throats the arrows which the others shot, and hanging themselves with the cords of some beds which happened to be in there with them and with strips made from their cloaks, and in every way, through most of the night (for night came on during their suffering), destroying themselves and being struck by those above, they perished.
And when day came, the Corcyraeans threw them crosswise like wicker on wagons and carried them out of the city. And the women, as many as were captured in the stronghold, they made slaves.

In such a way the Corcyraeans from the mountain were destroyed by the people, and the revolution, which had been great, ended in this, as far as this war at least was concerned; for there was no longer anything left of the other party worth mentioning.
The Athenians sailed away to Sicily, where they had set out for in the first place, and made war together with the allies there.

And the Athenians in Naupactus and the Acarnanians, at the end of the summer, made an expedition and took by treachery Anactorium, a city of the Corinthians which lies at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf; and expelling [the Corinthians] the Acarnanians themselves held the place with settlers from all their people. And the summer ended.

In the following winter Aristides son of Archippus, one of the generals of the Athenian ships collecting money, which had been sent out to the allies, arrested Artaphernes, a Persian, who was travelling from the King to Lacedaemon, at Eion on the Strymon.

And when he had been brought there, the Athenians had his letters transcribed from the Assyrian characters and read them, in which, among many other things written, the main point addressed to the Lacedaemonians was that the King did not know what they wanted; for though many envoys had come, none said the same thing; if then they wanted to say anything clear, they should send men to him with the Persian.

Artaphernes the Athenians later sent in a trireme to Ephesus, and envoys with him; and these, learning there that King Artaxerxes son of Xerxes had recently died (for about this time he died), returned home.

In the same winter the Chians too pulled down their new wall at the bidding of the Athenians, who suspected that they intended some revolt against them, after obtaining, however, pledges from the Athenians and assurance, as far as was possible, that they would plan nothing harsh concerning them. And the winter ended, and the seventh year ended for this war, which Thucydides wrote.
At the very beginning of the following summer there was a partial eclipse of the sun about the new moon, and early in the same month there was an earthquake.

and after this they marched against Antandrus and took the city through treachery. And it was their intention to free the other cities called the Actaean cities, which the Athenians had formerly held, though the Mytilenaeans had possessed them, and above all Antandrus; and having strengthened it (for there were good means of building ships, since there was timber on the spot and Ida was close by, and also of the other equipment), they could easily, using it as a base, harass Lesbos, which was near, and subdue the Aeolic towns on the mainland. And they were about to prepare these things.

In the same summer the Athenians, with sixty ships and two thousand hoplites and a few cavalry, and taking along the Milesians and some others of their allies, made an expedition against Cythera; and their generals were Nicias son of Niceratus and Nicostratus son of Diitrephes and Autocles son of Tolmaeus.

Cythera is an island, and it lies off Laconia near Malea; the inhabitants are Lacedaemonians of the perioeci, and a magistrate, the judge of Cythera, crossed over there from Sparta every year, and they always sent over a garrison of hoplites and paid much attention to it.

For it was a landing place for them for the merchant ships from Egypt and Libya, and at the same time pirates troubled Laconia less from the sea, by which alone it could be harmed; for the whole island juts out towards the Sicilian and Cretan sea.

So the Athenians, having put in with their army, with ten ships and two thousand Milesian hoplites took the city on the sea called Scandeia, while with the rest of the army they landed on the part of the island facing towards Malea and advanced against the [seaside] city of the Cytherians, and they found all the inhabitants at once encamped there.

And when a battle took place the Cytherians held their ground for a short time, then they turned and fled into the upper town, and later they came to terms with Nicias and his fellow commanders to leave their own fate to the Athenians, except for death.

There had also been some talks earlier between Nicias and certain of the Cytherians, for which reason the terms of the agreement were settled for them both more quickly and more favourably, for the present and for the future; for otherwise the Athenians would have removed the Cytherians, since they were Lacedaemonians and the island lay so close to Laconia.

After the agreement the Athenians took over Scandeia, the town at the harbour, and having set a garrison over Cythera they sailed to Asine and Helus and most of the places by the sea, and making landings and spending the night in the places where it was convenient they ravaged the land for about seven days.

The Lacedaemonians, although they saw that the Athenians held Cythera and expected that they would make such landings on their own land too, nowhere opposed them with their forces gathered together, but sent garrisons throughout the country, a number of hoplites as each place required, and in other respects they were very much on their guard, fearing that some revolution might happen to them in their constitution, since the disaster on the island had happened, unexpected and great, Pylos and Cythera were occupied, and on all sides a war surrounded them, swift and impossible to guard against,

so that, contrary to their custom, they raised four hundred cavalry and archers, and in military matters, if ever, they became especially hesitant, being engaged, contrary to the existing character of their forces, in a naval struggle, and that against Athenians, for whom whatever was not attempted was always a shortfall from what they expected to accomplish;

and at the same time the many reverses of fortune that had befallen them unexpectedly in a short time caused them the greatest dismay, and they feared that some disaster might happen to them again like the one on the island.

Because of this they were less daring in battle, and they thought that whatever move they made would fail, because their judgement had lost all confidence from their former unfamiliarity with misfortune.

So while the Athenians were then ravaging the seaboard they mostly kept quiet, whenever a landing was made at a particular garrison, each thinking themselves inferior in number and being in such a state; one garrison, however, which did resist around Cotyrta and Aphrodisia, frightened the scattered crowd of light-armed troops with a charge, but when the hoplites received it, it retreated again, and a few of its men were killed and arms were taken, and the Athenians, having set up a trophy, sailed back to Cythera.

From there they sailed round to Epidaurus Limera, and after ravaging some part of the land they came to Thyrea, which belongs to the land called Cynuria, but is on the border between the Argive and Laconian territory; the Lacedaemonians, who occupied it, had given it to the expelled Aeginetans to live in, because of the services done them at the time of the earthquake and of the revolt of the Helots and because, although subject to the Athenians, they had always stood on their side.

So while the Athenians were still sailing up, the Aeginetans abandoned the wall by the sea which they happened to be building, and withdrew to the upper town, in which they lived, about ten stadia away from the sea.

And one of the Lacedaemonian garrisons in the country, which had also been helping them build the wall, refused to go into the walled town with them although the Aeginetans asked them, but it seemed to them dangerous to be shut up within the wall; and having withdrawn to the high ground, since they did not think they were a match for the enemy, they kept quiet.

Meanwhile the Athenians landed and, advancing at once with their whole army, took Thyrea. And they burned the city and plundered what was in it, and the Aeginetans, as many as had not been killed in the fighting, they brought with them to Athens, together with the commander of the Lacedaemonians who was with them, Tantalus son of Patrocles; for he had been taken alive, wounded.

They also brought a few men from Cythera, whom they thought it best to remove for safety's sake. And the Athenians decided to put these away in the islands, and that the rest of the Cytherians should live in their own land and pay a tribute of four talents, but to put to death all the Aeginetans who had been captured because of their former and constant enmity, and to imprison Tantalus along with the other Lacedaemonians from the island.

In the same summer in Sicily an armistice was first made between the Camarinaeans and the Geloans with each other; then the other Siceliots also came together at Gela, envoys from all the cities, and held talks with one another, to see whether they could somehow be reconciled. And many other opinions were expressed on both sides, as they disagreed and made claims, according as each thought they were being wronged in some way, and Hermocrates son of Hermon, a Syracusan, who was in fact the one who persuaded them most, spoke to the assembly words of this kind.

‘It is neither as a man from the smallest city, Siceliots, that I shall speak, nor from the one suffering most in the war, but publicly declaring the opinion that seems to me best for the whole of Sicily.

And as for war, how grievous it is, why should anyone list everything in it and speak at length before those who know? For no one is either forced into it by ignorance, or turned away by fear, if he thinks he will gain some advantage. But it happens that to one side the gains appear greater than the dangers, while the other is willing to undergo the dangers rather than suffer some immediate loss;
but if both sides should happen to be doing these very things at the wrong moment, exhortations to reconciliation are useful.

This would be worth very much to us too at the present time, if we were persuaded; for it was in order to settle our private interests well, each of us, that we went to war in the first place and now try to be reconciled with one another through debate, and, if it turns out that each does not go away having his fair share, we shall go to war again.

‘And yet we must recognise that this conference will not be about our private interests only, if we are wise, but about whether we shall still be able to save the whole of Sicily, which, as I judge, is being plotted against by the Athenians; and we must consider the Athenians far more compelling mediators on these matters than my words, who, having the greatest power of the Greeks, are watching for our mistakes, being here with a few ships, and under the lawful name of alliance are speciously turning our natural hostility to their own advantage.

For if we take up war and call them in, men who march even against those who do not call them in, of their own accord, and if we harm ourselves at our own expense, and at the same time pave the way to their empire, it is likely that, when they see us worn out, they will at some time come with a larger expedition themselves and try to bring all this under their power.

‘And yet, if we are wise, each of us should call in allies and take on dangers for his own city when acquiring what does not belong to us rather than when harming what we already have, and we should consider that faction is what most destroys cities, and Sicily too, whose inhabitants are all plotted against together, but are divided city by city.

Knowing this we must be reconciled, private citizen with private citizen and city with city, and try in common to save the whole of Sicily, and let it occur to no one that the Dorians among us are enemies to the Athenians, while the Chalcidian race is safe because of its Ionian kinship.
For it is not because the races are divided in two, out of hatred of one of them, that they will attack, but because they covet the good things in Sicily, which we possess in common.

They have shown this just now at the appeal of the Chalcidian race; for to those who have never once helped them according to the alliance they themselves readily rendered their due beyond the treaty.

And that the Athenians should seek this advantage and plan ahead is quite pardonable, and I do not blame those who wish to rule, but those who are more ready to obey; for it is the nature of mankind always to rule what yields, and to guard against what attacks.

Those of us who know this and do not plan ahead rightly, or anyone who has come here not having judged this most important, that all of us together should deal well with the common danger, are mistaken.

and the quickest release from it would come if we came to terms with one another; for the Athenians do not set out from their own land, but from that of those who called them in. And in this way war is not ended by war, but quarrels are ended without trouble by peace, and those who were called in, having come with a fair pretext for injustice, will go away with good reason without success.
‘So much good, then, is found with regard to the Athenians by those who take good counsel;

but peace, which all agree is the best thing, why should we not make it among ourselves as well? Or do you think that, if one man has some good and another the opposite, it is not quiet rather than war that would end the latter for each and help preserve the former, and that peace does not hold honours and splendours with less danger, and all the other things one might go through in a long speech, as about war? Having considered these things you should not disregard my words, but each should rather foresee his own safety from them.

And if anyone thinks he will surely achieve something either by justice or by force, let him not be bitterly disappointed by the unexpected, knowing that many before now, some pursuing wrongdoers with vengeance and others hoping to gain an advantage by some power, the former, so far from avenging themselves, were not even saved, while it befell the latter, instead of having more, to lose what was their own besides.

For vengeance does not succeed as a matter of right because a wrong has been done; nor is strength sure because it is confident. But the incalculable nature of the future prevails for the most part, and though it is the most treacherous of all things, it nevertheless proves the most useful too; for fearing it equally we go against one another with more forethought.

‘And now, alarmed on both counts, by the vague fear of this unseen future and by the presence of the Athenians, already dreaded, and considering that the shortfall in what each of us thought he would achieve has been sufficiently checked by these hindrances, let us send away from the country the enemies who are upon us, and let us ourselves preferably come to terms for ever, or, if not, make a truce for as long as possible and postpone our private quarrels to another time.

In short, let us recognise that if we obey me we shall each have a free city, from which, being our own masters, we shall repay with equal valour him who does us good or harm; but if we distrust me and obey others, it will not be a question of avenging ourselves on anyone, but even at best we would of necessity become friends to our worst enemies and at odds with those with whom we should not be.

‘And I, as I said at the beginning, representing the greatest city and more likely to attack someone than to defend myself, think it right, foreseeing these things, to make concessions, and not to harm my opponents so badly that I myself am harmed the more, nor, through foolish contentiousness, to think myself as much master of fortune, which I do not rule, as of my own judgement, but to give way as far as is reasonable.
And I ask the others to do the same as I, and to suffer this at your own hands and not at those of the enemy.

For it is no disgrace for kinsmen to give way to kinsmen, a Dorian to a Dorian or a Chalcidian to his kindred, and in short to us who are neighbours and fellow dwellers in one land, and that surrounded by sea, and called by one name, Siceliots; we shall go to war, I think, when it happens, and we shall come to terms again among ourselves, using common conferences;
but foreigners who invade we shall always repel together, if we are wise, since when harmed one by one we are all endangered; and we shall never again in future call in allies or mediators.

For by doing this we shall at present not deprive Sicily of two good things, getting rid of the Athenians and of a war among ourselves, and in future we shall inhabit it by ourselves, free and less plotted against by others.’

When Hermocrates had spoken thus, the Siceliots were persuaded and agreed among themselves to end the war, each keeping what they had, except that the Camarinaeans were to have Morgantina on paying a fixed sum of money to the Syracusans;

and the allies of the Athenians called their officials and told them that they would make peace and that the treaty would include them too. When these approved, they made the agreement, and after this the ships of the Athenians sailed away from Sicily.

When the generals returned, the Athenians in the city punished two of them with exile, Pythodorus and Sophocles, and fined the third, Eurymedon, on the grounds that, when they could have subdued affairs in Sicily, they had been bribed to withdraw.

So, enjoying their present good fortune, they expected nothing to oppose them, but that they could achieve both what was possible and what was more difficult alike, with a great and with a smaller force equally. The cause was their unexpected success in most things, which lent strength to their hope.

In the same summer the Megarians in the city, hard pressed in the war by the Athenians, who always invaded their country in full force twice every year, and by their own exiles from Pegae, who had been expelled by the people in a revolution and were troublesome with their raids, began to say among themselves that they ought to receive the exiles back and not let the city be ruined from both sides.
And the friends of those outside, noticing the talk, themselves also demanded more openly than before that this proposal be adhered to.

But the leaders of the people, realising that the people would not be able to hold out with them because of their hardships, became afraid and made overtures to the generals of the Athenians, Hippocrates son of Ariphron and Demosthenes son of Alcisthenes, wishing to hand over the city and thinking that the danger to them was smaller than that those they had expelled should return. And they agreed that first the Athenians should take the long walls (these were about eight stadia long, from the city to Nisaea, their harbour), so that the Peloponnesians should not come to help from Nisaea, in which they alone formed the garrison to secure Megara, and then that they would try to hand over the upper city too; and they expected that the citizens would go over more easily once this had happened.

So the Athenians, when everything had been prepared by both sides in deeds and words, sailed at nightfall to Minoa, the island of the Megarians, with six hundred hoplites, whom Hippocrates commanded, and sat down in a pit, from which they had dug clay for the bricks of the walls and which was not far away;

and those with Demosthenes, the other general, light-armed Plataeans and other frontier patrols, lay in ambush at the Enyalium, which is a little less far away. And no one noticed except the men whose business it was to know, that night.

And when dawn was about to break, these Megarian traitors did the following. For a long time they had prepared for the opening of the gates by being accustomed, as pirates, to carry a sculling boat on a cart through the ditch down to the sea by night, having persuaded the commander, and to sail out; and before it was day they brought it back again on the cart and took it into the wall through the gates, so that the watch should be invisible to the Athenians on Minoa, since no boat was to be seen in the harbour.

And on this occasion the cart was already at the gates, and when they were opened as usual for the boat, the Athenians, seeing it (for this was done by arrangement), ran at full speed from the ambush, wishing to arrive before the gates were shut again and while the cart was still in them, being an obstacle to closing them; and at the same time the Megarians acting with them killed the guards at the gates.

And first the Plataeans and patrols with Demosthenes ran in where the trophy now stands, and immediately inside the gates (for the nearest Peloponnesians had noticed) the Plataeans fought and overcame those who came to help, and secured the gates for the hoplites of the Athenians as they came on;
and then each of the Athenians, as he got inside, advanced at once against the wall.

And the Peloponnesian garrison at first resisted and defended themselves, a few of them, and some of them were killed, but most took to flight, frightened because enemies had fallen on them at night and the Megarian traitors were fighting against them, thinking that all the Megarians had betrayed them.

For it also happened that the herald of the Athenians, on his own initiative, proclaimed that any Megarian who wished could come and take his stand with the Athenians. And when they heard this, they no longer waited, but, thinking they really were being attacked in common, fled to Nisaea.

At dawn, when the walls had already been taken and the Megarians in the city were in an uproar, those who had negotiated with the Athenians, and another crowd with them which was in the secret, said that they ought to open the gates and go out to battle.

It had been agreed between them that when the gates were opened the Athenians should rush in, while they themselves were to be clearly distinguishable (for they were to anoint themselves with oil), so that they should not be harmed. And they had more security for the opening; for the four thousand Athenian hoplites from Eleusis and six hundred cavalry, marching through the night according to the agreement, had arrived.

But when they had anointed themselves and were already near the gates, one of those in the secret betrayed the plot to the other party. And these gathered together and came in a body and said that they ought neither to go out (for never before, even when they were stronger, had they dared this) nor lead the city into obvious danger; and if anyone did not obey, the battle would take place right there. They gave no sign that they knew what was going on, but insisted that they were giving the best advice, and at the same time they stayed by the gates guarding them, so that the plotters were not able to do what they intended.

The generals of the Athenians, realising that some obstacle had arisen and that they would not be able to take the city by force, at once began to wall Nisaea round, thinking that, if they took it before any help came, Megara too would

come over more quickly (and iron arrived quickly from Athens, and stonemasons and the other things needed); beginning from the wall they held and building a cross-wall on the side facing the Megarians, from there on both sides of Nisaea down to the sea the army divided the ditch and walls among them and, using stones and bricks from the suburb, and cutting down trees and timber, they built a palisade wherever it was needed; and the houses of the suburb, once given battlements, themselves served as a fortification.

And they worked the whole of that day; on the next day, towards evening, the wall was all but finished, and those in Nisaea, alarmed by a shortage of food (for they drew it day by day from the upper city), and not thinking that the Peloponnesians would come quickly to help, and regarding the Megarians as enemies, agreed with the Athenians that each should be released for a fixed sum of money after handing over his arms, and that the Athenians should deal as they wished with the Lacedaemonians, the commander and anyone else who was there.
On these terms they came out, and the Athenians, having broken off the long walls from the city of the Megarians and taken over Nisaea, prepared the rest.

Brasidas son of Tellis, a Lacedaemonian, happened at this time to be near Sicyon and Corinth, preparing an expedition to Thrace. And when he learned of the capture of the walls, fearing for the Peloponnesians in Nisaea and that Megara might be taken, he sent to the Boeotians, telling them to meet him quickly with an army at Tripodiscus (this is a village of the Megarid with this name, below Mount Geraneia), and he himself came with two thousand seven hundred Corinthian hoplites, four hundred Phliasians, six hundred Sicyonians, and those of his own who had already been gathered, thinking that he would still find Nisaea not yet taken.

When he learned the news (for he happened to have set out by night for Tripodiscus), he picked three hundred of the army and, before his coming became known, approached the city of the Megarians unnoticed by the Athenians, who were by the sea, wishing ostensibly, and at the same time in reality if he could, to make an attempt on Nisaea, but above all to enter the city of the Megarians and secure it. And he asked them to receive his men, saying that he was in hope of recovering Nisaea.

But the factions of the Megarians were afraid, the one that he might bring in the exiles and drive them out, the other that the people, fearing this very thing, might attack them and the city, being at war with itself while the Athenians lay in wait nearby, might be destroyed; so they did not receive him, but both decided to keep quiet and watch what would happen.

For each side expected that there would be a battle between the Athenians and those who had come to help, and that it was thus safer for them to join the side each favoured once it had won; and Brasidas, when he could not persuade them, withdrew again to the rest of the army.

At dawn the Boeotians arrived, having intended even before Brasidas sent to go to the help of Megara, since the danger was not foreign to them, and being already at Plataea with their whole army; but when the messenger came too, they were much more encouraged, and having sent two thousand two hundred hoplites and six hundred cavalry, they went back home with the greater part.

When the whole army was now present, not less than six thousand hoplites, and the hoplites of the Athenians were in line around Nisaea and the sea, while the light-armed were scattered over the plain, the cavalry of the Boeotians fell unexpectedly on the light-armed troops and drove them to the sea (for until then no help had yet come to the Megarians from anywhere);
but the Athenian cavalry rode out against them in turn and came to close quarters, and there was a cavalry battle for a long time, in which each side claims not to have been worsted.

For the Athenians killed and stripped the cavalry commander of the Boeotians and a few others who had charged up to Nisaea itself, and having got possession of these bodies they gave them back under truce and set up a trophy; in the action as a whole, however, neither side parted having ended decisively, but the Boeotians went back to their own people, and the Athenians to Nisaea.

After this Brasidas and the army advanced nearer to the sea and the city of the Megarians, and having occupied a suitable position they drew up in line and kept quiet, thinking that the Athenians would come against them, and knowing that the Megarians were waiting to see which side would win.

And they thought that both things were in their favour, on the one hand not attacking first and not beginning a battle and danger of their own accord, since they had openly shown that they were ready to defend themselves, and so the victory would justly be credited to them as if without a struggle, and at the same time things would also turn out rightly with regard to the Megarians;

for if they had not been seen to come, there would have been no chance for them, but they would clearly have been deprived of the city at once as if defeated; but as it was, it might happen that the Athenians themselves would not want to fight, so that they would gain without a battle what they had come for. And this is in fact what happened.

For the Megarians, when the Athenians came out and drew up beside the long walls, but kept quiet themselves too since the enemy did not attack, their generals also reckoning that the danger was not equal for them, since most things had gone well for them, if they began a battle against superior numbers, either to take Megara if they won or, if they failed, to be damaged in the best of their hoplites, while for the others it was natural to be willing to risk it, since each part of their whole force and of those present was at stake, after waiting for some time, when nothing was attempted by either side, the Athenians went away first to Nisaea and then the Peloponnesians to where they had set out from. So then the friends of the exiles among the Megarians, taking courage, opened the gates to Brasidas himself and the commanders from the cities, as having won and since the Athenians had not been willing to fight any more, and having received them they entered into talks, while those who had negotiated with the Athenians were already dismayed.
And later, when the allies had been dispersed to their cities, he too went back to Corinth and prepared the expedition to Thrace, where he had been bound in the first place;

and the Megarians in the city, when the Athenians too had withdrawn home, those who had taken the largest part in the dealings with the Athenians, knowing that they had been detected, at once slipped away, while the others, after conferring with the friends of the exiles, brought back the men from Pegae, binding them with great oaths to bear no grudge, but to give the city the best counsel.

But these, when they had come into office and held a review of arms, separated the companies and picked out about a hundred men from their enemies and from those who seemed to have had the largest part in the dealings with the Athenians, and, having compelled the people to cast an open vote about them, when they were condemned, they put them to death, and they brought the city to an extreme oligarchy.
And this change of government, brought about by very few men after a revolution, lasted for a very long time.

In the same summer, when Antandrus was about to be fortified by the Mytilenaeans, as they intended, the generals of the Athenian tribute-collecting ships, Demodocus and Aristides, who were near the Hellespont (for the third of them, Lamachus, had sailed into the Pontus with ten ships), when they learned of the fortifying of the place and thought it dangerous that it might become like Anaea opposite Samos, where the exiles of the Samians had established themselves and helped the Peloponnesians in naval matters by sending them helmsmen, and threw the Samians in the city into confusion and received those who left it; so then they gathered an army from the allies and sailed there, and having defeated in battle those who came out from Antandrus against them, they recovered the place again.

And not long after, Lamachus, who had sailed into the Pontus and anchored in the territory of Heraclea at the river Cales, lost his ships when rain fell in the uplands and the flood came down suddenly; but he himself and the army went on foot through the Bithynian Thracians, who live across in Asia, and arrived at Calchedon, the colony of the Megarians at the mouth of the Pontus.
In the same summer Demosthenes, general of the Athenians, also arrived at Naupactus with forty ships, immediately after the withdrawal from the Megarid.

Some men were going to betray Siphae (Siphae belongs to the territory of Thespiae and lies on the sea in the Crisaean Gulf); Chaeronea, which pays contributions to Orchomenus, formerly called Minyan but now Boeotian, was to be handed over by others from Orchomenus, and the Orchomenian exiles were taking a very active part and were hiring men from the Peloponnese (Chaeronea is the last town of Boeotia, next to Phanotis in Phocis), and some Phocians were also involved.

The Athenians were to seize Delium, the sanctuary of Apollo in the territory of Tanagra facing Euboea, and all this was to happen at the same time on an appointed day, so that the Boeotians should not come in a body to help at Delium, but each should be busy with the troubles in their own territory.

And if the attempt succeeded and Delium was fortified, they confidently hoped that, even if no change in the constitutions of the Boeotians took place at once, while these places were held and the land was raided and each had a refuge close at hand, things would not remain as they were, but that in time, as the Athenians joined those who had revolted, while the others did not have their forces united, they would bring them into a favourable state.

Such then was the plot being prepared, and Hippocrates himself, with a force from the city, was to march, when the moment came, into Boeotia, but he sent Demosthenes ahead with the forty ships to Naupactus, so that, having gathered an army from those parts, of Acarnanians and the other allies, he should sail against Siphae, which was to be betrayed; and a day had been fixed for them on which they were to do these things at the same time.

And Demosthenes, on his arrival, finding that Oeniadae had been forced by all the Acarnanians into the Athenian alliance, and having himself raised all the allied force in that region, first marched against Salynthius and the Agraeans and won them over, and then made his other preparations to be at Siphae when he was needed.

At the same time in the summer Brasidas, marching with one thousand seven hundred hoplites to the regions of Thrace, when he reached Heraclea in Trachis and, after he had sent a messenger ahead to Pharsalus to his friends asking them to conduct him and his army through, there came to Melitia in Achaea Panaerus and Dorus and Hippolochidas and Torylaus and Strophacus, who was proxenus of the Chalcidians, then indeed he set out.

Other Thessalians also conducted him, and from Larissa Niconidas, who was a friend of Perdiccas. For Thessaly was in any case not easy to pass through without an escort, and certainly not with arms, and among all Greeks alike it was regarded with suspicion to pass through the land of neighbours without their consent; and the mass of the Thessalians had always been well disposed to the Athenians.

So if the Thessalians had not been governed in their country by a narrow oligarchy rather than by equal laws, he would never have got through, since even then, as he was marching, others of the party that wanted the opposite met him at the river Enipeus and tried to stop him, and said that he was doing wrong by marching on without the consent of the whole people.

But those who were conducting him said that they would not take him through against their will, and that, being his hosts, they were escorting him because he had arrived unexpectedly. And Brasidas himself said that he was coming as a friend to the land of the Thessalians and to themselves, and that he was bearing arms against the Athenians, who were enemies, and not against them, and that he did not know of any enmity between the Thessalians and the Lacedaemonians such that they should not use each other's land, and that now he would not go on against their will (for he would not be able to), but that he did not think he ought to be stopped.

And when they heard this they went away, while he, on the advice of his escort, before any larger force could gather to stop him, went on at full speed without stopping. And on that day on which he set out from Melitia he reached Pharsalus and encamped by the river Apidanus, and from there he went to Phacium, and from there to Perrhaebia.

From here the Thessalian escort went back, and the Perrhaebians, who are subjects of the Thessalians, brought him to Dium in the dominion of Perdiccas, a town of Macedonia which lies at the foot of Olympus facing Thessaly.
In this way Brasidas ran through Thessaly quickly before anyone could prepare to stop him, and arrived at the court of Perdiccas and in Chalcidice.

For it was from the Peloponnese, when the affairs of the Athenians were prospering, that those in Thrace who had revolted from the Athenians and Perdiccas, out of fear, had brought out the army, the Chalcidians thinking that the Athenians would set out against them first (and at the same time the neighbouring cities of theirs that had not revolted were secretly joining in calling it in), and Perdiccas, who was not openly an enemy, but himself feared the old quarrels with the Athenians and most of all wished to subdue Arrhabaeus, king of the Lyncestians.
And the present misfortune of the Lacedaemonians made it easier for them to bring an army out of the Peloponnese.

For since the Athenians were pressing on the Peloponnese and not least on their territory, they hoped to divert them most effectively if they harassed them in turn by sending an army against their allies, especially since these were ready to maintain it and were calling them in to help them revolt.
And at the same time they were glad to send out some of the Helots on a pretext, so that they should not attempt a revolution in the present situation while Pylos was occupied;

since they had in fact also done the following out of fear of their youth and their number (for most of the Lacedaemonians' institutions had always been set up mainly with regard to their security against the Helots); they proclaimed that those of them who claimed to have proved the best in the wars for them should be selected, as if they were going to free them, making a test and thinking that those who, out of pride, each claimed first to be freed would also be the most likely to attack them.
And having selected about two thousand, these crowned themselves and went round the temples as if freed, but not long after they made away with them, and no one knew in what way each was killed.
And on this occasion they gladly sent seven hundred of them with Brasidas as hoplites, while the rest he brought out from the Peloponnese, having persuaded them with pay.

And the Lacedaemonians sent Brasidas himself chiefly because he wished it (and the Chalcidians too were eager for him), a man who at Sparta was thought to be energetic in everything and who, after he went out, proved of the greatest value to the Lacedaemonians.

For at the time, by showing himself just and moderate towards the cities, he caused most of them to revolt, and others of the places he took by betrayal, so that the Lacedaemonians, when they wanted to come to terms, as they did, had places to give in exchange and receive back, and relief from the war for the Peloponnese; and in the war that came later, after the events in Sicily, the virtue and intelligence that Brasidas showed then, known to some by experience and believed by others from hearsay, did most to create in the allies of the Athenians a desire for the Lacedaemonians.
For he was the first to go out and be thought good in every way, and he left behind the firm hope that the others too were like him.

So then, when he had arrived in Thrace, the Athenians, on learning of it, declared Perdiccas an enemy, thinking that he was responsible for the passage, and established a stronger watch over their allies in that region.

Perdiccas at once took Brasidas and the army together with his own force and marched against Arrhabaeus son of Bromerus, king of the Lyncestian Macedonians, who was his neighbour, since he had a quarrel with him and wished to subdue him.

But when he and his army, together with Brasidas, arrived at the pass into Lyncus, Brasidas said that he wished first to go and confer before making war, and make Arrhabaeus an ally of the Lacedaemonians, if he could.

And at the same time the envoys from Perdiccas had said something of this kind in Lacedaemon, that he would make many of the places around him allies of theirs, so that on this ground Brasidas thought he had the more right to deal with the affairs of Arrhabaeus in common.

But Perdiccas said that he had not brought Brasidas to be a judge of their quarrels, but rather to be a destroyer of whatever enemies he himself should point out, and that he would do wrong if, while he himself maintained half the army, he should confer with Arrhabaeus.

But Brasidas conferred with him against Perdiccas' will and after a quarrel, and, persuaded by his arguments, he led the army away before invading the country. After this Perdiccas gave a third instead of half of the provisions, thinking that he had been wronged.
In the same summer, immediately, Brasidas, taking the Chalcidians with him as well, marched against Acanthus, the colony of the Andrians, a little before the vintage.

And the Acanthians were divided among themselves about receiving him, those who were joining the Chalcidians in calling him in, and the people. Nevertheless, because of fear for the fruit, which was still outside, the multitude was persuaded by Brasidas to receive him alone and to deliberate after hearing him, and they received him; and standing before the multitude (and he was not a bad speaker either, for a Lacedaemonian) he spoke as follows.

and if we have come late, having been disappointed in our expectation from the war there, by which we hoped to destroy the Athenians quickly by ourselves, without your danger, let no one blame us; for now, when the opportunity has offered, we have come and will try to subdue them together with you.
But I am surprised at the shutting of the gates against me, and that you are not glad that I have come.
and if you have anything else in mind, or if you are going to oppose your own freedom and that of the other Greeks, it would be a terrible thing.

For it is not only that you yourselves resist, but also all those whom I approach will be less inclined to come over to me, taking it ill that you, to whom I came first, who represent an important city and are thought to have good sense, did not receive me; and I shall not be able to give a credible reason, but shall seem either to be offering an unjust freedom or to have come weak and unable to defend you against the Athenians, if they attack.

And yet with this very army which I now have, when I came to help at Nisaea, the Athenians were not willing to engage, though they were more numerous, so that it is not likely that they will send against you by sea a force equal to the army at Nisaea.

And I myself have come not for harm but for the liberation of the Greeks, having bound the authorities of the Lacedaemonians by the most solemn oaths that those whom I bring over shall truly be independent allies, and at the same time not so that we may have you as allies, having won you over either by force or by deceit, but, on the contrary, to fight as your allies, enslaved as you are by the Athenians.
So I do not think that I myself should be suspected, since I give the strongest pledges, nor be considered a powerless protector, and I think you should come over with confidence.
And if anyone, privately fearing someone, is perhaps reluctant in case I should hand the city over to some party, let him trust me most of all.
For I have not come to join a faction, nor do I think I would be offering a clear freedom if, disregarding your ancestral constitution, I were to enslave the many to the few or the fewer to all.

For that would be harsher than foreign rule, and for us Lacedaemonians there would be no thanks for our labours, but instead of honour and glory rather blame; and we would be seen ourselves to be acquiring, by the very charges with which we are fighting down the Athenians, more hatefully than he who has not displayed virtue.

For it is more shameful for men of reputation to gain an advantage by specious deceit than by open force; for the one attacks by the claim of strength, which fortune has given, the other by the plotting of an unjust mind.

So great is the circumspection we use in matters of the highest importance to us, and you could not get greater assurance besides our oaths than from those whose deeds, examined in the light of their words, give the inevitable conviction that it is in their interest too, just as I have said.

‘But if, when I offer these things, you say that you are unable, but, being well disposed, you claim that you should not be harmed for rejecting me, and that freedom does not seem to you free from danger, and that it is right to offer it to those who are also able to receive it, and not to compel anyone against his will, I shall make the gods and heroes of the country witnesses that, having come for your good, I do not persuade you, and I shall try to compel you by ravaging your land,

and I shall no longer think that I am doing wrong, but that I have some justification for two compelling reasons, for the Lacedaemonians, that they may not, with your goodwill, if you are not won over, be harmed by the money brought from you to the Athenians, and for the Greeks, that they may not be prevented by you from being freed from slavery.
For otherwise we would not be justified in doing this, nor are we Lacedaemonians obliged, except for the sake of some common good, to free those who do not wish it;
nor again do we aim at empire, but rather, being eager to stop others, we would wrong the majority if, while bringing independence to all, we allowed you who oppose it to stand in the way.

In view of this, deliberate well, and strive to be the first to begin freedom for the Greeks and to lay up everlasting glory, and yourselves to escape harm to your private property and to give your whole city the fairest name.’

Brasidas said this much. The Acanthians, after much had been said before on both sides, voted secretly, and because Brasidas had spoken persuasively and out of fear for the fruit the majority decided to revolt from the Athenians, and having bound him by the oaths which the authorities of the Lacedaemonians had sworn when they sent him out, that those he should bring over would truly be independent allies, on these terms they received the army.
And not long after Stagirus too, a colony of the Andrians, joined in the revolt. These things then happened in this summer.

At the very beginning of the following winter, when the places in Boeotia were being betrayed to Hippocrates and Demosthenes, generals of the Athenians, and Demosthenes was to meet at Siphae with the ships and the other at Delium, a mistake was made about the days on which both were to march, and Demosthenes, having sailed to Siphae first, with Acarnanians and many of the allies from there in his ships, achieved nothing, since the plot had been revealed by Nicomachus, a Phocian from Phanoteus, who told the Lacedaemonians, and they told the Boeotians;

and when all the Boeotians came to help (for Hippocrates was not yet in their land to distract them) Siphae and Chaeronea were occupied in advance. And when the conspirators learned of the mistake, they made no move in the cities.

Hippocrates, having called out the Athenians in full force, citizens and resident aliens and all the foreigners who were present, arrived at Delium too late, when the Boeotians had already withdrawn from Siphae; and having encamped the army he fortified Delium in the following way [the sanctuary of Apollo].

They dug a ditch round the sanctuary and the temple, and from the excavation they threw up the earth instead of a wall, and fixing stakes alongside, they cut down the vines around the sanctuary and threw them in, together with stones and bricks which they took from the nearby buildings they pulled down, and in every way they raised the fortification high. And they set up wooden towers where it was suitable and where no building of the sanctuary stood; for the cloister that had been there had fallen down.
Beginning on the third day after they set out from home, they worked on that day and the fourth and on the fifth until the midday meal.

Then, when most of it had been finished, the army withdrew ahead from Delium about ten stadia, as if going home, and most of the light-armed troops went straight on, while the hoplites grounded their arms and halted; but Hippocrates, staying behind still, was arranging guards and the work on the outer fortification, as much as was left, how it was to be completed.

During these days the Boeotians were gathering at Tanagra; and when they had arrived from all the cities and learned that the Athenians were moving off home, although the other Boeotarchs, who are eleven, did not approve of fighting, since the enemy were no longer in Boeotia (for the Athenians were mostly on the borders of the territory of Oropus when they grounded their arms), Pagondas son of Aeoladas, Boeotarch from Thebes together with Arianthidas son of Lysimachidas, and holding the command at the time, wishing to fight the battle and thinking it better to run the risk, called each company to him separately, so that they should not all together leave their arms, and tried to persuade the Boeotians to go against the Athenians and to fight the battle, speaking as follows.

‘Men of Boeotia, it should not even have entered the mind of any of us commanders that it is not right to come to battle with the Athenians if we do not catch them still in Boeotia. For it is Boeotia that they intend to ravage, having come from the neighbouring land and built a fort in it, and they are surely enemies in whatever place they are caught and wherever they come from to commit hostile acts.

But now, if anyone did think it safer, let him change his mind. For prudence does not admit, for those whom another attacks, the same calculation about their own land as for one who holds his own possessions and, reaching out for more, attacks someone of his own free will.

And it is the custom of your fathers to repel a foreign army that attacks, both in your own land and in that of your neighbours alike. And against the Athenians, who are moreover your neighbours, it is necessary most of all.

For against neighbours equality of strength is what makes freedom for all, and against these men above all, who try to enslave not only those near them but also those far away, how should we not go to the utmost extremity of struggle (we have as an example the Euboeans across the strait and most of the rest of Greece, how they are treated by them), and recognise that, while for others neighbours fight battles about the boundaries of land, for us, if we are defeated, one undisputed boundary will be fixed for our whole land?

For they will come in and hold our possessions by force. So much more dangerous than others is the neighbourhood of these men that we have. And those who attack their neighbours in the confidence of strength, as the Athenians do now, are accustomed to march more fearlessly against one who keeps quiet and defends himself only in his own land, but to be less ready to take on one who meets them in advance outside his borders and, if the moment is right, begins the war.

We ourselves have experience of this against these men; for by defeating them at Coronea, when they had occupied our land while we were in civil strife, we established great security for Boeotia until this day.
