Remembering this, the older among us must equal their former deeds, and the younger, sons of fathers who proved brave then, must try not to disgrace the virtues that belong to them, and, trusting that the god will be on our side, whose sanctuary they have lawlessly fortified and occupy, and in the sacrifices, which appear favourable to us who have offered them, we must close with these men and show that what they desire they may acquire by attacking those who do not defend themselves, but from those to whom it is noble always to free their own land by battle and not to enslave that of others unjustly, they will not go away without a struggle.’

With such exhortations Pagondas persuaded the Boeotians to go against the Athenians. And quickly breaking camp he led the army on (for it was already late in the day), and when he came close to their army, he halted at a place from which, since there was a hill between them, they could not see each other, and drew up his men and prepared for battle.

And Hippocrates, who was near Delium, when it was reported to him that the Boeotians were advancing, sent to the army ordering it to form in line, and he himself came not long after, leaving about three hundred cavalry near Delium, so that they might at the same time be guards, if anyone attacked it, and might watch for an opportunity and fall upon the Boeotians during the battle.

But the Boeotians set men against these to ward them off, and when all was ready for them, they appeared over the hill and grounded their arms, drawn up as they were to fight, about seven thousand hoplites and more than ten thousand light-armed troops, and a thousand cavalry and five hundred peltasts.

The Thebans and those in their district held the right wing; in the centre were the Haliartians and Coronaeans and Copaeans and the others around the lake; the left was held by the Thespians and Tanagraeans and Orchomenians. On each wing were the cavalry and light-armed troops. The Thebans were drawn up twenty-five shields deep, and the others as each happened.
This was the force and order of battle of the Boeotians;

and of the Athenians, the hoplites were drawn up eight deep along the whole army, being equal in number to their opponents, and the cavalry on each wing. Light-armed troops regularly equipped were neither present then nor did the city have any; those who had joined in the invasion, being many times more numerous than the enemy, and many unarmed men who had followed, since it was a levy in full force of the foreigners present and of the citizens, as soon as they had started for home, were not present except a few.
When they had formed in line and were already about to engage, Hippocrates the general, passing along the army of the Athenians, encouraged them and spoke as follows.
‘Athenians, the exhortation is brief, but to brave men it has the same force and is a reminder rather than a command.

Let it not occur to any of you that we are running so great a risk in a foreign land where it does not concern us. For the struggle will be in their land for ours; and if we win, the Peloponnesians will never invade your country without the cavalry of these men, and in one battle you both win this land besides and free that one more.

So advance against them in a manner worthy of the city, which each of you is proud to have as his fatherland, the first among the Greeks, and of your fathers, who defeated these men in battle under Myronides at Oenophyta and once held Boeotia.’

While Hippocrates was exhorting them thus and had gone as far as the middle of the army, but had not had time for the rest, the Boeotians, after Pagondas had exhorted them too briefly there as well, raised the paean and came on from the hill. And the Athenians came on against them and closed at a run.
And the extremities of both armies did not come to close quarters, but suffered the same thing; for torrents prevented them. The rest were engaged in a stubborn battle with pushing of shields.

And the left of the Boeotians, as far as the centre, was worsted by the Athenians, and they pressed hard on the others there and not least the Thespians. For when those drawn up beside them gave way, and they were surrounded in a narrow space, those of the Thespians who perished were cut down defending themselves hand to hand; and some of the Athenians too, thrown into confusion by the encirclement, failed to recognise and killed one another.

So this part of the Boeotians was worsted and fled to the part still fighting, but the right, where the Thebans were, got the better of the Athenians, and, pushing them back step by step at first, followed them up.
and now, from both sides, because of this and because of the Thebans following up and breaking through, a rout of the whole army of the Athenians had set in.
And some rushed to Delium and the sea, others towards Oropus, others to Mount Parnes, and others wherever each had some hope of safety.

And the Boeotians followed and killed them, especially the cavalry, both their own and the Locrians who had come to help just as the rout was happening; but when night overtook the action, the mass of the fugitives escaped more easily.
And on the next day those from Oropus and those from Delium, leaving a garrison behind (for they still held it all the same), were carried home by sea.
And the Boeotians, having set up a trophy and taken up their own dead, and stripped those of the enemy and left a guard, withdrew to Tanagra, and they planned an attack on Delium.

From the Athenians a herald going to ask for the dead met a Boeotian herald, who turned him back, saying that he would achieve nothing until he himself had returned, and then came before the Athenians and delivered the message from the Boeotians, that they had acted unjustly in transgressing the customs of the Greeks;

therefore, on behalf of the god and of themselves, the Boeotians, invoking the deities who share the altar and Apollo, gave them notice to leave the sanctuary and then carry off what belonged to them.

When the herald had said this, the Athenians sent their own herald to the Boeotians and said that they had neither done any wrong to the sanctuary nor would willingly damage it in future; for they had not entered it in the first place for that purpose, but in order to defend themselves from it against those who were rather wronging them.

And the law among the Greeks was that those who held power over each land, whether larger or smaller, also always held the sanctuaries, which were to be tended in the ways customary besides any others they were able to use.

For the Boeotians too, and most of the others who had driven out some people by force and occupied their land, had first come upon the sanctuaries as belonging to others and now possessed them as their own.

And they themselves, if they had been able to conquer more of their land, would have held it; but now, from the part in which they were, they would not of their own will go away as if from something not their own.

And they had disturbed the water out of necessity, which they had not wantonly brought on themselves, but they had been forced to use it while defending themselves against those who had first come against their land.

And it was reasonable that anything done under the constraint of war and some danger should find some pardon even with the god. For the altars were a refuge for involuntary offences, and transgression was a name given to evils done without necessity and not to those who had dared something because of misfortunes.
And it was much more impious of them to claim to give back the dead in exchange for sanctuaries than of those who were unwilling to recover what was proper by giving up sanctuaries.

And they told them to say plainly that they might take up their dead, not on condition of leaving the land of the Boeotians (for they were no longer in their land, but in land they had won by the spear), but under a truce according to ancestral custom.

The Boeotians answered that, if they were in Boeotia, they should leave their land and then carry off what was theirs, but if in their own land, they themselves knew what to do, thinking that, while the territory of Oropus, in which the dead happened to lie, since the battle had taken place on the border, belonged to the Athenians as a subject territory, they could not still get possession of them by force against their will; nor again would they make a truce, of course, over the Athenians' land; and that it was a plausible answer to say ‘leave our land and then take back what you ask for.’ And the herald of the Athenians, having heard this, went away without success.

And the Boeotians at once sent for javelin-throwers and slingers from the Malian Gulf, and, since two thousand Corinthian hoplites had come to help them after the battle, and the Peloponnesian garrison that had come out of Nisaea, and Megarians with them, they marched against Delium and attacked the fortification, and after trying in other ways they brought up an engine, which took it, of the following kind.

They sawed a great beam in two and hollowed it all out and fitted it together again exactly like a pipe, and at one end they hung a cauldron on chains, and an iron bellows-pipe was let down from the beam, bending into it, and a great part of the rest of the wood was also covered with iron.
They brought it up from a distance on carts to the wall, where it was mostly built of vines and timber; and when it was near, they put large bellows into the end of the beam on their side and blew.

And the blast, passing airtight into the cauldron, which held lighted coals and sulphur and pitch, made a great flame and set fire to the wall, so that no one could stay on it any longer, but they abandoned it and took to flight, and the fortification was taken in this way.
Of the garrison some were killed, and two hundred were captured; the mass of the others went on board the ships and were carried home.

Delium was taken on the seventeenth day after the battle, and when the herald from the Athenians, who knew nothing of what had happened, came again not long after about the dead, the Boeotians gave them back and no longer gave the same answer.

There died in the battle a little less than five hundred of the Boeotians, and of the Athenians a little less than a thousand, including Hippocrates the general, and a great number of light-armed troops and baggage carriers.

After this battle Demosthenes too, a little later, since the business of the betrayal at Siphae had not succeeded for him when he sailed there, having on his ships his army of Acarnanians and Agraeans and four hundred Athenian hoplites, made a landing in the territory of Sicyon.

And before all the ships had come to shore, the Sicyonians came to help and routed those who had landed and pursued them to the ships, and killed some and took others alive. And having set up a trophy they gave back the dead under truce.

Sitalces too, king of the Odrysians, died about the same days as the events at Delium, having marched against the Triballi and been defeated in battle. And Seuthes son of Sparadocus, who was his nephew, became king of the Odrysians and of the rest of Thrace over which Sitalces had ruled.
In the same winter Brasidas with the allies in Thrace marched against Amphipolis, the Athenian colony on the river Strymon.

This place, on which the city now stands, Aristagoras the Milesian had tried earlier to colonise, when fleeing from King Darius, but he was driven out by the Edonians, and then the Athenians tried too, thirty-two years later, sending ten thousand settlers of their own and of any others who wished, who were destroyed at Drabescus by the Thracians.
And again, in the twenty-ninth year, the Athenians came, with Hagnon son of Nicias sent out as founder, drove out the Edonians and founded this place, which was formerly called Nine Ways.

They set out from Eion, which they themselves held as a trading place at the mouth of the river on the sea, twenty-five stadia away from the present city, which Hagnon named Amphipolis because, with the Strymon flowing around it on both sides [because it surrounds it], he enclosed it with a long wall from river to river and settled it conspicuous towards the sea and the mainland.

Against this city, then, Brasidas set out from Arnae in Chalcidice and marched with his army. And arriving towards evening at Aulon and Bromiscus, where Lake Bolbe flows out into the sea, he took supper and went on through the night.
It was stormy weather and snowing a little; for which reason he pressed on all the more, wishing to escape the notice of those in Amphipolis except for the traitors.
For there were settlers from Argilus in it (the Argilians are colonists of the Andrians) and others who were involved in this plot, some persuaded by Perdiccas, others by the Chalcidians.

But most of all the Argilians, who lived close by and had always been suspected by the Athenians and had designs on the place, when the opportunity came and Brasidas arrived, had negotiated for some time with their fellow citizens living there that the city should be handed over, and then, having received him into their city and revolted from the Athenians, that night they brought the army before dawn to the bridge over the river.

The town lies some distance from the crossing, and walls did not then come down to it as they do now, but a small guard had been posted; Brasidas easily forced this, partly because there was treachery, partly because it was stormy weather and he fell on them unexpectedly, and he crossed the bridge, and at once he held everything outside belonging to the Amphipolitans who lived throughout the whole district.

His crossing having happened suddenly for those in the city, and many of those outside being captured, while others fled into the walled town, the Amphipolitans were thrown into great confusion, especially as they were suspicious of one another.
And it is said that Brasidas, if he had chosen not to turn his army to plunder, but to march straight against the city, would probably have taken it.
But as it was, having settled his army in camp, since he had overrun the parts outside and nothing came to him from those inside as he expected, he kept quiet;

and the opponents of the traitors, being superior in number so that the gates were not opened at once, sent, together with Eucles the general, who had come from Athens to be their guardian of the place, to the other general in the regions of Thrace, Thucydides son of Olorus, who wrote this history, who was near Thasos (the island is a colony of the Parians, about half a day's sail from Amphipolis), asking him to come to their help.

And he, on hearing this, sailed in haste with seven ships which happened to be at hand, and he wished above all to reach Amphipolis first, before it yielded at all, or, if not, to occupy Eion in advance.

Meanwhile Brasidas, fearing the help from the ships from Thasos, and learning that Thucydides held the right of working the gold mines in that part of Thrace and through this had influence among the leading men of the mainland, hastened to seize the city first, if he could, so that, if Thucydides arrived, the mass of the Amphipolitans, hoping that he would gather an allied force from the sea and from Thrace and save them, would no longer come over to him.

And he offered moderate terms, making this proclamation, that any of the Amphipolitans and Athenians in the city who wished might remain with his own property, sharing equal and like rights, and that anyone unwilling might leave, taking his own property with him, within five days.

And the majority, on hearing this, changed their minds, especially since only a small part of the citizens were Athenians, while the greater part was mixed, and many of those taken outside had relatives inside; and in view of their fear they considered the proclamation just, the Athenians because they would gladly leave, thinking that the danger was not equal for them and at the same time not expecting help soon, and the rest of the multitude because they were not deprived of their city on equal terms and were released from danger unexpectedly.

So, since those acting for Brasidas were now openly justifying the proposals, since they also saw that the people had changed their minds and no longer listened to the Athenian general who was present, the agreement was made and they accepted him on the terms he had proclaimed.
And they handed over the city in this way, and Thucydides and the ships sailed into Eion late on that same day.
And Brasidas had just taken Amphipolis, and he missed taking Eion by a night; for if the ships had not come to help quickly, it would have been taken at dawn.

and Brasidas, having suddenly sailed down the river with many boats against Eion, in the hope of taking the point projecting from the wall and so gaining control of the entrance, and having made an attempt by land at the same time, was beaten back on both sides, and he set about arranging matters around Amphipolis.

And Myrcinus, an Edonian city, came over to him, after Pittacus, king of the Edonians, had been killed by the sons of Goaxis and by Brauro, his wife, and Galepsus not long after, and Oesyme; these are colonies of the Thasians. And Perdiccas too, who had come immediately after the capture, helped to settle these matters.

When Amphipolis was taken the Athenians fell into great fear, especially because the city was useful to them for the sending of ship timber and for the revenue of money, and because as far as the Strymon there was a passage for the Lacedaemonians, if the Thessalians conducted them, against their allies, but as long as they did not control the bridge, since above there was a large lake formed by the river over a great distance, and the parts towards Eion were watched by triremes, they would not have been able to advance; but now this [he thought] had become easy. And they feared that their allies would revolt.
For Brasidas showed himself moderate in other respects, and in his speeches everywhere declared that he had been sent out to free Greece.

And the cities subject to the Athenians, learning of the capture of Amphipolis and what he offered, and his mildness, were especially stirred up to revolt, and they sent heralds to him secretly, asking him to come to them and each of them wishing to be the first to revolt.

For it seemed to them that there was no danger, since they were mistaken about the power of the Athenians, which was as great as later became evident, and judged more by uncertain wishing than by sure foresight, since men are accustomed to entrust to thoughtless hope what they desire, and to thrust aside with sovereign reason what they do not welcome.

And at the same time, since the Athenians had recently been defeated in Boeotia and Brasidas said enticing things that were not true, that the Athenians had not been willing to engage him at Nisaea when he had only his own army, they were confident and believed that no one would come to help against them.

But most of all, because of the pleasure of the moment and because they were going to make trial for the first time of the Lacedaemonians in a passionate mood, they were ready to take risks in every way. Perceiving this, the Athenians sent garrisons to the cities, as far as was possible at short notice and in winter, while Brasidas, sending to Lacedaemon, asked them to send him an additional army, and he himself prepared the building of triremes on the Strymon.
But the Lacedaemonians did not support him, partly out of envy on the part of their leading men, partly also because they wished rather to recover the men from the island and to end the war.

In the same winter the Megarians took the long walls, which the Athenians held, and razed them to the ground, and Brasidas, after the capture of Amphipolis, marched with the allies against the peninsula called Acte.
It projects inward from the King's canal, and Athos, a high mountain, forms its end at the Aegean Sea.

these are inhabited by mixed tribes of bilingual barbarians, and there is also a small Chalcidian element, but the greatest part is Pelasgian, of those Tyrrhenians who once lived in Lemnos and Athens, and Bisaltian and Crestonian and Edonians; and they live in small towns.
And most of them came over to Brasidas, but Sane and Dium held out, and he stayed with his army and ravaged their land.

When they did not listen to him, he marched at once against Torone in Chalcidice, which was held by the Athenians; and a few men were inviting him in, being ready to hand over the city. And arriving while it was still night and towards dawn, he halted with his army by the temple of the Dioscuri, which is about three stadia from the city.

The rest of the city of the Toronaeans and the Athenians in the garrison did not notice him; but those acting for him, knowing that he would come, and a few of them having gone forward secretly, were watching for his approach, and when they saw that he was there, they brought in to them seven light-armed men with daggers (for only so many of the twenty men first appointed were not afraid to go in; and they were commanded by Lysistratus of Olynthus), who slipped through the wall facing the sea and, unnoticed, went up and killed the guards at the highest guard-post, since the city lies on a hill, and began breaking down the postern towards Canastraeum.

And Brasidas, having advanced a little, kept quiet with the rest of his army, but sent ahead a hundred peltasts, so that, when any gates were opened and the signal that had been agreed was raised, they might be the first to run in.

And these, as time went on and they wondered at the delay, had little by little come close to the city; and those of the Toronaeans who were making preparations inside with the men who had entered, when the postern had been broken down and the gates by the market-place had been opened by cutting through the bar, first brought some men round to the postern and let them in, so that they might suddenly frighten those in the city, who knew nothing, from the rear and from both sides, and then they raised the fire signal, as had been agreed, and now received the rest of the peltasts through the gates by the market-place.
And Brasidas, seeing the signal, set off at a run, having roused his army, who raised a shout all together and caused great dismay to those in the city.
And some burst in at once by the gates, others over some square beams which happened to be lying against the wall, which had fallen and was being rebuilt, for hauling up stones.

Brasidas, then, and the main body at once turned upwards and towards the high parts of the city, wishing to take it from top to bottom and securely; but the rest of the crowd scattered in all directions alike.
While the capture was taking place, the bulk of the Toronaeans, knowing nothing, were in confusion, but the conspirators and those who were pleased by this at once joined those who had come in.

The Athenians (for about fifty hoplites happened to be sleeping in the market-place), when they perceived it, a few of them were killed in hand-to-hand fighting, but of the rest, some by land, others to the ships, of which two were on guard, fled and got safely into Lecythus, the fort, which they themselves had seized and held, a height of the city cut off towards the sea on a narrow isthmus.
And those of the Toronaeans also who were friendly to them fled to them.

When day had now come and the city was securely held, Brasidas made a proclamation to the Toronaeans who had fled with the Athenians that whoever wished might come out to his own property and live as a citizen without fear, and to the Athenians he sent a herald and ordered them to leave Lecythus under truce, taking their own property, as the place belonged to the Chalcidians.

They said they would not leave, but asked him to make a truce with them for a day to take up their dead. He made a truce for two. During these he himself strengthened the nearby houses, and the Athenians their own positions.

And having called an assembly of the Toronaeans he spoke much as he had to those at Acanthus, saying that it was not just either to consider those who had negotiated with him for the capture of the city as worse men or traitors (for they had not done this for the sake of enslavement nor persuaded by money, but for the good and the freedom of the city) or for those who had not taken part to think that they would not get the same treatment; for he had not come to destroy either the city or any private citizen.

He had made the proclamation to those who had fled to the Athenians for this reason, that he thought them no worse for their friendship with those; and when they had tried them [the Lacedaemonians], he thought they would be not less but much more well disposed to them, inasmuch as they acted more justly, and that now they were afraid through inexperience.

And he told them all to prepare themselves to be steadfast allies and to bear the blame from now on for whatever mistakes they might make; as for the past, it was not the Lacedaemonians who had been wronged, but rather they themselves by others who were stronger, and it was pardonable if they had in any way opposed him.

And having said such things and encouraged them, when the truce had expired he made assaults on Lecythus; and the Athenians defended themselves from a poor fortification and from houses that had battlements,

and for one day they beat them back; but on the next day, when an engine was about to be brought against them by the enemy, from which they intended to throw fire on the wooden palisades, and the army was already advancing, at the point where they thought the enemy would most likely bring up the engine and where it was most open to attack, they set up a wooden tower on a building, and carried up many jars and casks of water and large stones, and many men went up.

But the building, taking on too great a load, suddenly broke down, and as a great crash occurred, it distressed rather than frightened those of the Athenians who were near and saw it, but those further off, and especially those at the greatest distance, thinking that the place had already been taken at that point, rushed in flight to the sea and the ships.
And Brasidas, when he perceived that they were leaving the battlements and saw what was happening, charged with the army and at once took the fortification, and killed all whom he caught in it.

And the Athenians, having left the place in this way with their boats and their ships, were carried across to Pallene; but Brasidas (for there is a temple of Athena in Lecythus, and he had happened to proclaim, when he was about to make the assault, that he would give thirty minas of silver to the first man to mount the wall), thinking that the capture had happened by some other means than human, paid the thirty minas to the goddess for the temple, and having pulled down Lecythus and cleared it he dedicated the whole as a sacred precinct.
And for the rest of the winter he settled the places that he held and plotted against the others; and as the winter ended, the eighth year of the war ended.

The Lacedaemonians and the Athenians, at the beginning of spring of the following summer, at once made a truce for a year, the Athenians thinking that Brasidas would then no longer cause any more of their allies to revolt before they had prepared at their leisure, and at the same time, if it suited them, they might also come to a more general agreement, and the Lacedaemonians thinking that the Athenians feared precisely what they themselves dreaded, and that once there was a respite from troubles and hardship, they would, having experienced it, be more eager to be reconciled and, giving back their men to them, to make a treaty also for the longer term.

For they valued recovering their men more highly, while Brasidas was still successful; and if he advanced further and established an equal balance, they were likely to be deprived of these, and, defending themselves on equal terms with the rest, to run a risk and perhaps prevail.
So the following truce is made for them and their allies.
‘Concerning the temple and the oracle of Pythian Apollo, we agree that whoever wishes may consult it without fraud and without fear according to the ancestral laws.
The Lacedaemonians and the allies who are present agree to this; and they say they will persuade the Boeotians and the Phocians as far as they can by sending heralds.

Concerning the treasures of the god, we agree to take care that we shall find out the wrongdoers, rightly and justly following the ancestral laws, both you and we and those of the others who wish, all following the ancestral laws.

Concerning these things, then, the Lacedaemonians and the other allies agreed on these terms; and the Lacedaemonians and the other allies agreed to the following, if the Athenians make a treaty, that each side remain in its own territory, keeping what we now hold, those in Coryphasium staying within Buphras and Tomeus, those in Cythera having no communication with the alliance, neither we with them nor they with us, those in Nisaea and Minoa not crossing the road from the gates by the shrine of Nisus to the Poseidonium, and from the Poseidonium straight to the bridge leading to Minoa (nor shall the Megarians and their allies cross this road), and keeping the island which the Athenians took, with neither side communicating with the other, and, in Troezen, whatever they now hold, according to what they agreed with the Athenians;

and as to using the sea, as far as along their own coast and that of their alliance, the Lacedaemonians and the allies may sail not in a ship of war, but in any other rowed vessel carrying a burden of up to five hundred talents.

For a herald and an embassy and attendants, as many as may seem fit, travelling to the Peloponnese and to Athens about ending the war and about arbitration, there shall be safe conduct, going and returning, both by land and by sea.
Deserters shall not be received during this time, neither free nor slave, neither by you nor by us.
And you shall give satisfaction to us and we to you according to ancestral custom, settling disputed matters by arbitration without war.

The Lacedaemonians and the allies agree to this; but if anything seems to you either better or more just than this, come to Lacedaemon and explain it; for neither the Lacedaemonians nor the allies will reject anything that you say that is just.
And let those who come come with full powers, just as you also ask of us. And the truce shall be for a year.
〈and〉 that the truce be for a year, and begin on this day, the fourteenth of the month Elaphebolion.
During this time envoys and heralds shall go to one another and hold discussions on what terms the ending of the war shall be.

And the generals and the prytanes, having called an assembly, the Athenians shall deliberate first about the peace ... on what terms the embassy about ending the war shall be admitted. And the embassies now present shall at once swear before the people that they will indeed abide by the truce for the year.
‘These terms the Lacedaemonians [and swore] and the allies agreed with the Athenians and their allies at Lacedaemon on the twelfth of the month Gerastius.
This, then, was the truce that was made, and during it they continually met in discussions about the larger treaty.

About the days on which they were making these mutual visits, Scione, a city in Pallene, revolted from the Athenians to Brasidas. The Scionaeans say that they are Pellenians from the Peloponnese, and that their first ancestors, sailing from Troy, were carried down to this place by the storm which the Achaeans met with, and settled there.

After they had revolted, Brasidas sailed across by night to Scione, with a friendly trireme sailing ahead and himself following at a distance in a skiff, so that, if he met any vessel larger than the skiff, the trireme might defend him, but if another trireme of equal strength came up, he thought it would turn not against the smaller boat but against the ship, and that meanwhile he would get through safely.

Having crossed over and called an assembly of the Scionaeans, he said what he had said at Acanthus and Torone, and further declared that they were most worthy of praise, since, when Pallene was cut off at the isthmus by the Athenians who held Potidaea and they were nothing else than islanders, they had of their own accord gone over to freedom and had not waited through lack of courage for necessity to come upon them concerning what was clearly their own good; and that this was a sign that they would bravely endure any other of the greatest trials also; and if matters were settled according to his wish, he would consider them in truth the most faithful friends of the Lacedaemonians and would honour them in other ways.

And the Scionaeans were elated by his words, and all alike took courage, even those to whom what was being done had not been pleasing before, and they resolved to carry on the war zealously, and they received Brasidas well in other respects, and publicly crowned him with a golden crown as the liberator of Greece, and privately decked him with ribbons and came up to him as to an athlete.

He, leaving some guard with them for the present, crossed back, and not much later brought over a larger army, wishing with them to make an attempt on Mende and Potidaea, thinking that the Athenians would come to help it as to an island and wishing to anticipate them; and something was also being negotiated by him with these cities concerning betrayal.

And he was about to attack these cities, but meanwhile those who were carrying round the news of the truce arrived to him in a trireme, for the Athenians Aristonymus, for the Lacedaemonians Athenaeus.
And the army crossed back to Torone, and they announced the agreement to Brasidas, and all the allies of the Lacedaemonians in Thrace accepted what had been done.

Aristonymus agreed for the others, but, perceiving from a calculation of the days that the Scionaeans had revolted later, he said they would not be included in the treaty. But Brasidas argued at length that they had revolted earlier, and would not give up the city.

When Aristonymus reported about them to Athens, the Athenians were at once ready to march against Scione. But the Lacedaemonians sent envoys and said that they would be breaking the treaty, and they laid claim to the city trusting Brasidas, and were ready to submit to arbitration about it.

But the Athenians were not willing to take the risk of arbitration, but to march as quickly as possible, being angry that even those who were in the islands now thought fit to revolt from them, trusting in the useless strength of the Lacedaemonians on land.

And the truth about the revolt was rather as the Athenians claimed; for the Scionaeans revolted two days later. And they at once passed a decree, persuaded by the proposal of Cleon, to destroy the Scionaeans and put them to death. And keeping quiet in other matters, they prepared for this.

Meanwhile Mende revolted from them, a city in Pallene, a colony of the Eretrians. And Brasidas received them, not thinking that he was doing wrong, although they openly came over during the truce; for there were matters in which he himself also charged the Athenians with breaking the treaty.

For this reason the Mendaeans too were bolder, seeing that the mind of Brasidas was ready, judging also from Scione that he did not abandon it, and at the same time because those who were negotiating among them were few and, once they had set about it, no longer held back, but feared for themselves being found out and forced the many against their will.
The Athenians, as soon as they learned of it, were much more angry still and prepared against both the cities.

And Brasidas, expecting their attack by sea, secretly conveyed to Olynthus in Chalcidice the children and women of the Scionaeans and Mendaeans, and sent across to them five hundred hoplites of the Peloponnesians and three hundred Chalcidian peltasts, and as commander of them all Polydamidas. And they together made ready their own defences, as the Athenians would soon be there.

Meanwhile Brasidas and Perdiccas marched together against Arrhabaeus for the second time, to Lyncus. And the one led the force of the Macedonians over whom he ruled and hoplites of the Greeks living among them, the other, in addition to his own remaining Peloponnesians, Chalcidians and Acanthians and of the others as many as each could. The whole hoplite force of the Greeks was about three thousand, and the cavalry of the Macedonians with the Chalcidians who followed numbered in all nearly a thousand, and there was another large crowd of barbarians.
Having invaded the land of Arrhabaeus and found the Lyncestians encamped against them, they too took up a position facing them.

And as the infantry held a hill on each side, and there was a plain in the middle, the cavalry of both sides rode down into it and first fought a cavalry battle, and then Brasidas and Perdiccas, as the Lyncestian hoplites had first come forward from the hill with the cavalry and were ready to fight, led their men against them in turn, engaged, and routed the Lyncestians, and killed many, while the rest escaped to the heights and kept quiet.

After this they set up a trophy and waited two or three days, waiting for the Illyrians, who happened to be about to come to Perdiccas as mercenaries; then Perdiccas wanted to advance against the villages of Arrhabaeus and not sit still, but Brasidas, being anxious about Mende, that it might suffer something if the Athenians sailed against it first, and at the same time, since the Illyrians were not present, was not eager, but rather wished to retreat.

And meanwhile, as they were disagreeing, it was announced that the Illyrians had betrayed Perdiccas and joined Arrhabaeus; so that, when it now seemed best to both to retreat because of fear of them, as they were warlike men, but nothing had been decided because of the disagreement about when they should set out, and night came on, the Macedonians and the mass of the barbarians at once took fright, as great armies are apt to be struck by panic for no clear reason, and thinking that many times more than had actually come were advancing and were all but there, broke into sudden flight and went homewards, and they forced Perdiccas, who at first did not perceive it, when he learned of it, before seeing Brasidas (for they were encamped far from each other), to depart first.

Brasidas, at dawn, when he saw that the Macedonians had gone ahead and that the Illyrians and Arrhabaeus were about to attack, himself also drew his hoplites together into a square formation and, taking the crowd of light troops into the middle, intended to retreat.

As skirmishers to run out, if the enemy attacked them anywhere, he posted the youngest men, and he himself with three hundred picked men, intending to be last, planned while retreating to stand and repel the foremost of the enemy as they pressed on.
And before the enemy were near, he encouraged his soldiers briefly as follows, as haste allowed.

‘If I did not suspect, men of the Peloponnese, that you were struck with alarm both by being left alone and because the attackers are barbarians and many, I would not in the same way be giving instruction together with my exhortation; but as it is, in view of the desertion of our side and the number of the enemy, I shall try to persuade you of the most important things with a brief reminder and advice.

For it befits you to be brave in war not because of the presence of allies on each occasion, but because of your own valour, and not to fear any number of others, you who do not even come from states such as theirs, in which the many do not rule the few, but rather the fewer rule the more, having acquired their power by no other means than by conquering in battle.

And as for the barbarians, whom you now fear through inexperience, you must learn, both from what you have already fought against the Macedonians among them and from what I myself infer and know by hearsay from others, that they will not be formidable.

For whatever things among the enemy are in reality weak but have an appearance of strength, true information about them, once it is gained, tends rather to embolden those who defend themselves; but against those who truly have some advantage, a man would attack more boldly if he did not know it beforehand.

These men have a menace that is frightening to the inexperienced; for they are terrible in the number of their appearance and unbearable in the loudness of their shouting, and the empty brandishing of their weapons conveys some show of threat. But in coming to close quarters with those who withstand these things they are not the same; for having no order they would not be ashamed to abandon any position when pressed, and their flight and their attack, having equal repute for honour, leave their courage also untested (and a battle in which each is his own master would most readily provide anyone with a pretext for saving himself decently), and they think it safer to frighten you without risk than to come to close quarters; for otherwise they would have done that rather than this.

And you clearly see that all that was at first formidable about them is in fact small, though to sight and hearing it is alarming. If you withstand this as it comes on and, when there is the right moment, withdraw again in good order and formation, you will both reach safety sooner and will know in future that such mobs, against those who have received their first onset, boast of their courage with threats from afar by their menace, but against those who give way to them, they are quick to display their bravery at their heels, when it is safe.’

Having given such advice, Brasidas began to lead his army away. And the barbarians, seeing this, pressed on with much shouting and uproar, thinking that he was fleeing and that they would overtake and destroy him.

And when the skirmishing parties met them wherever they attacked, and he himself with the picked men withstood them as they pressed on, they withstood the first onset contrary to expectation and thereafter received and repelled them when they attacked, and when they kept quiet they themselves withdrew, then indeed most of the barbarians held off from the Greeks with Brasidas in the open country, and, leaving some part to follow and attack them, the rest went on at a run against the fleeing Macedonians, killed those they met, and, getting there first, occupied in advance the pass which lies narrow between two hills into the land of Arrhabaeus, knowing that there was no other way of retreat for Brasidas. And as he was now approaching the most difficult part of the road itself, they began to surround him in order to cut him off.

But he, perceiving it, told the three hundred with him to go at a run, as quickly as each could, without order, to whichever of the hills he thought they could more easily take, and try to dislodge from it the barbarians already on it, before the larger encircling force of the enemy joined them there.

And they fell upon them and overcame those on the hill, and the main army of the Greeks now went more easily towards it; for the barbarians were frightened, since the rout of their own men had taken place there from the height, and they no longer followed further, thinking that the enemy were already at the frontier and had escaped.
And Brasidas, when he had gained the heights, going on in greater safety, arrived on the same day at Arnisa, the first place in the dominion of Perdiccas.

And the soldiers themselves, angry at the early retreat of the Macedonians, whatever teams of oxen of theirs they met on the road, or any baggage that had fallen off, as was likely to happen in a retreat by night and in fear, they unyoked and slaughtered the oxen, and appropriated the baggage.

And from this time Perdiccas first regarded Brasidas as an enemy, and for the future he had a hatred of the Peloponnesians in his mind which was not usual for him because of the Athenians, but, departing from his own pressing interests, he worked out how he might as quickly as possible come to terms with the one and get rid of the other.

Brasidas, having returned from Macedonia to Torone, found the Athenians already holding Mende, and, keeping quiet there, he thought it was now impossible to cross over to Pallene and give help, but he kept Torone under guard.

For about the same time as the events in Lyncus the Athenians had sailed against Mende and Scione, as they had been preparing to do, with fifty ships, of which ten were Chian, and with a thousand hoplites of their own and six hundred bowmen and a thousand Thracian mercenaries and other peltasts from the allies there; and Nicias son of Niceratus and Nicostratus son of Diitrephes were in command.

Setting out from Potidaea with the ships and putting in at the Poseidonium, they advanced against the Mendaeans. And these themselves and three hundred Scionaeans who had come to their aid and the Peloponnesian auxiliaries, seven hundred hoplites in all, and Polydamidas their commander, happened to be encamped outside the city on a strong hill.

And Nicias, with a hundred and twenty light-armed Methonaeans and sixty picked men of the Athenian hoplites and all the bowmen, trying to go up against them by a path up the hill, and being wounded by them, was not able to force his way; and Nicostratus, attacking with all the rest of the army by another approach from further off against the hill, which was hard to climb, was thrown into complete confusion, and the whole army of the Athenians came close to being defeated.
And on this day, as the Mendaeans and the allies did not give way, the Athenians withdrew and encamped, and the Mendaeans, when night came on, went back into the city.

On the next day the Athenians sailed round to the side facing Scione and took the suburb, and all day they ravaged the land, with no one coming out against them (for there was some civil strife in the city), and the three hundred Scionaeans departed home in the following night.

And on the next day Nicias with half of the army advanced as far as the borders of the Scionaeans and ravaged the land, while Nicostratus with the rest sat down before the city at the upper gates, where the road goes to Potidaea.
And Polydamidas (for in that quarter, inside the wall, the arms of the Mendaeans and the auxiliaries happened to be lying) drew them up as for battle and urged the Mendaeans to go out against them.

And when someone of the popular party answered him back in a factious spirit that he would not go out and had no need to fight, and when, as he answered back, he was dragged by the hand by him and roughly handled, the people at once took up their arms and in great anger advanced on the Peloponnesians and on those who with them had worked against them.

And falling upon them they routed them, partly by the sudden attack, and partly because they were afraid as the gates were being opened to the Athenians; for they thought that the attack on them had been made by some prior arrangement.

And those who were not killed at once fled to the acropolis, which they themselves had also held before; but the Athenians (for Nicias too had already turned back and was near the city) burst into the city of Mende, as it had not been opened by agreement, and plundered it with the whole army as if they had taken it by storm, and the generals with difficulty restrained them so that the people too should not be killed.

And after this they ordered the Mendaeans to live as citizens as they had been used to, themselves judging among themselves whether they thought any were responsible for the revolt; and those on the acropolis they walled off with a wall on each side down to the sea and set a guard over them. And when they had got control of the affairs of Mende, they advanced against Scione.
And they themselves and the Peloponnesians, having come out against them, took position on a strong hill in front of the city, and unless the enemy took it, there could be no wall built around them.
The Athenians, having attacked it by force and dislodged those on it in battle, encamped and, after setting up a trophy, prepared for the circumvallation.

And not long after, when they were already at work, the auxiliaries who were besieged in the acropolis at Mende forced their way through the guard along the sea and arrived by night, and most of them, slipping through the army before Scione, got into it.

While Scione was being walled round, Perdiccas, having sent a herald to the generals of the Athenians, made an agreement with the Athenians because of his hatred of Brasidas over the retreat from Lyncus, having begun negotiating right at that time.

And (for Ischagoras the Lacedaemonian happened at that time to be about to lead an army by land to Brasidas) Perdiccas, partly because Nicias urged him, since he had come to terms, to do something evident for the Athenians as a proof of his reliability, and partly because he himself no longer wished the Peloponnesians to come into his territory, worked upon his guest-friends in Thessaly, being always on good terms with the leading men, and stopped the army and the preparations, so that they did not even try the Thessalians.

Ischagoras, however, and Ameinias and Aristeus themselves came to Brasidas, as the Lacedaemonians had sent them to inspect the situation, and, contrary to custom, they brought some of their young men out of Sparta, in order to appoint them governors of the cities and not to entrust them to anyone who happened to be there. And he appointed Clearidas son of Cleonymus at Amphipolis, and Pasitelidas son of Hegesander at Torone.

In the same summer the Thebans pulled down the wall of the Thespians, accusing them of favouring Athens, having always wanted to do so, but it was now easier since in the battle against the Athenians whatever flower of their manhood there was had perished.

And the temple of Hera at Argos was burned down in the same summer, Chrysis the priestess having placed a lighted lamp near the garlands and fallen asleep, so that everything caught fire and was ablaze before she noticed.

And Chrysis, fearing the Argives, fled at once that night to Phlius; and they appointed another priestess according to the established law, Phaeinis by name. Chrysis had covered eight years of this war and half of the ninth when she fled.
And Scione, when the summer was already ending, had been completely walled round, and the Athenians, leaving a guard over it, withdrew with the rest of the army.

In the following winter matters between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians were quiet because of the truce, but the Mantineans and Tegeans and the allies of each side fought at Laodoceum in Oresthis, and the victory was disputed; for each side routed the wing opposite them, and both set up trophies and sent spoils to Delphi.

But after many had been killed on each side and the battle had been evenly matched and night had cut off the action, the Tegeans bivouacked on the field and at once set up a trophy, while the Mantineans withdrew to Bucolion and later set up a rival one.

In the same winter too, as it was ending and spring was already near, Brasidas made an attempt on Potidaea. For approaching by night and setting up a ladder, he escaped notice up to that point; for the setting up took place just in the interval after the bell had been carried past, before the man passing it on returned; then, however, as they noticed at once, before he could climb up, he led the army back again in haste and did not wait for day to come.
And the winter ended, and the ninth year ended of this war which Thucydides wrote down.

In the following summer the year's truce had expired, as far as the Pythian games, and during the truce the Athenians removed the Delians from Delos, thinking that on account of some ancient offence they had been consecrated while not pure, and that this was moreover a defect in their purification, in which, as I have shown before, they thought they had done right in removing the coffins of the dead. And the Delians settled at Atramyttium in Asia, which Pharnaces gave them, each as he had set out.

Cleon, having persuaded the Athenians, sailed out to the places in Thrace after the truce, with twelve hundred hoplites of the Athenians and three hundred cavalry, and a larger number of the allies, and thirty ships.
Putting in first at Scione, which was still under siege, and taking on from there hoplites from the garrison, he sailed down into the Silent Harbour of the Toronaeans, not far distant from the city.

From there, learning from deserters that neither was Brasidas in Torone nor were those in it a match for him in battle, he advanced against the city with the land army, and sent ten ships to sail round 〈into〉 the harbour.
And he came first to the outer wall which Brasidas had built around the city in addition, wishing to bring the suburb inside, and, pulling down part of the old wall, he had made it a single city.

Pasitelidas, the Lacedaemonian commander, and the garrison that was present came to the defence of it and fought off the Athenians as they attacked. And as they were hard pressed and at the same time the ships 〈that had been〉 sent round into the harbour were sailing round, Pasitelidas, fearing that the ships might get there first and take the city undefended and that he might be caught inside when the fortification was taken, left it and went at a run into the city.

But the Athenians got there first, both those from the ships, who took Torone, and the land force, which followed and at the first assault burst in with him at the breach in the old wall. And some of the Peloponnesians and Toronaeans they killed at once in hand-to-hand fighting, and others they took alive, including Pasitelidas the commander.
Brasidas was coming to help Torone, but learning on the way that it had been taken, he retreated, having missed arriving in time by about forty stades.

Cleon and the Athenians set up two trophies, one at the harbour, the other at the fortification, and they enslaved the women and children of the Toronaeans, and the men themselves and the Peloponnesians and any others who were Chalcidians, about seven hundred in all, they sent to Athens; and of these the Peloponnesians later went free in the treaty that was made, and the rest were brought back by the Olynthians, released man for man.
And about the same time the Boeotians also took Panactum, a fort of the Athenians on the border, by treachery.
And Cleon, having set a guard over Torone, set out and sailed round Athos as if towards Amphipolis.
About the same time Phaeax son of Erasistratus, with two others, sailed out as an envoy to Italy and Sicily with two ships, as the Athenians sent him.
For the Leontines, after the Athenians had left Sicily following the agreement, had enrolled many citizens, and the people were planning to redistribute the land.

But the powerful men, perceiving this, brought in the Syracusans and expelled the people. And these wandered off each their own way, while the powerful men, coming to terms with the Syracusans and leaving and abandoning their city, settled in Syracuse with citizenship.

And later again some of them, because they were not satisfied, left Syracuse and occupied Phoceae, a place so called in the city of the Leontines, and Bricinniae, which is a stronghold in the Leontine territory. And most of the people who had then been expelled came to them, and establishing themselves they made war from the fortifications.

Learning of this, the Athenians sent Phaeax, to see whether by persuading their own allies there and the other Siceliots, if they could, to make a joint expedition on the ground that the Syracusans were building up their power, they might save the people of the Leontines.

Phaeax on arriving persuaded the Camarinaeans and the Agrigentines, but at Gela, as the matter met opposition, he did not go on to the others, perceiving that he would not persuade them, but withdrew through the land of the Sicels to Catana, and at the same time on the way went also to Bricinniae and encouraged them, and sailed away.

And on the voyage along the coast to Sicily and on the way back, and in Italy, he negotiated with some cities about friendship with the Athenians, and he met the Locrian settlers who had been expelled from Messene, who, after the agreement of the Siceliots, when the Messenians fell into strife and one faction brought in the Locrians, had been sent out as settlers, and Messene belonged to the Locrians for some time.
Phaeax, then, meeting these men as they were being brought home, did them no harm; for an agreement had been made by the Locrians with him about coming to terms with the Athenians.

For alone of the allies, when the Siceliots were being reconciled, they made no treaty with the Athenians, nor would they have then, if the war against the Hipponians and Medmaeans, who were both their neighbours and their colonists, had not held them fast. And Phaeax arrived at Athens some time later.

Cleon, when he had then sailed round from Torone against Amphipolis, setting out from Eion attacked Stagirus, a colony of the Andrians, and did not take it, but took Galepsus, the colony of the Thasians, by storm.

And having sent envoys to Perdiccas, so that he might come with an army according to the alliance, and others to Thrace to Polles, the king of the Odomantians, to bring as many Thracian mercenaries as possible, he himself kept quiet, waiting at Eion.

Brasidas, learning this, himself also took up a position opposite at Cerdylium; this place belongs to the Argilians, on high ground across the river, not far from Amphipolis, and everything was visible from there, so that Cleon could not have set out with his army without his noticing; which he expected him to do, to go up against Amphipolis with his present army, despising their numbers.

And at the same time he also made preparations, calling to his aid fifteen hundred Thracian mercenaries and all the Edonians, peltasts and cavalry; and he had a thousand peltasts of the Myrcinians and Chalcidians in addition to those in Amphipolis.

The whole hoplite force that was assembled was about two thousand, and there were three hundred Greek cavalry. Of these Brasidas took about fifteen hundred and sat at Cerdylium, while the others were posted in Amphipolis with Clearidas.
Cleon for a while kept quiet, but then was forced to do just what Brasidas expected.

For as the soldiers were annoyed at sitting still, and were reckoning up his leadership, against what experience and daring it would be pitted, with what ignorance and cowardice, and how unwillingly they had come with him from home, he, perceiving the murmuring and not wishing them to become disaffected through sitting in the same place, took them and led them on.

And he used the same method in which, having been successful at Pylos too, he had come to believe that he had some sense; for he did not even expect that anyone would come out against him for battle, but he said he was going up rather to view the place, and he was waiting for the larger force, not in order to secure himself with safety if he should be forced to fight, but in order to surround the city on all sides and take it by force.
And having come and stationed the army on a strong hill in front of Amphipolis, he himself viewed the marshy part of the Strymon and how the position of the city lay in relation to Thrace.

And he thought he could depart, whenever he wished, without a battle; for no one was visible on the wall, nor was anyone coming out by the gates, and they were all shut. So he even thought that he had made a mistake in not coming up with siege engines; for he would have taken the city, since it was undefended.
And Brasidas, as soon as he saw the Athenians moving, himself also came down from Cerdylium and entered Amphipolis.

And he did not make a sally and draw up his troops against the Athenians, distrusting his own force and thinking that they were inferior, not in numbers (for they were roughly equal), but in quality (for the part of the Athenians that was on the campaign had come out pure, and the best of the Lemnians and Imbrians), but he prepared to attack them by a stratagem.

For if he showed the enemy both the number and the makeshift equipment of the men with him, he did not think he would be more likely to prevail than without their being seen beforehand and without contempt arising from the reality.

So he himself picked out a hundred and fifty hoplites, and assigning the others to Clearidas, he planned to attack suddenly before the Athenians departed, thinking that he would not catch them isolated in the same way again, if their reinforcements should happen to arrive. Having called together all the soldiers and wishing to encourage them and explain his plan, he spoke as follows.
but in what way I intend to make the attack, I shall explain, so that the fighting in small parts and not all together may not seem inadequate to anyone and cause lack of courage.

For I suppose that the enemy, both out of contempt for us and not expecting that anyone would come out against them for battle, have gone up to the place, and now, turned in disorder to viewing it, are careless.
and those stratagems have the finest reputation by which a man, deceiving the enemy most, would most help his friends.

So while they are still unprepared and confident, and have their minds on withdrawing more than on staying, from what appears to me, in the relaxation of their purpose and before their thinking is braced up again, I, taking those with me and getting there first, if I can, will fall at a run on the middle of their army;

and you, Clearidas, afterwards, when you see me already pressing on and, as is likely, frightening them, leading those with you, the Amphipolitans and the other allies, suddenly open the gates, rush out, and hurry to close with them as quickly as possible.
For there is the best hope that they will be frightened in this way; for what comes on later is more terrible to the enemy than what is present and fighting.

And show yourself a brave man, as is fitting for you as a Spartiate, and you, men of the allies, follow bravely, and consider that 〈three things〉 belong to fighting well: being willing, feeling shame, and obeying the commanders, and that on this day, if you prove brave, freedom is yours and to be called allies of the Lacedaemonians, or else to be slaves of the Athenians, if you fare as well as possible without enslavement or death, and to have a harsher slavery than you had before, and to become obstacles to the liberation of the rest of the Greeks.
But do not be faint-hearted, seeing how much the contest is about, and I will show that I am not more able to advise my neighbours than to carry it out myself in deed.’
Brasidas, having said so much, himself prepared for the sally and posted the others with Clearidas at the gates called the Thracian gates, so that they might come out as had been ordered.

And to Cleon, since Brasidas had been seen coming down from Cerdylium and, in the city, which is visible from outside, sacrificing at the temple of Athena and doing these things, it was reported (for he had then gone forward to view the place) that the whole army of the enemy was visible in the city and that many feet of horses and of men were showing under the gates, as if they were coming out.

Hearing this he came up; and when he saw it, not wishing to fight it out in battle before his reinforcements arrived and thinking that he would get away in time, he ordered the signal for retreat to be sounded at once and passed the word to those departing to withdraw towards the left wing, as was alone possible, in the direction of Eion.
And when it seemed to him that this was slow, he himself wheeled the right wing and, exposing his unprotected side to the enemy, led the army away.

And at this moment Brasidas, when he saw the opportunity and the army of the Athenians moving, said to those with him and to the others: ‘The men will not wait for us. They show it by the movement of their spears and of their heads; for those with whom this happens are not accustomed to wait for attackers. Now let someone open for me the gates that have been ordered, and let us go out as quickly as possible with confidence.’

And he went out by the gates towards the palisade and the first gates of the long wall which was then standing, and ran at full speed along this straight road, where now, for one going up the steepest part of the place, a trophy stands, and attacking the Athenians, who were frightened by their own disorder and at the same time astounded at his daring, he routed them in the middle of their army.

And Clearidas, as had been ordered, at the same time came out by the Thracian gates with the army and bore down on them. And the result was that, through the unexpectedness and suddenness from both sides, the Athenians were thrown into confusion,

and their left wing, the one towards Eion, which had indeed already gone ahead, was at once broken off and fled; and Brasidas, as it was already retreating, while advancing against the right wing, was wounded, and the Athenians did not notice that he had fallen, but those near him took him up and carried him away.

The right wing of the Athenians stood its ground better, and Cleon, as he had not intended from the first to stand, fled at once and, overtaken by a Myrcinian peltast, was killed, but his hoplites, rallying on the hill, beat off Clearidas even when he attacked two or three times, and did not give way until the Myrcinian and Chalcidian cavalry and the peltasts, surrounding them and throwing javelins at them, routed them.

Thus the whole army of the Athenians was now in flight, and with difficulty, turning by many roads over the mountains, all who were not killed either at once in hand-to-hand fighting or by the Chalcidian cavalry and the peltasts, the rest got back to Eion.
Those who had taken up Brasidas out of the battle and brought him safely brought him into the city still breathing; and he learned that his men were victorious, but not long after he died.
And the rest of the army, having returned with Clearidas from the pursuit, stripped the dead and set up a trophy.

After this all the allies, following in arms, buried Brasidas at public expense in the city, in front of what is now the market-place; and thereafter the Amphipolitans, having fenced in his monument, sacrifice to him as to a hero and have given him honours, games and annual sacrifices, and they assigned the colony to him as its founder, pulling down the buildings of Hagnon and obliterating whatever memorial of his founding was likely to survive anywhere, considering that Brasidas had been their saviour, and at the same time, in the present situation, courting the alliance of the Lacedaemonians out of fear of the Athenians, while Hagnon, because of their hostility to the Athenians, would not hold the honours equally to their advantage or with pleasure.

And they gave back the dead to the Athenians. About six hundred of the Athenians died, and seven of their opponents, because the battle took place not from a set line of battle, but rather from such an accident and prior panic.
After taking up the dead the Athenians sailed away home, and those with Clearidas settled the affairs of Amphipolis.

And about the same time, as the summer was ending, Rhamphias and Autocharidas and Epicydidas, Lacedaemonians, were leading a relief force of nine hundred hoplites to the places in Thrace, and arriving at Heracleia in Trachis they set in order what seemed to them not to be in good condition.
While they were staying there this battle happened to take place, and the summer ended.

At the very beginning of the following winter Rhamphias and his men went through as far as Pierium in Thessaly, but as the Thessalians hindered them and at the same time Brasidas was dead, to whom they were bringing the army, they turned back home, thinking that there was no longer any opportunity, since the Athenians had departed after their defeat and they themselves were not competent to do any of the things that he had been planning.
But most of all they went away because they knew that the Lacedaemonians, when they set out, had their minds more inclined towards peace.

And it happened that immediately after the battle at Amphipolis and the retreat of Rhamphias from Thessaly neither side engaged in war any longer, and they were more inclined in mind towards peace, the Athenians because they had been beaten at Delium and again shortly after at Amphipolis, and no longer had confident hope in their strength, relying on which they had not accepted the treaty before, thinking that with their present good fortune they would gain the upper hand;

and at the same time they feared that their allies, encouraged by their failures, might revolt further, and they regretted that after the events at Pylos, when a good opportunity offered, they had not come to terms;

and the Lacedaemonians, on the other hand, since the war was turning out contrary to their expectation, in which they had thought that within a few years they would destroy the power of the Athenians if they ravaged their land, and since they had met with the disaster on the island, such as had never yet befallen Sparta, and their country was being plundered from Pylos and Cythera, and the Helots were deserting, and there was always the fear that those too who remained, trusting in those outside, might in the present circumstances make a revolution as they had done before.

And it also happened that their thirty years' treaty with the Argives was about to expire, and the Argives were not willing to make another unless someone gave the land of Cynuria back to them, so that it seemed impossible to fight the Argives and the Athenians at the same time. And they suspected that some of the cities in the Peloponnese would revolt to the Argives; which in fact happened.

So, as both sides reckoned these things, it seemed that the agreement must be made, and not least to the Lacedaemonians, from their desire to recover the men from the island; for the Spartiates among them were of the first rank and † alike † their kinsmen.

They had indeed begun to negotiate immediately after their capture, but the Athenians were in no way willing, while they were faring well, to settle on equal terms. But when they had failed at Delium, the Lacedaemonians, knowing that they would now be more likely to accept, at once made the one-year truce, during which they were to meet and deliberate also about a longer period.

But when the defeat at Amphipolis too had befallen the Athenians and both Cleon and Brasidas were dead, who on both sides had most opposed the peace, the one because he was successful and honoured through war, the other thinking that if there were quiet he would be more clearly seen to be doing wrong and less believed when he slandered, then indeed those who were most eager for the leadership in each city, Pleistoanax son of Pausanias, king of the Lacedaemonians, and Nicias son of Niceratus, who had fared best of the men of that time in his commands, became much more eager, Nicias wishing, while he was unharmed and held in esteem, to preserve his good fortune, and both for the present to rest from toil himself and to give his fellow citizens rest, and for future time to leave behind a name as one who had lived through without ever bringing the city to disaster, thinking that this comes from avoiding risk and from whoever entrusts himself least to fortune, and that peace provides freedom from risk, and Pleistoanax because he was being slandered by his enemies about his return, and was always put forward by them to the Lacedaemonians as a matter for scruple, whenever they suffered some setback, as though these things happened because of his unlawful return.

and in time to have urged the Lacedaemonians, when he was in exile at Lycaeum because of his retreat from Attica, once thought to have been bribed, and living at that time in a house half of which belonged to the sanctuary of Zeus, out of fear of the Lacedaemonians, to bring him back in the nineteenth year with the same dances and sacrifices as when they first established their kings at the founding of Lacedaemon.

Vexed, therefore, by this slander, and thinking that in peace, when no setback occurred and at the same time the Lacedaemonians were recovering their men, he himself too would be beyond the reach of his enemies, whereas while war prevailed it was always inevitable that the leading men should be slandered because of the misfortunes, he was eager for the agreement.

And during this winter they went into discussions, and towards spring a preparation was already held out as a threat by the Lacedaemonians, being announced round the cities as 〈for〉 a fort to be built in Attica, so that the Athenians might listen more readily, and when, as a result of the meetings, after they had put forward many claims against each other, it was agreed that they should make peace by giving back what each side had gained in war, but that the Athenians should keep Nisaea (for when they demanded Plataea back, the Thebans said that they held the place not by force but because its people had come over by agreement and had not been betrayed, and the Athenians said they held Nisaea in the same way), then indeed the Lacedaemonians, having summoned their own allies, and as all the others except the Boeotians and Corinthians and Eleans and Megarians voted to make an end (these did not like what was being done), made the agreement and poured libations with the Athenians and swore, and the Athenians with the Lacedaemonians, as follows.
‘The Athenians and the Lacedaemonians and the allies have made a treaty on the following terms, and have sworn to it city by city.

Concerning the common sanctuaries, whoever wishes may sacrifice and go and consult the oracles and attend as envoys according to ancestral custom, both by land and by sea, without fear. The sanctuary and the temple of Apollo at Delphi and the Delphians shall be independent and self-taxing and self-judging, both as to themselves and their own land, according to ancestral custom.

The treaty shall be for fifty years between the Athenians and the allies of the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians and the allies of the Lacedaemonians, without fraud and without harm, both by land and by sea.

It shall not be permitted to bear arms with intent to harm, neither for the Lacedaemonians and the allies against the Athenians and the allies, nor for the Athenians and the allies against the Lacedaemonians and the allies, by any art or device. And if there is any dispute between them, they shall use legal process and oaths, in whatever way they may agree.

The Lacedaemonians and the allies shall give back Amphipolis to the Athenians. And from whatever cities the Lacedaemonians handed over to the Athenians, it shall be permitted for the people to depart wherever they wish, keeping their own property; and the cities, paying the tribute fixed in the time of Aristides, shall be independent. And it shall not be permitted for the Athenians or the allies to bear arms against them to their harm, as long as they pay the tribute, since the treaty has been made. They are Argilus, Stagirus, Acanthus, Scolus, Olynthus, Spartolus. They shall be allies of neither side, neither of the Lacedaemonians nor of the Athenians; but if the Athenians persuade the cities, it shall be permitted for the Athenians to make them their allies if they are willing.
The Mecybernaeans and Sanaeans and Singaeans shall live in their own cities, just as the Olynthians and Acanthians.

The Lacedaemonians and the allies shall give back Panactum to the Athenians. And the Athenians too shall give back to the Lacedaemonians Coryphasium and Cythera and Methana and Pteleum and Atalante, and all the men of the Lacedaemonians who are in the public prison of the Athenians or in public prison anywhere else that the Athenians rule; and they shall release those of the Peloponnesians besieged in Scione and all the others who are allies of the Lacedaemonians in Scione and those whom Brasidas sent in, and any of the allies of the Lacedaemonians who is in Athens in the public prison or in public prison anywhere else that the Athenians rule. And the Lacedaemonians and the allies too shall give back whomever they hold of the Athenians and the allies on the same terms.
Concerning the Scionaeans and Toronaeans and Sermylians and any other city that the Athenians hold, the Athenians shall decide about them and the other cities as they see fit.

The Athenians shall make oaths with the Lacedaemonians and the allies city by city. Each side shall swear its local oath, the most binding one, seventeen men from each city. And the oath shall be as follows: “I will abide by this agreement and this treaty justly and without fraud.” And for the Lacedaemonians and the allies there shall be an oath on the same terms with the Athenians,
and both sides shall renew the oath every year. And they shall set up pillars at Olympia and Delphi and the Isthmus and at Athens on the Acropolis and at Lacedaemon in the Amyclaeum.

And if either side forgets anything about any matter, it shall be consistent with their oath for both, using fair discussion, to make a change in it in whatever way both may see fit, the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians.

‘The treaty begins 〈in Lacedaemon〉 in the ephorate of Pleistolas, on the fourth day from the end of the month Artemisium, and at Athens in the archonship of Alcaeus, on the sixth day from the end of the month Elaphebolion. The following swore and poured libations.

For the Lacedaemonians, 〈Pleistoanax, Agis,〉 Pleistolas, Damagetus, Chionis, Metagenes, Acanthus, Daithus, Ischagoras, Philocharidas, Zeuxidas, Antippus, Tellis, Alcinadas, Empedias, Menas, Laphilus. For the Athenians, the following. Lampon, Isthmionicus, Nicias, Laches, Euthydemus, Procles, Pythodorus, Hagnon, Myrtilus, Thrasycles, Theagenes, Aristocrates, Iolcius, Timocrates, Leon, Lamachus, Demosthenes.’

This treaty was made as the winter was ending, at the beginning of spring, immediately after the City Dionysia, just ten years having passed and a few days more since the first invasion of Attica and the beginning of this war took place.

Let one reckon by the seasons, and not rather trusting the enumeration of the names of those who, in each place, either as archons or by virtue of some office, mark past events. For it is not exact, since something may have happened to them either at the beginning or in the middle or at whatever point it chanced.
But counting by summers and winters, as it has been written, he will find, as each of these amounts to half of the year, that ten summers and as many winters have passed in this first war.

The Lacedaemonians (for the lot fell on them to give back first what they held) at once released the prisoners of war whom they held, and having sent Ischagoras and Menas and Philocharidas as envoys to the places in Thrace, they ordered Clearidas to hand over Amphipolis to the Athenians and the others to accept the treaty, as had been laid down for each.
