But they were not willing, thinking that it was not favourable to them; nor did Clearidas hand over the city, to please the Chalcidians, saying that he was not able to hand it over against their will.

And having come himself in haste with envoys from there to Lacedaemon, to defend himself if Ischagoras and his colleagues should accuse him of disobedience, and at the same time wishing to know whether the agreement could still be altered, when he found that they were bound, he himself went back again in haste, as the Lacedaemonians sent him and ordered him preferably to hand over the place too, or if not, to bring out all the Peloponnesians that were in it.

The allies happened to be present in Lacedaemon themselves, and the Lacedaemonians ordered those of them who had not accepted the treaty to make it. But they, on the same pretext on which they had rejected it at first, said they would not accept it, unless they made one that was fairer than this.

And as they did not listen to them, they dismissed them, and themselves made an alliance with the Athenians, thinking that the Argives would be least likely to be dangerous to them, since they had not been willing to renew the treaty when Ampelidas and Lichas came, considering them not formidable without the Athenians, and that the rest of the Peloponnese would most likely keep quiet; for they would have gone over to the Athenians, if it had been possible.
So, as envoys from the Athenians were present and discussions took place, they came to an agreement, and the following oaths and alliance were made.

‘On the following terms the Lacedaemonians 〈and the Athenians〉 shall be allies for fifty years. If any enemies come into the land of the Lacedaemonians and do harm to the Lacedaemonians, the Athenians shall help the Lacedaemonians in whatever way they can most effectively, as far as possible; and if they ravage it and depart, that city shall be an enemy to the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians and shall suffer harm from both, and both cities shall make peace together. This shall be done justly and zealously and without fraud.

And if any enemies come into the land of the Athenians and do harm to the Athenians, the Lacedaemonians shall help 〈the Athenians〉 in whatever way they can most effectively, as far as possible; and if they ravage it and depart, that city shall be an enemy to the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians and shall suffer harm from both, and both cities shall make peace together.
This shall be done justly and zealously and without fraud. And if the slave population rises in revolt, the Athenians shall help the Lacedaemonians with all their strength, as far as possible.

These shall be sworn to by those of each side who also swore the other treaty. And they shall renew 〈the oath〉 every year, the Lacedaemonians going to Athens for the Dionysia, and the Athenians going to Lacedaemon for the Hyacinthia.
And each side shall set up a pillar, the one in Lacedaemon by Apollo in the Amyclaeum, the other at Athens on the Acropolis by Athena.
And if the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians see fit to add or take away anything concerning the alliance, whatever they see fit, it shall be consistent with their oath for both.

‘The oath was sworn, for the Lacedaemonians, by the following: Pleistoanax, Agis, Pleistolas, Damagetus, Chionis, Metagenes, Acanthus, Daithus, Ischagoras, Philocharidas, Zeuxidas, Antippus, Alcinadas, Tellis, Empedias, Menas, Laphilus, and for the Athenians, Lampon, Isthmionicus, Laches, Nicias, Euthydemus, Procles, Pythodorus, Hagnon, Myrtilus, Thrasycles, Theagenes, Aristocrates, Iolcius, Timocrates, Leon, Lamachus, Demosthenes.’

This alliance was made not long after the treaty, and the Athenians gave back the men from the island to the Lacedaemonians, and the summer of the eleventh year began. These ten years of the first war, which went on continuously, have now been written.

After the treaty and the alliance of the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians, which were made after the ten years' war, when Pleistolas was ephor in Lacedaemon and Alcaeus archon at Athens, there was peace for those who accepted them, but the Corinthians and some of the cities in the Peloponnese tried to upset what had been done, and at once another disturbance arose between the allies and Lacedaemon.
And at the same time the Lacedaemonians, as time went on, also became suspect to the Athenians, since in some matters they did not do what had been laid down in the agreement.

And for six years and ten months they refrained from marching against each other's land, but abroad, under an unstable cessation of hostilities, they did each other the greatest harm; then, however, being forced to break the treaty made after the ten years, they entered again into open war.

The same Thucydides, an Athenian, has also written these things in order, as each thing happened, by summers and winters, until the Lacedaemonians and the allies put an end to the empire of the Athenians and took the Long Walls and the Piraeus. Up to this point the years of the war amounted in all to twenty-seven.

And if anyone does not see fit to consider the interval of agreement as war, he will not judge rightly. For let him look at the facts as they have been set out, and he will find that it is not reasonable for it to be judged a peace, in which neither side gave back nor received everything that they had agreed, and apart from these things, in the Mantinean and Epidaurian war and in other matters, violations occurred on both sides, and the allies in Thrace were no less hostile, and the Boeotians kept a ten-day truce.

So that, with the first ten-year war and the suspicious cessation of hostilities after it and the war that followed from it, one will find so many years, reckoning by the seasons, and not many days over, and that for those who asserted anything on the strength of oracles this alone indeed came true with certainty.
For I myself always remember, both when the war was beginning and until it ended, that it was put forward by many that it had to last thrice nine years.

And I lived through the whole of it, being of an age to understand and applying my mind, so that I might know something accurately; and it befell me to be exiled from my own country for twenty years after my command at Amphipolis, and, being present at the affairs of both sides, and not least at those of the Peloponnesians because of my exile, to perceive something more of them at my leisure.
The dispute after the ten years, then, and the breaking of the treaty, and how the war was fought after that, I shall relate.

and the others went away home, but the Corinthians, turning first to Argos, held discussions with some of the Argives who were in office, saying that, since the Lacedaemonians, not for the good but for the enslavement of the Peloponnese, had made a treaty and alliance with the Athenians, formerly their bitterest enemies, the Argives ought to see how the Peloponnese could be saved, and to decree that any city of the Greeks that wished, which is independent and gives fair and equal justice, might make an alliance with the Argives for the mutual defence of each other's land, and to appoint a few men with full powers, and not to have the discussions before the people, so that those who failed to persuade the multitude might not be exposed; and they said that many would come over out of hatred of the Lacedaemonians.
And the Corinthians, having suggested this, went back home;

and the men of the Argives, having heard it, when they had brought the proposals before the authorities and the people, the Argives passed the decree and chose twelve men, with whom any of the Greeks who wished might make an alliance, except the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians; and neither of these should be permitted to make a treaty without the people of the Argives.

And the Argives accepted this the more readily, seeing that war with the Lacedaemonians was coming for them (for the treaty with them was about to expire) and at the same time hoping to lead the Peloponnese; for at this time Lacedaemon was in very bad repute and was despised because of its misfortunes, while the Argives were in the best condition in every respect, not having taken part in the Attic war, but rather, being at peace with both, having reaped the profits.
So the Argives in this way were receiving into the alliance those of the Greeks who were willing,

and the Mantineans and their allies were the first to come over to them, fearing the Lacedaemonians. For a part of Arcadia had been subjugated by the Mantineans as subjects while the war against the Athenians was still going on, and they thought that the Lacedaemonians would not allow them to rule, now that they had leisure; so they gladly turned to the Argives, considering it a great city and always at variance with the Lacedaemonians, and governed by a democracy just like themselves.

And when the Mantineans had revolted, the rest of the Peloponnese also began to murmur that they too should do this, thinking that they had changed sides because they knew something more, and at the same time being angry with the Lacedaemonians, among other things also because in the Attic treaty it had been written that it would be consistent with their oath to add and take away whatever both the cities saw fit, the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians.

For this clause above all was disturbing the Peloponnese and raising the suspicion that the Lacedaemonians wished to enslave them together with the Athenians; for it would have been just for the alteration to have been written as belonging to all the allies.
So, being afraid, most of them were eager each on their own part also to make an alliance with the Argives.

The Lacedaemonians, perceiving this murmuring that had arisen in the Peloponnese and that the Corinthians had been its instigators and were themselves about to make a treaty with Argos, sent envoys to Corinth wishing to forestall what was coming, and they blamed them for the instigation of the whole thing, and said that if they revolted from them and became allies of the Argives, they would be breaking their oaths, and that they were already doing wrong in not accepting the treaty with the Athenians, since it had been stated that whatever the majority of the allies voted should be binding, unless there were some hindrance from gods or heroes.

And the Corinthians, in the presence of those of their allies who had not accepted the treaty either (for they themselves had summoned them beforehand), replied to the Lacedaemonians, not stating openly how they were wronged, that they had not recovered for them Sollium from the Athenians nor Anactorium, nor anything else in which they thought they were getting less, but making as their pretext that they would not betray those in Thrace; for they had sworn oaths to them both privately, when they first revolted with the Potidaeans, and others later.
About the old oaths they said this much, and about the alliance with the Argives they would deliberate with their friends and do whatever was just.

And the envoys of the Lacedaemonians went back home; and there happened to be present in Corinth envoys of the Argives too, who urged the Corinthians to come into the alliance and not to delay; but they told them to come to their next assembly.

And an embassy of the Eleans also came at once and first made an alliance with the Corinthians, then, going from there to Argos, as had been arranged beforehand, they became allies of the Argives. For they happened to be at variance with the Lacedaemonians about Lepreum.

For once, when a war had arisen between the Lepreates and some of the Arcadians, and the Eleans had been called in by the Lepreates to an alliance in return for half of their land, and had ended the war, the Eleans let the Lepreates themselves keep the land and imposed on them a payment of a talent to Olympian Zeus.

And until the Attic war they paid it, but then, when they stopped on the pretext of the war, the Eleans tried to compel them, and they turned to the Lacedaemonians. And when the case had been entrusted to the Lacedaemonians, the Eleans, suspecting that they would not get fair treatment, gave up the arbitration and ravaged the land of the Lepreates.

The Lacedaemonians nonetheless gave judgment that the Lepreates were independent and that the Eleans were in the wrong, and, as they had not abided by the arbitration, sent a garrison of hoplites into Lepreum.

The Eleans, thinking that the Lacedaemonians had received a city of theirs that had revolted, and citing the agreement in which it had been stated that whatever places anyone held when they entered the Attic war, they should hold these also when they came out of it, revolted to the Argives on the ground that they were not getting fair treatment, and they too made the alliance, as had been arranged beforehand.

And immediately after them the Corinthians and the Chalcidians in Thrace also became allies of the Argives. But the Boeotians and the Megarians, though saying the same, kept quiet, being let alone by the Lacedaemonians and thinking that the democracy of the Argives was less advantageous for them, governed as they were by an oligarchy, than the constitution of the Lacedaemonians.

About the same time in this summer the Athenians, having reduced the Scionaeans by siege, killed the men of military age, and enslaved the children and women, and gave the land to the Plataeans to occupy, and they brought the Delians back again to Delos, taking to heart their misfortunes in the battles and since the god at Delphi had given an oracle.
And the Phocians and the Locrians began to make war.

And the Corinthians and the Argives, being now allies, came to Tegea to make it revolt from the Lacedaemonians, seeing that it was a large part and thinking that, if it were added to them, they would hold the whole Peloponnese.

But when the Tegeans said that they would in no way oppose the Lacedaemonians, the Corinthians, who up to then had been acting zealously, slackened in their eagerness and feared that none of the others would now come over to them.

Nevertheless they went to the Boeotians and asked them to become allies of themselves and the Argives and to act in common in other matters; and the ten-day truce, which the Athenians and the Boeotians had with each other, made not long after [this] fifty-year treaty, the Corinthians asked the Boeotians to accompany them to Athens and obtain for them too, [just as the Boeotians had it,] and, if the Athenians did not accept, to renounce the armistice and in future not to make a treaty without them.

The Boeotians, when the Corinthians asked them, told them to wait as regards the alliance with the Argives, but they went to Athens with the Corinthians and did not obtain the ten days' truce, but the Athenians answered that the Corinthians had a treaty, if indeed they were allies of the Lacedaemonians.

The Boeotians, then, did not renounce the ten days' truce any the more, although the Corinthians demanded it and accused them of having agreed to it with them; but between the Corinthians and the Athenians there was a cessation of hostilities without a treaty.

The same summer the Lacedaemonians marched out in full force, under the command of Pleistoanax son of Pausanias, king of the Lacedaemonians, into Arcadia against the Parrhasians, who were subjects of the Mantineans, since they had called them in during a faction quarrel, and at the same time also intending to demolish the fort at Cypsela, if they could, which the Mantineans had built and themselves garrisoned, lying in the Parrhasian territory, against the Sciritis of Laconia.

And the Lacedaemonians ravaged the land of the Parrhasians, while the Mantineans, handing over their city to the Argives as guards, themselves guarded the allied territory; but being unable to save both the fort at Cypsela and the towns in Parrhasia, they went away.
The Lacedaemonians, after making the Parrhasians independent and pulling down the fort, withdrew home.

And in the same summer, when the soldiers who had gone out from Thrace with Brasidas had now come back to them, whom Clearidas had brought after the treaty, the Lacedaemonians voted that the Helots who had fought with Brasidas should be free and live wherever they wished, and not long afterwards they settled them with the Neodamodes at Lepreum, which lies on the border of Laconia and Elis, as they were by now at variance with the Eleans;

but those of their own men who had been taken on the island and had given up their arms, fearing that they might think that because of their misfortune they would be degraded and, if they kept their full rights, might attempt a revolution, they disfranchised, although some of them were already holding offices, and with such a disfranchisement that they could neither hold office nor have power to buy or sell anything. Later, however, in the course of time, they regained their rights.
In the same summer the Dians also took Thyssus on the Acte of Athos, which was an ally of the Athenians.

And all this summer there was intercourse between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians, but the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians suspected one another right after the treaty because of the non-restoration of the places to each other.

For the Lacedaemonians, who had drawn the lot to restore first, had not restored Amphipolis and the rest, nor were they making their allies in Thrace accept the treaty, nor the Boeotians, nor the Corinthians, though they always said that together with the Athenians they would compel these jointly, if they were not willing; and they set times, without a written agreement, within which those who did not come in were to be enemies to both.

So the Athenians, seeing that none of these things was being done in fact, suspected that the Lacedaemonians intended nothing just, so that they did not restore Pylos when they demanded it, but even regretted having given back the prisoners from the island, and they held the other places, waiting until the others too should do for them what had been agreed.

The Lacedaemonians said that they had done what was possible; for they had given back the Athenian prisoners who were in their hands and had withdrawn the soldiers in Thrace and whatever else they had in their power; but they said that they did not control Amphipolis so as to hand it over, but that they would try to bring the Boeotians and Corinthians into the treaty and to get back Panactum and to recover all the Athenians who were prisoners among the Boeotians.

They demanded, however, that Pylos be given back to them; or if not, that they at least withdraw the Messenians and the Helots, just as they themselves had withdrawn their troops from Thrace, and that the Athenians garrison the place themselves, if they wished.

And after many discussions had been held, and often, in this summer, they persuaded the Athenians to withdraw from Pylos the Messenians and the rest of the Helots and all who had deserted from Laconia; and they settled them at Cranii in Cephallenia.
So during this summer there was quiet and visiting to and fro between them.

In the following winter (for it happened that other ephors were now in office and not those under whom the treaty had been made, and some of them were even opposed to 〈the 〉 treaty) when embassies had come from the alliance and Athenians and Boeotians and Corinthians were present, and they had said much among themselves and agreed on nothing, as they were going home, Cleobulus and Xenares, those of the ephors who most wished to dissolve the treaty, held private talks with the Boeotians and Corinthians, urging them as far as possible to hold the same views and that the Boeotians should try, after first becoming allies of the Argives themselves, next to make the Argives together with the Boeotians allies of the Lacedaemonians (for in this way the Boeotians would least be compelled to enter the Attic treaty; for the Lacedaemonians would choose, in preference to the enmity of the Athenians and the dissolution of the treaty, to have the Argives become their friends and allies; for they knew that the Lacedaemonians always desired Argos to become friendly to them on good terms), thinking that the war outside the Peloponnese would be easier.

They asked the Boeotians, however, to hand over Panactum to the Lacedaemonians, so that by getting back Pylos in exchange for it, if they could, they might more easily enter on war with the Athenians.

And the Boeotians and Corinthians, having been charged with these instructions by Xenares and Cleobulus and all those of the Lacedaemonians who were friends of theirs, to report them to their governments, withdrew each to their own homes.

But two men of the Argives from the highest office watched for them on the road as they were leaving, and meeting them, entered into discussion on whether the Boeotians might somehow become their allies as the Corinthians and Eleans and Mantineans had; for they thought that, if this went forward, they could then easily both make war and make peace, with the Lacedaemonians too, if they wished, following a common policy, and with anyone else, if it were necessary.

The envoys of the Boeotians were pleased to hear it; for by chance they were being asked for the very things that their friends from Lacedaemon had also instructed them to seek. And the men of the Argives, when they saw that they were receiving the proposal, said that they would send envoys to the Boeotians and went away.

On their arrival the Boeotians reported to the boeotarchs both what had been said at Lacedaemon and what came from the Argives who had met them; and the boeotarchs were pleased and much more eager, because it had turned out for them from both sides that their friends among the Lacedaemonians wanted the same things and the Argives were pressing toward the same ends.

And not long afterwards envoys of the Argives arrived making the proposals that had been mentioned; and the boeotarchs sent them away after approving their proposals and promising to send envoys to Argos about the alliance.

Meanwhile it was decided first by the boeotarchs and the Corinthians and the Megarians and the envoys from Thrace to swear oaths to one another that truly on any occasion they would help the one in need and would not make war on anyone nor come to terms without common consent, and that then the Boeotians and Megarians (for they were doing the same) should make a treaty with the Argives.

But before the oaths were taken, the boeotarchs communicated these things to the four councils of the Boeotians, which hold all the supreme authority, and urged that oaths be taken with the cities that wished to swear together with them for mutual help.

But those in the councils of the Boeotians did not accept the proposal, fearing that they might act against the Lacedaemonians by swearing with the Corinthians who had revolted from them; for the boeotarchs did not tell them what had happened at Lacedaemon, that Cleobulus and Xenares among the ephors and their friends advised them first to become allies of the Argives and Corinthians and afterwards to join with the Lacedaemonians, believing that the council, even if they did not tell it, would vote nothing other than what they had decided beforehand and were recommending.

And when the matter met this resistance, the Corinthians and the envoys from Thrace went away without achieving anything, and the boeotarchs, who had earlier intended, if they carried this, to try to make the alliance with the Argives as well, no longer brought anything about the Argives before the councils, nor did they send to Argos the envoys they had promised, but there was a certain neglect and delay in everything.
And in this same winter the Olynthians took Mecyberna, which the Athenians were garrisoning, by a sudden attack.

After this (for discussions were always going on between the Athenians and Lacedaemonians about the places they held of each other) the Lacedaemonians, hoping that, if the Athenians got back Panactum from the Boeotians, they themselves would recover Pylos, went to the Boeotians as envoys and asked them to hand over to them Panactum and the Athenian prisoners, so that in exchange for them they might recover Pylos.

But the Boeotians said that they would not give them up unless they made a separate alliance with them as with the Athenians. The Lacedaemonians, though they knew that they would be wronging the Athenians, since it had been agreed that neither should make a treaty or war with anyone without the other, yet wishing to take over Panactum in order to recover Pylos in exchange for it, and since at the same time those who were eager to wreck the treaty were zealous for the Boeotian cause, made the alliance when the winter was already ending and toward spring; and Panactum was at once being pulled down. And the eleventh year of the war ended.

At the very beginning of spring of the following summer the Argives, when the envoys of the Boeotians whom they had said they would send did not come, and they learned that Panactum was being pulled down and that a separate alliance had been made by the Boeotians with the Lacedaemonians, feared that they would be isolated and that the whole alliance would go over to the Lacedaemonians;

for they thought that the Boeotians had been persuaded by the Lacedaemonians both to pull down Panactum and to enter the treaty with the Athenians, and that the Athenians knew of this, so that it was no longer possible for them to make an alliance even with the Athenians, whereas before they had hoped, from the quarrels, that if their treaty with the Lacedaemonians did not last, they would at any rate become allies of the Athenians.

Being at a loss, then, the Argives, and fearing that they would be at war at once with the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans, the Boeotians and Athenians, having earlier refused the treaty with the Lacedaemonians and been proud in the thought that they would lead the Peloponnese, sent as quickly as they could to Lacedaemon as envoys Eustrophus and Aeson, who seemed to be most friendly to them, thinking that in the present circumstances it was best to make a treaty with the Lacedaemonians, on whatever terms might be granted, and to keep quiet.
And their envoys on arrival held discussions with the Lacedaemonians on the terms on which a treaty might be made with them.

And at first the Argives demanded that the case be referred to arbitration, either to some city or to a private person, about the Cynurian land, about which they are always in dispute as it is a border region (it contains the towns of Thyrea and Anthene, and the Lacedaemonians occupy it); then, when the Lacedaemonians would not allow it to be mentioned, but said that, if they wished to make a treaty as before, they were ready, the Argive envoys nevertheless induced the Lacedaemonians to agree to the following: for the present to make a treaty for fifty years, but that it should be possible for either side, after a challenge, provided there was neither plague nor war at Lacedaemon or Argos, to fight it out for this land, as once before when each side claimed to have won, but that it should not be allowed to pursue beyond the borders of Argos and Lacedaemon.

To the Lacedaemonians this at first seemed folly, but then (for they desired to have Argos friendly at any cost) they agreed on what they demanded and drew up the terms in writing. But the Lacedaemonians told them, before any of it took effect, first to go back to Argos and show it to the people, and, if it was acceptable, to come at the Hyacinthia to swear the oaths. And they withdrew;

but in this time during which the Argives were doing this, the envoys of the Lacedaemonians, Andromedes and Phaedimus and Antimenidas, who were to receive Panactum and the men from the Boeotians and give them back to the Athenians, found Panactum demolished by the Boeotians themselves, on the pretext that there had once been, after a quarrel about it, old oaths between the Athenians and Boeotians that neither should inhabit the place but that they should graze it jointly, while the men of the Athenians whom the Boeotians held as prisoners Andromedes and his colleagues took over and brought to the Athenians and gave back, and they told them of the demolition of Panactum, thinking that this too was a restoration; for no enemy of the Athenians would live in it any longer.

When this was said the Athenians were indignant, thinking they had been wronged by the Lacedaemonians both by the demolition of Panactum, which ought to have been handed over standing, and when they learned that they had also made a separate alliance with the Boeotians, though they had earlier said they would jointly compel those who did not accept the treaty. And they considered all the other points in which they had fallen short of the agreement and thought they had been deceived, so that they gave the envoys a harsh answer and sent them away.
While the Lacedaemonians were in such a quarrel with the Athenians, those in Athens who in their turn wished to dissolve the treaty at once pressed on.

Among them was Alcibiades son of Clinias, a man who was then still young in age, as it would be in any other city, but honoured for the distinction of his ancestors; he thought it was really better to side with the Argives, yet he opposed it also out of pride and rivalry, because the Lacedaemonians had negotiated the treaty through Nicias and Laches, having overlooked him because of his youth and having not honoured the old proxeny that had once existed, which, after his grandfather had renounced it, he himself intended to renew by his attentions to their prisoners from the island.

And thinking that he was slighted on all sides, he had both spoken against it at first, saying that the Lacedaemonians were not to be trusted, but that they were making the treaty so that, having made a treaty with the Athenians, they might crush the Argives and then go against the Athenians alone, and now, when the quarrel had arisen, he at once sent privately to Argos, urging them to come as quickly as possible with the Mantineans and Eleans and invite them to the alliance, since it was the right moment and he himself would cooperate to the utmost.

When the Argives heard the message and when they learned that the alliance of the Boeotians had not been made with the Athenians, but that they had fallen into a great quarrel with the Lacedaemonians, they paid no more attention to their envoys at Lacedaemon, who happened to be away about the treaty, and turned their thoughts rather to the Athenians, thinking that a city friendly to them from of old, and governed as a democracy as they themselves were, and possessing great power at sea, would fight on their side if they went to war.
So they at once sent envoys to the Athenians about the alliance; and the Eleans and Mantineans also joined in the embassy.

Envoys of the Lacedaemonians also arrived in haste, men who seemed acceptable to the Athenians, Philocharidas and Leon and Endius, fearing that the Athenians in their anger would make the alliance with the Argives, and at the same time to ask for Pylos in exchange for Panactum and to defend the Boeotian alliance, saying that they had not made it to harm the Athenians.

And by saying in the council both this and that they had come with full powers to settle all the points in dispute, they made Alcibiades afraid that, if they said the same before the people, they would win over the multitude and the Argive alliance would be rejected.

So Alcibiades contrived the following against them: he persuaded the Lacedaemonians, giving them a pledge, that if they did not admit before the people that they had come with full powers, he would give Pylos back to them (for he himself would persuade the Athenians, just as he was now opposing it) and would settle the other matters.

He did this wishing to detach them from Nicias and, by discrediting them before the people as having nothing true in mind and never saying the same things, to make the Argives and Eleans and Mantineans allies. And so it happened.

For when they came before the people and on being asked said that they had not come with full powers, as they had said in the council, the Athenians would no longer bear it, but as Alcibiades cried out against the Lacedaemonians much more than before, they listened to him and were ready to bring in the Argives and those with them at once and make them allies; but an earthquake happened before anything was ratified, and this assembly was adjourned.

At the assembly on the next day Nicias, although the Lacedaemonians had been deceived and he himself had been deceived about their not admitting that they had come with full powers, nevertheless said that they should rather become friends with the Lacedaemonians, and, putting off the matter of the Argives, send again to them and find out what they intended, saying that it was to their own honour and to the other side's discredit that the war should be put off; for while their affairs stood well it was best for them to preserve their prosperity as long as possible, but for the others, who were in misfortune, it was a windfall to run the risk as soon as possible.

And he persuaded them to send envoys, of whom he himself was one, to tell the Lacedaemonians, if they intended anything just, to give back Panactum standing and Amphipolis, and to give up the alliance with the Boeotians, if they did not enter the treaty, just as it had been agreed that neither should come to terms with anyone without the other.

And they told them to say that they too, if they had wished to do wrong, would already have made the Argives allies, since they were indeed present for this very purpose. And after instructing them on whatever else they complained of, they sent off Nicias and his fellow envoys.

And when they arrived and reported the other points and finally said that, unless they gave up the alliance with the Boeotians if they did not enter the treaty, they too would make the Argives and those with them allies, the Lacedaemonians said that they would not give up the alliance with the Boeotians, since Xenares the ephor and his party and all others who were of the same mind prevailed in having it so, but at Nicias' request they renewed the oaths; for he feared that he would go away with everything unaccomplished and be attacked, as indeed happened, since he was thought to be responsible for the treaty with the Lacedaemonians.

And when he had come back and the Athenians heard that nothing had been accomplished at Lacedaemon, they were at once in a rage, and thinking they had been wronged (for the Argives and their allies happened to be present), with Alcibiades introducing them, they made a treaty and alliance with them as follows.

‘The Athenians and the Argives and Mantineans and Eleans made a treaty for a hundred years 〈with one another〉, on behalf of themselves and the allies whom each rule, without fraud and without harm, both by land and by sea.

It shall not be allowed to bear arms with hostile intent, either for the Argives and Eleans and Mantineans and their allies against the Athenians and the allies whom the Athenians rule, or for the Athenians and their allies 〈whom the Athenians rule〉 against the Argives and Eleans and Mantineans and their allies, by any craft or contrivance.

On the following terms the Athenians and Argives and Mantineans and Eleans shall be allies for a hundred years. If enemies come against the land of the Athenians, the Argives and Mantineans and Eleans shall come to help to Athens, in whatever way the Athenians request, in the most vigorous manner they can, as far as possible; and if they ravage it and depart, this city shall be an enemy to the Argives and Mantineans and Eleans and Athenians and shall be punished by all these cities; and none of the cities shall be allowed to end the war against this city, unless all decide so.

And the Athenians too shall come to help to Argos and Mantinea and Elis, if enemies come against the land of the Argives or that of the Mantineans or that of the Eleans, in whatever way these cities request, in the most vigorous manner they can, as far as possible; and if they ravage it and depart, this city shall be an enemy to the Athenians and Argives and Mantineans and Eleans and shall be punished by all these cities; and 〈none of the cities〉 shall be allowed to end the war against this city, unless all [the cities] decide so.

They shall not allow armed men to pass for war through their own land or that of the allies whom each rule, nor by sea, unless all the cities have voted for the passage, the Athenians and Argives and Mantineans and Eleans.

For those who come to help, the city that sends them shall provide food for up to thirty days, once they come to the city that requested help, and likewise on their return; but if it wishes to use the army for a longer time, the city that sent for them shall give food, to the hoplite and light-armed soldier and archer three Aeginetan obols for each day, and to the horseman an Aeginetan drachma.

The city that sent for 〈the army〉 shall have the command, when the war is in its own territory; but if it is decided by 〈all〉 the cities to make an expedition jointly somewhere, the command shall be shared equally by all the cities.

The Athenians shall swear to the treaty on behalf of themselves and their allies, and the Argives and Mantineans and Eleans and their allies shall swear city by city. Each shall swear the oath of their own country that is the greatest, over full-grown victims. And the oath shall be as follows: “I will abide by the alliance according to the agreement, justly and without harm and without fraud, and I will not transgress it by any craft or contrivance.”

At Athens the council and the home magistrates shall swear, and the prytanes shall administer the oath; at Argos the council and the Eighty and the artynae, and the Eighty shall administer the oath; at Mantinea the demiurgi and the council and the other magistrates, and the theori and the polemarchs shall administer the oath; at Elis the demiurgi and the holders of the offices and the Six Hundred, and the demiurgi and the thesmophylaces shall administer the oath.

The oaths shall be renewed by the Athenians going to Elis and to Mantinea and to Argos thirty days before the Olympic games, and by the Argives and Eleans and Mantineans going to Athens ten days before the Great Panathenaea.

The agreement about the treaty and the oaths and the alliance shall be inscribed on a stone pillar, by the Athenians on the Acropolis, by the Argives in the marketplace in the temple of Apollo, and by the Mantineans in the temple of Zeus in the marketplace; and they shall also set up jointly at Olympia a bronze pillar at the present Olympic games.
And if these cities decide that it is better to add anything to the agreement, whatever all the cities decide in joint deliberation shall be binding.’
The treaty and the alliance were made in this way, and the treaty of the Lacedaemonians and Athenians was not renounced on this account by either side.

The Corinthians, though allies of the Argives, did not enter into it, but, even when an alliance had been made before this by the Eleans and Argives and Mantineans, to make war and peace with the same parties, they did not swear to it, but said that the first defensive alliance that had been made was enough for them, to help one another, but to join no one in attacking.
The Corinthians thus stood apart from the allies and again turned their thoughts toward the Lacedaemonians.

The Olympic games were held this summer, at which Androsthenes the Arcadian won the pancratium for the first time; and the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the sanctuary by the Eleans, so that they could neither sacrifice nor compete, as they had not paid them the fine which, under the Olympic law, the Eleans had imposed on them, alleging that they had borne arms 〈against〉 them against the fort of Phyrcus and sent hoplites of theirs into Lepreum during the Olympic truce. The fine was two thousand minas, two minas for each hoplite, as the law prescribes.
The Lacedaemonians sent envoys and argued that they had not been justly condemned, saying that the truce had not yet been announced at Lacedaemon when they sent in the hoplites.

The Eleans said that the armistice was already in force among them (for they proclaim it first to themselves), and that while they were keeping quiet and expecting nothing, as in time of truce, the others had done wrong unnoticed.

The Lacedaemonians replied that there was no need for them to make the announcement at Lacedaemon any longer, if they already considered them to be doing wrong, but that they had done so not as believing this, and that they had no longer borne arms against them anywhere.

The Eleans held to the same argument, that they could not be persuaded that the others were not doing wrong, but that if they were willing to give back Lepreum to them, they would remit their own share of the money, and what was due to the god they would pay themselves on their behalf.

When they would not listen, they next demanded this, that they need not give back Lepreum if they did not wish, but that, mounting the altar of Olympian Zeus, since they were eager to use the sanctuary, they should swear before the Greeks that they would truly pay the fine later.

When they would not do even this, the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the sanctuary [from sacrifice and contests] and sacrificed at home, and the other Greeks attended the festival, except the Lepreans.

And there was great fear at the festival that the Lacedaemonians would come in arms, especially since Lichas son of Arcesilaus, a Lacedaemonian, had been beaten by the umpires in the arena, because, when his own team won and was proclaimed as belonging to the Boeotian state, since he was not allowed to compete, he came forward into the arena and crowned the charioteer, wishing to show that the chariot was his; so that all were much more afraid and it seemed that something new would happen. The Lacedaemonians, however, kept quiet, and the festival passed thus for them.

After the Olympic games the Argives and their allies came to Corinth to ask them to join them. And envoys of the Lacedaemonians happened to be present, and after much discussion nothing was finally accomplished, but when an earthquake happened they all dispersed home. And the summer ended.
In the following winter the Heracleots in Trachis fought a battle against the Aenianians and Dolopians and Malians and some of the Thessalians.

For these peoples, living near the city, were hostile to it; for the place had been fortified against no other land than theirs. And they had opposed the city from the very moment it was being founded, damaging it as much as they could, and on this occasion they defeated the Heracleots in the battle, and Xenares son of Cnidis, the Lacedaemonian, their commander, was killed, and others of the Heracleots were also killed. And the winter ended, and the twelfth year of the war ended.

At the very beginning of the following summer the Boeotians took over Heraclea, as it was in a bad way after the battle, and sent away Agesippidas the Lacedaemonian for governing it badly. They took over the place fearing that, while the Lacedaemonians were in turmoil over affairs in the Peloponnese, the Athenians would take it; the Lacedaemonians, however, were angry with them.

And in the same summer Alcibiades son of Clinias, being a general of the Athenians, with the Argives and the allies cooperating, went into the Peloponnese with a few Athenian hoplites and archers, and taking along the allies from there, helped to settle various matters concerning the alliance as he went through the Peloponnese with his army, and persuaded the Patreans to carry their walls down to the sea, and himself intended to build another fort at Achaean Rhium. But the Corinthians and Sicyonians, and those to whom it would have been harmful if built, came to help and prevented it.

In the same summer war broke out between the Epidaurians and the Argives, on the pretext of the offering to Apollo Pythaeus, which the Epidaurians were obliged to bring but did not send in payment for pasture lands (the Argives had the chief authority over the temple); but even without this cause it seemed good to Alcibiades and the Argives to win over Epidaurus, if they could, both to keep Corinth quiet and because help from Aegina would be shorter for the Athenians than sailing around Scyllaeum. So the Argives prepared themselves to invade Epidaurus to exact the offering.

At about the same time the Lacedaemonians also marched out in full force to Leuctra on their own border toward Mount Lycaeum, under the command of Agis son of Archidamus, their king; but no one knew where they were marching, not even the cities from which the troops had been sent.

But when the sacrifices for crossing the border did not turn out favourably for them, they themselves went back home and sent word round to their allies to prepare to march after the coming month (it was the month Carneus, a holy month for the Dorians).
When they had withdrawn, the Argives marched out on the fourth day before the end of the month before Carneus, and, keeping this day the whole time, invaded the Epidaurian territory and ravaged it.
The Epidaurians called on their allies; some of them pleaded the month as an excuse, and others came as far as the border of the Epidaurian territory and kept quiet.

And during the time when the Argives were in Epidaurus, embassies from the cities met at Mantinea, at the invitation of the Athenians. And during the discussions Euphamidas the Corinthian said that their words did not agree with their deeds; for they were sitting together about peace, while the Epidaurians and their allies and the Argives were drawn up against each other in arms; so they ought first to go to each side and break up the armies, and then talk again about the peace.

And they were persuaded and went and led the Argives out of the Epidaurian territory. But later they met in the same place and even so were unable to agree, but the Argives again invaded the Epidaurian territory and ravaged it.
The Lacedaemonians also marched out to Caryae, and when the sacrifices for crossing were not favourable to them there either, they withdrew.

The Argives, after ravaging about a third of the Epidaurian territory, went back home. And a thousand Athenian hoplites came to help them, with Alcibiades as general; but on learning that the Lacedaemonians had ended their expedition, and as there was no longer any need of them, he went away. And so the summer passed.
In the following winter the Lacedaemonians, unnoticed by the Athenians, sent three hundred garrison troops and Agesippidas as commander by sea into Epidaurus.

The Argives came to the Athenians and complained that, although it was written in the treaty that each should not allow enemies to pass through their own territory, they had allowed them to sail past by sea; and that unless they in turn brought the Messenians and Helots to Pylos against the Lacedaemonians, they themselves would be wronged.

The Athenians, persuaded by Alcibiades, wrote at the foot of the Laconian pillar that the Lacedaemonians had not kept their oaths, and brought the Helots from Cranii to Pylos to plunder, but otherwise kept quiet.
During this winter, while the Argives and Epidaurians were at war, no pitched battle took place, but ambushes and raids, in which some on each side were killed as chance had it.

And at the end of the winter, when it was already toward spring, the Argives came with ladders against Epidaurus, intending to take it by force as it was empty of men because of the war; and they went away without success. And the winter ended, and the thirteenth year of the war ended.

In the middle of the following summer the Lacedaemonians, since the Epidaurians, their allies, were in distress and of the rest in the Peloponnese some had revolted and others were not well disposed, thinking that unless they acted quickly to forestall it, the matter would go further, marched in full force with the Helots against Argos; Agis son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, led them.

The Tegeans and all the other Arcadians who were allies of the Lacedaemonians marched with them. The allies from the rest of the Peloponnese and those from outside gathered at Phlius, the Boeotians with five thousand hoplites and as many light troops and five hundred horsemen and as many foot soldiers who fought with the horsemen, the Corinthians with two thousand hoplites, the others in varying numbers, and the Phliasians with their whole force, since the army was in their territory.

The Argives, having learned in advance first of the preparations of the Lacedaemonians and then that they were advancing to Phlius wishing to join the others, then marched out themselves too; and the Mantineans came to help them, with their own allies, and three thousand hoplites of the Eleans.

And advancing they met the Lacedaemonians at Methydrium in Arcadia. And each side occupied a hill; and the Argives prepared to fight the Lacedaemonians as they were isolated, but Agis broke camp by night and, unnoticed, marched to Phlius to join the other allies.
And the Argives, perceiving this, set out at dawn, first to Argos, and then to the road by which they expected the Lacedaemonians to come down with their allies, the road by Nemea.

Agis, however, did not take this road which they expected, but, giving orders to the Lacedaemonians and Arcadians and Epidaurians, went by another, difficult road and came down into the plain of the Argives; and the Corinthians and Pellenians and Phliasians marched by another steep road; and the Boeotians and Megarians and Sicyonians had been told to come down by the road from Nemea, where the Argives were posted, so that, if the Argives went into the plain against them to bring help, they could follow and use their horses.
And having made these dispositions and invaded the plain, he ravaged Saminthus and other places;

and the Argives, learning of it, came to help from Nemea when it was already day, and falling in with the army of the Phliasians and Corinthians they killed a few of the Phliasians, while they themselves lost not many more to the Corinthians.

And the Boeotians and Megarians and Sicyonians advanced, as they had been told, along the road to Nemea, and no longer found the Argives there, but went down and, when they saw their own land being ravaged, formed up for battle. And the Lacedaemonians too prepared themselves on the other side.

The Argives were cut off in the middle; for from the plain the Lacedaemonians and those with them shut them off from the city, from above the Corinthians and Phliasians and Pellenians, and on the side toward Nemea the Boeotians and Sicyonians and Megarians. They had no horsemen with them; for the Athenians alone of the allies had not yet come.

The mass of the Argives and their allies did not think the present situation so dangerous, but it seemed to them that the battle would be on favourable ground, and that they had cut off the Lacedaemonians in their own territory and near their own city.

But two men of the Argives, Thrasylus, who was one of the five generals, and Alciphron, proxenus of the Lacedaemonians, when the armies were already all but meeting, went up to Agis and urged him not to fight a battle; for the Argives were ready to give and accept arbitration on fair and equal terms, if the Lacedaemonians had any complaint against the Argives, and to keep peace in future after making a treaty.

And those of the Argives who said this spoke on their own authority and not by order of the people; and Agis accepted the proposals himself, and without consulting the majority, nor even deliberating himself, but only communicating with one man of those in authority who were serving with the army, made a truce for four months, within which they were to carry out what had been agreed. And he led the army away at once, without telling any of the other allies.

The Lacedaemonians and their allies followed as he led because of the law, but among themselves they blamed Agis greatly, thinking that when a fine chance had come for them to engage, with the enemy shut in on all sides by both horse and foot, they were going away having done nothing worthy of their preparations.

For this was indeed the finest Greek army that had been assembled up to that time; and it was seen best while it was still all together at Nemea, where the Lacedaemonians were with their whole force, and Arcadians and Boeotians and Corinthians and Sicyonians and Pellenians and Phliasians and Megarians, and all of these picked men from each people, who seemed a match not only for the Argive alliance but even if another were added to it.
So the army, thus blaming Agis, withdrew and dispersed, each to their own homes,

and the Argives themselves blamed even much more those who had made the truce without the people, they too thinking that the Lacedaemonians had escaped when a finer chance would never have come to them; for the contest would have taken place near their own city and with many good allies.

And on their return they began to stone Thrasylus in the Charadrus, where they try cases arising from campaigns before entering the city. But he took refuge at the altar and survived; they did, however, confiscate his property.

After this, when a thousand Athenian hoplites and three hundred horsemen came to help, commanded by Laches and Nicostratus, the Argives (for they still hesitated to break the truce with the Lacedaemonians) told them to go away and did not bring them before the people when they wished to negotiate, until the Mantineans and Eleans (for they were still present) compelled them by their insistence.

And the Athenians, with Alcibiades present as envoy, said before the Argives and the allies that the truce had not been rightly made without the other allies, and that now (for they had come at the right moment) they ought to take up the war.

And having persuaded the allies by these arguments, they at once all marched against Arcadian Orchomenus, except the Argives; these, although persuaded, stayed behind at first, but later they too came.

And all of them sat down before Orchomenus, besieged it and made assaults, wishing to win it over for various reasons and especially because hostages from Arcadia had been placed there by the Lacedaemonians.

The Orchomenians, fearing the weakness of their wall and the size of the army, and, as no one came to help them, that they would perish first, came to terms, to be allies and to give hostages of their own to the Mantineans and to hand over those whom the Lacedaemonians had deposited there.

After this, now holding Orchomenus, the allies deliberated which of the remaining places they should attack first. And the Eleans urged going against Lepreum, the Mantineans against Tegea; and the Argives and Athenians sided with the Mantineans.

And the Eleans, angry that they had not voted to go against Lepreum, went back home; the other allies prepared at Mantinea to go against Tegea. And some of those in the city itself were also offering to betray it to them.

The Lacedaemonians, when they had withdrawn from Argos after making the four months' truce, blamed Agis greatly for not having subdued Argos for them, when there had been a finer chance than ever before, as they themselves thought; for it was not easy to catch so many allies of such quality all together.

And when news came also of the capture of Orchomenus, they were much more angry and at once in their rage resolved, contrary to their own character, that they should raze his house and fine him a hundred thousand drachmas.
But he begged them to do none of these things; for he would make amends for the charges by a good deed on campaign, or else they could then do what they wished.

They put off the fine and the razing, but at that time they made a law which had never existed among them before; for they chose ten Spartiates as his advisers, without whom he had no authority to lead an army out of the city.
Meanwhile news came to them from their friends in Tegea that, unless they came quickly, Tegea would revolt from them to the Argives and their allies, and that it had all but revolted already.
Then the Lacedaemonians and the Helots set out to help in full force, quickly and as never before.

They marched to Orestheum in Maenalia; and they told those of the Arcadians who were their allies to gather and follow close behind them to Tegea, while they themselves all went as far as Orestheum, and from there, after sending back home the sixth part of their own men, in which were the older and the younger men, to guard things at home, they arrived at Tegea with the rest of the army. And not long afterwards the allies from Arcadia arrived.

They also sent to Corinth and to the Boeotians and Phocians and Locrians, telling them to come quickly to help to Mantinea. But for these it was short notice, and it was not easy to pass through the enemy territory unless they were together and had waited for one another (for it shut them off in the middle), but nevertheless they hurried on.
The Lacedaemonians, taking with them the Arcadian allies who were present, invaded the Mantinean territory, and encamping near the temple of Heracles they ravaged the land.
When the Argives and their allies saw them, they occupied a strong position, hard to approach, and drew up as if for battle.

And the Lacedaemonians at once advanced against them; and they came as far as a stone's or javelin's throw, but then one of the older men, seeing that they were going against a strong position, shouted to Agis that he was intending to cure one evil with another, meaning that he wanted his present untimely eagerness to make up for the blameworthy retreat from Argos.
And he, whether because of the shout or because some other thought, or the same, suddenly occurred to him, led the army back again in haste before engaging.

And arriving at the Tegean territory he turned the water into the Mantinean territory, the water over which, since it does much harm to whichever side it falls on, the Mantineans and Tegeans are at war. He wanted to make those who were on the hill come down to help against the diversion of the water, once they learned of it, [the Argives and their allies] and to fight the battle on level ground.

And having stayed that day there by the water, he diverted it; and the Argives and their allies, at first astonished at their sudden retreat at such short notice, did not know what to think; then, when the others had retreated and disappeared from sight and they themselves were keeping still and not following, they again blamed their own generals for having let the Lacedaemonians go before, when they had been finely caught near Argos, and now because no one pursued them as they ran away, but the enemy were getting safely away at their ease while they themselves were being betrayed.
The generals were at first confused, but later they led them down from the hill and, advancing into the plain, encamped as if to go against the enemy.

On the next day the Argives and their allies formed up as they intended to fight, if they came upon the enemy; and the Lacedaemonians, going back from the water to the temple of Heracles to the same camp, saw at a short distance their opponents all already in line and advanced from the hill.

On this occasion the Lacedaemonians were more alarmed than at any time they remembered. For their preparation had to be made at short notice, and at once they hurriedly fell into their own order, with King Agis directing everything according to the law.

For when a king leads, everything is commanded by him, and he himself tells the polemarchs what is needed, they tell the lochagoi, these the pentecontaters, and these in turn the enomotarchs, and these the enomoty.

On this occasion the Sciritae formed their left wing, who alone of the Lacedaemonians always hold this position by themselves; next to them were the Brasidean soldiers from Thrace and the Neodamodes with them; then came the Lacedaemonians themselves, who placed their companies in order, and next to them the Heraeans of Arcadia, after these the Maenalians, and on the right wing the Tegeans, with a few of the Lacedaemonians holding the extreme end, and their horsemen on each wing.

The Lacedaemonians were drawn up thus; their opponents had the Mantineans on the right wing, because the action was taking place in their territory, next to them were their Arcadian allies, then the thousand picked men of the Argives, to whom the city had long provided training in warfare at public expense, and next to them the other Argives, and after them their allies, the Cleonaeans and Orneates, then the Athenians last, holding the left wing, and their own horsemen with them.
Such was the order and preparation of both sides, but the army of the Lacedaemonians appeared larger.

But I could not write down the numbers accurately, either for each contingent on either side or for the whole; for the number of the Lacedaemonians was unknown because of the secrecy of their state, and that of the others in turn was distrusted because of men's tendency to boast about their own numbers. From the following calculation, however, one can estimate the number of the Lacedaemonians who were present on that occasion.

Seven companies fought, apart from the Sciritae, who were six hundred, and in each company there were four pentecostyes, and in each pentecostys four enomoties. Of each enomoty four men fought in the front rank; in depth they were not all drawn up alike, but as each company commander wished, though on the whole they were drawn up eight deep. And along the whole line, apart from the Sciritae, the front rank consisted of four hundred and forty-eight men.

When they were now about to engage, exhortations were also given to each contingent by their own generals, as follows: to the Mantineans, that the battle would be for their country and at the same time for empire and slavery, so that the one, having tasted it, they should not lose, and the other they should not taste again; to the Argives, that for their ancient leadership and their former equal share in the Peloponnese they should not put up with being deprived of them for ever, and that they should punish men who were at once their enemies and neighbours for many wrongs; and to the Athenians, that it was glorious, fighting with many good allies, to be second to none, and that by defeating the Lacedaemonians in the Peloponnese they would hold their empire more securely and enlarge it, and that no one else would ever come against their land.

Such were the exhortations given to the Argives and their allies, while the Lacedaemonians, man by man and with their war songs, made among themselves the exhortation to remember what they knew, as brave men, knowing that long practice in deeds gives more safety than an exhortation in words, finely spoken at short notice.

And after this came the clash, the Argives and their allies advancing vigorously and with fury, the Lacedaemonians slowly and to the music of many flute players stationed among them, not for religious reasons, but so that they might advance evenly, stepping in rhythm, and their line might not break up, as large armies tend to do in advancing.

While they were still closing, King Agis decided to do the following. All armies do this: in engagements they are pushed out rather toward their right wings, and both sides overlap the enemy's left with their right, because each man in his fear brings his unprotected side as close as possible to the shield of the man stationed on his right and thinks that the closeness of the locked ranks gives the best protection; and the man at the front of the right wing is responsible for this, as he is always eager to keep his own unprotected side away from the enemy, and the others follow from the same fear.
And on this occasion the Mantineans with their wing far overlapped the Sciritae, and the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans overlapped the Athenians still more, as their army was larger.

Agis, fearing that their left would be surrounded, and thinking that the Mantineans overlapped too far, signalled to the Sciritae and Brasideans to move out from their own line and make it equal to the Mantineans, and into this gap he ordered two companies from the right wing, under the polemarchs Hipponoidas and Aristocles, to move across and fill it by throwing themselves in, thinking that their own right would still have a surplus and that the line facing the Mantineans would be made firmer.

It happened, however, since he gave the order at the very moment of the advance and at short notice, that Aristocles and Hipponoidas refused to move across, and indeed for this offence they were afterwards banished from Sparta, being judged to have played the coward, and that the enemy engaged first, and, when he ordered the Sciritae, since the companies had not moved across, to rejoin his own line, they too were no longer able to close it up.
But although the Lacedaemonians had been at a disadvantage in skill in every respect on this occasion, they showed that they were no less superior in courage.

For when they came to close quarters with the enemy, the right of the Mantineans routed their Sciritae and Brasideans, and the Mantineans and their allies and the thousand picked men of the Argives, bursting in through the gap that had not been closed, cut down the Lacedaemonians and, surrounding them, routed them and drove them back to the wagons and killed some of the older men posted there.

And in this part the Lacedaemonians were defeated; but with the rest of the army, and especially the centre, where King Agis was and around him the three hundred so-called horsemen, they fell upon the older men of the Argives and the five companies so named, and the Cleonaeans and Orneates and those of the Athenians drawn up beside them, and routed them, most of them not even waiting to come to blows, but giving way at once as the Lacedaemonians came on, and some even being trampled down in their haste to escape being overtaken.

When the army of the Argives and their allies had given way in this part, it was now breaking off on both sides at once, and at the same time the right of the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans was surrounding the Athenians with its overlapping part, and danger had closed around them on both sides, on one side being surrounded, on the other already defeated. And they would have suffered most of the whole army, if their horsemen, who were present, had not been of help to them.
And it happened that Agis, when he saw his left in trouble against the Mantineans and the thousand Argives, ordered the whole army to move toward the part that was being defeated.

And when this happened, the Athenians meanwhile, as the army passed by and turned away from them, got away safely at their ease, and with them the defeated part of the Argives; while the Mantineans and their allies and the picked men of the Argives no longer thought of pressing on the enemy, but, seeing their own side defeated and the Lacedaemonians bearing down on them, they turned to flight.

And of the Mantineans many more were killed, but most of the picked men of the Argives escaped. The flight and retreat, however, were not hard pressed or long; for the Lacedaemonians, until they have routed the enemy, fight long and stubbornly, standing their ground, but once they have routed them their pursuits are short and not far.
Such, or as close as possible to this, was the battle, the greatest indeed of Greek battles for a very long time and fought by the most notable cities.

The Lacedaemonians, setting the arms of the enemy dead in front of them, at once set up a trophy and stripped the dead, and they took up their own dead and carried them to Tegea, where they were buried, and gave back those of the enemy under truce.

There died of the Argives and Orneates and Cleonaeans seven hundred, of the Mantineans two hundred, and of the Athenians with the Aeginetans two hundred, and both generals. Of the Lacedaemonians, the allies did not suffer so much that any notable loss occurred; of themselves it was hard to learn the truth, but it was said that about three hundred died.
When the battle was about to take place, Pleistoanax, the other king, also came to help with the older and younger men, and he got as far as Tegea, but on learning of the victory he went back.

And the Lacedaemonians sent and turned back the allies from Corinth and from beyond the Isthmus, and they themselves withdrew and, dismissing their allies (for it happened to be the Carnea for them), celebrated the festival.

And by this one action they cleared themselves of the charge then brought against them by the Greeks, both of cowardice because of the disaster on the island and of their general want of counsel and slowness, being thought ill of because of fortune, as it seemed, but being still the same men in spirit.

On the day before this battle it also happened that the Epidaurians invaded the Argive territory in full force, as it was empty of men, and killed many of the guards left behind by the Argives when they had marched out.

And when three thousand hoplites of the Eleans had come to help the Mantineans after the battle, and a thousand Athenians in addition to the earlier ones, all these allies at once marched against Epidaurus, while the Lacedaemonians were celebrating the Carnea, and dividing the work among themselves they began to wall the city round.

And the others gave up, but the Athenians, as they had been assigned, at once completed the headland where the temple of Hera stands. And they all left a garrison together in this part of the fortification and withdrew, each to their own cities. And the summer ended.
At the very beginning of the following winter the Lacedaemonians, after celebrating the Carnea, marched out, and on arriving at Tegea sent proposals for an agreement ahead to Argos.

They had men there even before who were friendly to them and who wished to overthrow the democracy at Argos; and after the battle had taken place, they were much better able to persuade the many to accept the agreement. They wanted first to make a treaty with the Lacedaemonians, then later an alliance as well, and only then to attack the people.

And Lichas son of Arcesilaus, who was proxenus of the Argives, came from the Lacedaemonians bringing two proposals to Argos, one on what terms they would make war, if they wished it, the other on what terms they would keep peace, if they preferred peace. And after much debate (for Alcibiades also happened to be present) the men who were working for the Lacedaemonians, now also daring to act openly, persuaded the Argives to accept the proposal for agreement. It is as follows.

‘On these terms the assembly of the Lacedaemonians resolves to make an agreement with the Argives: they shall give back the children to the Orchomenians and the men to the Maenalians, and give back the men in Mantinea to the Lacedaemonians, and withdraw from Epidaurus and demolish the fort.
And if the Athenians do not withdraw from Epidaurus, they shall be enemies to the Argives and to the Lacedaemonians and to the allies of the Lacedaemonians and to the allies of the Argives.
And if the Lacedaemonians hold any child, they shall give it back to all the cities.
Concerning the sacrifice to the god, if they wish, an oath shall be tendered to the Epidaurians, 〈if〉 not, they shall swear it themselves.
All the cities in the Peloponnese, both small and great, shall be independent according to ancestral custom.

And if anyone from outside the Peloponnese comes against the Peloponnesian land to do harm, they shall resist together, after deliberating in common, in whatever way seems most just to the Peloponnesians.

All the allies of the Lacedaemonians outside the Peloponnese shall be in the same position as the Lacedaemonians, and the allies of the Argives shall be in 〈the same position as the Argives〉, keeping their own territory.
After showing this to the allies, they shall conclude the agreement, if they approve. But if the allies think otherwise, they shall send them home.’

The Argives first accepted this proposal, and the army of the Lacedaemonians withdrew from Tegea home; after this, as there was now intercourse between them, not long afterwards the same men again brought it about that the Argives gave up the alliance with the Mantineans and with the Athenians and Eleans and made a treaty and alliance with the Lacedaemonians. And these were its terms.

‘On these terms the Lacedaemonians and Argives resolved that there shall be a treaty and alliance for fifty years, giving satisfaction on fair and equal terms according to ancestral custom; and the other cities in the Peloponnese shall share in the treaty and the alliance, independent and self-governing, keeping their own territory, giving satisfaction on fair and equal terms according to ancestral custom.

All the allies of the Lacedaemonians outside the Peloponnese shall be in the same position as the Lacedaemonians; and the allies of the Argives shall be in the same position as the Argives, keeping their own territory.
And if there is need of a joint expedition anywhere, the Lacedaemonians and Argives shall deliberate, deciding in the way most just for the allies.

And if any of the cities, either within or outside the Peloponnese, has a dispute, whether about boundaries or about anything else, it shall be settled. And if one allied city quarrels with another city, they shall go to a city that both cities consider impartial. Private citizens shall be judged according to ancestral custom.’

This treaty and alliance had been made; and whatever they held of each other's through war or in any other way, they settled. And now managing their affairs in common, they voted not to receive a herald or embassy from the Athenians unless they left the Peloponnese, abandoning their forts, and not to make peace or war with anyone except together.

And they pursued matters with zeal in general, and both sent envoys to the places in Thrace and to Perdiccas, and they persuaded Perdiccas to swear alliance with them. He did not, however, revolt at once from the Athenians, but he intended to, because he saw that the Argives had done so too; and he himself was originally from Argos. And they renewed the old oaths with the Chalcidians and swore new ones.

The Argives also sent envoys to the Athenians, telling them to abandon the fort at Epidaurus. And they, seeing that their men were few compared with the larger number of fellow garrison troops, sent Demosthenes to bring out their own men. And he, on arriving, held an athletic contest as a pretext outside the fort, and when the rest of the garrison had gone out, he shut the gates; and later the Athenians themselves, after renewing the treaty with the Epidaurians, gave back the fort.

After the defection of the Argives from the alliance, the Mantineans too, though at first holding out, then, being unable to do so without the Argives, came to terms themselves with the Lacedaemonians and gave up their rule over the cities.

And the Lacedaemonians and Argives, a thousand of each, marched out together, and the Lacedaemonians themselves went and put affairs in Sicyon into the hands of a narrower few, and after that both together also put down the democracy in Argos, and an oligarchy favourable to the Lacedaemonians was established. And this happened toward spring, as the winter was ending, and the fourteenth year of the war ended.
In the following summer the Dians on Athos revolted from the Athenians to the Chalcidians, and the Lacedaemonians settled affairs in Achaea, which had not been favourable to them before.

And the people of the Argives, gradually rallying and regaining courage, attacked the few, waiting for the very time of the Gymnopaediae of the Lacedaemonians; and in a battle in the city the people won, and they killed some and drove out others.

The Lacedaemonians, as long as their friends were summoning them, did not come for a long time, but putting off the Gymnopaediae they set out to help. And at Tegea, learning that the few had been defeated, they were no longer willing to advance, despite the entreaties of those who had escaped, but returned home and celebrated the Gymnopaediae.

And later, when envoys came both from those in the city [messengers] and from the Argives outside, and the allies were present and much was said by both sides, they decided that those in the city were in the wrong, and they resolved to march against Argos, but there were delays and postponements.

Meanwhile the people of the Argives, fearing the Lacedaemonians and again trying to win the alliance of the Athenians, and thinking that it would help them most, built long walls to the sea, so that, if they were shut off from the land, the import of supplies by sea with the help of the Athenians might help them.

Some of the cities in the Peloponnese also knew about the wall building. And the Argives in full force, themselves and their wives and slaves, built the walls; and from Athens carpenters and stonemasons came to them. And the summer ended.

In the following winter the Lacedaemonians, when they learned that they were building walls, marched against Argos, themselves and their allies except the Corinthians; and they also had something being worked for them from within Argos itself. The army was led by Agis son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians.

And what seemed to be prepared for them from within the city did not go forward any further; but they took and demolished the walls being built, and captured Hysiae, a place in the Argive territory, and killed all the free men they took, and then withdrew and dispersed to their cities.
After this the Argives too marched into the territory of Phlius and ravaged it and went away, because they were receiving their exiles; for most of them had settled there.

In the same winter the Athenians also blockaded the Macedonians, charging Perdiccas with the sworn league he had made with the Argives and Lacedaemonians, and with the fact that, when they had prepared to lead an army against the Chalcidians in Thrace and against Amphipolis, with Nicias son of Niceratus as general, he had broken the alliance and the expedition had been broken up chiefly because he †had withdrawn †; so he was an enemy. And this winter ended, and the fifteenth year of the war ended.

In the following summer Alcibiades sailed to Argos with twenty ships and seized three hundred men of the Argives who still seemed to be suspect and to favour the Lacedaemonians, and the Athenians deposited them in the nearby islands which they ruled; and the Athenians made an expedition against the island of Melos with thirty ships of their own, six Chian, and two Lesbian, and with twelve hundred hoplites of their own and three hundred archers and twenty mounted archers, and from the allies and islanders about fifteen hundred hoplites.

The Melians are colonists of the Lacedaemonians, and they would not submit to the Athenians like the other islanders, but at first, siding with neither, they kept quiet, and then, when the Athenians tried to compel them by ravaging their land, they entered into open war.
