Encamping, then, in their territory with this force, the generals Cleomedes son of Lycomedes and Tisias son of Tisimachus, before doing any harm to the land, first sent envoys to hold talks. The Melians did not bring them before the people, but told them to state the purpose for which they had come before the magistrates and the few.

The envoys of the Athenians spoke as follows. ‘Since the talks are not held before the people, so that, we suppose, the many may not be deceived by hearing from us in one continuous speech persuasive and unrefuted arguments all at once (for we see that this is what our being brought before the few means), you who are sitting here, make it still safer. For you too should not decide on each point in a single speech, but take up at once whatever seems not to be said properly and judge it. And first say whether what we propose pleases you.’

The councillors of the Melians answered: ‘The fairness of instructing one another at leisure is not to be blamed, but the acts of war, which are already present and not in the future, plainly differ from it. For we see that you have come yourselves as judges of what is to be said and that the outcome of it in all likelihood will bring us war if we prevail in justice and therefore do not give in, and slavery if we are persuaded.’

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: Well then, if you have met to reckon up suspicions about the future, or for anything else than to deliberate for the safety of your city on the basis of present facts and what you see, we would stop; but if for this, we would speak.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: It is natural and pardonable for men placed in such a situation to turn to many things in both speech and thought; this meeting, however, is about our safety, and let the discussion, if you agree, proceed in the way you propose.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: Then we ourselves shall not offer, with fine words, a long and unconvincing speech, saying either that we rule justly because we overthrew the Mede or that we are now attacking you because we have been wronged, nor do we ask you to think you will persuade us by saying either that you did not join the campaign because you were colonists of the Lacedaemonians, or that you have done us no wrong, but rather to achieve what is possible on the basis of what each of us really thinks, since you know as well as we do that in human reckoning justice is decided only when there is equal compulsion, while the strong do what they can and the weak give way.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: As we think, at any rate, it is useful (we must speak so, since you have thus laid it down that we speak of expediency instead of justice) that you should not destroy the common good, but that for whoever is at any time in danger what is fair and just should hold good, and that he should be helped if he persuades somewhat even short of strict right. And this concerns you no less, inasmuch as, if you fell, you would become an example to others of the greatest vengeance.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: We, for our part, are not disheartened about the end of our empire, even if it should be ended; for it is not those who rule others, like the Lacedaemonians, who are terrible to the conquered (and our contest is not with the Lacedaemonians), but subjects who themselves attack their rulers somewhere and overcome them.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: Let that risk be left to us; but that we are here for the benefit of our empire and that we shall now speak for the safety of your city, this we shall show, wishing to rule you without trouble and to have you saved to the advantage of both.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: And how could it be as useful for us to be slaves as it is for you to rule?

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: Because you would be able to submit instead of suffering the most terrible things, and we would gain by not destroying you.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: So you would not accept that we keep quiet and be friends instead of enemies, but allies of neither side?

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: No; for your enmity does not harm us so much as your friendship would, which would be shown to our subjects as a sign of our weakness, while your hatred would be a sign of our power.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: Do your subjects regard what is reasonable in such a way that they put those who have no connection with you in the same class as those who, being mostly your own colonists, and some of them having revolted, have been subdued?

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: For they think that neither lacks a claim of right, but that the ones survive by their power, and that we do not attack them out of fear; so that, apart from our ruling more people, you would also give us security by being subdued, especially since you are islanders and weaker than others, if you did not prevail against the masters of the sea.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: But do you not think there is security in that other course? For here too, just as you have forced us away from the language of justice and persuade us to submit to your interest, we in turn must try to persuade you, explaining what is useful to us, if it happens to coincide with what is useful to you as well. For how will you not make enemies of all who are now allied with neither side, when they look at this and think that some day you will come against them too? And what do you achieve by this other than strengthening the enemies you have, and bringing upon you, against their will, those who never even intended to become your enemies?

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: For we do not consider those more dangerous to us who, living somewhere on the mainland, because of their freedom will long put off taking precautions against us, but rather islanders who are anywhere not subject to us, like you, and those who are already irritated by the compulsion of our empire. For these are the most likely to give themselves up to unreason and bring both themselves and us into a danger they foresee.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: Surely then, if you run so great a risk so as not to lose your empire, and those who are already slaves to be freed from it, for us at any rate, who are still free, it would be great baseness and cowardice not to try everything before being enslaved.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: No, not if you deliberate wisely; for the contest for you is not one of manly courage on equal terms, to avoid incurring disgrace, but rather the deliberation is about safety, so as not to resist those who are much stronger.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: But we know that the fortunes of war are sometimes more impartial than the difference in numbers on each side would suggest; and for us to yield at once is to give up hope, but by acting there is still hope that we may stand upright.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: Hope, being a comfort in danger, does not ruin those who use it from abundance, even if it harms them; but for those who stake everything they have on it (for it is extravagant by nature), it is recognised for what it is at the moment they fall, and when it is recognised it leaves nothing by which one might still guard against it.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: Do not wish to suffer this, weak as you are and hanging on a single turn of the scale, nor to become like the many who, when it is still possible to be saved by human means, once visible hopes fail them in their distress, turn to invisible ones, prophecy and oracles and all such things that, together with hopes, bring ruin.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: We too, be well assured, think it difficult to contend against your power and fortune, unless it is to be on equal terms; nevertheless we trust that in fortune, which comes from the divine, we shall not be at a disadvantage, because we stand as godly men against unjust ones, and that for what we lack in power the alliance of the Lacedaemonians will make up, which is compelled, if for nothing else, at least for the sake of kinship and from shame to help us. And so our confidence is not so utterly unreasonable.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: As for the favour of the divine, then, we do not think that we shall fall short of it either; for nothing that we claim or do goes beyond men's belief about the divine or their wishes for themselves.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: For we believe of the divine by opinion, and of the human clearly, that by a necessity of nature it always rules wherever it has the power; and we neither laid down this law nor were the first to use it once laid down, but having received it in existence and being about to leave it existing for ever, we make use of it, knowing that you too and others, if you had the same power as we, would do the same.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: And so with regard to the divine we have good reason not to fear that we shall be at a disadvantage; but as for your expectation regarding the Lacedaemonians, your trust that out of shame, forsooth, they will come to your aid, while we bless your innocence of evil we do not envy your folly.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: For the Lacedaemonians, towards themselves and their own native institutions, practise virtue to the highest degree; but as to how they behave towards others, though one could say much, in summary one would show most clearly that, most conspicuously of all men we know, they consider what is pleasant honourable and what is expedient just. And yet such a way of thinking does not favour your present unreasonable hope of safety.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: But we, on this very point, now trust most of all in their own interest, that they will not be willing to betray the Melians, who are their colonists, and so become untrustworthy to those of the Hellenes who are well disposed to them and useful to their enemies.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: You do not think, then, that interest goes with safety, while what is just and honourable is practised with danger; a thing which the Lacedaemonians, as a rule, are least inclined to venture.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: But we believe that they would undertake even dangers for our sake rather than for others, and would consider them more secure than for others, inasmuch as we lie near the Peloponnese for any action there, and by kinship of sentiment we are more trustworthy than others.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: But what gives security to those about to join in a struggle is clearly not the goodwill of those who called them in, but whether one far surpasses in power for action; and to this the Lacedaemonians look somewhat more than the rest (at any rate, through distrust of their own resources they attack their neighbours only together with many allies), so that it is not likely that they will cross over to an island while we are masters of the sea.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: But they could also send others; and the Cretan sea is wide, on which capture is harder for those who control it than escape is for those who wish to slip through unnoticed.

div.p: And if they should fail in this, they would turn both against your land and against the rest of your allies, all those whom Brasidas did not reach; and your toil will be not for land that does not belong to you, but rather for your own alliance and country.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: Something of this kind might happen to you too, as it has to us who have experienced it, and you are not unaware that the Athenians have never once withdrawn from a single siege through fear of others.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: But we reflect that, although you said you would deliberate about your safety, you have said nothing in this long discussion in reliance on which men could expect to be saved, but your strongest supports are hopes deferred to the future, while your present resources are too slight to prevail against those already arrayed against you. And you show great unreasonableness of mind if, after letting us withdraw, you do not come to some decision wiser than these.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: For surely you will not turn to that sense of shame which, in dangers that are disgraceful and clearly foreseen, most often destroys men. For many, though they still foresaw what they were being carried into, have been drawn on by the power of a seductive word, the thing called disgrace, so that, overcome by the word, they have in fact willingly fallen into irremediable calamities and incurred in addition a disgrace more disgraceful because joined with folly rather than with misfortune.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: This you will guard against, if you take good counsel, and you will not think it unseemly to yield to the greatest city when it offers moderate terms, to become allies keeping your own land while paying tribute, and, when a choice is given between war and safety, not to contend obstinately for the worse; since those who do not give way to their equals, behave well towards their superiors and are moderate towards their inferiors would prosper most.

sp.speaker: Ath.
sp.p: Consider, then, also after we have withdrawn, and reflect again and again that you are deliberating about your fatherland, your one and only fatherland, whose fate will depend on one decision, whether it succeeds or fails.

div.p: So the Athenians withdrew from the conference; and the Melians, left by themselves, since they were of much the same opinion as they had expressed in their replies, answered as follows.

‘Our opinion, Athenians, is no other than it was at first, nor will we in a short time take away the freedom of a city that has already been inhabited for seven hundred years, but trusting in the fortune from the gods which has preserved it until now and in the help from men, the Lacedaemonians, we shall try to save ourselves.
But we invite you to let us be your friends and enemies to neither side, and to withdraw from our land after making a treaty such as seems suitable to both of us.’

So the Melians answered thus; and the Athenians, now breaking off the conference, said, ‘Well then, judging from these resolutions, you alone, as it seems to us, regard the future as clearer than what is before your eyes, and look on what is unseen, because you wish it, as already coming to pass, and having staked the most on the Lacedaemonians, on fortune and on hopes, and trusted them most, you will also be most utterly ruined.’

And the Athenian envoys returned to the army; and their generals, since the Melians would not submit at all, at once turned to war and, dividing the work among the cities, walled the Melians round in a circle.
And later the Athenians, leaving a garrison of their own men and of their allies both by land and by sea, withdrew with the greater part of the army. Those left behind stayed and besieged the place.
And at about the same time the Argives invaded Phliasia and, ambushed by the Phliasians and their own exiles, lost about eighty men.

And the Athenians at Pylos took much booty from the Lacedaemonians; and the Lacedaemonians, even because of this, did not renounce the treaty and make war on them, but proclaimed that any of their people who wished might plunder the Athenians.
And the Corinthians went to war with the Athenians because of some private quarrels; but the rest of the Peloponnesians kept quiet.

And the Melians, too, took the part of the Athenian wall of circumvallation facing the market-place by attacking at night, and they killed some men and, after bringing in grain and as many useful things as they could, withdrew and kept quiet; and the Athenians thereafter kept a better watch. And the summer ended.

In the following winter the Lacedaemonians, intending to march into Argive territory, withdrew, since the crossing [sacrifices at the boundaries ] did not turn out favourably for them. And the Argives, because of their intended invasion, suspected some of the men in the city and arrested some of them, while the others escaped.
And at about the same time the Melians again took another part of the Athenian wall of circumvallation, as not many of the guards were present.

And when another army came later from Athens because of these events, commanded by Philocrates son of Demeas, and they were now being besieged in force, and some treachery also occurred, they surrendered of their own accord to the Athenians on condition that these should decide about them.
And they killed all the Melians of military age whom they took, and enslaved the children and women; and they settled the place themselves, sending out five hundred colonists later.

In the same winter the Athenians wished to sail again to Sicily with a greater force than that with Laches and Eurymedon and subdue it, if they could, most of them being ignorant of the size of the island and of the number of its inhabitants, both Hellenes and barbarians, and that they were taking on a war not much smaller than that against the Peloponnesians.
For the voyage round Sicily is for a merchant ship not much less than eight days, and, large as it is, it is separated by a stretch of sea of only about twenty stadia from being mainland;

and it was settled in ancient times as follows, and these were all the peoples that held it. The most ancient said to have lived in a part of the country are the Cyclopes and Laestrygonians, of whom I can say neither their race nor whence they came or whither they went; let it suffice what has been said by the poets and what each man in some way knows about them.

After them the Sicanians appear to have been the first to settle there, as they themselves say, even before them, because they are indigenous, but as the truth is found to be, they were Iberians who had been driven out by the Ligurians from the river Sicanus in Iberia. And from them the island was then called Sicania, having previously been called Trinacria; and they still inhabit the western parts of Sicily even now.

When Ilium was being taken, some of the Trojans, having escaped the Achaeans, came in boats to Sicily, and settling on the borders of the Sicanians were all together called Elymi, and their cities were Eryx and Egesta. And there also settled with them some of the Phocians who, returning at that time from Troy, had been carried by a storm first to Libya and then from there to Sicily.

The Sicels crossed over from Italy (for they lived there) to Sicily, fleeing from the Opicans, as is likely and as is said, on rafts, having watched for the strait when the wind was blowing down, though they may perhaps also have sailed in some other way. There are still Sicels in Italy even now, and the country was thus named Italy after Italus, a king of the Sicels who had this name.

And coming into Sicily as a great host, they defeated the Sicanians in battle and drove them back to the southern and western parts of it and caused the island to be called Sicily instead of Sicania, and they settled and held the best parts of the land for nearly three hundred years after they crossed, before the Hellenes came to Sicily; and even now they still hold the central and northern parts of the island.

And the Phoenicians also lived all round Sicily, having taken possession of headlands on the sea and of the islets lying off the coast for the sake of trade with the Sicels; but when the Hellenes began to sail in by sea in great numbers, they abandoned most of these places and, settling together, lived in Motya, Soloeis and Panormus near the Elymi, both trusting in their alliance with the Elymi and because from there Carthage is the shortest voyage from Sicily. These, then, were the barbarians who lived in Sicily, and this was how they settled it.

Of the Hellenes, the first were Chalcidians from Euboea, who sailed with Thucles as founder and settled Naxos, and they set up an altar of Apollo Archegetes, which is now outside the city, on which the sacred envoys, whenever they sail from Sicily, first sacrifice.

In the following year Archias, one of the Heraclidae, from Corinth founded Syracuse, having first driven the Sicels out of the island on which the inner city now stands, though it is no longer surrounded by water; and at a later time the outer city too was walled in with it and became populous.

And Thucles and the Chalcidians, setting out from Naxos in the fifth year after the founding of Syracuse, drove out the Sicels by war and founded Leontini, and after it Catana; but the Catanaeans themselves chose Euarchus as their founder.

At about the same time Lamis also came to Sicily leading a colony from Megara, and after settling a place called Trotilus beyond the river Pantacyas, and later moving from there and sharing the city of Leontini with the Chalcidians for a short time, and being driven out by them and founding Thapsus, he himself died, and the others, having been removed from Thapsus, when Hyblon, a Sicel king, handed over the land and led them there, settled the Megarians who were called Hyblaean.

And after living there for two hundred and forty-five years they were removed from the city and the land by Gelon, tyrant of the Syracusans. But before they were removed, a hundred years after they had settled there, they sent Pammilus and founded Selinus, and he came from Megara, their mother city, and joined in founding it.

Gela was founded jointly by Antiphemus from Rhodes and Entimus from Crete, who led settlers there, in the forty-fifth year after the founding of Syracuse. And the city got its name from the river Gela, but the place where the city now is and which was first fortified is called Lindii; and Dorian institutions were established for them.

About one hundred and eight years after their own founding, the Geloans settled Acragas, naming the city after the river Acragas, making Aristonous and Pystilus founders, and giving it the institutions of the Geloans.

Zancle was settled at the beginning by pirates who came from Cyme, the Chalcidian city in Opicia, but later a large number also came from Chalcis and the rest of Euboea and shared the land with them; and its founders were Perieres and Crataemenes, one from Cyme, the other from Chalcis. Its name at first was Zancle, as it was called by the Sicels, because the place is sickle-shaped in form (the Sicels call a sickle zanklon), but later they themselves were driven out by Samians and other Ionians, who, fleeing the Medes, landed in Sicily,
and not long after Anaxilas, tyrant of the Rhegians, drove out the Samians and, settling the city himself with a mixed population, renamed it Messene after his own original fatherland.

And Himera was settled from Zancle by Eucleides, Simus and Sacon, and most of those who went to the colony were Chalcidians, but there also settled with them exiles from Syracuse who had been defeated in civil strife, the so-called Myletidae; and the language became a mixture of the Chalcidian and the Doric, but the Chalcidian institutions prevailed.
Acrae and Casmenae were settled by the Syracusans, Acrae seventy years after Syracuse, and Casmenae about twenty after Acrae.

And Camarina was first settled by the Syracusans, about one hundred and thirty-five years after the founding of Syracuse; its founders were Dascon and Menecolus. When the Camarinaeans had been removed by the Syracusans in a war because of a revolt, in time Hippocrates, later tyrant of Gela, taking the land of the Camarinaeans as ransom for Syracusan prisoners, himself became founder and resettled Camarina. And when it had again been depopulated by Gelon, it was resettled for the third time by the Geloans.

So many were the peoples of Hellenes and barbarians that inhabited Sicily,and against an island of this size the Athenians were eager to make an expedition, aiming, by the truest explanation, to rule the whole of it, but wishing at the same time, with a fair pretext, to help their own kinsmen and the allies they had acquired.

Most of all they were urged on by envoys of the Egestaeans who were present and called on them for help more eagerly. For bordering on the Selinuntians, they had gone to war with them over certain marriage questions and over disputed land, and the Selinuntians, bringing in the Syracusans as allies, were pressing them hard in the war both by land and by sea; so that the Egestaeans, reminding the Athenians of the alliance made with the Leontines in the time of Laches and the former war, begged them to send ships and help them, saying many other things and, in sum, that if the Syracusans, having depopulated Leontini, went unpunished, and by destroying their remaining allies got the whole power of Sicily for themselves, there was a danger that at some time, coming with a great force as Dorians to help Dorians by kinship and at the same time as colonists to help the Peloponnesians who had sent them out, they might join in destroying the power of the Athenians too; and that it was wise, with the allies still left, to resist the Syracusans, especially since they themselves would provide money enough for the war.

Hearing this in their assemblies, as the Egestaeans and their supporters said it often, the Athenians voted to send envoys first to Egesta to see about the money, whether it was there, as they said, in the public treasury and in the temples, and at the same time to learn how things stood with the war against the Selinuntians.

And the envoys of the Athenians were sent to Sicily; and in the same winter the Lacedaemonians and their allies, except the Corinthians, marched into Argive territory, ravaged a small part of the land and carried off some grain, having brought carts, and after settling the Argive exiles at Orneae and leaving a few of the rest of the army with them, and making a truce for a certain time on condition that the Orneates and the Argives should not harm each other's land, they went back home with the army.

When the Athenians came not long after with thirty ships and six hundred hoplites, the Argives went out in full force with the Athenians and besieged those in Orneae for one day; but at night, when the army had bivouacked at a distance, the men from Orneae escaped. And on the next day, when the Argives learned of it, they razed Orneae and withdrew, and later the Athenians went home with their ships.
And the Athenians, bringing by sea to Methone, which borders on Macedonia, cavalry of their own and the Macedonian exiles who were with them, ravaged the land of Perdiccas.

And the Lacedaemonians sent to the Chalcidians in Thrace, who had a ten-day truce with the Athenians, and urged them to join Perdiccas in the war; but they were unwilling. And the winter ended, and the sixteenth year ended of this war which Thucydides wrote the history of.

In the following summer, at the beginning of spring, the envoys of the Athenians came back from Sicily, and the Egestaeans with them, bringing sixty talents of uncoined silver as a month's pay for sixty ships, which they were going to ask them to send.

And the Athenians held an assembly and, having heard from the Egestaeans and from their own envoys things that were enticing but not true, in particular about the money, that it was ready in large amounts in the temples and in the treasury, voted to send sixty ships to Sicily, with Alcibiades son of Cleinias, Nicias son of Niceratus and Lamachus son of Xenophanes as generals with full powers, to help the Egestaeans against the Selinuntians, and also to join in resettling Leontini, if they had any success in the war, and to manage all other matters in Sicily in whatever way they judged best for the Athenians.

On the fifth day after this an assembly was held again, on how the equipment for the ships should be made ready most quickly, and to vote the generals whatever they might further need for the expedition.

And Nicias, who had been chosen to command against his will, and who thought that the city had not decided rightly but was aiming at all Sicily, a great undertaking, on a slight and specious pretext, came forward wishing to dissuade them, and advised the Athenians as follows.

‘This assembly was convened about our preparations, about how we should sail to Sicily; but it seems to me that we must still consider this very question, whether it is better to send out the ships at all, and that we should not, with such brief deliberation on great matters, be persuaded by men of another race to take up a war that does not concern us.

And yet I myself gain honour from such a thing, and fear less than others for my own person, though I consider that a man who takes some thought for his person and his property is just as good a citizen; for such a man would most wish, for his own sake, that the affairs of the city should also prosper. Nevertheless, neither in time past have I spoken against my judgment for the sake of being honoured, nor shall I now, but I shall say what I judge best.

Against your character my speech would be weak, if I should urge you to preserve what you have and not to risk what is ready at hand for what is unseen and in the future; but that your haste is untimely and that what you have set out for is not easy to achieve, this I shall show.
‘For I say that you, leaving many enemies behind you here, want to sail there and bring yet others here upon you.

And perhaps you think that the treaty you have made has something secure about it, a treaty which, as long as you keep quiet, will be a treaty in name (for so men both here and among the enemy have managed it), but if we should suffer a defeat somewhere with a considerable force, our enemies will quickly make their attack on us, since for them, first, the agreement was made under compulsion through misfortunes and on terms more disgraceful than for us, and then in this very agreement we have many points in dispute.

And there are some who have not yet accepted even this agreement, and not the weakest; but some are openly at war, and others, because the Lacedaemonians are still keeping quiet, are themselves also held back by ten-day truces.

And perhaps, if they found our power divided, which is just what we are now hastening to do, they would very readily join in an attack on us with the Siceliots, whose alliance they would in former times have valued above much else.

So one must consider these things, and not think fit to run risks with the city unsettled and reach out for another empire before we have secured the one we have, if indeed the Chalcidians in Thrace, after being in revolt from us for so many years, are still unsubdued, and some others on the mainlands obey us doubtfully. But we hasten to help the Egestaeans, forsooth, as allies who are wronged; while those by whose revolt we ourselves have long been wronged we still delay to punish.

And yet those, if we subdued them, we could also hold; but these, even if we conquered them, we could hardly rule, being far away and many. And it is foolish to go against men whom one will not hold even if one conquers them, and if one fails, one will not be in the same position as before the attempt.
And the Siceliots, it seems to me, as they now are, would become even less dangerous to us if the Syracusans ruled them; which is the very thing with which the Egestaeans most try to frighten us.

For now they might perhaps come, each of them, to please the Lacedaemonians, but in that case it is not likely that an empire would march against an empire; for in whatever way they took away ours together with the Peloponnesians, it is likely that their own would be destroyed by the same men in the same way.

And the Hellenes there would be most awed by us if we did not come, and next if, after showing our power, we went away after a short time; for we all know that what is farthest off and gives least test of its reputation is admired. But if we suffered any defeat, they would very quickly despise us and attack us together with our enemies here.

This is just what you, Athenians, have now experienced with regard to the Lacedaemonians and their allies; because you have got the better of them beyond expectation, compared with what you feared at first, you now despise them and are aiming even at Sicily.

But one must not be elated at the misfortunes of one's opponents, but feel confident only after mastering their spirits, nor think that the Lacedaemonians, because of their disgrace, have anything else in view than how, even now, if they can, they may defeat us and repair their own dishonour, all the more as they have cultivated a reputation for valour most of all and for the longest time.
So our struggle, if we are wise, is not about the Egestaeans in Sicily, barbarian men, but about how we shall keep a sharp watch on a city that is plotting against us through oligarchy.

‘And we must remember that we have only recently recovered a little from a great plague and from war, so as to have grown stronger in money and in men; and it is right to spend these here for ourselves, and not for these exiles who beg for help, for whom it is useful to lie well and, at the risk of their neighbour, providing only words themselves, either, if they succeed, to show no proper gratitude, or, if they fail somewhere, to ruin their friends with them.

And if someone, glad to have been chosen to command, urges you to sail, considering only his own interest, especially as he is still too young to command, so that he may be admired for his horse-breeding and, because of its great expense, may also get some profit from his command, do not allow this man either to make a private display at the risk of the city, but consider that such men wrong the public interest and waste their own, and that the matter is a great one and not such as a younger man can deliberate on and rashly take in hand.

‘It is these men that I fear when I see them sitting here now summoned by the same man, and I in turn appeal to the older men not to be shamed, if any of you is sitting beside one of these, into fearing that he will seem a coward if he does not vote for war, nor, as they themselves may feel, to be sick with longing for what is far away, knowing that very few things succeed through desire and most through foresight, but on behalf of the fatherland, which is now running the greatest risk it has ever run, to vote against it, and to vote that the Siceliots, keeping the same boundaries with us as now, which are not open to blame, the Ionian gulf if one sails along the coast and the Sicilian sea across the open water, should enjoy their own possessions and settle their affairs among themselves;

and to tell the Egestaeans separately that, since they began the war against the Selinuntians at first without the Athenians, they should also end it by themselves; and in future not to make allies as we are accustomed to, whom we shall help when they fare badly, but from whom we shall get no help when we ourselves need it.

‘And you, prytanis, if you think it your duty to care for the city and wish to be a good citizen, put these things to the vote and lay the question before the Athenians again, considering, if you hesitate to put the vote again, that breaking the laws would bring no blame with so many witnesses, but that you would become the physician of the city when it has deliberated 〈badly 〉, and that to govern well is this: whoever benefits his fatherland as much as possible, or at least does it no harm willingly.’
Thus Nicias spoke, and of the Athenians who came forward most advised making the expedition and not undoing what had been voted, while some also spoke against it.

The one who urged the expedition most eagerly was Alcibiades son of Cleinias, wishing to oppose Nicias, since he differed from him in other political matters too and because Nicias had mentioned him invidiously, and above all being eager to be general and hoping through himself to take both Sicily and Carthage and, if successful, at the same time to benefit his private affairs in both money and reputation.

For being held in high esteem by the citizens, he indulged desires greater than his actual property allowed, both in horse-breeding and in his other expenses; and this was just what later, not least, brought down the city of the Athenians.

For the many, fearing the extent of his lawlessness in his personal way of life and of the designs he pursued in every single thing he was involved in, became his enemies, believing that he desired a tyranny, and though in public he managed the affairs of the war excellently, each of them in private was offended by his habits, and entrusting affairs to others, they ruined the city not long after.
At that time, then, he came forward and advised the Athenians as follows.

‘It belongs to me more than to others, Athenians, to command (for I must begin from this point, since Nicias has attacked me), and at the same time I think I am worthy of it. For the things for which I am cried down bring glory to my ancestors and to me, and also benefit to the fatherland.

For the Hellenes thought our city even greater than its actual power because of the magnificence of my mission to Olympia, though they had previously hoped that it had been worn down by war, because I entered seven chariots, as many as no private man had ever entered before, and I won and also came second and fourth, and provided everything else in a manner worthy of the victory. For by custom such things are an honour, and from what is done power is also inferred at the same time.

And again, whatever splendour I display in the city by providing choruses or in any other way naturally arouses envy among the citizens, but to strangers this too appears as strength. And this folly is not useless, when a man by his private expenditure benefits not only himself but also the city.

Nor indeed is it unjust that one who thinks highly of himself should not be on an equal footing, since the one who fares badly does not share his misfortune equally with anyone; but just as when we are unfortunate we are not greeted, in the same way let a man endure being looked down on by the prosperous, or else let him give equal treatment and then claim the same in return.

And I know that such men, and all who have stood out in the splendour of anything, are a vexation in their own lifetime, most of all to their equals and then also to others who live with them, but that to later generations they leave some men claiming kinship with them even where there is none, and to whatever fatherland they belong, they leave it a boast that they were not strangers nor wrongdoers, but its own men who did noble deeds.

Aiming at this, and cried down in my private life for these reasons, consider whether I manage public affairs worse than anyone. For having united the strongest powers of the Peloponnese without great danger or expense to you, I compelled the Lacedaemonians to stake everything on one day at Mantinea; as a result of which, though they were victorious in the battle, they are not yet even now firmly confident.

‘And this is what my youth and my seemingly unnatural folly accomplished, dealing with the power of the Peloponnesians in fitting words and, giving credibility by its passion, persuading them. And now do not be afraid of it, but while I am still in my prime with it and Nicias is thought to be fortunate, make full use of the services of each of us.

And do not change your minds about the voyage to Sicily as if it would be against a great power. For the cities there are populous with mixed crowds and easily accept changes and additions of citizens.

And for this reason no one is equipped, as he would be for his own fatherland, either with arms for his person or with lasting improvements in the country; but whatever each man thinks he can take from the common stock by persuasive speech or by sedition, and then, if he fails, live in another land, this is what he provides himself with.

And it is not likely that such a crowd will either listen to advice with one mind or turn to action in common; but quickly, each of them, if something were said to please them, would come over, especially if they are in civil strife, as we hear.

And indeed they do not have as many hoplites as they boast, nor have the other Hellenes turned out to be as many as each counted themselves, but Hellas, very greatly deceived about them, was barely armed sufficiently in this war.

So the situation there, from what I learn by hearsay, is like this and will be even easier (for we shall have many barbarians who out of hatred of the Syracusans will join us in attacking them), and matters here will not hinder us, if you take good counsel.

For our fathers, having as enemies these same men whom they now say we would be leaving behind if we sailed, and the Mede as a foe besides, acquired the empire, being strong in nothing else than the superiority of their fleet.

And now the Peloponnesians have never been more hopeless against us, and even if they are very strong, they are able to invade our land even if we do not sail out, but with their fleet they could not harm us; for we have a fleet left over that is a match for them.

So what reasonable thing could we say to hold back ourselves, or what excuse could we offer our allies there for not helping them? We ought to help them, since we have sworn to it, and not object that they did not help us either. For we did not take them on so that they would come here to help us in return, but so that by being troublesome to our enemies there they would prevent them from coming here.

And this is how we acquired our empire, both we and all others who have ruled, by readily coming to the aid of those, barbarians or Hellenes, who at any time called on us, since if all kept quiet or drew distinctions of race as to whom we ought to help, we would add little to it and would rather run a risk about this very empire. For one does not only defend oneself against a superior when he attacks, but also forestalls him so that he will not attack.

And it is not possible for us to ration out how far we wish to rule, but it is necessary, since we are placed in this position, to plot against some and not to let go of others, because there is a danger of being ruled by others ourselves, if we do not ourselves rule others. And you cannot look at inaction from the same point of view as others, unless you also change your practices to be like theirs.

‘Reckoning, then, that we shall rather increase our power here if we go against those there, let us make the voyage, so that we may lay low the pride of the Peloponnesians, if we are seen to despise the present peace and to sail even against Sicily; and at the same time we shall either, in all likelihood, rule all Hellas when those there have been added to us, or at least damage the Syracusans, by which both we ourselves and our allies will benefit.
And safety, both to remain, if things go well, and to come away, our ships will provide; for we shall be masters of the sea even against all the Siceliots together.

And do not let the inaction of Nicias' speech and his setting the young against the older turn you aside, but in our accustomed order, just as our fathers, young together with old in their counsels, raised these affairs to this height, so now too try in the same way to advance the city, and consider that youth and old age without each other can do nothing, but that the simple and the middling and the very exact, mixed together, would be strongest, and that the city, if it keeps quiet, will wear itself out upon itself like anything else, and its skill in all things will grow old, but if it is in constant struggle, it will continually gain experience and will have the habit of defending itself not in word but rather in deed.

And in general I judge that a city that is not inactive would, it seems to me, be most quickly ruined by a change to inactivity, and that those men live most safely who govern themselves least differently from their present customs and laws, even if these are worse.’

Such were the words of Alcibiades; and the Athenians, having heard him and the Egestaeans and the Leontine exiles, who came forward and begged them and, reminding them of their oaths, implored them to help them, were far more eager than before to make the expedition.

And Nicias, realizing that with the same arguments he could no longer dissuade them, but that by the size of the armament, if he demanded a large one, he might perhaps change their minds, came forward and spoke to them again as follows.
‘Since I see, Athenians, that you are wholly bent on making the expedition, may these things turn out as we wish, but for the present I shall declare what I think.

For we are about to go, as I learn by hearsay, against cities that are large and neither subject to one another nor in need of a change by which a man would gladly pass from forced slavery to an easier condition, nor likely to accept our rule in place of freedom, and the Hellenic cities are many in number for a single island.

For apart from Naxos and Catana, which I expect will join us because of their kinship with the Leontines, there are seven others, equipped in all respects very much like our own power, and not least those against which we are chiefly sailing, Selinus and Syracuse.

For they have many hoplites and archers and javelin-men, and many triremes and a crowd to man them. And they have money, partly private, and partly also in the temples at Selinus, and to the Syracusans tribute is also brought from some barbarians; but where they most surpass us is that they possess many horses and use home-grown, not imported, grain.

‘Against such a power, then, we need not only a naval and slight force, but a large infantry force must also sail with us, if we wish to do something worthy of our design and not be shut out from the land by numerous cavalry, especially if the cities, in fear, stand together and no others besides the Egestaeans become our friends and provide us with cavalry with which to defend ourselves

(and it would be shameful to be forced to come away or to send for more later, having planned without consideration at first); we must set out from here with an adequate armament, knowing that we are about to sail far from our own land and to make a campaign not on the same terms as when you came as allies against someone among your subjects here, where supplies of whatever more you needed were easily brought from friendly territory, but that we shall be cutting ourselves off in an entirely foreign land, from which it is not easy for a messenger to come even in four winter months.

So it seems to me that we must take many hoplites, both of our own and of our allies, both from the subjects and any we can persuade or attract by pay from the Peloponnese, and many archers and slingers, so that they may hold out against their cavalry, and that we must greatly surpass them in ships too, so that we may also bring in supplies more easily, and that we must also take in merchant ships grain from here, wheat and parched barley, and bakers from the mills, pressed into service in proportion and paid, so that if we are held up anywhere by inability to sail, the army may have supplies (for being large, it will not be for every city to receive it), and that we must prepare everything else as far as possible and not become dependent on others, and above all have as much money as possible from here. As for the money from the Egestaeans, which is said to be ready there, consider that it is most likely ready in word only.

For if we ourselves go from here having prepared a force not only equal to theirs,except of course for their fighting strength, the hoplites, but even surpassing them in everything, even so we shall hardly be able to conquer those there and also to bring our own forces through safely.

And we must consider that we are going to found a city among foreign and hostile peoples, who must, on the very first day they land, at once be masters of the land, or know that, if they fail, they will find everything hostile.

Fearing this, and knowing that we must plan well in many things, and be fortunate in still more (which is hard, being men), I wish to sail having entrusted myself as little as possible to fortune, but to sail out safe, as far as is reasonable, through preparation.
For this I consider most secure for the whole city and safest for us who are going on the expedition. But if anyone thinks otherwise, I yield the command to him.’
Nicias said this much, thinking that he would either deter the Athenians by the magnitude of the requirements or, if he were forced to make the expedition, would in this way sail out most safely;

but they were not deprived of their desire for the voyage by the burdensomeness of the preparations, but were far more eager, and the opposite of what he intended happened to him; for he seemed to have given good advice, and there would now be ample security indeed.

And a passion fell on all alike to sail out; for the older men thought they would either subdue the places they were sailing against or that a great force could suffer no harm, while those in the prime of life longed for far-off sights and spectacles and were confident they would come back safe; and the great mass of the soldiers expected to get money for the present and to acquire in addition a power from which there would be perpetual pay.
So because of the excessive desire of the majority, if anyone was not in fact pleased, he kept quiet, fearing that by voting against it he might seem ill-disposed to the city.
And finally one of the Athenians came forward and, calling on Nicias, said that he should not make excuses or delay, but say now, in front of all, what armament the Athenians should vote him.

And he said, unwillingly, that he would rather deliberate at leisure with his fellow commanders, but as far as it seemed to him already, they must sail with no fewer than a hundred triremes (and of the Athenians themselves there would be as many troop-transports as they decided, and others must be sent for from the allies), and with hoplites, Athenians and allies together, no fewer than five thousand, and more if they could; and that they would prepare and bring the rest of the armament in proportion, archers from home and from Crete, and slingers, and anything else that seemed suitable.

When the Athenians heard this, they at once voted that the generals should have full powers both about the size of the army and about the whole expedition, to act as seemed best to them [for the Athenians ].

And after this the preparation went on, and they sent to the allies and made levies at home, and the city had just recovered from the plague and the continuous war both in the number of young men who had grown up and in the accumulation of money because of the truce, so that everything was provided more easily. And they were busy with the preparation.

Meanwhile, of all the stone Hermae there were in the city of the Athenians (there are, by local custom, square-cut works, many both in the doorways of private houses and in sanctuaries), most had their faces mutilated in one night.

And no one knew who had done it, but they were sought with large public rewards for information, and they voted besides that if anyone knew of any other impious act that had been committed, whoever wished, citizens, foreigners or slaves, should inform without fear.

And they took the matter very seriously; for it seemed to be an omen for the expedition and at the same time to have been done as part of a conspiracy for revolution and the overthrow of the democracy.

Information was then given by some metics and attendants, nothing about the Hermae, but that some mutilations of other statues had previously been committed by young men in play and drink, and at the same time that the mysteries were being performed in houses in mockery; and of these they also accused Alcibiades.

And taking these charges up, those who were most hostile to Alcibiades, because he stood in the way of their own secure leadership of the people, and thinking that if they drove him out they would be first, exaggerated them and cried out that both the affair of the mysteries and the mutilation of the Hermae had been done to overthrow the democracy, and that none of it had been done without him, adding as proof his other undemocratic lawlessness in his habits.

And he defended himself at the time against the informations and was ready to be tried before sailing, as to whether he had done any of these things (for the preparations had already been provided), and, if he had done any of them, to pay the penalty, but if he was acquitted, to command.

And he called on them to witness that they should not accept slanders about him in his absence, but put him to death now, if he was guilty, and that it would be wiser not to send him at the head of so great an army with such a charge on him before they had decided.

But his enemies, fearing that he would have the army well disposed to him if he were tried at once, and that the people would go soft in favouring him because through him the Argives and some of the Mantineans were joining in the campaign, tried to prevent and put off the trial, putting forward other speakers who said that he should sail now and not hold up the departure, but come back and be tried within a fixed number of days, as they wished, on a greater slander, which they would more easily procure in his absence, to have him recalled and brought home to stand trial. And it was decided that Alcibiades should sail.

After this, when it was already midsummer, the departure for Sicily took place. Most of the allies, and the grain-carrying merchant ships and the smaller vessels and all the rest of the armament that accompanied them, had been ordered beforehand to gather at Corcyra, so that from there they might cross the Ionian gulf together to the promontory of Iapygia; but the Athenians themselves, and any of the allies who were present, went down to the Piraeus on an appointed day at dawn and began manning the ships in order to put out to sea.

And with them went down also the whole of the rest of the crowd in the city, so to speak, both citizens and foreigners, the natives each sending off their own, some their friends, some their kinsmen, some their sons, and they went with hope and with lamentation at once, hope that they would make conquests, and lamentation as to whether they would ever see them again, reflecting how long a voyage from their own land they were being sent on.

And at the present moment, as they were now about to leave each other amid dangers, the terrors came home to them more than when they were voting to sail; but still, at the sight of their present strength, because of the abundance of everything they saw, they took courage again. The foreigners and the rest of the crowd had come for the spectacle, as to an enterprise that was noteworthy and beyond belief. For this armament, the first to sail out with the Hellenic forces of a single city, was the costliest and most splendid of those up to that time.

In the number of ships and hoplites, both the expedition to Epidaurus under Pericles and the same one to Potidaea under Hagnon were not smaller; for four thousand hoplites of the Athenians themselves and three hundred horsemen and a hundred triremes, and fifty of the Lesbians and Chians, and many allies besides sailed on it.

But they had set out on a short voyage and with poor equipment, whereas this expedition, as one that would be long and was fitted out for both kinds of service, as needed, with ships and infantry at once, had its fleet built up at great expense both of the trierarchs and of the city, the public treasury giving a drachma a day to each sailor and providing empty ships, sixty fast ones and forty troop-transports, and the best crews for these, and the trierarchs giving bounties in addition to the pay from the public treasury to the thranitae among the sailors and to the crews, and using costly figureheads and equipment for the rest,and each one striving to the utmost that his own ship should most excel in fine appearance and in swift sailing, while the infantry was picked from good muster-rolls and vied with one another with great zeal in their arms and personal equipment.

And it came about that there was rivalry among themselves, in whatever post each had been assigned, and that it looked to the rest of the Hellenes more like a display of power and resources than an armament against enemies.

For if one had reckoned the public expenditure of the city and the private expenditure of those serving in the expedition, of the city both what it had already spent in advance and what it was sending with the generals, and of the private persons both what each had spent on his person and, as trierarch, on his ship, and all that he was still going to spend, and besides what everyone was likely to have provided as travelling money for a long campaign, even apart from his pay from the public treasury, and all that any soldier or merchant sailed with for trade, many talents in all would have been found to be taken out of the city.

And the expedition became famous no less for amazement at its daring and the splendour of the spectacle than for the superiority of its force over those they were going against, and because it was the longest voyage from home yet attempted and undertaken with the greatest hope for the future compared with their present resources.

When the ships were manned and everything they were going to take with them on the voyage had now been put on board, silence was signalled by the trumpet, and they made the prayers customary before putting to sea, not ship by ship, but all together, led by a herald, mixing bowls of wine throughout the whole army, and the marines and the officers pouring libations from gold and silver cups.

And the rest of the crowd on land, of the citizens and anyone else present who was well disposed to them, joined in the prayers. And having sung the paean and finished the libations, they put out, and after sailing out first in column they then raced as far as Aegina. And they hastened to reach Corcyra, where the rest of the army of the allies was also gathering.

To Syracuse news about the expedition came from many quarters, but for a long time nothing was believed, and even when an assembly was held, speeches of the following kind were made by various others, some believing the reports about the expedition of the Athenians, others saying the opposite, and Hermocrates son of Hermon came forward, believing that he knew the facts clearly, and spoke and advised them as follows.

‘Perhaps I shall seem to you, like some others, to say incredible things about the reality of the expedition, and I know that those who either say or report things that seem not credible not only do not persuade but are also thought foolish; but nevertheless I shall not be frightened into silence when the city is in danger, being convinced that I speak with clearer knowledge than another.

For the Athenians, which greatly surprises you, have set out against you with a large force both naval and infantry, on the pretext of their alliance with the Egestaeans and the resettlement of the Leontines, but in truth from desire for Sicily, and most of all for our city, thinking that if they got this, they would easily get the rest as well.

So, as they will soon be here, consider from your present resources in what way you will best defend yourselves against them, and do not be caught unguarded by despising them nor neglect the whole matter by disbelieving.

And if anyone does believe it, let him not be dismayed at their daring and power. For neither will they be able to harm us more than they suffer, nor is it without advantage to us that they come with a great expedition, but it is much better with regard to the other Siceliots (for in their alarm they will be more willing to be our allies), and if in the end we either subdue them or drive them away without achieving what they aim at (for I certainly do not fear that they will attain what they expect), it will turn out to be a most glorious deed for us, and not one beyond my hopes.

For few great expeditions, either of Hellenes or of barbarians, that set out far from their own land have succeeded. For they do not come in greater numbers than the inhabitants and their neighbours (for everything unites through fear), and if they fail in a foreign land for lack of supplies, they nevertheless leave a name to those they plotted against, even if they come to grief mostly through their own fault.

This is just how these very Athenians grew great, when the Mede failed in many things beyond expectation, on the name that he was going against Athens, and it is not beyond hope that the same will happen to us.

‘With confidence, then, let us make our preparations here and, sending to the Sicels, make some more secure and try to make friendship and alliance with others, and let us send envoys to the rest of Sicily, showing that the danger is common, and to Italy, so that we may either make an alliance for ourselves or they may not receive the Athenians.

And it seems to me better to send to Carthage as well; for it is not beyond their expectation, but they are always in fear that the Athenians may some time come against their city, so that perhaps, thinking that if they abandon things here they themselves too will be in trouble, they would be willing to help us either secretly or openly or in some way at least. And they are the most able of men today to do so, if they wish; for they possess very much gold and silver, by which war and everything else prospers.
And let us send also to Lacedaemon and to Corinth, asking them to come here quickly with help and to stir up the war over there.

But what I myself think most opportune, and what you, because of your habitual quietness, would be least likely to be quickly persuaded of, shall nevertheless be said. If we Siceliots, all together, or if not, as many as possible with us, were willing to launch the whole of our existing navy and, with two months' provisions, meet the Athenians at Tarentum and the promontory of Iapygia, and make it clear to them that the struggle will not be for Sicily before it is for their crossing of the Ionian sea, we should greatly alarm them and bring them to reckon that we set out as guards from a friendly country (for Tarentum receives us), while for them the open sea is wide to cross with their whole armament, and it is hard, because of the length of the voyage, to stay in formation, and it would be easy for us to attack, coming on slowly and a few at a time.

If, on the other hand, they lightened their ships and attacked with their faster-sailing part in a more compact body, then if they used their oars, we would attack them when they were worn out, and if that did not seem wise, we can also withdraw to Tarentum; while they, having crossed with few provisions as if for a sea battle, would be in difficulties in deserted places, and either, if they stayed, they would be blockaded, or, if they tried to sail along the coast, they would leave behind the rest of their armament and, not being sure about the cities, whether they would receive them, they would lose heart.

So I for my part think that, shut in by this reckoning, they would not even set sail from Corcyra, but either, after deliberating and sending out spies to see how many we are and in what position, they would be pushed by the season into winter, or, dismayed by the unexpected, they would give up the voyage, especially since the most experienced of their generals, as I hear, is leading against his will and would gladly seize a pretext, if anything considerable were seen on our part.

And we would be reported, I know well, as stronger than we are; and men's opinions are formed according to what is said, and those who attack first, or at least make it clear beforehand to the attackers that they will defend themselves, are more feared, being thought equal to the danger.

This is just what would now happen to the Athenians. For they are coming against us thinking that we will not defend ourselves, having justly judged us because we did not join the Lacedaemonians in destroying them; but if they saw us showing daring beyond their expectation, they would be more dismayed by the unexpected than by our real power.

‘Be persuaded, then, above all to dare this, but if not, to prepare everything else for the war as quickly as possible, and let it be clear to everyone that contempt for attackers is shown by valour in action, but that for now it would turn out most useful to regard preparations made in fear as the safest and to act as if in danger. And the men are both coming and, I know well, are already on their voyage and all but here.’

So much Hermocrates said; and the people of the Syracusans were in great strife with one another, some saying that the Athenians would by no means come and that what he said was not true, and others asking, even if they did come, what they could do to them that they would not suffer worse in return. Others, quite contemptuously, turned the matter into a joke. Few were those who believed Hermocrates and feared what was coming.
And Athenagoras, who was a leader of the people and at that time most persuasive to the many, came forward and spoke to them as follows.

‘As for the Athenians, whoever does not wish them to be so foolish as to come here and fall into our hands is either a coward or not well disposed to the city; but as for those who report such things and fill you with fear, I do not wonder at their daring, but at their stupidity, if they think they are not seen through.

For those who have some private fear wish to throw the city into alarm, so that they may cover up their own fear under the common one. And now this is what these reports mean; they have not arisen of themselves, but have been put together by men who are always stirring up such things here.
But you, if you take good counsel, will reckon what is likely by considering not what these men report, but what clever men of much experience, as I consider the Athenians to be, would do.

For it is not likely that they, leaving the Peloponnesians behind and before they have firmly ended the war there, would willingly come to another war no smaller, since I for my part think they are content that we, so many and so great cities, are not coming against them.

But if they should indeed come, as they are said to, I consider Sicily more capable than the Peloponnese of fighting the war to the end, inasmuch as it is better equipped in every respect, and our city by itself much stronger than the army that, as they say, is now coming, even if it should come twice as large, since I know that no horses will accompany them, nor will any be provided here, except a few from the Egestaeans, nor hoplites equal in number to ours, coming as they do on ships (for it is a great thing to be carried so long a voyage here even in the ships alone, lightly laden), nor the rest of the armament that must be provided against a city as large as this, which is not small.

So, so far do I differ from them, it seems to me that, if they came bringing another city as large as Syracuse is and settled on our border and made war, they would hardly escape being utterly destroyed, still less, surely, in a Sicily that is wholly hostile (for it will unite), with a camp set up from their ships, and not going far from their wretched tents and bare necessities because of our cavalry. And in short I do not think they would even get control of the land; so much stronger do I consider our armament.
‘But, as I say, the Athenians know this and, I know well, are looking after their own interests, and men from here are inventing stories of things that neither are nor could be,

men whom I know, not now for the first time but always, to be wishing, either by such words as these and others still more mischievous, or by deeds, to frighten your people and rule the city themselves. And indeed I fear that some day, by trying often, they may even succeed; for we are poor at taking precautions before we are in the midst of suffering, and at prosecuting them when we have found them out.
Therefore, because of this, our city is seldom at rest, and takes on many factions and struggles, not more against the enemy than against itself, and sometimes tyrannies and unjust cliques.

I shall try, if you are willing to follow me, never to let any of this happen in our time, by persuading you, the many, and by punishing those who contrive such things, not only when caught in the act (for it is hard to come upon them), but also for what they wish but cannot do (for one must forestall an enemy not only in what he does but also in his intentions, since if one does not take precautions first, one will also be the first to suffer), and as for the few, by sometimes exposing them, sometimes watching them, and sometimes also instructing them; for in this way I think I could best turn them away from wrongdoing.

And indeed, as I have often asked myself, what is it you want, young men? To hold office already? But that is not lawful; and the law was laid down because you are not capable, rather than to exclude you when you are capable. But then, not to have equal rights with the many? And how is it just that the same people should not be thought worthy of the same rights?

Someone will say that democracy is neither wise nor fair, but that those who have money are the best fitted to rule well. But I say, first, that the people is the name for the whole, oligarchy for a part, and next, that the rich are the best guardians of money, the wise would give the best counsel, and the many, after hearing, would judge best, and that these, both separately and all together, have an equal share in a democracy.

An oligarchy gives the many a share in the dangers, but of the benefits it not only takes the larger part but takes away and keeps everything; and this is what the powerful and the young among you are eager for, things impossible to obtain in a great city. ‘But even now, most senseless of all men, if you do not understand that you are pursuing evil, you are either the most ignorant of all the Hellenes I know, or the most wicked, if you dare it knowingly.

But either learning or repenting, increase the common good of the city for all, considering that the good among you would have an equal or even a greater share in it [than the mass of the city ], but that if you want other things, you risk being deprived of everything; and have done with reports like these, knowing that you are dealing with people who see through them and will not allow it.

For this city, even if the Athenians do come, will defend itself against them in a manner worthy of itself, and we have generals who will look after these things; and if none of it is true, as I do not think it is, the city will not, alarmed by your reports and choosing you as rulers, place a self-chosen slavery upon itself, but, considering matters by itself, it will judge your words as having the force of deeds, and will not be deprived of its present freedom by listening to you, but will try to preserve it by guarding in deed against allowing it.’
Such were the words of Athenagoras. And one of the generals stood up and allowed no one else to come forward, but himself spoke as follows about the present situation.

‘It is not wise either for anyone to utter slanders against one another or for those who hear them to accept them, but rather to look to the reports coming in, so that each one of us and the whole city may prepare to defend ourselves well against the invaders.
And if after all there is no need, there is no harm in the commonwealth being equipped with horses and arms

and the other things in which war takes pride (and we shall have the care and inspection of these), and in sending men round to the cities, both for observation and for anything else that seems useful. Some of this we have already seen to, and whatever we learn we shall bring before you.’ And the Syracusans, when the general had said this much, dispersed from the assembly.

The Athenians themselves and all their allies were now at Corcyra. And first the generals held a final review of the army and arranged in what order they were to anchor and encamp, and dividing it into three parts they allotted one to each general, so that they would neither, sailing together, be short of water and harbours and provisions at their landing places, and would in other respects be more orderly and easier to command, being assigned by divisions to a general;

and then they sent ahead to Italy and Sicily three ships to find out which of the cities would receive them. And these had been told to come back to meet them, so that they might know before putting in.

After this the Athenians, with an armament now of this size, set out from Corcyra and crossed to Sicily, with a hundred and thirty-four triremes in all and two Rhodian fifty-oared ships (of these a hundred were Attic, of which sixty were fast ships and the others troop-ships, and the rest of the fleet was of the Chians and the other allies), with five thousand one hundred hoplites in all (and of these, of the Athenians themselves, fifteen hundred were from the muster-roll and seven hundred were thetes serving as marines on the ships, and the others were allies who joined the expedition, some from the subjects, and five hundred from the Argives, and two hundred and fifty of the Mantineans and mercenaries), with four hundred and eighty archers in all (and eighty of these were Cretans), and seven hundred Rhodian slingers, and a hundred and twenty light-armed Megarian exiles, and one horse-transport carrying thirty horsemen.

Such was the size of the first armament that crossed over for the war. And for these, thirty grain-carrying merchant ships brought the provisions, carrying also the bakers and stonemasons and carpenters and all the tools for wall-building, and a hundred boats, which sailed with the merchant ships under compulsion; and many other boats and merchant ships voluntarily accompanied the army for the sake of trade; and all these then crossed the Ionian gulf together from Corcyra.

And when the whole armament had reached the Iapygian promontory and Tarentum, and wherever each found it convenient, they sailed along the coast of Italy, the cities not receiving them with a market nor into the town, but only with water and anchorage, and Tarentum and Locri not even with these, until they came to Rhegium, a promontory of Italy.

And there they now gathered, and outside the city, since they would not receive them inside, they set up a camp in the sanctuary of Artemis, where they also provided them with a market, and drawing their ships up on shore they rested. And they held talks with the Rhegians, claiming that, being Chalcidians, they should help the Leontines, who were Chalcidians; but they said that they would not side with either party, but would do whatever the rest of the Italiots also agreed on.

And they considered in what way they would best deal with affairs in Sicily; and at the same time they awaited the ships sent ahead to Egesta, wishing to know about the money, whether what the messengers had said in Athens was there.

Meanwhile clear news was now coming to the Syracusans from many quarters and from their spies that the ships were at Rhegium, and in view of this they began preparing with all their mind and were no longer incredulous. And they sent round to the Sicels, to some places guards, to others envoys, and brought garrisons into the outposts in the country, and in the city they examined, by an inspection of arms and horses, whether they were complete, and arranged everything else as for a war that was imminent and all but upon them.
The three ships that had gone ahead came back from Egesta to the Athenians at Rhegium, reporting that the rest of the money they had promised was not there, but only thirty talents were to be seen.

And the generals were at once disheartened, because this had at the very first gone against them, and because the Rhegians were unwilling to join the expedition, whom they had first tried to persuade and who were most likely to agree, being kinsmen of the Leontines and always friendly to them. And Nicias had expected the news from the Egestaeans, but to the other two it was rather unexpected.

The Egestaeans had contrived the following trick at the time when the first envoys of the Athenians came to them to inspect the money. They brought them into the sanctuary of Aphrodite at Eryx and showed them the offerings, bowls and wine-jugs and censers and no small amount of other furnishings, which, being of silver, made a much greater show than their small value in money; and holding private entertainments for the crews of the triremes, they collected the drinking cups, both gold and silver, from Egesta itself and borrowed those from the neighbouring cities, both Phoenician and Hellenic, and brought them to the banquets, each as their own.

And as all mostly used the same ones and many were to be seen everywhere, it caused great amazement to the Athenians from the triremes, and when they arrived in Athens they spread the word that they had seen much money.

And these men, who had themselves been deceived and had then persuaded the others, when the story went round that the money was not in Egesta, were much blamed by the soldiers; but the generals deliberated in view of the present situation.

Nicias' opinion was to sail against Selinus with the whole army, which was the chief purpose for which they had been sent, and if the Egestaeans provided money for the whole army, to decide accordingly, but if not, to require them to provide maintenance for the sixty ships they had asked for, and to stay and reconcile the Selinuntians with them either by force or by agreement, and so, after sailing past the other cities and displaying the power of the city of the Athenians and showing their zeal towards their friends and allies, to sail back home, unless they should be able, in a short time and unexpectedly, either to help the Leontines or to bring over some of the other cities, and not to endanger the city by spending its own resources.

Alcibiades said that, having sailed out with so great a force, they ought not to go away disgracefully and without achieving anything, but should send heralds to the cities, all except Selinus and Syracuse, and try to detach some of the Sicels from the Syracusans and make friends of others, so as to have grain and troops, and first persuade the Messenians (for they were best placed on the line of passage and the approach to Sicily, and would be a harbour and a most suitable naval station for the army); and having brought over the cities, and knowing with whom they would fight, they should then attack Syracuse and Selinus, unless the latter came to terms with the Egestaeans and the former allowed them to resettle the Leontines.
Lamachus said that they ought to sail straight to Syracuse and fight the battle near the city as soon as possible, while they were still unprepared and most dismayed.

For every army is most formidable at first; but if it delays before coming into sight, men regain courage in their minds and, at the sight of it, rather despise it. But if they fell upon them suddenly, while the enemy were still awaiting them in great fear, they would most surely prevail and would terrify them in every way, both by the sight of them (for they would now appear most numerous) and by the expectation of what they would suffer, but most of all by the immediate danger of the battle.

And it was likely that many had also been cut off outside in the fields because they did not believe that they would come, and while these were bringing in their property the army would not lack supplies, if it sat down before the city in control of the field.
