And the other Siceliots would in this way at once be more inclined not to ally themselves with the Syracusans but to come over to them, and would not delay, looking around to see which side would prevail. And he said that they ought to withdraw and make Megara their naval station and base of operations, which was deserted, being not far from Syracuse either by sea or by land.

Lamachus, having said this, nevertheless himself also came over to the opinion of Alcibiades. After this Alcibiades sailed across in his own ship to Messene and made proposals to them about an alliance, and when he did not persuade them, but they answered that they would not receive him in the city, but would provide a market outside, he sailed back to Rhegium.
And at once the generals manned sixty ships out of the whole fleet and, taking provisions, sailed along the coast to Naxos, leaving the rest of the army at Rhegium and one of their own number.
The Naxians received them into the city, and they sailed along to Catana. And as the Catanaeans would not receive them (for there were men there who favoured the cause of the Syracusans),

they went on to the river Terias, and after bivouacking there, on the next day they sailed to Syracuse with the rest of the ships in single file; but they sent ten of the ships ahead into the great harbour to sail in and see whether any fleet had been launched, and, sailing up close, to proclaim from the ships that the Athenians had come to restore the Leontines to their own land in accordance with their alliance and kinship; that therefore those of the Leontines who were in Syracuse should without fear come away to the Athenians as to friends and benefactors.
And when the proclamation had been made and they had reconnoitred the city and the harbours and the features of the country from which they would have to make war, they sailed back to Catana.

And when an assembly had been held, the Catanaeans would not receive the army, but they told the generals to come in and say what they wished. And while Alcibiades was speaking, and the people in the city had turned their attention to the assembly, the soldiers broke down unnoticed a small gate that had been badly built up, and having entered they went to market in the city.

Of the Catanaeans, those who favoured the Syracusans, when they saw the army inside, at once became very frightened and slipped away, not very many of them, while the rest voted an alliance with the Athenians and told them to bring the rest of the army from Rhegium.
After this the Athenians sailed across to Rhegium, and setting out now with the whole army for Catana, when they arrived, they set up their camp.

And word was brought to them from Camarina that, if they came, the Camarinaeans would come over to them, and that the Syracusans were manning a fleet. So with the whole army they sailed along first to Syracuse; and when they found no fleet being manned, they went along again to Camarina, and putting in to the beach they sent a herald. But the Camarinaeans would not receive them, saying that their oaths were to receive the Athenians if they sailed in with a single ship, unless they themselves sent for more.

Having accomplished nothing, they sailed away; and after landing at a point in Syracusan territory and making plunder, and when the Syracusan cavalry came to the rescue and killed some of the light troops who were scattered, they returned to Catana.

And they find the Salaminia, the ship from Athens, which had come for Alcibiades, to order him to sail home to make his defence against the charges which the city brought against him, and for certain others of the soldiers with him who had been informed against as committing impiety concerning the mysteries, and some also concerning the Hermae.

For the Athenians, after the army had sailed away, had been no less active in investigating what had been done concerning the mysteries and concerning the Hermae, and not testing the informers, but accepting everything in a suspicious spirit, on the word of rascals they arrested and imprisoned some very good citizens, thinking it more useful to sift the matter and find out the truth than that anyone, even one who seemed to be good, when accused through the wickedness of an informer, should escape without examination.

For the people, knowing by hearsay that the tyranny of Pisistratus and his sons had become harsh at the end, and moreover that it had been put down not by themselves and Harmodius, but by the Lacedaemonians, were always afraid and took everything suspiciously.

For the daring deed of Aristogiton and Harmodius was undertaken because of a love affair, and by relating it at some length I shall show that neither the others nor the Athenians themselves give any accurate account about their own tyrants or about what happened.

For when Pisistratus died in old age while holding the tyranny, it was not Hipparchus, as most people think, but Hippias, being the eldest, who obtained the rule. And when Harmodius was in the bloom of youthful beauty, Aristogiton, a man of the townspeople, a citizen of the middle class, became his lover and had him.

And Harmodius, having been solicited by Hipparchus son of Pisistratus and not being won over, tells Aristogiton. And he, deeply pained as a lover and fearing the power of Hipparchus, lest he should take him by force, at once plots, as far as his existing station allowed, the overthrow of the tyranny.

And meanwhile Hipparchus, when on a second attempt he had no more success in persuading Harmodius, did not wish to do anything violent, but prepared to insult him in some covert way, as if it were not for this reason.

For neither in the rest of his rule was he oppressive to the many, but he conducted it without giving offence; and indeed these tyrants practised virtue and intelligence to a very great degree, and, exacting from the Athenians only a twentieth of their produce, they adorned their city finely and carried on their wars and offered sacrifices at the temples.

In all other respects the city itself used the laws previously established, except that they always took care that one of their own family should be in the offices. And among others of them who held the annual archonship at Athens was Pisistratus, the son of Hippias who had been tyrant, bearing the name of his grandfather, who when he was archon dedicated the altar of the twelve gods in the marketplace and that of Apollo in the Pythian precinct.

And later the Athenian people, building on to the altar in the marketplace to make it longer, obliterated the inscription; but that of the altar in the Pythian precinct is still clearly visible even now, in faint letters, saying this:
This memorial of his archonship Pisistratus son of Hippias
set up in the precinct of Pythian Apollo.

That Hippias ruled as the eldest I firmly assert, knowing it also from report more accurately than others, but one might learn it also from this very fact: for of the legitimate brothers he alone appears to have had children, as the altar shows and the pillar about the wrongdoing of the tyrants set up on the Athenian acropolis, on which no child of Thessalus or of Hipparchus is recorded, but five of Hippias, who were born to him by Myrrhine the daughter of Callias son of Hyperechides; for it was likely that the eldest would marry first.
And on the same pillar he is recorded first after his father, and this too not unnaturally, because he was the eldest after him and had been tyrant.

Nor indeed, it seems to me, would Hippias ever have easily seized the tyranny on the spot, if Hipparchus had died while in power and he himself had been establishing himself on that same day; but, through his earlier familiarity, which was formidable to the citizens and strict towards the mercenaries, he prevailed with a great margin of safety, and he was not at a loss as a younger brother would be, who had not previously been continuously familiar with the rule.
But it was the lot of Hipparchus, becoming famous through the misfortune of his fate, to acquire also the reputation of the tyranny for the time to come.

So then he insulted Harmodius, who had rejected his solicitation, as he had intended; for after summoning his sister, a maiden, to come and carry a basket in a certain procession, they turned her away, saying that they had never summoned her at all because she was not worthy.

Harmodius took this badly, and Aristogiton too was much more exasperated on his account. And for them everything else had been arranged with those who were to join them in the deed, but they were waiting for the Great Panathenaea, the only day on which it aroused no suspicion that those of the citizens who were to conduct the procession should gather together in arms; and they themselves were to begin, and the others were to help them at once against the bodyguards.

Those who had sworn to the conspiracy were not many, for the sake of security; for they hoped that even those not in the secret, if any number at all should be bold, would be willing, since they had arms at least, to join on the spot in setting themselves free.

And when the festival came, Hippias was outside in the so-called Ceramicus with his bodyguards, arranging how each part of the procession was to go forward, while Harmodius and Aristogiton, already holding their daggers, advanced to the deed.

And when they saw one of their fellow conspirators talking familiarly with Hippias (and Hippias was easy of access to everyone), they were afraid and thought that they had been informed against and were all but on the point of being arrested.

So they wished first, if they could, to take vengeance beforehand on the man who had wronged them and on whose account they were running all this risk, and just as they were they rushed inside the gates, and they came upon Hipparchus by the so-called Leocorium, and at once falling upon him without forethought and in the greatest possible anger, the one through jealous love, the other as having been insulted, they struck him and kill him.
And Aristogiton escapes the bodyguards for the moment, as the crowd ran together, but later he was caught and was not gently dealt with; but Harmodius is killed on the spot.

When the news was brought to Hippias in the Ceramicus, he went at once, not to the scene of the deed, but to the armed men of the procession, before they, being some distance away, perceived it, and, composing his face so as not to betray anything of the disaster, he pointed out a certain place and ordered them to go off to it without their arms.

And they withdrew, thinking that he would say something, but he, having told his mercenaries to take up the arms, at once picked out those whom he held guilty and anyone who was found with a dagger; for it was customary to conduct the processions with shield and spear.
In such a way, because of a lover's grief, both the beginning of the plot and the reckless daring arising from sudden fright came about for Harmodius and Aristogiton.

For the Athenians the tyranny became harsher after this, and Hippias, being now more in fear, put many of the citizens to death and at the same time looked abroad, to see whether he might see any safe refuge available to him anywhere if a revolution took place.

At any rate, after this he, an Athenian, gave his daughter Archedice to a Lampsacene, Aeantides, the son of Hippoclus the tyrant of Lampsacus, perceiving that they had great influence with King Darius. And her tomb is in Lampsacus, bearing this inscription:
Of a man who was the best in Hellas of those in his day,
Hippias, this dust hides the daughter Archedice,
who, though her father and husband and brothers were tyrants
and her children too, was not lifted up in mind to arrogance.

And after being tyrant of the Athenians for three more years and being deposed in the fourth by the Lacedaemonians and the exiled Alcmaeonidae, Hippias went under a truce to Sigeum and to Aeantides at Lampsacus, and from there to King Darius, from whose court he also set out twenty years later, already an old man, and joined the Medes in the expedition to Marathon.

Bearing these things in mind, and remembering all that they knew by hearsay about them, the Athenian people were then harsh and suspicious towards those who had been accused in the matter of the mysteries, and everything seemed to them to have been done as part of an oligarchic and tyrannical conspiracy.

And as, because of their anger at such things, many men of note were already in prison and there appeared to be no end to it, but day by day they went further towards greater savagery and arresting still more, then one of the prisoners, who was thought to be most guilty, is persuaded by one of his fellow prisoners to give information, whether it was true or not; for there is conjecture on both sides, and no one either then or later can say anything certain about those who did the deed.

By his argument he persuaded him that he ought, even if he had not done it, to save himself by obtaining immunity and to free the city from its present suspicion; for his safety would be surer if he confessed with immunity than if he denied it and went to trial.

And he informs both against himself and against others in the matter of the Hermae; and the Athenian people, gladly accepting what they thought was the truth, and having previously thought it terrible if they should not discover those who were plotting against their democracy, at once released the informer and with him the others whom he had not accused, while those who were charged they put on trial, and they executed all who had been arrested, and condemning to death those who had escaped, they proclaimed a reward in silver for whoever killed them.
And in this it was unclear whether those who suffered had been punished unjustly, but the rest of the city was for the present manifestly benefited.

As for Alcibiades, at the urging of his enemies, who had attacked him even before he sailed, the Athenians took it hard; and when they thought they had the truth about the Hermae, they believed much more that the matter of the mysteries too, of which he was accused, had been done by him with the same purpose and as part of the conspiracy against the democracy.

For it happened also that a Lacedaemonian army, not a large one, at the very time when they were in this uproar, had advanced as far as the Isthmus, carrying on some negotiation with the Boeotians. So it seemed that it had come by agreement at his instigation and not on account of the Boeotians, and that, if they had not forestalled it by arresting the men according to the information, the city would have been betrayed. And for one night they even slept in arms in the Theseum within the city.

And at the same time the friends of Alcibiades at Argos were suspected of plotting an attack on the democracy, and for this reason the Athenians then handed over to the Argive people the Argive hostages who were kept in the islands, to put them to death.

And from every side suspicion surrounded Alcibiades. So, wishing to bring him to trial and put him to death, they thus send the ship Salaminia to Sicily for him and for the others about whom information had been given.

The instructions were to order him to follow and make his defence, but not to arrest him, since they were careful both not to cause disturbance among their own soldiers in Sicily and among the enemy and, not least, wished the Mantineans and Argives to stay, thinking that it was through him that they had been persuaded to join the expedition.

And he, with his own ship, and those accused with him sailed away from Sicily with the Salaminia as if to Athens; and when they were at Thurii, they no longer followed, but leaving the ship they disappeared, fearing to sail home to trial under such a prejudice.

The men from the Salaminia for a while searched for Alcibiades and those with him; but as they were nowhere to be found, they sailed off. And Alcibiades, now an exile, not long afterwards crossed over in a boat from the territory of Thurii to the Peloponnese; and the Athenians condemned him and those with him to death by default.

After this the remaining Athenian generals in Sicily, dividing the army into two parts and each taking one by lot, sailed with the whole force for Selinus and Egesta, wishing to know whether the Egestaeans would give the money, and also to look into the affairs of the Selinuntines and learn their differences with the Egestaeans.

Sailing along with Sicily on their left, on the side towards the Tyrrhenian gulf, they put in at Himera, which is the only Hellenic city in this part of Sicily; and as it would not receive them, they went on along the coast.

And on their voyage along the coast they take Hyccara, a Sicanian town, but hostile to the Egestaeans; it was on the sea. And having enslaved the inhabitants they handed the town over to the Egestaeans (for their cavalry had come to join them), while they themselves went back with the infantry through the territory of the Sicels until they reached Catana, and the ships sailed round carrying the captives.

Nicias, sailing directly from Hyccara to Egesta, after transacting other business and receiving thirty talents, rejoined the army; and they sold the captives, and from them one hundred and twenty talents were realised.

And they sailed round to their Sicel allies, ordering them to send troops; and with half of their own army they went against Hybla Geleatis, which was hostile, and did not take it. And the summer ended.
In the following winter the Athenians at once began preparing for their attack on Syracuse, and the Syracusans also on their part as if to go against them.

For since the Athenians did not at once attack them, as they had at first feared and expected, with each passing day they regained more courage, and when the Athenians were seen sailing far away from them along the other side of Sicily, and after going to Hybla and attempting it they did not take it by force, they despised them still more and demanded of their generals, as a crowd is apt to do when it has grown bold, to lead them against Catana, since the enemy were not coming against them.

And Syracusan horsemen, constantly riding up as scouts to the army of the Athenians, insulted them, asking among other things whether they had come rather to settle with them themselves in a foreign land than to resettle the Leontines in their own.

Knowing this, the generals of the Athenians, wishing to draw them out in full force as far as possible from the city, while they themselves meanwhile sailed along by night with the ships and occupied a camping place in a suitable spot at their leisure, knowing that they would not be equally able to do this if they disembarked from the ships in face of an enemy prepared, or if they were detected going by land (for the Syracusan horsemen, who were numerous, would do great harm to their light troops and their crowd of followers, since they themselves had no horsemen present, but in this way they would seize a position where they would suffer no harm worth mentioning from the horsemen; and Syracusan exiles who accompanied them told them of the position near the Olympieum, which they in fact occupied), the generals accordingly contrive something like the following for what they wanted.

They send a man faithful to them, but in the opinion of the Syracusan generals no less friendly to them; the man was a Catanaean, and he said that he came from men in Catana whose names they knew and whom they knew to be still remaining in the city among those well disposed to them.

He said that the Athenians were passing the nights away from their arms in the city, and that if the Syracusans wished to come in full force against the army on an appointed day at dawn, they themselves would shut in those who were with them and set fire to the ships, and the Syracusans, attacking the stockade, would easily take the army; and that those who would help in this were many of the Catanaeans and were already prepared, those from whom he himself had come.

The generals of the Syracusans, since they were confident in other respects as well and had intended even without this to prepare to march on Catana, trusted the man much too inconsiderately and at once, after agreeing on a day when they would be there, sent him back, and they themselves (for by now the Selinuntines and some others of their allies had arrived) gave orders for all the Syracusans to march out in full force. And when their preparations too were complete and the days on which they had agreed to come were near, marching towards Catana they bivouacked on the river Symaethus in the territory of Leontini.

But the Athenians, when they perceived them approaching, took up their whole army and those of the Sicels or anyone else who had joined them, and embarking them on the ships and boats, sailed by night for Syracuse.

And at dawn the Athenians were disembarking at the place opposite the Olympieum to occupy their camp, while the Syracusan horsemen, having ridden first up to Catana and perceiving that the whole army had put to sea, turned back and report to the infantry, and then all of them, turning back, hastened to the defence of the city.

Meanwhile the Athenians, since the Syracusans had a long way to go, at their leisure settled their army in a suitable position, where they would be able to begin battle whenever they wished and the Syracusan horsemen would be least able to harm them both in the action and before it; for on one side walls and houses and trees and a marsh shut them in, and along the other side there were cliffs.

And felling the trees nearby and carrying them down to the sea, they fixed a stockade beside the ships, and at Dascon, where it was most accessible to the enemy, they quickly raised a fort of unhewn stones and timber, and they broke down the bridge over the Anapus.

While they were making these preparations no one came out from the city to hinder them, but first the Syracusan horsemen came up in support, and then later the whole infantry too was assembled. And at first they came near the army of the Athenians, but then, as the Athenians did not advance against them, they withdrew and, crossing the Helorine road, bivouacked.

On the next day the Athenians and their allies prepared for battle, and were drawn up as follows. The Argives and Mantineans held the right wing, the Athenians the centre, and the other allies the rest. And half of their army was drawn up in front, eight deep, and half beside the tents in a hollow square, also drawn up eight deep; these had been told to watch where any part of the army was most hard pressed, and to come to its support. And they placed the baggage-carriers inside this reserve.

The Syracusans drew up all their hoplites sixteen deep, being the Syracusans in full force and all the allies who were present (the Selinuntines above all had come to their help, and then also cavalry from Gela, about two hundred in all, and from Camarina about twenty horsemen and about fifty archers), and they placed their horsemen on the right, not fewer than twelve hundred, and beside them the javelin-throwers.
As the Athenians were about to attack first, Nicias, going along the line to each nation in turn and to them all together, exhorted them as follows.
‘What need is there, men, of a long exhortation, when we are here for the same struggle? For the preparation itself seems to me more capable of giving courage than fine words with a weak army.

For where we are Argives and Mantineans and Athenians and the foremost of the islanders, how should not everyone, with such and so many allies, have great hope of victory, especially against men who are defending themselves in a mass levy and are not picked men, as we are too, and moreover against Siceliots, who despise us but will not stand their ground against us, because their skill is less than their daring?

And let each of you also bear this in mind, that we are far from our own land and near no friendly land, except what you yourselves win by fighting. And I remind you of the opposite of what I am sure the enemy are urging on one another; for they say that the struggle will be for their fatherland, but I say that it is not in our fatherland, from which we must conquer or not easily withdraw; for the many horsemen will press upon us.
So, remembering your own worth, advance eagerly against the enemy, and consider the present necessity and difficulty more formidable than the enemy.’

Nicias, after exhorting them in such words, at once led the army forward. The Syracusans were not expecting to have to fight at that moment, and some of them, since the city was near, had even gone away; and those who in their haste were running up to help came too late, but they took their places wherever each could join the main body. For indeed they were not lacking in eagerness or in daring either in this battle or in the others, but in courage they were not inferior as far as their skill held out, and when it fell short they betrayed their resolution too against their will. Nevertheless, though they did not think that the Athenians would attack them first and were forced to defend themselves in haste, they took up their arms and at once advanced to meet them.

And first the stone-throwers and slingers and archers of each side skirmished in front and routed one another, as light troops would be likely to; then the seers brought forward the customary sacrifices and the trumpeters urged the hoplites to engage,

and they advanced, the Syracusans to fight for their fatherland and each for his own safety for the present and for his freedom in the future, and of their opponents the Athenians to win another's land for their own and not to injure their own by defeat, the Argives and the independent allies to help them win what they had come for and, having conquered, to see again their own fatherland; while the subject allies had their greatest eagerness for their immediate safety, which was hopeless if they did not prevail, and then, as a secondary matter, that if they helped the Athenians subdue anything else, their subjection would be easier for them.

When the battle came to close quarters, they held out against each other for a long time, and it happened that at the same time there were some claps of thunder and lightning and heavy rain, so that for those who were fighting for the first time and had had very little experience of war this too added to their fear, while to the more experienced what was happening seemed to come about through the season of the year, but the fact that their opponents were not being defeated caused them much greater alarm.

And when the Argives first pushed back the left wing of the Syracusans, and after them the Athenians the part facing themselves, the rest of the Syracusan army too was now broken through and put to flight.

And the Athenians did not pursue far (for the Syracusan horsemen, being numerous and undefeated, held them back, and charging their hoplites, if they saw any pursuing ahead of the rest, drove them back), but having followed in a body as far as was safe they withdrew again and set up a trophy.

The Syracusans, having gathered on the Helorine road and having formed up as well as they could in the circumstances, nevertheless sent a guard of their own men to the Olympieum, fearing that the Athenians might lay hands on the treasures that were there, and the rest withdrew to the city.

The Athenians did not go to the temple, but having gathered their own dead and laid them on a pyre they bivouacked there. On the next day they gave back their dead to the Syracusans under a truce (there died of them and of their allies about two hundred and sixty), and they gathered the bones of their own (there died of them and of their allies about fifty), and with the spoils of the enemy they sailed back to Catana;

for it was winter, and it did not yet seem possible to carry on the war from where they were, until they had sent for horsemen from Athens and collected them from their allies there, so as not to be wholly outmatched in cavalry, and at the same time had collected money there and received it from the Athenians, and had won over some of the cities, which they hoped would be more ready to listen to them after the battle, and had provided both other things and corn and whatever was needed, intending to attack Syracuse in the spring.
With this intention they sailed away to Naxos and Catana to pass the winter, and the Syracusans, after burying their own dead, held an assembly.

And Hermocrates son of Hermon came forward to them, a man who was in general inferior to no one in intelligence and in the war had shown himself competent in experience and distinguished for courage, and he encouraged them and did not let them give in because of what had happened;

for their spirit had not been defeated, but their lack of discipline had done the harm. And yet they had not been outdone by as much as might have been expected, especially since they had contended, as mere amateurs, so to speak, against craftsmen, the foremost of the Hellenes in experience.

Great harm had also been done by the number of the generals and the division of command (for they had fifteen generals) and by the disorderly lack of discipline of the many. But if a few experienced generals were chosen and during this winter they prepared the hoplite force, providing arms for those who had none, so that they might be as many as possible, and compelling them to undergo the other training as well, he said that in all likelihood they would overcome their opponents, since courage was theirs already and discipline in action would be added; for both these qualities would increase, discipline being practised amid dangers, while their courage would of itself become more daring through confidence in their skill.

And they ought to choose generals both few and with full powers, and to swear to them the oath that they would surely let them command as they judged best; for in this way what had to be kept secret would be better concealed, and everything else would be prepared in an orderly way and without excuses.
And the Syracusans, having heard him, voted everything as he urged and chose as generals Hermocrates himself and Heraclides son of Lysimachus and Sicanus son of Execestus, these three,

and they sent envoys to Corinth and to Lacedaemon, so that an alliance might come to them and that they might persuade the Lacedaemonians to wage the war against the Athenians more resolutely and openly on their behalf, so that they might either draw them away from Sicily or be less able to send further help to the army in Sicily.

The Athenian army at Catana sailed at once to Messene, expecting it to be betrayed to them. And what was being negotiated did not come about; for Alcibiades, when he was leaving his command after being summoned home, knowing that he would go into exile, informs the friends of the Syracusans in Messene, being privy to what was to happen; and they first put the men to death, and then, being in revolt and in arms, those who wished this prevailed so that the Athenians were not received.

After staying about thirteen days, the Athenians, as they were suffering from the weather and had no provisions and nothing was going forward, went away to Naxos and, having made ditches and stockades round their camp, spent the winter there; and they sent a trireme to Athens for money and horsemen, so that they might arrive at the beginning of spring.

During the winter the Syracusans too built walls, at the city, taking in the Temenites, a wall along the whole side facing Epipolae, so that, if they should after all be defeated, they might not be easily walled off within a smaller space, and a fort at Megara, and another at the Olympieum; and they set stakes along the sea wherever there were landing places.

And knowing that the Athenians were wintering at Naxos, they marched in full force against Catana, and ravaged part of their land and, after setting fire to the tents and the camp of the Athenians, returned home.

And learning that the Athenians were sending an embassy to Camarina on the basis of the alliance made in the time of Laches, to see whether they might win them over, they themselves sent a counter-embassy; for they suspected the Camarinaeans of not having sent eagerly what they had sent for the first battle, and that in future they might no longer be willing to help them, seeing that the Athenians had done well in the battle, and might go over to them, persuaded by their former friendship.

So when Hermocrates and others had arrived at Camarina from Syracuse, and Euphemus with others from the Athenians, Hermocrates, when an assembly of the Camarinaeans had been held, wishing to discredit the Athenians in advance, spoke as follows.

‘We have come on this embassy, Camarinaeans, not because we feared that you would be dismayed by the present force of the Athenians, but rather that the words which are about to come from them might persuade you before you heard anything from us too.

For they have come to Sicily on the pretext which you hear of, but with the intention which we all suspect; and to me they seem to wish not to resettle the Leontines but rather to unsettle us. For surely it is not reasonable that they should lay waste the cities there but settle those here, and should care for the Leontines because they are Chalcidians, on the ground of kinship, while they keep enslaved the Chalcidians in Euboea, of whom these are colonists.

And by the same method they acquired their power there and are now trying to do so here; for having become leaders of the Ionians, who were willing, and of all who were their allies by descent from them, as if to take vengeance on the Mede, they subdued them, bringing against some the charge of desertion, against others of making war on one another, and against others whatever plausible charge they had in each case.

And so neither did these men stand up against the Mede for the freedom of the Hellenes, nor the Hellenes for their own, but the one for the enslavement of the Hellenes to themselves instead of to him, the others for a change of master, to one not less intelligent but more intelligent for evil.

‘But indeed we have not come now to set out before those who know them all the wrongs of the city of the Athenians, which is easy to accuse, but much rather to blame ourselves, because, having examples of how the Hellenes there were enslaved for not defending themselves, and now that the same sophistries are being used against us, resettlements of Leontine kinsmen and aid to Egestaean allies, we are not willing to unite and show them more resolutely that here there are no Ionians, or Hellespontines and islanders, who are always changing their master, either the Mede or some other, and remaining slaves, but free Dorians from the independent Peloponnese living in Sicily.

Or are we waiting until we are taken one by one, city by city, knowing that this is the only way in which we can be conquered, and seeing them turning to this method, so as to divide some of us by words, to set others at war with one another by the hope of alliance, and to do harm to others by saying whatever pleasant thing they can to each? And do we think that, if a distant fellow-dweller perishes first, the danger will not come to each of us too, but that the one who suffers before him is unfortunate by himself alone?

And if it has occurred to anyone that it is the Syracusan, but not himself, who is the enemy of the Athenian, and he thinks it hard to run risks on behalf of my country at any rate, let him consider that he will be fighting in my country not more for mine than equally for his own at the same time, and all the more safely in that he will contend not after I have been destroyed beforehand, but having me as an ally and not alone; and that the Athenian wishes not to punish the enmity of the Syracusan, but on the pretext of me to secure no less the friendship of that man.

And if anyone envies or even fears us (for greater powers are exposed to both these things), and for these reasons wishes Syracuse to be injured so that we may be taught moderation, but to survive for the sake of his own security, he hopes for what is beyond human power to wish; for it is not possible for the same man to be equally the steward both of his desires and of fortune.

And if his judgement should fail, lamenting over his own misfortunes he might perhaps some day wish to envy my good fortune again. But that is impossible for one who has abandoned us and has not been willing to take on the same dangers, which concern not names but realities; for in word a man would be preserving our power, but in fact his own safety.

And it would have been most fitting for you above all, Camarinaeans, being our neighbours and the next to be in danger, to foresee these things and not to be lukewarm allies as now, but rather to come to us yourselves, and, as you would have called on us with entreaties if the Athenians had come first to the territory of Camarina, in the same way now too to exhort us to show that we will not give way at all. But neither you nor the others have as yet bestirred yourselves to do this.

‘But perhaps out of cowardice you will pay court to justice both towards us and towards the invaders, saying that you have an alliance with the Athenians; but you did not make it against your friends, but in case any of your enemies should attack you, and to help the Athenians, at any rate, when they are wronged by others and not when they themselves, as now, wrong their neighbours,

since not even the Rhegians, who are Chalcidians, are willing to help in resettling the Leontines, who are Chalcidians. And it is strange if they, suspecting the reality behind the fair plea, are prudent without giving a reason, while you, on a plausible pretext, wish to help your natural enemies and, together with your bitterest foes, to destroy those who are by nature still more your kinsmen.

But that is not just; you ought to defend us and not fear their armament; for it is not formidable if we all stand together, but only if, as these men are striving for, we do the opposite and stand apart, since not even when they came against us alone and won the battle did they achieve what they wished, but they went away quickly.

So when we are united there is surely no reason to lose heart, but rather to enter the alliance more eagerly, especially since help will come from the Peloponnese, whose men are altogether superior to these in military matters; and let no one think that the well-known caution of yours is fair to us and safe for you, namely to help neither side, as being allies of both.

For it is not as fair in fact as it is in principle. For if through your not joining the alliance the sufferer is overthrown and the conqueror prevails, what else have you done by this same abstention than fail to help the one to be saved and fail to prevent the other from being wicked? And yet it is nobler to side with those who are wronged and who are at the same time your kinsmen, and so to guard the common interest of Sicily and not to allow the Athenians, who are indeed your friends, to do wrong.

‘To sum up, we Syracusans say that there is no point in teaching clearly either you or the others about things which you yourselves know no worse than we; but we entreat you and at the same time solemnly declare, if we do not persuade you, that we are being plotted against by Ionians, our perpetual enemies, and are being betrayed by you, Dorians by Dorians.

And if the Athenians subdue us, they will owe their victory to your decisions, but will be honoured in their own name, and as the prize of victory they will take none other than the one who gave them the victory; and if, on the other hand, we prevail, you, the same people, will pay the penalty for being the cause of our dangers.

So consider and choose now either immediate slavery without danger, or, if you prevail together with us, not to take these men as masters in shame and to escape our enmity, which would not prove short-lived.’
Such were the words of Hermocrates. After him Euphemus, the envoy of the Athenians, spoke as follows.
‘We came for the renewal of the former alliance, but since the Syracusan has attacked us, it is necessary to speak also about our empire, and show that we hold it with good reason.

Now he himself stated the greatest proof, that the Ionians are at all times enemies of the Dorians. And it is indeed so; for we, being Ionians, considered how we might least be subject to the Peloponnesians, who are Dorians and more numerous and live near us,

and after the Persian Wars, having acquired a fleet, we freed ourselves from the rule and leadership of the Lacedaemonians, since it was no more fitting for them to give orders to us than for us to them, except in so far as they were stronger at that time, and having ourselves become leaders of those who were formerly subject to the King, we dwell in safety, thinking that in this way we should be least under the Peloponnesians, having a power with which to defend ourselves, and, to speak precisely, not unjustly subduing the Ionians and islanders, whom the Syracusans say we have enslaved though they are our kinsmen.

For they came against their mother city, against us, with the Mede, and did not dare to revolt and destroy their homes, as we did when we abandoned our city, but they themselves wished for slavery and to bring the same upon us.

In return for this we rule, both because we are worthy of it, since we provided the largest fleet and an unhesitating zeal for the Hellenes, and because these, readily doing this for the Mede, were harming us, and at the same time because we were reaching out for strength against the Peloponnesians.

And we do not use fine words, saying that we rule with good reason because we alone overthrew the barbarian, or that we ran our risks for the freedom of these men rather than for that of all and of ourselves. But no one can be blamed for securing his proper safety. And now too it is for the sake of our own security that we are present here, and we see that the same things are to your advantage too.

And we prove it from the very things which these men slander and which you in your suspicion take in the more alarming sense, knowing that those who are suspicious out of great fear are delighted for the moment by the pleasure of a speech, but later, when it comes to action, do what is to their advantage.

For we have said that we hold our empire there through fear, and that it is for the same reason that we have come here, to settle affairs safely with our friends, and not to enslave them, but rather to prevent them from suffering this.

‘And let no one suppose that we care for you though it is no concern of ours, knowing that if you are preserved and, through not being weak, hold out against the Syracusans, we should be less harmed by their sending some force to the Peloponnesians.

And in this respect you are already of the greatest concern to us. For this reason too it is reasonable for us to resettle the Leontines, not as subjects like their kinsmen in Euboea, but as strong as possible, so that, being neighbours of these men from their own land, they may be troublesome to them on our behalf.

For there we are a match for our enemies even by ourselves, and the Chalcidian, whom he says we are unreasonably freeing here after enslaving him there, is useful to us when he is without armament and contributes money only, while here both the Leontines and our other friends are useful when they are as independent as possible.

For a tyrant or a city holding empire nothing is unreasonable if it is expedient, nor is anyone a kinsman unless he can be trusted; in each case one must become enemy or friend according to the occasion. And what benefits us here is not to harm our friends, but that our enemies should be powerless through the strength of our friends.

And you should not distrust us; for we also lead our allies there as each of them is useful, the Chians and Methymnaeans as independent on condition of providing ships, most of them more forcibly by payment of money, and others again as quite free allies, although they are islanders and easy to take, because they are in favourable positions round the Peloponnese.

So it is natural that our arrangements here too should be made with a view to our advantage and, as we say, to fear of the Syracusans. For they aim at ruling over you and wish, after uniting you on the ground of suspicion of us, either by force or because you are left isolated when we have gone away without success, themselves to rule over Sicily. And this is inevitable if you unite with them; for neither will so great a strength, united into one, be easy for us to deal with any longer, nor would these men be weak against you if we were not present.

And whoever does not think so is refuted by the facts themselves. For the first time you called us in, you held out no other fear than that, if we allowed you to fall under the Syracusans, we ourselves too would be in danger.

And now it is not just to distrust the same argument by which you thought fit to persuade us, nor to be suspicious because we are present with a force greater than is needed against the strength of these men, but much rather to distrust these men.

We, at any rate, are neither able to remain here without you, and even if we turned wicked and subdued you, we should be unable to hold you because of the length of the voyage and the difficulty of guarding large cities that are equipped like those of the mainland; but these men, living next to you not with an army but with a city greater than our force here, are always plotting against you and, whenever they get an opportunity against each of you,

they do not let it go (they have shown this already in other cases and in the matter of the Leontines), and now they dare to call on you, as if you were without sense, against those who are hindering this and who have so far kept Sicily from being under them.

But we call on you in our turn to a far more genuine safety, begging you not to betray the safety which both of us have from each other, and to consider that for these men, because of their numbers, the way against you is always open even without allies, while you will not often have the opportunity to defend yourselves with so great an auxiliary force; and if out of suspicion you allow it to go away either without success or even after a defeat, you will yet wish to see even the smallest fraction of it, when its coming will no longer achieve anything for you.

‘But do not you, Camarinaeans, or the others either, be won over by the slanders of these men; we have told you the whole truth about the things of which we are suspected, and we shall still remind you of them in summary and expect to persuade you.

For we say that we rule over those there so as not to be subject to another, and that we free those here so that we may not be harmed by them, and that we are compelled to do many things because we also have many things to guard against, and that both now and before we have come as allies to those of you here who are wronged, not uninvited, but having been called in.

And do not, setting yourselves up either as judges of what we do or as correctors, which would be difficult by now, try to turn us aside, but in so far as anything in our busy meddling and character is also to your advantage, take hold of this and make use of it, and consider that these things do not harm all alike, but benefit a far greater number of the Hellenes;

for everyone in every place, even where we are not established, both the man who thinks he will be wronged and the man who is plotting, because a ready hope is at hand for the one to obtain help from us in return, and for the other to think that, if we come, it will not be without fear for him to run the risk, both are compelled, the one to be moderate against his will, the other to be saved without trouble of his own.

So do not reject this security, common to anyone who needs it and now present for you, but, putting yourselves on an equal footing with the others, together with us, instead of always being on your guard against the Syracusans, share in plotting against them in your turn on equal terms at last.’

Such were the words of Euphemus. And the Camarinaeans were affected in the following way. They were well disposed to the Athenians, except in so far as they thought they would enslave Sicily, but they were always at variance with the Syracusans because they were neighbours; and fearing no less that the Syracusans, being near, might prevail even without them, they had at first sent them the few horsemen, and for the future they decided to serve the Syracusans rather in fact, but as sparingly as they could, while for the present, so that they might not seem to give less to the Athenians either, since they had also proved the stronger in the battle, to give an equal answer in words to both.

And having so resolved they answered that, since there happened to be a war between both parties, who were both their allies, they thought it consistent with their oaths for the present to help neither. And the envoys of each side departed.
And the Syracusans were making their own preparations for the war, while the Athenians, encamped at Naxos, were negotiating with the Sicels so that as many as possible might come over to them.

And those of the Sicels who lived more towards the plains, being subjects of the Syracusans, for the most part had not revolted; but 〈the〉 settlements of those who held the interior, which had always been independent even before, at once, except for a few, were on the side of the Athenians, and they brought down corn to the army and there are some who brought money too.

And marching against those who did not come over, the Athenians forced some to do so, while from others they were kept off by the Syracusans, who sent garrisons and came to their help. And moving their station for the winter from Naxos to Catana and setting up again the camp which had been burnt by the Syracusans, they spent the winter there.

And they sent a trireme to Carthage about friendship, to see whether they might obtain some help, and they also sent to Tyrrhenia, since some cities were offering of their own accord to join in the war. And they sent round to the Sicels too and, sending to Egesta, ordered them to send as many horses as possible, and they prepared the other things for the circumvallation, bricks and iron, and whatever was needed, intending to take up the war at the beginning of spring.

The Syracusan envoys who had been sent to Corinth and Lacedaemon tried, as they sailed along, to persuade the Italiots too not to look on at what the Athenians were doing, since it was being plotted against them alike, and when they were in Corinth, they made speeches asking them to help them on the ground of kinship.

And the Corinthians at once voted, being themselves the first to do so, to help them with all zeal, and they sent envoys with them to Lacedaemon, so that they might join in persuading the Lacedaemonians too both to wage the war there more openly against the Athenians and to send some help to Sicily.

And the envoys from Corinth arrived at Lacedaemon, and also Alcibiades with his fellow exiles, who had then crossed over at once in a merchant ship from the territory of Thurii, first to Cyllene in Elis, and then later came to Lacedaemon under a safe-conduct, the Lacedaemonians themselves having sent for him; for he was afraid of them because of his conduct in the affair of Mantinea.

And it happened that in the assembly of the Lacedaemonians the Corinthians and the Syracusans and Alcibiades, making the same request, persuaded the Lacedaemonians. And while the ephors and those in authority were intending to send envoys to Syracuse to prevent them from coming to terms with the Athenians, but were not eager to send help, Alcibiades came forward and roused and stirred up the Lacedaemonians, speaking as follows.
‘I must first speak to you about the prejudice against me, so that you may not, through suspicion of me, listen less favourably to what concerns the common interest.

When my ancestors had renounced their proxeny for you because of some grievance, I myself took it up again and paid court to you in various ways and especially in connection with your disaster at Pylos. And while I continued zealous, you, in making your peace with the Athenians, procured power for my enemies through their agency, and brought dishonour upon me.

And for this reason you were justly harmed by me when I turned to the side of the Mantineans and Argives and in whatever else I opposed you; and now, if anyone was then unreasonably angry with me while he was suffering, let him look at it in the light of the truth and change his mind. Or if anyone thought worse of me because I inclined rather to the people's side, let him not think that in this way either he is right to be offended.

For we have always been opposed to tyrants (and everything that is opposed to absolute power is called the people), and from that the leadership of the multitude has remained with us. And at the same time, as the city was a democracy, it was necessary in most things to conform to the existing conditions.

But we tried to be more moderate in politics than the prevailing licence. But there were others, both in the past and now, who led the mob on to worse things; and they are the very men who drove me out.

But we were leaders of the whole people, thinking it right to help preserve the form of government in which the city happened to be greatest and freest and which one had received, since as for democracy, those of us who had any sense knew it for what it was, and I myself no worse than anyone, inasmuch as I could even rail at it. But nothing new could be said about acknowledged folly; and to change it did not seem safe to us while you, our enemies, were close at hand.
‘So much for the charges against me; but now learn about the matters on which you must deliberate and on which I, if I know anything more, must advise you.
We sailed to Sicily, first, if we could, to subdue the Siceliots, and after them the Italiots in turn, and then to make an attempt on the empire of the Carthaginians and on Carthage itself.

And if these plans succeeded, either wholly or for the most part, we were then going to attack the Peloponnese, bringing with us the whole force of the Hellenes there that had been added to us, and having hired many barbarians, Iberians and others of the barbarians there who are now admittedly the most warlike, and having built many triremes in addition to our own, since Italy has timber in abundance; and with these, blockading the Peloponnese all round, and at the same time with our infantry attacking from the land, taking some of the cities by storm and walling in others, we hoped easily to defeat them in war and after that to rule over the whole Hellenic world as well.
And money and corn, so that some of these plans might be more easily carried out, the places acquired there were themselves going to provide in sufficient quantity, without the revenue from here.

Such, concerning the expedition that has now gone, you have heard from the man who knows most exactly what we intended; and the generals who remain will, if they can, carry it out in the same way. And now learn how affairs there will not survive unless you help.

For the Siceliots are rather inexperienced, but nevertheless, if they united in a body, they might even now still prevail; but the Syracusans alone, already defeated in battle with their whole force and at the same time hemmed in by ships, will be unable to hold out against the armament of the Athenians now there.
And if this city is taken, the whole of Sicily is held too, and at once Italy as well; and the danger from there which I just foretold would fall upon you before long.

So let no one think that he is deliberating only about Sicily, but also about the Peloponnese, unless you do the following quickly: send to that place an army on ships of such a kind that the men will row themselves there and serve as hoplites at once, and, what I consider still more useful than the army, a Spartan man as commander, so that he may organise those who are there and compel those who are unwilling; for in this way your existing friends will be more confident and those who are wavering will come over with less fear.

And at the same time you must make war more openly here, so that the Syracusans, thinking that you care for them, may hold out better, and the Athenians may be less able to send further help to their own men.

And you must fortify Decelea in Attica, which is the thing the Athenians have always feared most, and the only one of the hardships in war that they think they have not experienced. And one would most surely harm one's enemies in this way, if, perceiving what they most fear, one learned it clearly and brought it upon them; for it is likely that they, each knowing most exactly their own dangers, fear them.

And of the advantages that you yourselves will gain by the fortification and will deprive the enemy of, I shall pass over many and sum up the greatest. For the things with which the country is stocked will for the most part come to you, some captured, others of their own accord; and they will at once be deprived of the revenues of the silver mines of Laurium and of all the profits they now get from the land and from the law-courts, and above all of the revenue from the allies, which will be less regularly paid, since they, thinking that the war on your side is now being waged in full force, will slight them.

And whether any of these things is done both quickly and with greater zeal rests with you, Lacedaemonians, since that they are possible (and I do not think I shall be mistaken in my judgement) I am quite confident.

‘And I claim that I should not seem worse to any of you if I, who once was thought to love my city, now attack it with all my might together with its bitterest enemies, nor that my words should be suspected as coming from an exile's eagerness.

For I am an exile from the wickedness of those who drove me out, and not, if you listen to me, from service to you; and the worse enemies are not you, who have harmed your enemies somewhere, but those who have forced their friends to become enemies.

And the love of my city I do not have where I am wronged, but where I lived as a citizen in security. Nor do I think that I am now going against a country that is still mine, but much rather that I am recovering one that is no longer mine. And the true lover of his city is not the man who, having unjustly lost his own, does not attack it, but the man who, because of his longing for it, tries by every means to recover it.

So I ask you, Lacedaemonians, to make use of me without hesitation for every danger and every hardship, recognising this saying put forward by everyone, that if as an enemy I did you great harm, I might also as a friend help you sufficiently, inasmuch as I know the affairs of the Athenians, while I could only guess at yours; and I ask you, considering that you are now deliberating about matters of the very greatest importance, not to shrink from the expedition both to Sicily and to Attica, so that by being present there with a small part of your force you may save great interests and destroy both the present and the future power of the Athenians, and after this may yourselves live in safety and lead the whole of Hellas, which will follow willingly and not by force, but out of goodwill.’

Alcibiades said this much, and the Lacedaemonians, who had themselves been intending even before to march against Athens, but were still delaying and looking about them, were much more strengthened when he gave them detailed information on each of these points, thinking that they had heard it from the man who knew most clearly;

so that they now turned their attention to the fortification of Decelea and to sending some help immediately to those in Sicily as well. And appointing Gylippus son of Cleandridas as commander for the Syracusans, they told him to consult with them and the Corinthians and to act so that some help might come to those there in the best and quickest way possible in the circumstances.

And he told the Corinthians to send him two ships at once to Asine, and to prepare the rest, as many as they intended to send, and to be ready to sail when the time came. And having agreed on this, they departed from Lacedaemon.

And the Athenian trireme from Sicily arrived too, which the generals had sent for money and horsemen. And the Athenians, having heard them, voted to send the maintenance for the army and the horsemen. And the winter ended, and the seventeenth year ended of this war which Thucydides wrote.

At the very beginning of spring in the following summer the Athenians in Sicily set out from Catana and sailed along the coast to Megara in Sicily, whose inhabitants the Syracusans had expelled in the time of Gelon the tyrant, as has also been told by me before, and they themselves hold the land.

And landing, they laid waste the fields and, after going against a fort of the Syracusans and failing to take it, they went along again both by land and by sea to the river Terias, and going up into the plain they laid it waste and set fire to the corn, and falling in with some of the Syracusans, not many, they killed some of them and set up a trophy and withdrew to their ships.

And sailing back to Catana and taking in provisions there, they went with their whole army against Centoripa, a town of the Sicels, and having brought it over by agreement they went away, burning at the same time the corn of the Inessaeans and the Hyblaeans.

And arriving at Catana they find the horsemen who had come from Athens, two hundred and fifty, without their horses but with their equipment, as horses were to be procured there, and thirty mounted archers and three hundred talents of silver.

In the same spring the Lacedaemonians also marched against Argos and came as far as Cleonae, but when an earthquake occurred they went back. And after this the Argives invaded the Thyreatis, which borders on their land, and took much plunder from the Lacedaemonians, which was sold for not less than twenty-five talents.

And in the same summer, not long afterwards, the people of Thespiae attacked those who held the offices but did not succeed, and when the Thebans came to the rescue some were arrested and others fled to Athens.

And in the same summer the Syracusans, when they learned that the horsemen had come to the Athenians and that they were already about to march against them, thinking that, unless the Athenians got control of Epipolae, a steep place lying directly above the city, they could not easily be walled off, not even if they were defeated in battle, intended to guard the approaches to it, so that the enemy might not go up by these unnoticed; for they could not do so at any other point.
For the rest of the place is steep, and as far as the city it slopes down and is all visible from within; and because it lies on top of the rest it has been named Epipolae by the Syracusans.

And they went out in full force at daybreak to the meadow beside the river Anapus (for Hermocrates and his fellow generals had just taken over their command), held a review of arms, and first picked out six hundred chosen men of the hoplites, commanded by Diomilus, an exile from Andros, so that they might be guards of Epipolae and, if they were needed for anything else, might quickly be on hand together.

But the Athenians, on the day following this night, while the Syracusans were holding their review, had already, unnoticed by them, put in with their whole army from Catana at the place called Leon, which is six or seven stades from Epipolae, and had landed the infantry, and anchored with their ships at Thapsus; it is a peninsula jutting out into the sea on a narrow isthmus, and it is not far from the city of the Syracusans either by sea or by land.

And the naval force of the Athenians, having fenced off the isthmus with a stockade at Thapsus, remained quiet; but the infantry went at once at a run towards Epipolae and gets up by Euryelus before the Syracusans, perceiving it, came up from the meadow and the review.
And they came to the rescue, the others as fast as each could, and the six hundred with Diomilus; and the distance from the meadow before they engaged was for them not less than twenty-five stades.

So attacking them in this way in rather disorderly fashion and being defeated in battle on Epipolae, the Syracusans withdrew into the city; and Diomilus is killed and about three hundred of the others.

And after this the Athenians, having set up a trophy and given back the dead to the Syracusans under a truce, went down on the next day towards the city itself, and when they did not come out against them, they withdrew and built a fort at Labdalum, on the edge of the cliffs of Epipolae, looking towards Megara, so that it might be a storehouse for their baggage and money whenever they advanced either to fight or to build walls.

And not long afterwards there came to them three hundred horsemen from Egesta and about a hundred of the Sicels and Naxians and some others; and the Athenians already had two hundred and fifty, for whom they got horses, some from the Egestaeans and Catanaeans, while others they bought, and altogether six hundred and fifty horsemen were assembled.

And having placed a garrison in Labdalum, the Athenians advanced to Syca, where they took up position and quickly built the circle wall. And they caused consternation to the Syracusans by the speed of their building; and they went out and intended to give battle and not to look on.

And when the armies were already drawn up against each other, the generals of the Syracusans, seeing that their army was scattered and not easily formed into line, led it back again into the city, except for a part of the horsemen; and these, remaining, prevented the Athenians from carrying stones and from dispersing too far.
And one tribe of the Athenian hoplites and all the horsemen with them charged and routed the Syracusan horsemen, and they killed some of them and set up a trophy for the cavalry battle.

And on the next day some of the Athenians were building the wall of the circle on the north side, while others, collecting stones and timber, kept laying them along towards the place called Trogilus, where the wall of circumvallation from the great harbour to the other sea would be shortest for them.

But the Syracusans, at the suggestion above all of Hermocrates among their generals, no longer wished to risk battles with their whole force against the Athenians, but it seemed better to build a counter-wall where the Athenians were going to carry their wall, and, if they were first, the Athenians would be cut off, and at the same time, if the Athenians came against them while they were doing this, to send part of their army against them and themselves to be first in occupying the approaches with the stockade, while the Athenians would stop their work and all turn against them.
So they went out and began building from their own city, carrying a cross wall below the circle of the Athenians, cutting down the olive trees of the sacred precinct and setting up wooden towers.

The ships of the Athenians had not yet sailed round from Thapsus into the great harbour, but the Syracusans were still masters of the coast, and the Athenians brought in their provisions by land from Thapsus.

And when the Syracusans thought that what had been staked and built of the counter-wall was sufficient, and the Athenians had not come to hinder them, fearing that the Syracusans might fight them more easily when they were divided, and at the same time hastening on with their own circumvallation, the Syracusans left one tribe to guard the construction and withdrew into the city, while the Athenians destroyed their pipes, which had been laid underground to bring drinking water into the city, and, watching for the time when the rest of the Syracusans were in their tents at midday and some had even gone off into the city and those in the stockade were keeping careless guard, they placed in front three hundred picked men of their own and some chosen light troops, armed as hoplites, to run suddenly at full speed to the counter-wall, while the rest of the army, in two divisions, went one with one general towards the city, in case they should come out to help, and the other with the other general to the stockade by the postern gate.

And the three hundred attack and take the stockade; and its guards abandoned it and fled into the outwork round the Temenites. And the pursuers burst in with them, and once inside they were driven out again by force by the Syracusans, and some of the Argives and not many of the Athenians were killed there.
And the whole army, coming back, pulled down the counter-wall and tore up the stockade and carried off the stakes to their own camp and set up a trophy.

On the next day the Athenians, starting from the circle, began to fortify the cliff above the marsh, which on this side of Epipolae looks towards the great harbour, and where the wall of circumvallation would be shortest for them going down through the level ground and the marsh to the harbour.

And meanwhile the Syracusans also went out and again began a stockade, starting from the city, through the middle of the marsh, and at the same time dug a ditch alongside, so that it might not be possible for the Athenians to carry their wall down to the sea.

But the Athenians, when the part towards the cliff had been completed by them, attack the stockade and ditch of the Syracusans again, ordering the ships to sail round from Thapsus into the great harbour of the Syracusans, while they themselves, about dawn, went down from Epipolae into the level ground and, through the marsh, where it was clayey and firmest, laying doors and broad planks on it and walking across on them, at daybreak they take the stockade, except for a small part, and the ditch, and later they took what was left as well.

And a battle took place, and in it the Athenians were victorious. And of the Syracusans, those who held the right wing fled towards the city, and those on the left along the river. And the three hundred picked men of the Athenians, wishing to cut them off from crossing, hastened at a run to the bridge.

But the Syracusans, alarmed (for most of their horsemen were there too), close with these three hundred, and rout them and charge into the right wing of the Athenians; and as they fell upon it the first tribe of the wing was also thrown into panic.

Seeing this, Lamachus came to help from their own left wing with a few archers, taking the Argives with him, and after crossing a ditch and being isolated with a few of those who had crossed with him, he is killed himself and five or six of those with him. And the Syracusans at once quickly succeed in snatching these up and carrying them across the river to safety, and they themselves withdrew as the rest of the Athenian army was now coming up.

Meanwhile those of them who had at first fled to the city, when they saw this happening, themselves took courage again and from the city drew up against the Athenians opposite them, and they send a part of their force against the circle on Epipolae, thinking that they would take it undefended.

And they take and destroy the outwork of ten plethra, but Nicias prevented them from taking the circle itself; for he happened to have been left behind in it because of illness. For he ordered the servants to set fire to the engines and all the timber that had been thrown down in front of the wall, since he knew that through lack of men they would be unable to survive in any other way.

And so it turned out: for the Syracusans no longer came on because of the fire, but withdrew again. For help was already coming up to the circle from below, from the Athenians who had driven off the enemy there, and at the same time their ships were sailing down from Thapsus, as had been ordered, into the Great Harbour.

Seeing this, the men on the heights and the whole army of the Syracusans went off in haste into the city, thinking that with their present force they would no longer be able to prevent the building of the wall to the sea.

After this the Athenians set up a trophy, gave back their dead to the Syracusans under truce, and recovered the bodies of Lamachus and those who fell with him; and now that their whole armament was with them, both the fleet and the land force, starting from Epipolae and the cliffs they began to wall off the Syracusans with a double wall down to the sea.

Provisions for the army were brought in from all parts of Italy. Many of the Sicels too, who had earlier been waiting to see how things went, came as allies to the Athenians, and from Tyrrhenia three fifty-oared ships. And everything else was going forward for them in line with their hopes.

For the Syracusans no longer thought they could prevail by war, since no help had come to them even from the Peloponnese, and they were holding talks about terms both among themselves and with Nicias; for he alone now held the command, Lamachus being dead.

No decision was reached, but, as is natural with men in difficulties and more closely besieged than before, much was said both to him and still more within the city. For under their present misfortunes they had also come to some suspicion of one another, and they deposed the generals under whom these things had happened to them, as if they were being harmed by their bad luck or their treachery, and chose others in their place, Heraclides, Eucles and Tellias.

Meanwhile Gylippus the Lacedaemonian and the ships from Corinth were already off Leucas, wishing to bring help to Sicily in haste. And as the reports that kept reaching them were alarming and all false in the same way, saying that Syracuse had already been completely walled off, Gylippus no longer had any hope for Sicily, but wishing to save Italy, he himself and Pythen the Corinthian crossed the Ionian gulf to Tarentum as fast as possible with two Laconian and two Corinthian ships, while the Corinthians were to sail later, after manning two Leucadian and three Ambraciot ships in addition to their own ten.

Gylippus, after first going on an embassy from Tarentum to Thuria and renewing his father's citizenship there, and being unable to win them over, put out and sailed along the coast of Italy, and being caught by a wind off the Terinaean gulf, which blows hard there from a steady northerly quarter, he was carried out to sea, and after a very severe storm he reached Tarentum again; and hauling ashore the ships that had suffered most from the storm, he repaired them.

Nicias, hearing that he was sailing up, despised the small number of his ships, as the Thurians had also done, and thought they were sailing equipped more like pirates, and as yet took no precautions.

About the same time in this summer the Lacedaemonians too invaded Argos, they and their allies, and ravaged most of the land, and the Athenians came to the help of the Argives with thirty ships; these broke their treaty with the Lacedaemonians in the most open way.

For before this they had joined the Argives and Mantineans in the war by raids from Pylos and by landings around the rest of the Peloponnese rather than in Laconia, and though the Argives often urged them just to touch Laconia with their arms, ravage even the smallest part together with them, and go away, they refused; but now, under the command of Pythodorus, Laespodias and Demaratus, they landed at Epidaurus Limera, Prasiae and other places and ravaged the land, and so gave the Lacedaemonians at last a more plausible ground for defending themselves against the Athenians.
When the Athenians had withdrawn from Argos with their ships, and the Lacedaemonians too, the Argives invaded Phliasia, laid waste part of their land and killed some of them, and went back home.

Gylippus and Pythen, after repairing their ships, sailed along the coast from Tarentum to Epizephyrian Locri; and now learning more clearly that Syracuse was not yet completely walled off, but that it was still possible for men arriving with an army to get in by way of Epipolae, they deliberated whether they should keep Sicily on the right and risk sailing in, or keep it on the left, sail first to Himera, and taking on both the Himeraeans themselves and any other force they could persuade, go by land.

And they decided to sail to Himera, especially since the four Attic ships were not yet at Rhegium, which Nicias, hearing that they were at Locri, had sent out after all. Getting ahead of this guard, they crossed the strait, and after touching at Rhegium and Messana they reached Himera.

While there they persuaded the Himeraeans to join in the war, both to follow them themselves and to provide arms for those of the sailors from their ships who had none (for they had hauled their ships ashore at Himera), and they sent to the Selinuntians and told them to meet them with their whole force at a certain place.

The Geloans and some of the Sicels also promised to send them a force, not a large one; these were ready to come over with much more eagerness, both because Archonidas had recently died, who, as king of some of the Sicels in that region and a man of no small power, had been a friend of the Athenians, and because Gylippus seemed to have come from Lacedaemon full of zeal.

And Gylippus, taking of his own sailors and marines those that were armed, about seven hundred, Himeraean hoplites and light troops together a thousand, and a hundred horsemen, some light troops and horsemen of the Selinuntians, a few Geloans, and of the Sicels about a thousand in all, marched towards Syracuse;

meanwhile the Corinthians from Leucas were coming to help with the rest of their ships as fast as they could, and Gongylus, one of the Corinthian commanders, who set out last with a single ship, arrived first at Syracuse, though only a little before Gylippus, and finding them about to hold an assembly on ending the war, he prevented it and encouraged them, saying that still other ships were sailing up, and Gylippus son of Cleandridas as commander, sent by the Lacedaemonians.
And the Syracusans took heart and at once went out with their whole army to meet Gylippus; for they now learned that he was already near.

He, having taken Ietae, a fort of the Sicels, on his way, and drawn up his men as for battle, arrived at Epipolae; and going up by Euryelus, where the Athenians too had gone up at first, he advanced with the Syracusans against the wall of the Athenians.

He happened to arrive at the very moment when the Athenians had already completed a double wall of seven or eight stades to the Great Harbour, except for a short stretch towards the sea (this they were still building), while along the rest of the circle towards Trogilus on the other sea stones had already been laid down for the greater part, and some parts had been left half-finished, others fully finished. So near did Syracuse come to danger.

The Athenians, when Gylippus and the Syracusans suddenly came upon them, were thrown into confusion at first, but drew up in line.
