He grounded his arms nearby and sent a herald to them, saying that if they were willing to leave Sicily within five days, taking their own belongings, he was ready to make a truce.
They treated this with contempt and sent him away without any answer. And after this they made ready against each other as for battle.

And Gylippus, seeing the Syracusans in confusion and not easily forming in line, led his army back into the more open ground. And Nicias did not lead the Athenians against him, but kept still by their own wall. When Gylippus saw that they were not coming on, he led the army off to the height called Temenitis, and they camped there for the night.

The next day he led out the greater part of his army and drew it up facing the walls of the Athenians, so that they would not send help elsewhere, while he sent a detachment against the fort of Labdalum and took it, and killed all whom he captured in it; the place was not visible to the Athenians.
And on the same day a trireme of the Athenians that was lying in wait off the harbour was captured by the Syracusans.

After this the Syracusans and their allies began to build a single wall through Epipolae, starting from the city and running up towards the cross wall, so that the Athenians, if they could not stop it, would no longer be able to wall them off.
The Athenians had by now gone up to the heights, having finished the wall by the sea, and Gylippus (for part of the Athenians' wall was weak) took his army by night and advanced against it.

The Athenians (for they happened to be bivouacking outside) went out to meet him as soon as they noticed; and he, seeing this, quickly led his men back again. The Athenians built it up higher and guarded it themselves at that point, and now posted the rest of the allies along the rest of the fortification, where each were to keep guard.

Nicias decided to fortify the place called Plemmyrium; it is a headland opposite the city, which juts out and makes the mouth of the Great Harbour narrow, and if it were fortified, it seemed to him that bringing in supplies would be easier: for they would be lying in wait at a shorter distance from the harbour of the Syracusans, and would not, as now, have to put out from the far end of the harbour if the enemy made any move with their fleet. He was by now giving more attention to the war at sea, seeing that matters on land were now less hopeful for them, since Gylippus had come.
So he brought over an army and the ships and built three forts; and in them most of the baggage was stored, and the large transports and the fast ships were now moored there.

And so it was then for the first time that the crews began to suffer badly: for they had scarce water, and not from close by, and at the same time, whenever the sailors went out for firewood, they were cut down by the horsemen of the Syracusans, who were masters of the land; for a third of the Syracusan cavalry had been posted at the little town at the Olympieum because of the men at Plemmyrium, so that they would not come out to do damage.

Nicias also learned that the rest of the Corinthian ships were sailing up; and he sent twenty ships to watch for them, which had been ordered to lie in wait for them around Locri and Rhegium and the approach to Sicily.

Gylippus at the same time went on building the wall through Epipolae, using the stones that the Athenians had laid down beforehand for themselves, and at the same time kept leading out the Syracusans and the allies and drawing them up in front of the fortification; and the Athenians drew up against them.
When Gylippus thought the moment had come, he began the attack; and coming to close quarters they fought between the fortifications, where the Syracusan cavalry was of no use.

And when the Syracusans and their allies had been defeated and had taken up their dead under truce, and the Athenians had set up a trophy, Gylippus called the army together and said that the mistake had not been theirs but his own: for by drawing up his line too far inside the walls he had deprived them of the help of the cavalry and the javelin-men; now, therefore, he would lead them on again.

And he told them to bear in mind that in equipment they would be no worse off, and that in spirit it would be intolerable if they, Peloponnesians and Dorians, did not resolve to defeat Ionians and islanders and a motley rabble and drive them out of the country.

After this, when the moment came, he led them on again. Nicias and the Athenians, thinking that even if the enemy were unwilling to begin a battle, they themselves could not stand by and let the wall be built alongside theirs (for the enemy's wall had already all but passed the end of the Athenians' wall, and if it went further, it would then be all the same for them whether they fought and won every time or did not fight at all), went out against the Syracusans.

And Gylippus led his hoplites further out beyond the walls than before and engaged them, posting his horsemen and javelin-men on the flank of the Athenians in the open space where the works of both walls came to an end.

And in the battle the horsemen charged the left wing of the Athenians, which was opposite them, and routed it; and because of this the rest of the army too was defeated by the Syracusans and driven headlong into the fortifications.

And the following night they got ahead by building their wall alongside and past the Athenians' building, so that they themselves could no longer be hindered by them, and had completely deprived the Athenians, even if they won, of any chance of still walling them off.

After this the remaining twelve ships of the Corinthians, Ambraciots and Leucadians sailed in, slipping past the Athenian guard (Erasinides, a Corinthian, commanded them), and helped the Syracusans build the rest of the wall as far as the cross wall.

And Gylippus went off into the rest of Sicily to raise an army, both naval and land forces, and at the same time to win over any of the cities that either was not eager or had so far kept entirely out of the war.

Other envoys of the Syracusans and Corinthians were sent to Lacedaemon and Corinth, so that a further army might be brought over in whatever way it could, in merchant ships or boats or any other way that might work, since the Athenians too were sending for reinforcements.
The Syracusans were manning a fleet and making trials, intending to try their hand at this too, and in other respects they were greatly encouraged.

Nicias, perceiving this and seeing the strength of the enemy and his own difficulties growing day by day, himself also sent to Athens, as he had often done at other times, reporting on everything that happened, but especially now, thinking that they were in danger and that, unless they recalled them as quickly as possible or sent out others in no small numbers, there was no safety.

But fearing that the men he sent, either through inability to speak or through failing memory or by saying something to please the crowd, might not report the facts, he wrote a letter, thinking that in this way above all the Athenians would learn his own opinion, with nothing of it lost in the messenger, and would deliberate about the truth.
And the men he sent went off carrying the letter and what they had to say; and he looked after the affairs of the camp, now relying more on guarding it than on taking risks of his own accord.

At the end of the same summer Euetion too, an Athenian general, campaigned with Perdiccas against Amphipolis with many Thracians, and did not take the city, but bringing triremes round into the Strymon he besieged it from the river, using Himeraeum as his base. And the summer ended.

In the following winter the men from Nicias came to Athens, said what they had been told to say by word of mouth, answered any questions that anyone asked, and delivered the letter. The clerk of the city came forward and read it to the Athenians; it ran as follows.
‘Our earlier actions, Athenians, you know from many other letters; but now it is time for you to learn our present situation no less and to deliberate.

For when we had defeated in most of the battles the Syracusans against whom we were sent, and had built the walls in which we now are, Gylippus, a Lacedaemonian, came with an army from the Peloponnese and from some of the cities in Sicily. In the first battle he was defeated by us, but on the next day, forced back by many horsemen and javelin-men, we withdrew within the walls.

So now, because of the number of our opponents, we have stopped the circumvallation and are keeping quiet (for we could not use our whole army either, since guarding the walls has taken up part of our hoplite force); and they have built a single wall alongside ours, so that it is no longer possible to wall them in, unless someone attacks this counter-wall with a large army and takes it.
And it has turned out that we, who seem to be besieging others, are rather suffering this ourselves, at least on land; for we cannot even go far out into the country because of the horsemen.

‘They have also sent envoys to the Peloponnese for another army, and Gylippus has gone to the cities in Sicily, to persuade those that are now keeping quiet to join in the war, and from the others to bring yet more land forces and naval equipment, if he can.
For they intend, as I learn, to make an attempt on our walls with their land forces and at the same time with their ships by sea.

And let none of you think it strange that they will do so by sea too. For our navy, as they too are learning, was at first in its prime, both in the dryness of the ships and in the soundness of the crews; but now the ships are waterlogged from having been at sea so long already, and the crews have been ruined.
For it is not possible to haul the ships ashore and dry them out, because the enemy's ships, being equal to ours in number and even more, keep us always expecting that they will sail against us.
They can be seen making trials, and the initiative lies with them, and they have more opportunity to dry out their own ships; for they are not blockading others.

We could hardly have this even with a great surplus of ships, and if we were not forced as now to keep guard with all of them; for if we take away even a little from our watch, we shall not have our supplies, since even now we bring them in with difficulty past their city.

Our crews have been ruined and are still being ruined for this reason: of the sailors, some are being killed by the horsemen while gathering firewood, foraging and fetching water from far off; the servants, since we have been reduced to an even fight, are deserting, and of the foreigners, those who were pressed on board go off at once to their cities, while those who were at first attracted by high pay and thought they would make money rather than fight, now that against their expectation they see a navy and everything else on the enemy's side standing up to us, either leave on the pretext of desertion or as each one can (and Sicily is large), and there are some who, trading on their own account, have persuaded the trierarchs to take Hyccaric slaves on board in their place, and so have destroyed the precision of our navy.
I am writing to you who know that the prime of a crew is short, and that few of the sailors are able to get a ship under way and keep the rowing together.

Of all this the most baffling thing is that I, the general, cannot prevent these things (for your natures are hard to command), and that we have nowhere from which to fill up the crews of our ships, which the enemy can do from many places, but both what we have and what we lose must necessarily come from what we brought with us; for the cities that are now our allies, Naxos and Catana, are powerless.

And if one more thing goes the enemy's way, so that the places in Italy that feed us, seeing the state we are in and that you are not coming to help, go over to them, [the war] will be fought out for them without a battle, with us starved into surrender.

‘I could have sent you other news more pleasant than this, but certainly not more useful, if you must deliberate knowing clearly how things stand here. And at the same time, knowing your natures, that you wish to hear what is most pleasant but blame people afterwards if anything turns out for you differently from that, I thought it safer to reveal the truth.

And now, regarding what we came for in the first place, take the view that neither the soldiers nor the commanders have deserved your blame; but since all Sicily is uniting and another army from the Peloponnese is expected by them, deliberate at once in the knowledge that the forces here are not a match even for the present enemy, but that you must either recall them or send out another army, no smaller, both land and naval, and no little money, and for me a successor, since I am unable to stay on because of a disease of the kidneys.

I think I deserve to receive your indulgence; for when I was in health I did you much good service in my commands. Whatever you intend to do, do it at once at the start of spring and without delays, since the enemy will provide what they get from Sicily within a short time, and what comes from the Peloponnese more slowly, but still, if you do not pay attention, some of it will escape your notice, as before, and some will get here first.’

This was what the letter of Nicias set out, and the Athenians, when they had heard it, did not relieve Nicias of his command, but until other colleagues chosen for him should arrive, they appointed two of the men there with him, Menander and Euthydemus, so that he would not bear the hardship alone in his sickness, and they voted to send another army, both naval and land, of Athenians from the muster-roll and of the allies.

And they chose as his colleagues Demosthenes son of Alcisthenes and Eurymedon son of Thucles. And they sent Eurymedon off to Sicily at once, around the winter solstice, with ten ships, bringing 〈a hundred and〉 twenty talents of silver, and at the same time to announce to the men there that help would come and that they would be cared for;
Demosthenes stayed behind and prepared the expedition, intending to sail at the start of spring, calling for troops from the allies and getting ready money, ships and hoplites at home.
The Athenians also sent twenty ships round the Peloponnese, to make sure that no one crossed from Corinth and the Peloponnese to Sicily.

For the Corinthians, when the envoys came to them and reported that matters in Sicily were improving, thinking that they had not been wrong to send the earlier ships either, took much more heart, and prepared to send hoplites to Sicily in merchant ships themselves, while the Lacedaemonians were to send some from the rest of the Peloponnese in the same way;

and the Corinthians manned twenty-five ships, to try a sea battle against the squadron at Naupactus, and so that the Athenians at Naupactus would be less able to stop their merchant ships from putting out, having to keep watch against the line of triremes drawn up against them.

The Lacedaemonians were also preparing their invasion of Attica, as they had decided before, and with the Syracusans and Corinthians urging them on, since they were learning of the Athenians' help for Sicily, so that it might be stopped by an invasion. And Alcibiades kept pressing them and advising them to fortify Decelea and not to slacken the war.

But above all the Lacedaemonians had gained a certain confidence because they thought that the Athenians, having a double war, against them and against the Sicilian Greeks, would be easier to overthrow, and because they considered that the Athenians had been the first to break the treaty; for in the earlier war the breach of law had been rather theirs, both because the Thebans had come into Plataea during a truce, and because, though it had been stated in the earlier agreement that no one should take up arms if the other side was willing to submit to arbitration, they themselves had not listened when the Athenians called on them to go to arbitration. And for this reason they thought that their misfortunes were deserved, and they took to heart the disaster at Pylos and any other that had befallen them.

But when the Athenians, setting out from Argos with their thirty ships, had ravaged part of Epidaurus and Prasiae and other places, and at the same time were raiding from Pylos, and whenever disputes arose about any of the points contested under the treaty, they refused to submit to arbitration when the Lacedaemonians called on them to do so, then at last the Lacedaemonians, thinking that the breach of law that had earlier been their own fault had now in turn come round to the Athenians, were eager for the war.

And during this winter they sent round to their allies for iron and got ready the other tools for the fortification, and at the same time, intending to send help to the men in Sicily in the merchant ships, they provided it themselves and compelled the other Peloponnesians to do so too. And the winter ended, and the eighteenth year of this war, of which Thucydides wrote the history, ended.

At the very beginning of the following spring, earlier than ever before, the Lacedaemonians and their allies invaded Attica; Agis son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, led them. And first they ravaged the parts of the country around the plain, then they began to fortify Decelea, dividing the work among the cities.

Decelea is about a hundred and twenty stades from the city of the Athenians, and about the same distance, not much more, from Boeotia. The fort was built to do harm to the plain and the richest parts of the country, and was visible all the way to the city of the Athenians.

While the Peloponnesians and their allies in Attica were building the fort, those in the Peloponnese were sending off the hoplites to Sicily in the merchant ships at about the same time, the Lacedaemonians picking out the best of the Helots and the neodamodes, about six hundred hoplites of both together, with Eccritus, a Spartiate, as commander, and the Boeotians three hundred hoplites, commanded by Xenon and Nicon, Thebans, and Hegesander, a Thespian.

These set out among the first from Taenarum in Laconia and put out to sea; after them, not much later, the Corinthians sent off five hundred hoplites, some from Corinth itself and some hired in addition from among the Arcadians, appointing Alexarchus, a Corinthian, as their commander. The Sicyonians too sent two hundred hoplites together with the Corinthians, commanded by Sargeus, a Sicyonian.

The twenty-five ships of the Corinthians that had been manned during the winter lay at anchor facing the twenty Attic ships at Naupactus, until these hoplites had got away from the Peloponnese in their merchant ships; it was for this purpose that they had been manned in the first place, so that the Athenians would pay attention to the triremes rather than to the merchant ships.

Meanwhile the Athenians too, at the same time as the fortification of Decelea and at the very beginning of spring, sent thirty ships round the Peloponnese with Charicles son of Apollodorus as commander, who had been ordered to go also to Argos and, under the alliance, call on the Argives for hoplites for the ships,

and they sent off Demosthenes to Sicily, as they had intended, with sixty Athenian ships and five Chian ones, twelve hundred Athenian hoplites from the muster-roll, and as many islanders as could be used from each place, having also gathered from the other subject allies anything they had that was useful for the war. He had been ordered first to sail round together with Charicles and join him in operations against Laconia.
And Demosthenes sailed to Aegina and waited there for any of the army that had been left behind, and for Charicles to pick up the Argives.
In Sicily, at about the same time this spring, Gylippus too came to Syracuse, bringing from the cities he had persuaded as large a force as he could get from each.
And calling the Syracusans together he said that they must man as many ships as they could and try a sea battle; for he hoped to achieve by it something for the war that would be worth the risk.

Hermocrates too joined in persuading them, not least, not to lose heart about attacking the Athenians with their ships, saying that the Athenians too did not have their experience of the sea from their fathers or from all time, but had been landsmen even more than the Syracusans and had been forced by the Medes to become seamen. And against daring men, such as the Athenians were, those who dared in return would seem most formidable [to them]; for the very means by which the Athenians terrify their neighbours, not by being superior in strength at times, but by attacking with boldness, they themselves could use in the same way against their opponents.

And he said he knew well that the Syracusans, by daring unexpectedly to stand up to the Athenian navy, would gain more through the Athenians being taken aback by such a thing than the Athenians would harm the Syracusans' inexperience by their skill. So he urged them to go and make trial of their navy and not to hold back.
And the Syracusans, with Gylippus and Hermocrates and anyone else urging them, were eager for the sea battle and began manning their ships;

and when Gylippus had got the fleet ready, he led out the whole land army at nightfall and was himself about to attack the forts at Plemmyrium by land, while at the same time and at a signal the triremes of the Syracusans sailed out, thirty-five from the Great Harbour, and the forty-five from the smaller one, where their dockyard also was, [and] sailed round, wishing to join those inside and at the same time to sail against Plemmyrium, so that the Athenians would be thrown into confusion on both sides.

The Athenians quickly manned sixty ships against them, and with twenty-five of them fought the thirty-five ships of the Syracusans in the Great Harbour, while with the rest they went to meet those sailing round from the dockyard. And they fought at once in front of the mouth of the Great Harbour, and held out against each other for a long time, the one side wishing to force the entrance, the other to prevent it.

Meanwhile Gylippus, when the Athenians at Plemmyrium had gone down to the sea and were giving their attention to the sea battle, got in first by falling suddenly on the forts at dawn, and took the largest first, and then the two smaller ones as well, since the guards did not stand their ground when they saw the largest easily taken.

From the first fort that was captured, the men who took refuge in the boats and a merchant ship got away to the camp with difficulty; for while the Syracusans were winning the sea battle with their ships in the Great Harbour, they were pursued by a single fast-sailing trireme; but when the two forts were being taken, by then the Syracusans happened to be already losing, and the men fleeing from them sailed past more easily.

For the Syracusan ships fighting in front of the mouth, having forced back the Athenian ships, were sailing in without any order, and falling foul of one another they handed the victory to the Athenians; for they routed both these and those by which they had at first been beaten in the harbour.

And they sank eleven ships of the Syracusans and killed most of the men, except those from three ships whom they took alive; of their own, three ships were destroyed. Hauling up the wrecks of the Syracusans and setting up a trophy on the islet in front of Plemmyrium, they went back to their own camp.

Such was the outcome of the sea battle for the Syracusans, but they held the forts at Plemmyrium, and set up three trophies for them. And one of the two forts taken last they demolished, while the other two they repaired and garrisoned.

Many men were killed or taken alive in the capture of the forts, and a great deal of property was taken in all; for since the Athenians used the forts as a storehouse, there was much property of merchants and grain in them, and much belonging to the trierarchs too, since the sails of forty triremes and the rest of their gear were captured there, and three triremes that had been hauled ashore.

The capture of Plemmyrium was the greatest and the first among the things that damaged the army of the Athenians; for not even the entrances for bringing in supplies were safe any longer (for the Syracusans blockaded them with ships stationed there, and the convoys now took place only by fighting), and in other respects too it caused dismay and despondency in the army.

After this the Syracusans sent out twelve ships with Agatharchus, a Syracusan, in command of them. And one of them went to the Peloponnese, carrying envoys who were to explain that their own affairs were hopeful and to urge that the war there be pushed on even more; the eleven ships sailed to Italy, having learned that boats full of goods were sailing to the Athenians.
And falling in with the boats they destroyed most of them, and burned timber for shipbuilding in the territory of Caulonia, which was ready for the Athenians.
After this they went to Locri, and while they were lying at anchor there one of the merchant ships from the Peloponnese sailed in, carrying Thespian hoplites;

and the Syracusans took them on board their ships and sailed along the coast for home. The Athenians watched for them with twenty ships near Megara and took one ship, crew and all, but could not take the others, and these escaped to Syracuse.

There was also skirmishing in the harbour about the stakes which the Syracusans had driven into the sea in front of the old ship-sheds, so that their ships might lie at anchor inside them and the Athenians might not sail up and harm them by ramming.

For the Athenians brought up against them a ship of ten thousand talents' burden, which had wooden towers and screens, and from boats they tied ropes to the stakes and winched them up and broke them off, and diving down they sawed them through. The Syracusans shot at them from the ship-sheds; and the men on the merchant ship shot back, and in the end the Athenians removed most of the stakes.

The most troublesome part of the palisade was the hidden part; for there were some of the stakes which they had driven in so that they did not rise above the water, so that it was dangerous to sail up, for fear that someone, not seeing them in advance, might run his ship on them as on a reef. But divers went down and sawed off these too for pay. Still, the Syracusans drove in stakes again.
And they devised many other things against each other, as was natural with the armies being close and facing each other, and they made use of skirmishes and attempts of every kind.

The Syracusans also sent envoys, Corinthians, Ambraciots and Lacedaemonians, to the cities, to report the capture of Plemmyrium and to say about the sea battle that they had been defeated not by the strength of the enemy so much as by their own confusion, and to make clear [in turn] that in other respects they were hopeful, and to ask them to come to their help with both ships and land forces, since the Athenians too were expected with another army, and if they themselves managed first to destroy the army the Athenians had there, the war would be finished. And the people in Sicily were doing these things.

Demosthenes, when the army had been gathered that he was to take to help in Sicily, set out from Aegina, sailed to the Peloponnese and joined Charicles and the thirty ships of the Athenians, and taking Argive hoplites on board their ships, they sailed to Laconia;

and first they ravaged part of Epidaurus Limera, then, putting in at the coast of Laconia opposite Cythera, where the temple of Apollo is, they ravaged parts of the land and fortified a place like an isthmus, so that the Helots of the Lacedaemonians might desert to it, and at the same time raiders might make plundering expeditions from it, as from Pylos.

And Demosthenes, as soon as he had helped to occupy the place, sailed along to Corcyra, so that he might pick up allies there too and make the voyage to Sicily as quickly as possible; Charicles waited until he had finished fortifying the place, and leaving a garrison in it he himself went back home later with the thirty ships, and the Argives at the same time.
In this same summer there also came to Athens thirteen hundred peltasts of the sword-bearing Thracians of the Dian tribe, who were to sail with Demosthenes to Sicily.

The Athenians, since they had come too late, intended to send them back to Thrace, where they had come from. For keeping them for the war from Decelea seemed expensive; for each man received a drachma a day.

For since Decelea, after being first fortified by the whole army during this summer, and later occupied as a threat to the country by garrisons from the cities coming in succession at intervals, was doing the Athenians much harm, and was among the chief things that ruined their affairs, by destruction of property and loss of men.

For before, the invasions were short and did not prevent them from enjoying the land for the rest of the time; but now, with the enemy constantly sitting on them, and sometimes with larger forces attacking, and at other times with the regular garrison necessarily overrunning the country and making raids, and with the king of the Lacedaemonians, Agis, present, who was making war in no half-hearted way, the Athenians suffered great harm.

For they had been deprived of the whole of their land, and more than twenty thousand slaves had deserted, a large part of them craftsmen, and all their sheep and beasts of burden had been lost; and of the horses, since the horsemen rode out every day, making forays towards Decelea and keeping guard over the country, some went lame from the hard ground and constant toil, and others were wounded.

The transport of supplies from Euboea, which had earlier gone more quickly by land from Oropus through Decelea, now went round Sunium by sea at great cost; and the city needed everything alike to be imported, and instead of being a city it had become a fortress.

For the Athenians, keeping guard on the battlements by turns during the day, and at night all of them except the horsemen, some at the arms-posts † on duty †, others on the wall, were worn out summer and winter.

What pressed them most was that they had two wars at once, and they had come to such a pitch of rivalry that no one would have believed it if he had heard of it before it happened. For that they, while being besieged by the Peloponnesians with a fort in their own land, should not even so withdraw from Sicily, but should there in the same way besiege in turn Syracuse, a city in itself no smaller than that of the Athenians, and should cause the Greeks so great a surprise at their power and daring, given that at the beginning of the war some thought they would hold out for a year, some for two, and none for more than three years, if the Peloponnesians invaded their country, so that in the seventeenth year after the first invasion they went to Sicily, already worn down by the war in every way, and took on a war no smaller than the one they already had with the Peloponnese.

For these reasons, and because Decelea was then doing them great harm and other great expenses fell upon them, they became short of money. And about this time they imposed on their subjects, instead of the tribute, a tax of one twentieth on goods carried by sea, thinking that more money would come in to them in this way. For their expenses were not the same as before, but had become much greater, as the war too was greater; while their revenues were being lost.

So, not wishing to spend money on the Thracians who had come too late for Demosthenes, because of their present shortage of money, they sent them back at once, ordering Diitrephes to take them home and telling him at the same time on the voyage along the coast (for they were going through the Euripus) to do the enemy any harm he could with them.
He landed them at Tanagra and made a quick raid for plunder, and from Chalcis in Euboea in the evening crossed the Euripus, and landing them in Boeotia, led them against Mycalessus.

During the night he bivouacked unnoticed near the Hermaeum (it is about sixteen stades from Mycalessus), and at daybreak he attacked the city, which is not large, and took it, falling on the people when they were off their guard and did not expect that anyone would ever come up so far from the sea to attack them, since the wall was weak and in some places had even fallen down, and in others was built low, and the gates were also open because they felt secure.

The Thracians burst into Mycalessus and sacked the houses and the temples and slaughtered the people, sparing neither old nor young, but killing everyone in turn whom they met, both children and women, and besides even the beasts of burden and every other living thing they saw; for the race of the Thracians, like the most bloodthirsty of the barbarians, is most murderous whenever it feels secure.

And then there was great confusion of every other kind and every form of destruction, and falling upon a boys' school, the largest in the place, which the boys had just entered, they cut them all down; and this disaster fell upon the whole city, a disaster inferior to none, and more than any other unexpected and terrible.

The Thebans, learning of it, came to help, and catching up with the Thracians when they had not yet gone far, they took the plunder away from them and, putting them to flight, pursued them to the Euripus and the sea, where the boats that had brought them were moored.

And they killed most of them as they were getting on board, since they did not know how to swim and the men in the boats, when they saw what was happening on land, had anchored the boats out of bowshot, since in the rest of the retreat the Thracians defended themselves quite skilfully against the Theban cavalry, which attacked first, running out ahead and closing their ranks again in their native formation, and few of them were killed in this part. A number were also caught in the city itself because of plundering and perished. In all two hundred and fifty of the Thracians were killed out of thirteen hundred.

They killed of the Thebans and the others who came to help about twenty horsemen and hoplites together, and of the Thebans Scirphondas, one of the Boeotarchs; and a part of the Mycalessians was wiped out. Such was what happened to Mycalessus, which suffered a calamity that, for its size, was less to be lamented than none in the war.

Demosthenes, sailing off at that time towards Corcyra after the fortification on the Laconian coast, found a merchant ship lying at Pheia in Elis, in which the Corinthian hoplites were to cross to Sicily, and destroyed it, but the men escaped and later took another one and sailed.

After this Demosthenes came to Zacynthus and Cephallenia, took on hoplites, sent for some of the Messenians from Naupactus, and crossed to the opposite mainland of Acarnania, to Alyzia and Anactorium, which the Athenians themselves held.

While he was engaged in this, Eurymedon met him, sailing back from Sicily, who had been sent out during the winter with the money for the army, and reported among other things that he had learned, when already on his voyage, that Plemmyrium had been taken by the Syracusans.

Conon too, who commanded at Naupactus, came to them, reporting that the twenty-five Corinthian ships lying at anchor opposite them were not giving up the war and were about to fight a sea battle; so he urged them to send ships, since their own eighteen were not enough to fight against the twenty-five of the enemy.

So Demosthenes and Eurymedon sent with Conon ten ships, the best sailers of those they had, to join those at Naupactus; and they themselves made preparations for the gathering of the army, Eurymedon sailing to Corcyra, telling the Corcyraeans to man fifteen ships and enlisting hoplites (for he was now sharing the command with Demosthenes, having turned back, as he had been chosen to do), and Demosthenes collecting slingers and javelin-men from the places around Acarnania.

The envoys who had gone from Syracuse to the cities at that time, after the capture of Plemmyrium, had persuaded them and, having gathered the army, were about to bring it, when Nicias, learning of it beforehand, sent to those of the Sicels who controlled the route and were his allies, the Centoripans, the Halicyaeans and others, asking them not to let the enemy through, but to unite and prevent them from passing; for they would not even try another way; for the Acragantines were not granting them a passage through their territory.

When the Sicilian Greeks were already on the march, the Sicels, as the Athenians had asked, laid an ambush in three places, and falling on them suddenly while they were off their guard, killed about eight hundred of them and all the envoys except one, the Corinthian; and he brought those who escaped, about fifteen hundred, to Syracuse.

About the same days the Camarinaeans too arrived to help them, five hundred hoplites, three hundred javelin-men and three hundred archers. The Geloans also sent a naval force of about five ships, four hundred javelin-men and two hundred horsemen.

For by now almost the whole of Sicily, except the Acragantines (and these were not on either side), but the others, who had earlier been waiting to see how things went, had joined together with the Syracusans and were helping them against the Athenians.

The Syracusans, after the disaster among the Sicels had befallen them, held back from attacking the Athenians at once; and Demosthenes and Eurymedon, the army from Corcyra and from the mainland being now ready, crossed the Ionian gulf with the whole army to the Iapygian promontory;

and setting out from there they put in at the Choerades islands of Iapygia, and took on board their ships some javelin-men of the Iapygians, a hundred and fifty of the Messapian tribe, and having renewed an old friendship with Artas, who as their ruler had provided them with the javelin-men, they came to Metapontum in Italy.

And having persuaded the Metapontines, under their alliance, to send with them three hundred javelin-men and two triremes, they took these on and sailed along the coast to Thuria. And they found that the opponents of the Athenians had recently been expelled in a revolution;

and wishing to gather the whole army there and review it, in case anyone had been left behind, and to persuade the Thurians to join their campaign as eagerly as possible and, since they were in this state of fortune, to regard the same people as enemies and friends as the Athenians did, they waited in Thuria and worked at this.

About this same time the Peloponnesians in the twenty-five ships, who were lying at anchor opposite the ships at Naupactus to cover the convoy of merchant ships to Sicily, got ready as for a sea battle, and manning still more ships, so that they had only slightly fewer than the Attic ships, they anchored off Erineus in Achaea, in the territory of Rhypes.

And since the place where they lay at anchor was crescent-shaped, the land forces of the Corinthians and of the allies from there, who had come to help, were drawn up on either side on the headlands jutting out, and the ships held the space between, closing it off; Polyanthes, a Corinthian, commanded the fleet.
The Athenians sailed against them from Naupactus with thirty-three ships (Diphilus commanded them).

The Corinthians at first kept still, then, when the signal was raised for them, since the moment seemed to have come, they rushed against the Athenians and engaged them. And they held out against each other for a long time.

Three ships of the Corinthians were destroyed, while of the Athenians not one was sunk outright, but some seven were disabled, struck prow to prow and having their outriggers smashed by the Corinthian ships, which had thicker catheads for this very purpose.

After fighting an even battle, such that each side claimed the victory, though the Athenians got possession of the wrecks because the wind drove them out to sea and because the Corinthians did not put out again, they separated from each other, and there was no pursuit, and no men were taken on either side; for the Corinthians and Peloponnesians, fighting close to the land, easily got to safety, and of the Athenians not one ship was sunk.

When the Athenians had sailed away to Naupactus, the Corinthians at once set up a trophy as victors, because they had disabled more of the enemy's ships, and thinking that they were not beaten for the very reason that the others were not victorious; for the Corinthians considered that they were winning if they were not badly beaten, while the Athenians thought they were beaten because they had not won by much.

When the Peloponnesians had sailed away and their land force had dispersed, the Athenians also set up a trophy in Achaea as victors, about twenty stades from Erineus, where the Corinthians had been anchored. And so the sea battle ended.

Demosthenes and Eurymedon, when the Thurians had got ready to join their campaign with seven hundred hoplites and three hundred javelin-men, ordered the ships to sail along the coast to the territory of Croton, while they themselves first reviewed the whole land force at the river Sybaris and then led it through the territory of Thuria.

And when they reached the river Hylias and the Crotoniates sent to them and said that they would not be willing for the army to go through their land, they went down and camped by the sea at the mouth of the Hylias; and their ships met them at the same place. The next day they embarked and sailed along the coast, putting in at the cities except Locri, until they reached Petra in the territory of Rhegium.

Meanwhile the Syracusans, learning of their approach, wished to make another attempt with their ships and with the rest of their land force, which they had been gathering for this very purpose, wishing to strike before they arrived.

They equipped the rest of their fleet in the way they had seen from the earlier sea battle would give them some advantage, and cutting down the prows of their ships to a shorter length they made them more solid, and put thick catheads on the prows, and fixed stays from these to the ships' sides, about six cubits long, inside and outside; in the same way as the Corinthians had refitted their ships at the prow before fighting the ships at Naupactus.

For the Syracusans thought that against the ships of the Athenians, which were not built in the same way but were light at the prow because they used their rams not so much prow to prow as after sailing round, they would not have the worse, and that the sea battle in the Great Harbour, with many ships in a small space, would be in their favour; for by ramming prow to prow they would smash the Athenians' bows, striking hollow and weak bows with solid and thick rams.

And the Athenians would have neither room to sail round nor to break through their line in the narrow space, the manoeuvres in which they most trusted their skill; for they themselves would, as far as possible, not allow them to break through, and the narrow space would prevent them from sailing round.

And what had earlier seemed to be a lack of skill in their helmsmen, ramming prow to prow, they themselves would make the most use of; for in it they would have the greatest advantage: for the Athenians, when pushed back, would have no room to back water except towards the land, and that only for a short way and into a small space, right by their own camp; while they themselves would control the rest of the harbour, and the Athenians, if they were hard pressed anywhere, crowding together

into a small space and all into the same place, would fall foul of one another and be thrown into confusion (which was in fact what harmed the Athenians most in all the sea battles, since they did not have the whole harbour to back water in, as the Syracusans did); and they would not be able to sail round into the open water, since the Syracusans would control the approach from the open sea and the backing away, especially as Plemmyrium would be hostile to them and the mouth of the harbour was not wide.

Having devised such plans to suit their own skill and strength, and being at the same time more confident now after the earlier sea battle, the Syracusans attacked with their land force and their ships at once.

Gylippus led out the land force from the city a little earlier and brought it up to the wall of the Athenians, at the part of it that faced the city; and the men from the Olympieum, the hoplites who were there and the horsemen and the light troops of the Syracusans, approached the wall from the other side; and immediately after this the ships of the Syracusans and their allies sailed out.

And the Athenians, who had at first thought that they would make an attempt with the land force alone, were thrown into confusion when they saw the ships too suddenly bearing down on them, and some took up position on the walls and in front of the walls against the attackers, others went out against the many horsemen and javelin-men advancing quickly from the Olympieum and the outer parts, and others manned the ships and at the same time ran to help along the shore, and when the ships were manned, they put out seventy-five ships against them; and the Syracusans had about eighty.

For much of the day they sailed up and backed away and tested each other, and neither side could achieve anything worth mentioning, except that the Syracusans sank one or two ships of the Athenians, and then they separated; and at the same time the land force withdrew from the walls.

The next day the Syracusans kept quiet, giving no sign of what they would do next; but Nicias, seeing that the sea battle had been evenly matched and expecting them to attack again, compelled the trierarchs to repair their ships, if any had suffered damage, and moored merchant ships in front of their own palisade, which they had driven into the sea in front of their ships instead of a closed harbour.

He placed the merchant ships about two plethra apart from each other, so that if any ship were hard pressed, there would be a safe refuge and a way out again at leisure. The Athenians spent the whole day until nightfall making these preparations.
On the next day the Syracusans engaged the Athenians earlier in the day, but with the same kind of attack by land and sea,

and taking position opposite them with their ships, they again spent much of the day in the same way testing each other, until Ariston son of Pyrrhichus, a Corinthian, the best helmsman on the Syracusan side, persuaded the commanders of their fleet to send to the officials in the city and tell them to move the market of things for sale down to the sea as quickly as possible, and to compel everyone to bring whatever food he had there and sell it, so that they could land the sailors and have them take their meal at once beside the ships, and after a short while attack the Athenians again on the same day when they were not expecting it.
They were persuaded and sent a messenger, and the market was got ready, and the Syracusans suddenly backed water, sailed back to the city, and landing at once took their meal on the spot;

and the Athenians, thinking that they had withdrawn to the city because they had been beaten by them, landed at their leisure and saw to their other business and to their meal, thinking that at least on that day they would not fight a sea battle again.

But suddenly the Syracusans manned their ships and sailed against them again; and they, in great confusion and most of them without having eaten, embarked in no order and with difficulty put out against them.

For some time they held off from each other, keeping on their guard; then the Athenians decided not to let themselves be worn out by their own delay, but to attack as quickly as possible, and charging with a cheer they engaged.

The Syracusans received them, and using their ships prow to prow, as they had planned, with the build of their rams they smashed in the bows of the Athenian ships over a large part of their outriggers, and the javelin-men on their decks did the Athenians great harm, and still much greater harm was done by the Syracusans who sailed round in small boats, slipping in under the oar-banks of the enemy ships and sailing along their sides and hurling javelins from them at the sailors.
In the end, fighting hard in this way, the Syracusans won, and the Athenians turned and fled between the merchant ships to their own anchorage.
The Syracusan ships pursued them as far as the merchant ships; then the yards hung with dolphins, raised from the merchant ships over the passages, stopped them.
Two ships of the Syracusans, carried away by the victory, came close to them and were destroyed, and one of them was taken with its crew.

The Syracusans, having sunk seven ships of the Athenians and damaged many, and having taken most of the men alive and killed others, withdrew, and they set up trophies for both sea battles, and they now had a firm hope that they were far superior with their ships, and they thought they would master the land force too.

And while they were preparing to attack again on both fronts, meanwhile Demosthenes and Eurymedon arrived with the reinforcements from Athens, about seventy-three ships including the foreign ones, about five thousand hoplites of their own and of the allies, no small number of javelin-men, barbarian and Greek, and slingers and archers and the rest of the equipment in good supply.

And for the moment the Syracusans and their allies were thrown into no small dismay, wondering whether there would ever be any end to their deliverance from danger, seeing that, in spite of the fortification of Decelea, an army equal to and like the first had come against them no less, and that the power of the Athenians appeared great everywhere; while the first army of the Athenians had regained a certain strength, as far as was possible after their misfortunes.

Demosthenes, seeing how matters stood, and thinking that it was not possible to delay and to suffer what Nicias had suffered (for Nicias, who was formidable when he first arrived, when he did not at once attack Syracuse but spent the winter at Catana, came to be despised, and Gylippus got in ahead of him by arriving from the Peloponnese with an army, which the Syracusans would not even have sent for if he had attacked at once; for thinking themselves strong enough, they would have learned at the same time that they were weaker and would have been walled off, so that even if they had sent for it, it would no longer have helped them in the same way), considering this, then, Demosthenes, and recognising that he himself too was at this moment, on the first day, most formidable to the enemy, wished to make use as quickly as possible of the present dismay of their army.

And seeing that the counter-wall of the Syracusans, with which they had prevented the Athenians from walling them in, was a single one, and that if one gained control of the ascent to Epipolae and then of the camp on it, it would easily be taken (for none of them would stand their ground),

he hurried to make the attempt, and he thought this would be the quickest way to end the war; for either he would succeed and take Syracuse, or he would lead the army away and not wear out to no purpose the Athenians serving in the expedition and the whole city.

So first the Athenians went out and ravaged the land of the Syracusans around the Anapus, and they had the upper hand with their army as at first, both by land and with their ships (for the Syracusans did not come out against them on either front, except with the horsemen and javelin-men from the Olympieum);

Then Demosthenes decided first to try the counter-wall with siege engines. But when he brought them up and the engines were burned by the enemy defending themselves from the wall, and when they attacked with the rest of the army at many points and were beaten back, he decided to delay no longer, but having persuaded Nicias and his other colleagues, he made the attack on Epipolae as he had planned.

It seemed impossible to approach and make the ascent unnoticed by day, so he gave orders for five days' provisions, took all the stonemasons and carpenters and other equipment, arrows and everything they would need to have for building walls if they won, and himself, at the first sleep, with Eurymedon and Menander, took the whole army and marched towards Epipolae, while Nicias was left behind in the walls.

And when they reached it at Euryelus, where the earlier army too had first gone up, they escaped the notice of the Syracusan guards, and going up to the fort of the Syracusans that was there they took it and killed some of the guards.

But most of them escaped at once to the camps, of which there were three on Epipolae in outworks, one of the Syracusans, one of the other Sicilian Greeks, and one of the allies, and they reported the attack and told the six hundred Syracusans, who were also the first guards on this part of Epipolae.

These came to help at once, and Demosthenes and the Athenians, meeting them, routed them though they defended themselves eagerly. And they themselves at once pressed forward, so that they would not be slow, with the present impetus, in accomplishing what they had come for; while others from the first contingent took the counter-wall of the Syracusans, since the guards did not stand their ground, and began to tear down the battlements.

The Syracusans and their allies and Gylippus and his men came to help from the outworks, and as the bold stroke had come upon them unexpectedly at night, they attacked the Athenians in a state of alarm, and being forced back by them they at first gave way.

But as the Athenians advanced now in greater disorder, as if they had won, and wished to pass as quickly as possible through all the part of the enemy that had not yet fought, so that they would not rally again if they themselves slackened the attack, the Boeotians were the first to stand up to them, and charging them they routed them and put them to flight.

And here the Athenians now fell into great confusion and difficulty, of which it was not easy to learn, even from either side, in what way each thing happened. For by day things are clearer, but even so those who are present hardly know everything, except each what happened near himself; but in a night battle, which was the only one between great armies in this war at least, how could anyone know anything clearly?

For there was a bright moon, but they saw one another only as one naturally does by moonlight, seeing the form of a body ahead but not trusting the recognition of a friend. And hoplites of both sides, in no small numbers, were moving about in a narrow space.

And of the Athenians some were already being defeated, while others were still advancing unbeaten from the first attack. And of the rest of their army a large part had just come up, and part was still coming up, so that they did not know which way to go. For in front, since the rout had happened, everything was already in confusion and it was hard to make anything out because of the shouting.

For the Syracusans and their allies, as victors, were cheering one another on with no small outcry, since it was impossible at night to give signals in any other way, and at the same time they were receiving those who charged them; and the Athenians were looking for one another and thought everything coming from the opposite direction hostile, even if it was friendly and belonged to those already fleeing back, and by constantly asking for the watchword, because there was no other way of recognising one another, they caused much confusion among themselves, all asking at once, and made it known to the enemy;

but they did not learn the enemy's watchword in the same way, because these, being victorious and not scattered, were less difficult to recognise, so that if they met any of the enemy while being stronger than them, these escaped them, since they knew their watchword, while if they themselves did not answer, they were killed.

What harmed them most, and not least, was the singing of the paean; for being very similar on both sides, it caused perplexity. For whenever the Argives and the Corcyraeans and all the Dorian contingent with the Athenians sang the paean, it caused alarm to the Athenians, and the enemy did so likewise.

So that in the end, once they had been thrown into confusion, they ran into one another at many points of the army, friends against friends and citizens against citizens, and not only fell into panic but even came to blows with one another and were separated only with difficulty.

And being pursued, many perished throwing themselves down the cliffs, since the way back down from Epipolae was narrow, and when those who escaped from above came down into the level ground, most of them, and all who belonged to the earlier army, escaped to the camp because they knew the country better, but of those who had come later there were some who missed the roads and wandered about the country; and these, when day came, the horsemen of the Syracusans rode round and killed.
The next day the Syracusans set up two trophies, one on Epipolae where the ascent was and one at the place where the Boeotians first made a stand, and the Athenians took up their dead under truce.

No small number of them and of their allies were killed, but still more arms were taken than in proportion to the dead; for those who were forced to leap down the cliffs, lightly equipped [without their shields], some perished and others were saved.

After this the Syracusans, encouraged again by their unexpected success, as they had been before, sent Sicanus with fifteen ships to Acragas, which was in a state of faction, to bring the city over if he could; and Gylippus went off again by land into the rest of Sicily, to bring yet more troops, in the hope of taking even the walls of the Athenians by force, since matters on Epipolae had turned out as they had.

Meanwhile the generals of the Athenians took counsel in view of the disaster that had happened and the general weakness now in the camp. For they saw that they were not succeeding in their attempts and that the soldiers were weary of staying;

for they were suffering from sickness for two reasons, both because this was the season of the year in which men are most liable to illness, and at the same time because the place in which they were encamped was marshy and unhealthy, and because everything else seemed hopeless to them.

So Demosthenes thought they should no longer stay, but, in line with the plan with which he had risked the attack on Epipolae, now that it had failed, he voted to leave and not to delay, while it was still possible to cross the sea and, with the ships that had joined them at least, to have the upper hand over the enemy's force.

And he said that it was more useful for the city to wage war against those who were building forts in their country than against the Syracusans, whom it was no longer easy to subdue; nor was it reasonable, either, to go on besieging them spending a great deal of money to no purpose.

Such was the view of Demosthenes; Nicias too thought that their situation was bad, but he did not want to reveal its weakness in words, nor that they should openly vote for the withdrawal in a large council and so have it reported to the enemy; for they would be much less likely to escape notice when they wished to do this.

And to some extent the enemy's affairs too, which he understood better than the others, still gave some hope that they would turn out worse than their own, if they persevered with the siege; for they would wear the enemy out through shortage of money, especially as they were now more fully masters of the sea with the ships they had. And since there was also a party in Syracuse that wished to hand matters over to the Athenians, it kept sending messages to him and would not let him withdraw.

Knowing this, he in fact still held back, wavering between the two courses and considering, but in his open speech at that time he said he would not lead the army away. For he knew well that the Athenians would not accept this from them, if they left without the Athenians themselves having voted for it. For those who would vote about them would not be men who saw the facts as they themselves did and would not judge them after hearing the criticism of others, but they would be persuaded by whatever slanders some clever speaker might make.

And of the soldiers present, he said, many, indeed most, who now cried out that they were in a terrible plight, would on arriving there cry out the opposite, that the generals had been bribed to betray them and had come away. He himself, at any rate, knowing the nature of the Athenians, did not wish to be put to death by the Athenians on a shameful charge and unjustly, rather than, if he must, to run the risk and suffer this fate at the hands of the enemy on his own account.

And the affairs of the Syracusans, he said, were even so still worse than their own; for, maintaining mercenaries with their money and at the same time spending on guard-posts and having now kept a large navy for a year already, they were partly in difficulty already and would partly be at a loss; for they had already spent two thousand talents and owed many more besides, and if they lost even any part whatever of their present force through not giving it pay, their affairs would be ruined, being mercenary rather than, like their own, compulsory.
They ought therefore, he said, to wear them down by staying on before the city, and not to go away beaten by money, in which they were far superior.

Nicias spoke so positively in saying all this because he knew the state of things in Syracuse accurately, both their lack of money and that there was a large party there that wished the state to fall to the Athenians and kept sending messages to him not to withdraw; and at the same time he was more confident than before of prevailing, at least with his ships.

But Demosthenes would not in any way accept staying on in the siege; but if they must not lead the army away without a decree of the Athenians, but wear the war out there, he said they ought to do this after removing either to Thapsus or to Catana, from where with their land army they could overrun much of the country and support themselves by plundering the property of the enemy and so harm them, and with their ships they would fight their battles in the open sea and not in a narrow space, which was more in favour of the enemy, but in wide waters, in which the advantages of their experience would be useful to them, and they would have room for retreats and attacks without setting out from and putting in to a short and circumscribed space.

And to put the whole in a word, he said that it in no way pleased him to remain any longer in the same place, but to remove now as quickly as possible and not delay. And Eurymedon spoke in support of him in this.

But as Nicias spoke against it, a certain hesitation and delay arose, and at the same time a suspicion that Nicias might be so positive because he knew something more. And so the Athenians in this way delayed and stayed where they were.

Meanwhile Gylippus and Sicanus arrived at Syracuse, Sicanus having failed to gain Acragas (for while he was still at Gela the party friendly to the Syracusans had been driven out); but Gylippus came with another large army from Sicily and with the hoplites sent out from the Peloponnese in the spring in the merchant ships, who had arrived at Selinus from Libya.

For they had been carried away to Libya, and after the Cyrenaeans had given them two triremes and pilots for the voyage, and on their way along the coast they had fought as allies of the Euesperitae, who were being besieged by the Libyans, and had defeated the Libyans, and from there had sailed along the coast to Neapolis, a Carthaginian trading-post, from which Sicily is nearest, a voyage of two days and a night away, and from there they had crossed over and arrived at Selinus.

And the Syracusans, as soon as they arrived, prepared to attack the Athenians again on both elements, with ships and with infantry; but the generals of the Athenians, seeing that another army had joined the enemy and that their own affairs at the same time were not going towards the better, but were growing daily worse in every respect, and above all were oppressed by the sickness of the men, repented that they had not removed earlier, and since not even Nicias opposed them as much any longer, except by asking that it should at least not be put openly to the vote, they gave notice to all, as secretly as they could, of a sailing out from the camp, and to be ready whenever the signal was given.

And when they were about to sail away, since all was ready, the moon was eclipsed; for it happened to be full moon. And most of the Athenians, taking it to heart, urged the generals to wait, and Nicias (for he was somewhat too much given to divination and the like) said that he would not even deliberate any further about how they might move until they had waited thrice nine days, as the soothsayers prescribed. And so for the Athenians, having delayed for this reason, the staying on had come about.

And the Syracusans too, learning of this, were far more roused not to let the Athenians alone, since these themselves had already confessed that they were no longer superior to them either with their ships or with their infantry (for otherwise they would not have planned the sailing out), and at the same time not wishing them to settle somewhere else in Sicily and become harder to make war on, but rather to force them to fight at sea there, as quickly as possible and in a place that suited themselves.

So they manned their ships and practised for as many days as seemed sufficient to them. And when the moment came, on the first day they attacked the walls of the Athenians, and when a small part both of the hoplites and of the horsemen came out against them by certain gates, they cut off some of the hoplites and, routing them, pursued them; and as the entrance was narrow, the Athenians lost seventy horses and not many of the hoplites.

And on this day the army of the Syracusans withdrew; but on the next day they sailed out with their ships, seventy-six in number, and at the same time advanced with their infantry against the walls. The Athenians put out against them with eighty-six ships, and closing with them fought at sea.

And Eurymedon, who held the right wing of the Athenians and wished to surround the ships of the enemy and was extending his line in his course more towards the land, the Syracusans and their allies, after first defeating the centre of the Athenians, cut off as well in the hollow and recess of the harbour, and they destroyed both him and the ships that followed with him; and then they also pursued all the ships of the Athenians and drove them ashore.

And Gylippus, seeing the ships of the enemy being defeated and carried ashore outside the stockades and their own camp, and wishing to destroy the men as they landed and that the Syracusans might more easily tow the ships off the shore, as it was friendly, came to help at the causeway with part of the army.

And the Tyrrhenians (for these were keeping guard for the Athenians at this point), seeing them advancing in disorder, came out against them and, falling on the first, routed them and drove them into the marsh called Lysimeleia.

But later, when a larger part of the army of the Syracusans and allies was already present, the Athenians too, coming to help and fearing for their ships, joined battle with them and, having defeated them, pursued them and killed not many hoplites, and as for the ships, they saved most of them and brought them together at the camp, but eighteen of them the Syracusans and their allies took, and killed all the men.

And wishing to burn the rest too, they filled an old merchant ship with brushwood and pine-wood (for the wind was blowing fair towards the Athenians) and let [the ship] go after throwing fire into it. And the Athenians, fearing for their ships, devised in turn means of quenching and stopping it, and having put an end to the flame and to the merchant ship's coming near, they got clear of the danger.

After this the Syracusans set up a trophy both for the sea-battle and for the cutting off of the hoplites up at the wall, where they also took the horses, and the Athenians for the rout of the infantry that the Tyrrhenians drove into the marsh and for the one they themselves made with the rest of the army.

Now that the victory of the Syracusans had become brilliant at sea too (for before they had feared the ships that had come with Demosthenes), the Athenians were in utter despondency, and their disappointment was great, but much greater still their regret for the expedition.

For these were the only cities they had yet attacked that were similar in character to their own, governed by democracies, as they themselves were, and possessing ships and horses and size, and as they were unable to bring in any element of discord among them, either through a change of government, by which they might have been won over, or through a much superior force, but failed in most things, they were at a loss even before this, and when they were beaten even with their ships, which they would never have expected, much more so still.
The Syracusans at once sailed along the harbour without fear and planned to close its mouth, so that the Athenians might no longer, even if they wished, sail out without their notice.

For they were no longer concerned only with saving themselves, but also with how they might prevent the Athenians, thinking, as was the case, that from the present situation their affairs were far superior, and that, if they could defeat the Athenians and their allies both by land and by sea, the achievement would appear a glorious one for them in the eyes of the Hellenes; for of the other Hellenes some would at once be set free and others released from fear (for the remaining power of the Athenians would no longer be able to bear the war that would afterwards be brought against it), and they themselves, being thought the authors of this, would be greatly admired both by the rest of mankind and by posterity.

And the contest was indeed worth it, both for these reasons and because they were getting the better not only of the Athenians but also of their many other allies, and again not by themselves alone, but also together with those who had come to help them, having become leaders together with the Corinthians and Lacedaemonians and having offered their own city to bear the brunt of the danger and having advanced their navy a great part of the way.
For the greatest number of peoples came together against this one city, except at least for the whole number that in this war gathered round the city of the Athenians and that of the Lacedaemonians.

For so many peoples on each side made war at Syracuse, coming against Sicily and on behalf of Sicily, some to help conquer the land, others to help save it, standing with one another not so much according to right or according to kinship, but as the circumstances befell each, either from interest or from necessity.

The Athenians themselves, Ionians, went willingly against the Syracusans, who were Dorians, and with them, still using the same speech and customs, the Lemnians and Imbrians and the Aeginetans, who then held Aegina, and also the Hestiaeans, who lived at Hestiaea in Euboea, being colonists, joined the campaign.
Of the others, some served as subjects, some as independent allies, and there were also some who served as mercenaries.

And of the subjects and tribute-payers there were the Eretrians and Chalcidians and Styrians and Carystians from Euboea, from the islands the Ceans and Andrians and Tenians, and from Ionia the Milesians and Samians and Chians. Of these the Chians, not being tribute-payers but providing ships, followed as independent allies. And these were all for the most part Ionians and descended from the Athenians, except the Carystians (these are Dryopes), and though they were subjects and under compulsion, still they were Ionians at least following against Dorians.

Besides them there were Aeolians, the Methymnaeans, subjects bound to provide ships and not tribute, and the Tenedians and Aenians, tribute-payers. These Aeolians fought under compulsion against Aeolians, their founders, the Boeotians 〈who were〉 with the Syracusans, but the Plataeans alone, Boeotians directly against Boeotians, did so naturally, from hatred.

The Rhodians and Cytherians were both Dorians; the Cytherians, colonists of the Lacedaemonians, bore arms with the Athenians against the Lacedaemonians who were with Gylippus, and the Rhodians, Argives by descent, were forced to make war on the Syracusans, who were Dorians, and on the Geloans, who were even their own colonists and were serving with the Syracusans.

And of the islanders around the Peloponnese, the Cephallenians and Zacynthians followed as independent allies, yet were rather constrained by their island position, because the Athenians controlled the sea; and the Corcyraeans, not only Dorians but plainly Corinthians, followed against the Corinthians and Syracusans, though they were colonists of the one and kinsmen of the other, under compulsion as a decent pretext, but by choice from their hatred of the Corinthians no less.

And those now called Messenians were taken into the war from Naupactus and from Pylos, which was then held by the Athenians. And also a few exiles of the Megarians, by a misfortune, fought against the Selinuntines, who were Megarians.

For the rest, the campaign was now rather voluntary. For the Argives followed, Dorians against Dorians with the Ionian Athenians, not so much for the sake of the alliance as from hatred of the Lacedaemonians and for the immediate private advantage of each, and the Mantineans and other Arcadian mercenaries, accustomed to go against whoever was pointed out to them at any time as enemies, and now for gain regarding the Arcadians who had come with the Corinthians as enemies no less, and the Cretans and Aetolians, these too persuaded by pay; and it happened that the Cretans, who had founded Gela together with the Rhodians, came willingly for pay not with their colonists but against their colonists.
And some of the Acarnanians came to help, partly for gain, but more from friendship for Demosthenes and goodwill towards the Athenians, being their allies.

And these were bounded by the Ionian Gulf; of the Italiots the Thurians and Metapontines served with them, caught at that time in such necessities of revolutionary times, and of the Siceliots the Naxians and Catanians, and of the barbarians the Egestaeans, who had called them in, and most of the Sicels, and of those outside Sicily some of the Tyrrhenians, because of their quarrel with the Syracusans, and Iapygian mercenaries. So many peoples served with the Athenians.

On the other side, the Syracusans were helped by the Camarinaeans, who were their neighbours, and the Geloans, who lived next to them, and then, as the Acragantines remained neutral, by the Selinuntines, settled beyond them.

And these inhabit the part of Sicily facing Libya, and the Himeraeans came from the part towards the Tyrrhenian sea, in which they are also the only Hellenes living; and these alone came to help from there.

And of the Hellenes in Sicily so many peoples, Dorians and all independent, fought with them, and of the barbarians only the Sicels who had not gone over to the Athenians; and of the Hellenes outside Sicily the Lacedaemonians, providing a Spartan commander, and for the rest Neodamodes and Helots [Neodamodes means men already free], and the Corinthians, the only ones who came both with ships and with infantry, and the Leucadians and Ambraciots because of kinship, and from Arcadia mercenaries sent by the Corinthians, and Sicyonians serving under compulsion, and of those outside the Peloponnese the Boeotians.

But compared with these who came from outside, the Siceliots themselves provided a greater number in every arm, as they inhabited great cities; for many hoplites and ships and horses and an abundant other crowd were gathered. And again, compared with all the others, so to speak, the Syracusans themselves provided more, because of the size of their city and because they were in the greatest danger.
Such were the auxiliary forces gathered on each side, and by then all of them were present for both sides, and nothing more came to either afterwards.

So the Syracusans and their allies naturally thought it would be a glorious achievement for them, after the victory they had won in the sea-battle, both to capture the whole army of the Athenians, great as it was, and not to let them escape by either way, neither by sea nor by land.

So they at once began to close the Great Harbour, which has a mouth of about eight stades, mooring triremes broadside and boats and small craft at anchor, and they prepared everything else in case the Athenians should still dare to fight at sea, and they planned nothing small in any respect.
The Athenians, seeing the closing of the harbour and perceiving the rest of their plan, decided they must take counsel.

And the generals and the taxiarchs met and, in view of their present difficulty in other respects and because they no longer had provisions for the moment (for they had sent ahead to Catana, as they were going to sail away, and told them not to bring any) and were not going to have any in future unless they won control of the sea, they decided to abandon the upper walls, and close to the ships themselves to cut off with a cross-wall as small a space as possible, sufficient for the baggage and the sick, and guard this, and from the rest of the infantry to man all the ships, as many as there were, both the serviceable and the less seaworthy, putting every man on board, and to fight it out at sea, and if they won, to make their way to Catana, but if not, to burn their ships and, formed up together, to retreat by land in whatever direction they might soonest reach some friendly place, either barbarian or Hellenic.

And they, as they had decided this, so they did; for they came down gradually from the upper walls and manned all the ships, forcing to embark anyone who seemed in any way to be of age and fit for service.

And in all about one hundred and ten ships were manned; and they put on board many archers and javelin-men from the Acarnanians and the other foreigners, and they provided everything else as far as was possible from necessity and from such a plan.

And Nicias, when most things were ready, seeing the soldiers disheartened both by having been defeated at sea, contrary to their custom, and, because of the scarcity of provisions, wishing to risk a decisive battle as soon as possible, called them all together and first encouraged them and spoke as follows.

‘Soldiers of the Athenians and of the other allies, the coming contest will be common alike to all, for the safety and the country of each, no less than for the enemy; for if we now win with our ships, each can see his own native city again, wherever it may be.
