And you must not lose heart or suffer what the most inexperienced of men suffer, who, having failed in their first contests, afterwards keep their expectation of fear throughout like their misfortunes.

But as many of you as are present of the Athenians, being already experienced in many wars, and as many of the allies, who have always served with us, remember the surprises in wars, and prepare yourselves in the hope that fortune too may yet stand on our side, and as men who will renew the fight in a manner worthy of this great number which you see for yourselves.

‘And what we saw would help against the narrowness of the harbour, with regard to the crowd of ships there is going to be and to their forces on the decks, by which we were harmed before, all this has now been considered by us too with the helmsmen, as far as present means allow, and made ready.

For many archers and javelin-men will go on board, and a crowd which, if we were fighting a sea-battle in the open sea, we would not use, because it would hinder our skill by the weight of the ships, but in the land-battle from the ships that we are forced into here it will be useful.

And we have found out all that we must build in reply, and against the thickness of their cat-heads, by which indeed we were most harmed, grappling-irons, which will prevent the backing water of the ship that has rammed, if the marines do their part in this.

For we have indeed been forced to this, to fight on foot from the ships, and it seems advantageous neither to back water ourselves nor to let them do so, especially as the land, except for as much as our infantry holds, is hostile.

‘Remembering this, you must fight it out as far as you can and not be driven ashore, but when ship has struck ship, you must not think of separating before you have swept the hoplites off the enemy's deck.

And I urge this on the hoplites no less than on the sailors, inasmuch as this task belongs rather to those above; and we still have the advantage, at least now, of being superior for the most part with the infantry.

And the sailors I exhort, and in the same breath also beg, not to be too dismayed at all by the misfortunes, as you now have the equipment on the decks better and the ships more numerous, and to consider that pleasure, how worth preserving it is, you who, being until now considered Athenians, though you are not, were admired throughout Hellas for your knowledge of our speech and your imitation of our ways, and shared in our empire no less in its benefits, both in being feared by the subjects and in not being wronged, by far the more.

So, being the only free partners of our empire, do not now justly betray it, but, despising the Corinthians, whom you have often defeated, and the Siceliots, none of whom thought fit even to stand up against us while our navy was in its prime, ward them off, and show that even with weakness and misfortunes your skill is superior to another's strength that is enjoying good fortune.

And those of you who are Athenians I remind once again of this as well, that you have left behind no other ships like these in the docks, nor any hoplites of military age, and that if anything other than victory befalls you, the enemy here will at once sail against Athens, and those of us left there will be unable to ward off both their own enemies there and those who come against them. And you here would at once fall under the Syracusans, against whom you yourselves know with what intention you came, and those there under the Lacedaemonians.

So, standing in this one contest for both, hold out, if ever you did, and consider, each one of you and all together, that those of you who will now be in the ships are for the Athenians both their infantry and their ships and the rest of their city and the great name of Athens, for which, if anyone surpasses another in anything, either in skill or in courage, he could not show it at any other moment better, so as to be both useful to himself and a saviour to all.’

Nicias, having given this exhortation, at once ordered the ships to be manned. And Gylippus and the Syracusans could perceive, as they saw the very preparations, that the Athenians were going to fight at sea, and the throwing of the grappling-irons had also been reported to them beforehand,

and they made ready against this as well as against everything else, each in its own way; for they covered the prows and the upper part of the ship for a great distance with hides, so that the iron hand when thrown might slip off and have no hold.
And when everything was ready, the generals and Gylippus encouraged them and spoke as follows.

‘That what has been achieved before is glorious, and that the coming contest will be for glorious things to come, Syracusans and allies, most of you seem to us to know (for otherwise you would not have taken them up so eagerly), and if anyone has not perceived it as fully as he should, we will show him.

For the Athenians came to this country first for the enslavement of Sicily, and then, if they succeeded, also of the Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas, and though they possessed the greatest empire of the Hellenes of the past and of the present, you, the first of men to stand up against their navy, by which they had mastered everything, have already won some sea-battles, and in all likelihood you will win this one now.

For when men are cut short in that in which they claim to excel, what remains of their opinion of themselves is weaker than it would have been if they had never thought so at all, and, failing contrary to the expectation of their boasting, they give way even beyond the real strength of their power; which is likely to be what the Athenians have now suffered.

And with us, the advantage we had before, with which we ventured even while still unskilled, is now more secure, and since the belief has been added to it that we are the strongest if we have defeated the strongest, the hope of each man is doubled; and for the most part the greatest hope also brings the greatest eagerness for undertakings.

‘And as for their imitation of our equipment, it is familiar to our way of fighting, and we shall not be unprepared against each part of it; but they, when many hoplites are on their decks, contrary to their custom, and many javelin-men too, landsmen so to speak, Acarnanians and others, have gone on board the ships, who will not even find out how they must throw their missile while sitting, how will they not endanger their ships, and all be thrown into confusion among themselves, moving not in their own way?

For they will not be helped by the number of their ships either, if any of you is also afraid of this, that he will fight with unequal numbers; for many ships in a small space will be slower at doing anything they want, and easiest to be harmed by the means we have prepared.

And learn the very truth from what we think we have clearly found out; for, as their troubles are overwhelming them and they are hard pressed by their present difficulty, they have been reduced to desperation, to take a risk, trusting not so much in their equipment as in fortune, in whatever way they can, so that either they may force their way out and sail away, or after this make their retreat by land, since they could not fare worse than their present state.

So against such disorder and the fortune of our bitterest enemies, which has given itself up, let us close with anger, and let us consider both that it is most lawful against opponents for those who think it right, as a punishment for the aggressor, to satisfy the anger of their spirit, and at the same time that to take vengeance on enemies, which will be granted to us, is, as the saying goes, the sweetest thing.

And that they are enemies, and the worst of enemies, you all know, since they came against our land to enslave it, and in this, if they had succeeded, they would have inflicted the most painful things on the men, the most shameful on the children and women, and on the whole city the most disgraceful name.

Therefore no one should grow soft or think it a gain that they go away without danger. For this they will do equally even if they win; but if, as is likely, we achieve what we want, that these men should be punished and that we should hand over to all Sicily, which already enjoys it, a more secure freedom, the contest is a glorious one. And the rarest of risks are those which, if they fail, do the least harm, and if they succeed, bring the most benefit.’
And the generals of the Syracusans and Gylippus, having likewise exhorted their own soldiers in this way, at once manned their ships in turn, when they perceived that the Athenians too were doing so.

And Nicias, dismayed by the situation and seeing how great the danger was and how near it [was] already, since they were all but about to put out, and thinking, as happens in great contests, that in deed everything was still lacking to them and that in word enough had not yet been said to them, again called on each of the trierarchs one by one, naming them by their fathers' names and by their own names and their tribes, asking each one who had any distinction of his own not to betray it, and not to obscure the virtues of their fathers, for which their ancestors were famous, reminding them of their country, the freest of all, and of the unrestricted freedom for all in it to live as they pleased, and saying other things that men in such a crisis would say, not guarding against seeming to anyone to talk in an old-fashioned way, and appeals that are brought forward much the same on all occasions, about wives and children and ancestral gods, but which they cry out because they think them useful in the present terror.

And he, thinking he had given exhortations not so much sufficient as necessary, withdrew and led the infantry to the sea and drew them up along as great a length as he could, so that the greatest possible help might come to those in the ships in keeping up their courage;

and Demosthenes and Menander and Euthydemus (for these had gone on board the Athenian ships as generals) set out from their own camp and sailed straight for the barrier of the harbour and the passage left open in it, wishing to force their way out.

But the Syracusans and their allies, having put out before them with about the same number of ships as before, guarded with a part of them the way out and the rest of the harbour in a circle, so that they might fall on the Athenians from all sides at once, and their infantry at the same time came to help wherever the ships put in. And the fleet of the Syracusans was commanded by Sicanus and Agatharchus, each holding a wing of the whole, and by Pythen and the Corinthians in the centre.

And when the rest of the Athenians came up to the barrier, in the first charge of their attack they overcame the ships stationed at it and tried to break the fastenings; but after this, as the Syracusans and allies bore down on them from all sides, the sea-battle was no longer at the barrier only, but also throughout the harbour, and it was fierce and like none of the earlier ones.

For on each side there was great eagerness on the part of the sailors to attack whenever the order was given, and great was the contest of skill of the helmsmen and their rivalry with one another; and the marines took care, whenever ship struck ship, that the work on the deck should not fall short of the other skill; and every man, each in the post to which he had been assigned, was eager to be seen first.

And as many ships met in a small space (for indeed these were the most ships that ever fought in the smallest space; for both together fell little short of two hundred), the rammings were few, because there was no backing water or breaking through the line, but the collisions, as ship happened to fall on ship either in fleeing or in attacking another, were more frequent.

And as long as a ship was bearing down, the men on the decks used javelins and arrows and stones against it unsparingly; but when they closed, the marines, coming to close quarters, tried to board each other's ships.

And it happened in many places, because of the narrow space, that some had rammed others and had themselves been rammed, and that two ships, and sometimes even more, were of necessity entangled with one, and that the helmsmen had to deal with defence against some and attack on others, not one at a time but many from all sides, and that the great din from many ships crashing together caused both terror and the inability to hear what the boatswains called out.

For there was indeed much exhortation and shouting from the boatswains on each side, both in the way of their craft and from the eagerness of the moment for victory, crying out to the Athenians to force the way out and now, if ever again, to lay hold eagerly of their safe return to their country, and to the Syracusans and allies that it would be glorious to prevent them from escaping and, by winning, to exalt each his own country.

And the generals on each side besides, if they saw anyone anywhere backing water without necessity, called the trierarch by name and asked, the Athenians whether they were retreating because they thought the most hostile land more their own than the sea that had been won by no small toil, the Syracusans whether they themselves were fleeing from those who were fleeing, the Athenians, whom they clearly knew to be eager to escape in any way.

And the infantry of both sides on the land, while the sea-battle hung in the balance, had great anguish and conflict of mind, the native troops being eager now for still greater glory, and the invaders fearing that they might fare even worse than at present.

For as everything for the Athenians depended on their ships, their fear for the future was like nothing else, and because of the 〈unevenness〉 of the sea-battle they were forced to have an uneven view of it from the land too.

For as the sight was at close range and not all were looking at the same point at once, if some saw their own side winning anywhere, they would take heart and turn to calling on the gods not to deprive them of safety, while those who looked at a part that was being beaten broke out in lamentation together with shouting, and from the sight of what was being done were more enslaved in spirit than those in the action; and others, looking at some part of the sea-battle that was evenly balanced, because of the undecided continuance of the struggle, swaying in terror with their very bodies in time with their feelings, were in the most distressing state of all; for they were always just on the point of escaping or of perishing.

And in the same army of the Athenians, as long as they fought at sea on even terms, one could hear everything at once, lamentation, shouting, "we are winning," "we are beaten," and all the other various cries that a great army in great danger would be forced to utter.

And the men on board their ships suffered much the same, until at last the Syracusans and their allies, after the sea-battle had held out for a long time, routed the Athenians and, pressing on them brilliantly with much shouting and cheering each other on, chased them to the land.

And then the naval force, as many as had not been captured afloat, ran ashore, one here, one there, and rushed into the camp; and the infantry, no longer divided, but all with one impulse, with wailing and groaning, unable to bear what was happening, some ran to help at the ships, others to guard the rest of the wall, and others, the greater number, now began to look to themselves and how they would be saved.

And at that moment the panic was not less than any of all the others. And they had suffered much the same as they themselves had inflicted at Pylos; for when the ships of the Lacedaemonians were destroyed, the men who had crossed over to the island were also lost to them, and now for the Athenians there was no hope of being saved by land, unless something unexpected happened.

The sea-battle having been fierce and many ships and men having been lost on both sides, the Syracusans and their allies, being victorious, took up the wrecks and the dead, and sailed back to the city and set up a trophy,
but the Athenians, because of the greatness of their present troubles, did not even think of asking for the taking up of their dead or wrecks, but planned to retreat at once that night.

And Demosthenes went to Nicias and gave his opinion that they should man the rest of the ships once more and force the way out, if they could, at dawn, saying that the ships left that were serviceable were still more numerous for them than for the enemy; for the Athenians had about sixty remaining, and their opponents fewer than fifty.
And when Nicias agreed with the opinion and they wished to man the ships, the sailors refused to go on board, because they were dismayed by their defeat and no longer thought they could win.

And they had all now made up their minds to retreat by land, but Hermocrates the Syracusan, suspecting their intention and thinking it dangerous if so great an army, having retreated by land and settled somewhere in Sicily, should wish to make war on them again, went to those in authority and proposed that they ought not to allow them to withdraw by night, stating what he himself thought, but that all the Syracusans and their allies should now go out and wall off the roads and occupy beforehand and guard the narrow passes of the country.

And they themselves agreed with this no less than he, and thought it ought to be done, but they thought that the men, who had just gladly taken their rest after a great sea-battle and since it was also a festival (for it happened that there was a sacrifice to Heracles on that day), would not easily be willing to obey; for in their great joy at the victory most of them had turned to drinking at the festival, and they would expect them to obey them in anything rather than take up arms and go out at present.

And as these considerations made it appear impracticable to the magistrates and Hermocrates could no longer persuade them, he himself thereupon contrived the following, fearing that the Athenians might quietly get ahead of them by passing the most difficult places during the night. He sent some of his own companions with horsemen to the camp of the Athenians, when it was getting dark; and they, riding up to within earshot and calling out to some men as if they were friends of the Athenians (for there were some who brought reports to Nicias from inside), told them to tell Nicias not to lead the army away during the night, as the Syracusans were guarding the roads, but to prepare at his leisure and withdraw by day.
And having said this they went away, and those who had heard it reported it to the generals of the Athenians;

and they, on the strength of the message, waited for that night, thinking it was no deception. And since even so they had not set out at once, they decided to wait also for the following day, so that the soldiers might pack up the most useful things as well as possible, and to leave everything else behind and set out taking with them only what was necessary for their personal subsistence.

But the Syracusans and Gylippus, going out first with their infantry, blocked the roads through the country by which the Athenians were likely to go, and guarded the crossings of the streams and rivers, and posted themselves to receive the army and stop it where they thought best; and with their ships they sailed up and towed the ships of the Athenians away from the beach (a few of them the Athenians themselves had burnt, as they had intended), and the rest, at their leisure, with no one hindering, they made fast wherever each had been driven ashore and brought them to the city.
After this, when Nicias and Demosthenes thought they had made sufficient preparations, the removal of the army at last took place, on the third day after the sea-battle.

It was a terrible thing, then, not in one respect only of their affairs, that they were withdrawing after losing all their ships, and that instead of great hope they themselves and their city were in danger, but also in the abandonment of the camp it happened that each man saw things painful to the eye and to the mind.

For as the dead were unburied, whenever anyone saw one of his friends lying there, he was plunged into grief together with fear, and the living who were being left behind, the wounded and the sick, were to the living far more grievous than the dead and more wretched than those who had perished.

For, turning to entreaties and lamentation, they threw them into distress, begging to be taken with them and calling out to each one, if they saw anywhere any of their comrades or relatives, hanging on to their tent-mates as they were already going away and following as far as they could, and when someone's strength and body failed him, being left behind not without many appeals to the gods and wailing, so that the whole army, filled with tears and in such distress, did not easily get away, even though it was leaving a hostile country and had already suffered things too great for tears and feared to suffer others in the unknown future.

And there was also a certain dejection and much self-reproach. For they were like nothing else than a city that had been starved out and was escaping, and that no small one; for of the whole multitude no fewer than forty thousand were on the march together. And of these all the others carried whatever each could that was useful, and the hoplites and the horsemen, contrary to custom, carried their own food themselves under their arms, some for lack of servants, others from distrust of them; for they had deserted long before and most of them at that very moment. And even so they did not carry enough; for there was no longer food in the camp.

And indeed the rest of their misery and the equal share of their misfortunes, though it had some lightening in being shared with many, was not even so thought easy at the time, especially when they considered from what splendour and boasting at first they had come to what an end and humiliation.

For this was indeed the greatest reversal that had befallen a Hellenic army, since instead of coming to enslave others it was their lot to go away fearing rather to suffer this themselves, and instead of the prayers and paeans with which they had sailed out, to set out back with omens the opposite of these, going on foot instead of on board ship, and relying on the hoplite force rather than the naval. Yet because of the greatness of the danger still hanging over them, all this seemed bearable to them.

And Nicias, seeing the army disheartened and in a great change of fortune, went along the ranks and encouraged and comforted them as far as circumstances allowed, raising his voice still more to each group he came to, out of eagerness, and wishing to do some good by being heard as widely as possible.

‘Even in your present situation, Athenians and allies, you must have hope (some have been saved before now even from worse situations than these), and you must not reproach yourselves too much either for your misfortunes or for your present undeserved sufferings.

I too, who am superior to none of you in strength (but you see indeed how I am suffering from my illness), and who was thought, I believe, second to no one in good fortune both in my private life and in other respects, am now hanging in the same danger as the meanest; and yet I have lived my life performing many customary duties towards the gods, and many just and blameless acts towards men.

For this reason my hope for the future is nevertheless confident, though the misfortunes do frighten us beyond what we deserve. But perhaps they may also abate; for the enemy have had enough good fortune, and if we made our expedition hateful to any of the gods, we have by now been sufficiently punished.

For others too, no doubt, have before now attacked their neighbours, and having done what men do, have suffered what men can bear. And it is reasonable for us now to hope that the dealings of the god will be kinder (for we are by now more deserving of his pity than of his jealousy), and seeing yourselves, what fine hoplites and how many of you are marching in your ranks, do not be too dismayed, but consider that you yourselves are a city at once, wherever you settle, and that no other city in Sicily would either easily withstand your attack or drive you out once settled anywhere.

And make sure yourselves that the march is safe and orderly, each man thinking of nothing else than that whatever place he is forced to fight in, that he will have, if he wins, as his country and his fortress.

And we shall make haste on our way by night and by day alike; for we have short provisions, and if we reach some friendly place of the Sicels (for these are still loyal to us through their fear of the Syracusans), consider yourselves at once in safety. A message has been sent ahead to them, and they have been told to meet us and bring other food.

‘And to sum up, soldiers, know both that it is necessary for you to be brave men, as there is no place near where you could be saved if you turn coward, and that, if you now escape the enemy, the rest of you will see again what you long for, wherever it may be, and the Athenians will restore the great power of their city, fallen though it is; for men make the city, and not walls or ships empty of men.’

Nicias, while giving such exhortations, at the same time went along the army, and wherever he saw it scattered and not advancing in order, he brought it together and set it in place, and Demosthenes did no less, saying such and similar things to those under him.
And the army marched drawn up in a hollow square, Nicias' division leading first and Demosthenes' following; and the hoplites had the baggage-carriers and the greater part of the crowd inside.

And when they reached the crossing of the river Anapus, they found some of the Syracusans and allies drawn up at it, and having routed them and won the ford, they advanced; but the Syracusans pressed on them, their horsemen riding alongside, and their light troops throwing javelins at them.

And on this day the Athenians advanced about forty stades and bivouacked by a certain hill; and on the next day they marched early and advanced about twenty stades, and they went down into a level place and encamped there, wishing to get something to eat from the houses (for the place was inhabited) and to take water with them from there; for in front of them, for many stades along the way they were going to go, there was not plenty.
Meanwhile the Syracusans went ahead and walled off the pass in front of them; it was a steep hill with a precipitous ravine on each side of it, and it was called the Acraean cliff.

On the next day the Athenians advanced, and the horsemen and javelin-men of the Syracusans and allies, who were numerous, hindered them on both sides and threw javelins and rode alongside them. And the Athenians fought for a long time, then retreated again to the same camp. And they no longer had provisions as before; for it was no longer possible to leave the camp because of the horsemen.

And setting out early they marched again, and forced their way to the hill that had been walled off, and found in front of them, above the wall, the infantry drawn up many shields deep; for the place was narrow.

And the Athenians attacked and assaulted the wall, and being shot at by many from the hill, which was steep (for those above reached them more easily), and being unable to force it, they retreated again and rested.

And it also happened that there were some thunderclaps and rain at the same time, as usually happens when the year is already turning towards autumn; and from this the Athenians were still more disheartened and thought that all this too was happening for their destruction.

And while they were resting, Gylippus and the Syracusans sent part of their army to wall them off again in the rear, where they had come from; but they in turn sent some of their own men and prevented it.

And after this the Athenians retreated with the whole army more towards the plain and bivouacked. On the next day they advanced, and the Syracusans attacked them on every side all around and wounded many, and if the Athenians advanced, they gave way, but if they retreated, they pressed on them, falling especially on those in the rear, in the hope that by routing them little by little they might throw the whole army into a panic.
And for a long time the Athenians held out in this way, then, having advanced five or six stades, they rested in the plain; and the Syracusans too withdrew from them to their own camp.

During the night Nicias and Demosthenes decided, since their army was in a bad state from the lack of all provisions by now, and many had been wounded in the many attacks of the enemy that had been made, to light as many fires as possible and lead the army away, no longer by the same road they had intended, but in the opposite direction to the one the Syracusans were watching, towards the sea.
And this whole route for the army led not towards Catana, but to the other part of Sicily, towards Camarina and Gela and the cities there, both Hellenic and barbarian.

So they lit many fires and marched in the night. And, as is apt to happen to all armies, and above all to the largest, that fears and terrors arise, especially when they are marching at night and through hostile country and with the enemy not far away, confusion fell upon them;
and the army of Nicias, as it was leading, kept together and got far ahead, while that of Demosthenes, about half or more, was separated and marched in more disorder.

Yet at dawn they reached the sea, and, entering the road called the Helorine road, they marched on, so that, when they reached the river Cacyparis, they might go up along the river through the interior; for they hoped that the Sicels whom they had sent for would also meet them there.

And when they reached the river, they found there too a guard of the Syracusans walling off and staking off the ford. And forcing their way past it, they crossed the river and marched on again towards another river, the Erineus; for the guides told them to go this way.

Meanwhile the Syracusans and their allies, when day came and they learned that the Athenians had gone, most of them blamed Gylippus for having let the Athenians go on purpose, and, pursuing in haste by the way they could easily perceive they had gone, they overtook them about the time of the midday meal.

And when they came up with those with Demosthenes, who were behind and marching more slowly and in more disorder, as they had been thrown into confusion that night, they at once fell on them and fought, and the horsemen of the Syracusans surrounded them the more easily since they were separated, and drove them together into one place.

And the army of Nicias was as much as fifty stades ahead; for Nicias led more quickly, thinking that safety lay not in staying of their own accord in such a situation and fighting, but in retreating as fast as possible, fighting only as much as they were forced to.

But Demosthenes happened to be for the most part in more continuous toil, because, as he was retreating in the rear, the enemy pressed upon him first, and now, learning that the Syracusans were pursuing, he did not advance but rather formed up for battle, until, by lingering, he was surrounded by them, and he himself and the Athenians with him were in great confusion; for, being driven into a place which had a low wall around it, with a road on this side and on that, and which had a good many olive trees, they were shot at from all around.

And the Syracusans naturally used such attacks and not hand-to-hand fighting; for to risk all against desperate men was no longer to their advantage rather than to the Athenians', and at the same time there was a certain sparing of themselves, now that success was clear, so that no one should be lost beforehand, and they thought that even so, by subduing them in this manner, they would take them.

So when, after shooting at the Athenians and allies all day from every side, they saw that they were now worn out by their wounds and the rest of their distress, Gylippus and the Syracusans and the allies made a proclamation, first to the islanders, that whoever wished might come over to them on condition of freedom; and some cities, not many, went over.

Then later an agreement was made with all the rest who were with Demosthenes, that they should hand over their arms and that no one should be put to death, either by violence or by imprisonment or by want of the barest means of life.

And they surrendered, six thousand in all, and laid down all the money they had, throwing it into upturned shields, and they filled four shields. And these they at once took away to the city; but Nicias and those with him reached the river Erineus on this day, and he crossed it and posted the army on some high ground.
On the next day the Syracusans overtook him and told him that those with Demosthenes had surrendered, calling on him to do the same; but he, not believing it, made a truce to send a horseman to see.

And when the man had gone and reported back that they had surrendered, he sent a herald to Gylippus and the Syracusans saying that he was ready to agree on behalf of the Athenians to repay all the money the Syracusans had spent on the war, on condition that they let the army with him go; and until the money was paid, he would give men of the Athenians as hostages, one for each talent.
But the Syracusans and Gylippus did not accept the proposals, but, falling on them and surrounding them on all sides, shot at these too until late.

And these too were in a wretched state from the lack of food and provisions. Yet, waiting for the quiet of the night, they intended to march on. And they took up their arms, and the Syracusans perceived it and raised the paean.

But the Athenians, realising that they were not escaping notice, laid down their arms again, except for about three hundred men; and these forced their way through the guards and went on during the night wherever they could.
And Nicias, when day came, led the army on; but the Syracusans and their allies pressed on them in the same way, shooting at them from every side and striking them down with javelins.

And the Athenians pushed on towards the river Assinarus, partly because they were hard pressed by the attack from every side of many horsemen and of the rest of the crowd, thinking that things would be somewhat easier for them if they crossed the river, and partly from their exhaustion and their desire to drink.

And when they reached it, they rushed in without any order any longer, but every man, wishing to be the first to cross himself, and the enemy pressing on them, made the crossing difficult by now; for, being forced to advance in a mass, they fell on one another and trampled each other down, and some were killed at once on the spears and baggage, while others, getting entangled, were swept away.

And the Syracusans, standing along the other bank of the river (which was steep), shot down from above at the Athenians, most of whom were drinking greedily and were thrown into confusion among themselves in the hollow bed of the river.

And the Peloponnesians came down after them and slaughtered especially those in the river. And the water was at once fouled, but it was drunk no less, muddy and bloody as it was, and most of them fought over it.

At last, when many dead were already lying on one another in the river, and the army had been destroyed, part of it at the river, and part, if any escaped, by the horsemen, Nicias surrendered himself to Gylippus, trusting him more than the Syracusans; and he told him and the Lacedaemonians to do with him whatever they wished, but to stop slaughtering the other soldiers.

And after this Gylippus at last ordered them to take prisoners; and they brought together alive all the rest, as many as were not hidden away (and these were many), and they sent men to pursue the three hundred, who had got through the guard during the night, and captured them.

So the part of the army that was collected as public property was not large, but the part that was stolen away was large, and all Sicily was filled with them, since they had not been taken by agreement as were those with Demosthenes.

And no small part were also killed; for this slaughter was indeed very great, and not less than any in this [Sicilian] war. And in the other attacks, which had been frequent during the march, not a few had died. But many nevertheless also escaped, some at once, others after serving as slaves and running away later; and for these the place of refuge was Catana.
And the Syracusans and their allies gathered together, took up as many of the prisoners as they could and the spoils, and went back to the city.

And all the others of the Athenians and the allies whom they had taken they sent down into the stone-quarries, thinking this the safest way of keeping them, but Nicias and Demosthenes they put to death, against the will of Gylippus. For Gylippus thought it would be a glorious achievement for him, on top of everything else, to bring the enemy generals as well to the Lacedaemonians.

And it happened that one of them, Demosthenes, was their greatest enemy, because of the events on the island and at Pylos, and the other, for the same reasons, their greatest friend; for Nicias had been eager that the men of the Lacedaemonians from the island should be released, by persuading the Athenians to make a treaty.

For this reason the Lacedaemonians were friendly to him, and he had surrendered himself to Gylippus trusting not least in this. But some of the Syracusans, as was said, some fearing, because they had been in communication with him, that if he were tortured he might cause them trouble on that account in the midst of their success, and others, especially the Corinthians, that, being rich, he might bribe some people with money and escape and that some fresh trouble might arise for them again from him, persuaded the allies and put him to death.

And he died for this reason or one very close to it, the man who of all the Hellenes of my time least deserved to come to such misfortune, because of his whole way of life, devoted to virtue as it was considered.

And those in the stone-quarries the Syracusans treated harshly in the first period. For as they were many in a hollow and small place, the sun at first and the stifling heat still distressed them because it was unroofed, and the nights that followed, on the contrary, autumnal and cold, brought on sickness by the change,

and as they did everything in the same place for lack of room, and moreover the dead were heaped together on one another, who died from their wounds and from the change and such causes, there were also smells that could not be borne, and they were at the same time oppressed by hunger and thirst (for they gave each of them for eight months a cotyle of water and two cotylae of food), and of all the other sufferings that men who have fallen into such a place are likely to endure there was none that did not befall them;
and for about seventy days they lived thus all together; then, except for the Athenians and any Siceliots or Italiots who had served with them, they sold the rest.
The number of all those taken is hard to state accurately, but they were no fewer than seven thousand.

And this turned out to be the greatest [Hellenic] action of those in this war, and, as it seems to me at least, of all Hellenic actions we know of by report, and the most brilliant for the victors and the most disastrous for the vanquished;

for, being beaten utterly at every point and having suffered no small misery in any respect, with total destruction, as the saying goes, both army and ships, and there was nothing that did not perish, and few out of many returned home. Such were the events in Sicily.

When it was reported at Athens, for a long time they disbelieved even the most credible of the soldiers, who had escaped from the action itself and reported it clearly, that things had been so completely destroyed; and when they did realise it, they were angry with those of the orators who had joined in promoting the expedition, as though they had not voted for it themselves, and they were enraged also with the oracle-mongers and soothsayers and all who at that time, by some divination, had raised their hopes that they would take Sicily.

Everything on every side distressed them, and fear and the very greatest dismay surrounded them after what had happened. For at the same time, deprived, both each man privately and the city, of many hoplites and horsemen and of men of military age such as they saw no others left, they were weighed down; and at the same time, seeing neither enough ships in the docks nor money in the treasury nor crews for the ships, they had no hope at present of being saved, and they thought that the enemy from Sicily would sail straight against the Piraeus with their fleet, especially after so great a victory, and that the enemy here, now doubly prepared in every way, would attack them with all their might both by land and by sea, and their own allies would revolt and join them.

Nevertheless, as far as their means allowed, they decided they must not give in, but must prepare a fleet, getting timber together wherever they could, and money, and must make their allies secure, and above all Euboea, and must reform affairs in the city towards economy, and choose a board of older men, who would give preliminary counsel on present affairs as occasion should require.
And in their immediate terror, as a people is apt to do, they were ready to keep good order in everything. And as they had decided, so they did, and the summer ended.

In the following winter, in view of the great disaster of the Athenians in Sicily, all the Hellenes were at once roused: those who were allies of neither side thought that, even if no one called on them, they should no longer stand aloof from the war, but should go of their own accord against the Athenians, considering that the Athenians would have come against each of them if they had succeeded in Sicily, and at the same time that the rest of the war would be short, and that it would be glorious to take part in it, while the allies of the Lacedaemonians in turn were more eager than before to be quickly rid of their great hardship.

But above all the subjects of the Athenians were ready to revolt even beyond their power, because they judged the situation in their passion and would not even allow the argument that the Athenians would be able to hold out the coming summer at least.

And the city of the Lacedaemonians was encouraged by all this, and above all because their allies from Sicily, with a great force, now that their navy had of necessity been added to theirs, would in all likelihood be with them at the beginning of spring.

And being full of hope on all sides, they intended to take up the war without reserve, reckoning that if it ended well they would be freed in future from such dangers as the one from the Athenians that would have surrounded them if they had added Sicily to their power, and that, having overthrown them, they would themselves now securely lead the whole of Hellas.

At once, then, Agis their king, setting out with some troops from Decelea during this winter, levied money from the allies for the fleet, and, turning towards the Malian Gulf, he carried off most of the booty of the Oetaeans, on account of their old enmity, and exacted money, and he forced the Achaeans of Phthiotis and the other subjects of the Thessalians in those parts, in spite of the complaints and unwillingness of the Thessalians, to give some hostages and money, and he deposited the hostages at Corinth and tried to bring them into the alliance.

And the Lacedaemonians made their requisition on the cities for the building of a hundred ships, and they assigned twenty-five to themselves and to the Boeotians each, fifteen to the Phocians and Locrians, and fifteen to the Corinthians, ten to the Arcadians and Pellenians and Sicyonians, ten to the Megarians and Troezenians and Epidaurians and Hermionians; and they prepared everything else to set about the war at once with the spring.

And the Athenians too made their preparations, as they had planned, in this same winter, both the shipbuilding, after getting timber together, and fortifying Sunium, so that their corn-ships might have safety in sailing round, and abandoning the fort in Laconia that they had built while sailing along to Sicily, and cutting down other expenses for economy, wherever anything seemed to be spent uselessly, and above all keeping a watch on the affairs of their allies so that they should not revolt from them.

While both sides were doing this and were, just as if they were beginning, engaged in nothing else but preparing for the war, the Euboeans were the first to send envoys to Agis about revolting from the Athenians, in this winter. And he accepted their proposals and sent for Alcamenes son of Sthenelaidas and Melanthus from Lacedaemon to command in Euboea; and they came with about three hundred of the Neodamodes, and he began preparing their crossing.

But meanwhile the Lesbians too came, wishing to revolt as well; and as the Boeotians supported them, Agis was persuaded to put off the matter of Euboea and prepared the revolt for the Lesbians, giving them Alcamenes as governor, who was to have sailed to Euboea, and the Boeotians promised ten ships, and Agis ten.

And this was done without the city of the Lacedaemonians; for Agis, as long as he was at Decelea with his own force, had the power to send troops wherever he wished, and to raise them, and to levy money. And at this period, one may say, the allies obeyed him much more [than] the Lacedaemonians in the city; for, having a force himself, he was formidable wherever he went at once.

And while he was acting for the Lesbians, the Chians and Erythraeans, who were also ready to revolt, did not turn to Agis but to Lacedaemon. And with them came also an envoy from Tissaphernes, who was the general of King Darius son of Artaxerxes in the coastal provinces.

For Tissaphernes too was inviting the Peloponnesians and promising to provide maintenance. For he had recently been called on by the King for the tribute from his own province, which he owed because he could not exact it from the Hellenic cities on account of the Athenians; so he thought that by injuring the Athenians he would more readily get the tribute, and at the same time make the Lacedaemonians allies of the King, and either bring alive or kill Amorges, the bastard son of Pissuthnes, who had revolted in Caria, as the King had ordered him.

The Chians and Tissaphernes, then, were acting together for the same end, but Calligeitus son of Laophon, a Megarian, and Timagoras son of Athenagoras, a Cyzicene, both exiles from their own countries living with Pharnabazus son of Pharnaces, arrived at Lacedaemon about the same time, sent by Pharnabazus to get ships brought to the Hellespont, so that he himself, if he could, might do what Tissaphernes was eager for, cause the cities in his own province to revolt from the Athenians because of the tribute, and win for the King on his own account the alliance of the Lacedaemonians.

As both parties, those from Pharnabazus and those from Tissaphernes, were negotiating this separately, there was great rivalry among those at Lacedaemon, as to whether the one side would persuade them first to send ships and troops to Ionia and Chios, or the other to the Hellespont.

The Lacedaemonians, however, received the proposals of the Chians and Tissaphernes far more favourably; for Alcibiades too was working with them, being a very close hereditary guest-friend of Endius, who was ephor, from which their family had also taken its Laconian name because of this guest-friendship; for Endius was called son of Alcibiades.

Nevertheless the Lacedaemonians first sent a man of the perioeci, Phrynis, to Chios as a spy, to see whether they had as many ships as they said and whether the city was in other respects as strong as its reputation, and when he reported to them that what they had heard was true, they at once made the Chians and Erythraeans allies and voted to send them forty ships, since there were already there, from what the Chians said, no fewer than sixty.

And at first they themselves were going to send ten of these, and Melanchridas, who was their admiral; then, after an earthquake had occurred, they sent Chalcideus instead of Melanchridas and instead of ten ships prepared five in Laconia. And the winter ended, and the nineteenth year ended of this war of which Thucydides wrote the history.

At the beginning of spring of the following summer, as the Chians were at once pressing for the ships to be sent and were afraid that the Athenians might find out what was going on (for all their embassies were sent secretly from them), the Lacedaemonians sent three Spartans to Corinth, to have the ships hauled across the Isthmus as quickly as possible from the other sea to the one facing Athens and to order them all to sail to Chios, both those that Agis was preparing for Lesbos and the others; and the ships of the allies there numbered in all thirty-nine.

Calligeitus and Timagoras, then, acting for Pharnabazus, did not join in the expedition to Chios, nor did they give the money they had brought with them for the expedition, twenty-five talents, but planned to sail later on their own with another expedition;

and Agis, when he saw that the Lacedaemonians were set on going to Chios first, did not himself think otherwise either, but the allies met at Corinth and deliberated, and they decided to sail first to Chios under the command of Chalcideus, who was preparing the five ships in Laconia, then to Lesbos under the command of Alcamenes, whom Agis also intended, and finally to go to the Hellespont (Clearchus son of Ramphias had been appointed commander for it),

and to carry half of the ships across the Isthmus first, and these to sail off at once, so that the Athenians might not pay more attention to those that were setting out than to those that were carried across later.

For they were making the voyage this way openly, despising the weakness of the Athenians, because no navy of theirs of any size had yet appeared. And as they had decided, they at once carried across twenty-one ships.

But the Corinthians, though the others were pressing for the voyage, were not eager to sail with them before they had celebrated the Isthmian festival, which was then taking place. And Agis was ready for them not to break the Isthmian truce, but to make the expedition his own.

But as the Corinthians did not agree and delay ensued, the Athenians became more aware of the affairs of the Chians, and they sent one of their generals, Aristocrates, and accused them, and when the Chians denied it, they ordered them to send ships with them as a pledge of good faith, according to the alliance; and they sent seven.

And the reason for the sending of the ships was that the majority of the Chians did not know what was going on, and the few who were in the secret did not yet wish to have the people hostile before they had got some strength, and no longer expected the Peloponnesians to come, because they were delaying.

Meanwhile the Isthmian games were held, and the Athenians (for they had been notified) attended them as spectators, and the affairs of the Chians became more evident to them. And when they returned, they at once made preparations so that the ships should not set out from Cenchreae without their knowledge.

After the festival they put to sea for Chios with twenty-one ships, with Alcamenes as their commander. And the Athenians at first sailed up to them with an equal number of ships and drew back towards the open sea. But when the Peloponnesians did not follow them far, but turned back, the Athenians also withdrew; for they did not consider trustworthy the seven ships of the Chians which they had in their number with them,

but afterwards they manned additional ships, bringing their number up to thirty-seven, and chased the enemy as they sailed along the coast into Spiraeum in the Corinthian territory; this is a deserted harbour and the last towards the borders of Epidauria. And the Peloponnesians lost one ship out at sea, but brought the rest together and anchored them.

And when the Athenians attacked both by sea with their ships and by landing on the shore, there was great and disorderly confusion, and the Athenians disabled most of the ships on the shore and killed the commander Alcamenes; and some of their own men also died.

After separating, they assigned a sufficient number of ships to blockade the enemy ships, and with the rest anchored at the islet, on which, as it was not far away, they made their camp, and they sent to Athens for help.

For the Corinthians had also come to the Peloponnesians on the next day to help the ships, and not long afterwards the other people of the neighbourhood as well. And seeing that the guarding in a deserted place was laborious, they were at a loss, and they thought of burning the ships, but then they decided to draw them up on shore and, sitting down beside them with their land force, to keep guard until some suitable opportunity of escape should present itself. And Agis too, on learning this, sent them a Spartan, Thermon.

Now the Lacedaemonians had first been told that the ships had put out from the Isthmus (for Alcamenes had been ordered by the ephors to send a horseman when this happened), and they at once wanted to send their own five ships with Chalcideus as commander and Alcibiades with him; then, when they were eager to set out, the news about the flight of the ships into Spiraeum was reported, and, disheartened because they had stumbled at their first step in the Ionian war, they no longer intended to send the ships from their own country, but even to recall some that had put to sea before.

On learning this, Alcibiades again persuaded Endius and the other ephors not to shrink from the voyage, saying that they would complete the voyage before the Chians learned of the disaster to the ships, and that he himself, when he reached Ionia, would easily persuade the cities to revolt by telling them of the weakness of the Athenians and the zeal of the Lacedaemonians; for he would appear more trustworthy than others.

And to Endius himself he said privately that it would be a fine thing for him, through Alcibiades, to make Ionia revolt and to make the King an ally of the Lacedaemonians, and that this achievement should not become Agis'; for he himself happened to be at odds with Agis.
And having persuaded the other ephors and Endius, he put to sea with the five ships together with Chalcideus the Lacedaemonian, and they made the voyage with all speed.

About this same time the sixteen ships of the Peloponnesians from Sicily which had fought through the war with Gylippus were also returning home; and after being cut off near Leucadia and roughly handled by the twenty-seven Attic ships commanded by Hippocles son of Menippus, who was keeping watch for the ships from Sicily, the rest, except one, escaped the Athenians and sailed into Corinth.

Chalcideus and Alcibiades, as they sailed, seized all whom they met, so that their coming might not be reported, and after touching first at Corycus on the mainland and releasing them there, they themselves, having first met with some of the Chians who were cooperating with them and who urged them to sail into the city without announcing it beforehand, arrived suddenly upon the Chians.

And the many were in wonder and consternation; but the few had arranged that the council should happen to be assembling, and when speeches were made by Chalcideus and Alcibiades saying that many other ships were sailing up, but not revealing the facts about the blockade of the ships in Spiraeum, the Chians revolted from the Athenians, and afterwards the Erythraeans.

And after this they sailed with three ships and made Clazomenae revolt too. And the Clazomenians immediately crossed over to the mainland and fortified Polichna, for a retreat for themselves from the islet on which they lived, if there should be any need. And those in revolt were all engaged in fortifying and in preparation for war;

and news of Chios quickly reached Athens; and thinking that a danger already great and manifest surrounded them, and that the rest of the allies would not be willing to keep quiet when the greatest city had changed sides, under their present consternation they at once lifted the penalties laid upon anyone who proposed or put to the vote the use of the thousand talents, which throughout the whole war they had been anxious not to touch, and they voted to use them and to man not a few ships, and of the ships blockading at Spiraeum to send at once the eight which had left the guard, pursued those with Chalcideus, and, not overtaking them, had returned (their commander was Strombichides son of Diotimus), and that twelve others under Thrasycles should go to help not long afterwards, these too leaving the blockade.

And they withdrew the seven ships of the Chians which were joining them in blockading the ships in Spiraeum, freed the slaves from them, and put the free men in bonds. And they speedily manned and sent out in their place 〈ten〉 other ships for the blockade of the Peloponnesians, instead of all the ships that had gone away, and intended to man thirty others. And their zeal was great, and nothing trivial was done for the relief of Chios.

Meanwhile Strombichides arrived at Samos with the eight ships, and after taking on one Samian ship he sailed to Teos and asked them to keep quiet. And Chalcideus was also sailing against Teos from Chios with twenty-three ships, and at the same time the land force of the Clazomenians and Erythraeans was coming along the shore.
But Strombichides, perceiving this in advance, put out to sea, and when, out on the open sea, he saw the ships from Chios were many, he fled towards Samos; and they pursued him.

The Teians, though at first not admitting the land force, brought it in when the Athenians fled. And the land troops waited for a while, also expecting Chalcideus back from the pursuit; but when he was long in coming, they themselves began to demolish the wall which the Athenians had built on the mainland side of the city of the Teians, and a few of the barbarians who had come up also helped them demolish it, commanded by Stages, a lieutenant of Tissaphernes.

Chalcideus and Alcibiades, after chasing Strombichides into Samos, armed the sailors from the ships from the Peloponnese and left them at Chios, and after manning these ships with substitutes from Chios, as well as twenty others, they sailed to Miletus to make it revolt;

for Alcibiades, being friendly with the leading men of the Milesians, wished to win them over before the arrival of the ships from the Peloponnese, and to give the credit, as he had promised, to the Chians, to himself, to Chalcideus and to Endius who had sent them out, for having made as many of the cities as possible revolt with the Chian force and Chalcideus.

So, having escaped notice for most of the voyage and arriving not much before Strombichides and Thrasycles, who happened to have just come from Athens with twelve ships and to be joining in the pursuit, they made Miletus revolt. And the Athenians, sailing up at their heels with nineteen ships, since the Milesians did not admit them, took up a blockading station at Lade, the island lying off the city.
And the first alliance of the Lacedaemonians with the King, made through Tissaphernes and Chalcideus immediately after the Milesians revolted, was as follows.

'On these terms the Lacedaemonians and the allies made an alliance with the King and Tissaphernes. Whatever territory and cities the King holds and the King's fathers held shall be the King's; and from these cities whatever money or anything else came in to the Athenians, the King and the Lacedaemonians and the allies shall jointly prevent, so that the Athenians receive neither money nor anything else.

And the war against the Athenians shall be waged jointly by the King and the Lacedaemonians and the allies; and it shall not be permitted to end the war against the Athenians unless both sides agree, the King and the Lacedaemonians and the allies.

And if any revolt from the King, they shall be enemies both to the Lacedaemonians and to the allies; and if any revolt from the Lacedaemonians and the allies, they shall be enemies to the King in the same way.'
This alliance was made; and after this the Chians at once manned ten more ships and sailed to Anaea, wishing to learn about the situation in Miletus and at the same time to make the cities revolt.

And when a message came to them from Chalcideus to sail back again, and that Amorges would be there by land with an army, they sailed to the temple of Zeus; and they sighted sixteen ships, with which Diomedon, still later than Thrasycles, was sailing up from Athens.

And when they saw them, they fled, one ship to Ephesus and the rest towards Teos. And the Athenians took four of them empty, the men having got to land first; the others took refuge in the city of the Teians.

And the Athenians sailed away towards Samos, while the Chians, putting to sea with their remaining ships, and the land force with them, made Lebedos revolt and then Haerae. And after this each returned home, both the land force and the ships.

About the same time the twenty ships of the Peloponnesians in Spiraeum, which had been chased there earlier and were being blockaded by an equal number of Athenians, made a sudden sally, won a sea battle and took four ships of the Athenians, and after sailing back to Cenchreae they again prepared for the voyage to Chios and Ionia. And Astyochus came to them from Lacedaemon as admiral, to whom the whole command of the fleet now belonged.

When the land force had withdrawn from Teos, Tissaphernes too came there in person with an army, demolished whatever was left of the wall at Teos, and withdrew. And not long after his departure Diomedon arrived with ten ships of the Athenians and made a treaty with the Teians that they should receive them too. And after sailing along the coast to Haerae and attacking it, since he could not take the city, he sailed away.

At this time there also took place the uprising at Samos by the people against the powerful, with the help of Athenians who happened to be there in three ships. And the people of the Samians killed some two hundred in all of the most powerful, and having punished four hundred with exile and divided their land and houses among themselves, and the Athenians having after this voted them autonomy as being now reliable, they governed the city thereafter, and they gave the landowners a share in nothing else, and no one of the people was any longer allowed to give a daughter in marriage to them or to take a wife from them.

After this, in the same summer, the Chians, as they had begun, losing nothing of their zeal, and being present in force to make the cities revolt even without the Peloponnesians, and at the same time wishing as many as possible to share the danger with them, made an expedition themselves with thirteen ships against Lesbos, as they had been told by the Lacedaemonians to go against it second and from there to the Hellespont, and at the same time the land force, both of the Peloponnesians who were present and of the allies from there, moved along the shore towards Clazomenae and Cyme; its commander was Eualas, a Spartan, and that of the ships was Deiniadas, a perioecus.
And the ships put in at Methymna and first made it revolt, and four ships were left in it; and then the rest made Mytilene revolt.

Astyochus, the Lacedaemonian admiral, sailing from Cenchreae with four ships, as he had set out to do, arrived at Chios. And on the third day after he came, the Attic ships, twenty-five of them, sailed to Lesbos, commanded by Leon and Diomedon; for Leon had later come with ten ships to help from Athens.

And Astyochus, putting to sea late on the same day and taking with him one Chian ship, sailed to Lesbos, to give help, if he could. And he arrived at Pyrrha, and from there on the next day at Eresus, where he learned that Mytilene had been taken by the Athenians at the first assault:

for the Athenians, sailing in unexpectedly just as they were, put into the harbour and got the better of the Chian ships, and after landing and defeating in battle those who resisted, they took the city.

Learning this from the Eresians and from the Chian ships from Methymna with Eubulus, which had been left there earlier and, fleeing when Mytilene was taken, fell in with him, three of them (for one was taken by the Athenians), Astyochus no longer pressed on to Mytilene, but, after making Eresus revolt and arming it, he sent the hoplites from his own ships by land along the coast to Antissa and Methymna, putting Eteonicus in command; and he himself sailed along the coast with the ships he had with him and the three Chian ones, hoping that the Methymnaeans would take courage on seeing them and stand by their revolt.

But when everything in Lesbos went against him, he took up his own land army and sailed back to Chios. And the land force of the allies, which was to have gone to the Hellespont, was also conveyed back to their cities. And after this six of the allied Peloponnesian ships at Cenchreae came to them at Chios.

And the Athenians restored affairs in Lesbos, and sailing from there they took Polichna of the Clazomenians, which was being fortified on the mainland, and carried them back again to the city on the island, except the authors of the revolt; these went away to Daphnus. And Clazomenae came over to the Athenians again.

In the same summer the Athenians blockading Miletus with the twenty ships at Lade made a landing at Panormus in Milesian territory and killed Chalcideus, the Lacedaemonian commander, who had come to the rescue with a few men, and on the third day afterwards they sailed across and set up a trophy, which the Milesians took down as having been set up without command of the land;

and Leon and Diomedon, with the ships of the Athenians from Lesbos, setting out from the Oenussae, the islands off Chios, and from Sidussa and from Pteleum, forts which they held in Erythraean territory, and from Lesbos, made war on the Chians from the ships; and they had as marines hoplites from the muster-roll, pressed into service.

And landing at Cardamyle and at Boliscus, they defeated in battle those of the Chians who came out against them, killed many, and laid waste the places in that region, and at Phanae they won again in another battle, and in a third at Leuconium. And after this the Chians no longer came out against them, while they ravaged the country, which was finely furnished and had been unharmed from the Persian wars until then.

For the Chians alone, after the Lacedaemonians, of those I have known, were both prosperous and prudent at the same time, and the more their city grew in greatness, the more securely they ordered themselves.

And not even this revolt, if they seem to have done it against the safer course, did they dare to make before they were going to share the danger with many good allies and perceived that the Athenians themselves no longer denied after the Sicilian disaster that their affairs were [certainly] in a very bad state; and if they were deceived in some way by the unexpected turns of human life, they made their mistake together with many who held the same opinion, that the power of the Athenians would quickly be destroyed.

So when they were shut off from the sea and were being ravaged by land, some attempted to bring the city over to the Athenians; the magistrates, perceiving them, themselves kept quiet, but they brought the admiral Astyochus from Erythrae with the four ships that he had with him, and considered how they could stop the plot in the most moderate way, either by taking hostages or by some other means. And they were thus engaged.

From Athens, at the end of the same summer, a thousand Athenian hoplites and fifteen hundred Argive ones (for the Athenians had armed the five hundred of the Argives who were light-armed) and a thousand of the allies, in forty-eight ships, some of which were hoplite transports, under the command of Phrynichus, Onomacles and Scironides, sailed into Samos, and crossing over to Miletus they encamped there.

And the Milesians came out, both themselves, eight hundred hoplites, and the Peloponnesians who had come with Chalcideus and some [foreign] auxiliary force of Tissaphernes, with Tissaphernes himself present and his cavalry, and engaged the Athenians and the allies.

And the Argives, rushing out ahead with their own wing and despising the enemy, advancing in rather disorderly fashion as against Ionians who would not stand their charge, were defeated by the Milesians, and a little fewer than three hundred of their men were killed;

but the Athenians, having defeated the Peloponnesians first and pushed back the barbarians and the rest of the crowd, without engaging the Milesians, who had withdrawn into the city from the rout of the Argives when they saw the rest of their army being defeated, grounded their arms right by the city of the Milesians as already victorious.

And it happened in this battle that the Ionians on both sides got the better of the Dorians: for the Athenians defeated the Peloponnesians opposed to them, and the Milesians the Argives. After setting up a trophy, the Athenians began preparing to wall in the place, which was shaped like an isthmus, thinking that if they won over Miletus, the other places too would easily come over to them.

Meanwhile, when it was already late in the afternoon, word was brought to them that the fifty-five ships from the Peloponnese and Sicily were all but there. For of the Siceliots, with Hermocrates the Syracusan most of all urging them to take part also in the remaining destruction of the Athenians, twenty ships of the Syracusans came and two of Selinus, and the ships from the Peloponnese, which they had been preparing, were now ready; and both squadrons, entrusted to Therimenes the Lacedaemonian to take to Astyochus the admiral, put in first at Leros, the island off Miletus;
then, perceiving from there that the Athenians were at Miletus, they first sailed into the Iasic Gulf, wishing to know the state of affairs at Miletus.

And when Alcibiades came on horseback to Teichiussa in Milesian territory, the part of the gulf to which they had sailed and where they had camped for the night, they learned about the battle (for Alcibiades had been present and had fought on the side of the Milesians and Tissaphernes), and he urged them, if they did not want to ruin their affairs in Ionia and their whole cause, to help Miletus as quickly as possible and not to let it be walled off.

And they were going to bring help at dawn; but Phrynichus, the general of the Athenians, when he had learned clearly from Leros about the ships, though his colleagues wished to stay and fight it out at sea, said that he would neither do this himself nor allow them or anyone else to do it, as far as he could.

For where [it is possible] to fight later, knowing clearly against how many enemy ships and with how many of their own against them they would fight after preparing adequately and at leisure, he would never yield to the reproach of disgrace and run an unreasonable risk.

For it was not disgraceful for Athenians to give way with their navy when the moment required, but it would turn out more disgraceful in whatever way it happened if they were defeated; and the city would fall not only into disgrace but also into the greatest danger, since after the misfortunes that had occurred it could hardly afford to take the offensive anywhere voluntarily, even with a secure force, or unless under absolute necessity, much less to go into self-chosen dangers when not forced to.

And he ordered them to take up as quickly as possible their wounded, their land force and as much of the equipment as they had come with, and, leaving behind what they had taken from enemy territory so that the ships might be light, to sail back to Samos, and from there, after bringing all the ships together, to make their attacks if an opportunity should arise anywhere.

And as he persuaded them, so he also acted; and Phrynichus was thought, not at that moment more than later, not in this matter only but also in everything else he was put in charge of, to be a man of good sense.
And the Athenians in this way broke up from Miletus at once in the evening with their victory incomplete, and the Argives sailed home from Samos in haste and in anger at their disaster;

and the Peloponnesians, setting out from Teichiussa at dawn, put in after them, and after staying one day, on the next day, having also taken on the Chian ships which had at first been chased into port with Chalcideus, they wished to sail back to Teichiussa for the equipment they had put ashore there.

And when they came, Tissaphernes arrived with his land force and persuaded them to sail against Iasus, which Amorges, an enemy, held. And attacking Iasus suddenly, while the inhabitants expected nothing but that the ships were Attic, they took it; and the Syracusans were most praised in the action.

And taking Amorges alive, the bastard son of Pissuthnes and a rebel against the King, the Peloponnesians handed him over to Tissaphernes to take to the King, if he wished, as the King had ordered him, and they sacked Iasus, and the army took a very great deal of money; for the place was of ancient wealth.

And they took the mercenaries who had served with Amorges into their own ranks without harming them, since most of them were from the Peloponnese; and after handing over the town to Tissaphernes, and all the captives, both slave and free, for each of whom they agreed to receive a Daric stater from him, they then withdrew to Miletus.

And Pedaritus son of Leon, whom the Lacedaemonians had sent to Chios as governor, they sent by land as far as Erythrae with the mercenary force from Amorges, and they set up Philippus there as governor of Miletus. And the summer ended.

In the following winter, after Tissaphernes had put Iasus in a state of defence, he came to Miletus, and distributed a month's pay to all the ships, as he had undertaken at Lacedaemon, at the rate of an Attic drachma for each man, but for the rest of the time he wished to give three obols, until he should ask the King; and if the King ordered it, he said he would give the full drachma.

But when Hermocrates the Syracusan general objected (for Therimenes, not being admiral, but sailing with them to hand over the ships to Astyochus, was soft about the pay), it was nevertheless agreed that each man should receive more than three obols by the amount of five ships. For he gave thirty talents a month for fifty-five ships; and to the others, as far as there were more ships than this number, pay was given at this same rate.

In the same winter the Athenians at Samos (for thirty-five other ships had also arrived from home, and generals Charminus, Strombichides and Euctemon) gathered together the ships from Chios and all the others and wished, after casting lots, to blockade Miletus with the navy and to send both a navy and a land force against Chios.

And they did so; for Strombichides, Onomacles and Euctemon, with thirty ships and taking part of the thousand hoplites who had come to Miletus in hoplite transports, sailed against Chios, which had fallen to them by lot, while the others, remaining at Samos with seventy-four ships, held command of the sea and made attacks on Miletus.

Astyochus, who happened at that time to be at Chios selecting the hostages because of the treachery, stopped this, when he perceived that the ships with Therimenes had come and that the affairs of the alliance were in a better state, and taking ten ships of the Peloponnesians and ten Chian ships he put to sea,

and after attacking Pteleum and failing to take it he sailed along the coast to Clazomenae and ordered those of them who favoured the Athenians to move inland to Daphnus and come over to their side; and Tamos, who was lieutenant-governor of Ionia, joined in the order.

But when they did not listen, after making an attack on the city, which was unwalled, and being unable to take it, he sailed away in a strong wind, himself to Phocaea and Cyme, while the other ships put in at the islands lying off Clazomenae, Marathussa, Pele and Drymussa.

And of whatever property of the Clazomenians had been stored away there, after staying eight days because of the winds, they plundered and consumed some, and putting the rest on board they sailed away to Phocaea and Cyme to Astyochus.

While he was there, envoys of the Lesbians arrived, wishing to revolt again; and they persuaded him, but since the Corinthians and the other allies were unwilling because of the former failure, he weighed anchor and sailed for Chios. And after the ships had been caught in a storm, they arrived later at Chios, some from one place and some from another.

And after this Pedaritus, who was at that time travelling by land from Miletus, reached Erythrae and crossed over to Chios, he and his army; and he also had at his disposal soldiers from the five ships, about five hundred, who had been left behind with their arms by Chalcideus.

And when some Lesbians offered to revolt, Astyochus put the proposal to Pedaritus and the Chians that they ought to go with the ships and make Lesbos revolt; for they would either have more allies or, if they failed in anything, they would harm the Athenians. But they did not listen, and Pedaritus said he would not give up the ships of the Chians to him.

And he, taking the five ships of the Corinthians and a sixth from Megara and one from Hermione and the Laconian ones he had come with himself, sailed for Miletus to take up his command as admiral, after threatening the Chians many times that he would certainly not help them if they should need anything.

And touching at Corycus in Erythraean territory he camped there for the night. And the Athenians from Samos, sailing against Chios with their army, were themselves separated from them by the hill on the other side, and they anchored, and they escaped each other's notice.

But when a letter came from Pedaritus during the night saying that some Erythraean prisoners, released from Samos, had come to Erythrae to betray it, Astyochus at once put to sea back to Erythrae, and by so little did he escape falling in with the Athenians.

And Pedaritus too sailed across to him, and after they had investigated the matter of those who were thought to be betraying the city, when they found that the whole thing had been a pretext for the men's escape from Samos, they acquitted them of the charge and sailed away, the one to Chios, while the other went on to Miletus, as he had intended.
