Meanwhile the army of the Athenians too, sailing round from Corycus with the ships, fell in off Arginus with three warships of the Chians, and when they saw them, they gave chase; and a great storm came on, and the ships of the Chians barely escaped into the harbour, while of the Athenian ships the three that had pressed on hardest were wrecked and cast ashore near the city of the Chians, and of the men some were captured and others killed, and the other ships took refuge in the harbour called Phoenicus below Mimas. And from there they later anchored at Lesbos and prepared for the fortification.

From the Peloponnese in the same winter Hippocrates the Lacedaemonian sailed out with ten Thurian ships, commanded by Dorieus son of Diagoras with two colleagues, one Laconian and one Syracusan ship, and put in at Cnidus; this had already revolted at the instigation of Tissaphernes.

And when those at Miletus learned of them, they ordered them to guard Cnidus with half of the ships, and with those stationed around Triopium to seize the merchant ships putting in from Egypt; Triopium is a headland projecting from the Cnidian territory, sacred to Apollo.

But the Athenians, learning of it and sailing from Samos, captured the six ships keeping guard at Triopium; the men escaped from them. And after this they sailed into Cnidus, attacked the city, which was unwalled, and almost took it.

On the next day they attacked again, and as the inhabitants had fenced themselves in better during the night and those who had escaped from the ships at Triopium had come in to join them, they no longer did as much damage, so they withdrew, ravaged the land of the Cnidians and sailed back to Samos.

About the same time, when Astyochus came to Miletus to the fleet, the Peloponnesians were still well supplied with everything in the camp; for pay was being given sufficiently, and the great sums plundered from Iasus were in the hands of the soldiers, and the Milesians were bearing the burdens of the war zealously.

Still, the Peloponnesians thought that the first agreement with Tissaphernes, made with Chalcideus, was defective and not more in their favour, and they made another while Therimenes was still present; and it is as follows.
'Agreement of the Lacedaemonians and the allies with King Darius and the sons of the King and Tissaphernes, that there shall be a treaty and friendship on the following terms.

Whatever territory and cities belong to King Darius or belonged to his father or to his ancestors, against these neither the Lacedaemonians nor the allies of the Lacedaemonians shall go for war or for any harm, nor shall either the Lacedaemonians or the allies of the Lacedaemonians exact tribute from these cities; nor shall King Darius or those whom the King rules go against the Lacedaemonians or the allies for war or for any harm.
And if the Lacedaemonians or the allies need anything from the King, or the King from the Lacedaemonians or the allies, whatever they persuade each other to do, it shall be right for them to do it.

And the war against the Athenians and the allies both shall wage jointly; and if they make peace, both shall make it jointly. And whatever army is in the King's territory at the King's summons, the King shall pay its expenses.

And if any of the cities that have made the agreement with the King goes against the King's territory, the others shall stop it and defend the King as far as they can; and if any of those in the King's territory or in the territory the King rules goes against the territory of the Lacedaemonians or of the allies, the King shall stop it and defend them as far as he can.'
After this agreement Therimenes, having handed over the ships to Astyochus, sailed away in a light boat and disappeared,

and the Athenians from Lesbos, having already crossed over to Chios with their army and being masters of both land and sea, began to fortify Delphinium, a place strong on the landward side in any case, possessing harbours and not far from the city of the Chians.

And the Chians, having been beaten in the many earlier battles, and besides not being on very good terms among themselves, but even suspicious of one another, since the party of Tydeus son of Ion had already been put to death by Pedaritus for Atticism and the rest of the city was held down by force under the few, kept quiet, and for these reasons neither they themselves nor the mercenaries with Pedaritus seemed to them a match for the enemy.
They did, however, send to Miletus, urging Astyochus to help them; and when he did not listen, Pedaritus sent a letter about him to Lacedaemon, accusing him of wrongdoing.

And affairs at Chios had come to this point for the Athenians; and their ships from Samos made attacks on those at Miletus, but since these did not put out against them, they withdrew again to Samos and kept quiet.

From the Peloponnese in the same winter the twenty-seven ships prepared by the Lacedaemonians for Pharnabazus [by] the agency of Calligeitus the Megarian and Timagoras the Cyzicene set out and sailed for Ionia about the time of the solstice, and Antisthenes, a Spartan, sailed as their commander.

And the Lacedaemonians also sent with them eleven Spartans as advisers to Astyochus, one of whom was Lichas son of Arcesilaus; and they had been told, on arriving at Miletus, to share in the oversight of everything else in whatever way would turn out best, and to send these ships, either the same number or more or even fewer, to the Hellespont to Pharnabazus, if they thought fit, appointing Clearchus son of Ramphias, who sailed with them, as commander, and, if the eleven men thought fit, to remove Astyochus from the office of admiral and to appoint Antisthenes; for because of the letters of Pedaritus they were suspicious of him.

So the ships, sailing across the open sea from Malea, touched at Melos, and falling in with ten ships of the Athenians they took three of them empty and burned them. And after this, fearing that the ships of the Athenians which had escaped from Melos might, as in fact happened, inform those at Samos of their approach, they sailed towards Crete, and after making the voyage longer as a precaution, they put in at Caunus in Asia.
From there, as being in safety, they sent a message to the ships at Miletus to be convoyed along the coast.

And the Chians and Pedaritus at the same time, no less, though he kept delaying, sent messengers to Astyochus asking him to help them, since they were being besieged, with all the ships, and not to look on while the greatest of the allied cities in Ionia was shut off from the sea and ravaged by raids on land.

For the slaves of the Chians, being many and indeed the most numerous in any one city except that of the Lacedaemonians, and at the same time, because of their number, being punished more harshly for their offences, when the army of the Athenians seemed to be firmly established with a fortification, at once went over to them in large numbers as deserters, and these, knowing the country, did it the most harm.

So the Chians said that he ought to help them while there was still hope and it was possible to stop the enemy, while Delphinium was being fortified and was unfinished, and a larger rampart was being thrown around the camp and the ships. And Astyochus, although not intending to because of his earlier threat, when he saw that the allies too were eager, set out to give help.

Meanwhile news arrived from Caunus that the twenty-seven ships and the advisers of the Lacedaemonians were there; and thinking that everything else came second to convoying so many ships, so that they might command the sea more fully, and to getting the Lacedaemonians, who had come as overseers of him, safely across, he at once gave up the expedition to Chios and sailed to Caunus.

And landing on the way at Cos Meropis, he sacked the city, which was unwalled and had collapsed from an earthquake, the greatest that had befallen them within our memory, the people having fled to the mountains, and he plundered the country by raids, except for the free persons; these he let go.

And arriving from Cos at Cnidus by night, he was compelled by the urging of the Cnidians not to land the sailors, but to sail just as he was straight against the twenty ships of the Athenians, with which Charminus, one of the generals from Samos, was watching for these twenty-seven ships sailing up from the Peloponnese, the very ships which Astyochus too was sailing along the coast to meet.
For those at Samos had learned from Melos of their approach, and Charminus' watch was around Syme and Chalce and Rhodes and around Lycia; for he already perceived that they were at Caunus.

So Astyochus sailed just as he was to Syme before his coming was reported, in case he might somehow catch the ships somewhere out at sea. And rain and the clouded state of the sky caused his ships to wander in the darkness and fall into confusion.

And at dawn, when the fleet had been scattered and the left wing was already visible to the Athenians, while the rest was still wandering around the island, Charminus and the Athenians hastily put out against them with fewer than their twenty ships, thinking that these were the ships from Caunus which they were watching for.

And falling on them at once they sank three and disabled others, and they were getting the better in the action until, contrary to their expectation, the greater part of the ships came into view and they were being shut in from all sides.

And then, turning to flight, they lost six ships, and with the rest they took refuge at the island of Teutlussa, and from there at Halicarnassus. And after this the Peloponnesians put in at Cnidus, and when the twenty-seven ships from Caunus had joined them, they sailed with all together, set up a trophy at Syme and anchored again at Cnidus;

and the Athenians, when they learned of the sea battle, sailed with all the ships from Samos to Syme, and without setting out against the fleet at Cnidus, nor they against them, they took the ships' gear at Syme, touched at Lorymi on the mainland and sailed back to Samos.

And the ships of the Peloponnesians, now all together at Cnidus, were being repaired where anything was needed, and the eleven men of the Lacedaemonians held talks with Tissaphernes (for he had come) about what had already been done, if anything did not please them, and about the war to come, in what way it would be waged best and most advantageously for both.

And Lichas examined most closely what was being done, and said that neither treaty, neither that of Chalcideus nor that of Therimenes, was well drawn up, but that it was monstrous if the King should claim to rule now as well all the territory which he and his ancestors had ruled before; for this would mean that all the islands would again be enslaved, and Thessaly and the Locrians and everything as far as the Boeotians, and that instead of freedom the Lacedaemonians would put Median rule on the Hellenes.

So he told them to make another, better treaty, or at any rate they would not abide by these, nor did they need any of his maintenance on these terms. And Tissaphernes, indignant, went away from them in anger and with nothing done,

and they, as overtures were being made from the most powerful men there, had the intention of sailing to Rhodes, hoping to win over an island not without strength in its number of seamen and its land force, and at the same time thinking that they would be able by themselves, from the existing alliance, to maintain the ships without asking Tissaphernes for money.

So sailing at once in the same winter from Cnidus and touching first at Camirus in Rhodian territory with ninety-four ships, they frightened the many, who did not know what was being negotiated, and they fled, especially since the city was unwalled; then the Lacedaemonians called together these and those from the two cities, Lindus and Ialysus, and persuaded the Rhodians to revolt from the Athenians; and Rhodes went over to the Peloponnesians.

And the Athenians at this moment, having learned of it, sailed with the ships from Samos wishing to arrive first, and appeared out at sea, but being not much too late, for the moment they sailed away to Chalce, and from there to Samos, and later, making their attacks from Chalce and from Cos [and from Samos], they waged war on Rhodes.
And the Peloponnesians collected money from the Rhodians to the amount of thirty-two talents, but otherwise they kept quiet for eighty days, having drawn up their ships on shore.

Meanwhile, and even earlier, before they removed to Rhodes, the following was being done. Alcibiades, being suspected by the Peloponnesians after the death of Chalcideus and the battle at Miletus, and a letter having come from them from Lacedaemon to Astyochus to put him to death (for he was an enemy of Agis, and in other respects too appeared untrustworthy), first withdrew in fear to Tissaphernes, and then damaged the affairs of the Peloponnesians with him as much as he could,

and becoming his instructor in everything, he cut down the pay, so that instead of an Attic drachma three obols were given, and that not regularly, telling Tissaphernes to say to them that the Athenians, who had had knowledge of naval matters for a longer time, gave three obols to their own men, not so much from poverty as so that their sailors should not grow insolent from abundance and some of them make their bodies worse by spending money on things from which weakness results, while others desert the ships, not leaving behind the arrears of pay as a pledge;

and he taught him to persuade the trierarchs and the generals of the cities by giving them money, so that they would concede these things to him, except the Syracusans; of these Hermocrates alone opposed it on behalf of the whole alliance.

And the cities asking for money he sent away himself, answering on behalf of Tissaphernes that the Chians were shameless, being the richest of the Hellenes and yet saved by auxiliary help, to expect others to risk both their lives and their money for their freedom;

and he said that the other cities, which had spent money on the Athenians before they revolted, were doing wrong if they would not be willing now as well to contribute as much and even more for themselves.

And he pointed out that Tissaphernes, now waging war with his own money, was reasonably sparing, but if ever maintenance came down from the King, he would pay them their full wages and give the cities reasonable help.

And he also advised Tissaphernes not to be in too great a hurry to end the war, nor to wish, either by bringing up the Phoenician ships which he was equipping or by providing pay for more Hellenes, to give the power over both land and sea to the same people, but to let both hold the rule divided, and the King would always be able to lead the one side against those who were troublesome to him.

But if the rule over land and sea came into one hand, he would be at a loss for people with whom to bring down the dominant party, unless he himself wished at some point to rise up at great expense and risk and fight it out. And this was cheaper, to wear the Hellenes out against one another at a small fraction of the expense and at the same time with his own safety.

And he said that the Athenians were more suitable partners in the empire for him; for they were less eager for possessions on land, and had a policy and practice of making war most advantageous to him; for they would join in subjugating the sea for themselves and for him all the Hellenes living in the King's territory, while the others, on the contrary, had come to liberate them, and it was not likely that the Lacedaemonians would now be freeing the Hellenes from the Hellenes, themselves Hellenes, but not freeing them from those [the barbarians], unless at some point they failed to remove them.
So he urged him first to wear out both, and after cutting off as much as possible from the Athenians, then to get the Peloponnesians out of the country.

And Tissaphernes for the most part intended this, as far at least as could be conjectured from what he did. For having for this reason given his confidence to Alcibiades as advising well on these matters, he provided maintenance poorly to the Peloponnesians and would not let them fight at sea, but by saying that the Phoenician ships would come and that they would then contend with an abundant superiority, he ruined their affairs and took away the vigour of their navy, which had become very strong, and in everything else, too plainly to escape notice, he was not zealously helping in the war.

Alcibiades gave this advice to Tissaphernes and the King, while he was with them, partly because he thought it was best, and partly because he was at the same time working for his own return to his fatherland, knowing that, if he did not destroy it, it would some day be possible for him to persuade his countrymen and return; and he thought he could best persuade them by this means, if Tissaphernes were seen to be friendly to him; which is just what happened.

For when the soldiers of the Athenians at Samos perceived that he had influence with him, partly because Alcibiades had also sent word to the most powerful men among them to mention him to the best people, saying that he wished to return on condition of an oligarchy, and not of the villainy and the democracy that had banished him, and, having made Tissaphernes their friend, to share in the government with them, but more because of their own accord, the trierarchs of the Athenians at Samos and the most powerful men were bent on overthrowing the democracy.

And this movement was started first in the camp, and from there it came later to the city. And some men crossed over from Samos and came to talks with Alcibiades, and when he held out that he would make Tissaphernes their friend first and then the King too, if they were not governed by a democracy (for in this way the King would trust them more), the most powerful of the citizens, who also suffer the most hardship, had great hopes for themselves of getting affairs into their own hands and of prevailing over the enemy.

And going to Samos they gathered the suitable men into a conspiracy and openly told the many that the King would be their friend and would supply money if Alcibiades returned and they were not governed by a democracy.

And the crowd, even if they were somewhat annoyed for the moment at what was being done, kept quiet because of the easy prospect of pay from the King; and those who were organizing the oligarchy, after they had communicated it to the multitude, again examined the proposals of Alcibiades among themselves and with the greater part of their club.

And to the others they appeared practicable and trustworthy, but nothing pleased Phrynichus, who was still general, and Alcibiades seemed to him, as was indeed the case, to want an oligarchy no more than a democracy, and to look to nothing else than how, by changing the city from its present order, he might return at the invitation of his associates, while they themselves had to see to this above all, that they did not fall into faction; and it was not easy for the King, when the Peloponnesians were now on an equal footing at sea and held cities in his empire, and not the smallest ones, to attach himself to the Athenians, whom he did not trust, and to have trouble, when he could make friends of the Peloponnesians, from whom he had never yet suffered any harm.

And as for the allied cities, to which they had supposedly promised an oligarchy, since they themselves too would no longer be governed by a democracy, he said that he knew well that neither would those that had revolted come over to them any the more, nor would those that remained be more steadfast; for they would not want to be slaves with an oligarchy or a democracy rather than to be free with whichever of these they happened to have;

and they thought that the so-called good and noble men would give them no less trouble than the people, being the providers and proposers to the people of the evils from which they themselves benefited most; and, as far as it depended on those men, they would be put to death even without trial and more violently, whereas the people was both their own refuge and a check on those men.
And he himself knew clearly that the cities, having learned this from the facts themselves, thought so. So, to him at least, nothing of what was being done by Alcibiades at present was pleasing.

But those of the conspiracy who had gathered, just as they had decided at first, accepted the present proposals and prepared to send Peisander and others as envoys to Athens, to negotiate about the return of Alcibiades and the overthrow of the democracy there, and to make Tissaphernes a friend of the Athenians.

But Phrynichus, knowing that there would be a proposal about the return of Alcibiades and that the Athenians would accept it, and fearing, because of the opposition shown in what he had said, that, if he returned, he would do him harm as one who had stood in his way, resorted to the following.

He sent to Astyochus, the admiral of the Lacedaemonians, who was then still near Miletus, informing him secretly that Alcibiades was ruining their affairs by making Tissaphernes a friend to the Athenians, and writing everything else down clearly; and he said that he should be pardoned for plotting some harm against a man who was an enemy, even to the disadvantage of the city.

But Astyochus had no intention of punishing Alcibiades, especially since he no longer came into his hands as before, but going up to him at Magnesia and to Tissaphernes he at once told them what had been written from Samos and became an informer himself, and, as was said, he had attached himself to Tissaphernes for his own gain, to share with him both on these matters and on others; and that is why he was softer in pressing [about] the pay, which was not being given in full.
And Alcibiades at once sent a letter against Phrynichus to Samos, to those in authority, telling what he had done and demanding that he be put to death.

And Phrynichus, thrown into confusion and in the very greatest danger because of the disclosure, sent again to Astyochus, both blaming him for the earlier matter, that it had not been well kept secret, and saying now that he was ready to give them the whole army of the Athenians at Samos to destroy, writing in detail, since Samos was unwalled, how he would do it, and that he could not now be blamed, being in danger of his life because of them, for doing this and anything else rather than being destroyed himself by his worst enemies. And Astyochus revealed this too to Alcibiades.

And when Phrynichus perceived in advance that he was betraying him and that a letter from Alcibiades about these matters was all but there, he himself got ahead of it and announced to the army that the enemy, since Samos was unwalled and at the same time not all the ships were anchored inside, intended to attack the camp, and that he had learned this clearly, and that they ought to fortify Samos as quickly as possible and keep everything else under guard; and he was general and had authority to do this himself.

And they set about preparing the fortification, and because of this Samos, which was to be fortified in any case, was fortified more quickly; and the letters from Alcibiades came not long afterwards, saying that the army was being betrayed by Phrynichus and that the enemy was about to attack.

But Alcibiades, being thought untrustworthy, and, having learned the enemy's plans in advance, to be attributing them to Phrynichus as an accomplice out of enmity, did him no harm, but rather confirmed his testimony by reporting the same things.

After this Alcibiades worked on Tissaphernes and tried to persuade him to be a friend to the Athenians, since, though he feared the Peloponnesians because they were there with more ships than the Athenians, he nevertheless wished to be persuaded, if he somehow could, especially since he had perceived the dispute of the Peloponnesians at Cnidus about the treaty of Therimenes (for it had already happened, as they were at Rhodes at this time); in which Lichas had proved true the statement made earlier by Alcibiades about the Lacedaemonians freeing all the cities, saying that it was not tolerable to have agreed that the King should rule the cities which at any time before either he himself or his fathers had ruled. And Alcibiades, as one contending for great stakes, was eagerly devoting himself to courting Tissaphernes;

and the envoys of the Athenians sent from Samos with Peisander, arriving at Athens, made speeches before the people, summarizing many points, but chiefly that it would be possible for them, if they brought back Alcibiades and were not governed by a democracy in the same way, both to have the King as an ally and to prevail over the Peloponnesians.

And when many others also spoke against it on the matter of the democracy, and at the same time the enemies of Alcibiades cried out that it would be monstrous if he returned by violating the laws, and the Eumolpidae and Ceryces protested about the mysteries, for which he had gone into exile, and called on the gods not to bring him back, Peisander came forward in the face of much opposition and indignation and, taking each of the objectors aside, asked him whether he had any hope of safety for the city, when the Peloponnesians had no fewer ships than they confronting them at sea and more allied cities, and the King and Tissaphernes were supplying them with money, while they themselves no longer had any, unless someone should persuade the King to come over to their side.

And when, on being asked, they said they had none, he then told them plainly: 'Well then, this cannot happen for us unless we govern ourselves more prudently and put the offices more into the hands of a few, so that the King may trust us, and unless at present we deliberate less about the form of government than about our safety (for later it will be possible for us to change it again, if anything does not please us), and unless we bring back Alcibiades, who alone of men now living is able to accomplish this.'

And the people, on first hearing it, took the proposal about the oligarchy badly; but being clearly shown by Peisander that there was no other way of safety, out of fear and at the same time in the hope that it would also be changed back, they gave way.
And they voted that Peisander and ten men with him should sail and conduct affairs with Tissaphernes and Alcibiades in whatever way seemed to them would turn out best.

And at the same time, when Peisander also slandered Phrynichus, the people removed him from his office together with his colleague Scironides, and they sent Diomedon and Leon in their place as generals to the fleet. And Peisander slandered Phrynichus by saying that he had betrayed Iasus and Amorges, because he did not think him suited to the negotiations with Alcibiades.

And Peisander, after visiting all the sworn associations which happened to exist already in the city for lawsuits and offices, and urging them to band together and, taking counsel in common, to overthrow the democracy, and after making the other preparations required by the present circumstances so that there should be no more delay, himself made the voyage to Tissaphernes with the ten men.

And Leon and Diomedon, having in the same winter already reached the ships of the Athenians, made an attack on Rhodes. And they found the ships of the Peloponnesians hauled up on shore, and after making a landing and defeating in battle those of the Rhodians who came to the rescue, they withdrew to Chalce, and they made war from there rather 〈than〉 from Cos; for it was easier for them to keep watch from there, in case the fleet of the Peloponnesians should set out anywhere.

And Xenophantidas, a Laconian, also came to Rhodes from Pedaritus from Chios, saying that the wall of the Athenians had now been completed, and that unless they came to help with all their ships, the cause at Chios would be lost. And they intended to help.

Meanwhile Pedaritus, with the mercenaries he had with him and the Chians in full force, attacked the Athenians' rampart around the ships, took part of it and got possession of some ships that had been hauled up; but when the Athenians came out to the rescue and first routed the Chians, the rest of the force around Pedaritus was also defeated, and he himself was killed, and many of the Chians, and many arms were taken.

After this the Chians were besieged by land and sea even more than before, and the famine there was great; and the envoys of the Athenians with Peisander, arriving at Tissaphernes, held talks about the agreement.

But Alcibiades (for things with Tissaphernes were not quite secure for him, since Tissaphernes feared the Peloponnesians more and still wished, just as he had been taught by him, to wear out both sides) resorted to a device of this kind, that Tissaphernes, by asking for as much as possible from the Athenians, should not come to an agreement.

And it seems to me that Tissaphernes too wished the same thing, he himself out of fear, while Alcibiades, when he saw that the other would not come to an agreement even so, wished it to seem to the Athenians that he was not unable to persuade him, but that, when Tissaphernes had been persuaded and wished to come over, the Athenians were not giving enough.

For Alcibiades, speaking himself on behalf of Tissaphernes, who was present, made such excessive demands that the Athenians' side, although they conceded for a long time whatever he asked, nevertheless became responsible for the failure; for he demanded that all Ionia should be given up, and then the islands lying off it and other things, and when the Athenians did not oppose these, finally, at the third meeting, fearing that he would be completely exposed as powerless, he demanded that they allow the King to build ships and sail along his own coast wherever and with as many ships as he wished. At this point no longer ... but the Athenians, thinking matters were hopeless and that they had been deceived by Alcibiades, went away in anger and made their way to Samos.

Immediately after this, in the same winter, Tissaphernes went along to Caunus, wishing to bring the Peloponnesians back to Miletus and, after making yet another agreement, whatever he could, to supply them with maintenance and not to become completely hostile to them, fearing that if they were at a loss for maintenance for many ships, they might either be compelled to fight the Athenians at sea and be defeated, or, with their ships emptied of men, the Athenians might get what they wanted without him. And further, he feared most of all that in their search for maintenance they might ravage the mainland.

So, from calculating and foreseeing all this, as he wished to keep the Hellenes equal against one another, he sent for the Peloponnesians, gave them maintenance and made the following third treaty with them.

'In the thirteenth year of the reign of Darius, while Alexippidas was ephor at Lacedaemon, an agreement was made in the plain of the Maeander between the Lacedaemonians and the allies and Tissaphernes and Hieramenes and the sons of Pharnaces concerning the affairs of the King and of the Lacedaemonians and the allies.
The King's territory, as much of it as is in Asia, shall be the King's; and concerning his own territory the King shall decide as he wishes.
And the Lacedaemonians and the allies shall not go against the King's territory for any harm, nor the King against the territory of the Lacedaemonians or of the allies for any harm.

And if any of the Lacedaemonians or the allies go against the King's territory for harm, the Lacedaemonians and the allies shall prevent it; and if anyone from the King's territory goes against the Lacedaemonians or the allies for harm, the King shall prevent it.
And Tissaphernes shall provide maintenance for the ships now present according to what has been agreed until the King's ships come;

and the Lacedaemonians and the allies, after the King's ships arrive, shall be free to maintain their own ships, if they wish. And if they wish to receive the maintenance from Tissaphernes, Tissaphernes shall provide it, and the Lacedaemonians and the allies, when the war ends, shall repay Tissaphernes whatever money they have received.

And after the King's ships arrive, the ships of the Lacedaemonians and those of the allies and those of the King shall wage the war in common, in whatever way seems best to Tissaphernes and to the Lacedaemonians and the allies. And if they wish to make peace with the Athenians, peace shall be made on equal terms.'

This treaty was made, and after this Tissaphernes prepared to bring the Phoenician ships, as had been stated, and everything else that he had promised, and he wished at least to be seen making preparations;

and when the winter was already ending the Boeotians took Oropus by treachery, though the Athenians held it with a garrison. And men of the Eretrians and of the Oropians themselves cooperated, plotting the revolt of Euboea; for as the place lies opposite Eretria, it was impossible, while the Athenians held it, for it not to do great harm both to Eretria and to the rest of Euboea.

So, now holding Oropus, the Eretrians came to Rhodes, inviting the Peloponnesians into Euboea. But they were more intent on helping Chios, which was in distress, and setting out with all their ships they sailed from Rhodes.

And when they were near Triopium they sighted the ships of the Athenians out at sea sailing from Chalce; and as neither sailed against the other, they arrived, the one side at Samos and the other at Miletus, and they saw that it was no longer possible to help Chios without a sea battle. And this winter ended, and the twentieth year of this war which Thucydides wrote down ended.

In the following summer, right at the beginning of spring, Dercylidas, a Spartan, was sent along by land with a not large army to the Hellespont to make Abydos revolt (they are colonists of the Milesians), and the Chians, while Astyochus was at a loss how to help them, were compelled, pressed by the siege, to fight at sea.

And it happened, while Astyochus was still at Rhodes, that they had brought from Miletus as commander after the death of Pedaritus Leon, a Spartan, who had come out with Antisthenes as a marine, and twelve ships which happened to be on guard at Miletus, of which five were Thurian and four Syracusan and one from Anaea and one Milesian and one Leon's own.

And when the Chians had come out in full force and seized a strong position, and at the same time their ships, thirty-six of them, had put out against the thirty-two of the Athenians, they fought at sea; and after a hard-fought sea battle, the Chians and the allies, who had not had the worse of it in the action (for it was already late), withdrew into the city.
Immediately after this, when Dercylidas had marched along by land from Miletus, Abydos on the Hellespont revolted to Dercylidas and Pharnabazus, and Lampsacus two days later.

And Strombichides, learning of it at Chios, came quickly to the rescue with twenty-four ships of the Athenians, some of which were troop-ships carrying hoplites, and, after defeating in battle the Lampsacenes who came out against him and taking Lampsacus, which was unwalled, at the first assault, and making booty of the goods and slaves, but settling the free men there again, he went against Abydos.

And when they neither came over nor could he take it by assault, he sailed across to the coast opposite Abydos and set up Sestus, a city of the Chersonese which the Medes once held, as a fort and guard-post for the whole Hellespont.
Meanwhile the Chians became more masters of the sea, and those at Miletus and Astyochus, learning about the sea battle and that Strombichides and the ships had gone away, took courage.

And Astyochus, sailing along the coast with two ships to Chios, brought the ships from there and with all of them together now made an attack on Samos; and when, because they were suspicious of one another, they did not put out against him, he sailed back again to Miletus.

For about this time and even earlier the democracy at Athens had been overthrown. For when the envoys with Peisander came from Tissaphernes to Samos, they secured their position in the army itself still more firmly and urged the most powerful of the Samians themselves to try with them to establish an oligarchy, although these had risen against one another in order not to be governed by an oligarchy;

and at the same time the Athenians at Samos, conferring among themselves, decided to leave Alcibiades alone, since he was unwilling (and indeed he was not a suitable man to come into an oligarchy), but to see for themselves, as being already in danger, by what means their cause should not be given up, and at the same time to hold out in the war and to contribute money zealously themselves from their own private houses, and anything else that might be needed, as they were no longer toiling for others but for themselves.

So, having encouraged one another in this way, they at once sent Peisander and half of the envoys home to manage affairs there, and they had been told to establish an oligarchy in the subject cities at which they might put in; and they sent the other half to the other subject places, some to one place and some to another,
and they sent Dieitrephes, who was near Chios but had been elected to command in the Thracian region, to his command. And on arriving at Thasos he overthrew the democracy.

And about the second month after he left, the Thasians began to fortify their city, as no longer needing an aristocracy together with the Athenians, and expecting freedom from the Lacedaemonians day by day;

for there was also a party of them in exile, banished by the Athenians, with the Peloponnesians, and this party, together with their friends in the city, was working with all its might to bring ships and make Thasos revolt. So what they most wanted happened to them, that the city was set right without danger and the democracy that would have opposed them was overthrown.

So at Thasos the opposite happened to what the Athenians establishing the oligarchy wanted, and so, it seems to me, also in many other of the subject states; for the cities, having gained moderation and freedom from fear in their actions, went on to outright freedom, not preferring the hollow good order offered by the Athenians.

And Peisander and his colleagues, sailing along the coast, as had been decided, overthrew the democracies in the cities, and at the same time, having from some places hoplites as allies for themselves, they came to Athens.

And they found most of the work already done by their associates. For some of the younger men had banded together and secretly killed a certain Androcles, the foremost leader of the people, who had also been chiefly responsible for driving out Alcibiades, and they killed him for both reasons, because of his popular leadership and because they thought they would gratify Alcibiades, as he was going to return and make Tissaphernes their friend, rather more; and they secretly did away with some others who were inconvenient in the same way.

And a proposal had been openly prepared by them that no others should receive pay than those serving in the war, and that no more than five thousand should share in affairs, and these such as were most able to serve with both their property and their persons.

But this was a fair pretext for the majority, since those who were changing the constitution were going to hold the city themselves. Nevertheless the people and the council chosen by the bean still met; but they deliberated on nothing that was not approved by the conspirators, and indeed the speakers were from among them, and what was to be said had been considered by them beforehand.

And none of the others spoke against them any longer, being afraid and seeing that the conspiracy was large; and if anyone did speak against them, he was at once put to death in some convenient way, and there was neither any search for those who had done it nor any prosecution if they were suspected, but the people kept quiet and were in such consternation that anyone who suffered no violence thought it a gain, even if he kept silent.

And thinking that the conspiracy was much larger than it actually was, they were beaten in their minds, and being unable to find it out because of the size of the city and because they did not know one another, they could not [find it out themselves].

And for this same reason it was also impossible for anyone who was indignant to pour out his grievance to another so as to defend himself by plotting; for he would have found either a stranger to whom he would speak or an acquaintance who was untrustworthy.

For all those of the popular party approached one another with suspicion, as if each had a share in what was happening. For there were among them also men whom no one would ever have thought would turn to oligarchy; and these created the greatest distrust among the many and contributed most to the safety of the few, by making the people's distrust of itself firm.

So at this moment Peisander and his colleagues arrived and at once took up what remained. And first, having assembled the people, they proposed that ten men be chosen as commissioners with full powers to draft laws, and that these, after drafting them, should bring a proposal before the people on a fixed day about how the city would best be governed;

then, when the day came, they confined the assembly at Colonus (it is a sanctuary of Poseidon outside the city, about ten stades away), and the commissioners brought forward nothing else but just this, that any Athenian should be allowed to propose with impunity whatever motion he wished; and if anyone indicted the proposer for an illegal proposal or harmed him in any other way, they imposed heavy penalties on him.

Then at last it was said openly that no one should hold any office any longer under the same constitution or receive pay, and that they should choose five men as presidents, and these should choose a hundred men, and each of the hundred three in addition to himself; and they, being four hundred, should enter the council-chamber and rule with full powers in whatever way they judged best, and should convene the Five Thousand whenever they saw fit.

And the one who made this proposal was Peisander, who in other respects too most eagerly and openly helped to overthrow the democracy; but the man who planned the whole affair, how it was brought to this point, and who had given it attention for the longest time, was Antiphon, a man second to none of the Athenians of his time in excellence, and most able both to think things out and to express what he had concluded, and who did not come forward before the people nor willingly into any other contest, but was viewed with suspicion by the multitude because of his reputation for cleverness, yet was the one man most able to help those who were engaged in contests, both in court and before the people, whoever consulted him about anything.

And he himself, when † the democracy was changed and the affairs of the Four Hundred came into trials † and, having later been overturned, were being harshly treated by the people †, appears to have made the best defence of anyone up to my time, when accused on these very matters of having helped to set it up, in a trial for his life.

And Phrynichus too showed himself more eager than anyone for the oligarchy, fearing Alcibiades and knowing that he was aware of all he had done at Samos with Astyochus, thinking that in all likelihood he would never be brought back by an oligarchy; and in the face of dangers, once he had taken the task on, he proved by far the most reliable.

Theramenes too, the son of Hagnon, was foremost among those who joined in overthrowing the democracy, a man incapable neither of speaking nor of judging. So, carried out by many able men, the business not unnaturally succeeded, great as it was; for it was difficult to deprive the Athenian people of their freedom in about the hundredth year after the tyrants had been overthrown, a people that had not only not been subject to others, but for more than half of this time had itself been accustomed to rule over others.

When the assembly, with no one speaking against it, had ratified these measures and been dissolved, they afterwards brought the Four Hundred into the council-chamber in the following way. All the Athenians were always under arms, some on the wall, others in the ranks, because of the enemy at Decelea;

so on that day they let those who were not in the secret go away as they were accustomed, while those in the conspiracy had been told to wait quietly, not at the arms themselves, but at some distance, and if anyone opposed what was being done, to take up the arms and not permit it.

There were also Andrians and Tenians and three hundred Carystians and some of the settlers in Aegina, whom the Athenians had sent to live there, who had come for this very purpose in their own arms, and to whom the same orders had been given beforehand.

When these had been arranged in this way, the Four Hundred came, each with a hidden dagger, and with them the hundred and twenty [Greek] young men whom they used whenever there was any need for violence, and they confronted the councillors chosen by the bean who were in the council-chamber and told them to take their pay and leave; and they themselves brought them the pay for the whole of the remaining time and gave it to them as they went out.

When in this way the council had withdrawn without saying anything against it, and the other citizens made no disturbance but kept quiet, the Four Hundred entered the council-chamber and for the time chose prytanes from among themselves by lot and performed toward the gods all the prayers and sacrifices usual on entering office, but later they departed widely from the democratic administration (except that they did not recall the exiles, because of Alcibiades) and in other respects governed the city by force.

They put to death some men, not many, who seemed suitable to be got out of the way, and imprisoned others, and removed others from the city; and they sent heralds to Agis, the king of the Lacedaemonians, who was at Decelea, saying that they wished to be reconciled and that it was reasonable for him to come to terms with them rather than with the faithless democracy, which no longer existed.

But he, thinking that the city was not quiet, and that the people would not so suddenly give up their ancient freedom, and that if they saw a large army of theirs they would not stay quiet, and not at all trusting at present that they were no longer in turmoil, gave no conciliatory answer to those who had come from the Four Hundred, but sent for a large additional army from the Peloponnese and not long afterwards himself went down, with the garrison from Decelea and those who had come, to the very walls of the Athenians, hoping that they, being in turmoil, would more readily be subdued to them as they wished, or even at the first shout, because of the uproar likely to arise both inside and outside; for he thought he could not fail to take the long walls at least, because they were left undefended.

But when he came close and the Athenians made no move whatever inside, but sent out the cavalry and a part of the hoplites and light troops and archers and struck down some of his men because they came too close, and got possession of some arms and corpses, then at last he recognised the situation and led his army back again.

He himself and those with him stayed where they were at Decelea, but the newcomers, after they had stayed a few days in the country, he sent back home. After this the Four Hundred nonetheless kept sending envoys to Agis, and as he now received them more readily and advised it, they also sent envoys to Lacedaemon about an agreement, wishing to make peace.

They also sent ten men to Samos to reassure the army and to explain that the oligarchy had not been established to the harm of the city and the citizens, but for the preservation of the whole state, and that those taking part were five thousand and not four hundred only; and yet, because of their expeditions and their business abroad, the Athenians had never yet come to deliberate on any matter so great that five thousand assembled.

And having instructed them in the other things that were fitting to say, they sent them off immediately after their own establishment, fearing, as in fact happened, that the crowd of sailors would not itself be willing to remain under the oligarchic order, and that, the trouble beginning there, they would remove them from power.
For in Samos there was already a revolution concerning the oligarchy, and the following things happened at just the very time when the Four Hundred were combining.

For those of the Samians who earlier had risen against the powerful and were the popular party changed sides again and, persuaded both by Peisander, when he came, and by the Athenians at Samos who were in the conspiracy, they became sworn conspirators, about three hundred, and were about to attack the others as being the popular party.

And they killed a certain Hyperbolus, one of the Athenians, a worthless man, who had been ostracised not from fear of his power and standing, but because of his wickedness and the disgrace he brought on the city, acting together with Charminus, one of the generals, and some of the Athenians who were with them, giving them a pledge of faith, and they did other such things together with them, and they were eager to attack the majority.

But the people, perceiving it, revealed what was coming to Leon and Diomedon among the generals (for these bore the oligarchy unwillingly, because they were honoured by the people) and to Thrasybulus and Thrasyllus, the one serving as trierarch, the other as hoplite, and to others who were thought always to be most opposed to the conspirators; and they asked them not to look on while they themselves were destroyed and Samos was estranged from the Athenians, through which alone their empire had [until now] held together to this point.

And they, on hearing this, went to the soldiers one by one, urging them not to permit it, and not least to the Paralians, Athenians and free men all of them, who sailed in the ship and had always been hostile to oligarchy even when it was not present; and Leon and Diomedon used to leave them some ships as guards whenever they sailed anywhere.

So when the three hundred attacked them, all these came to help, and especially the Paralians, and the majority of the Samians prevailed, and they killed some thirty of the three hundred and punished the three most guilty with exile; and bearing no grudge against the rest, they lived together as citizens under a democracy from then on.

And when they sailed in, the Four Hundred immediately imprisoned two or three of the Paralians, and taking the ship from the rest and transferring them to another ship, a troop-ship, they ordered them to keep guard around Euboea.

But Chaereas, getting away unnoticed somehow at once, when he saw the state of affairs, went back to Samos and reported to the soldiers everything from Athens, making it all worse than it was, saying that they were punishing everyone with blows, and that it was not possible to say anything against those who held the government, and that their wives and children were being outraged, and that they intended to seize and imprison the relatives of all those who served at Samos without being of their way of thinking, so that, if they did not obey, these would be put to death; and he told many other lies besides.

On hearing this they at first rushed to stone those who had chiefly set up the oligarchy and those of the others who had taken part in it, but then, restrained by those in the middle and told not to ruin the cause while the enemy was lying close by with prows facing them, they stopped.

After this, wishing now openly to change affairs in Samos to a democracy, Thrasybulus son of Lycus and Thrasyllus (for these had been the chief leaders of the change) bound all the soldiers by the greatest oaths, and especially those from the oligarchic party themselves, that they would truly be governed democratically and be of one mind and would carry on the war against the Peloponnesians zealously and would be enemies to the Four Hundred and would make no overtures to them.

All the Samians of military age also swore the same oath, and the soldiers shared all their affairs and whatever might result from their dangers with the Samians, believing that there was no refuge of safety either for them or for themselves, but that, whether the Four Hundred prevailed or the enemy from Miletus, they would be destroyed.
And at this time they had fallen into a contest, the one side forcing the city to be a democracy, the other forcing the army to be an oligarchy.

The soldiers also held an assembly at once, in which they deposed their former generals, and any of the trierarchs whom they suspected, and chose others in their place, both trierarchs and generals, among whom were Thrasybulus and Thrasyllus.

And standing up among themselves they made various exhortations, in particular that they must not lose heart because the city had revolted from them; for it was the fewer who had seceded from them, the more numerous and in every way better provided.

For since they held the whole fleet, they would compel the other cities which they ruled to give money just as if they set out from there (for they had a city, Samos, which was not weak, but had come within a very little of taking away the Athenians' command of the sea when it had made war on them, and they would defend themselves against the enemy from the same place as before), and they, having the ships, were better able to provide themselves with supplies than those in the city.

And it was through them, stationed in advance at Samos, that even before those at home had commanded the entrance to the Piraeus, and now they would be brought to such a state, if they were unwilling to give them back the constitution, that they themselves would be better able to shut them out from the sea than to be shut out by them.

And it was a small thing and worth nothing in which the city had been useful to them toward overcoming the enemy, and they had lost nothing, since those at home no longer had money to send, but the soldiers provided it for themselves, nor good counsel, for the sake of which a city commands armies; but even in these matters the others had done wrong by abolishing the ancestral laws, while they themselves preserved them and would try to compel those others too, so that not even those who would give some good counsel were worse among them.

And Alcibiades, if they granted him immunity and return, would gladly procure the alliance of the King for them. And most important of all, if they failed in everything, they had, possessing so large a fleet, many places of retreat in which they would find both cities and land.

Having held such an assembly among themselves and encouraged one another, they went on preparing for the war no less than before. And those sent to Samos by the Four Hundred [the ten envoys], when they learned of this while already at Delos, stayed quiet there.

About this time the soldiers of the Peloponnesians in the fleet at Miletus were also crying out among themselves that their cause was being ruined by Astyochus and Tissaphernes, since the one had been unwilling to fight at sea either before, while they themselves were still stronger and the fleet of the Athenians was small, or now, when they were said to be in civil strife and their ships were not yet together, but by waiting for the Phoenician ships from Tissaphernes, a mere name and not a fact, they would risk being worn out; and Tissaphernes in turn did not bring these ships, and harmed the fleet by giving pay neither continuously nor in full. So they said they must delay no longer, but fight a decisive sea-battle.

And the Syracusans urged this most of all. The allies and Astyochus, perceiving the murmuring, and having resolved in council to fight a decisive sea-battle, since the disturbance at Samos was also being reported to them, put out with all their ships, one hundred and twelve, and ordering the Milesians to go along by land to Mycale, they sailed toward Mycale.

But the Athenians with the eighty-two ships from Samos, which happened to be lying at Glauce of Mycale (Samos is only a short distance from the mainland here toward Mycale), when they saw the ships of the Peloponnesians sailing against them, withdrew to Samos, not thinking themselves sufficient in number to risk everything.
So they withdrew to Samos in this way, while the Peloponnesians, putting in at Mycale, encamped, and so did the land force of the Milesians and of the neighbouring peoples.
And on the next day, as they were about to sail against Samos, word came that Strombichides had arrived with the ships from the Hellespont; and they at once sailed back again to Miletus.

And the Athenians, the ships having joined them, themselves made an attack on Miletus with one hundred and eight ships, wishing to fight a decisive sea-battle; and when no one put out against them, they sailed back again to Samos.

In the same summer, immediately after this, the Peloponnesians, since they did not put out against the enemy, thinking themselves no match for them even with their ships together, being at a loss where they would get money for so many ships, especially as Tissaphernes paid badly, sent to Pharnabazus, as had been ordered from the Peloponnese at the start, Clearchus son of Rhamphias with forty ships.
For Pharnabazus was calling them to him and was ready to provide pay, and at the same time Byzantium was also sending envoys to them about revolting.

And these ships of the Peloponnesians, putting out into the open sea so that they might escape the notice of the Athenians on the voyage, were caught by a storm, and most of them with Clearchus reached Delos and later came back again to Miletus (Clearchus again went by land to the Hellespont and held the command), while ten, with Helixus the Megarian as general, got through safely to the Hellespont and caused Byzantium to revolt.
And after this those at Samos, learning of it, sent ships as reinforcement and guard to the Hellespont, and a short sea-battle took place before Byzantium, eight ships against eight.

Those in charge at Samos, and especially Thrasybulus, who had always held to the same view, ever since he had changed the government, of recalling Alcibiades, finally persuaded the mass of the soldiers in an assembly, and when they had voted recall and immunity for Alcibiades, he sailed to Tissaphernes and brought Alcibiades back to Samos, thinking that their only safety lay in winning Tissaphernes over to them from the Peloponnesians.

And when an assembly was held, Alcibiades complained of and lamented his personal misfortune of exile, and speaking much about public affairs he raised in them no small hopes for the future, and magnified to excess his own influence with Tissaphernes, so that those at home who held the oligarchy might fear him and the conspiracies might be more surely broken up, and those at Samos might hold him in greater honour and themselves take more courage, and the enemy might be set against Tissaphernes as much as possible and fall [from] their present hopes.

So Alcibiades, boasting greatly, made these promises: that Tissaphernes had assured him solemnly that, as long as anything of his own remained, if he could trust the Athenians, they would not lack pay, not even if in the end he had to turn his own bed into silver, and that he would bring the Phoenician ships already at Aspendus to the Athenians and not to the Peloponnesians; but he would trust the Athenians only if Alcibiades himself, safely restored, should guarantee them to him.

And hearing these and many other things, they at once chose him general together with the former ones and entrusted all their affairs to him, and each of them would not have exchanged for anything his present hope both of safety and of revenge on the Four Hundred, and they were already ready, because of what had been said, to despise at once the enemy at hand and to sail to the Piraeus.

But he completely prevented the sailing to the Piraeus, which would leave behind the nearer enemy, though many were pressing for it, and said that, since he had also been chosen general, he would first sail to Tissaphernes and arrange the affairs of the war.

And straight from this assembly he went off, so that he might seem to share everything with him, and at the same time wishing to be more honoured by him and to show that he had now been chosen general and was able to do him good or harm [now]. And it turned out that Alcibiades frightened the Athenians with Tissaphernes and Tissaphernes with them.
The Peloponnesians at Miletus, learning of the recall of Alcibiades, though they had distrusted Tissaphernes even before, were now set against him much more still.

For it had happened to them, at the time of the Athenians' attack on Miletus, when they were unwilling to put out against them and fight at sea, that Tissaphernes became much slacker in paying wages and that his unpopularity with them, which even before this had arisen because of Alcibiades, increased.

And gathering in groups, as before, the soldiers reckoned up, and so did some of the others, men of consideration, and not only the soldiery, that they had never yet received their pay in full, and that what was given was small and not even that paid regularly; and that unless they either fought a decisive sea-battle or went away to some place where they would have provisions, the men would desert the ships; and that Astyochus was to blame for everything, humouring Tissaphernes for his private gain.
While they were engaged in this reckoning, the following disturbance also occurred concerning Astyochus.

For the sailors of the Syracusans and Thurians, the more free they were as a body, the more boldly they assailed him and demanded their pay. He answered rather haughtily and threatened them, and against Dorieus, who was speaking for his own sailors, he even raised his stick.

When the mass of the soldiers saw this, being sailors, they burst out and rushed at Astyochus to stone him; but he, seeing it in time, took refuge at an altar. He was not struck, however, but they separated from one another.

The Milesians also took the fort of Tissaphernes that had been built in Miletus, falling on it secretly, and drove out the guards in it; and the other allies also approved of this, and not least the Syracusans.

Lichas, however, was not pleased with them, and said that the Milesians and the others in the King's land must serve Tissaphernes within reason and court him until they had settled the war well. And the Milesians were angry with him both for this and for other such things, and when he later died of sickness, they did not allow him to be buried where those of the Lacedaemonians who were present wished.
While their affairs were in such discord with both Astyochus and Tissaphernes, Mindarus came from Lacedaemon as successor to Astyochus as admiral and took over the command; and Astyochus sailed away.

And Tissaphernes sent with him as envoy one of his own people, named Gaulites, a Carian who spoke two languages, to accuse the Milesians about the fort and at the same time to defend himself, since he knew that the Milesians were going chiefly to denounce him, and Hermocrates with them, who intended to show that Tissaphernes was ruining the cause of the Peloponnesians together with Alcibiades and playing a double game.

He had always been at enmity with him over the payment of the wages; and finally, when Hermocrates had been exiled from Syracuse and other generals had come to Miletus for the ships of the Syracusans, Potamis and Myscon and Demarchus, Tissaphernes pressed on Hermocrates, now an exile, much more still, and accused him, among other things, of having once asked him for money and, not getting it, having declared his enmity toward him.
So Astyochus and the Milesians and Hermocrates sailed away to Lacedaemon. Alcibiades had already crossed back from Tissaphernes to Samos.

And the [envoys] from the Four Hundred arrived from Delos, whom they had sent at that time to reassure and inform those at Samos, while Alcibiades was present, and when an assembly was held they tried to speak.
The soldiers at first were unwilling to listen, but shouted to kill those who were overthrowing the democracy, but then, having with difficulty calmed down, they listened.

And they reported that the change had been made neither for the destruction of the city, but for its preservation, nor so that it might be handed over to the enemy (for it had been possible to do this when they invaded while they themselves were already in power), and that all of the Five Thousand would share in turn, and that their relatives were neither being outraged, as Chaereas had slanderously reported, nor suffering any harm, but each remained in place in possession of his own property.

Though they said much else, they listened no more willingly, but were angry, and different men gave different opinions, but chiefly to sail against the Piraeus. And Alcibiades seems then for the first time, and as much as anyone, to have benefited the city; for when the Athenians at Samos were set on sailing against their own people, in which case the enemy would most certainly have held Ionia and the Hellespont at once, he prevented it.
And at that time no other single man would have been able to restrain the crowd, but he stopped the expedition and, by rebuking those who were personally angry with the envoys, turned them aside.

And he himself sent them away with an answer, that he did not prevent the Five Thousand from ruling, but he ordered them to remove the Four Hundred and to set up the council as before, the Five Hundred; and if anything had been cut back for economy so that those serving in the field might have better provisions, he fully approved.

And in other respects he told them to hold out and give in to the enemy in nothing; for with regard to themselves, if the city was saved, there was great hope of coming to terms, but if once one side or the other should fall, either that at Samos or those at home, there would no longer be anyone left for one to be reconciled with.

There were also envoys of the Argives present, offering to the Athenian democracy at Samos to help them; and Alcibiades, after praising them and telling them to come when someone called them, sent them away so.

The Argives had come with the Paralians, who had at that time been ordered by the Four Hundred to sail around Euboea in the troop-ship, and who, conveying to Lacedaemon Athenian envoys [sent] from the Four Hundred, Laespodias and Aristophon and Melesias, [who], when they were sailing off Argos, seized the envoys and handed them over to the Argives as being among those who had done most to overthrow the democracy, while they themselves no longer went to Athens, but came from Argos to Samos bringing the envoys in the trireme which they had.

In the same summer Tissaphernes, at this time, when the Peloponnesians were most annoyed with him, both for other reasons and because of the recall of Alcibiades, as now openly siding with Athens, wishing, as it seemed, to clear himself of the charges before them, prepared to go to Aspendus for the Phoenician ships, and told Lichas to go with him; and he said he would put Tamos, his lieutenant, in charge of the army, to give pay for as long as he himself was away.
It is not told in the same way, nor is it easy to know with what intention he went to Aspendus and, having gone, did not bring the ships.

For that the Phoenician ships, one hundred and forty-seven, came as far as Aspendus is clear, but why they did not come on is conjectured in many ways. Some say it was so that by going away he might wear down, as he had in fact intended, the affairs of the Peloponnesians (at any rate Tamos, to whom the task was assigned, provided pay no better but even worse), others that he might bring the Phoenicians on to Aspendus and make money by discharging them (for in any case he was not going to use them at all), others that it was because of the outcry against him at Lacedaemon, so that it might be said that he was doing no wrong, but had plainly gone for ships that were truly manned.

To me, however, it seems most clear that it was for the sake of wearing out and holding in check the Greek forces that he did not bring the fleet, wearing them out while he was going there and delaying, and keeping them equal, so that by joining neither side he might make it stronger, since, if he had wished, he could surely have finished the war by appearing, beyond doubt; for by bringing it he would in all probability have given the victory to the Lacedaemonians, who even at present lay opposite the enemy with their fleet more as equals than as inferiors.

And what convicts him most is the excuse he gave for not bringing the ships. For he said they were fewer than the King had ordered to be collected; but he would surely have won still greater favour in this, by not spending much of the King's money and achieving the same results at less cost.

Alcibiades, when he learned that Tissaphernes too was going to Aspendus, sailed there himself as well, taking thirteen ships, promising those at Samos a sure and great benefit (for he would either bring the Phoenician ships to the Athenians himself or at least prevent them from coming to the Peloponnesians), knowing, as is likely, from long acquaintance the intention of Tissaphernes, that he was not going to bring them, and wishing to discredit him with the Peloponnesians as much as possible on account of his friendship with himself and the Athenians, so that he might be the more compelled by this to come over to their side. And he put out and made his voyage up the coast, straight for Phaselis and Caunus.

When the envoys sent from the Four Hundred came from Samos to Athens and reported the message from Alcibiades, that he urged them to hold out and give in to the enemy in nothing, and that he had great hopes of reconciling the army to them and of prevailing over the Peloponnesians, they greatly encouraged the many among those who shared in the oligarchy, who were discontented even before and would gladly have been rid of the business somehow in safety.

And they were already forming groups and finding fault with the state of affairs, having as leaders some of the very leading [generals] of the oligarchy and men in office, such as Theramenes son of Hagnon and Aristocrates son of Scellias and others, who had been among the foremost in taking part in affairs, but who feared, as they said, the army at Samos and Alcibiades very seriously, and also those [they were sending] as envoys to Lacedaemon, lest without the majority they might do some harm to the city, not that they † wanted to escape the government's falling too much into the hands of a few, but they said that the Five Thousand must be appointed in fact and not in name and the constitution made more equal.

This was the political form of their talk, but most of them, from private ambition, devoted themselves to the very thing by which above all an oligarchy that arises out of a democracy is destroyed; for all at once claim not to be equals, but each to be by far the first himself; whereas when an election is held under a democracy, a man bears the result more easily, because he is not beaten by his equals.

What most clearly encouraged them was the strong position of Alcibiades at Samos, and that it did not seem to them that the oligarchy would last; so each one strove to become himself the first leader of the people.

But those of the Four Hundred who were most opposed to such a form of government and were its leaders, Phrynichus, who as general at Samos [once] had then quarrelled with Alcibiades, and Aristarchus, a man most and longest opposed to the democracy, and Peisander and Antiphon and the others who were most powerful, both earlier, as soon as they had been established and when their forces at Samos had revolted to democracy, had been sending envoys of their own to Lacedaemon and were eager for an agreement and were building the wall in the place called Eetionea, and much more still after their envoys from Samos came, seeing both the majority and those of their own who had earlier seemed trustworthy changing sides.

And they sent off Antiphon and Phrynichus and ten others in haste, fearing both matters at home and those at Samos, instructing them to make terms with the Lacedaemonians in any way that was at all tolerable,

and they built the wall in Eetionea still more eagerly. The purpose of the wall was this, as Theramenes and those with him said: not so that they might not admit those at Samos into the Piraeus, if they sailed in by force, but rather so that they might admit the enemy, whenever they wished, with both ships and infantry.

For Eetionea is a mole of the Piraeus, and directly beside it is the entrance. So it was being walled in such a way, together with the wall already existing on the landward side, that, with a few men posted in it, they could command the entrance; for both the old wall facing the land and the new inner wall being built facing the sea ended at the very tower at the mouth of the harbour, which was narrow, the second one.

They also walled off a portico, which was the largest and immediately adjoining this wall in the Piraeus, and they controlled it themselves, and they compelled everyone to unload into it the corn, both what was on hand and what came in by sea, and to take it out from there when they sold it.

So Theramenes had long been spreading talk about these things, and especially after the envoys returned from Lacedaemon having achieved no agreement for all the people, saying that this wall was likely to destroy the city as well.

For at the same time there also happened to be, at the invitation of the Euboeans, at this same time, forty-two ships from the Peloponnese, among which were Italian ships from Tarentum and Locri and some Sicilian ones, already lying at Las in Laconia and preparing for the voyage to Euboea (Hegesandridas son of Hegesander, a Spartan, commanded them); and Theramenes said that these were sailing not to Euboea so much as to those who were fortifying Eetionea, and that unless one took precautions now, they would be destroyed before they knew it.

And there was in fact something of this kind on the part of those who were accused, and it was not merely slander in words. For those men wished above all to rule the allies too while keeping the oligarchy, but if not, to keep the ships and the walls and be independent, and if shut out from this too, not at least to be themselves destroyed first of all by the democracy when it was restored, but even to bring in the enemy and come to terms without walls and ships and keep the city's affairs on any terms, if only there was immunity for their own persons.
For this reason they were also eagerly building this wall, which had posterns and entrances and ways for bringing in the enemy, and they wished to get it finished in time.

Before, then, what was said was confined to a few and rather secret; but when Phrynichus, on his return from the embassy to Lacedaemon, was struck by a man of the frontier patrol by design in the crowded marketplace and, having gone not far from the council-chamber, died on the spot, and the man who struck him escaped, while his accomplice, an Argive, was seized and tortured by the Four Hundred but named no one who had ordered it, nor anything else except that he knew of many men gathering at the house of the commander of the frontier patrol and elsewhere at houses, then, since nothing new had come of it, Theramenes now went more boldly, and Aristocrates and all the others, of the Four Hundred themselves and of those outside, who were of the same mind, went to work.

For at the same time the ships had already sailed round from Las and, having anchored at Epidaurus, had overrun Aegina; and Theramenes said it was not likely that ships sailing to Euboea would have put into the gulf as far as Aegina and lie again at Epidaurus, unless they had come on invitation for the very purposes of which he himself had always been accusing them; so it was no longer possible to keep quiet.

Finally, after many seditious speeches and suspicions had arisen, they now set to work in earnest on affairs; for the hoplites in the Piraeus who were building the wall of Eetionea, among whom was Aristocrates, commanding as taxiarch his own tribe, seized Alexicles, a general of the oligarchy who was especially inclined toward the clubs, and took him into a house and confined him.
Others joined them in this, and among them Hermon, commander of the frontier patrol stationed at Munichia; and, most important of all, the mass of the hoplites wanted this.

When it was reported to the Four Hundred (they happened to be sitting together in the council-chamber), at once, except those who did not like this state of things, they were ready to go to arms and threatened Theramenes and those with him. And he, defending himself, said he was ready to go at once to help rescue him. And taking one of the generals who was of his mind, he went to the Piraeus; and Aristarchus and young men of the cavalry also went to help.

There was a great and alarming uproar; for those in the city thought that the Piraeus had already been taken and the man arrested killed, and those in the Piraeus that those from the city were all but upon them.

With difficulty, as the older men held back those in the city who were running about and rushing to the arms, and as Thucydides the Pharsalian, the city's proxenus, was present and eagerly threw himself in everyone's way and shouted to them not to destroy their country while the enemy lay in wait close by, they calmed down and kept their hands off one another.
And Theramenes, coming to the Piraeus (for he too was a general), as far as shouting went, was angry with the hoplites; but Aristarchus and the opponents of the people were angry in earnest.

But most of the hoplites went to grips with the work and did not change their minds, and they asked Theramenes whether he thought the wall was being built for any good and whether it would be better pulled down. And he said that if they thought it right to pull it down, he agreed too. And thereupon at once the hoplites and many of the people from the Piraeus climbed up and began to demolish the fortification.

And the appeal to the crowd was that whoever wanted the Five Thousand to rule instead of the Four Hundred should go to the work. For they still hid nonetheless behind the name of the Five Thousand, so as not to say outright "whoever wants the people to rule", fearing that they might really exist and that someone speaking to someone might come to grief through ignorance.
