And for this reason the Four Hundred did not want the Five Thousand either to exist or to be shown not to exist, thinking that to appoint so many as partners would be outright democracy, and that the uncertainty, on the other hand, would cause fear of one another.

On the next day the Four Hundred gathered in the council-chamber nevertheless, though in disarray; and the hoplites in the Piraeus, having released Alexicles whom they had arrested and pulled down the fortification, went to the theatre of Dionysus near Munichia, and grounding their arms they held an assembly, and when they had so resolved, they marched at once to the city and grounded their arms again in the Anaceum.

And some men chosen by the Four Hundred came to them and talked with them man to man and tried to persuade those they saw to be reasonable people both to keep quiet themselves and to restrain the others, saying that they would publish the names of the Five Thousand, and that from these, in turn, in whatever way the Five Thousand decided, the Four Hundred would be appointed, and that meanwhile they should in no way ruin the city or drive it into the arms of the enemy.

And the whole mass of the hoplites, as many speeches were made by many and to many, was calmer than before and was most afraid for the whole state; and they agreed to hold an assembly on an appointed day in the precinct of Dionysus about concord.

When the day of the assembly [in the precinct of Dionysus] came and they had all but gathered, word came that the forty-two ships and Hegesandridas were sailing from Megara along Salamis; and every one [of the mass of the hoplites] thought that this was the very thing long said by Theramenes and those with him, that the ships were sailing to the fortification, and it seemed to have been pulled down usefully.

Hegesandridas was perhaps hovering about Epidaurus and those parts by some prearranged agreement, but it is likely that he also lingered there in view of the present civil strife of the Athenians, in the hope that he might arrive at the right moment.

And the Athenians, on their side, when it was reported to them, at once ran to the Piraeus in full force, thinking that a war greater [than] their private one, from the enemy, was not far off, but at the harbour. And some went aboard the ships that were at hand, others launched more, and some ran to help at the walls and the mouth of the harbour.
But the ships of the Peloponnesians sailed along the coast and, doubling Sunium, anchored between Thoricus and Prasiae, and later arrived at Oropus.

And the Athenians, forced to use untrained crews in haste, as was natural with the city in civil strife and since they wished to go quickly to the help of their greatest possession (for Euboea, now that Attica was shut off to them, was everything), sent Thymochares as general with ships to Eretria,

So when he sailed against them, the Athenians too at once began to man their ships, thinking that the soldiers were by the ships; but they happened to be getting their midday meal not from the marketplace (for nothing was being sold, by design of the Eretrians), but from the houses at the edge of the town, so that, as they were slow in manning, the enemy might fall on them first and force the Athenians to put out just as they happened to be. And a signal was raised for them at Oropus from Eretria, when they should put out.

So with such preparation the Athenians put out and fought a sea-battle off the harbour of the Eretrians, and for a short time they held out nevertheless, then they turned to flight and were chased to the shore.

And those of them who fled to the city of the Eretrians as a friendly one fared worst, being slaughtered by them; but those who reached the fortification in Eretria which they themselves held survived, and so did those of the ships that reached Chalcis.

And the Peloponnesians, having taken twenty-two ships of the Athenians and having killed some of the men and taken others alive, set up a trophy. And not long after, having caused all Euboea to revolt except Oreus (this the Athenians themselves held), they also settled the other affairs concerning it.

When what had happened in Euboea reached the Athenians, the greatest consternation of all before came over them. For neither the disaster in Sicily, though it had seemed great at the time, nor anything else had ever yet frightened them so much.

For when the army at Samos had revolted, and there were no other ships nor men to man them, and they themselves were in civil strife, and it was uncertain when they would clash with one another, and so great a disaster had come on top of it, in which they had lost their ships and, most important, Euboea, from which they derived more benefit than from Attica, how could they not naturally be despondent?

But what disturbed them most and most closely was whether the enemy, having won, would dare to sail straight against them to the Piraeus, which was empty of ships; and they thought they were all but there already.

And this, if they had been bolder, they could easily have done, and either they would have divided the city still more by lying off it or, if they had stayed and besieged it, they would have compelled even the ships from Ionia, though hostile to the oligarchy, to come to the help of their own relatives and of the whole city; and meanwhile the Hellespont would have been theirs, and Ionia and the islands and everything as far as Euboea and, so to speak, the whole empire of the Athenians.

But not only in this did the Lacedaemonians prove the most convenient of all people for the Athenians to make war on, but in many other things too; for being most different in character, the one quick, the other slow, the one enterprising, the other timid, they were of very great help, especially to a naval empire. And the Syracusans showed it; for being most similar in character, they also made war on them best.

At any rate, in response to the news the Athenians nevertheless manned twenty ships and called an assembly, one immediately, then for the first time in the place called the Pnyx, where they had been accustomed to meet at other times too, in which they deposed the Four Hundred and voted to hand over affairs to the Five Thousand (and all those who furnished arms were to be of their number), and that no one should receive pay for any office; and if anyone did, they made him accursed.

And later there were also many other assemblies, from which they voted for lawgivers and the other measures concerning the constitution. And not least in this first period, in my time at least, the Athenians appear to have been well governed; for there was a moderate blending of the few and the many, and this first raised the city up out of the bad state into which affairs had fallen.
They also voted to recall Alcibiades and others with him, and sending both to him and to the army at Samos they urged them to take up affairs.

In this change those around Peisander and Alexicles and all who were most of the oligarchy at once slipped away to Decelea; and Aristarchus alone of them (for he happened to be a general) quickly took some archers, the most barbarous ones, and marched to Oenoe.

It was a fort of the Athenians on the borders of Boeotia, and the Corinthians were besieging it as volunteers, because of a disaster that had befallen them from Oenoe, the destruction of men returning from Decelea, having called in the Boeotians as well.

So Aristarchus, having conferred with them, deceived those in Oenoe, saying that those in the city had come to terms with the Lacedaemonians on everything, and that they too must hand over the place to the Boeotians; for the agreement had been made on these terms. And they, trusting him as a general and knowing nothing because they were being besieged, came out under a truce.
In this way the Boeotians took and occupied Oenoe, and the oligarchy and civil strife at Athens came to an end.

About the same time of this summer the Peloponnesians at Miletus too, since none of those appointed by Tissaphernes at that time [when he went to Aspendus] was giving them pay, and neither the Phoenician ships nor Tissaphernes had come anywhere as yet, and Philippus, who had been sent with him, had written to Mindarus the admiral, and another man, Hippocrates, a Spartan who was at Phaselis, that the ships would not come and that they were being wronged in everything by Tissaphernes, and Pharnabazus was calling them to him and was eager, if he got the ships, himself too to make the remaining cities of his province revolt from the Athenians, just as Tissaphernes had, hoping to gain something more from it, then Mindarus, in good order and on sudden notice, so as to escape the notice of those at Samos, put out from Miletus with seventy-three ships and sailed for the Hellespont (earlier in this same summer sixteen ships had sailed into it, which also overran some part of the Chersonese); but caught by a storm and forced by it, he put in at Icarus, and having stayed there because of bad sailing weather for five or six days, he arrived at Chios.
And Thrasyllus, when he learned that he had put out from Miletus, also sailed at once from Samos with fifty-five ships, hurrying so that he might not enter the Hellespont first.

But learning that he was at Chios, and thinking that he would keep him there, he posted scouts both on Lesbos and on the mainland opposite, so that, if the ships moved anywhere, they should not escape notice, and he himself, sailing along to Methymna, ordered barley-meal and the other provisions to be prepared, intending, if more time passed, to make his attacks on Chios from Lesbos.

At the same time (for Eresus on Lesbos had revolted) he wanted to sail against it and, if he could, take it. For exiles of the Methymnaeans, not the least powerful ones, having brought over from Cyme about fifty hoplites who were associates of theirs and having hired some from the mainland, about three hundred in all, with Anaxander the Theban leading them on the ground of kinship, first attacked Methymna, and, beaten back in the attempt because of the Athenian guards who came out from Mytilene, and driven off again in a battle outside, they crossed over the mountain and caused Eresus to revolt.

And two ships returning home from the Hellespont also joined them, and 〈five〉 Methymnaean ones; and the ships present were sixty-seven in all, with whose forces they were preparing to take Eresus by storm with engines and in every way, if they could.

Meanwhile Mindarus and the ships of the Peloponnesians from Chios, having taken in provisions for two days and having each received from the Chians three Chian fortieths, on the third day put out in haste from Chios, 〈not〉 into the open sea, so that they might not fall in with the ships at Eresus, but keeping Lesbos on their left they sailed toward the mainland.

And putting in at the harbour of Carteria in the territory of Phocaea and taking their midday meal, they sailed along the coast of Cyme and had their supper at Arginusae on the mainland, opposite Mytilene.

From there they sailed along the coast while it was still deep night and, arriving at Harmatus on the mainland opposite Methymna, they took their meal and quickly sailed past Lectum and Larisa and Hamaxitus and the places there, and arrived at Rhoeteum, already in the Hellespont, before midnight. And some of the ships also put in at Sigeum and at other places there.

The Athenians at Sestus, who were with eighteen ships, when the fire-signallers gave them signals and they saw the many fires suddenly appearing in the enemy's land, knew that the Peloponnesians were sailing in. And that same night, as fast as they could, keeping close to the Chersonese, they sailed along toward Elaeus, wishing to sail out into the open water away from the ships of the enemy.

And they escaped the notice of the sixteen ships at Abydus, although a watch had been ordered in advance by the friendly fleet sailing up, that they should be on their guard against them if they sailed out; but sighting those with Mindarus at dawn, and as these at once gave chase, they did not all get away first, but most of them escaped to Imbros and Lemnos, while four of the ships, sailing last, were overtaken off Elaeus.
And one, which had run aground at the sanctuary of Protesilaus, they took with its crew, and two others without their crews; and the other one they burned, empty, near Imbros.
After this, with the ships from Abydus that had joined them and the others, eighty-six in all, they besieged Elaeus that day, and when it did not come over, they sailed back to Abydus.

And the Athenians, deceived by their scouts and not thinking that the enemy ships' voyage along the coast could escape their notice, but assaulting the walls at their leisure, when they perceived it, at once left Eresus and hurried to help at the Hellespont;

and they took two ships of the Peloponnesians, which had put out too boldly into the open sea in the pursuit and fell in with them, and a day later they arrived and anchored at Elaeus, and they brought in the ships from Imbros that had fled there, and for five days they prepared for the sea-battle.

After this they fought at sea in the following way. The Athenians were sailing along in column close by the shore toward Sestus, and the Peloponnesians, perceiving it, themselves also put out against them from Abydus.

And when they knew that they were going to fight, they extended their line, the Athenians along the Chersonese, starting from Idacus as far as Arrhiana, seventy-six ships, and the Peloponnesians in turn from Abydus as far as Dardanus, eighty-six ships.

On the Peloponnesian side, the Syracusans held the right wing, and Mindarus himself the other, with the best-sailing ships, and on the Athenian side Thrasyllus held the left, and Thrasybulus the right; and the other generals were placed as each had been assigned.

As the Peloponnesians were eager to engage first, and, outflanking the right of the Athenians with their own left, to shut them off from sailing out, if they could, and in the centre to push them toward the land, which was not far off, the Athenians, recognising this, where their opponents wanted to block them off, extended their own line against them and outdid them in sailing,

and their left had already passed the headland called Cynossema. But as a result of this, their centre was made up of weak and scattered ships, especially as they had fewer in number and the ground around Cynossema had a sharp and angular outline, so that what was happening on the other side of it could not be seen.
So the Peloponnesians, attacking in the centre, drove the ships of the Athenians onto dry land and went ashore after them, having much the better of the action.

And neither could Thrasybulus' men on the right help the centre because of the number of the ships pressing on them, nor Thrasyllus' men on the left (for it was out of sight because of the headland of Cynossema, and at the same time the Syracusans and the others, ranged against them in no smaller numbers, held them back), until the Peloponnesians, fearlessly, because they had won, pursuing some one ship, others another, began to fall into disorder in some part of their force.

But Thrasybulus' men, seeing that the ships opposite them were holding off, stopped extending their wing and, turning about, at once engaged them and put them to flight, and cutting off the ships of the victorious part of the Peloponnesians that had strayed, they struck them and threw most of them into panic without a fight. And the Syracusans, as it happened, had themselves already given way to Thrasyllus' men and rushed into flight all the more when they saw the others too.

When the rout had taken place and the Peloponnesians had fled mostly to the river Meidius at first, and later to Abydus, the Athenians took few ships (for the Hellespont, being narrow, gave their opponents short distances to safety), but nevertheless this victory in the sea-battle that they won was most opportune.

For having until then feared the fleet of the Peloponnesians because of their small reverses and because of the disaster in Sicily, they were freed from blaming themselves and from thinking the enemy still worth anything at sea.

They took, however, of their opponents' ships eight Chian, five Corinthian, two Ambraciot and two Boeotian, and of the Leucadians and Lacedaemonians and Syracusans and Pellenians one each; and they themselves lost fifteen ships.

And having set up a trophy on the headland where Cynossema is, and brought in the wrecks, and given back the dead to their opponents under a truce, they also sent a trireme to Athens as messenger of the victory.

And the Athenians, when the ship arrived and they heard of the unexpected good fortune, after the recent disasters around Euboea and those that had happened in the civil strife, were greatly encouraged and believed that it was still possible for their cause to prevail, if they took it up zealously.

On the fourth day after the sea-battle, having hastily repaired their ships, the Athenians at Sestus sailed against Cyzicus, which had revolted; and sighting the eight ships from Byzantium lying at anchor off Harpagium and Priapus, they sailed against them, defeated in battle those on land, and took the ships. And arriving also at Cyzicus, which was unwalled, they brought it over again and exacted money.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesians too sailed from Abydus to Elaeus and recovered those of their captured ships that were sound (the Elaeusians had burned the others), and sent Hippocrates and Epicles to Euboea to bring the ships from there.

About this same time Alcibiades also sailed back to Samos with the thirteen ships from Caunus and Phaselis, reporting that he had turned back the Phoenician ships from the Peloponnesians so that they did not come, and that he had made Tissaphernes more friendly to the Athenians than before.

And having manned nine ships in addition to those he had, he exacted much money from the Halicarnassians and fortified Cos. And having done this and set up a governor in Cos, when it was already near autumn, he sailed back to Samos.
And Tissaphernes, when he learned that the ships of the Peloponnesians had sailed from Miletus to the Hellespont, broke camp from Aspendus and marched toward Ionia.

While the Peloponnesians were in the Hellespont, the Antandrians (they are Aeolians), bringing hoplites from Abydus by land over Mount Ida, brought them into the city, being wronged by Arsaces the Persian, the lieutenant of Tissaphernes, the very man who, when the Delians who had settled at Atramyttium after they had been removed by the Athenians for the purification of Delos, pretending an undeclared enmity and offering service to their best men, led them out as if in friendship and alliance, watched for them while they were taking their midday meal, surrounded them with his own men, and shot them down.

So, fearing him because of this deed, lest he might at some time commit some outrage against them too, and as he was imposing other burdens on them which they could not bear, they drove his guards out of the acropolis.

And Tissaphernes, learning of this act of the Peloponnesians too, and not only of the one at Miletus and Cnidus (for there too his guards had been expelled), and thinking that he had been greatly discredited with them and fearing that they might do him some further harm, and at the same time annoyed if Pharnabazus, having received them with less time and expense, should achieve more success against the Athenians, decided to go to them at the Hellespont, so that he might complain of what had happened at Antandrus and defend himself as plausibly as possible against the charges, both about the Phoenician ships and about the other matters. And arriving first at Ephesus he offered a sacrifice to Artemis.
[When the winter after this summer ends, the twenty-first year is completed.]
